HumanSightBench contains 2,876 visual questions with short answers across 7 top-level perceptual categories and 21 subcategories. We only include items that pass five inclusion gates: question clarity, answer uniqueness, visual grounding, human solvability, and text-only shortcut filtering. According to the protocol, errors are defined as incorrect answers on human-validated visual tasks with the evaluated interface. The inclusion gates are intended to reduce confounds from ambiguity and external knowledge. The best pass@3 score is 65.6% across eight evaluated MLLMs. No evaluated model exceeds 27.5% on Counting. These results identify capability gaps that are hidden by overall scores and can help future training experiments and held-out evaluation.

AI.tldr: HumanSightBench is a benchmark of 2,876 short-answer visual questions that are easy for humans and hard for MLLMs, filtered through five inclusion gates. The best pass@3 score across eight evaluated MLLMs is 65.6%, and no model exceeds 27.5% on Counting.
AI.motivation: MLLMs succeed on knowledge-heavy vision-language benchmarks but still fail on visual questions people solve easily, and end-to-end evaluation confounds perception with language priors, knowledge, ambiguity and underspecified answers.
AI.method: Items are constructed to be human-easy by construction and model-hard by evaluation, and must pass five gates: question clarity, answer uniqueness, visual grounding, human solvability and text-only shortcut filtering. Items span 7 top-level perceptual categories and 21 subcategories, and errors are incorrect answers on human-validated tasks.
AI.result: The best pass@3 score is 65.6% across eight MLLMs, and no evaluated model exceeds 27.5% on Counting. The overall scores hide these category-level capability gaps.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark identifies perception gaps that aggregate scores hide and can support future training experiments and held-out evaluation.

title: Unprompted coordination through shared memory in LLM agents: a locked two-implementation replication and extension
comment: 13 pages, 7 tables, 2 figures. Replication package: this https URL
summary: Coordination between large language-model agents has become a central question for AI safety and software engineering, as such agents are deployed in groups that share infrastructure. Existing research tells the agents that partners exist or asks them to coordinate. Whether coordination arises through shared state alone, with nothing disclosing that anyone else is present, is the key question for deployments that share caches and memory between agents, yet it has rarely been examined, and never with independent replication; this study does both. Four agents each received a short arithmetic task and a key-value store presented to each as its own scratch space; two held complementary halves of one computation, and no prompt mentioned other agents, sharing or collaboration. For reliability, the environment was rebuilt independently from a written protocol, and both implementations ran under hashed locks on design, data and analysis. The results bear novelty value in three respects. Joint success occurred only through the shared store. Whether a model coordinated depended not on its vendor tier but on whether it wrote its intermediate result and looked at the store again, and one ordinary sentence, "check your workspace again before submitting", switched that second look on and off. The findings held under replication. For practice, state shared between agents is a communication channel and should be separated, namespaced and logged. For research, designs should be locked before the data, and the parse rule, endpoint and parameters reported. Future work should test open-weight models and separate using another agent's output from intending to communicate.

AI.tldr: A locked, two-implementation replication finds that four LLM agents coordinate through a shared key-value store alone, with no prompt mentioning other agents. Whether a model coordinated depended on whether it wrote its intermediate result and re-read the store, and one added sentence switched that second look on and off.
AI.motivation: Coordination through shared state alone, without disclosure that others are present, matters for deployments where agents share caches and memory, and it has rarely been examined or independently replicated.
AI.method: Four agents each receive an arithmetic task and a key-value store presented as their own scratch space, with two holding complementary halves of one computation. The environment was rebuilt independently from a written protocol, and both implementations ran under hashed locks on design, data and analysis.
AI.result: Joint success occurred only through the shared store. Coordination depended on whether a model wrote its intermediate result and looked at the store again rather than on its vendor tier, and the sentence "check your workspace again before submitting" toggled this second look. The findings held under replication.
AI.conclusion: Shared agent state is a communication channel and should be separated, namespaced and logged, and studies should lock designs before data and report parse rules, endpoints and parameters. Open-weight models and the separation of using another agent's output from intent to communicate remain for future work.

title: Can the Confidence and Decisions of System 1 Models Be Trusted? An Explainability and Perturbation Audit of Jev-Style Decision Models
comment: 36 pages, 4 figures, 16 tables. Code and benchmark artifacts available at this https URL
summary: "System 1" decision models (pioneered by TypeSafe AI's Jev) replace autoregressive text generation with a single forward pass returning typed probability distributions over declared schemas (Choice, Score, Noul). While deployed for low-latency routing and automated triage, their statistical calibration and post-hoc explainability remain uncharacterized. We introduce an open, deterministic audit benchmark evaluating System 1 decision models across calibration under label-preserving perturbations, cross-question interference, and post-hoc attribution faithfulness. Evaluating five open-weight models (0.8B to 27B) alongside generative System 2 baselines -- both single-token logprob scoring and structured JSON/CoT decoding -- across NLI (e-SNLI), adversarial syntactic shortcuts (HANS), synthetic clinical triage (N=900), prompt injection defense (Tensor Trust, N=250), and an 86-case logic-gate trigger suite yields five findings: (1) provider confidence is an exact closed-form dispersion transform (1 - H(p)/ln K on sub-10B models; normalized margin on Clef-27B) rather than empirical accuracy; (2) bundling multiple questions in one request induces directional cross-question interference (11.7% to 22.4% binary flips on Tev1-0.8B, vs. 0.1% to 0.2% on Tev1-4B); (3) System 1 models with >= 4B parameters are faster and better calibrated under syntactic shifts (ECE_w = 0.030 to 0.087) than logprob (0.144) and JSON (0.378) baselines; (4) for prompt-injection defense (N=250), >= 4B models achieve 0.988 to 0.998 AUROC with up to 95.2% recall and 0.0% false alarms at 48 to 60 ms; and (5) single-pass inference makes 512-coalition XAI interactive (1.3 to 3.2 s/input), while KernelSHAP with a logit link (S1-SHAP) mitigates softmax saturation on disjunctive OR gates (89.3% to 100.0% gate recovery vs. 57.1% to 82.1% in prob space; p_adj = 0.004).

AI.tldr: The paper audits System 1 decision models (single-forward-pass typed probability outputs) for calibration, cross-question interference and explanation faithfulness across five open-weight models from 0.8B to 27B. It finds that provider confidence is a closed-form dispersion transform rather than empirical accuracy.
AI.motivation: System 1 models are deployed for low-latency routing and triage, but their calibration and post-hoc explainability have not been characterized.
AI.method: An open deterministic audit benchmark covers label-preserving perturbations, bundled multi-question requests, post-hoc attribution, and tasks including e-SNLI, HANS, a synthetic clinical triage set (N=900), Tensor Trust prompt injection (N=250) and an 86-case logic-gate suite. System 1 models are compared with logprob and JSON/CoT System 2 baselines, and KernelSHAP with a logit link (S1-SHAP) is used for attribution.
AI.result: Provider confidence matches a closed-form dispersion transform rather than accuracy. Bundling questions causes directional interference, with 11.7% to 22.4% binary flips on the 0.8B model versus 0.1% to 0.2% on the 4B model. Models of 4B or more parameters are faster and better calibrated under syntactic shifts (ECE_w 0.030 to 0.087) than logprob (0.144) and JSON (0.378) baselines. For prompt-injection defense, models of 4B or more reach 0.988 to 0.998 AUROC with up to 95.2% recall and 0.0% false alarms. S1-SHAP recovers 89.3% to 100.0% of OR gates versus 57.1% to 82.1% in probability space.
AI.conclusion: System 1 models are fast and often well calibrated at 4B and above, but their confidence reflects a dispersion transform rather than accuracy, and bundling questions should be avoided. Single-pass inference also makes 512-coalition explanations interactive.

title: Evaluating Cross-Signal Coherence in Mammography Vision-Language Models
summary: As vision-language models (VLMs) move toward interpreting medical images directly, their outputs increasingly include not just a label but a stated confidence and a written justification. Yet the field still predominantly evaluates VLMs using just accuracy. We evaluate the coherence between answer, confidence, and explanation across four VLMs on breast density and BI-RADS categorization, using two mammography datasets. We perform controlled perturbations of the question, multiple choice option orders, and the images and assess changes in the three outputs. Our results suggest confidence does not decrease even as the mammography image is changed. Shuffling the options also changes most VLMs' answers. Notably, there are cases where a model's own stated reasoning contradicts its final answer, a distinction accuracy alone cannot capture but one that governs whether an AI-generated answer can be trusted.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates coherence among answer, stated confidence and written explanation in four vision-language models on breast density and BI-RADS categorization across two mammography datasets. It finds that confidence stays stable even when the image changes, and that some models' explanations contradict their final answers.
AI.motivation: VLMs for medical imaging increasingly output confidence and justifications, yet they are still evaluated mainly by accuracy, which cannot reveal whether the three outputs are consistent or trustworthy.
AI.method: Controlled perturbations change the question, the multiple-choice option order and the images, and changes in answer, confidence and explanation are assessed across four VLMs on two mammography datasets.
AI.result: Confidence does not decrease even when the mammography image is changed. Shuffling the options changes most models' answers. Some models' stated reasoning contradicts their final answer.
AI.conclusion: Accuracy alone cannot capture answer-explanation-confidence incoherence, which governs whether AI-generated medical answers can be trusted.

title: Type-logical grammars and formal languages
summary: We show that type-logical grammars with the standard rules for product, associativity, extraction and infixation have an NP-complete fixed recognition problem, adapting a construction for first-order linear logic from Pshenitsyn (2025), who already showed that grammars in first-order linear logic are closed under intersection and therefore not semilinear and not mildly context-sensitive. We strengthen these results and shown that grammars in first-order linear logic can simulate the quasi-linear grammars of Book \& Greibach (1970), the grammars recognised in non-deterministic linear time (NSPACE(n) or. NLIN). I argue that NLIN is an interesting class of formal languages as well, and a useful upper bound on the time complexity of formalisms used for natural language, just like LOGCFL is a useful upper bound on the space complexity. Taken together this means that first-order linear logic can be seen as the logic of non-deterministic linear-time string languages, graph languages and automata.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that type-logical grammars with standard product, associativity, extraction and infixation rules have an NP-complete fixed recognition problem. It also shows that first-order linear logic grammars can simulate quasi-linear grammars, the class recognized in nondeterministic linear time.
AI.motivation: Earlier work showed that first-order linear logic grammars are closed under intersection and so are not semilinear or mildly context-sensitive, and the complexity and generative power of such formalisms for natural language needed sharpening.
AI.method: The paper adapts a construction for first-order linear logic from Pshenitsyn (2025) to type-logical grammars with the standard rules, and it relates grammars to the quasi-linear grammars of Book and Greibach (1970) and to NSPACE(n).
AI.result: The fixed recognition problem for these type-logical grammars is NP-complete. First-order linear logic grammars can simulate quasi-linear grammars, which are recognized in NSPACE(n) or NLIN.
AI.conclusion: First-order linear logic can be seen as the logic of nondeterministic linear-time string, graph and automaton languages, and NLIN is proposed as a useful upper bound on the time complexity of natural language formalisms, analogous to LOGCFL for space.

title: TrialDesignBench: Benchmarking Language Models for Phase-I Trial Design Against Clinical Knowledge
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Presented as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on World Models for High-Stakes Health (WMHS). Code and data: this https URL
summary: AI is used in much of the clinical trial pipeline. However, selecting the statistical design of a trial, a crucial step that determines how drug doses are tested on humans and evaluated, has seen almost no AI progress. LLMs appear to be a natural fit given their strengths in biomedical knowledge and statistical reasoning. Nevertheless, there is currently no appropriate way to evaluate such abilities because recent regulatory and methodological shifts, most notably FDA's Project Optimus, have redefined what constitutes a reasonable design and rendered many previous designs obsolete. To lay the groundwork for AI-assisted trial design, we introduce TrialDesignBench, a benchmark of 617 Phase-I/I-II oncology dose-finding trials, each paired with an expert-validated reference design that is consistent with the latest FDA regulatory initiatives. This reference standard is produced through a formalization of the expert design process. We evaluate five frontier LLMs, none of which matches the reference standard. Our ablation experiments trace this performance gap to two main causes, inference of latent, unrecorded design determinants from trial sources (supplying them raises class-wise balanced accuracy by 0.22) and structured decision-tree reasoning (+0.24). TrialDesignBench offers a reproducible, contemporary-standard objective for evaluating and enhancing AI-assisted trial design.

AI.tldr: TrialDesignBench is a benchmark of 617 Phase-I/I-II oncology dose-finding trials, each paired with an expert-validated reference design consistent with recent FDA initiatives such as Project Optimus, and none of five frontier LLMs matches the reference standard.
AI.motivation: AI has made almost no progress on selecting the statistical design of early-phase trials, and no appropriate evaluation exists because regulatory and methodological shifts such as Project Optimus have made many previous designs obsolete.
AI.method: The authors formalize the expert design process to produce reference designs for 617 trials and evaluate five frontier LLMs, with ablations that supply latent unrecorded design determinants inferred from trial sources and that test structured decision-tree reasoning.
AI.result: No model matches the reference standard; supplying the latent design determinants raises class-wise balanced accuracy by 0.22, and structured decision-tree reasoning adds 0.24.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark gives a reproducible, contemporary-standard objective for evaluating and enhancing AI-assisted trial design, and the ablations identify inferring hidden determinants and structured reasoning as the two main gaps.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Clinical Agents: When Dense Rewards Beat Outcome Rewards
comment: 31 pages, 11 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is increasingly used to improve language model reasoning, yet its effects on sequential decision procedures remain poorly understood. We study this problem in clinical multi-turn agents that must decide what information to request, when to stop gathering evidence, and which action to take. We introduce three controlled environments: medication refill triage, acute diagnostic work-up, and dosing titration, each with hidden clinical states, query costs, exact adaptive oracles, and deterministic outcome verifiers. Across these tasks, outcome-only group relative policy optimization often improves aggregate reward while producing undesirable procedures, including premature commitment, one-question collapse, and failures on rare high-risk cases. In diagnostics, assigning dense credit to questions that reduce uncertainty improves held-out value and moderate-case support across three training seeds relative to outcome-only reinforcement learning, without the high-risk seed collapse observed under outcome-only training. Separating exploration from exploitation further increases high-risk support at its best checkpoint, but at the cost of excessive information gathering on low-acuity cases. Additional experiments show that the optimal strength of process credit is task-dependent; that after a supervised warmup that already gathers carefully, reinforcement learning raises aggregate reward by trimming questions while degrading high-risk performance; and that reinforcement learning does not reliably repair rare behavior gaps inherited from biased supervised data. Verifiable final outcomes are therefore insufficient for training reliable multi-turn agents: reward design must account for the procedure used to reach an answer, and evaluation must distinguish adaptive information gathering from reward-exploiting shortcuts.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that outcome-only reinforcement learning for clinical multi-turn agents can improve aggregate reward while producing unsafe procedures, and that dense credit for uncertainty-reducing questions improves held-out value and high-risk support in diagnostics.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is widely used for language model reasoning, but its effects on sequential decision procedures, such as deciding what to ask and when to stop gathering evidence, are poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors build three controlled clinical environments (medication refill triage, acute diagnostic work-up, and dosing titration) with hidden states, query costs, adaptive oracles and deterministic outcome verifiers, and compare outcome-only group relative policy optimization with variants that assign dense process credit and separate exploration from exploitation.
AI.result: Outcome-only training produces premature commitment, one-question collapse and failures on rare high-risk cases; dense credit improves held-out value and moderate-case support across three seeds without the high-risk seed collapse, and separating exploration further increases high-risk support at its best checkpoint at the cost of excessive questioning on low-acuity cases.
AI.conclusion: Verifiable final outcomes are insufficient for training reliable multi-turn clinical agents, so reward design must account for the procedure used to reach an answer and evaluation must distinguish adaptive information gathering from reward-exploiting shortcuts.

title: Curbside Chatbots: Auditing the Mental Health Interventions Large Language Models Recommend to Clinicians, Caregivers, and Patients
comment: 100 pages: 30 page main text and references, 70 page appendix. 7 figures, 2 tables. Results explorer: this https URL
summary: Users are asking language models mental health questions and are receiving answers. We audited what 41 language models recommend to users when the same clinical information reaches them from three footings: a clinician describing a patient, a caregiver describing a loved one, or a person describing themselves. Across 19 case vignettes and five questions, we collected 35,055 free-text responses, extracted every intervention named with a validated judge, and had 29 models rate the full option lists on a seven-point Likert scale for the same cases. Models largely recommend what they rate well, with recommendation behavior differing by footing, and many models offering clinicians a consultation-style response and lay users hedged, simplified advice. When asked about recommendations for a specific intervention type, models more often named options they themselves rated below zero as initial choices, usually with conditions attached. We will release the instrument, code, and full corpus on publication as a living audit.

AI.tldr: An audit of 41 language models finds that the mental health interventions they recommend depend on whether the same clinical information comes from a clinician, a caregiver or the person themselves, and that models often name options they rate below zero as initial choices.
AI.motivation: Users increasingly ask language models mental health questions, but it is unclear what interventions models recommend to clinicians, caregivers and patients given the same clinical information.
AI.method: The authors present 19 case vignettes and five questions under three footings (clinician, caregiver, self), collect 35,055 free-text responses, extract every named intervention with a validated judge, and have 29 models rate the full option lists on a seven-point Likert scale.
AI.result: Models largely recommend the options they rate well, recommendation behavior differs by footing, clinicians receive consultation-style responses while lay users receive hedged, simplified advice, and for specific intervention types models more often name options they rated below zero as initial choices, usually with conditions attached.
AI.conclusion: The audit documents footing-dependent and sometimes inconsistent mental health recommendations from language models, and the authors plan to release the instrument, code and full corpus on publication as a living audit.

title: Video-DCI: How Far Are VLM Agents from Human Viewers in Direct Video Corpus Interaction?
summary: Humans answer complex visual questions by inspecting short moments, updating what they know, and redirecting attention toward missing evidence. Existing video benchmarks, however, often provide the relevant video, evaluate only final answers or isolated localization, or permit textual shortcuts, leaving multi-round visual evidence seeking underexplored. We introduce Video-DCI, a diagnostic benchmark and functionally matched human-agent protocol for Direct Video-Corpus Interaction. It comprises DCI-Loc for temporal evidence localization and DCI-QA for end-to-end discovery, retention, and composition of cross-video evidence. In DCI-QA, videos within each pool are topically related, yet every answer requires hidden temporal evidence from multiple videos. Given only the question and video pool, humans and agents iteratively inspect bounded local windows, retain supporting evidence, and answer with cited temporal spans. Human trajectories provide reference curves for evidence acquisition and use across rounds. Experiments reveal a consistent retrieval-to-grounding gap. On DCI-Loc, frontier VLMs often retrieve and expose the reference moment, yet convert far less of this exposure into precise final citations than the human reference. On DCI-QA, the loss begins earlier and compounds across videos. Ablation studies further confirm that iterative search outperforms one-shot retrieval. Multi-round search is therefore necessary but insufficient: current agents accumulate candidates and observations more readily than precise, jointly sufficient evidence.

AI.tldr: Video-DCI is a diagnostic benchmark for direct video-corpus interaction in which humans and VLM agents iteratively inspect local windows across related videos to answer questions with cited temporal evidence, and frontier VLM agents show a retrieval-to-grounding gap relative to humans.
AI.motivation: Existing video benchmarks supply the relevant video, evaluate only final answers or isolated localization, or permit textual shortcuts, leaving multi-round visual evidence seeking underexplored.
AI.method: The authors introduce DCI-Loc for temporal evidence localization and DCI-QA for end-to-end discovery, retention and composition of evidence across topically related videos, with a functionally matched human-agent protocol that records human trajectories as reference curves.
AI.result: Frontier VLMs often retrieve and expose the reference moment on DCI-Loc yet convert far less of it into precise final citations than humans do, and on DCI-QA the loss begins earlier and compounds across videos; ablations show iterative search outperforms one-shot retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Multi-round search is necessary but insufficient, since current agents accumulate candidates and observations more readily than precise, jointly sufficient evidence.

title: Confusion-Adaptive Margin Learning for Handwritten Letter Recognition: A Controlled Study on EMNIST Letters
summary: Handwritten character recognition systems can achieve high accuracy while retaining concentrated errors among visually similar classes. Motivated by residual letter confusions in earlier geometry-based recognition work, we investigate whether these errors can be addressed through the training objective. We introduce Confusion-Adaptive Margin Learning (CAML), which constructs a sparse weighted confusion graph from a discovery partition held out from pilot training and applies pair-specific cosine-separation constraints during final training. CAML adds no classifier, routing rule, or inference-time parameters. We evaluate CAML on EMNIST Letters against a strictly matched cross-entropy CNN baseline, using the same architecture, final training data, deterministic augmentation, optimizer, and checkpoint selection. Eight confusion pairs are targeted: I/L, G/Q, U/V, R/V, D/O, C/E, I/J, and H/N. On the official clean test set, accuracy changes from 95.6346% to 95.6731%, and macro-F1 from 0.956326 to 0.956724. Mean accuracy across ten predefined corrupted conditions increases from approximately 95.3812% to 95.4303%; symmetric errors within targeted pairs decrease from 614 to 605 (1.47%). The global differences are small and not statistically reliable. CAML fixes 124 baseline errors but introduces 116 new errors on clean data (exact McNemar p=0.6515), and no corruption-specific difference remains significant after Holm correction. Thus, CAML does not establish global superiority, but shows that a leakage-controlled, pair-specific margin objective can alter targeted error structure with limited overall benefit for an already strong classifier.

AI.tldr: Confusion-Adaptive Margin Learning (CAML) adds pair-specific cosine-separation constraints for eight confusable letter pairs on EMNIST Letters and changes the targeted error structure, but its global gains over a matched cross-entropy CNN are small and not statistically reliable.
AI.motivation: Handwritten character recognizers keep errors concentrated among visually similar classes, and the authors ask whether these residual confusions can be addressed through the training objective instead of the architecture.
AI.method: CAML builds a sparse weighted confusion graph from a held-out discovery partition and applies pair-specific cosine-separation constraints during final training, adding no classifier, routing rule or inference-time parameters, and is compared with a strictly matched cross-entropy CNN baseline on EMNIST Letters.
AI.result: On the clean test set accuracy changes from 95.6346% to 95.6731% and macro-F1 from 0.956326 to 0.956724, mean accuracy over ten corrupted conditions rises from about 95.3812% to 95.4303%, and symmetric errors within targeted pairs fall from 614 to 605; CAML fixes 124 baseline errors but adds 116 new ones (exact McNemar p=0.6515), and no corruption-specific difference survives Holm correction.
AI.conclusion: CAML does not establish global superiority, but a leakage-controlled, pair-specific margin objective can alter targeted error structure with limited overall benefit for an already strong classifier.

title: DiffusedSplitFed: Latent Diffusion-based Obfuscation for Reconstruction-Resilient Split Federated Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Federated Learning (FL), Split Learning (SL), and Split Federated Learning (SplitFed) enable collaborative medical image analysis without sharing raw patient data. However, intermediate features and gradients exchanged during SplitFed training may reveal sensitive information through reconstruction attacks. To address this vulnerability, we propose \textbf{DiffusedSplitFed}, a SplitFed framework that integrates Latent Denoising Diffusion Models (LDDMs) at client--server split points to obfuscate transmitted representations while preserving segmentation performance. Three architectural variants (V1--V3) are developed using different combinations of dual conditioning and global feature fusion to investigate trade-offs among reconstruction resistance, segmentation accuracy, and computational complexity. Experiments on three medical imaging datasets (HAM10K, Blastocysts, and FHPsAOPMSB), supported by multiple independent runs and paired statistical analyses, demonstrate improved resistance to the evaluated image reconstruction attacks compared with Baseline SplitFed, while maintaining competitive segmentation performance. Comparisons with existing diffusion-based segmentation methods further demonstrate competitive segmentation accuracy under the evaluated settings. A conditional convergence analysis is also provided to characterize the effects of LDDM-induced gradient perturbations and local optimization on training. These findings highlight the potential of latent diffusion-based representation obfuscation for reconstruction-resilient collaborative medical image segmentation. The implementation is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: DiffusedSplitFed inserts latent denoising diffusion models at the client-server split points of SplitFed training to obfuscate transmitted features and gradients, improving resistance to the evaluated reconstruction attacks while keeping competitive segmentation performance on three medical imaging datasets.
AI.motivation: Intermediate features and gradients exchanged during SplitFed training can leak sensitive patient information through reconstruction attacks, and existing protection of these exchanges reduces utility.
AI.method: The authors develop three variants (V1 to V3) of latent diffusion obfuscation at split points using different combinations of dual conditioning and global feature fusion, and provide a conditional convergence analysis of the effect of LDDM-induced gradient perturbations.
AI.result: Across HAM10K, Blastocysts and FHPsAOPMSB, with multiple runs and paired statistical tests, the variants resist the evaluated reconstruction attacks better than Baseline SplitFed while staying competitive in segmentation accuracy, and also compare competitively with existing diffusion-based segmentation methods.
AI.conclusion: Latent diffusion-based representation obfuscation is a promising route to reconstruction-resilient collaborative medical image segmentation, with trade-offs among resistance, accuracy and computational cost across variants.

title: RadAI: Gaze-Intention Fusion Pipeline for Attention-Guided Educational Videos in Chest X-Ray Interpretation
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 1 table, accepted to 2026 MIT IEEE URTC conference
summary: Chest radiograph interpretation errors often arise from failures in visual search: although trainees may correctly identify an abnormality once pointed out, they frequently fail to fixate on the relevant region, while expert search strategies (where radiologists look, in what sequence, and for how long) remain largely implicit. Eye movement modeling examples (EMME), which replay a recorded expert's gaze over the image, have been shown to improve novice detection of findings on chest radiographs, but producing one requires an eye-tracking session on that specific case, so teaching sets are limited to recorded sessions by experts. In this work, RadAI is presented, the first end-to-end framework for transforming predicted radiologist gaze into narrated instructional videos, enabling scalable gaze-guided training without collecting new eye-tracking data. Given only a chest X-ray and its report, RadAI predicts an expert fixation sequence, associates each interval of that sequence with the diagnostic finding it pursues, extracts the corresponding image region, and renders the result as an EMME-style video in which each highlighted finding is narrated with synthesized speech. RadAI is evaluated on 97 cases from the EGD-CXR dataset, assessing whether the highlighted regions correspond to annotated abnormality locations. We position this work as a framework for scalable generation of educational content for residents and medical students in the field of radiology.

AI.tldr: RadAI is an end-to-end framework that predicts a radiologist's gaze sequence from a chest X-ray and its report and renders it as a narrated, eye-movement-modeling-style educational video, without new eye-tracking data.
AI.motivation: Eye movement modeling examples improve novice detection of chest radiograph findings, but they require an eye-tracking session on each case, which limits teaching sets to recorded expert sessions.
AI.method: RadAI predicts an expert fixation sequence, associates each fixation interval with the finding it pursues, extracts the corresponding image region, and renders an EMME-style video in which each highlighted finding is narrated with synthesized speech.
AI.result: The highlighted regions are evaluated on 97 cases from the EGD-CXR dataset by checking whether they correspond to annotated abnormality locations.
AI.conclusion: The authors position RadAI as a framework for scalable generation of gaze-guided educational content for residents and medical students in radiology.

title: MAPA: Mode-Aware Prototype Allocation for Latent Dataset Distillation in 3D Medical Classification
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027. 17 pages including supplementary material
summary: Dataset distillation (DD) synthesizes a small training set from a large one, but applying it to 3D medical classification is constrained by the memory and optimization costs of synthesizing full volumetric samples. Under a storage-equivalent budget, distilling in the latent space of a frozen autoencoder reduces this cost and fits more synthetic samples (prototypes) than in voxel space. However, class-level matching, such as distribution matching, causes prototypes to concentrate in dense latent regions while underrepresenting sparser intra-class regions, a consistent imbalance that we term prototype concentration. To address this, we propose MAPA (Mode-Aware Prototype Allocation), a latent distillation method that spreads prototypes across intra-class modes while preserving class-level matching. MAPA marks these modes with fixed anchors estimated by clustering the real latents and distributes prototypes over them through a soft assignment, together with a lightweight anti-collapse regularizer and curriculum weighting that stabilize the optimization. Across five 3D medical classification tasks, MAPA improves the aggregate balanced accuracy by +4.2 points over the strongest latent baseline while using the same number of prototypes. An exploratory severity analysis on MosMedData suggests improved worst-stratum recall without loss of normal-case specificity.

AI.tldr: MAPA is a latent dataset distillation method for 3D medical classification that spreads prototypes across intra-class modes to counter prototype concentration, improving aggregate balanced accuracy by 4.2 points over the strongest latent baseline at the same prototype count.
AI.motivation: Dataset distillation of volumetric medical data is costly in voxel space, and class-level matching in latent space concentrates prototypes in dense regions while underrepresenting sparser intra-class modes.
AI.method: MAPA estimates fixed mode anchors by clustering real latents, distributes prototypes over the anchors through a soft assignment, and adds a lightweight anti-collapse regularizer and curriculum weighting while preserving class-level matching.
AI.result: Across five 3D medical classification tasks, MAPA improves aggregate balanced accuracy by +4.2 points over the strongest latent baseline with the same number of prototypes, and an exploratory severity analysis on MosMedData suggests better worst-stratum recall without loss of normal-case specificity.
AI.conclusion: Spreading prototypes across intra-class modes is a practical way to make latent dataset distillation more representative for 3D medical classification, although the severity result is exploratory.

title: HALMES: Knowing When to Intervene in LVLM Hallucination Mitigation
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in multimodal tasks. Nevertheless, their outputs remain prone to object hallucinations that are inconsistent with visual content. Contrastive decoding, as a training-free inference-time mitigation approach, typically intervenes in the output distribution at every decoding step. However, such indiscriminate full-stage intervention may disrupt originally correct generations and even induce new hallucinations. To address this issue, we first analyze the relationship between internal attention features and hallucinated token segments in LVLMs, revealing that hallucination-related abnormalities already emerge progressively in preceding token segments. Based on this observation, we propose HALMES, a lightweight plug-and-play module that identifies hallucination precursor segments from attention features during generation and selectively triggers contrastive decoding. HALMES can be integrated with various full-stage contrastive decoding methods, transforming indiscriminate intervention into on-demand targeted correction. Extensive experiments across different LVLM architectures and multiple benchmarks show that HALMES further improves the hallucination mitigation performance of existing contrastive decoding methods while reducing the negative impact of full-stage intervention on normal outputs, validating the importance of modeling and selectively intervening on hallucination-prone segments.

AI.tldr: HALMES is a lightweight module that detects hallucination precursor segments from attention features during generation and triggers contrastive decoding only on those segments, improving existing contrastive decoding methods while reducing harm to correct outputs.
AI.motivation: Contrastive decoding mitigates object hallucination in LVLMs but intervenes at every decoding step, which can disrupt correct generations and introduce new hallucinations.
AI.method: The authors analyze internal attention features and hallucinated token segments, find that abnormalities emerge progressively in preceding segments, and build HALMES to identify these precursor segments and selectively trigger contrastive decoding, pluggable into various full-stage methods.
AI.result: Experiments across different LVLM architectures and multiple benchmarks show that HALMES further improves the mitigation performance of existing contrastive decoding methods and reduces the negative impact of full-stage intervention on normal outputs.
AI.conclusion: Selectively intervening on hallucination-prone segments, rather than intervening indiscriminately, is an important design choice for inference-time hallucination mitigation in LVLMs.

title: HippoMamba: A Mamba-augmented network for hippocampal segmentation and serial volumetry in Alzheimers disease
summary: Hippocampal atrophy is among the earliest structural markers of Alzheimer's disease, and reliable hippocampal segmentation across serial MRI visits is a prerequisite for measuring it. We present HippoMamba, a network that combines a 3D convolutional encoder and decoder with a Mamba selective state space block at the bottleneck, designed to process one or more MRI visits of a subject. On the Medical Segmentation Decathlon hippocampus dataset (260 subjects, five-fold cross-validation), HippoMamba obtained a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 0.8861 $\pm$ 0.0094, the highest among six convolutional and transformer-based methods trained with the same folds and patch size, and its per-subject Dice was significantly higher than that of each method (Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests, $p \leq 0.013$). Its mean 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (1.45 mm) and average surface distance (0.44 mm) were the lowest of the compared methods, although they did not differ significantly from those of Attention U-Net, and the Hausdorff distance did not differ significantly from that of SegResNet. Without retraining, the five-fold ensemble was applied to 600 T1-weighted sessions from 150 participants of the OASIS-3 cohort. In sessions meeting a registration quality criterion, predicted hippocampal volumes ranked consistently with FreeSurfer volumes (Pearson r = 0.778, 95% CI 0.699 to 0.838; ICC(3,1) = 0.772) but were systematically smaller by about 27%. In a pre-specified analysis of participants followed for at least two years, annualised volume change derived from per-visit segmentation was moderately correlated with that of FreeSurfer (r = 0.503, 95% CI 0.319 to 0.659), with a larger mean rate. These results support the use of HippoMamba for hippocampal segmentation and for ranking hippocampal volume within a cohort, with absolute volumes and rates of change interpreted relative to the reference method.

AI.tldr: HippoMamba combines a 3D convolutional encoder-decoder with a Mamba state space block for hippocampal segmentation and serial volumetry, reaching a mean Dice of 0.8861 on the Medical Segmentation Decathlon hippocampus dataset and correlating with FreeSurfer volume change on OASIS-3, though with systematically smaller volumes.
AI.motivation: Reliable hippocampal segmentation across serial MRI visits is needed to measure the early atrophy that marks Alzheimer's disease.
AI.method: HippoMamba places a Mamba selective state space block at the bottleneck of a 3D convolutional encoder-decoder that can process one or more MRI visits per subject, and is compared with six convolutional and transformer methods under five-fold cross-validation with the same folds and patch size.
AI.result: HippoMamba obtains a mean Dice of 0.8861 plus or minus 0.0094, the highest of the compared methods with significant per-subject differences, and the lowest mean 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (1.45 mm) and average surface distance (0.44 mm); on 600 OASIS-3 sessions without retraining, predicted volumes correlate with FreeSurfer (Pearson r = 0.778) but are about 27% smaller, and annualised volume change correlates moderately (r = 0.503) in participants followed for at least two years.
AI.conclusion: HippoMamba supports hippocampal segmentation and ranking of volumes within a cohort, with absolute volumes and rates of change to be interpreted relative to the reference method.

title: A four-view smartphone video dataset of a robot-held flexible strip, with camera poses and a 3D LaGSplat baseline
comment: 2 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Dataset and checkpoints: doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23601189. Training code: this https URL. Interactive demo: this https URL
summary: This note describes a multi-view video dataset of a deformable object driven by a measured input, with the measured pose of every camera, and a first 3D result obtained on it with LaGSplat. LaGSplat learns from video a low-dimensional latent state that is both the generalized coordinate of a learned dissipative Lagrangian and the conditioning variable of a Gaussian Splatting decoder; fitting the decoder in 3D calls for synchronized multi-view footage, which the original paper only had from synthetic renderings. Here a robot arm moves a flexible strip by oscillating along a one-dimensional path, and four iPhones, three fixed and one handheld, film it for ten minutes. The videos are synchronized, the cameras are posed from the scene, and the position of the gripper is given per frame as the input of the system. LaGSplat fitted on this data with the gripper acceleration as a forcing term renders held-out views at 26 to 33 dB PSNR and runs as a real-time interactive demo in a web browser. Dataset, checkpoints and training code are public.

AI.tldr: The paper releases a four-view smartphone video dataset of a robot-held flexible strip with measured camera poses and gripper inputs, and reports a first 3D result in which LaGSplat renders held-out views at 26 to 33 dB PSNR.
AI.motivation: The original LaGSplat work had multi-view data only from synthetic renderings, so fitting its Gaussian Splatting decoder in 3D needs real synchronized multi-view footage.
AI.method: A robot arm oscillates a flexible strip along a one-dimensional path while four iPhones (three fixed, one handheld) film it for ten minutes, with synchronized videos, cameras posed from the scene and per-frame gripper position as input, and LaGSplat is fitted with gripper acceleration as a forcing term.
AI.result: LaGSplat fitted on this data renders held-out views at 26 to 33 dB PSNR and runs as a real-time interactive demo in a web browser.
AI.conclusion: The dataset, checkpoints and training code are public, providing a real-data testbed for 3D learned Lagrangian models of deformable objects.

title: SceneShifter: Training-free Multi-Scene Temporal Control for Audio-driven Human Animation
summary: Although audio-driven human animation has achieved impressive realism, it still lacks effective Multi-Scene Temporal Control: orchestrating background transitions at precise timestamps while preserving a coherent foreground subject. We show that this challenge stems from the diffusion transformer's self-attention mechanism, and addressing it requires two capabilities: (1) Semantic-Aware Temporal Decoupling, which isolates background attention across scenes while retaining cross-scene foreground attention for subject consistency; and (2) Foreground Motion Localization, which accurately tracks the foreground subject across latent frames, especially under large motion. To address these challenges, we introduce SceneShifter, a training-free framework for precise multi-scene control in audio-driven human animation. SceneShifter guides spatio-temporal self-attention by suppressing cross-scene attention among background tokens while preserving cross-scene attention among foreground tokens. To support this guidance under large motion, SceneShifter extracts dynamic foreground masks from the self-attention layers and heads that best capture subject trajectories. We further introduce SceneShifterBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate scene-timing accuracy, foreground preservation, and visual quality under large motion, multiple subjects. Experiments show that SceneShifter achieves frame-level scene timing, strong subject preservation, and high visual quality, outperforming existing baselines. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: SceneShifter is a training-free method for audio-driven human animation that enables frame-level background scene transitions at chosen timestamps while keeping the foreground subject consistent, and it comes with SceneShifterBench for scene timing, foreground preservation and visual quality.
AI.motivation: Audio-driven human animation lacks precise multi-scene temporal control, because the diffusion transformer's self-attention entangles background transitions with foreground subject consistency, especially under large motion.
AI.method: SceneShifter suppresses cross-scene attention among background tokens while preserving it among foreground tokens, and extracts dynamic foreground masks from the self-attention layers and heads that best track the subject trajectory.
AI.result: The authors report frame-level scene timing, strong subject preservation and high visual quality on the new SceneShifterBench, outperforming existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Guiding spatio-temporal self-attention without training is an effective route to precise multi-scene control in audio-driven human animation, including for multiple subjects under large motion.

title: How Many Demonstrations Does a VLA Need? On the Sample Efficiency of VLA Finetuning
summary: Pretrained vision language action (VLA) models show strong zero-shot performance, but are rarely deployed directly and are often first post-trained on demonstrations from the target setting. Yet VLAs are typically compared by zero-shot or full-data fine-tuned success, revealing little about the data and compute required for adaptation. We study adaptation efficiency for six VLAs ($\pi_{0}$, $\pi_{0.5}$, and GR00T N1-N1.7) on four LIBERO suites, varying both demonstrations and training steps. This reveals differences hidden by full-data fine-tuning: models within two points on the full LIBERO-Spatial dataset differ by up to $3\times$ in success with 50 demonstrations. $\pi_{0.5}$ needs $2$--$5\times$ fewer demonstrations than $\pi_{0}$ and is the most sample-efficient model at every budget, with the largest gap on the long-horizon suite. Within GR00T, N1.5 adapts more efficiently than N1.6 and N1.7 on three of four suites, despite their stronger zero-shot performance. We study one pretraining factor behind these differences by freezing the VLM during finetuning: this severely degrades the $\pi$ models, whose VLM is jointly trained with the action expert during pretraining, but barely affects GR00T models. Finally, validation loss on held-out demonstrations tracks closed-loop success within a suite, but understates how much more sample-efficient $\pi_{0.5}$ is than $\pi_{0}$.

AI.tldr: A study of six VLA models across four LIBERO suites finds large differences in sample efficiency hidden by full-data fine-tuning, with pi0.5 needing 2 to 5 times fewer demonstrations than pi0 and GR00T N1.5 adapting more efficiently than N1.6 and N1.7.
AI.motivation: VLAs are usually compared by zero-shot or full-data fine-tuned success, which reveals little about the data and compute needed to adapt them to a target setting.
AI.method: The authors vary both the number of demonstrations and the training steps for pi0, pi0.5 and GR00T N1 through N1.7 on four LIBERO suites, and freeze the VLM during finetuning to test one pretraining factor.
AI.result: Models within two points on the full LIBERO-Spatial dataset differ by up to 3 times in success with 50 demonstrations; pi0.5 is the most sample-efficient at every budget with the largest gap on the long-horizon suite; freezing the VLM severely degrades the pi models but barely affects GR00T models; validation loss tracks closed-loop success within a suite but understates the efficiency gap.
AI.conclusion: Adaptation efficiency is a distinct axis from zero-shot or full-data performance, and it depends on how the VLM is pretrained, so it should be measured directly when choosing a VLA for post-training.

title: Clinically Informed Colour Encoding Improves the Localisation and Stability of Explanations in Deep Learning ECG Models: External Validation in a UK Biobank Epilepsy Cohort
summary: Objective: It is not known whether the input representation governs the quality of explanations of deep learning models for electrocardiogram analysis. Risk of dangerous ventricular repolarisation is judged from the QT-interval and the shape of the T-wave, features that are hard to assess visually and harder still to verify in a model's reasoning. We evaluate a pseudo-colour encoding filling the area beneath the QT interval, its colour sequence designed from clinical electrophysiology knowledge and mapped to a validated risk prediction model, the QT-nomogram. Methods: Two identically configured residual networks were trained on single-heartbeat images from a clinical trial, differing only in whether pseudo-colour encoding was applied, so that any difference is attributable to the chromatic channel alone. To externally validate the effect, both models were applied without fine-tuning or threshold tuning to a previously unseen epilepsy cohort from the UK-Biobank at two visits, and eight explanation methods compared on faithfulness, localisation and stability. Results: The pseudo-colour model achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.903 and 0.914 at the first and follow-up visits, against 0.719 and 0.720 for the monochrome model, recovering three to five times as many at-risk heartbeats at comparable specificity. Pseudo-colour encoding improved explanation localisation and stability for almost every method, and the improvement reproduced across both visits. Conclusion: The input representation is a controllable and previously overlooked determinant of both predictive performance and explanation quality. Significance: Treating interpretability as a representation-design problem offers a route towards explanations clinicians can check against known electrophysiology.

AI.tldr: Pseudo-colour encoding of the QT interval in ECG images, with a colour sequence designed from clinical electrophysiology knowledge, raises external AUROC from about 0.72 to 0.90 or higher in a UK Biobank epilepsy cohort and improves localisation and stability of explanations for almost every method.
AI.motivation: The representation of ECG inputs is an unexamined determinant of explanation quality for deep learning models, and clinicians need explanations they can verify against electrophysiology knowledge.
AI.method: Two identically configured residual networks were trained on single-heartbeat images from a clinical trial, differing only in whether pseudo-colour filling beneath the QT interval was applied, and both were applied without fine-tuning to a UK Biobank epilepsy cohort at two visits, with eight explanation methods compared on faithfulness, localisation and stability.
AI.result: The pseudo-colour model achieves AUROC of 0.903 and 0.914 at the first and follow-up visits versus 0.719 and 0.720 for the monochrome model, recovers three to five times as many at-risk heartbeats at comparable specificity, and improves explanation localisation and stability for almost every method across both visits.
AI.conclusion: Input representation is a controllable and previously overlooked determinant of both predictive performance and explanation quality, and treating interpretability as a representation-design problem is a route to explanations clinicians can check.

title: ReelCache: An Efficient KV Cache Compression and Management System for Multi-Round Video Generation
comment: 18 pages total, 11 pages body plus 5 pages appendix
summary: Autoregressive video diffusion models produce large KV caches during multi-round video generation. Keeping all these KV chunks would consume substantial memory, while rebuilding discarded caches would significantly delay video chunk generation. This paper presents ReelCache, a KV cache compression system for efficient multi-round, long video generation. ReelCache combines an intra-chunk compressor with an inter-chunk cache manager. The compressor applies low-rank decomposition across channels and video coding to the resulting coefficients, predicting the decomposition rank per transformer layer online to meet retained-energy targets. The cache manager shares basis directions across consecutive chunks and organizes chunk states in a tree, allowing generation branches to share historical state while supporting restoration for resume, rewind, and fork. Experiments across five video generation models show that ReelCache reduces KV storage by 14.46-21.13x relative to baselines and accelerates next-chunk generation by 1.25-3.36x, with less than 1% drop in six representative VBench metrics. GitHub: this https URL

AI.tldr: ReelCache compresses and manages KV caches for multi-round autoregressive video generation, reducing KV storage by 14.46 to 21.13 times and accelerating next-chunk generation by 1.25 to 3.36 times with less than 1% drop in six VBench metrics across five models.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive video diffusion models produce large KV caches during multi-round generation, and keeping all chunks costs substantial memory while rebuilding discarded caches delays each new chunk.
AI.method: ReelCache combines an intra-chunk compressor that applies low-rank decomposition across channels followed by video coding, with online per-layer rank prediction for retained-energy targets, and an inter-chunk cache manager that shares basis directions across chunks and organizes chunk states in a tree to support branching, resume, rewind and fork.
AI.result: Across five video generation models, ReelCache reduces KV storage by 14.46 to 21.13 times relative to baselines and speeds up next-chunk generation by 1.25 to 3.36 times, with less than 1% drop in six representative VBench metrics.
AI.conclusion: Structured KV compression combined with tree-organized cache management makes long multi-round video generation more memory-efficient while preserving quality and supporting interactive generation operations.

title: Seeing Like a Shopper: Validating Vision-Language Models as Synthetic Consumers
summary: Language models are widely used as synthetic respondents in surveys, behavioral experiments, and market research. Most of these respondents read text, whereas shoppers in a store choose by looking at shelves, which makes vision-language models (VLMs) natural synthetic shoppers. We test whether VLM shoppers follow real consumers at two levels. At the purchase level, VLM shoppers built from household records plan their trips from a store directory and select products from shelf images, and we compare their purchases with six public datasets from three countries. The synthetic baskets hit held-out purchases as often as the households' own past trips, and synthetic group differences correlate with real ones twice as strongly as those of a trained regression. Without fitting, VLM shoppers reproduce alcohol purchases by gender and age in Russia and trip sizes by store distance in Taiwan, and respond to situations, prices, and displays within measured ranges. At the level of a single shelf choice, a model's answer confounds the product with its position and letter label. We therefore introduce ShelfSight, shelf renderings that vary products, positions, labels, viewpoints, and prices independently, together with a factor model that separates product preferences from the effects of label and position, which we call answer effects. On ShelfSight, hosted VLMs read the shelf, follow stated needs, keep their product preferences across views, and respond to price as budget shoppers. These answer effects, a preference for the letter A and for positions in the image, are estimated once per image type and removed. VLMs are thus good synthetic shoppers whose corrected shelf choices reflect product preferences.

AI.tldr: VLM shoppers reproduce several real purchase patterns from household and shelf evidence, and the authors introduce ShelfSight with a factor model that removes answer effects for letter labels and positions so that shelf choices reflect product preferences.
AI.motivation: Language models are used as synthetic survey respondents, but shoppers choose by looking at shelves, so the authors test whether vision-language models can serve as validated synthetic consumers at purchase and shelf-choice levels.
AI.method: VLM shoppers built from household records plan trips from a store directory and select products from shelf images, and are compared with six public datasets from three countries; ShelfSight renders shelves that vary products, positions, labels, viewpoints and prices independently, and a factor model separates product preferences from answer effects estimated once per image type.
AI.result: Synthetic baskets hit held-out purchases as often as households' own past trips, synthetic group differences correlate with real ones twice as strongly as a trained regression, and without fitting VLM shoppers reproduce alcohol purchases by gender and age in Russia and trip sizes by store distance in Taiwan; on ShelfSight VLMs keep product preferences across views and respond to price, but show a preference for letter A and for certain image positions.
AI.conclusion: VLMs can act as good synthetic shoppers once answer effects are removed, since their corrected shelf choices reflect product preferences.

title: Preconditioned Implicit Midpoint Langevin Sampling for Non-Smooth Bayesian Imaging
summary: We introduce P-IMLA, a preconditioned implicit-midpoint Langevin sampler for high-dimensional log-concave targets with non-smooth regularization. The obstruction is that the large steps enabled by matrix preconditioning are precisely where preconditioned Euler-Maruyama inflates stationary variance. Implicit midpoint removes this surplus via a Cayley-transform identity, making P-IMLA Gaussian-exact at any step size. Beyond Gaussians, whitening transfers the sharp IMLA contraction rate to $\kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and backward-error analysis gives drift-only rather than Euler-type diffusion bias under explicit smoothness assumptions. An $M$-norm Moreau envelope yields a proximal non-smooth variant with a three-term error budget. Controlled Gaussian and TV-regularized imaging experiments confirm the predicted separation: the unpreconditioned midpoint scheme retains long transients as $\kappa_f$ grows, whereas P-IMLA remains $\kappa_{\mathrm{eff}}$-governed and near variance-exact.

AI.tldr: P-IMLA is a preconditioned implicit-midpoint Langevin sampler for high-dimensional log-concave targets with non-smooth regularization that is Gaussian-exact at any step size and avoids the variance inflation of preconditioned Euler-Maruyama.
AI.motivation: Matrix preconditioning enables large steps in Langevin sampling, but in exactly that regime preconditioned Euler-Maruyama inflates the stationary variance.
AI.method: Implicit midpoint removes the surplus variance through a Cayley-transform identity, whitening transfers the IMLA contraction rate to an effective condition number, backward-error analysis gives drift-only bias under explicit smoothness assumptions, and an M-norm Moreau envelope yields a proximal non-smooth variant with a three-term error budget.
AI.result: In controlled Gaussian and TV-regularized imaging experiments, the unpreconditioned midpoint scheme keeps long transients as the condition number grows, whereas P-IMLA remains governed by the effective condition number and is near variance-exact.
AI.conclusion: Preconditioning combined with the implicit midpoint scheme gives a stable, variance-accurate sampler for non-smooth Bayesian imaging, with the predicted separation confirmed in experiments.

title: QCVS: Question-Contrastive Visual Steering for Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Inference-time steering in vision-language models often entangles query-relevant reasoning dynamics with low-level perceptual noise, causing collateral degradation on correct predictions. We propose Question-Contrastive Visual Steering (QCVS) to isolate task-specific intervention directions via double-differential activation probing. By contrasting spatial layout perturbations under the target query against a generic description reference, QCVS cancels task-agnostic visual artifacts without ground-truth supervision. A dual-threshold gating mechanism then evaluates relative interaction strength and signal amplitude, selectively applying a single bounded hidden-state update only when necessary. Empirical evaluations across multiple scales of Qwen3.5 (2B to 9B) and DeepSeek-VL2 on DynaMath and We-Math demonstrate that QCVS achieves state-of-the-art accuracy gains under sparse coverage (approximately 22%-30%). Crucially, QCVS yields repair rates up to 13.98% while suppressing collateral damage down to 0.41%, proving high intervention precision and computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: QCVS isolates task-specific steering directions for vision-language models by contrasting query-conditioned and generic description references, and applies a single bounded hidden-state update only when a dual-threshold gate deems it necessary, yielding accuracy gains of about 22 to 30 percent under sparse coverage with collateral damage of 0.41 percent.
AI.motivation: Inference-time steering of vision-language models mixes query-relevant reasoning with low-level perceptual noise, which degrades predictions that were already correct.
AI.method: QCVS uses double-differential activation probing that contrasts spatial layout perturbations under the target query against a generic description reference to cancel task-agnostic artifacts without ground-truth supervision, then gates the intervention with dual thresholds on relative interaction strength and signal amplitude.
AI.result: On DynaMath and We-Math with several Qwen3.5 scales (2B to 9B) and DeepSeek-VL2, QCVS achieves accuracy gains of approximately 22 to 30 percent under sparse coverage, repair rates up to 13.98 percent, and collateral damage down to 0.41 percent.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that query-contrastive gating gives high intervention precision and computational efficiency for multimodal reasoning steering, with the reported gains limited to the evaluated models and benchmarks.

title: Stochastic Deep Supervision for Gallery-Consistent Early-Exit Face Recognition
summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) perform strongly in face recognition (FR), yet their fixed-depth inference limits deployment in resource-constrained settings. We propose SD-ViT, a training framework that gives a usable exit at every block depth by making every depth produce discriminative embeddings, for budget-selected fixed-depth exits. Standard ViTs supervise intermediate layers only through backpropagation, so their intermediate representations are not directly optimized to form usable identity embeddings. SD-ViT adds a stochastic auxiliary signal: at each iteration a randomly selected intermediate block is passed through the same embedding head as the final layer and trained with a weighted margin-penalty softmax loss. The objective is thus stochastically sampled deep supervision through a shared classifier. Because both loss terms share that head and classifier, intermediate tokens are trained to map into the same embedding space as final-layer tokens. This matters for FR, where matching is by similarity: a probe processed at an early exit can be compared directly against full-depth gallery embeddings, with no gallery recomputation or adaptation layers. On established benchmarks, SD-ViT stays within 0.4 IJB-C points of the same backbone trained conventionally at full depth, while its early-exit probes recover over 96% of their own full-depth performance at 50% of the computational cost without modifying the reference gallery. A single verification threshold calibrated at full depth remains usable from quarter depth onward.

AI.tldr: SD-ViT trains a Vision Transformer for face recognition with a stochastic auxiliary loss so that every depth yields embeddings in the final embedding space, allowing early-exit probes to be matched directly against full-depth galleries while staying within 0.4 IJB-C points of the conventionally trained model.
AI.motivation: Fixed-depth Vision Transformers limit face recognition deployment in resource-constrained settings, and intermediate layers of standard ViTs are not directly optimized to produce usable identity embeddings.
AI.method: At each iteration a randomly selected intermediate block is passed through the same embedding head and classifier as the final layer and trained with a weighted margin-penalty softmax loss, so intermediate tokens map into the same embedding space as final-layer tokens.
AI.result: SD-ViT stays within 0.4 IJB-C points of the same backbone trained conventionally at full depth, and its early-exit probes recover over 96 percent of their full-depth performance at 50 percent of the computational cost without modifying the gallery; a verification threshold calibrated at full depth remains usable from quarter depth onward.
AI.conclusion: Stochastic deep supervision through a shared classifier makes early exits usable for face recognition without gallery recomputation or adaptation layers.

title: Retrieval-Grounded Multi-View Reasoning for Clinically Reliable Radiology Report Generation
summary: Chest radiograph report generation is hampered by retrieved reports that resemble the current image but are clinically inconsistent with it, and by diagnostic-label imbalance. We present RG-MVR, a retrieval-grounded framework comprising Retrieval-Augmented Evidence Grounding, which combines dense memory summaries with visually gated sparse retrieved evidence; Adaptive Multi-view Evidential Reasoning, which weights image, memory, and retrieved evidence per case; and a Clinical Prompt Learner, which models finding mention separately from positive, negative, or uncertain status. On MIMIC-CXR, RG-MVR achieved a clinical-label F1 of 0.483 and a BLEU-4 of 0.118 (IU X-ray: 0.202 and 0.110). In an exploratory external cohort of 22 examinations, clinical-label agreement declined markedly (F1, 0.071) and unsupported statements remained common, although physicians found fewer unsupported temporal comparisons (9 vs. 20 cases) and device-related statements (7 vs. 15) than with the baseline. Evidence-aware retrieval and structured diagnostic prompting may reduce specific reporting errors, but broader external validation is required.

AI.tldr: RG-MVR combines memory summaries, visually gated sparse retrieved evidence, adaptive multi-view evidential reasoning and a clinical prompt learner for chest radiograph report generation, reaching a clinical-label F1 of 0.483 on MIMIC-CXR but showing markedly lower agreement in a 22-examination external cohort.
AI.motivation: Retrieved reports for chest radiograph report generation can resemble the current image while being clinically inconsistent with it, and diagnostic labels are imbalanced.
AI.method: RG-MVR uses Retrieval-Augmented Evidence Grounding that combines dense memory summaries with visually gated sparse retrieved evidence, Adaptive Multi-view Evidential Reasoning that weights image, memory and retrieved evidence per case, and a Clinical Prompt Learner that models finding mention separately from positive, negative or uncertain status.
AI.result: On MIMIC-CXR the model achieves a clinical-label F1 of 0.483 and BLEU-4 of 0.118 (IU X-ray: 0.202 and 0.110); in an exploratory external cohort of 22 examinations clinical-label F1 falls to 0.071 and unsupported statements remain common, although physicians found fewer unsupported temporal comparisons (9 vs. 20 cases) and device-related statements (7 vs. 15) than with the baseline.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-aware retrieval and structured diagnostic prompting may reduce specific reporting errors, but broader external validation is required before the approach can be relied on.

title: SurvAD: How Anomalies Survive Diffusion Reconstruction
summary: Diffusion-based anomaly detectors reconstruct a test image towards normality, yet how much of an anomaly survives, its leak, remains uncharacterized. We show that a first-order deterministic sampler obeys an exact recursion along the anomaly, whose continuous limit is a survival law. The anomaly decays exponentially as the noise falls, at a rate set by the retention $r$, the share the model keeps on the states it visits. Because $r$ depends on the noise level and not on the step count, one measured path predicts the leak of other step counts, samplers and schedules from a nearby start to within a few hundredths, on four diffusion models and real defects. The law also shows that the leak's growth over steps is exposure bias and that normal details obey the same law, so changing the path or the training trades leak for detail error. We introduce SurvAD, which fine-tunes the reconstructor on inference-like starts and fits a comparator that adds evidence to the residual map without suppressing its ranking elsewhere. For under $2\%$ more inference time, SurvAD raises the multi-class pixel average precision (P-AP) of DeCo-Diff from $76.8$ to $80.7$ on MVTec AD and from $57.5$ to $60.0$ on VisA. It matches CostFilter-AD on the same reconstructor with $9\times$ fewer trainable parameters and, under Dinomaly's protocol, exceeds its reported P-AP on Dinomaly on both benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Shows that the leak of an anomaly through a diffusion-based reconstruction follows an exponential survival law set by a retention rate, and proposes SurvAD, which fine-tunes the reconstructor and adds a residual comparator to raise pixel-level AP on MVTec AD and VisA.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based anomaly detectors reconstruct test images towards normality, but how much of an anomaly survives this reconstruction, its leak, has not been characterized.
AI.method: The authors derive an exact recursion for a first-order deterministic sampler along the anomaly, whose continuous limit is a survival law governed by a retention rate that depends on the noise level and not the step count. SurvAD fine-tunes the reconstructor on inference-like starting points and fits a comparator that adds evidence to the residual map without suppressing its ranking elsewhere.
AI.result: One measured path predicts the leak for other step counts, samplers and schedules to within a few hundredths on four diffusion models. For under 2% more inference time, SurvAD raises DeCo-Diff multi-class pixel AP from 76.8 to 80.7 on MVTec AD and from 57.5 to 60.0 on VisA, matches CostFilter-AD with 9x fewer trainable parameters, and exceeds Dinomaly's reported P-AP on both benchmarks under Dinomaly's protocol.
AI.conclusion: Leak growth over steps is exposure bias, and normal details obey the same law, so changing the sampling path or the training trades leak against detail error; the law gives a principled handle on that trade-off.

title: Quality-Governed Deep Learning Network for Brain Tumor MRI Segmentation
summary: The segmentation of brain tumors from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an essential step for computer-aided neuro-oncology, treatment planning and follow-up. While effective encoder-decoder representations are achieved by U-Net and Attention U-Net, the skip sections of the network can generate weak-contrast or noisy responses in the case of heterogeneous boundaries of the tumor. In this paper, we introduce a Quality-Governed Deep Learning Network (QGDL-Net) that can be used for binary tumor segmentation from FLAIR MRI slices. The proposed model is able to predict the slice quality based on contrast and SNR statistics and to fine-tune the encoder features prior to decoding by learnable quality gates. We used the 80:20 train-validation split for experiments with BraTS 2021. QGDL-Net achieved a Dice of 0.9747, IoU of 0.9506, precision of 0.9755, recall of 0.9739, F1 of 0.9747 and accuracy of 0.9982, outperforming U-Net and Attention U-Net. The EigenCAM maps and segmentation overlays provide better tumor localization and interpretable activation around the lesion regions.

AI.tldr: Proposes QGDL-Net, which predicts slice quality from contrast and SNR statistics and uses learnable quality gates to refine encoder features before decoding, reaching a Dice of 0.9747 for binary tumor segmentation on FLAIR MRI from BraTS 2021.
AI.motivation: U-Net and Attention U-Net skip connections can generate weak-contrast or noisy responses when tumor boundaries are heterogeneous.
AI.method: The quality-governed network estimates slice quality from contrast and SNR statistics and applies learnable quality gates that fine-tune encoder features before decoding, trained with an 80:20 train-validation split.
AI.result: On BraTS 2021 it reaches Dice 0.9747, IoU 0.9506, precision 0.9755, recall 0.9739, F1 0.9747 and accuracy 0.9982, outperforming U-Net and Attention U-Net; EigenCAM maps and segmentation overlays are reported to give better tumor localization.
AI.conclusion: Quality-gated feature refinement is presented as a way to improve tumor segmentation and interpretability on MRI slices, with gains reported over both baselines.

title: Optimized Car Damage Detection Using CNN and Object Detection Model
summary: Car damage detection systems play a vital role in scenarios, like the insurance claims process, accident reporting systems, or a documented write-up of the various damages a vehicle in a car garage exhibits upon entry and exit. This paper presents a two-fold model architecture encompassing a convolutional neural network used to classify the collected input samples as clear or damaged, thereby filtering out the undamaged images, before the input is passed on to the object detection layer for further localization and classification of defects into Scratch, Dent, Glass Shatter, and Smash. A deviation from the focus of related work, this paper poses the use of unified models while applying transfer learning techniques to augment performance that caters to multiple use cases. The design of this model has been made to optimize performance by incorporating the two models to streamline the processing of input samples. The model boasts significant performance with accuracies of 98% for the CNN layer and 0.5 mAP for the object detection layer. However, the metric for the object detection layer seems to understate its performance due to reasons discussed within the paper.

AI.tldr: Combines a CNN that filters out undamaged car images with an object detector that localizes and classifies Scratch, Dent, Glass Shatter and Smash, reporting 98% CNN accuracy and 0.5 mAP for the detection layer.
AI.motivation: Car damage detection for insurance claims, accident reporting and garage inspection needs both to filter clean images and to localize defect types, and prior work often addresses these separately.
AI.method: A two-stage architecture uses a CNN to classify inputs as clear or damaged and passes only the damaged images to an object detection layer; transfer learning is applied so that unified models serve multiple use cases.
AI.result: The CNN reaches 98% accuracy and the object detection layer reaches 0.5 mAP; the authors argue the detection metric understates performance for reasons discussed in the paper.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage cascade is presented as a practical way to streamline damage assessment across use cases, although the detection score may understate its true performance.

title: Reliability-Aware Benchmarking of Self-Supervised Learning in Histopathology Under 1-10% Label Regimes
