comment: Oral presentation, CIBB 2026 (21st International Conference on Computational Intelligence Methods for Bioinformatics and Biostatistics, Rome, Italy). 6 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Expert annotation in digital pathology is expensive, and low-label regimes remain common in realistic histopathology workflows. Self-supervised learning (SSL) offers a practical way to learn transferable representations from unlabeled pathology images, but performance-only evaluation can hide unreliable confidence behavior under domain shift. We present a reliability-aware benchmark of SimCLR, BYOL, and an MAE-inspired masked-reconstruction baseline on PatchCamelyon (PCam; 96x96) and PANDA (prostate cancer) under 1%, 5%, and 10% labeled regimes with frozen-encoder linear probing. To address common single-run concerns, ResNet-18 results are repeated over 3 splits x 3 seeds (n=9) and ViT-B/16 over 1 split x 3 seeds (n=3) under practical compute constraints, with mean+/-std reporting and per-run logs. Beyond AUROC, accuracy, and F1-score, we report Expected Calibration Error and Brier score, OOD confidence diagnostics for cross-dataset PCam<->PANDA scoring, federated-vs-centralized SimCLR comparisons on PCam, and cross-dataset transfer to colorectal histology tiles. SSL improves label efficiency on the more controlled PCam task, while PANDA's noisier patch-level proxy can remain near coin-flip with higher variance. The study highlights that histopathology SSL should be assessed not only by ranking performance but also by calibration, robustness, and transparent reproducibility diagnostics before clinical interpretation.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks SimCLR, BYOL and an MAE-inspired baseline on PatchCamelyon and PANDA under 1%, 5% and 10% labels, assessing calibration, OOD confidence and transfer alongside accuracy.
AI.motivation: Performance-only evaluation of self-supervised learning in histopathology can hide unreliable confidence under domain shift, while expert annotation in pathology is expensive.
AI.method: Frozen-encoder linear probing, with ResNet-18 repeated over 3 splits x 3 seeds (n=9) and ViT-B/16 over 1 split x 3 seeds (n=3), reporting AUROC, accuracy, F1, Expected Calibration Error, Brier score, OOD confidence diagnostics, federated versus centralized SimCLR, and transfer to colorectal histology tiles.
AI.result: SSL improves label efficiency on the more controlled PCam task, while PANDA's noisier patch-level proxy can remain near coin-flip with higher variance.
AI.conclusion: Histopathology SSL should be assessed by calibration, robustness and reproducibility diagnostics as well as ranking performance before clinical interpretation.

title: MATA: Motion-aligned Temporal Adapter
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027. Joint first authors with equal contributions. Code - this https URL
summary: Few-shot fine-grained video action recognition requires recognizing novel action classes from only a few labeled examples. The difficulty is that visually similar actions often share actors, scenes, poses, and objects, differing only in the order, timing, and short duration of motion changes. We study this problem under three practical constraints: few tunable parameters, low compute cost, and use of the video modality alone. We propose Motion-aligned Temporal Adapter (MATA), a parameter-efficient adapter on top of a frozen CLIP backbone. MATA specializes CLIP features along the temporal dimension using two components: temporal phase alignment through learnable temporal positional embeddings, and a local motion transition operator through depth-wise convolution. With only ~3.6M tunable parameters, MATA achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple fine-grained benchmarks while remaining robust to both visual corruptions and temporal disruptions induced by frame dropping. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: Introduces MATA, a parameter-efficient temporal adapter on a frozen CLIP backbone for few-shot fine-grained video action recognition, with about 3.6M tunable parameters and state-of-the-art results across several benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Visually similar actions share actors, scenes, poses and objects and differ mainly in the order, timing and short duration of motion changes, under constraints of few tunable parameters, low compute and video-only input.
AI.method: MATA adds temporal phase alignment through learnable temporal positional embeddings and a local motion transition operator implemented as a depth-wise convolution on CLIP features.
AI.result: It achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple fine-grained benchmarks and stays robust to visual corruptions and to temporal disruption from frame dropping.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight temporal specialization of a frozen image-language backbone is sufficient for fine-grained few-shot action recognition under the stated constraints.

title: EarthJev: Efficient Visual Evidence Acquisition and Decision for UHR Remote Sensing Understanding
summary: Ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing visual question answering (VQA) requires locating fine-grained evidence in large scenes under limited visual input budgets. Active observation addresses this challenge through selective exploration, but repeated generative judgments can make region search costly. Its decisions also concern distinct prediction targets: spatial pointer validity, evidence presence, and reasoning correctness. We propose EarthJev, a framework that separates region scoring from answer generation and uses target-specific decision signals while keeping the answering model frozen. A spatial pointer verifier uses visual and geometric cues to guide exploration or bypass search. An evidence-aware decision mechanism scores compact candidate views in batches using a lightweight head on frozen representations, without generating textual region judgments. Format-specific confidence calibration then guides selection between candidate answers generated from memory and overview presentations of the acquired evidence. Across five benchmarks, EarthJev achieves a mean accuracy of 53.06% with Qwen3.5-9B, outperforming ZoomSearch with the same answering model by 2.33 to 14.73 percentage points per benchmark while reducing mean latency from 11.30 - 1.67 seconds per question. With four additional frozen answering models, model-specific fitting of the decision modules and calibration mappings yields mean accuracy gains of 3.41 - 6.53 percentage points over the corresponding single-pass baselines. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: Proposes EarthJev, which separates region scoring from answer generation for ultra-high-resolution remote sensing VQA, reaching 53.06% mean accuracy with Qwen3.5-9B while cutting latency relative to ZoomSearch.
AI.motivation: Active observation for UHR remote sensing VQA makes repeated generative region judgments costly, and its decisions target distinct quantities: spatial pointer validity, evidence presence and reasoning correctness.
AI.method: A spatial pointer verifier uses visual and geometric cues to guide exploration or bypass search, and an evidence-aware decision mechanism scores compact candidate views in batches with a lightweight head on frozen representations. Format-specific confidence calibration chooses between answers generated from memory and answers from overview presentations of the acquired evidence, while the answering model stays frozen.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks EarthJev averages 53.06% accuracy with Qwen3.5-9B, beating ZoomSearch with the same model by 2.33 to 14.73 points per benchmark and reducing mean latency from 11.30 to 1.67 seconds per question. With four other frozen answering models, fitted decision modules and calibration give gains of 3.41 to 6.53 points over single-pass baselines.
AI.conclusion: Target-specific decision signals on frozen models offer an efficient alternative to generative region search for UHR visual question answering.

title: Representation Learning for 3D Brain Imaging: A Benchmark
summary: Many deep learning architectures for computer vision tasks rely on features extracted by a pre-trained encoder on large databases of natural 2D RGB images. However, the wide domain gap with medical images hampers the direct transfer of optimized deep learning models from computer vision to clinical applications. Recently, self-supervised pre-training and foundation models emerged as promising alternatives to mitigate these limitations. Yet, constructing such models for medical imaging faces critical challenges, including designing and adapting training strategies for large 3D volume datasets, and the need for standardized benchmarks to evaluate feature extraction performance. In this study, we propose an extensive comparison of vision encoders with a focus on 3D brain MRI. First, we consider 8 fully and self-supervised models pretrained on natural images (e.g. ResNet, DINO, CLIP) and 10 backbone architectures trained on medical images, either based on supervised (e.g. RadImageNet) or self-supervised (e.g. BiomedCLIP, SimCLR) tasks. All pre-trained encoders are evaluated on various downstream tasks to assess the representation power of their latent representations, including age and sex prediction as well as disease classification on the ADNI and PPMI datasets. Our study shows that 2D encoders pre-trained on natural images perform the most favorably, even compared to models pre-trained on more than 100k brain MRI volumes, highlighting the need for more suitable and robust methods for representation learning in 3D medical imaging. The source code for this study is publicly available at: https: //github.com/PierreFalconnier/brain-representation-benchmark.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks 8 natural-image encoders and 10 medical-image encoders on 3D brain MRI and finds that 2D encoders pretrained on natural images perform most favourably.
AI.motivation: The domain gap between natural and medical images, and the large size of 3D volumes, hinder direct transfer of pretrained models, and standardized benchmarks for 3D medical feature extraction are lacking.
AI.method: Compares 18 encoders, including self-supervised and fully supervised natural-image models such as ResNet, DINO and CLIP, and medical backbones trained with supervised methods such as RadImageNet or self-supervised methods such as BiomedCLIP and SimCLR. The frozen latent representations are evaluated on age and sex prediction and disease classification on ADNI and PPMI.
AI.result: 2D encoders pretrained on natural images perform most favourably, even compared with models pretrained on more than 100k brain MRI volumes.
AI.conclusion: More suitable and robust representation learning methods are needed for 3D medical imaging; the source code is publicly released.

title: Nanopath: Fast, Fair, Open Experimentation for Pathology Foundation Models
comment: 17 pages, 2 figures, 10 tables. NeurIPS 2026 workshop: AI at Scale for Clinical Impact: Cancer Pathology Foundation Models
summary: We introduce nanopath, an open-source framework and benchmark for rapidly training and evaluating small-scale pathology foundation models. Using a single H100 GPU, a typical nanopath model trains in a little over an hour on up to one million TCGA pathology tile presentations and evaluates within 25 minutes on a broad suite of tile-level and slide-level tasks. Nanopath enables rapid exploration of research ideas at small scale, so promising training recipes can subsequently be tested with more data and compute. To enable fair comparisons between ideas, we constrain submissions to fixed data and compute budgets while keeping the downstream evaluation protocol fixed. Anyone may clone the codebase, automatically download the data, reproduce or modify existing models, and submit a run to Labless, our public experiment ledger where researchers and AI agents can search through prior attempts. Since its public release in June 2026, nanopath has received 1,269 experiments from 20 contributors. Here, we detail its design and assess how well its rapid evaluation tracks standardized THUNDER, HEST, and PathoBench (CPTAC) benchmarks across six nanopath and 14 reference foundation models. Nanopath's fast evaluation suite strongly tracked these standardized benchmarks, and a few 22M parameter nanopath models even outperformed giant 1.1B parameter models on a subset of downstream tasks. We subsequently discuss how we have since optimized nanopath's evaluation suite to be an even more faithful, quick proxy for external benchmarking. Nanopath provides an accessible testbed for students, researchers, and AI agents to explore pathology foundation modeling through fair, transparent, and directly comparable experiments.

AI.tldr: Introduces nanopath, an open-source framework and benchmark for training and evaluating small pathology foundation models under fixed data and compute budgets, and shows that its fast evaluation tracks standardized benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Comparing pathology foundation models fairly and quickly is hard when experiments are large and their protocols vary, so researchers need a small-scale, reproducible testbed.
AI.method: A single H100 trains a typical model in a little over an hour on up to one million TCGA tile presentations and evaluates within 25 minutes on tile-level and slide-level tasks. Submissions are constrained to fixed data and compute budgets with a fixed downstream protocol, and runs are recorded in the public Labless experiment ledger.
AI.result: The fast evaluation strongly tracks THUNDER, HEST and PathoBench (CPTAC) across six nanopath and 14 reference foundation models, and some 22M-parameter nanopath models outperform 1.1B-parameter models on a subset of downstream tasks. Since its June 2026 release, nanopath has received 1,269 experiments from 20 contributors.
AI.conclusion: Nanopath gives students, researchers and AI agents an accessible testbed for pathology foundation modeling, and its evaluation suite has since been optimized as a more faithful quick proxy for external benchmarks.

title: Beyond Hash Matching: AI-Based Detection of Previously Unidentified CSAM and its Legal Implications in the EU
summary: The detection of previously unidentified Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) remains a significant challenge for law enforcement authorities, online service providers, and child protection organizations, as traditional hash-matching technologies are primarily designed to identify previously verified material. This paper reviews and classifies existing AI-based technologies that could complement hash-based approaches and support the detection, analysis, and prioritization of potentially harmful content. The reviewed approaches are organized into three categories: real-time image and video analysis, image and video classification and tagging, and AI-based behavioral monitoring. A comparative analysis examines the capabilities, limitations, and potential integration of general-purpose computer vision platforms, content moderation services, and specialized CSAM detection tools within existing detection workflows. An experimental evaluation was conducted using Google Cloud Vision AI and Sightengine to investigate sexual-content classification and child-adult age estimation. The results highlight differences in classification taxonomies and outputs across providers, as well as significant limitations in age classification, particularly for adolescents. These findings highlight the importance of using AI-based assessments as complementary tools for analysis and prioritization, rather than as definitive determination of CSAM. Finally, the paper examines the relevant European Union regulatory framework, with particular attention to the EU AI Act, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), fundamental rights, transparency, accountability, and human oversight. The legal analysis highlights how regulatory obligations and safeguards may differ depending on the deployment context, potentially creating inconsistencies across interconnected detection and reporting workflows.

AI.tldr: Reviews AI-based technologies that could complement hash matching for detecting previously unidentified CSAM, tests Google Cloud Vision AI and Sightengine on sexual-content classification and age estimation, and analyzes the EU legal framework.
AI.motivation: Hash matching identifies only material that has already been verified, so law enforcement and online providers need complementary AI detection that also fits the legal framework.
AI.method: The reviewed approaches fall into real-time image and video analysis, image and video classification and tagging, and AI-based behavioural monitoring. The paper compares general-purpose vision platforms, content moderation services and specialized tools, runs an experimental evaluation with Google Cloud Vision AI and Sightengine, and analyzes the EU AI Act, GDPR, fundamental rights, transparency, accountability and human oversight.
AI.result: Providers differ in classification taxonomies and outputs, and age classification, particularly for adolescents, shows significant limitations.
AI.conclusion: AI assessments should complement rather than replace determination by humans, and regulatory obligations and safeguards may differ by deployment context, potentially creating inconsistencies across detection and reporting workflows.

title: GMD-Mamba: Lightweight 3D Medical Image Segmentation Using a Grouped Multi-Directional Mamba
comment: It is a four pages paper with 2 figures and submitted to ISBI2027
summary: Mamba has the capability to capture global context in linear time for 3D medical image segmentation. However, existing methods employ Mamba with full-width directional scans at every resolution, keeping the model large (64-138M parameters and high FLOPs). We propose Grouped Multi-Directional (GMD) Mamba, a lightweight network based on the GMD scan that divides input channels $C$ into groups $G$ and flattens each group in different directions in one pass. This gives multi-directional context at $O(C^2/G)$ instead of $O(K \cdot C^2)$, where $K$ is the number of scan directions. Additionally, we employ Mamba only at the deepest encoder stages, resulting in 19.2M parameters. On BraTS2023, it achieves the best average Dice of 92.0% and the lowest HD95 of 2.7 at $\sim$1/7 the parameters of SegMamba-V2. For model validation, we also ran experiments on the MSD Spleen dataset, achieving competitive performance. The implementation details and code are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes GMD-Mamba, a lightweight 3D medical segmentation network built on Grouped Multi-Directional Mamba scans, reaching 92.0% average Dice on BraTS2023 with 19.2M parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing Mamba segmentation models use full-width directional scans at every resolution, which keeps them large at 64-138M parameters with high FLOPs.
AI.method: The GMD scan divides the input channels into groups and flattens each group in a different direction in one pass, giving multi-directional context at O(C^2/G) instead of O(K*C^2) for K scan directions. Mamba is used only at the deepest encoder stages.
AI.result: On BraTS2023 it achieves the best average Dice of 92.0% and the lowest HD95 of 2.7 at about one-seventh the parameters of SegMamba-V2; it is competitive on MSD Spleen.
AI.conclusion: Grouped multi-directional scanning with selective placement of Mamba blocks gives a much smaller model that still reaches the best reported Dice in the experiments.

title: Ultra-Lightweight 3D Medical Image Segmentation via Knowledge Distillation in Label-Scarce Domains
comment: This is a four pages paper having 3 figures and is submitted to ISBI2027
summary: Mamba is a neural network architecture that reduces computational complexity, and has been shown to be effective for 3D medical image segmentation. However, existing models still remain computationally expensive. We propose compressing Mamba by distillation while achieving competitive performance. Specifically, we demonstrate compression of a 139M-parameter SegMamba-V2 teacher into a lightweight TinyUNet3D student with about 0.96M parameters, achieving about 145$\times$ compression with a performance drop of just over one Dice point. We further investigate the utility of knowledge distillation in a range of data-labeling scenarios under identical experimental settings, and show that its advantage is most prominent when labeled data is scarce. To demonstrate the generalizability of our approach, experiments are conducted on three datasets: BraTS 2023, MSD Spleen and MSD Hippocampus. The code for TinyUNet3D is publicly available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Distills a 139M-parameter SegMamba-V2 teacher into a 0.96M-parameter TinyUNet3D student, about 145x compression at a cost of just over one Dice point, and shows that distillation helps most when labels are scarce.
AI.motivation: Mamba-based 3D segmentation models remain computationally expensive, and the value of distillation under different labeling conditions has not been established.
AI.method: Knowledge distillation from SegMamba-V2 to TinyUNet3D, with experiments under identical settings across a range of data-labeling scenarios on BraTS 2023, MSD Spleen and MSD Hippocampus.
AI.result: The student achieves about 145x compression with a Dice drop of just over one point, and the advantage of distillation is most prominent when labeled data is scarce.
AI.conclusion: Distillation is a practical route to lightweight 3D segmentation, particularly in label-scarce domains, and the TinyUNet3D code is publicly available.

title: REFORM-3D: A Representation-Centric Evaluation Framework for 3D Medical Vision Foundation Models
comment: 32 pages, 6 figures, Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 ED Track
summary: Evaluation of 3D medical foundation models is typically dominated by downstream task scores, which entangle representation quality with adaptation choices. This is especially critical in volumetric imaging, where spacing and anisotropy can substantially alter image statistics while the anatomy itself remains unchanged. We therefore introduce \textbf{REFORM-3D}, a \textbf{R}epresentation-centric \textbf{E}valuation \textbf{F}ramew\textbf{OR}k for benchmarking frozen 3D medical vision foundation \textbf{M}odels across three questions: Acquisition Robustness, asking whether features remain stable when spacing varies while anatomy is fixed; Cross-Modal Anatomical Alignment, asking whether labeled anatomical structures remain recoverable across modalities under balanced bidirectional retrieval; and Anatomical Transfer, asking whether organ identity remains recoverable from limited labeled support under case-disjoint evaluation. These are also pretraining questions, because what a 3D encoder learns depends on how volumes are geometrically presented during self-supervised pretraining. We further introduce Med3DINO encoder family, pretrained on $62.6$K unlabeled MR, CT, PET, CTA, and CBCT volumes under three explicit geometric assumptions: isotropic normalization, voxel-relative sampling, and spacing-aware resampling. Across Med3DINO and heterogeneous external encoders, REFORM-3D reveals module-specific strengths rather than a single model ordering. Within the controlled Med3DINO comparison, voxel-relative sampling yields lower embedding drift, whereas spacing-aware resampling favors anatomical transfer; semantic-transfer advantages depend on the dataset and feature type. Project link: \href{this https URL}{\highlightLR{REFORM-3D}}.

AI.tldr: Introduces REFORM-3D, a representation-centric framework that evaluates frozen 3D medical vision foundation models on acquisition robustness, cross-modal anatomical alignment and anatomical transfer, together with the Med3DINO encoder family pretrained under three geometric assumptions.
AI.motivation: Downstream task scores entangle representation quality with adaptation choices, and in volumetric imaging spacing and anisotropy can change image statistics while the anatomy stays the same.
AI.method: Three probes: acquisition robustness when spacing varies with anatomy fixed, cross-modal anatomical alignment under balanced bidirectional retrieval, and anatomical transfer from limited labeled support under case-disjoint evaluation. Med3DINO is pretrained on 62.6K unlabeled MR, CT, PET, CTA and CBCT volumes under isotropic normalization, voxel-relative sampling, or spacing-aware resampling.
AI.result: REFORM-3D reveals module-specific strengths rather than a single model ordering. Within the Med3DINO comparison, voxel-relative sampling yields lower embedding drift while spacing-aware resampling favours anatomical transfer, and semantic-transfer advantages depend on dataset and feature type.
AI.conclusion: The geometric presentation of volumes during self-supervised pretraining shapes what a 3D encoder learns, so representation evaluation should cover these pretraining questions.

title: VLM as an Editing Pilot: VLM-Steered Velocity Control for Flow-Based Image Editing
summary: Text-guided image editing requires realizing the requested semantic change while preserving content unrelated to the instruction. FlowEdit provides an efficient inversion-free solution, but its source-anchored coupling can become overly restrictive, causing zero-edit, where the output remains close to the source and the requested change fails to emerge. We find that source coupling directly governs the preservation--editing trade-off, while a fixed coupling schedule cannot adapt to timestep-specific editing needs. Motivated by this observation, we propose V2C-Edit, a training-free VLM-steered velocity control framework. V2C-Edit constructs complementary coupling-controlled velocities and dynamically selects among them using Instruction-Level Similarity (ILS), which evaluates whether the predicted transformation follows the editing instruction. Adaptive spatial masking further preserves regions unrelated to the edit. Experiments on MagicBrush and PIE-Bench with FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3 show that V2C-Edit consistently improves instruction alignment over FlowEdit while maintaining competitive structural preservation, and that ILS better reflects editing effectiveness than target-caption CLIP similarity. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes V2C-Edit, a training-free framework that uses a VLM-based Instruction-Level Similarity score to select among coupling-controlled velocities in flow-based image editing, improving instruction alignment over FlowEdit.
AI.motivation: FlowEdit's source-anchored coupling can cause zero-edit, where the output stays close to the source and the requested change fails to appear, and a fixed coupling schedule cannot adapt to timestep-specific editing needs.
AI.method: The method constructs complementary coupling-controlled velocities and dynamically selects among them using Instruction-Level Similarity, which evaluates whether the predicted transformation follows the editing instruction. Adaptive spatial masking preserves regions unrelated to the edit.
AI.result: On MagicBrush and PIE-Bench with FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3, V2C-Edit consistently improves instruction alignment over FlowEdit while staying competitive on structural preservation, and ILS reflects editing effectiveness better than target-caption CLIP similarity.
AI.conclusion: Timestep-adaptive selection of coupling through instruction-level evaluation addresses the preservation-editing trade-off in training-free flow-based editing.

title: Adapting Frozen Promptable Segmenters to User-Defined Taxonomies via Few-Shot Proposal Learning
summary: Promptable segmenters of the SAM family turn a click or a phrase into an instance mask, so the costly part of a label is now its class. However, each annotation project draws its own class boundary, often through objects these models already know: people from cars, sedans from trucks, one sedan model from another. A generic model's boundary is fixed by its training vocabulary. We present SNAP, an annotation pipeline that learns the project's boundary from the labels the annotator draws anyway. On one frozen SAM2.1 pass per image, we fit a per-project head, SnapHead, that classifies every proposal and refits in seconds after each labeled image. Where SAM 3 is available, the same labels decide class by class whether to keep its boundary or ours. Given the true masks of eight look-alike cell lines, SAM 3 assigns classes at Cohen's kappa = 0.038 and SnapHead at 0.754 (60 labeled images), and when only the class names change, SAM 3 falls to chance and SnapHead's score is unchanged. End to end, with 20 labeled images, SNAP beats a SAM 3 oracle tuned on the evaluation labels on five microscopy projects (0.484 against 0.441 F1), and run unchanged on five held-out datasets, it beats SAM 3 as shipped on four. Our results suggest that frozen foundation features already encode the class boundaries a generic vocabulary misses, and that a project's own labels are enough to read them out.

AI.tldr: Presents SNAP, an annotation pipeline that learns a project-specific class boundary on top of a frozen SAM2.1 using a lightweight per-project head, SnapHead, so that a few labeled images fix class assignment for look-alike categories.
AI.motivation: Promptable segmenters of the SAM family fix class boundaries to a generic training vocabulary, while each annotation project draws its own boundary, often among objects these models already know.
AI.method: One frozen SAM2.1 pass per image produces proposals, and SnapHead classifies every proposal and is refit within seconds after each labeled image. Where SAM 3 is available, the labels decide class by class whether to keep its boundary or the learned one.
AI.result: Given the true masks of eight look-alike cell lines, SAM 3 reaches Cohen's kappa 0.038 and SnapHead 0.754 with 60 labeled images; when only the class names change, SAM 3 falls to chance while SnapHead is unchanged. With 20 labeled images, SNAP beats a SAM 3 oracle tuned on the evaluation labels on five microscopy projects (F1 0.484 against 0.441) and beats SAM 3 as shipped on four of five held-out datasets.
AI.conclusion: Frozen foundation features already encode class boundaries that a generic vocabulary misses, and a project's own labels are enough to read them out.

title: Contrastive fine-tuning against stain and scanner bias improves robustness and downstream performance across pathology foundation models
summary: Histopathology foundation models achieve strong performance across diverse downstream tasks, yet their representations have been shown to encode scanner- and site-specific biases, creating generalization gaps and potentially limiting real-world utility. We introduce SPECTRA (Scanner and Pathology Embedding Contrastive Tuning for Robust Alignment), a model-agnostic contrastive learning post-training framework which explicitly encourages scanner- and stain-robust representations, to optimize performance and generalization on downstream applications. Using parameter-efficient LoRA adapters trained on matched multi-scanner and multi-stain whole-slide images sourced from the PLISM dataset, our method aligns spatially corresponding regions across acquisition conditions (scanner, stain), using other locations within each candidate condition as negatives. SPECTRA improved PathoROB robustness index, gene-expression prediction on HEST, slide-level classification AUC on CPTAC, and held-out PLISM retrieval for every model. Overall tile-level classification on THUNDER also improved, with exceptions for segmentation and calibration tasks. We open-source our training and evaluation codebases and release adapters and model weights for selected backbones.

AI.tldr: Introduces SPECTRA, a model-agnostic contrastive post-training framework with LoRA adapters that aligns spatially corresponding regions across scanners and stains, improving robustness and downstream performance across pathology foundation models.
AI.motivation: Histopathology foundation models encode scanner- and site-specific biases, which create generalization gaps and limit real-world utility.
AI.method: Parameter-efficient LoRA adapters are trained on matched multi-scanner and multi-stain whole-slide images from PLISM. Corresponding regions across acquisition conditions serve as positives, and other locations within each candidate condition serve as negatives.
AI.result: SPECTRA improved the PathoROB robustness index, HEST gene-expression prediction, CPTAC slide-level AUC and held-out PLISM retrieval for every model. THUNDER tile-level classification also improved overall, with exceptions for segmentation and calibration tasks.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive alignment across acquisition conditions is an effective post-training step for pathology encoders, and the training and evaluation codebases, adapters and weights for selected backbones are released.

title: A Privacy-Aware Deep Learning Benchmark for Facial Emotion Recognition
summary: Facial Expression Recognition (FER) traditionally relies on raw RGB images, introducing privacy risks, sensitivity to illumination variations, and susceptibility to identity-confounding visual shortcuts. As an alternative, this work proposes a lightweight, privacy-aware pipeline using exclusively geometric representations-facial landmarks (478 points) and blendshapes (52 coefficients, ARKit standard)-eliminating persistent raw video storage. Six neural architectures trained from scratch on fused CREMA-D and RAVDESS datasets were benchmarked against an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 baseline under a 5-fold subject-independent cross-validation protocol. Geometric models consistently outperformed the pixel baseline on unseen subjects with 12-124 times fewer parameters, while demonstrating superior robustness on subtle emotional expressions such as sadness. Ablation studies reveal that blendshapes capture the primary discriminative signal, while landmarks provide essential complementary spatial topology. These results demonstrate that compact geometric representations preserve affective semantics, eliminate downstream transfer learning dependency on visual backbones, and enable efficient, privacy-aware emotion recognition.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks a privacy-aware facial emotion recognition pipeline that uses only facial landmarks and ARKit blendshapes, finding that geometric models outperform an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 on unseen subjects with 12 to 124 times fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: RGB-based facial expression recognition raises privacy risks, is sensitive to illumination, and is prone to identity-confounding visual shortcuts.
AI.method: Uses 478 facial landmarks and 52 ARKit blendshape coefficients, with six neural architectures trained from scratch on fused CREMA-D and RAVDESS and compared with an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 under 5-fold subject-independent cross-validation; ablations separate the contributions of the two representations.
AI.result: Geometric models consistently outperform the pixel baseline on unseen subjects and are more robust on subtle expressions such as sadness. Blendshapes capture the primary discriminative signal, while landmarks provide essential complementary spatial topology.
AI.conclusion: Compact geometric representations preserve affective semantics without persistent raw video storage or visual-backbone transfer learning, enabling efficient privacy-aware emotion recognition.

title: Improving the Diffusability of Motion Tokenizer
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 (Spotlight). 26 pages, including appendix
summary: Latent diffusion models paired with a variational auto-encoder (VAE) tokenizer have shown promising performance for efficient text-driven human motion generation. However, motion latent diffusion suffers from a generation-reconstruction trade-off: simply increasing tokenizer capacity enhances reconstruction but fails to proportionally improve text-conditioned generation quality. We assume this trade-off stems from a spectral mismatch inside the VAE tokenizer: the encoder yields a latent space biased toward high frequencies, and the decoder introduces temporal artifacts. In this paper, we propose the Diffusable Motion Tokenizer (DiMoT) to improve the diffusability of the tokenizer, rather than scaling up the diffusion backbone. To improve text-conditioned optimization, Critic Spectral Adaptation (CSA) leverages a pretrained diffusion model as the critic to suppress high-frequency latent energy. To preserve motion dynamics, the Alpha-Flow Motion Decoder (AMD) performs generative decoding via average-velocity prediction, enabling efficient one-step decoding. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiMoT achieves state-of-the-art performance across various challenging text-to-motion benchmarks, yielding superior motion fidelity and text-motion alignment. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes DiMoT, a motion tokenizer designed for diffusability, which uses critic-guided spectral adaptation and an average-velocity decoder to improve text-to-motion generation without scaling the diffusion backbone.
AI.motivation: Enlarging a motion VAE tokenizer improves reconstruction but not text-conditioned generation proportionally; the authors attribute this to a spectral mismatch, with a latent space biased toward high frequencies and temporal artifacts from the decoder.
AI.method: Critic Spectral Adaptation uses a pretrained diffusion model as the critic to suppress high-frequency latent energy. The Alpha-Flow Motion Decoder performs generative decoding via average-velocity prediction, enabling efficient one-step decoding.
AI.result: DiMoT achieves state-of-the-art performance across several challenging text-to-motion benchmarks, with superior motion fidelity and text-motion alignment.
AI.conclusion: Improving the diffusability of the tokenizer is presented as an alternative to scaling the diffusion backbone for latent motion generation.

title: CXR-CMFA: A Cross-Modal Feature Aggregation Network for Chest X-Ray Pathology Classification
summary: Chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation remains challenging because subtle pathology can be obscured by overlapping anatomy, image-quality variation, and limited visual evidence in isolated radiographs. Although image-only deep learning models provide useful baselines, they discard the complementary diagnostic context available in radiology reports, while large vision-language models can be computationally expensive for practical deployment. This paper presents CXR-CMFA, a lightweight cross-modal feature aggregation network for binary CXR pathology classification. The proposed framework combines a dual-stream visual encoder, using EfficientNet-B0 for global anatomical representation and DenseNet-121 for local pathological detail, with a TF-IDF-MLP report encoder. Two fusion modules integrate these modalities: the Dual-Modal Spatial Attention Module (DMSAM) uses the report embedding to gate global and local visual features, and the Cross-Modal Gated Feature Fusion (CGFF) module learns per-instance weights for visual and textual contributions. Experiments on the MIMIC-CXR benchmark, using the provided train, validation, and test splits, show that CXR-CMFA achieves 93.45% accuracy, 99.88% precision, 91.8% recall, 95.7% F1-score, and 99.19% AUC on the held-out test set. The model produces only four false positives among 984 normal test cases, supporting its suitability for high-specificity screening workflows. An ablation study further demonstrates a 22.47 percentage-point AUC improvement over the global-image-only variant, confirming the value of adaptive cross-modal fusion. These results indicate that compact report-conditioned fusion can provide strong discriminative performance without relying on large pretrained language models.

AI.tldr: Proposes CXR-CMFA, a lightweight network that fuses a dual-stream CNN visual encoder with a TF-IDF-MLP report encoder for binary chest X-ray pathology classification, reporting 93.45% accuracy and 99.19% AUC on the MIMIC-CXR test set.
AI.motivation: Image-only models discard the diagnostic context in radiology reports, while large vision-language models are computationally expensive for practical deployment.
AI.method: EfficientNet-B0 provides global anatomical representation and DenseNet-121 local pathological detail, and a TF-IDF-MLP encodes the report. The Dual-Modal Spatial Attention Module uses the report embedding to gate global and local visual features, and the Cross-Modal Gated Feature Fusion module learns per-instance weights for visual and textual contributions.
AI.result: On the held-out MIMIC-CXR test set it reaches 93.45% accuracy, 99.88% precision, 91.8% recall, 95.7% F1-score and 99.19% AUC, with only four false positives among 984 normal test cases. An ablation shows a 22.47-point AUC improvement over the global-image-only variant.
AI.conclusion: Compact report-conditioned fusion can give strong discrimination without large pretrained language models, which suits high-specificity screening workflows.

authors: Ronald L. P. D. de Jong
title: ATLAS: A Multi-Procedure Benchmark and Context-Aware Model for Surgical Anatomy Segmentation
summary: Recognizing anatomical structures during minimally invasive surgery (MIS) could support intraoperative navigation and improve patient safety, but progress is limited by small, single-procedure datasets and by segmentation methods developed for natural scenes. This work addresses both limitations through a new dataset and model. First, we introduce ATLAS-120k, a clip-level semantic segmentation dataset of 121,018 annotated frames from 100 surgical videos, covering 14 laparoscopic and robot-assisted procedures and 41 classes. Annotations were created with a pipeline that combines manual labeling, tracker-based propagation, and review by surgeons. Second, we propose ATLAS (Anatomy Recognition with Context Learning using Foundation Representations), a video semantic segmentation model for surgical anatomy recognition. ATLAS builds on in-domain foundation-model embeddings and adds context queries for the procedure and surgical phase, together with query propagation between frames for short-term memory. ATLAS outperforms state-of-the-art natural-image and in-domain foundation models in both segmentation accuracy and temporal consistency, achieving a Dice score of 0.70 with ViT-L while running in real time at 76.2 FPS. Ablations show that the context queries improve accuracy and that query propagation improves temporal consistency. ATLAS also generalizes well, matching a dedicated model zero-shot on CholecSeg8k and improving phase recognition on AutoLaparo over SurgeNet initialization. The model weights, dataset annotations, and annotation tool are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Introduces ATLAS-120k, a 121,018-frame surgical anatomy segmentation dataset spanning 14 procedures, and ATLAS, a context-aware video segmentation model that reaches a Dice of 0.70 with ViT-L at 76.2 FPS.
AI.motivation: Progress in surgical anatomy recognition is limited by small single-procedure datasets and by segmentation methods developed for natural scenes.
AI.method: ATLAS-120k is annotated by manual labeling, tracker-based propagation and surgeon review across 100 surgical videos with 41 classes. ATLAS builds on in-domain foundation-model embeddings, adds context queries for the procedure and surgical phase, and propagates queries between frames as short-term memory.
AI.result: ATLAS outperforms natural-image and in-domain foundation models in segmentation accuracy and temporal consistency, reaching a Dice of 0.70 with ViT-L at 76.2 FPS. Context queries improve accuracy and query propagation improves temporal consistency; the model matches a dedicated model zero-shot on CholecSeg8k and improves phase recognition on AutoLaparo over SurgeNet initialization.
AI.conclusion: Context-aware, memory-equipped foundation-model segmentation, together with a public dataset and annotation tool, supports practical intraoperative anatomy recognition.

title: RigidGS: Geometry-Aware Object Decoupling for Rigid-Body Interaction in 3D Gaussian Splatting
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Accepted at WACV 2027 (Applications Track). Project page: this https URL
summary: Interactive VR/MR applications demand photorealistic 3D representations that support real-time rendering and object-level manipulation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves high rendering quality, it represents scenes as unstructured, monolithic primitives. Existing object-aware 3DGS methods jointly optimize geometry and semantic states but suffer from two key failure modes: noisy foundation-model masks on complex geometry, and label-geometry coupling, in which co-optimized identity gradients mislabel boundary Gaussians. We introduce RigidGS, an end-to-end pipeline that decouples geometric learning from object identity. We propose a depth- and temporally-aware mask refinement module that addresses two complementary SAM2 failures: over-inclusion on thin structures and under-inclusion on multimodal-depth objects. We then determine object identities entirely upstream via COLMAP projection voting and freeze them during training, directing mask supervision solely toward geometric optimization. Refined masks alone substantially improve competing methods, yet a residual gap in label-geometry coupling persists that our fixed-identity design eliminates. RigidGS outperforms prior object-aware 3DGS methods on LLFF/NVOS, Mip-NeRF~360, and iNeRF360, improving segmentation and boundary IoU by 7.7 and 14.5 points on LLFF/NVOS. Finally, RigidGS enables real-time rigid-body manipulation on Meta Quest~2 without mesh extraction. Our code and project page are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes RigidGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting pipeline that decouples geometry from object identity through refined masks and identities fixed by COLMAP projection voting, enabling real-time rigid-body manipulation on Meta Quest 2.
AI.motivation: Existing object-aware 3DGS methods suffer from noisy foundation-model masks on complex geometry and from label-geometry coupling, in which co-optimized identity gradients mislabel boundary Gaussians.
AI.method: A depth- and temporally-aware mask refinement module corrects SAM2 over-inclusion on thin structures and under-inclusion on multimodal-depth objects. Object identities are assigned upstream by COLMAP projection voting and frozen during training, so mask supervision targets geometric optimization only.
AI.result: Refined masks alone substantially improve competing methods, and the fixed-identity design removes the residual label-geometry coupling gap. RigidGS outperforms prior object-aware 3DGS methods on LLFF/NVOS, Mip-NeRF 360 and iNeRF360, improving segmentation and boundary IoU by 7.7 and 14.5 points on LLFF/NVOS, and enables real-time rigid-body manipulation on Meta Quest 2 without mesh extraction.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling object identity from geometric optimization makes object-level 3DGS editable in real time, which supports interactive VR and MR applications.

title: Anatomy-Preserving Unpaired Medical Image Translation via Shared Latent Anchoring
summary: Unpaired medical image-to-image translation requires synthesizing target-modality images from source-modality images without aligned supervision. Existing methods learn a direct source-to-target mapping that entangles structure preservation and appearance generation within a single model, often distorting clinically meaningful anatomy in the translated output. We argue that these two objectives should be decoupled entirely: anatomical structure should be captured independently of generation, and the generator should operate only on a frozen structural representation. To this end, we propose a two-stage framework for unpaired medical image translation. In the first stage, we learn a shared structure space by training a structure encoder-decoder on source images, target images, and structural masks jointly, using mask reconstruction to anchor the latent space to modality-agnostic anatomy. For source images without mask annotations, a target-domain memory bank provides soft structural supervision via prototype retrieval. In the second stage, a conditional flow model learns to render target-domain appearance under fixed structural conditions. This ensures the generator inherits target appearance statistics and can focus entirely on structural conditioning rather than learning appearance from scratch. We validate our framework on OCT-to-OCTA synthesis and brain MR-to-CT translation. Our method outperforms all unpaired baselines on both tasks and, despite requiring no paired supervision, also surpasses paired baselines, improving PSNR by up to 11.2% and SSIM by up to 26.4% on OCT-to-OCTA, and achieving consistent gains across whole-image, soft-tissue, and bone regions on MR-to-CT. The project repository is available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-stage framework for unpaired medical image translation that decouples anatomical structure from appearance, learning a shared structure space and then rendering target appearance with a conditional flow model under fixed structure. On OCT-to-OCTA and brain MR-to-CT it outperforms unpaired baselines and even paired baselines.
AI.motivation: Direct source-to-target mappings in unpaired medical image translation entangle structure preservation and appearance generation in one model, which often distorts clinically meaningful anatomy.
AI.method: A structure encoder-decoder is trained jointly on source images, target images and structural masks, with mask reconstruction anchoring the latent space to modality-agnostic anatomy. A target-domain memory bank gives soft structural supervision to source images without masks via prototype retrieval. A conditional flow model then renders target appearance under the frozen structural conditions.
AI.result: On OCT-to-OCTA the method improves PSNR by up to 11.2% and SSIM by up to 26.4%, and on MR-to-CT it gives consistent gains across whole-image, soft-tissue and bone regions. It surpasses paired baselines despite using no paired supervision.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling structure from generation, with the generator working only on a frozen structural representation, yields anatomically faithful translation without paired data.

title: From Weapons to Events: Evaluating Evidential Support in Multimodal AI for Policing
comment: 34 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables; appendices include annotation guidelines, prompt templates and a datasheet
summary: Computer vision (CV) for policing has centred on recognising objects such as seized weapons, while body-worn video (BWV) is still reviewed by people, with existing AI tools using only its audio. Multimodal video AI could make BWV review faster and cheaper. At the object level, we present the KnifeHunter dataset, developed with UK law enforcement, with over 25,000 images of 543 knife classes and a protocol reflecting investigative conditions, and KHNet, a retrieval architecture fusing local and global features, which with about 125,000 distractor images attains 85.7% and 63.4% mean Average Precision (mAP) on the medium and hard protocols. At the event level, we present an evaluation protocol for video understanding pipelines, which describe a video as events and a transcript, that scores transcription, speaker attribution, event detection, temporal localisation and unsupported events. Whether each event is supported by the recording is labelled by a judge validated against blinded human labels. We apply it to complete pipelines, three 2026 omni-modal models and our hybrid NarrativeBridge-PAL-GPT-5 pipeline, on UKBWV-27, a pilot stress-test set of 27 publicly released UK BWV recordings (118 minutes). On this set the hybrid pipeline leads on five of six measures, yet it leaves 13.6% of predicted events unsupported and misattributes 27.7% of utterances, and every pipeline degrades on recordings from edited releases, long recordings and noisy audio. We propose readiness levels separating assistive tasks from those requiring verification of every output.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the KnifeHunter dataset and KHNet retrieval model for object-level knife recognition, and an event-level protocol for evaluating video understanding pipelines on UK body-worn video. Evaluated on a 27-recording pilot set, the best hybrid pipeline still leaves 13.6% of predicted events unsupported and misattributes 27.7% of utterances.
AI.motivation: Policing computer vision has focused on recognising seized objects, while body-worn video is still reviewed manually and existing AI tools use only its audio. Multimodal video AI could speed up this review, but its reliability for investigative use was unknown.
AI.method: KnifeHunter contains over 25,000 images of 543 knife classes with an investigative protocol, and KHNet fuses local and global features for retrieval. The event-level protocol scores transcription, speaker attribution, event detection, temporal localisation and unsupported events, with support labelled by a judge validated against blinded human labels.
AI.result: KHNet reaches 85.7% and 63.4% mAP on the medium and hard protocols with about 125,000 distractor images. On UKBWV-27 (27 recordings, 118 minutes) the hybrid NarrativeBridge-PAL-GPT-5 pipeline leads on five of six measures, yet leaves 13.6% of predicted events unsupported and misattributes 27.7% of utterances, and all pipelines degrade on edited, long or noisy recordings.
AI.conclusion: Current pipelines are suitable only for assistive tasks, so the authors propose readiness levels that separate assistive uses from those requiring verification of every output.

title: Beyond Frame-Level Accuracy: Analyzing Video-Level Stability in Transformer-Based Deepfake Forensics
comment: Paper submitted to international journal of intelligent systems, Wiley publishers, accepted version of open-access paper
summary: Deepfake videos generated by advanced generative models pose serious threats to digital security, misinformation control, and media forensics. Although numerous detection methods have been proposed, their reported performances are often based on heterogeneous preprocessing pipelines, inconsistent data splits, and model-specific training protocols, hindering fair architectural comparison. This work presents a controlled and reproducible comparative study of convolutional neural networks (ResNet-18 and EfficientNet-B0) and a transformer-based architecture (ViT-B/16) within a unified, face-centric deepfake detection framework. All models are trained using identical preprocessing, augmentation, optimization settings, and data splits on Celeb-DF v2 and FaceForensics++, and results are validated across three independent random seeds with bootstrapped confidence intervals. Experimental results show that while CNN-based models perform competitively at the frame level, their performance degrades after video-level aggregation. In contrast, ViT-B/16 demonstrates more stable video-level performance, achieving 92.8\% [95\% CI: 91.7--94.0] video-level accuracy and an AUC of 0.950 [95\% CI: 0.934--0.964] on Celeb-DF v2 (3-seed bootstrapped). Cross-dataset evaluation across the same three random seeds reveals a large, asymmetric generalization gap (AUC 0.79 FF++$\rightarrow$Celeb-DF vs. 0.64 Celeb-DF$\rightarrow$FF++), indicating that in-domain video-level stability does not transfer to unseen manipulation domains. These findings indicate that global self-attention improves robustness and video-level stability for deepfake detection within a given data domain, while highlighting the need for further work on cross-domain generalization.

AI.tldr: The paper compares ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0 and ViT-B/16 for deepfake detection under a controlled, reproducible protocol. CNNs are competitive per frame but degrade after video-level aggregation, while ViT-B/16 is more stable at video level, and cross-dataset generalisation remains weak.
AI.motivation: Reported deepfake detection performance is hard to compare because studies use heterogeneous preprocessing, inconsistent data splits and model-specific training protocols.
AI.method: All three architectures are trained with identical preprocessing, augmentation, optimisation settings and data splits on Celeb-DF v2 and FaceForensics++, and results are validated over three random seeds with bootstrapped confidence intervals.
AI.result: ViT-B/16 reaches 92.8% video-level accuracy (95% CI 91.7 to 94.0) and an AUC of 0.950 (95% CI 0.934 to 0.964) on Celeb-DF v2. Cross-dataset AUC is 0.79 from FF++ to Celeb-DF and 0.64 from Celeb-DF to FF++.
AI.conclusion: Global self-attention improves video-level robustness within a single data domain, but in-domain stability does not transfer to unseen manipulation domains, so cross-domain generalisation needs further work.

title: STAIRS: Staging the Inverse Problem via Admissible-Support Scheduling for Unrolled MRI Reconstruction
summary: Accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) forms images from incomplete Fourier measurements, shifting acquisition burden to computational reconstruction. Deep unrolled networks interleave learned regularization and data consistency, yet typically estimate the full unmeasured spectrum at every cascade. We propose STAIRS (Staging the Inverse Problem via Admissible-Support Scheduling), which projects intermediate reconstructions onto nested Fourier supports that expand to the full spectrum and conditions each update on its support transition. Conditional increments of a regularized log-determinant score of training covariance define a normalized spectral coordinate, accounting for dependencies between newly and previously admitted frequencies. Dyadic targets allocate larger coordinate increments to earlier cascades and are mapped to fixed supports before training, enabling coarse-to-fine reconstruction with unchanged sampling masks and data consistency. On fastMRI and Stanford2D, STAIRS improves matched Transformer (HUMUSNet) and convolutional (NAFNet) backbones in single- and multi-coil reconstruction, including radiologist-annotated pathology regions. It also outperforms predictor-based progression with lower parameter overhead and inference latency. Stage-wise analysis shows repeated error correction by projection and lower intermediate reconstruction errors than the backbones alone throughout support expansion. Ablations favor dyadic allocation over uniform expansion for square and line-band supports and over manual front-loading for square windows. Support projection alone improves reconstruction, and transition conditioning strengthens the gain. Cross-dataset evaluation shows improvements for both backbones in both directions. Support allocation thus complements regularizer design in unrolled MRI reconstruction.

AI.tldr: STAIRS is a training scheme for unrolled MRI reconstruction that projects intermediate reconstructions onto nested Fourier supports expanding to the full spectrum, so the network reconstructs coarse-to-fine across cascades. It improves HUMUSNet and NAFNet backbones on fastMRI and Stanford2D with lower parameter overhead than predictor-based progression.
AI.motivation: Deep unrolled MRI networks typically estimate the full unmeasured spectrum at every cascade, and existing progressive alternatives add predictor overhead.
AI.method: Intermediate reconstructions are projected onto nested Fourier supports and each update is conditioned on its support transition. A normalised spectral coordinate is defined from conditional increments of a regularised log-determinant score of the training covariance, and dyadic targets allocate larger increments to earlier cascades and are mapped to fixed supports before training.
AI.result: STAIRS improves both HUMUSNet (Transformer) and NAFNet (convolutional) backbones in single- and multi-coil reconstruction, including on radiologist-annotated pathology regions, and outperforms predictor-based progression in parameters and latency. Dyadic allocation beats uniform expansion and manual front-loading in ablations, and cross-dataset evaluation improves both backbones in both directions.
AI.conclusion: Support allocation complements regularizer design as a way to improve unrolled MRI reconstruction, with the gains coming from projection and transition conditioning.

title: Domain Generalization for Style-Debiased Object Detection via Label-Consistent Training across Multiple Styles
summary: Domain generalization (DG) for object detection aims to improve model performance on unseen target domains. Existing detectors, however, suffer substantial degradation on visually distinct unseen domains, as models confined to limited training styles tend to overfit superficial statistical cues rather than object-level semantics. Motivated by human perception, which attends primarily to semantically relevant features while ignoring irrelevant style cues, we propose Origin-Anchored Multi-Style Consistency (OAMSC), a source-only framework that couples multi-style data synthesis with cross-style consistency learning to suppress style-sensitive shortcut learning. For data preparation, we leverage off-the-shelf diffusion models to expand the source datasets into 20 distinct styles, with all generated images manually verified to ensure that object instances and annotations remain consistent across style variants. During training, we impose Origin-anchored consistency constraints at scene and object levels to reinforce the learning of domain-stable features while suppressing the influence of style-sensitive cues. Extensive experiments and ablation studies on multiple challenging DG benchmarks demonstrate the consistent effectiveness and strong generalization performance of OAMSC across diverse domain shifts. Notably, our approach applies to both one-stage and two-stage detectors, while its data-centric design is complementary in principle to other DG methods. The training code and two style-transfer datasets constructed for the experiments, comprising approximately 180K images in total, are publicly available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: OAMSC is a source-only domain generalisation framework for object detection that uses diffusion models to expand source data into 20 styles and enforces cross-style consistency at scene and object levels. It works with one-stage and two-stage detectors across multiple DG benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Detectors trained on limited styles overfit superficial style cues rather than object-level semantics, and degrade substantially on visually distinct unseen domains.
AI.method: Off-the-shelf diffusion models expand each source dataset into 20 styles, and all generated images are manually verified for consistent objects and annotations. Origin-anchored consistency constraints at scene and object levels encourage domain-stable features and suppress style-sensitive cues during training.
AI.result: The paper reports consistent effectiveness and strong generalisation across diverse domain shifts on multiple challenging DG benchmarks, with ablations supporting each component. The method applies to both one-stage and two-stage detectors.
AI.conclusion: A data-centric multi-style design with consistency learning suppresses style-sensitive shortcuts and is complementary in principle to other DG methods. The training code and two style-transfer datasets of about 180K images are released on GitHub.

title: DAC-MACE: Context-Conditioned Expert Routing for Compact Scene Coordinate Regression in Camera Relocalization
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to IEEE Sensors Journal
summary: A camera becomes an absolute pose sensor when its images can be relocalized against a prebuilt map of the scene. On mobile robots and augmented-reality devices, that map must be small and quick to build. Scene coordinate regression (SCR) stores the scene in a compact network that predicts a 3D coordinate for every pixel, and mixture-of-experts (MoE) variants extend its capacity to larger outdoor scenes. In existing MoE-based SCR, however, the router assigns each pixel to an expert from the same local descriptor that the experts regress from, so repeated facades and windows at different locations receive similar routing inputs. We present DAC-MACE, which conditions soft expert routing on recalibrated and contextualized features. A residual context adapter (RCA) reweights the channels and locations of frozen encoder features, a global context encoder (GCE) mixes them with multi-scale self-attention, and an image-level pooled descriptor is added to the router input. A dual-threshold RANSAC--Levenberg--Marquardt estimator recovers the pose. On Cambridge Landmarks, DAC-MACE attains a mean per-scene median translation error of 13.0 cm over three seeds, the lowest among the RGB-only SCR methods compared (GLACE 13.6 cm, MACE 14.4 cm), and reduces the error on the largest scene from 24 to 19 cm relative to MACE. In a cumulative study, the MoE head, GCE, RCA, and the dual-threshold estimator lower the mean error from 17.0 cm to 14.4, 14.0, 13.6, and 13.0 cm. On 7-Scenes, adding GCE to a single ACE head raises Recall@(5 cm, 5$^\circ$) from 86.56% to 87.60%.

AI.tldr: DAC-MACE improves mixture-of-experts scene coordinate regression for camera relocalisation by conditioning expert routing on contextualised features rather than local descriptors alone. It reaches 13.0 cm mean median translation error on Cambridge Landmarks, the lowest among the RGB-only SCR methods compared.
AI.motivation: In existing MoE-based scene coordinate regression, the router assigns pixels to experts from the same local descriptor the experts regress from, so repeated structures such as facades and windows receive similar routing inputs.
AI.method: A residual context adapter reweights channels and locations of frozen encoder features, and a global context encoder mixes them with multi-scale self-attention. An image-level pooled descriptor is added to the router input, and a dual-threshold RANSAC and Levenberg-Marquardt estimator recovers the pose.
AI.result: On Cambridge Landmarks the mean per-scene median translation error is 13.0 cm over three seeds, against 13.6 cm for GLACE and 14.4 cm for MACE, and the error on the largest scene drops from 24 to 19 cm relative to MACE. In a cumulative study the components lower the mean error from 17.0 cm to 14.4, 14.0, 13.6 and 13.0 cm, and on 7-Scenes adding GCE to a single ACE head raises Recall at (5 cm, 5 degrees) from 86.56% to 87.60%.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning soft expert routing on context features resolves routing ambiguity among repetitive scene structures, improving compact scene coordinate regression for large outdoor scenes.

title: Uncertainty, Not Concealment: A Mechanistic Reappraisal of Sycophancy in Vision-Language Models
comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Med-Reasoner Workshop
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) in medical retrieval-augmented generation must be able to say when a retrieved report contradicts the X-ray, so understanding whether they can detect such conflicts is important for safe deployment. The sycophancy mask hypothesis holds that these models internally detect conflicts but refuse to report them, concealing a detected contradiction. We introduce a three-part diagnostic that separates concealment from uncertainty: representation probing, activation steering, and two-way forced choice. Across four instruction-tuned VLMs on chest X-rays, we confirm behavioral suppression of contradiction and find that a linear probe separates matched from mismatched inputs, beyond what a simple CLIP model achieves. Steering the learned conflict direction never elicits contradiction, and forcing a binary choice does not recover one; instead, cross-modal attention to the image drops on mismatched pairs. We conclude that these models fail to contradict because the mismatch registers as hedged, gated uncertainty rather than concealed knowledge, calling for re-grounding and uncertainty surfacing. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper tests the sycophancy mask hypothesis, which claims VLMs detect medical report-image conflicts but conceal them, and finds instead that the mismatch registers as hedged uncertainty. Across four instruction-tuned VLMs on chest X-rays, the models suppress contradiction behaviourally, but a linear probe separates matched from mismatched inputs.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models used in medical retrieval-augmented generation must recognise when a retrieved report contradicts an X-ray, and the sycophancy mask hypothesis suggests they detect such conflicts yet refuse to report them.
AI.method: A three-part diagnostic separates concealment from uncertainty: representation probing, activation steering along a learned conflict direction, and two-way forced choice. Cross-modal attention to the image is also examined on matched and mismatched pairs.
AI.result: A linear probe separates matched from mismatched inputs beyond what a simple CLIP model achieves. Steering the conflict direction never elicits contradiction, forcing a binary choice does not recover it, and cross-modal attention to the image drops on mismatched pairs.
AI.conclusion: The models fail to contradict because the mismatch is treated as gated uncertainty rather than concealed knowledge, which calls for re-grounding and surfacing of uncertainty.

title: AI-Driven Repair of Missing Automotive Components
summary: Due to supply constraints, replacing damaged automotive components can be expensive and time-consuming, while replacing the entire component can be wasteful when much of it remains usable. This paper presents a pipeline to investigate whether missing geometry can be reconstructed as a repair patch using paired observations of the intact models and synthetically damaged components. Noise-free color, depth, and silhouette images were produced using the camera viewpoints. Depth differences were then used to identify the potential missing regions, while multi-view voxel reconstruction was used to estimate the missing portion. A pretrained DINOv2 model was also added to validate missing candidates and determine whether pretrained visual features could improve reconstruction. We tested the pipeline on 20 automotive CAD models, each with a synthetically removed portion. Each model was tested under four different conditions using two reconstruction methods for a total of 160 trials. The predictions were compared with the missing geometry of the unchanged ground-truth using predefined thresholds of the voxel intersection-over-union over 0.85 and the absolute relative volume error less than 15%. Of the 160 experimental trials, 109 of them satisfied both thresholds. Geometry-only reconstruction passed 16 of 20 components with eight views but only 10 of 20 with four adjacent views. Further analysis showed that 24 out of the 37 failed reconstructions could be categorized as unsuccessful because extra material was incorrectly added to areas that should have been empty. The implementation of DINOv2 into the pipeline did not improve the overall reconstruction accuracy and made prediction generation slower. For 13 verified tests, printing only the repaired sections instead of the entire parts reduced filament use by 93.08% and printing time by 89.39% based on the median results.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a pipeline that reconstructs missing automotive geometry as a repair patch by combining depth-difference detection with multi-view voxel reconstruction, and tests it on 20 CAD models with synthetic damage. Of 160 trials, 109 met both thresholds, and printing only the repaired sections cut filament use by 93.08% for verified cases.
AI.motivation: Replacing a damaged automotive component is expensive and slow during supply shortages, and replacing whole parts wastes much material that is still usable.
AI.method: Noise-free colour, depth and silhouette images are rendered from camera viewpoints. Depth differences identify missing regions, multi-view voxel reconstruction estimates the missing portion, and a pretrained DINOv2 model is tested for validating candidates. Two reconstruction methods are run under four conditions on 20 models.
AI.result: Trials pass when voxel IoU exceeds 0.85 and absolute relative volume error is below 15%, and 109 of 160 trials passed. Geometry-only reconstruction passed 16 of 20 components with eight views but 10 of 20 with four adjacent views. DINOv2 did not improve accuracy and slowed prediction, and for 13 verified tests printing only repaired sections reduced filament use by 93.08% and printing time by 89.39% (medians).
AI.conclusion: Geometry-based patch reconstruction is feasible for some components and can save substantial printing material and time, but over-filled extra material remains the main failure mode.

title: LoCo: Selective Local Competition for Discriminative Open-Vocabulary Multi-Label Recognition
comment: The paper is accepted by NeurIPS 2026
summary: Open-Vocabulary Multi-Label Recognition (OV-MLR) aims to identify all queried semantic concepts present in an image. Existing methods mainly improve global image-text matching or text-side representations, leaving local prediction largely under-explored. In this paper, we revisit local prediction and reveal that it can serve as a strong discriminative branch once two properties are properly handled: spatial consistency of local visual features and compatibility-aware local competition. This perspective is motivated by local semantic sparsity: each image region is related to only a small subset of queried concepts, while compatible concepts of different granularities or types may still coexist locally. We instantiate this perspective with LoCo, a selective Local Competition framework for OV-MLR. LoCo adopts a spatially consistent visual encoder to reduce local feature entanglement, and introduces Selective Softmax to impose competition only among locally incompatible categories while preserving compatible responses. Multi-scale inference further improves local prediction at different scales. LoCo can also be ensembled with an existing global predictor to provide complementary image-level context. Experiments on four multi-label benchmarks show that standalone LoCo improves average F1-score and mAP over TagCLIP by 3.4% and 3.8%, respectively. LoCo + DualPrompt achieves the highest averages among the compared methods, with gains of 4.8% and 5.2% over TagCLIP. Our results suggest that local semantic sparsity offers a useful basis for developing more discriminative open-vocabulary multi-label recognition methods. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: LoCo is an open-vocabulary multi-label recognition framework that revives local region prediction as a discriminative branch, using a spatially consistent encoder and Selective Softmax that applies competition only among locally incompatible categories. It improves over TagCLIP by 3.4% in average F1 and 3.8% in mAP standalone, and 4.8% and 5.2% when combined with DualPrompt.
AI.motivation: Existing open-vocabulary multi-label recognition methods focus on global image-text matching or text-side representations and leave local prediction under-explored, even though each region relates to only a small subset of queried concepts.
AI.method: A spatially consistent visual encoder reduces local feature entanglement, and Selective Softmax imposes competition only among locally incompatible categories while preserving compatible responses. Multi-scale inference refines local predictions, and LoCo can be ensembled with a global predictor for image-level context.
AI.result: Across four multi-label benchmarks, standalone LoCo improves average F1 and mAP over TagCLIP by 3.4% and 3.8%. LoCo with DualPrompt achieves the highest averages among compared methods, with gains of 4.8% and 5.2% over TagCLIP.
AI.conclusion: Local semantic sparsity is a useful basis for more discriminative open-vocabulary multi-label recognition, and local prediction can be a strong complement to global matching.

title: TimeTraveler: Temporal Strategy Planning with Time Dictionary for Streaming Video Understanding
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires models to answer user queries over continuously evolving video streams. Unlike offline video QA, SVU must handle queries whose evidence may lie in the past, appear in the current scene, or emerge only after future observations. Existing streaming video systems often rely on compact visual memories or fixed evidence-access schemes, which can lose fine-grained details and fail to adapt the answering process to the temporal intent of each query. In this paper, we propose TimeTraveler, a streaming VQA framework that performs temporal strategy planning with a Time Dictionary. Inspired by the need to search across different temporal regions of a stream, TimeTraveler stores each observed moment as a timestamp-indexed structured caption and uses this dictionary as an explicit source of queryable evidence. Given a query, TimeTraveler determines whether to recall past evidence, read the present context, or wait for future observations, and then applies a strategy-specific evidence acquisition process. Comparative experiments on streaming video QA benchmarks show that TimeTraveler improves streaming question answering by preserving fine-grained temporal evidence and selecting the appropriate temporal strategy for each query. The project page is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TimeTraveler is a streaming video QA framework that stores each observed moment as a timestamp-indexed structured caption in a Time Dictionary and plans, per query, whether to recall past evidence, read the present or wait for future observations. It improves streaming question answering on benchmarks by keeping fine-grained temporal evidence and choosing an appropriate strategy.
AI.motivation: Existing streaming video systems rely on compact visual memories or fixed evidence-access schemes, which lose fine-grained detail and do not adapt to the temporal intent of each query.
AI.method: Each observed moment is stored as a timestamp-indexed structured caption forming an explicit, queryable Time Dictionary. Given a query, the system selects a temporal strategy (recall, read present context or wait) and then applies a strategy-specific evidence acquisition process.
AI.result: Comparative experiments on streaming video QA benchmarks show improved question answering, attributed to preserving fine-grained temporal evidence and selecting the right temporal strategy per query.
AI.conclusion: Explicit temporal strategy planning over a structured dictionary of past observations is an effective way to handle streaming video understanding.

title: MaRiO: Multi-agent Collaborative Reasoning via Shared Observations in MLLMs
comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations & Datasets Track (poster). First two authors contributed equally
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) show strong visual perception capabilities, but existing evaluations largely focus on single-view or multi-view settings with shared camera parameters, leaving the challenge of multi-agent collaborative scenarios underexplored. In such settings, multiple agents observe a shared environment from independent viewpoints, and reliable decisions require reasoning across these independent observations of the same environment. To study this problem, we introduce MaRiO, a benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaborative reasoning, and evaluate 23 state-of-the-art MLLMs on it.
