title: Understanding the Effect of Visual Attention in CNNs: A Decision-Space Alignment Perspective
summary: Visual Attention enhances convolutional neural networks (CNNs) by modulating intermediate features, yet their effects on downstream decisions remain less understood. We present a decision-space framework that models multiplicative attention as an intermediate feature perturbation and derives a first-order prediction of its effect on the target-versus-competitor classification margin. We further introduce the Decision Alignment Score (DAS) to quantify the directional alignment between the perturbation and the local margin gradient. We evaluate the framework on CIFAR-100 using SimAM and CBAM across five popular CNN backbones, ResNet-18, ResNet-20, ResNet-50, ResNet-56, and MobileNetV2. The analysis examines prediction agreement, DAS margin correlations, and downstream activation-state changes. Across most final-attention configurations, predicted and actual margin changes show good agreement, while DAS exhibits positive correlations with actual margin changes. Single-attention experiments further show that prediction agreement and DAS margin correlations depend on attention placement, with stronger associations at later stages.

AI.tldr: The paper frames multiplicative visual attention in CNNs as an intermediate feature perturbation, derives a first-order prediction of its effect on the target-versus-competitor margin, and introduces the Decision Alignment Score (DAS) to measure how well that perturbation aligns with the local margin gradient.
AI.motivation: Visual attention modulates intermediate CNN features, yet its effects on downstream classification decisions are less well understood.
AI.method: Multiplicative attention is modeled as an intermediate feature perturbation; a first-order margin prediction is derived and DAS quantifies the directional alignment between the perturbation and the local margin gradient; SimAM and CBAM are evaluated on CIFAR-100 across ResNet-18, ResNet-20, ResNet-50, ResNet-56 and MobileNetV2, analyzing prediction agreement, DAS-margin correlations and activation-state changes.
AI.result: For most final-attention configurations predicted and actual margin changes agree well and DAS correlates positively with actual margin changes; for single-attention placements, agreement and DAS correlations depend on placement, with stronger associations at later stages; the abstract gives no numeric values.
AI.conclusion: The decision-space framework gives a usable first-order account of how attention changes decisions, with the strongest explanatory power for attention placed at later stages.

title: ROLECUE: Diagnosing Cross-Lingual Role-Binding Failures in Vision-Language Models
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027, Evaluations and Datasets Track
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can recognize events in images and parse sentences, but it remains unclear when they bind visual Agent-Patient structure to linguistic semantic roles across languages whose role cues depend on morphology, word order or construction. We introduce ROLECUE, a controlled diagnostic that pairs 192 validated two-person action images with German, Turkish, Japanese, English, Korean and Bangla sentences in canonical and patient-first orders. The evaluation separates image-only role recognition, text-only role parsing, direct image-sentence matching, response-compliance behavior and an external modular composition of the model's own component predictions. Across eight recent open-weight VLMs, ROLECUE reveals a structured spectrum: some models fail visual or linguistic component tests, some largely solve the diagnostic, some collapse to constant semantic assent and several show component-joint gaps in which reliable image-only and text-only role predictions do not survive direct joint inference. The largest non-degenerate gaps reach 44.9 percentage points, with final bootstrap intervals confirming that the effect is not a point-estimate artifact. These results reveal multilingual component-joint performance gaps and acceptance biases hidden by aggregate VLM benchmarks and show why component diagnostics are necessary before interpreting joint multimodal errors.

AI.tldr: ROLECUE is a controlled diagnostic that tests whether VLMs bind visual Agent-Patient structure to semantic roles across six languages, showing that component-level role recognition often does not survive joint image-sentence inference, with gaps up to 44.9 percentage points.
AI.motivation: It is unclear when VLMs link visual agent-patient structure to linguistic roles in languages whose role cues depend on morphology, word order or construction, and aggregate benchmarks can hide component-joint failures and acceptance biases.
AI.method: The benchmark pairs 192 validated two-person action images with German, Turkish, Japanese, English, Korean and Bangla sentences in canonical and patient-first orders, and separates image-only role recognition, text-only role parsing, direct image-sentence matching, response-compliance behavior and an external modular composition of the model's own component predictions.
AI.result: Across eight recent open-weight VLMs some models fail component tests, some largely solve the diagnostic, some collapse to constant semantic assent, and several show component-joint gaps; the largest non-degenerate gaps reach 44.9 percentage points, and final bootstrap intervals confirm the effect is not a point-estimate artifact.
AI.conclusion: Component diagnostics are needed before interpreting joint multimodal errors, since aggregate benchmarks can hide multilingual component-joint gaps and acceptance biases.

title: MotionGraphicsBench: Evaluating Motion Graphics Generation with Programmatic Verification
summary: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models can follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. We introduce MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark of 100 instances for animating an input static SVG with a motion edit prompt. By supplying all required visual elements, our editing task reflects a designer-like workflow and isolates motion generation from graphic generation. Derived from real-world Lottie motion designs, our benchmark contains diverse combinations of spatio-temporal animation behaviors. Each benchmark instance pairs its model input with a deterministic, human-readable verification program that accepts different valid implementations and reports which prompt requirements pass or fail, rather than comparing against a reference animation or using a VLM judge. We construct these programs with a multi-agent pipeline using human-labeled animations and synthesized test cases. On a balanced test set of 180 animations, our programs achieve 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments, compared with 83.3% for a GPT-6 Astra VLM baseline, and outperform the baseline in both approval and rejection recall. Across 47 configurations from 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 6.0% to 67.7%. Across 15 models evaluated at their highest available reasoning effort with 32 attempts per instance, additional attempts improve every model, but pass@32 still ranges from 38.0% to 95.0%. Our analysis of verification programs reveals that generated animations often fail to match reference poses, follow requested motion trajectories, or coordinate related events. We release our benchmark at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MotionGraphicsBench evaluates LLM-generated motion graphics for a static SVG using deterministic, human-readable verification programs rather than reference animations or VLM judges, with programs agreeing with human judgments on 93.3% of cases versus 83.3% for a GPT-6 Astra VLM baseline.
AI.motivation: It is hard to evaluate whether models follow requests that combine spatial, appearance and temporal requirements for animating a static graphic, and reference comparison or VLM judging is unreliable for this.
AI.method: The benchmark has 100 expert-curated instances derived from real Lottie motion designs, each pairing an SVG and a motion edit prompt with a verification program built by a multi-agent pipeline from human-labeled animations and synthesized test cases, which reports which prompt requirements pass or fail.
AI.result: On a balanced set of 180 animations the programs reach 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments versus 83.3% for the VLM baseline and outperform it in approval and rejection recall; across 47 configurations from 32 LLMs and 12 providers pass@1 ranges from 6.0% to 67.7%; across 15 models at their highest reasoning effort with 32 attempts per instance, pass@32 ranges from 38.0% to 95.0%.
AI.conclusion: Generated animations often fail to match reference poses, follow requested trajectories or coordinate related events, and programmatic verification gives a more reliable evaluation than a VLM judge.

title: The RenAIssance: Caption-Guided Diffusion Models for Historical-Art Visual Media
comment: Accepted at ACMMM26 RichMediaGAI. This work is co-funded by the European Union's Horizon Europe research and innovation programme under MSCA with grant agreement No 101081674
summary: Generative AI can expand cultural collections into prompt-responsive visual media, but historical artworks rarely provide the paired descriptions needed to adapt modern image generators. We present The RenAIssance, a scalable pipeline that turns a collection of historical European artworks into a reusable text-to-image media resource. The pipeline generates scene-level captions with BLIP and uses the resulting approximately 15,000 image--text pairs from DEArt to train a compact LoRA adapter for Stable Diffusion v1.5. The adapter shifts generated images toward the historical-art distribution while retaining the base model's ability to render novel concepts. On historical and contemporary prompts of different lengths, it improves FID to the DEArt reference distribution in every setting with only a modest decrease in CLIP text--image similarity. Qualitative results show that the same adapter can render both period-appropriate subjects and contemporary concepts in a coherent historical visual language. By decoupling a reusable style representation from the base generator, the approach offers a practical building block for controllable historical-art media creation, interactive authoring, and rich-media experiences.

AI.tldr: The RenAIssance builds a reusable text-to-image resource for historical European art by captioning the DEArt collection with BLIP and training a compact LoRA adapter for Stable Diffusion v1.5 on about 15,000 image-text pairs, improving FID to the historical reference distribution.
AI.motivation: Historical artworks rarely come with paired descriptions, which prevents adapting modern image generators to their visual style.
AI.method: Scene-level captions generated with BLIP are paired with DEArt images to train a compact LoRA adapter for Stable Diffusion v1.5 that shifts generation toward the historical-art distribution while preserving the base model's ability to render new concepts.
AI.result: On historical and contemporary prompts of different lengths the adapter improves FID to the DEArt reference distribution in every setting, with only a modest decrease in CLIP text-image similarity; qualitative results show period-appropriate and contemporary subjects rendered in a coherent historical visual language.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling a reusable style representation from the base generator gives a practical building block for controllable historical-art media creation and interactive authoring.

title: Reason First, Retrieve What Matters: Hypothesis-Guided Keyframe Selection for Long Video Understanding
summary: Long video understanding requires models to identify and reason over sparse, temporally distributed evidence within limited frame budgets. Existing keyframe selection methods typically retrieve query-relevant frames from a densely sampled candidate set before inference. However, global image-text matching incurs unnecessary computation when a small set of uniformly sampled frames already provides sufficient evidence. Query relevance alone may also overlook evidence that distinguishes competing answers, while one-shot selection offers no opportunity to correct earlier selection errors. We propose HypoKFS, a training-free, plug-and-play framework that couples keyframe selection with iterative inference by multimodal large language models (MLLMs). HypoKFS first reasons over sparsely sampled frames to construct an initial hypothesis space. The resulting answer distribution determines whether additional frame selection is needed. When needed, the retained hypotheses guide the selection of discriminative frames, followed by renewed inference and hypothesis refinement. This iterative process directs additional visual computation toward unresolved hypotheses while avoiding unnecessary global frame matching. Experiments on Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU demonstrate consistent improvements across multiple MLLM backbones. HypoKFS improves accuracy by up to 6.7 percentage points and achieves 72.9% accuracy on Video-MME at only 1.3% of the reference frame-hypothesis matching cost.

AI.tldr: HypoKFS is a training-free, plug-and-play framework that couples keyframe selection with iterative MLLM inference, selecting frames guided by retained answer hypotheses. It improves long video understanding accuracy by up to 6.7 points, reaching 72.9% on Video-MME at 1.3% of the reference frame-hypothesis matching cost.
AI.motivation: Existing keyframe selection retrieves query-relevant frames from a densely sampled set via global image-text matching, which is costly when sparse uniform frames already suffice. Query relevance alone can miss evidence that distinguishes competing answers, and one-shot selection cannot correct earlier errors.
AI.method: HypoKFS first reasons over sparsely sampled frames to build an initial hypothesis space, and the answer distribution decides whether more frame selection is needed. When it is, the retained hypotheses guide the choice of discriminative frames, followed by renewed inference and hypothesis refinement.
AI.result: On Video-MME, LongVideoBench and MLVU, HypoKFS gives consistent gains across several MLLM backbones, improving accuracy by up to 6.7 percentage points and reaching 72.9% on Video-MME.
AI.conclusion: Directing extra visual computation toward unresolved hypotheses, rather than doing global frame matching, makes keyframe selection both cheaper and more accurate for long video understanding.

title: EndoSCOP-V: A Multi-Turn Video Understanding Evaluation Framework for Multimodal Models in Endoscopy Reporting and Clinical Reasoning
summary: Endoscopic diagnosis unfolds over native video, where a single positive finding during traversal of the gastrointestinal tract sets off a multi-minute chain of reasoning over location, morphology, severity and intervention. Existing endoscopy multimodal benchmarks test only static images or single-disease videos, which miss the temporal and clinical reasoning that real-world reporting demands. We introduce EndoSCOP-V, a video-grounded multi-turn evaluation framework for structured endoscopy reporting and clinical reasoning. It contains 1,307 real-world endoscopy and colonoscopy videos (63.2 h; 97% 1080p) averaging about 174 s. Its 20,274 question-answer turns are instantiated deterministically from clinician-filled structured endoscopy-reporting EHRs, so no per-case annotation is synthetic or LLM-rephrased. They come from 1,033 clinician-reviewed templates, about 18 per disease, that span a clinically aligned 9-task x 30-sub-task reporting taxonomy over 54 World Endoscopy Organization (WEO) MST 3.0 diseases. 22% of procedures carry co-existing pathologies, up to six per case. A Markovian context-pruned oracle-forcing protocol evaluates the dialogue turn by turn, injecting the gold answer before each subsequent turn so that per-turn reasoning is isolated from cascading dialogue errors. A panel of 15 board-certified endoscopists sets a 78% strict-accuracy baseline on 1,500 questions. Across 14 open-weight LMMs, the best 27B-class model reaches 59.8% strict accuracy, falling to 53.4% once format-trivial disease-rejection items are excluded. On a between-subjects spot-check, the best of 3 frontier proprietary models trails the clinician panel by 23 pp on strict NDR accuracy. Sub-task analysis reveals consistent gaps in quantitative measurement, multi-variable grading and intervention reasoning on long-horizon video. Data: Hugging Face (EndoSCOP-V). Code: GitHub (abhi25t/EndoSCOP-V).

AI.tldr: EndoSCOP-V is a video-grounded multi-turn benchmark for structured endoscopy reporting and clinical reasoning, with 1,307 real endoscopy and colonoscopy videos and 20,274 question-answer turns generated deterministically from clinician-filled reporting EHRs. Evaluated on 14 open-weight LMMs and frontier proprietary models, it shows a clear gap to clinicians.
AI.motivation: Existing endoscopy multimodal benchmarks test only static images or single-disease videos, missing the temporal and clinical reasoning that real reporting requires.
AI.method: The benchmark spans 1,033 clinician-reviewed templates covering a 9-task by 30-sub-task reporting taxonomy over 54 WEO MST 3.0 diseases, with QA turns instantiated from structured EHRs rather than LLM-rephrased. A Markovian context-pruned oracle-forcing protocol evaluates each turn with the gold answer injected, isolating per-turn reasoning from cascading errors.
AI.result: A panel of 15 board-certified endoscopists reaches 78% strict accuracy on 1,500 questions. The best of 14 open-weight LMMs, a 27B-class model, reaches 59.8% strict accuracy, or 53.4% after excluding format-trivial disease-rejection items. On a spot-check, the best of three frontier proprietary models trails the clinicians by 23 percentage points on strict NDR accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Current multimodal models remain well short of clinicians on long-horizon endoscopy video, with the largest gaps in quantitative measurement, multi-variable grading and intervention reasoning.

title: Latent-WAM++: Shaping World and Action Representations for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: We introduce Latent-WAM++, a representation-centered World Action Model (WAM) for end-to-end autonomous driving. Existing WAMs are primarily trained to predict future states or final actions, leaving the intermediate world and action representations that connect prediction to planning only indirectly constrained. Latent-WAM++ matches the supervision of each representation to its role in planning. World Representation Construction combines scene-ego future prediction, SIGReg-based distribution stabilization, and frozen geometric priors to learn a temporally predictive, non-degenerate, and geometry-aware world representation without an EMA target encoder. Trajectory MeanFlow Planner directly predicts multimodal trajectory proposals while being optimized with an Improved MeanFlow velocity-space objective, enabling one-step sampling. Visual-Action Representation Alignment further aligns the resulting pre-output action features with a stop-gradient target derived from current visual semantics. Latent-WAM++ achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM v2 and under zero-shot evaluation on HUGSIM, reaching 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and 47.0 average RC and 30.1 average HD-Score on HUGSIM. Training the planner end to end costs 190 GPU-hours for Latent-WAM++ versus 1,600 for Latent-WAM, a reduction of 88.1%.

AI.tldr: Latent-WAM++ is a representation-centred World Action Model for end-to-end autonomous driving that supervises intermediate world and action representations according to their role in planning. It reaches 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and cuts training cost by 88.1% relative to Latent-WAM.
AI.motivation: Existing World Action Models train prediction of future states or final actions, so the intermediate representations linking prediction to planning are only indirectly constrained.
AI.method: World Representation Construction combines scene-ego future prediction, SIGReg-based distribution stabilisation and frozen geometric priors, without an EMA target encoder. A Trajectory MeanFlow Planner predicts multimodal trajectory proposals with an Improved MeanFlow velocity-space objective, allowing one-step sampling. Visual-Action Representation Alignment aligns pre-output action features to a stop-gradient target from current visual semantics.
AI.result: Latent-WAM++ reaches state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM v2, with 90.1 EPDMS, and under zero-shot evaluation on HUGSIM, with 47.0 average RC and 30.1 average HD-Score. End-to-end planner training takes 190 GPU-hours versus 1,600 for Latent-WAM, a reduction of 88.1%.
AI.conclusion: Matching supervision to each representation's role in planning yields strong driving performance at a much lower training cost.

title: VAComp: View-Aware Full Projector Compensation
summary: Full projector compensation adjusts a projector's input image to compensate for both geometric and photometric distortions introduced by the projection surface. Existing methods generally treat the viewing condition as a static camera viewpoint. When applied to a moving viewer, existing methods face two key challenges: (1) view-dependent methods require model retraining or recalibration to compensate for novel viewpoints; and (2) NeRF/GS-based view-agnostic methods use structure from motion (SfM) to calibrate the projector-camera systems (ProCams) with an unknown global scale, while view-aware tracking requires calibrating a camera oriented opposite to the projector, which introduces an additional calibration challenge. To address these challenges, we introduce VAComp, the first view-aware framework for full projector compensation for a moving viewer in a naked-eye setting. Using a projector, VAComp enables the viewer to perceive a virtual object that visually replaces the real object or to observe view-consistent modifications of the real object's appearance and material properties. To resolve the SfM scale ambiguity, we use metric calibration as a reference to recover the global scale; to calibrate the oppositely facing camera, we use two checkerboards, one facing the RGB camera and the other facing the depth camera. To balance compensation quality and runtime efficiency, we develop two non-iterative hybrid methods, VAComp-SD and VAComp-SI. Both combine 2D Gaussian-based view-conditioned geometric correction with learned photometric compensation, predicting each compensation image through a single forward pass without per-frame iterative optimization. Real-world experiments show that both methods achieve competitive compensation quality, with VAComp-SD enabling real-time updates and VAComp-SI operating at interactive rates. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: VAComp is a view-aware full projector compensation framework that lets a moving viewer see a virtual object or view-consistent modifications of a real object in a naked-eye setting. It uses two non-iterative hybrid methods, VAComp-SD for real-time updates and VAComp-SI for interactive rates.
AI.motivation: Existing compensation methods assume a static viewpoint. View-dependent methods need retraining or recalibration for new viewpoints, while NeRF/GS view-agnostic methods suffer from SfM scale ambiguity and view-aware tracking needs calibration of an oppositely facing camera.
AI.method: Metric calibration serves as a reference to recover the SfM global scale, and two checkerboards, one facing the RGB camera and one facing the depth camera, calibrate the opposing camera. VAComp-SD and VAComp-SI combine 2D Gaussian-based view-conditioned geometric correction with learned photometric compensation, predicting each compensation image in a single forward pass.
AI.result: Real-world experiments show both methods achieve competitive compensation quality, with VAComp-SD supporting real-time updates and VAComp-SI running at interactive rates.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid, non-iterative, view-aware compensation can handle a moving viewer without per-frame optimisation, trading quality against runtime.

title: VisProve: Learning Typed Visual Provenance for Scientific Document Question Answering
summary: Visual citations show where an answer is supported, but not how the cited content contributes to it. In scientific document question answering, a model may read a value directly, compress several observations, or combine evidence to infer a conclusion. We study typed visual provenance, where a system generates an answer together with source regions and explicit support relations. We introduce ReViE, a dataset of 3,941 questions over complete scientific documents, with page, section, and region annotations labeled as Quotation, Compression, or Inference. We further propose VisProve, which augments joint answer and provenance generation with differentiable Spatial Evidence Reading and Evidence-Answer Relation Feedback. VisProve conditions next-token prediction on localized visual evidence and its estimated support relation through a gated norm-bounded residual. On the document-disjoint ReViE test set, VisProve improves Typed-F1 from 3.52 to 5.48 and Section-F1 from 45.99 to 53.24 over joint supervised fine-tuning with the same backbone, while Page-F1 changes only marginally. These results suggest that coupling visual grounding with support relation modeling mainly improves fine-grained provenance, while the low absolute Typed-F1 reveals a substantial gap between answer generation and precise visual evidence attribution.

AI.tldr: VisProve learns typed visual provenance for scientific document question answering, generating an answer together with source regions and labelled support relations (Quotation, Compression or Inference). It is trained on ReViE, a dataset of 3,941 questions over complete scientific documents.
AI.motivation: Visual citations show where an answer is supported but not how the cited content contributes to it, such as direct reading, compression of several observations, or inference.
AI.method: The authors build ReViE, with page, section and region annotations labelled by support type, and propose VisProve. It augments joint answer and provenance generation with differentiable Spatial Evidence Reading and Evidence-Answer Relation Feedback, conditioning next-token prediction on localised visual evidence through a gated norm-bounded residual.
AI.result: On the document-disjoint ReViE test set, VisProve raises Typed-F1 from 3.52 to 5.48 and Section-F1 from 45.99 to 53.24 over joint supervised fine-tuning with the same backbone, while Page-F1 changes only marginally.
AI.conclusion: Coupling visual grounding with support-relation modelling mainly improves fine-grained provenance, but the low absolute Typed-F1 shows a large gap between answer generation and precise visual evidence attribution.

title: Agent2BIM: A Systematic Evaluation of Reality-Capture Configurations and Prior Models for As-Built Modeling
summary: AI agents can generate as-built Building Information Models (BIMs) from reality-capture data, but the evidence required for accurate reconstruction remains unclear. This paper presents Agent2BIM, an agent-based Scan-to-BIM framework, and evaluates seven capture configurations in a research laboratory and a mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) scene. Inputs include 360° panoramas, smartphone video, smartphone LiDAR, terrestrial laser scanning (TLS), TLS with posed panoramas, and imagery supplemented by prior IFC models. Outputs are compared against TLS-verified reference models for component detection, geometric accuracy, and MEP connectivity. In the laboratory, component recall ranged from 84% to 100%, but only 9% of components reconstructed from panoramas were within 20 cm of their reference positions, compared with 86% using smartphone LiDAR. In the MEP scene, scale-free inputs recovered 11 - 43% of components, versus 75 - 93% for metric inputs. Prior IFC models improved MEP reconstruction but could propagate inaccuracies. The results highlight the complementary roles of visual and metric evidence in agent-based Scan-to-BIM.

AI.tldr: Agent2BIM is an agent-based Scan-to-BIM framework that is systematically evaluated across seven reality-capture configurations in a laboratory and an MEP scene. The results show that visual and metric evidence play complementary roles in as-built BIM generation.
AI.motivation: It is unclear what capture evidence is needed for AI agents to generate accurate as-built BIMs from reality-capture data.
AI.method: The framework is tested on inputs including 360-degree panoramas, smartphone video, smartphone LiDAR, terrestrial laser scanning (TLS), TLS with posed panoramas, and imagery supplemented by prior IFC models. Outputs are compared with TLS-verified reference models for component detection, geometric accuracy and MEP connectivity.
AI.result: In the laboratory, component recall ranges from 84% to 100%, but only 9% of panorama-based components lie within 20 cm of their reference positions, versus 86% with smartphone LiDAR. In the MEP scene, scale-free inputs recover 11-43% of components against 75-93% for metric inputs, and prior IFC models improve MEP reconstruction but can propagate inaccuracies.
AI.conclusion: Visual and metric evidence are complementary, and metric inputs are essential for accurate agent-based Scan-to-BIM.

title: SHIN: Scalable Hierarchy for INcremental 3D Gaussian Splatting
comment: 8 pages of main text (13 pages including references and supplementary material), 7 figures
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis, but deployment budgets vary across devices and network conditions. Most compact methods target one operating point, so another budget requires a separate representation. SHIN is a scalable 3DGS hierarchy with a reusable Base and additive enhancement layers, so each higher-quality operating point extends rather than replaces the decoded representation. Constructing this hierarchy requires deciding which Gaussians each stage adds and how much spherical-harmonic (SH) appearance each retains, because these choices remain fixed in later prefixes. SHIN derives one shared Gaussian order from multi-scale position-scale sensitivity and divides each stage budget between adding Gaussians and retaining SH bands using calibrated gradient-based scores per byte. Lightweight opacity updates adjust compositing while transmitted geometry and SH coefficients remain unchanged. Across three benchmarks, SHIN progressively improves one cumulative representation and achieves the best PSNR-size efficiency in every overlapping comparison with the multi-rate and progressive baselines.

AI.tldr: SHIN is a scalable 3D Gaussian Splatting hierarchy with a reusable Base and additive enhancement layers, so each higher-quality operating point extends the decoded representation rather than replacing it. It achieves the best PSNR-size efficiency in every overlapping comparison against multi-rate and progressive baselines.
AI.motivation: Compact 3DGS methods usually target a single operating point, so different device or network budgets require separate representations.
AI.method: SHIN derives one shared Gaussian order from multi-scale position-scale sensitivity. Each stage budget is split between adding Gaussians and retaining spherical-harmonic bands, using calibrated gradient-based scores per byte. Lightweight opacity updates adjust compositing while transmitted geometry and SH coefficients stay fixed.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks, SHIN progressively improves one cumulative representation and achieves the best PSNR-size efficiency in every overlapping comparison with the multi-rate and progressive baselines.
AI.conclusion: A single cumulative, layered 3DGS representation can serve multiple deployment budgets without sacrificing rate-distortion efficiency.

title: FG-DSA: Frequency-Guided Depthwise Separable Attention for Efficient Dense Prediction
summary: Dense prediction and generative modeling in resource-constrained scenarios remain challenging, as repeated downsampling substantially reduces spatial detail and degrades boundaries. Although recent attention mechanisms have alleviated the problem of semantic ambiguity, they often fail to preserve high-frequency features or do so at the expense of a very high computational cost. In this paper, we propose the Frequency Guided Depthwise Separable Attention for Efficient Dense Prediction (FG-DSA), a novel framework for efficient dense visual understanding and generation. FG-DSA employs a 2D FFT high-pass filtering module to explicitly inject frequency domain priors into the spatial attention mechanism, allowing lightweight networks to recover sharp boundary transitions with linear complexity. A range of experiments show that FG-DSA is effective at recovering fine object boundaries and leads to a consistent performance gain in the task of semantic segmentation. Importantly, we show that FGA-DSA can be used as a module in diffusion-based generative U-Nets, leading to a significant improvement in the detail of the generated images with very little additional parameter and Floating Point Operation (FLOP) cost.

AI.tldr: FG-DSA is a frequency-guided depthwise separable attention module that injects frequency-domain priors through a 2D FFT high-pass filter to recover sharp boundaries in efficient dense prediction. It improves semantic segmentation and can be added to diffusion U-Nets to enhance generated detail.
AI.motivation: Repeated downsampling in resource-constrained dense prediction degrades spatial detail and boundaries, and existing attention mechanisms either miss high-frequency features or are computationally expensive.
AI.method: A 2D FFT high-pass filtering module injects frequency priors into spatial attention, letting lightweight networks recover sharp boundary transitions with linear complexity.
AI.result: Experiments show better recovery of fine object boundaries and consistent gains in semantic segmentation. As a module in diffusion-based U-Nets, it improves generated image detail with very little extra parameter and FLOP cost.
AI.conclusion: Explicit frequency guidance is a cheap way to restore boundary detail in lightweight dense prediction and generative U-Nets.

title: Dynamics-Informed Action Learning for Goal-Conditioned Latent Planning
summary: Latent world models enable visual control by planning action sequences in compact representation spaces, but a gap remains between how latent dynamics are learned and how they are used for planning. First, teacher-forced training does not expose the dynamics model to the recursively predicted latent states encountered during planning. Second, sampling-based planners typically initialize action search from goal-agnostic proposals, without exploiting the action-conditioned dynamics learned by the world model. We introduce Dynamics-Informed Action Learning (DIAL) to bridge these two gaps. During training, rollout alignment exposes the forward model to its own autoregressive latent predictions, while multi-step inverse supervision trains a lightweight inverse dynamics head to infer actions from latent-state transitions. We further apply the inverse head to model-generated transitions with its parameters held fixed, encouraging predicted rollouts to retain action-relevant information. At test time, DIAL autoregressively couples the inverse and forward dynamics to construct a dynamics-informed action sequence toward the goal, which initializes the mean of the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) proposal distribution. The subsequent CEM search then refines this initialization using the standard sampling and updating procedure. Experiments across four visual control benchmarks demonstrate that DIAL outperforms existing latent world models and planning baselines in both standard and long-horizon scenarios.

AI.tldr: DIAL couples a forward dynamics model and a lightweight inverse dynamics head to build a dynamics-informed action sequence that initialises the CEM planner for goal-conditioned latent planning. It outperforms existing latent world models and planning baselines on four visual control benchmarks, including long-horizon scenarios.
AI.motivation: Latent world models are trained with teacher forcing, which never exposes the forward model to its own recursive predictions, and sampling-based planners start action search from goal-agnostic proposals rather than the learned dynamics.
AI.method: Rollout alignment exposes the forward model to its autoregressive latent predictions, and multi-step inverse supervision trains an inverse dynamics head on latent transitions. The inverse head is applied to model-generated transitions with frozen parameters to keep rollouts action-relevant. At test time, the inverse and forward models are coupled autoregressively to set the mean of the CEM proposal distribution, which CEM then refines.
AI.result: DIAL outperforms existing latent world models and planning baselines in both standard and long-horizon scenarios across four visual control benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Training the dynamics model on its own rollouts and initialising planning from learned dynamics closes the gap between how latent dynamics are learned and used for planning.

title: Physically Guided TeX Generation for Low-Light Visual Tasks
summary: Low-light conditions reduce visible contrast and obscure details, while infrared images lack color and texture, motivating the fusion of infrared and visible information for visual tasks. Existing fusion methods primarily optimize image appearance or task-specific features without explicitly disentangling the coupled factors underlying thermal observations, limiting their physical interpretation under thermal degeneracy. Hyperspectral thermal measurements enable physical decomposition, but they require specialized imaging hardware, while pixel-level physical annotations for supervision or evaluation incur additional costs. We propose TeX-Gen, a physically guided framework for TeX generation from paired visible and infrared images in low-light visual tasks. TeX Generation constructs complementary multi-view features and employs independent branch-specific gates to route cues into the Temperature, Emissivity, and Texture maps. TeXMetric integrates radiometric reconstruction, channel structure, and material consistency to assess the generated maps without requiring pixel-level physical labels. TeX Tune improves performance through task-guided adjustments, jointly optimizing the adjustment modules and task network while keeping the generator frozen. Experiments show that TeX-Gen achieves competitive task performance in low-light environments on the FLIR, LLVIP, M3FD, and MSRS datasets. Experiments on HADAR also examine the association between TeXMetric scores and downstream detection performance.

AI.tldr: TeX-Gen generates Temperature, Emissivity and Texture maps from paired visible and infrared images for low-light visual tasks, without requiring hyperspectral hardware or pixel-level physical labels. Its TeXMetric score, together with task-guided TeX Tune adjustments, supports competitive task performance on several datasets.
AI.motivation: Fusion methods for low-light scenes mainly optimise appearance or task features, and do not disentangle the physical factors behind thermal observations. Hyperspectral measurements enable such decomposition but require specialised hardware, and pixel-level physical annotations are costly.
AI.method: TeX Generation builds complementary multi-view features and routes cues through independent branch-specific gates into the Temperature, Emissivity and Texture maps. TeXMetric assesses the maps by combining radiometric reconstruction, channel structure and material consistency. TeX Tune jointly optimises the adjustment modules and the task network while the generator stays frozen.
AI.result: TeX-Gen achieves competitive task performance in low-light conditions on FLIR, LLVIP, M3FD and MSRS. Experiments on HADAR also examine the association between TeXMetric scores and downstream detection performance.
AI.conclusion: Physically interpretable decomposition of thermal observations can support low-light visual tasks without hyperspectral hardware or pixel-level physical labels.

title: Heterogeneous Asymmetric Contrastive Distillation
summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) between architectural families, e.g., from a Transformer teacher to a CNN student, is difficult because the two networks learn different representations. Logits share a label space, but heterogeneous teachers differ in logit offset, scale, and sharpness, and their non-target classes are less semantically organized. Conventional logit distillation matches these values sample by sample, asking the student to imitate how another architecture expresses its predictions. We argue that a heterogeneous teacher should pass on the relational structure of its predictions, i.e., how it arranges samples relative to one another, and propose Heterogeneous Asymmetric Contrastive Distillation (HACD) to transfer this structure. HACD maps teacher and student logits to centered, temperature-softened probability directions on a shared unit hypersphere, which removes architecture-dependent offsets and lets the temperature control how sharply peaked outputs enter the representation while keeping informative non-target classes. Each student output must then identify its own teacher target within the batch. Because every teacher target also acts as a negative for the others, HACD computes the targets on a moderately augmented view and contrasts both a moderate and a strong student view against them. HACD adds no learnable parameters and needs one teacher pass per sample. It achieves the best or second-best accuracy on 11 of 12 heterogeneous pairs on CIFAR-100, without ground-truth labels, and on 14 of 15 pairs on ImageNet-1K, improving over the reported vanilla KD results by 8.82 and 1.33 percentage points on average. Checkpoints are available at this https URL the code will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: HACD transfers the relational structure of a heterogeneous teacher's predictions to the student by contrasting sample-level probability directions on a shared hypersphere. It achieves the best or second-best accuracy on 11 of 12 heterogeneous pairs on CIFAR-100 and 14 of 15 on ImageNet-1K, improving on vanilla KD by 8.82 and 1.33 percentage points on average.
AI.motivation: Logit distillation across architecture families matches raw logit values, which differ in offset, scale and sharpness between heterogeneous teachers and students, so the student imitates how another architecture expresses its predictions.
AI.method: Teacher and student logits are mapped to centred, temperature-softened probability directions on a shared unit hypersphere, which removes architecture-dependent offsets. Each student output must identify its own teacher target within the batch, with teacher targets computed on a moderately augmented view and contrasted against moderate and strong student views. HACD adds no learnable parameters and needs one teacher pass per sample.
AI.result: HACD achieves the best or second-best accuracy on 11 of 12 heterogeneous pairs on CIFAR-100, without ground-truth labels, and on 14 of 15 pairs on ImageNet-1K. It improves on the reported vanilla KD results by 8.82 and 1.33 percentage points on average.
AI.conclusion: Relational, contrastive transfer of teacher predictions is an effective way to distil knowledge across architectures without extra parameters.

title: MGE: A Membership Guided Data Extraction Attack against Diffusion Models
summary: Recently, diffusion models have achieved remarkable performance in image generation. However, their inherent memory properties introduce a potential safety risk of training data leakage, i.e., data extraction attack. To illustrate such risk, we propose a membership guided extraction (MGE) framework to effectively extract training data from a pre-trained diffusion model. Our core idea is to formulate the data extraction as a conditional generation, where the condition signal is from a membership inference classifier. To improve the success rate and efficiency of MGE, we propose adversarial gradient and parallel branch decoding. Our experiments on image generation benchmarks demonstrate that our MGE can extract hundreds of images, which shows that more attention should be paid to privacy-preserving of diffusion model.

AI.tldr: MGE is a membership-guided data extraction attack that recovers training images from a pre-trained diffusion model by casting extraction as conditional generation driven by a membership inference classifier. It extracts hundreds of training images, highlighting a privacy risk of diffusion models.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models can memorise training data, creating a risk of training data leakage through extraction attacks.
AI.method: The core idea is to frame data extraction as conditional generation, with the condition signal coming from a membership inference classifier. Adversarial gradient and parallel branch decoding are proposed to raise the success rate and efficiency of extraction.
AI.result: Experiments on image generation benchmarks show that MGE can extract hundreds of training images.
AI.conclusion: The results call for more attention to privacy-preserving methods for diffusion models.

title: JoVox: Joint Hierarchical Flow Matching for Lightweight Voxel Generation
summary: Generating high-fidelity voxels while keeping their lightweight nature remains an open problem in computer vision. Current generators are either high-fidelity but computationally heavy, or lightweight but of lower fidelity. Hierarchical methods keep the lightweight nature of voxels. However, their coarse levels, which decide where all finer cells can appear, are generated with the least information about the shape and are never revisited, so they are often plausible but wrong. Our key insight is to let finer cells take part in deciding coarse cells. To this end, we propose JoVox, a discrete flow matching framework that learns the joint distribution of all levels of the voxel hierarchy, instead of a separate distribution for each level, so that coarse cells can be predicted with finer cells already generated nearby. Within this framework, we further introduce a two-level prediction, which outputs the cells two levels finer at once instead of one level finer, halving the number of levels that the network processes and yielding voxels of higher fidelity. We also introduce an unmasking strategy that revisits early decisions once finer cells are generated and corrects inconsistencies in masked diffusion models. Our framework outperforms the baselines on both unconditional and image-conditioned voxel generation. Compared with the current state-of-the-art TRELLIS.2, we achieve 8x higher training throughput, 1/15 of the FLOPs in a forward pass, train on 4 vs. 32 GPUs, and obtain higher quality with an 11% lower Chamfer distance.

AI.tldr: JoVox is a discrete flow matching framework that jointly models all levels of a voxel hierarchy, so coarse cells can be predicted with finer cells already generated. It matches or beats baselines in unconditional and image-conditioned voxel generation while being much cheaper than TRELLIS.2.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity voxel generators are computationally heavy, and lightweight hierarchical generators produce plausible but wrong coarse levels, since those levels are generated with the least shape information and never revisited.
AI.method: JoVox learns the joint distribution of all hierarchy levels rather than a separate distribution per level. A two-level prediction outputs cells two levels finer at once, halving the number of levels the network processes. An unmasking strategy revisits early decisions once finer cells exist and corrects inconsistencies in masked diffusion models.
AI.result: JoVox outperforms baselines on unconditional and image-conditioned voxel generation. Compared with TRELLIS.2, it achieves 8x higher training throughput, 1/15 of the forward-pass FLOPs and training on 4 rather than 32 GPUs, with an 11% lower Chamfer distance.
AI.conclusion: Letting finer cells inform coarse decisions yields higher-fidelity voxels at lower computational cost.

title: Permute-then-Adapt: Weak-to-Strong Contrastive Image-Text Adaptation
summary: Image-text alignment models such as CLIP are typically trained with contrastive learning, where unpaired examples are treated as strict negatives. While this assumption introduces noise by penalising semantically related pairs, existing solutions often rely on heuristic similarity thresholds that lack statistical grounding and sensitivity to dataset-specific noise distributions. In this paper, we propose Permute-then-Adapt (PTA), a framework that leverages efficient weak models to identify missed positives while controlling Type-I error relative to a conditional permutation reference, up to calibration approximation error. Unlike standard distillation or arbitrary thresholding, PTA estimates a random-pairing reference distribution from the weak teacher's similarity scores and uses its upper tail, determined by $\alpha$, to select auxiliary positives. The calibrated positive set is then trained against by a single multi-positive contrastive objective: each anchor maximises the total probability mass it assigns to its positive set. Offline calibration with the weak model adds negligible training overhead. Experiments show gains over heuristic soft-label approaches in object recognition, cross-modal retrieval, and data efficiency. Project repository: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Permute-then-Adapt (PTA) identifies missed positives in image-text contrastive learning using a weak model, with the selection threshold set by a permutation-based reference that controls Type-I error. It improves object recognition, cross-modal retrieval and data efficiency over heuristic soft-label approaches.
AI.motivation: Contrastive training such as CLIP treats unpaired examples as strict negatives, penalising semantically related pairs, while existing heuristic similarity thresholds lack statistical grounding and sensitivity to dataset-specific noise.
AI.method: PTA estimates a random-pairing reference distribution from the weak teacher's similarity scores and uses its upper tail, set by alpha, to select auxiliary positives. A single multi-positive contrastive objective then maximises the total probability mass each anchor assigns to its positive set. Offline calibration adds negligible training overhead.
AI.result: Experiments show gains over heuristic soft-label approaches in object recognition, cross-modal retrieval and data efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Statistically calibrated selection of positives from a weak model is a cheap and principled alternative to arbitrary thresholds or distillation.

title: Disentangled Stylized Image Generation via IP-Cross-Attention Rearrangement
summary: With a solid theoretical foundation and pretraining on large-scale datasets, diffusion-based methods have achieved controllable generation leveraging text and image conditions, and generating excellent stylized images is possible using diffusion models. However, previous methods face significant challenges. First, because diffusion generation is iterative, the common approach of learning implicit style representations via cycle-consistency strategies is too costly and not well-suited to diffusion, even for LoRA-based methods. Second, decoupling style is difficult in the latent space of diffusion models. Representations of attributes are coupled in the latent space of diffusion models; thus, extracting style attributes with diffusion models usually suffers from the issue of content leakage. Furthermore, because style is hard to represent in natural language, capturing style using text prompts or textual inversion is deficient. In this paper, we propose a method for achieving disentangled stylized image generation through IP-cross-attention rearrangement, based on our experimental observations. We also propose negative content guidance, inspired by classifier-free guidance, to reduce content leakage in stylized image generation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a diffusion-based method for disentangled stylised image generation that rearranges IP-cross-attention and adds negative content guidance to reduce content leakage. It targets style extraction without costly cycle-consistency training.
AI.motivation: Learning implicit style via cycle-consistency is too costly for iterative diffusion, style is coupled with content in diffusion latents causing content leakage, and style is hard to express through text prompts or textual inversion.
AI.method: Based on experimental observations, the authors rearrange IP-cross-attention to achieve disentangled stylised generation. Negative content guidance, inspired by classifier-free guidance, is introduced to reduce content leakage.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Rearranging image-prompt cross-attention together with negative content guidance is presented as a route to disentangled stylised generation.

title: Locating and Repairing Domain Shift in VLM Trajectory Planning
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Main Track). 30 pages, 7 figures, 16 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly adopted as end-to-end driving planners, yet they suffer from cross-city domain shift. Existing methods treat this shift as a single quantity addressed by uniform alignment or single-site editing. We challenge this view on two counts: (i) domain shift in VLM trajectory planners is inherently structured across modality and layer, and (ii) a locate-then-repair recipe matched to this structure outperforms every uniform-objective baseline. We analyse domain shift via activation patching and uncover two regularities. (F1) Modality axis. Image and text tokens exhibit distinct shift patterns in each VLM. (F2) Layer axis. The layer-wise shift partition is architecture-dependent and dataset-stable. These findings recast domain shift as a two-dimensional tensor indexed by modality (image vs. text tokens) and layer, motivating a simple principle: locate where shift occurs, and repair only there. We instantiate this principle in MoLaRx (Modality-Layer Repair), a locate-then-repair framework. The Causal Importance Score (CIS) estimates the domain shift as a modality-layer tensor and partitions the layers into functional zones. CIS-Guided Selective Repair (CISR) then applies a matched operator (Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) / low-rank adaptation (LoRA) / freezing) to repair each zone, with the composition adapting automatically to each architecture. We evaluate MoLaRx on three architecturally distinct VLMs (LFM2-VL-1.6B, Qwen2-VL-2B, and PaliGemma2-3B) across two cross-city benchmarks (nuScenes and Argoverse 2). MoLaRx attains the lowest cross-city trajectory-error gap among adaptation methods in all six main-table settings, while using 50-60% fewer trainable parameters and 8.4-10.9 ms lower inference latency. In contrast, uniform MMD-only adaptation collapses in all six settings, highlighting the importance of structure-guided repair.

AI.tldr: MoLaRx is a locate-then-repair framework for cross-city domain shift in VLM trajectory planners, repairing each modality-layer zone with a matched operator. It achieves the lowest cross-city trajectory-error gap among adaptation methods in all six main-table settings, using 50-60% fewer trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing methods treat VLM domain shift as a single quantity, addressed by uniform alignment or single-site editing, although the shift may be structured across modality and layer.
AI.method: Activation patching reveals a modality axis, where image and text tokens shift differently, and a layer axis, where the layer-wise partition is architecture-dependent and dataset-stable. The Causal Importance Score estimates the shift as a modality-layer tensor and partitions layers into functional zones. CIS-Guided Selective Repair then applies MMD, LoRA or freezing to each zone.
AI.result: Evaluated on LFM2-VL-1.6B, Qwen2-VL-2B and PaliGemma2-3B across nuScenes and Argoverse 2, MoLaRx attains the lowest cross-city trajectory-error gap among adaptation methods in all six main-table settings, with 50-60% fewer trainable parameters and 8.4-10.9 ms lower inference latency. Uniform MMD-only adaptation collapses in all six settings.
AI.conclusion: Locating where shift occurs and repairing only there outperforms uniform objectives, highlighting the value of structure-guided repair.

title: 3D Segmentation in the Clinic: A Grand Challenge
comment: 9 pages, 1 table. Published in the proceedings of the MICCAI 2007 workshop 3D Segmentation in the Clinic: A Grand Challenge
summary: This paper describes the set-up of a segmentation competition for automatic and semi-automatic extraction of the liver from computed tomography scans and the caudate nucleus from brain MRI data. This competition was held in the form of a workshop at the 2007 Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention conference. The rationale for organizing the competition is discussed, the training and test data sets for both segmentation tasks are described and the scoring system used to evaluate the segmentation is presented.

AI.tldr: The paper describes the design of a 2007 MICCAI workshop competition for semi-automatic and automatic segmentation of the liver from CT and the caudate nucleus from brain MRI. It covers the rationale, training and test data, and the scoring system.
AI.motivation: The authors explain why a segmentation competition was organised for clinically relevant structures, which is the stated purpose of the workshop.
AI.method: The competition is set up as a workshop at MICCAI 2007, with training and test datasets for liver CT and caudate nucleus MRI segmentation and a defined scoring system for evaluation.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The paper documents the set-up of a segmentation challenge as a benchmark resource for clinical 3D segmentation.

title: LIFT: Local Metric Alignment and Foundation-guided Propagation for Few-shot Depth Completion
summary: Few-shot depth completion aims to recover dense metric depth from sparse measurements using only a small number of target-domain annotations, offering a favorable balance between annotation cost and model adaptation. We propose LIFT, a framework that harnesses both depth and feature priors from a frozen pretrained monocular depth estimation (MDE) foundation model for few-shot depth completion. Specifically, LIFT first estimates local scale and shift parameters on a coarse grid and interpolates them into smooth, dense parameter fields, providing a spatially adaptive metric depth initialization. It then progressively refines this initialization through multi-scale depth propagation guided by foundation features. Finally, a lightweight residual decoder combines multi-level foundation features with propagation correction to refine the metric depth. Extensive experiments on NYUv2 and KITTI-DC demonstrate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art few-shot performance. The source code will soon be released.

AI.tldr: LIFT is a few-shot depth completion framework that uses a frozen monocular depth foundation model to produce dense metric depth from sparse measurements with few target-domain annotations. It reports state-of-the-art few-shot performance on NYUv2 and KITTI-DC.
AI.motivation: Dense metric depth from sparse measurements usually needs many target-domain annotations, while few-shot adaptation should balance annotation cost and model adaptation.
AI.method: LIFT estimates local scale and shift on a coarse grid and interpolates them into dense parameter fields for spatially adaptive metric initialisation. Multi-scale depth propagation guided by foundation features then refines it, and a lightweight residual decoder combines multi-level foundation features with propagation correction.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on NYUv2 and KITTI-DC show state-of-the-art few-shot performance.
AI.conclusion: Combining local metric alignment with foundation-guided propagation gives accurate metric depth from very few annotations.

title: Tiny Evidence Region Localization with Selective Contrastive On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: Multimodal large language models have made progress in general visual tasks. However, limitations remain in fine-grained visual tasks requiring evidence from minute image regions. Existing methods primarily train models using evidence-related regions while overlooking the influence of extensive background regions, resulting in a limited ability to resist interference from irrelevant regions. We propose selective positive-negative on-policy self-distillation (SPN-OPSD), which considers both evidence and background regions. Supervision from both views improves the model's ability to resist interference from irrelevant regions. Furthermore, selective token-level distillation provides more informative supervision, improving the model's ability to attend to evidence regions in Fine-Grained Visual Tasks. On Qwen3.5-2B, SPN-OPSD improves accuracy on V* Bench, ZoomBench, and MME-RealWorld-Lite from 76.44%, 45.92%, and 57.43% to 84.82%, 54.56%, and 59.56%, respectively. Similar gains are also observed on Qwen3.5-0.8B.

AI.tldr: SPN-OPSD is a selective positive-negative on-policy self-distillation method that supervises both evidence and background regions to help multimodal LLMs localise tiny evidence regions. It lifts Qwen3.5-2B on V* Bench, ZoomBench and MME-RealWorld-Lite, and similar gains are reported on Qwen3.5-0.8B.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained visual tasks need evidence from minute image regions, but training on evidence regions alone ignores the interference of extensive background regions.
AI.method: SPN-OPSD supervises the model on both evidence and background views. Selective token-level distillation provides more informative supervision for attending to evidence regions.
AI.result: On Qwen3.5-2B, accuracy rises from 76.44% to 84.82% on V* Bench, from 45.92% to 54.56% on ZoomBench, and from 57.43% to 59.56% on MME-RealWorld-Lite. Similar gains are observed on Qwen3.5-0.8B.
AI.conclusion: Modelling both evidence and background regions makes multimodal models more robust to irrelevant regions in fine-grained visual tasks.

title: Writer-independent handedness identification from offline Bangla handwriting under controlled acquisition
summary: Handedness is a soft-biometric cue for forensic document examination and writer profiling, yet reported accuracies from offline handwriting rarely keep writers, texts and image acquisition apart, so models may recognise the writer or capture conditions rather than the writing hand. Such controlled evidence is missing for Bangla. Using our BanglaHand dataset of 42 writers (21 left- and 21 right-handed), who each wrote six shared prompts and two own texts under controlled collection and photography, we evaluate handedness identification with all images of each test writer held out, whole-writer permutation tests and photometric controls. An ink-gradient descriptor identified the handedness of unseen writers with 77.4% balanced accuracy (95% writer-bootstrap interval 67.7-86.5%; p=0.001) and frozen ImageNet embeddings with 69.5-72.0%. Part of this signal is stroke darkness: in a post hoc analysis, right-handed writers' strokes were darker at their centres for equal stroke width, consistent with higher pen pressure and not explained by lighting drift. With ink density and brightness regressed out, the descriptor still reached 64.5% (p=0.027), whereas writing-only shape features were weaker (60.8%; p=0.090). Handedness is thus identifiable from offline Bangla handwriting under controlled acquisition, and photometric controls are essential to interpret such cues.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that handedness can be identified from offline Bangla handwriting under controlled acquisition, using writer-independent evaluation on the BanglaHand dataset of 42 writers. It also shows that photometric controls are needed, since part of the signal is stroke darkness.
AI.motivation: Reported handedness accuracies from offline handwriting often fail to separate writers, texts and acquisition conditions, so models may recognise the writer or capture conditions rather than the writing hand. Controlled evidence is missing for Bangla.
AI.method: BanglaHand has 42 writers (21 left-handed, 21 right-handed) writing six shared prompts and two own texts under controlled collection and photography. The evaluation holds out all images of each test writer and uses whole-writer permutation tests and photometric controls. An ink-gradient descriptor and frozen ImageNet embeddings are compared.
AI.result: The ink-gradient descriptor identifies unseen writers' handedness with 77.4% balanced accuracy (95% writer-bootstrap interval 67.7-86.5%; p=0.001), and frozen ImageNet embeddings reach 69.5-72.0%. With ink density and brightness regressed out, the descriptor still reaches 64.5% (p=0.027), while writing-only shape features reach 60.8% (p=0.090).
AI.conclusion: Handedness is identifiable from offline Bangla handwriting under controlled acquisition, but photometric controls are essential to interpret such cues because stroke darkness contributes to the signal.

title: RoadState: A Domain-Prior-Enhanced Vision-Language System for Industrial-Grade Lane-Level Map Updating
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, including appendices. Accepted to AAAI-IAAI 2027, poster presentation
summary: Lane-level map updating requires temporally consistent, physically valid, and auditable road-scene semantics despite occlusions, ambiguous lane markings, temporary obstacles, and viewpoint changes. We present RoadState, a production-deployed vision-language system that transforms sequential road-scene observations into structured lane-level semantics for Baidu Maps' map-updating pipeline. Its core model, RoadState-VLM, formulates road-scene understanding as autoregressive state estimation, predicting the current structured road state from the previous observation and symbolic state together with the current observation. We introduce Geometric Chain-of-Thought (Geo-CoT), which uses a directed acyclic graph of semantic dependencies as a domain prior to improve semantic consistency and reasoning fidelity across interdependent road-state dimensions. Extensive experiments on a real-world dataset show that RoadState-VLM achieves 94.33% mean accuracy across six road-state dimensions, outperforming the strongest fine-tuned VLM baseline. Ablation studies further demonstrate the complementary effectiveness of Geo-CoT and temporal transition context. A cascaded routing pipeline directs routine cases to lightweight models while reserving complex cases for RoadState-VLM. Since its deployment in March 2025, RoadState has supported lane-level map updating across more than 360 cities and reduced overall production costs by 30%. Together with human-in-the-loop auditing, the system maintains robust performance under stress-test conditions. These results demonstrate how domain-prior-enhanced reasoning, structured state interfaces, selective routing, and human quality control can bridge the gap between VLM-based road-scene understanding and large-scale lane-level map updating.

AI.tldr: RoadState is a production vision-language system that turns sequential road-scene observations into structured lane-level semantics for Baidu Maps' map-updating pipeline. Its core model, RoadState-VLM, uses Geometric Chain-of-Thought over a dependency DAG and reaches 94.33% mean accuracy across six road-state dimensions.
AI.motivation: Lane-level map updating needs temporally consistent, physically valid and auditable road-scene semantics despite occlusions, ambiguous lane markings, temporary obstacles and viewpoint changes.
AI.method: The model treats road-scene understanding as autoregressive state estimation, predicting the current structured road state from the previous observation and symbolic state plus the current observation. Geometric Chain-of-Thought (Geo-CoT) uses a directed acyclic graph of semantic dependencies as a domain prior, and a cascaded router sends routine cases to lightweight models and complex cases to RoadState-VLM.
AI.result: RoadState-VLM reaches 94.33% mean accuracy across six road-state dimensions on a real-world dataset, beating the strongest fine-tuned VLM baseline. Ablations show Geo-CoT and temporal transition context are complementary. Since deployment in March 2025 the system has supported more than 360 cities and cut overall production costs by 30%.
AI.conclusion: Domain-prior-enhanced reasoning, structured state interfaces, selective routing and human quality control can bridge VLM-based road-scene understanding and large-scale lane-level map updating.

title: Unified Framework with Convex-Concave Decomposition and Sparse Topological Learning for Skeleton-Based Clinical Assessment
summary: Skeleton-based rehabilitation assessment faces fundamental limitations of fixed topologies which cannot model compensatory patterns, uniform joint treatments overlook clinically important deviations, and lack of geometric understand- ing. We propose Concave-Convex Decomposition Sparse Topological Graph Convolutional Network (CC2-STG), a multi-stream model that combines geo- metric decomposition, sparse feature learning, and adaptive topology. Our framework decomposes joint relationships into complementary convex-concave distance functions to model both local and global movement characteristics, with sparse regularization with proximal optimization selecting clinically relevant geo- metric features, while multi-scale topological analysis captures non-anatomical joint dependencies in pathological movements. Experiments on the KiMoRe and UIPRMD datasets validate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance on clinical pathological movement assessment.

AI.tldr: CC2-STG is a multi-stream graph convolutional network for skeleton-based rehabilitation assessment that combines convex-concave geometric decomposition, sparse feature learning and adaptive topology. It reports state-of-the-art performance on clinical pathological movement assessment on KiMoRe and UIPRMD.
AI.motivation: Fixed skeleton topologies cannot model compensatory movement patterns, uniform joint treatment overlooks clinically important deviations, and existing methods lack geometric understanding.
AI.method: Joint relationships are decomposed into complementary convex-concave distance functions to capture local and global movement characteristics. Sparse regularization with proximal optimization selects clinically relevant geometric features, and multi-scale topological analysis captures non-anatomical joint dependencies in pathological movements.
AI.result: The approach is validated on the KiMoRe and UIPRMD datasets and achieves state-of-the-art performance on clinical pathological movement assessment. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Modelling geometric decomposition, sparse selection and adaptive topology together improves skeleton-based clinical movement assessment.

title: BAPLe++: Cross-Model Transferability and Prompt-Level Defense of Backdoors in Medical Foundation Models
summary: Medical foundation models (Med-FMs) are increasingly adapted to clinical tasks through prompt learning, which tunes a small set of prompt tokens while the backbone remains frozen. Recent work has shown that this efficiency introduces a vulnerability: jointly optimizing learnable prompts and an imperceptible noise trigger during few-shot adaptation implants a backdoor that leaves clean performance intact but steers triggered inputs to an attacker-chosen class. Since prompts are compact and readily shared, this raises two questions: whether a backdoored prompt remains effective on a different Med-FM, and whether it can be repaired without retraining the backbone. We address both in BAPLe++. First, we present the first study of cross-model transferability of prompt-based backdoors, quantified by two proposed metrics, Clean Accuracy Difference (CAD) and Backdoor Accuracy Difference (BAD). Second, we propose DePLe (Defense via Prompt Learning), which uses the infected prompt as a fixed anchor and learns a new prompt on a small clean set that preserves the clean task while diverging from the compromised embedding region. Experiments on four Med-FMs and six chest X-ray and histopathology datasets show that backdoors transfer across models, but asymmetrically and in a dataset-dependent manner. Compared with four training-free input transformations, DePLe reduces backdoor accuracy more consistently while preserving, and in several settings improving, clean accuracy. Our code can be accessed on this https URL

AI.tldr: BAPLe++ studies whether backdoors implanted in prompt-tuned medical foundation models transfer across models and can be repaired without retraining the backbone. It proposes the DePLe defense, which learns a new prompt that diverges from the infected prompt and beats four training-free input transformations on backdoor accuracy.
AI.motivation: Prompt learning on frozen medical foundation models is efficient but exposes a backdoor vulnerability, and compact shareable prompts raise the questions of whether a backdoored prompt works on other models and whether it can be repaired cheaply.
AI.method: The paper gives the first study of cross-model transferability of prompt-based backdoors, measured with Clean Accuracy Difference (CAD) and Backdoor Accuracy Difference (BAD). The defense DePLe uses the infected prompt as a fixed anchor and learns a new prompt on a small clean set that preserves the clean task while moving away from the compromised embedding region.
AI.result: Experiments on four Med-FMs and six chest X-ray and histopathology datasets show that backdoors transfer across models asymmetrically and in a dataset-dependent way. Compared with four training-free input transformations, DePLe reduces backdoor accuracy more consistently and preserves, and in several settings improves, clean accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-level backdoors are a real transfer risk for shared medical foundation model prompts, and prompt-level defenses offer a backbone-free repair route.

title: How reliable is an embedding of the seabed? Repeat-look measurement of frozen encoders on synthetic aperture sonar
comment: Accepted at the Maritime Computer Vision Workshop (MaCVi) at WACV 2027
summary: Pretrained encoders from self-supervised representation learning are increasingly applied to sonar imagery of the seafloor, where they are evaluated with protocols that take one embedding per target. A target patch of seabed, by contrast, is re-imaged from an alternate look on overlapping survey passes, so each embedding is one measurement of that target. Standard protocols cannot say how consistent those measurements are, or how much of their spread belongs to the patch and how much to the acquisition geometry. We treat this as a measurement-reliability problem. Using a synthetic-aperture sonar (SAS) survey, we measure the repeat-look reliability of embeddings from a frozen natural-image encoder (DINOv3 ViT-S/16). Standard single-look metrics, effective rank, clustering and a linear probe for coral, are all stable to the look, and the probe performs well (AUC 0.93). Yet the repeat-look reliability of the same embeddings is poor, with a distance-based intraclass correlation (dbICC) of 0.20 and nearest neighbours and clusters that barely agree across looks. This contradiction resolves as we find the probe learns a stable direction, whose ICC of 0.60 is 3.0 times that of the full embedding. Variance components, calculated from generalizability theory, attribute under a tenth of the within-cell spread to look acquisition geometry. The rest is cell-specific and cannot be separated without repeat passes at matched geometry. A sonar-pretrained encoder (BenthicDINO) and a classical SAS texture descriptor show the same pattern. For this dataset and the tested representations, uses that depend on patch identity fail, such as cross-pass comparison and retrieval, while uses at the level of habitat type (e.g. coral classification) do not. Because the standard metrics did not detect this, we argue that repeat-look reliability should accompany any evaluation of representations of the seafloor.

AI.tldr: The paper measures how repeatable frozen encoder embeddings are when the same seabed patch is imaged from alternate looks in synthetic aperture sonar. It finds that repeat-look reliability is poor even though standard single-look metrics and a coral linear probe look good, so patch-identity uses fail while habitat-type uses hold.
AI.motivation: Standard protocols use one embedding per target, but a seabed patch is re-imaged on overlapping passes, so each embedding is a measurement. Existing protocols cannot say how consistent these measurements are or how much of their spread comes from the patch versus the acquisition geometry.
AI.method: The authors treat the problem as measurement reliability on a SAS survey and measure repeat-look reliability of DINOv3 ViT-S/16 embeddings using distance-based intraclass correlation (dbICC), nearest-neighbour and cluster agreement across looks, and variance components from generalizability theory. They also test a sonar-pretrained encoder (BenthicDINO) and a classical SAS texture descriptor.
AI.result: Single-look metrics, effective rank, clustering and a coral linear probe (AUC 0.93) are stable across looks, yet the full embedding has dbICC 0.20 and neighbours and clusters barely agree across looks. The probe's stable direction has ICC 0.60, 3.0 times the full embedding's. Under a tenth of the within-cell spread is attributed to look acquisition geometry, and BenthicDINO and the texture descriptor show the same pattern.
AI.conclusion: For this dataset and these representations, patch-identity uses such as cross-pass comparison and retrieval fail while habitat-level uses such as coral classification do not, so repeat-look reliability should accompany evaluation of seafloor representations.

title: WorldFoundry: Towards Unified Infrastructure for World Intelligence
comment: 39 pages, 10 figures. This technical report will be updated periodically
summary: Visual generative models increasingly blur the line between synthesizing observations and simulating environments. Yet visual plausibility alone does not constitute successful world modeling: compelling outputs may lack persistent state, physical dynamics, or causally consistent responses to interactions. We define a generative world model as a predictive dynamical system that maintains a persistent, history-conditioned representation of an environment, updates that representation in response to actions or interventions, and generates temporally coherent trajectories that reflect outcomes under observed and counterfactual interventions. From this definition, we derive an intelligence-oriented framework spanning perceptual grounding, persistent state modeling, controllable transformation, dynamics-aware prediction, and closed-loop interaction.
