Experiments across photogrammetry, classical multi-view stereo, neural implicit surfaces, Gaussian-splatting-based reconstruction, and multi-view photometric stereo show that Martine enables regime-aware evaluation with explicit control over reference-data accuracy. The benchmark resolves sub-millimetric reconstruction differences, with a best observed Chamfer distance of 0.058 mm over the evaluated visible surface.

AI.tldr: Martine is a benchmark for controlled multi-view 3D surface reconstruction with 28 objects, including transparent and fine-structured ones, captured at 9568 x 6376 pixels from 84 views under single-light and multi-light regimes. The best observed Chamfer distance over the visible surface is 0.058 mm.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-view benchmarks restrict viewpoint coverage, resolution or illumination, and others lack accurate 3D ground truth or quantified image-to-geometry alignment, which limits metric surface evaluation.
AI.method: The benchmark provides object-independent camera calibration, accurate 3D ground-truth scans, calibration and image-to-geometry accuracy measured on test images, and 3D property masks for analyzing errors by material, visibility, curvature and fine structures.
AI.result: Experiments across photogrammetry, classical multi-view stereo, neural implicit surfaces, Gaussian-splatting-based reconstruction and multi-view photometric stereo show regime-aware evaluation with explicit control over reference-data accuracy. The best observed Chamfer distance is 0.058 mm, and the benchmark resolves sub-millimetric differences.
AI.conclusion: Martine enables fair, regime-aware comparison of reconstruction methods under controlled acquisition, with reference-data accuracy made explicit.

title: Rethinking Geometric Depth in Monocular 3D Object Detection: A Projection-Consistent Reformulation
summary: Monocular 3D detection (Mono3D) hinges on recovering depth from a single image, for which the geometric formulation $z \approx f \cdot H / h_{2D}$ is widely adopted due to its simplicity and direct grounding in projective geometry. We show that this formulation harbors a systematic, projection-induced bias: substituting the 2D bounding-box height $h_{2D}$ recovers the depth of an object's visible front surface rather than its center, causing size-dependent underestimation that persists even under ground-truth inputs. We address this front-surface bias with MonoPCA, a unified framework built on a projection-consistent reformulation. At its core, PCDepth retains the measurable $h_{2D}$ and closes the gap to center depth through an orientation- and size-aware correction derived from perspective geometry, eliminating the bias without introducing ill-posed regression targets. Because PCDepth couples depth to predicted object size and orientation, attribute perception becomes essential. We therefore introduce GeoAlign, a teacher-student framework that transfers geometric representations from Vision Foundation Models into a lightweight student, strengthening attribute perception at no inference cost. Across four challenging benchmarks, MonoPCA achieves SoTA performance, including a +1.44% AP$_{3D}$ gain on the KITTI leaderboard and +2.80% on Omni3D$_{OUT}$. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The common depth formula for monocular 3D detection, which uses the 2D box height, has a projection-induced bias; MonoPCA corrects it with a projection-consistent reformulation and transfers geometric attributes from Vision Foundation Models via GeoAlign.
AI.motivation: Substituting the 2D bounding-box height into the geometric depth formula recovers the depth of an object's visible front surface rather than its center, causing size-dependent underestimation even with ground-truth inputs.
AI.method: PCDepth keeps the measurable 2D height and applies an orientation- and size-aware correction derived from perspective geometry, avoiding ill-posed regression targets; GeoAlign is a teacher-student framework that transfers geometric representations from Vision Foundation Models into a lightweight student at no inference cost.
AI.result: MonoPCA achieves state-of-the-art performance across four benchmarks, including a +1.44% AP3D gain on the KITTI leaderboard and +2.80% on Omni3D OUT.
AI.conclusion: Removing the front-surface projection bias and strengthening attribute perception improves monocular 3D object detection.

title: MICE: Multi-animal Interaction Context Encoder - A Hierarchical Foundation Model for Mouse Behavior
comment: NeurIPS 2026 (Spotlight). 25 pages, 4 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Quantifying mouse behavior from pose is a foundational tool in neuroscience, ethology, drug discovery, and animal welfare. Self-supervised foundation models are a natural fit, but a foundation model for mouse behavior must handle social behavior - many behaviors that matter (aggression, courtship, mounting, allogrooming) are inherently multi-animal. Existing self-supervised pose models fall short: they encode each animal independently and discard interaction signal, hard-code the animal count, and pretrain one dataset at a time. We introduce MICE (Multi-animal Interaction Context Encoder), a hierarchical foundation model for mouse behavior that pretrains jointly on six mouse-pose corpora spanning one to four mice and 7 to 27 keypoints. MICE combines a hierarchical individual encoder capturing per-mouse kinematics at multiple temporal scales with a Perceiver-style social encoder whose learned latent codebook decouples parameter count from animal count, so a single checkpoint serves any group size without retraining. Across four evaluation protocols spanning six datasets, MICE matches or exceeds prior keypoint-based baselines, and layer-wise probing shows the social stage incrementally improves discriminability beyond the individual encoder. Code, weights, and data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MICE is a hierarchical self-supervised foundation model for mouse behavior that pretrains jointly on six mouse-pose corpora and encodes social interaction so that one checkpoint serves any group size.
AI.motivation: Existing self-supervised pose models encode each animal independently, discard interaction signal, hard-code the animal count, and pretrain on one dataset at a time.
AI.method: A hierarchical individual encoder captures per-mouse kinematics at multiple temporal scales, and a Perceiver-style social encoder with a learned latent codebook decouples parameter count from animal count.
AI.result: Across four evaluation protocols spanning six datasets, MICE matches or exceeds prior keypoint-based baselines, and layer-wise probing shows the social stage incrementally improves discriminability beyond the individual encoder.
AI.conclusion: A single checkpoint can serve any group size without retraining, and modeling social context adds discriminative information to mouse behavior representations.

title: SurfScaff3D: Bridging Geometric and Semantic Representations for LLM-based 3D Object Generation
summary: Creating high-quality 3D content has traditionally required specialist expertise and experience with complex tools. The growing ecosystem of AI-assisted creativity demands accessible and intuitive 3D generation systems. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising directions, yet extending their generative capabilities to 3D remains fundamentally challenging because existing 3D representations are not naturally compatible with language-based reasoning. Current approaches either depend on expensive fine-tuning or impose restrictive structural priors that sacrifice expressiveness and exclude organic shapes. We argue that the mismatch between LLM-native reasoning and conventional 3D parameterizations is a core bottleneck of LLM-driven 3D generation. To address this, we introduce the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS), a representation designed around semantically meaningful, interpretable part-level abstractions that are naturally understood by both humans and LLMs, enabling expressive, editable, and open-domain 3D generation without imposing restrictive geometric priors or expensive fine-tuning. Building upon HPS, we introduce SurfScaff3D, an interactive framework for text and image-to-3D generation. HPS inherits the flexibility of B-spline patches, while exposing an interface that leverages open-world capabilities of foundation models to reliably generate 3D. Its hierarchical part-level semantic labels enable targeted, natural-language edits at any level of granularity without re-running generation. Further, HPS offers explicit per-patch control over surface detail, enabling more expressive geometry capable of representing arbitrary objects. Extensive experiments against state-of-the-art LLM-based 3D generation methods demonstrate strong geometric fidelity, semantic alignment, and flexible editing across diverse object categories.

AI.tldr: SurfScaff3D is an interactive text and image-to-3D generation framework built on the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold, a B-spline patch representation with part-level semantic labels that LLMs can reason over.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based 3D generation either depends on expensive fine-tuning or imposes restrictive structural priors that sacrifice expressiveness and exclude organic shapes.
AI.method: The Hierarchical Patch Scaffold uses semantically meaningful, interpretable part-level abstractions that inherit the flexibility of B-spline patches, with hierarchical part labels enabling natural-language edits and explicit per-patch control over surface detail.
AI.result: Experiments against state-of-the-art LLM-based 3D generation methods demonstrate strong geometric fidelity, semantic alignment, and flexible editing across diverse object categories.
AI.conclusion: Aligning the 3D representation with LLM-native reasoning removes a core bottleneck, enabling expressive, editable, open-domain 3D generation without expensive fine-tuning.

title: LocateAnyMesh: Grounding 3D Mesh Queries in 2D Images with Vision-Language Models
summary: Textured 3D meshes specify object geometry and appearance, making them a natural query for finding a particular asset in an image. We introduce LocateAnyMesh, a vision-language model that uses the mesh itself as part of its prompt. A frozen 3D encoder maps colored surface points to a compact token sequence, which a learned connector places alongside image and instruction tokens. We evaluate two grounding models with PPAT mesh tokens: LAM-Select selects image-region proposals, while LAM-Direct predicts coordinates directly. Neither requires rendered query views or view-template matching. New objects require a single encoder pass and no object-specific fine-tuning. LAM-Select improves localization on the reported real-image suites and the official BOP YCB-V evaluation. Secondary experiments compare mesh encoders, and a LAM-Direct study isolates surface color. A single-seed LAM-Select continuation supplies pointing and mesh-only description evidence without replacing the reported localization model. The results support mesh tokens as a query representation, with remaining limitations in presence decisions, identity binding, proposal coverage, and descriptive fidelity.

AI.tldr: LocateAnyMesh is a vision-language model that uses a textured 3D mesh as part of its prompt to ground the queried object in 2D images, with a frozen 3D encoder mapping colored surface points to tokens.
AI.motivation: A textured mesh is a natural query for finding a particular asset in an image, and the work aims to use it directly without rendered query views or view-template matching.
AI.method: A frozen 3D encoder maps colored surface points to a compact token sequence that a learned connector places alongside image and instruction tokens; LAM-Select selects image-region proposals, and LAM-Direct predicts coordinates directly.
AI.result: LAM-Select improves localization on the reported real-image suites and the official BOP YCB-V evaluation; secondary experiments compare mesh encoders and isolate surface color, and a single-seed continuation adds pointing and mesh-only description evidence.
AI.conclusion: Mesh tokens are a viable query representation, with remaining limitations in presence decisions, identity binding, proposal coverage, and descriptive fidelity.

title: SurgTAP-3D: A Large-Scale Cross-Surgery Video Dataset with Contact-Aware 3D Motion Tracking
comment: Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics (T-RO)
summary: Understanding 3D scene dynamics in minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is a fundamental step toward physically intelligent and autonomous surgical systems. However, existing public datasets offer limited scalability and diversity in real-world clinical scenarios. Moreover, annotations typically focus on either tissue or instruments alone, overlooking tool-tissue interactions. This gap limits applications such as augmented reality guidance and autonomous surgery driven by vision-language-action (VLA) models or world models, which demand large-scale, high-quality 3D supervision. In this work, we construct SurgTAP-3D, a large-scale in-vivo pseudo-3D surgical motion tracking dataset and benchmark, comprising 520K frames, 4,549 action clips, and 1.4M 2D/3D point trajectories from diverse robotic and manual procedures under unified action categories. To make annotation scalable, we design a unified framework for surgical 3D point tracking that converts uncalibrated monocular surgical videos into structured 4D annotations through contact-region prompting, active-tool segmentation, dynamic bundle adjustment, and global 4D refinement. This pipeline adapts foundation priors to surgical videos and produces temporally consistent trajectories, pseudo-scale geometry, camera poses, and instrument masks. The dataset captures realistic challenges inherent to surgical environments, including occlusions, smoke, bleeding, and rapid instrument motion. We establish a comprehensive benchmark on SurgPose, SurgT, and STIR, covering both instrument and tissue tracking. We demonstrate instrument displacement estimation, deformable surface reconstruction, and foundation-model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of our dataset and annotation framework for 3D surgical point tracking, reconstruction, and surgical action understanding. Homepage: this https URL

AI.tldr: SurgTAP-3D is a large-scale in-vivo pseudo-3D surgical motion tracking dataset and benchmark of 520K frames, 4,549 action clips and 1.4M 2D/3D point trajectories, built with a scalable annotation framework.
AI.motivation: Existing public surgical datasets offer limited scalability and diversity, and their annotations usually cover either tissue or instruments alone, overlooking tool-tissue interactions.
AI.method: A unified surgical 3D point tracking framework converts uncalibrated monocular surgical videos into structured 4D annotations through contact-region prompting, active-tool segmentation, dynamic bundle adjustment, and global 4D refinement.
AI.result: A benchmark on SurgPose, SurgT and STIR covers instrument and tissue tracking, and the authors demonstrate instrument displacement estimation, deformable surface reconstruction, and foundation-model fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The dataset and annotation framework are effective for 3D surgical point tracking, reconstruction, and surgical action understanding.

title: Correctness Metric Matters: NWD-Based Calibration Loss for Tiny Person Detection in UAV Infrared Imagery
summary: Detection calibration aligns predicted confidence with empirical correctness. Existing calibration losses inherit their correctness definition from box regression, specifically IoU against a hard threshold. We show that this target is geometrically ill-posed for tiny objects in UAV infrared imagery, where persons occupy less than 0.1\% of the image. The same pixel error is penalized more heavily as the target shrinks, so binary prediction calibration (BPC) actively suppresses confidences that should be high. On HIT-UAV, BPC with an IoU target degrades image-level localization-aware ECE (LaECE) from 0.0689 to 0.0761, 0.0649 to 0.0733, and 0.0653 to 0.0682 across Low, Mid, and High signal-to-clutter ratio (SCR) groups. We replace the IoU target with a continuous, scale-invariant normalized Wasserstein distance (NWD). The NWD target reduces LaECE\(_{\mathrm{NWD}}\) relative to BPC+IoU on all three groups (\(p<10^{-7}\)) with mAP neutral (0.9356 vs.\ 0.9347), and an independent center-offset anchor confirms that the gain is a genuine geometric correction. The improvement holds across a broad plateau of calibration weights. The NWD formulation requires no inference-time mapping layer. If a validation-fitted isotonic map is applied on top of it, calibration is lowered further, and the two corrections act on different components of the same error. The metric-level remedy has a measurable boundary. Target-background thermal pairing in the training distribution and detection-level aggregation under per-image detection-count heterogeneity lie outside it. Both are quantified independently of the NWD target.

AI.tldr: Replacing the IoU correctness target in a calibration loss with a scale-invariant normalized Wasserstein distance (NWD) improves calibration for tiny person detection in UAV infrared imagery without changing mAP.
AI.motivation: Calibration losses inherit an IoU-based hard-threshold correctness target that is geometrically ill-posed for tiny objects, where persons occupy under 0.1% of the image, so binary prediction calibration suppresses confidences that should be high.
AI.method: The IoU target is replaced by a continuous, scale-invariant normalized Wasserstein distance that needs no inference-time mapping layer; a validation-fitted isotonic map can optionally be applied on top of it.
AI.result: On HIT-UAV the NWD target reduces LaECE relative to BPC with an IoU target on all three SCR groups (p < 1e-7) with mAP neutral (0.9356 vs 0.9347), whereas BPC with IoU raised LaECE from 0.0689 to 0.0761, 0.0649 to 0.0733, and 0.0653 to 0.0682 across the Low, Mid, and High SCR groups.
AI.conclusion: The gain is a genuine geometric correction confirmed by a center-offset anchor, and the metric-level remedy has a measurable boundary: target-background thermal pairing and detection-level aggregation under varying detection counts lie outside it.

title: Dense Flow from Adaptive Correspondence
summary: Optical flow requires reliable matching from sufficient visual context and precise motion at every pixel. Existing methods such as WAFT match and estimate flow on the same coarse grids, then recover dense flow through learned upsampling, without explicitly linking visual support for matching to dense flow reconstruction. Our key insight is that dense pixel-level flow does not require equally dense matching. We decouple correspondence scale from flow resolution by adapting the size and shape of spatial supports to image structure for reliable matching, while reusing these supports for precise dense flow reconstruction. We realize this in Flow from Adaptive Token Estimation (FATE), whose token supports expand within coherent regions and contract near motion boundaries. Shared pixel-to-token associations pool features for matching and reconstruct pixel flow from token motions. Flow supervision jointly trains pixel grouping, token matching, and flow estimation without grouping labels, allowing FATE to anticipate which pixels are likely to move together from appearance alone. Trained on FlyingChairs/FlyingThings3D, FATE achieves the highest zero-shot accuracy on Sintel Final and KITTI, a critical setting given scarce real-world flow labels. For visible pixels, FATE improves accuracy within coherent regions, and more near motion boundaries. Its largest gains occur where direct matches are unavailable: Occluded or out-of-frame pixels account for roughly 10% of valid pixels but 50% of WAFT's total error. Experiments show that adaptive correspondence through pixel-to-token grouping enables reliable matching and precise pixel-level flow, improving generalization to unseen real scenes.

AI.tldr: FATE (Flow from Adaptive Token Estimation) decouples correspondence scale from flow resolution by adapting token supports to image structure, achieving the highest zero-shot accuracy on Sintel Final and KITTI when trained on FlyingChairs and FlyingThings3D.
AI.motivation: Existing methods such as WAFT match and estimate flow on the same coarse grids and recover dense flow through learned upsampling, without explicitly linking the visual support used for matching to dense flow reconstruction.
AI.method: Token supports expand within coherent regions and contract near motion boundaries; shared pixel-to-token associations pool features for matching and reconstruct pixel flow from token motions, and flow supervision jointly trains pixel grouping, token matching, and flow estimation without grouping labels.
AI.result: FATE achieves the highest zero-shot accuracy on Sintel Final and KITTI and improves accuracy within coherent regions and near motion boundaries; its largest gains are on occluded or out-of-frame pixels, which are about 10% of valid pixels but 50% of WAFT's total error.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive correspondence through pixel-to-token grouping enables reliable matching and precise pixel-level flow, improving generalization to unseen real scenes.

title: GeoPilot: Diagnosis-Guided Interventions and Geometric Evaluation for Aerial Reconstruction
summary: When a mesh reconstructed from aerial remote-sensing imagery disagrees with reference geometry, deciding what to change requires a diagnosis of the reconstruction process. We present GeoPilot, a workflow that turns diagnostics and prior observations into executable program or camera-configuration interventions. A large language model proposes the change, numerical tools reconstruct the mesh, and an external evaluator measures its geometry under a stated coordinate and reference protocol. The main case tests a shared-intrinsics hypothesis proposed before the comparison. On 224 Metashape-raster development images, shared intrinsics improved all six native-coordinate measures and reduced mean surface-to-reference distance by 7.04%. Reference-assisted alignment fitted and evaluated on separate within-scene checkerboard samples reversed the mean-distance ranking, limiting that gain to native-frame delivery. A separate matched comparison on publisher-undistorted images favored fixed published cameras on all six measures, reducing mean distance by 12.11%; the cameras retain upstream image and laser-scanning adjustment information. With one reconstruction per configuration, these comparisons provide conditional evidence for camera handling. Three end-to-end runs each delivered a mesh and six-metric evaluation from all 327 images of a second development scene.

AI.tldr: GeoPilot is a workflow in which an LLM proposes diagnosis-guided program or camera-configuration interventions for aerial mesh reconstruction, and an external evaluator measures the resulting geometry under a stated protocol.
AI.motivation: When a mesh reconstructed from aerial remote-sensing imagery disagrees with reference geometry, deciding what to change requires a diagnosis of the reconstruction process.
AI.method: An LLM proposes the change, numerical tools reconstruct the mesh, and an external evaluator measures its geometry under a stated coordinate and reference protocol; the main case tests a shared-intrinsics hypothesis stated before the comparison.
AI.result: On 224 Metashape-raster development images, shared intrinsics improved all six native-coordinate measures and reduced mean surface-to-reference distance by 7.04%; reference-assisted alignment reversed the mean-distance ranking, limiting that gain to native-frame delivery; on publisher-undistorted images, fixed published cameras beat the alternative on all six measures, reducing mean distance by 12.11%.
AI.conclusion: Evidence for camera handling is conditional because each configuration was reconstructed once, but three end-to-end runs on a second 327-image scene each delivered a mesh and a six-metric evaluation.

title: SpinSCI: Mask-Conditioned Spatial-Temporal Spin Transformer for Video Snapshot Compressive Imaging
summary: Video snapshot compressive imaging (SCI) recovers multiple frames from one spatiotemporally coded measurement. This paper proposes SpinSCI, a mask-conditioned Spatial-Temporal Spin Transformer whose Mask-Conditioned Ising Refinement Block (MC-IRB) combines attention logits and sensing information to form signed spin couplings. Finite mean-field updates gate residual feature refinement. Physics-guided initialization and final data consistency incorporate the measurement model. Compared with HiSViT$_9$, SpinSCI achieves average PSNR gains of 0.51 dB, 0.23 dB, and 0.04 dB on small-scale gray, mid-scale color, and large-scale color benchmarks, respectively, with 16.9% fewer parameters, 21.0-21.6% fewer FLOPs, 17.1-49.9% lower latency, and 62.3-63.3% lower peak memory. Relative to DU-9stg, average PSNR differs by at most 0.13 dB across these benchmarks, with 28.2-28.7% fewer FLOPs, 64.6-71.7% lower inference latency, and 30.1-35.0% lower peak memory. Qualitative comparisons on the real benchmark further show recovery of fine details and textures. Code and reference checkpoints are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: SpinSCI is a mask-conditioned Spatial-Temporal Spin Transformer for video snapshot compressive imaging that raises PSNR over HiSViT_9 while using fewer parameters, FLOPs, latency and peak memory.
AI.motivation: Video snapshot compressive imaging must recover multiple frames from one spatiotemporally coded measurement, so the reconstruction network should be accurate and efficient while using the sensing mask.
AI.method: The Mask-Conditioned Ising Refinement Block combines attention logits and sensing information to form signed spin couplings, finite mean-field updates gate residual feature refinement, and physics-guided initialization and final data consistency incorporate the measurement model.
AI.result: Against HiSViT_9, average PSNR gains are 0.51, 0.23 and 0.04 dB on small-scale gray, mid-scale color and large-scale color benchmarks, with 16.9% fewer parameters, 21.0-21.6% fewer FLOPs, 17.1-49.9% lower latency and 62.3-63.3% lower peak memory; against DU-9stg, PSNR differs by at most 0.13 dB with 28.2-28.7% fewer FLOPs.
AI.conclusion: The model offers a better accuracy-efficiency trade-off than the compared baselines and recovers fine details and textures in qualitative comparisons on a real benchmark.

title: Calibrated Alarm Thresholds for Compact Fire and Smoke Detectors
summary: Compact object detectors such as YOLOv8n are a common choice for camera-based fire and smoke detection on low-power devices. These detectors are usually evaluated with box-level metrics such as mean average precision, and their outputs are turned into decisions with a fixed confidence threshold such as 0.25 or 0.5. A fire monitoring system, however, makes one decision per image: raise an alarm or not. In this paper we evaluate two publicly available compact detectors on the D-Fire test set at the image level. We compare three simple rules for turning box detections into one alarm score per image, and we use a split conformal procedure to choose the alarm threshold from held-out images so that the expected fraction of missed fire and smoke images stays below a chosen target. We find that the same fixed threshold leads to very different miss rates for the two detectors, 17.3 and 8.4 percent at a threshold of 0.5, while the calibrated threshold meets miss-rate targets of 10, 5 and 1 percent for both detectors and all three rules. At a 5 percent target, the false alarm rate on images without fire or smoke stays between 1.2 and 3.0 percent. We also find that smoke-only images stay below the target even when the overall target is met, and we describe the main failure cases.

AI.tldr: A fixed confidence threshold gives very different image-level miss rates for two compact fire and smoke detectors, and a split conformal procedure can choose alarm thresholds that meet miss-rate targets for both.
AI.motivation: A fire monitoring system makes one alarm decision per image, yet compact detectors are usually evaluated with box-level metrics and used with fixed confidence thresholds such as 0.25 or 0.5.
AI.method: Three simple rules convert box detections into one alarm score per image, and a split conformal procedure on held-out images chooses the alarm threshold so that the expected fraction of missed fire and smoke images stays below a target; two public compact detectors are evaluated on the D-Fire test set.
AI.result: At threshold 0.5 the miss rates are 17.3% and 8.4% for the two detectors, while calibrated thresholds meet targets of 10, 5 and 1% for both detectors and all three rules; at the 5% target the false alarm rate on images without fire or smoke stays between 1.2% and 3.0%, and smoke-only images stay below the target.
AI.conclusion: Image-level threshold calibration is needed because one fixed threshold behaves very differently across detectors, and the paper describes the main failure cases that remain.

title: LangDepth: Vision-Language Scene Priors for Semantic Binning and Cross-Domain Monocular Depth Estimation
summary: Monocular depth estimation has advanced through large-scale pretraining and strong visual backbones, yet metric depth remains sensitive to scene-level scale. Indoor rooms and outdoor driving scenes occupy very different depth ranges, but most depth decoders infer this global structure implicitly from visual features. We ask whether scene-level semantic structure can instead act as an upstream prior that shapes the metric output space before dense prediction. We present LangDepth (SemanticBins), a monocular depth architecture that couples strong visual features with a scene-conditioned output space. A frozen CLIP encoder and a learnable bank of scene- and geometry-oriented concept keys convert image features into a compact scene descriptor, without requiring per-image text or an external captioner. A Scene Prior Module (SPM) maps this descriptor to a scene-conditioned metric depth interval, providing a global range anchor before dense decoding. In parallel, a DINOv2-L backbone with a lightweight FPN extracts dense visual features, and a Per-Pixel Assignment Network (PPAN) assigns pixels to the scene-prescribed bin structure. A confidence gate fuses the dense visual estimate with the SPM prior. We train LangDepth jointly on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI under a modest supervised depth budget, without web-scale depth supervision or pseudo-labelled depth data. A single model achieves delta_1 = 0.960 on NYU, 0.960 on KITTI, 0.887 on DIODE indoor, 0.946 on iBims-1, and 0.861 on SUN RGB-D. Beyond aggregate accuracy, the SPM predicts compact indoor ranges and much wider outdoor KITTI ranges, the gate becomes SPM-dominant on outdoor scenes, and perturbing the routed scene context causes large drops on KITTI and iBims-1. These results support scene-conditioned output spaces as a practical and interpretable mechanism for cross-domain monocular depth estimation.

AI.tldr: LangDepth is a monocular depth architecture that predicts a scene-conditioned metric depth interval from CLIP-based scene descriptors and fuses it with dense DINOv2 features, reaching strong cross-domain accuracy with a modest supervised depth budget.
AI.motivation: Most depth decoders infer global scale implicitly from visual features, although indoor rooms and outdoor driving scenes occupy very different depth ranges.
AI.method: A frozen CLIP encoder and a learnable bank of concept keys form a compact scene descriptor; a Scene Prior Module maps it to a scene-conditioned depth interval, a DINOv2-L backbone with an FPN and a Per-Pixel Assignment Network assign pixels to the prescribed bins, and a confidence gate fuses the dense estimate with the prior, trained jointly on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI.
AI.result: delta_1 is 0.960 on NYU, 0.960 on KITTI, 0.887 on DIODE indoor, 0.946 on iBims-1 and 0.861 on SUN RGB-D; the Scene Prior Module predicts compact indoor ranges and much wider outdoor KITTI ranges, and perturbing the routed scene context causes large drops on KITTI and iBims-1.
AI.conclusion: Scene-conditioned output spaces are a practical and interpretable mechanism for cross-domain monocular depth estimation.

title: Towards Rotation-Only Imaging Geometry: Multi-View Pose Estimation
summary: Global structure-from-motion (SfM) commonly refines relative poses on individual image pairs and then estimates global rotations by rotation averaging. Pairwise refinement does not explicitly combine feature-level constraints with multi-view consistency during rotation initialization. We introduce Global Rotations from Aggregated Matches (GRAM), which estimates global rotations directly from initial relative rotations and inlier matches by minimizing edge-wise rotation-only algebraic residuals. GRAM replaces two-view relative-pose optimization and rotation averaging with a single stage. We further extend rotation- only imaging geometry to multiple views and develop Multi-view Optimization with Rotation-only Reprojection Error (MORE) for nonlinear global rotation refinement. Analytical Rotation-guided Translation (ART) derives locally scaled triplet translations from Linear Global Translation (LiGT) constraints and recovers global translations using weighted least squares. Synthetic and real-world experiments demonstrate the accuracy, robustness, and efficiency of the proposed methods.

AI.tldr: GRAM estimates global rotations directly from initial relative rotations and inlier matches in a single stage, and ART recovers global translations, giving a rotation-only multi-view pose estimation pipeline for global structure-from-motion.
AI.motivation: Global SfM refines relative poses on individual image pairs before averaging rotations, so pairwise refinement does not combine feature-level constraints with multi-view consistency during rotation initialization.
AI.method: GRAM minimizes edge-wise rotation-only algebraic residuals in place of two-view pose optimization and rotation averaging; MORE performs nonlinear global rotation refinement with a rotation-only reprojection error; ART derives locally scaled triplet translations from LiGT constraints and recovers global translations by weighted least squares.
AI.result: Synthetic and real-world experiments are reported to demonstrate the accuracy, robustness, and efficiency of the proposed methods.
AI.conclusion: Extending rotation-only imaging geometry to multiple views yields a single-stage rotation estimator and a translation recovery step that the authors present as accurate, robust, and efficient.

title: FMA-Net: Flexible Modality Adaptation for Robust Multimodal Face Presentation Attack Detection
summary: Multimodal face presentation attack detection (fPAD) improves robustness using complementary RGB, depth, and infrared (IR) cues, but deployment remains challenging when modalities are unavailable or incomplete. Existing flexible-modality methods mainly use zero-filling or modality omission, potentially discarding cross-modal information and introducing modality-dependent bias. We propose the Flexible Modality Adaptation Network (FMA-Net), a unified framework that compensates for missing modalities through instruction-guided latent-space translation. The Face Modality Instruct Translator (FMIT) estimates target modality observations from RGB inputs, while context-aware category enhancement uses learnable text prompts as modality-invariant semantic anchors. A Facial Feature Adapter (F2A) integrates global facial structure and local spoof-relevant cues to enhance discriminative representations. Synthetic-to-Real Face Domain Alignment (SR-FDA) reduces feature discrepancies between translated and real modalities, with benefits depending on the missing-modality pattern and data domain. Experiments on WMCA and PADISI-Face validate the framework. On WMCA with a 70% modality missing ratio, FMA-Net achieves a mean ACER of 3.22% across four intra-domain missing-modality protocols, compared with 4.24% for the strongest baseline by the same criterion. When both depth and IR are entirely unavailable, it achieves 5.23% ACER, compared with 5.99% for the best competing result. Cross-domain experiments also reveal limitations of synthetic-to-real alignment under dataset shifts. These results support FMA-Net as a practical approach to fPAD with flexible and incomplete modalities.

AI.tldr: FMA-Net is a flexible-modality face presentation attack detection framework that compensates for missing depth and IR inputs by instruction-guided latent-space translation from RGB, improving ACER under missing modalities on WMCA.
AI.motivation: Multimodal face PAD relies on complementary RGB, depth and IR cues, but the zero-filling or modality-omission strategies of existing flexible methods can discard cross-modal information and introduce modality-dependent bias.
AI.method: The Face Modality Instruct Translator estimates target modality observations from RGB inputs, learnable text prompts serve as modality-invariant semantic anchors, a Facial Feature Adapter combines global facial structure with local spoof cues, and Synthetic-to-Real Face Domain Alignment reduces discrepancies between translated and real modalities.
AI.result: On WMCA with a 70% modality missing ratio, mean ACER is 3.22% across four intra-domain protocols versus 4.24% for the strongest baseline; with depth and IR entirely unavailable, ACER is 5.23% versus 5.99%; cross-domain experiments reveal limits of synthetic-to-real alignment under dataset shift.
AI.conclusion: FMA-Net is a practical approach to fPAD with flexible and incomplete modalities, though its benefit depends on the missing-modality pattern and the data domain.

title: Benchmarking CNNs, Vision Transformers, and Foundation Models for Explainable Brain Tumor MRI Classification: Calibration, Decision Analysis, and External Validation
comment: Under review at Scientific Report Journal, Springer
summary: Deep learning models for brain tumor MRI classification are usually compared by accuracy alone, on public datasets whose independence is rarely checked. We benchmarked six architectures: two convolutional networks (EfficientNetV2-M and ConvNeXt-V2-Tiny), two vision transformers (Swin-V2-S and ViT-L/16), and two foundation models (DINOv2-L and MedSigLIP-448), for four-class classification of 7,216 public MRI images. We assessed accuracy, calibration, explainability, ensembles, and decision curves, with every fitted quantity estimated on validation data only. Pixel-verified duplicate screening showed that 36% of the test images had a near-duplicate in the training data. Test accuracy ranged from 94.5% to 95.6%, with no pairwise difference after Holm correction, and fell to 90.3% to 91.7% on the 773 test images free of duplicates and shared patients. Ensembles did not outperform the best single model. Attribution maps passed a model-randomization test but localized expert-annotated tumors poorly. On 1,675 external BDNeuro-MRI images that did not duplicate the training data, accuracy ranged from 77.6% (MedSigLIP-448) to 95.0% (ViT-L/16), and 12 of 15 pairwise differences were significant. Internal accuracy on this public collection therefore did not distinguish the architectures, whereas the duplicate-filtered external test did.

AI.tldr: Benchmarking six architectures for four-class brain tumor MRI classification shows that internal public-test accuracy does not separate them, whereas a duplicate-filtered external test does.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for brain tumor MRI are usually compared by accuracy alone on public datasets whose independence from the training data is rarely checked.
AI.method: EfficientNetV2-M, ConvNeXt-V2-Tiny, Swin-V2-S, ViT-L/16, DINOv2-L and MedSigLIP-448 are evaluated on 7,216 public images for accuracy, calibration, explainability, ensembles and decision curves, with every fitted quantity estimated on validation data only and pixel-verified duplicate screening applied.
AI.result: 36% of test images had a near-duplicate in the training data, and test accuracy of 94.5% to 95.6% showed no pairwise difference after Holm correction, falling to 90.3% to 91.7% on 773 duplicate-free test images; on 1,675 external BDNeuro-MRI images accuracy ranged from 77.6% (MedSigLIP-448) to 95.0% (ViT-L/16) with 12 of 15 pairwise differences significant; ensembles did not beat the best single model.
AI.conclusion: Internal accuracy on this public collection did not distinguish the architectures, whereas the duplicate-filtered external test did, so independence checks are needed for benchmarking.

title: Direct Trajectory Optimization for Inference-Time Alignment of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
summary: Alignment of text-to-image diffusion models with reward functions is a key challenge in controllable generation. Existing approaches typically rely on optimizing model inputs or fine-tuning denoising networks, which requires computationally expensive backpropagation through large denoising models. In this work, we propose Direct Trajectory Optimization (DTO), a training-free framework that performs alignment by directly optimizing the sampling trajectory of diffusion models. Specifically, DTO treats intermediate denoising scores and sampled noise as the optimization variables, eliminating the need for gradients through the denoising network. To mitigate the out-of-distribution problem, we introduce Reward-Optimized Score Guidance, which interpolates between the optimized scores and the pretrained model predictions to stabilize sampling, while providing a provable theoretical guarantee of reward improvement under constrained distributions. Empirically, DTO improves alignment performance across three diffusion models on two benchmarks, outperforming existing inference-time alignment methods while maintaining high efficiency. These results suggest that trajectory-level optimization is a promising direction for efficient and effective diffusion model alignment.

AI.tldr: Direct Trajectory Optimization (DTO) is a training-free inference-time alignment method for text-to-image diffusion models that optimizes the sampling trajectory and avoids backpropagation through the denoising network.
AI.motivation: Existing alignment approaches optimize model inputs or fine-tune denoising networks, which requires computationally expensive backpropagation through large denoising models.
AI.method: DTO treats intermediate denoising scores and sampled noise as optimization variables, and Reward-Optimized Score Guidance interpolates between the optimized scores and pretrained predictions to stabilize sampling, with a theoretical guarantee of reward improvement under constrained distributions.
AI.result: DTO improves alignment performance across three diffusion models on two benchmarks, outperforming existing inference-time alignment methods while remaining efficient.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-level optimization is a promising direction for efficient and effective diffusion model alignment.

title: When to Trust Adaptation: Contextual Fusion for Transferable Vision-Language Prompting
summary: When a vision-language model encounters a new class or domain, how much should it trust its learned prompts? Because source adaptation can correct pretrained errors on some target images while disturbing valid predictions on others, we introduce Contextual Adaptive Fusion (CAF), which retains four prediction branches by pairing frozen and prompted visual and textual representations. To arbitrate when branches disagree on an image, CAF combines each branch's predictive confidence with how frequently the branches favor its proposed class across the unlabeled target collection, placing greater trust in predictions that are locally confident yet less dominated by collection-wide frequency bias. The fusion coefficients are learned once on source data and remain fixed at inference. Trained on ImageNet, CAF achieves 69.96% average accuracy across ten cross-dataset benchmarks (1.92 percentage points above ManiPT) and remains highly competitive across four ImageNet variants, setting a new best of 52.21% on ImageNet-S. In base-to-novel transfer across eleven datasets, CAF further reaches 79.77% novel-class accuracy and an 82.81% harmonic mean. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Contextual Adaptive Fusion (CAF) arbitrates among four prediction branches that pair frozen and prompted vision-language representations, reaching 69.96% average accuracy across ten cross-dataset benchmarks when trained on ImageNet.
AI.motivation: Source prompt adaptation can correct pretrained errors on some target images while disturbing valid predictions on others, so the model needs a way to decide how much to trust its learned prompts for each image.
AI.method: CAF combines each branch's predictive confidence with how often the branches favor its proposed class across the unlabeled target collection, and its fusion coefficients are learned once on source data and fixed at inference.
AI.result: Trained on ImageNet, CAF achieves 69.96% average accuracy across ten cross-dataset benchmarks, 1.92 points above ManiPT, and sets a new best of 52.21% on ImageNet-S among four ImageNet variants; in base-to-novel transfer over eleven datasets it reaches 79.77% novel-class accuracy and an 82.81% harmonic mean.
AI.conclusion: Trusting predictions that are locally confident yet less dominated by collection-wide frequency bias makes prompt adaptation more robust across domains.

title: End-to-End Joint Training of Super-Resolution and Compression Artifact Removal for Industrial Machine Vision
summary: In industrial machine vision, images captured by edge devices are often downsampled and compressed to reduce bandwidth, introducing resolution loss and compression artifacts that severely degrade the performance of downstream tasks, such as defect detection. Existing quality enhancement methods typically apply super-resolution (SR) or compression artifact removal (CAR) independently or in a sequential manner and are largely optimized for human visual fidelity rather than machine perception. This paper proposes an end-to-end quality enhancement framework that integrates SR and CAR with a unified training strategy that optimizes both human-perception and machine-perception objectives. We investigate fixed-weight and uncertainty-based dynamic-weight loss functions to balance reconstruction quality and machine vision task performance. Extensive experiments on PCB Defect, DeepPCB, and NEU-DET datasets show that the proposed jointly trained model generally outperforms standalone and separately trained SR-CAR pipelines. In particular, under severe JPEG compression, our method improves defect detection performance from 0.461 to 0.887 mAP@50 on PCB Defect over sequential SR-CAR baselines, with only a slight reduction in PSNR. These results demonstrate that joint optimization is critical for compression-aware industrial machine vision systems.

AI.tldr: A jointly trained super-resolution and compression artifact removal model improves defect detection under severe JPEG compression over sequential SR-CAR pipelines, raising mAP@50 on PCB Defect from 0.461 to 0.887.
AI.motivation: Images from edge devices are downsampled and compressed to save bandwidth, and existing SR or CAR methods are applied independently or in sequence and optimized for human visual fidelity rather than machine perception.
AI.method: An end-to-end framework integrates SR and CAR under a unified training strategy that optimizes both human-perception and machine-perception objectives, comparing fixed-weight and uncertainty-based dynamic-weight loss functions.
AI.result: On PCB Defect, DeepPCB and NEU-DET the jointly trained model generally outperforms standalone and separately trained SR-CAR pipelines; under severe JPEG compression it improves PCB Defect mAP@50 from 0.461 to 0.887 over sequential SR-CAR baselines, with only a slight reduction in PSNR.
AI.conclusion: Joint optimization is critical for building compression-aware industrial machine vision systems.

title: Answer or Defer? Testing VLMs' Stated Confidence on Brain MRI
comment: Accepted to the WACV 2027 FABRIC Workshop
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) could support medical-image interpretation, but their use requires deciding which interpretations to accept and which images to refer to a clinician. We test whether thresholding stated confidence can retain useful coverage while limiting errors among accepted answers, and how this depends on the population. Eight open-weight VLMs, including two reasoning models, assess 3,888 brain MRI slices from post-treatment glioma patients (BraTS 2024) and healthy volunteers (IXI) for tumor or gross abnormality. BraTS labels are mask-derived; IXI slices are treated as negatives. On BraTS, no threshold selects a nonempty set with at most 5% empirical error for any model, even when chosen retrospectively. This also holds for four models evaluated on a large-lesion, distant-negative subset. At a 10% error budget, Gemma-4-12B retains 24.4% of slices and every other model at most 2.5%. To investigate this limited selection ability, we separate confidence differences between predicted answers from differences within each answer. For four models with available outcome-level summaries, pooled mean confidence differs more between answers than between correct and incorrect responses within each answer. A covariance decomposition explains how this pattern can produce opposite confidence-correctness associations across populations. At a 20% error budget, accepting every "tumor" answer covers more slices than any confidence threshold for two models. These findings caution against using unvalidated stated confidence as a standalone deferral signal and support population-specific validation before deployment. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Eight open-weight VLMs assessed on brain MRI slices show that no confidence threshold yields a nonempty answer set with at most 5% error on BraTS, so stated confidence is unreliable as a standalone deferral signal.
AI.motivation: Deciding which VLM interpretations to accept and which images to refer to a clinician requires that stated confidence retain useful coverage while limiting errors among accepted answers, and this may depend on the population.
AI.method: Eight open-weight VLMs, including two reasoning models, assess 3,888 brain MRI slices from post-treatment glioma patients (BraTS 2024) and healthy volunteers (IXI) for tumor or gross abnormality, and a covariance decomposition separates confidence differences between answers from differences within each answer.
AI.result: On BraTS no threshold selects a nonempty set with at most 5% empirical error for any model, while at a 10% error budget Gemma-4-12B retains 24.4% of slices and every other model at most 2.5%; for four models pooled mean confidence differs more between answers than between correct and incorrect responses within each answer.
AI.conclusion: Unvalidated stated confidence should not be used alone as a deferral signal, and population-specific validation is needed before deployment.

title: MDA framework: multi-architecture domain adaptation for unsupervised person re-identification
summary: Unsupervised person re-identification not only faces the challenge of domain gaps, but existing methods also rarely support multiple network architectures. To tackle both issues, this paper proposes a multi-architecture auto-adaptive domain adaptation method: Mamba augmented multi-architecture domain adaptation framework. Specifically, this paper constructs the multi-architecture domain adaptation capability at two levels. At the first level, we propose a composite operator(MDA operator) that encapsulates Mamba as a component for enhancing domain adaptation. At the second level, based on this operator, we propose a Mamba-enhanced multi-architecture Domain Adaptation framework(MDA framework). Comprehensive experiments on person re-identification benchmarks validate the consistency and flexibility of the proposed framework. The MDA framework supports versatile deployment strategies without being confined to a single integration point. Under a single deployment configuration, it surpasses several SOTA methods. Moreover, it demonstrates substantial performance improvements across both CNN and Transformer architectures. When embedded into a CNN backbone, the framework achieves a 10.2% mAP improvement on the adaptation task from CUHK03 to Market-1501. Integrated with a Transformer backbone, it yields a 19.8% mAP improvement on the same task.

AI.tldr: The MDA framework is a Mamba-enhanced multi-architecture domain adaptation method for unsupervised person re-identification that works with both CNN and Transformer backbones.
AI.motivation: Unsupervised person re-identification faces domain gaps, and existing methods rarely support multiple network architectures.
AI.method: A composite MDA operator encapsulates Mamba as a component for enhancing domain adaptation, and an MDA framework built on this operator supports versatile deployment strategies without being confined to a single integration point.
AI.result: Under a single deployment configuration it surpasses several SOTA methods; with a CNN backbone it improves mAP by 10.2% on the CUHK03 to Market-1501 adaptation task, and with a Transformer backbone by 19.8% on the same task.
AI.conclusion: The framework's consistency and flexibility across CNN and Transformer architectures make it a versatile domain adaptation approach for person re-identification.

title: Aggregation-Induced Calibration Failure in Sum-Based Label Expansion for Multi-Label Facial Expression Recognition: A Diagnostic Study
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 14 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Label-space expansion - predicting a larger joint space and summing back to the original labels - is a natural design for multi-label facial expression recognition, but its failure modes have not been characterised. We evaluate Condition-Aware Label Expansion (CALE) on a self-built dataset (30,240 training images, 3,460 multi-label test images), on seven backbones, and on the public RAF-DB and RAF-ML benchmarks. The central finding is that the aggregation rule, not the representation, decides whether the method works. With a fixed threshold of 0.5, the aggregate score spans 28x across five backbones at 10% of the training data (0.24 to 6.79) and collapses to a 1.9x range at full data, while threshold-free mAP stays within 1.28x over the same backbones, which localises the fault to the summation step. The mechanism is the uncalibrated aggregation rule, which adds the main-branch score to half the sum of the three non-main branches; we verify it by measuring main- and non-main-branch activations. Two plain seven-dimensional sigmoid baselines (BCE, ASL) reach mAP 0.5055 and 0.5175; ASL exceeds three of the five CALE configurations and falls within 0.03 of the best. On single-label FER the gain over a seven-dimensional baseline is nominally significant (paired t-test, p = 0.0436) but does not survive Benjamini-Hochberg correction (p_BH = 0.2055) or a Wilcoxon test (p = 0.1250). We conclude that sum-based label expansion requires threshold calibration at the deployment data scale, or a learned aggregation, before it can support multi-label decisions.

AI.tldr: A diagnostic study shows that in sum-based label expansion for multi-label facial expression recognition, the uncalibrated aggregation rule rather than the representation decides whether the method works, so threshold calibration or learned aggregation is required.
AI.motivation: Label-space expansion is a natural design for multi-label facial expression recognition, but its failure modes have not been characterised.
AI.method: Condition-Aware Label Expansion (CALE) is evaluated on a self-built dataset of 30,240 training and 3,460 multi-label test images, seven backbones, and the RAF-DB and RAF-ML benchmarks; its aggregation adds the main-branch score to half the sum of the three non-main branches, and the authors verify this by measuring branch activations.
AI.result: At a fixed 0.5 threshold the aggregate score spans 28x across five backbones at 10% of training data (0.24 to 6.79) and collapses to 1.9x at full data, while threshold-free mAP stays within 1.28x; plain BCE and ASL baselines reach mAP 0.5055 and 0.5175, and ASL exceeds three of the five CALE configurations; the single-label FER gain is nominally significant (p = 0.0436) but not after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (p_BH = 0.2055) or a Wilcoxon test (p = 0.1250).
AI.conclusion: Sum-based label expansion requires threshold calibration at the deployment data scale, or a learned aggregation, before it can support multi-label decisions.

title: Where Does Proposal Selection Fail? Diagnosing Frozen Vision-Language Queries over Detector Proposals
summary: In modular grounding a frozen detector proposes regions and a vision-language model (VLM) selects one, at lower cost than letting the VLM decode a box, but it is unclear where such systems fail. We hold perception fixed---every trained selector chooses among the same frozen proposals, which contain the referent for at least $99.8\%$ of RefCOCO/+/g queries---and vary the selection interface one factor at a time for two VLMs of one family (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B). On RefCOCOg, what the selector reads matters more than how it is built: the VLM's image-conditioned query encodes the referent's location and beats a text-only query by $0.15$--$0.18$ with every head tested (by less for InternVL3-8B, whose vision encoder differs; one head tested). The remaining errors are rankings among a few top candidates; a cross-attention selector supervised with every valid box reaches the VLM's coordinate decoding on RefCOCOg, and with Qwen2.5-VL on RefCOCO/+ when also trained on their data. Beyond that distribution it does not: on Ref-L4's Objects365 images, mostly of categories outside training, every trained head falls to $0.19$--$0.28$ while Qwen decoding keeps about $0.8$ (InternVL3's drops too), neither a wider detector prompt nor a class-agnostic proposer closes the gap, and on public reasoning benchmarks Ref-Adv-s and RefBench-PRO full-budget heads trail decoding by $0.19$--$0.37$ although proposals cover most referents. A trained verifier reduces to an existence probe on the VLM's query state and does not beat the VLM's yes/no answer on public no-target benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper diagnoses where frozen-proposal, VLM-selector grounding fails by holding the detector proposals fixed and varying only the selection interface for two Qwen VLMs. The selector's visual input matters more than its architecture on RefCOCOg, but trained selectors collapse out of distribution where VLM coordinate decoding stays strong.
AI.motivation: Modular grounding lets a frozen detector propose regions and a VLM select one, which is cheaper than decoding a box, but it was unclear where such systems fail. The paper isolates the selection step, since the proposals already contain the referent for at least 99.8% of RefCOCO/+/g queries.
AI.method: Every trained selector chooses among the same frozen proposals, and the selection interface is varied one factor at a time for Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B. The compared factors include the query type, with the VLM's image-conditioned query versus a text-only query, and the selector head, including a cross-attention selector supervised with every valid box. A trained verifier is also tested as an existence probe.
AI.result: On RefCOCOg the image-conditioned query beats a text-only query by 0.15 to 0.18 across every head tested, and a cross-attention selector reaches the VLM's coordinate decoding there. On Ref-L4 Objects365 images every trained head falls to 0.19 to 0.28 while Qwen decoding keeps about 0.8, and on Ref-Adv-s and RefBench-PRO the full-budget heads trail decoding by 0.19 to 0.37. A wider detector prompt and a class-agnostic proposer do not close the gap.
AI.conclusion: The main limitation of proposal-based selection is generalization beyond the training distribution and the rankings among a few top candidates, not the head design, so VLM coordinate decoding remains the stronger option out of distribution. A trained verifier does not beat the VLM's own yes/no answer on public no-target benchmarks.

title: Beyond Head Importance: Collective Computation in Video Transformers
summary: Attention heads in video Transformers vary greatly in functional importance. Understanding their contributions requires examining not only which heads are important, but also how they participate in collective computation within the network. We study this collective computation from two perspectives: the downstream use of head outputs and the composition of interactions across layers. Ablation analyses of four video Transformers show that high-importance heads identified on a single task also support other video understanding tasks and help preserve the representational structure that distinguishes different videos. Representational responses to head ablation correlate weakly with head importance after the attention module, but more strongly after the MLP in the same block. Adapting this downstream processing through MLP-only fine-tuning further improves the use of lower-importance head outputs. Meanwhile, through composition across layers, sets of heads with shorter spatiotemporal attention distances support stronger perturbation responses at distant tokens than sets with longer distances. Their joint ablation causes even greater performance loss than ablating equally sized sets of high-importance heads, revealing collective contributions not fully captured by individual importance rankings. These findings highlight collective computation as a key perspective for understanding attention head function: functional contributions depend on both how head outputs are used downstream and how local interactions compose across layers.

AI.tldr: The paper studies attention heads in video Transformers as a collective computation rather than by individual importance rankings. Ablations show that heads with shorter spatiotemporal attention distances have a larger effect on distant tokens than equally sized sets of high-importance heads.
AI.motivation: Attention heads in video Transformers differ greatly in functional importance, but importance rankings alone do not show how heads participate in computation across the network. The paper argues that downstream use of head outputs and cross-layer composition must also be examined.
AI.method: Ablation analyses are run on four video Transformers from two perspectives: the downstream use of head outputs, measured by representational responses after the attention module and the MLP in the same block, and the composition of interactions across layers. The paper also tests MLP-only fine-tuning to adapt downstream processing.
AI.result: High-importance heads identified on one task also support other video understanding tasks and help preserve representational structure that separates videos. Representational responses to ablation correlate weakly with head importance after attention but more strongly after the MLP. MLP-only fine-tuning further improves the use of lower-importance head outputs. Sets of heads with shorter spatiotemporal attention distances cause greater performance loss when jointly ablated than equally sized sets of high-importance heads.
AI.conclusion: Functional contributions of attention heads depend on how their outputs are used downstream and how local interactions compose across layers, so collective computation is a key perspective beyond individual head importance.

title: Training Vision Transformers to Focus: Emergence of Spatial Attention Head Specialization
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Self-supervised learning in Vision Transformer models, such as DINO, enables robust visual perception without requiring labeled data by leveraging large-scale image datasets. However, these models lack a focusing mechanism during training, resulting in perceptual representations that are often ambiguous or overly similar. In this work, we introduce two visual focusing loss functions designed to establish correspondence between the model's attention and specific regions within images. Specifically, we leverage the multi-head attention mechanism within the model to selectively steer the model's focus, leading to the emergence of spatial attention head specialization, characterized by diverse and spatially focused perceptual capabilities without requiring annotations. Through both qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we demonstrate that our method substantially increases the spatial selectivity and diversity of attention heads, improving both interpretability and performance on dense prediction tasks such as zero-shot image segmentation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces two visual focusing loss functions for DINO-style self-supervised Vision Transformers that align attention heads with specific image regions. The method yields spatially specialized heads that improve interpretability and dense prediction such as zero-shot image segmentation.
AI.motivation: Self-supervised Vision Transformers such as DINO learn robust perception without labels, but they have no focusing mechanism during training, so their representations are often ambiguous or overly similar.
AI.method: Two visual focusing loss functions establish correspondence between the model's multi-head attention and specific regions within images, steering each head's focus without requiring annotations.
AI.result: The method substantially increases the spatial selectivity and diversity of attention heads in qualitative and quantitative evaluations. It also improves performance on dense prediction tasks, with zero-shot image segmentation given as the example.
AI.conclusion: Spatial attention head specialization can emerge through focusing losses without annotations, improving both interpretability and dense prediction performance.

title: Developing a Street View Imagery Processing Pipeline for Building-Level Vacant House Assessment
summary: Street view imagery (SVI) is widely used to audit urban environments remotely. Automated assessments usually assume that each image shows the target building clearly. In practice, an image may lack task-relevant evidence or show a neighboring house. If this goes unchecked, a model's score cannot show whether it judged the correct building. We present a reproducible SVI processing pipeline that makes image suitability and target identity explicit and checkable. We apply it to vacant house assessment in South Korea, using 10,311 images of 1,609 detached-house parcels. Task-suitability filtering adapts its criteria to image composition and administrative area. This keeps coverage even across areas. While keeping as many images as a single uniform filter, our filtering left 101 more parcels with a usable image. Target-house alignment identifies the parcel's house from camera metadata and parcel boundaries. It needs no building footprints or additional training. Alignment matched human labels for 85.6% of images, compared with 79.8% for the best simple rule. In vacancy classification, filtering and alignment raised AUROC from 0.684 to 0.719, but marking a different house in the same image still gave 0.709. Grad-CAM showed that the model often looked at areas outside the target house. Image suitability, target identification, and model evidence are therefore separate problems, and scores alone do not resolve them. Recording which images were used and which house was selected lets reviewers verify each assessment and can support human virtual audits.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a reproducible street view imagery pipeline that makes image suitability and target-house identity explicit for building-level vacant house assessment in South Korea. Alignment and filtering improve AUROC from 0.684 to 0.719, but the model often attends to areas outside the target house.
AI.motivation: Automated street view assessments usually assume each image clearly shows the target building, yet images may lack task-relevant evidence or show a neighboring house, so a model score alone cannot show whether the correct building was judged.
AI.method: The pipeline has two steps. Task-suitability filtering adapts its criteria to image composition and administrative area, and target-house alignment identifies the parcel's house from camera metadata and parcel boundaries without building footprints or extra training. The dataset has 10,311 images of 1,609 detached-house parcels, and Grad-CAM is used to inspect model evidence.
AI.result: Adaptive filtering keeps as many images as a uniform filter while leaving 101 more parcels with a usable image. Alignment matches human labels for 85.6% of images versus 79.8% for the best simple rule. Filtering and alignment raise AUROC from 0.684 to 0.719, and marking a different house in the same image still gives 0.709. Grad-CAM shows the model often looks outside the target house.
AI.conclusion: Image suitability, target identification and model evidence are separate problems that scores alone do not resolve, and recording the images and selected house lets reviewers verify each assessment and supports human virtual audits.

title: RBA: A Read-out Basis Adapter for Parameter-Efficient Interactive OCTA Vessel Segmentation with SEEM
summary: Retinal disease monitoring with optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) relies on segmentation of vessels and the foveal avascular zone (FAZ). Promptable models such as SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) allow click-based refinement, but without adaptation SEEM segments thin vessels poorly and needs many clicks. Fully fine-tuning its 342 million parameters on a few hundred images is costly and risks overfitting, and parameter-efficient methods such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) usually adapt only the encoder. Yet SEEM reads every candidate mask from one feature map at quarter resolution, too coarse for vessels one to three pixels wide. This study introduces the Read-out Basis Adapter (RBA), whose read-out branch generates 32 image-specific basis maps at half resolution. Each candidate accesses them through its own vector and a zero-initialised projection, so the model starts exactly as SEEM. The encoder branch, a standard rank-1 LoRA, supplies the information needed to tell arteries from veins. RBA adds 0.47 million trainable parameters. Under simulated error-driven clicks, with the ground truth used only to place them, RBA outperforms LoRA, Conv-LoRA andAdaptFormer on OCTA-500 3mmlarge vessels. Averaged over three seeds, it reaches an intersection over union (IoU) of 85.16% and a Dice score of 91.93%, 2.90 and 1.72 percentage points above Conv-LoRA. On the 6 mm subset, one run gives margins of 4.35 and 2.76 points. The gain extends to arteries, veins and ROSE-O but not to the FAZ. In SEEM, adaptation capacity pays more at the mask read-out than in the encoder.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Read-out Basis Adapter (RBA), a parameter-efficient adapter for the SEEM promptable model that improves click-based OCTA vessel segmentation. It adds 0.47 million trainable parameters and reaches 85.16% IoU and 91.93% Dice on OCTA-500 3mm large vessels, averaged over three seeds.
AI.motivation: SEEM segments thin retinal vessels poorly and needs many clicks, full fine-tuning of its 342 million parameters risks overfitting on a few hundred images, and LoRA usually adapts only the encoder even though SEEM reads each mask from a coarse quarter-resolution feature map.
AI.method: RBA's read-out branch generates 32 image-specific basis maps at half resolution, and each candidate accesses them through its own vector and a zero-initialised projection so the model starts exactly as SEEM. A standard rank-1 LoRA encoder branch supplies the information needed to separate arteries from veins.
AI.result: RBA outperforms LoRA, Conv-LoRA and AdaptFormer on OCTA-500 3mm large vessels, reaching 85.16% IoU and 91.93% Dice averaged over three seeds, 2.90 and 1.72 points above Conv-LoRA. On the 6 mm subset a single run gives margins of 4.35 and 2.76 points. The gain extends to arteries, veins and ROSE-O but not to the FAZ.
AI.conclusion: In SEEM, adaptation capacity pays more at the mask read-out than in the encoder.

title: LO-World: Unified BEV Latent Modeling for Joint 4D Occupancy and LiDAR Forecasting
summary: LiDAR point clouds and 3D semantic occupancy represent two distinct modalities capturing fine-grained metric geometry and dense volumetric semantics, respectively, holding natural potential for mutual complementarity. However, existing world models typically forecast these modalities independently or cascade them heuristically, missing the opportunity for reciprocal cross-modal regularization. To address this, we propose \textbf{LO-World}, a unified 4D world model that forecasts both modalities within a shared BEV latent space. This single-stream formulation enables dense semantics and metric geometry to mutually reinforce each other, while eliminating multi-pipeline redundancy. Specifically, LO-World couples an efficient hybrid range-voxel autoencoder with a flow-matching generator that caches historical context to reduce iterative sampling latency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LO-World outperforms prior state-of-the-art baselines, improving occupancy forecasting IoU by 10.9% and reducing LiDAR Chamfer Distance by 30.1%. Meanwhile, it sustains a real-time throughput exceeding $25$~FPS on a single RTX 4090. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: LO-World is a unified 4D world model that forecasts LiDAR point clouds and 3D semantic occupancy jointly in a shared BEV latent space. It improves occupancy forecasting IoU by 10.9% and reduces LiDAR Chamfer Distance by 30.1%, running above 25 FPS on a single RTX 4090.
AI.motivation: Existing world models forecast LiDAR and occupancy independently or cascade them heuristically, which misses reciprocal cross-modal regularization between dense semantics and metric geometry and leaves redundant pipelines.
AI.method: LO-World uses a single-stream formulation in a shared BEV latent space. It couples an efficient hybrid range-voxel autoencoder with a flow-matching generator that caches historical context to reduce iterative sampling latency.
AI.result: LO-World outperforms prior state-of-the-art baselines, improving occupancy forecasting IoU by 10.9% and reducing LiDAR Chamfer Distance by 30.1%. It sustains real-time throughput above 25 FPS on a single RTX 4090.
AI.conclusion: A unified latent formulation lets dense semantics and metric geometry reinforce each other while removing multi-pipeline redundancy, and it can run in real time.

title: Text Alone Predicts Which Classes a Segmentation Readout Keeps
summary: An open-vocabulary segmentation readout silently loses a class deployed beyond its training categories. It still emits masks with high confidence, but the class never wins a single pixel. The training loss falls anyway, and mIoU can even rise while classes die. We show that which classes collapse is written in the class-name list alone. Before any image is seen, we rank each class's collapse risk from its text similarity to the training vocabulary alone. The ranking holds at AUROC 0.69-0.96 across nine model families, twelve backbones and eight pretraining recipes. Two further families, measured only after the predictions were written down, land in the same band. What the list writes, it can rewrite. With identical images and a class's counterpart moved in or out of the training list, retraining flips that class's gain over the frozen baseline by 21 IoU points; swapping in unrelated names changes nothing. We find a vocabulary-distance mechanism behind the collapse. Collapsed classes lose every vote to near-name neighbors, but in the frozen features they survive. Turning down the readout's amplitude, or stopping training early, brings them back, up to +16 points, without retraining; trained with its amplitude held down, the readout never collapses.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that an open-vocabulary segmentation readout silently drops classes deployed beyond the training vocabulary, and that which classes collapse can be predicted from the class-name list alone using text similarity to the training vocabulary. The predicted ranking reaches AUROC 0.69 to 0.96 across nine model families, twelve backbones and eight pretraining recipes.
AI.motivation: A class deployed beyond its training categories can lose every pixel while the model still emits confident masks, the training loss falls and mIoU can even rise, so the failure is hidden by standard metrics.
AI.method: Before any image is seen, each class's collapse risk is ranked from its text similarity to the training vocabulary. The method is tested by moving a class's counterpart in or out of the training list and retraining, and by swapping in unrelated names. The mechanism is analysed through votes in the readout and the frozen features, and by lowering the readout amplitude or stopping training early.
AI.result: The ranking holds at AUROC 0.69 to 0.96 across nine model families, twelve backbones and eight pretraining recipes, and two further families measured after predictions were recorded fall in the same band. Moving a counterpart in or out of the training list flips a class's gain over the frozen baseline by 21 IoU points, while unrelated names change nothing. Lowering the amplitude or stopping early recovers collapsed classes by up to 16 points without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Collapse is determined by vocabulary distance, since collapsed classes lose votes to near-name neighbours even though they survive in the frozen features, and a readout trained with its amplitude held down never collapses.

title: Scale-Consistent Monocular Fisheye Visual Odometry via Spherical Bundle Adjustment-Guided Unsupervised Depth Learning
summary: The wide field of view of fisheye cameras and the simplicity of a monocular setup make monocular fisheye visual odometry (VO) attractive for robotic localization and mapping. Nevertheless, scale drift remains a major challenge over long trajectories. Unsupervised depth learning can help to mitigate this issue, but the pronounced distortion of fisheye images poses challenges for accurate depth estimation. This article presents S$^2$D-FVO, a monocular fisheye VO framework integrating spherical bundle adjustment (SBA)-guided unsupervised depth learning to improve scale consistency and depth estimation accuracy. Given that pixel reprojection residuals do not uniformly reflect angular deviations between viewing rays and that the first-order linearization of a scalar angular reprojection residual is insensitive to perturbations along one tangent direction, SBA employs tangent-space angular reprojection residuals derived from the spherical logarithmic map. These residuals retain sensitivity along both tangent directions, with their norms equal to the corresponding scalar angular residuals. A median depth-based scale regularization term is further integrated into SBA to constrain the reconstruction scale.
