Learning from them requires recovering motion from completed interactions and using it to anticipate what could happen next. We present $\textit{Grasping-the-Future}$, a unified generative model of joint 3D hand-object motion, including wrist motion, finger articulation, and object position and orientation. Through masked spatiotemporal completion and flow matching, we train a single model for several prediction tasks: forecasting future interactions, predicting hand motion given object motion or vice versa, generating both trajectories toward a desired final object pose, and completing partially observed interactions. We explicitly model hand-object relations and incorporate contact constraints to help preserve grasp relationships during motion. To obtain 3D supervision from internet videos, we develop a scalable pipeline that combines pretrained perception models with joint geometric optimization to reconstruct completed interactions. We combine these recovered trajectories with annotated interaction datasets as training data for all tasks. We demonstrate strong performance across all tasks, outperforming released forecasters on datasets with 3D annotations. Moreover, we show geometric and physical plausibility of the predicted trajectories by retargeting them to a robotic embodiment. Videos are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Grasping-the-Future is a unified generative model of joint 3D hand-object motion that is trained with masked spatiotemporal completion and flow matching on 3D data recovered from internet videos. It handles forecasting, conditional hand or object prediction, goal-directed trajectory generation and completion, and outperforms released forecasters on datasets with 3D annotations.
AI.motivation: Anticipating an interaction requires predicting how an object will move and how the hands should move with it. Human videos capture these relations, but 3D supervision for them is scarce and must be recovered from completed interactions.
AI.method: One model jointly generates wrist motion, finger articulation, and object position and orientation through masked spatiotemporal completion and flow matching. Hand-object relations are modelled explicitly and contact constraints are added to preserve grasp relationships. A scalable pipeline combines pretrained perception models with joint geometric optimisation to reconstruct 3D interactions from internet videos.
AI.result: The model shows strong performance on all tasks and outperforms released forecasters on datasets with 3D annotations. Predicted trajectories, when retargeted to a robotic embodiment, are shown to be geometrically and physically plausible.
AI.conclusion: A single generative model can cover several hand-object prediction tasks, and internet-video reconstruction can supply useful 3D training data for them.

title: Beyond Modality Preference: Controlling Multimodal Arbitration under Modality Conflict in MLLMs
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) integrate information across modalities, but become unreliable when those modalities disagree. Under conflicting inputs, MLLMs may favor modalities that are not the most reliable for the task, thus motivating inference-time control of modality arbitration. We identify a small set of attention heads, termed arbitration heads, that causally influence whether predictions follow visual or textual evidence. Building on this, we introduce a lightweight, training-free intervention that biases these heads toward a designated trusted modality at inference time. The identified heads are stable across calibration set sizes and generalize across settings, and steering them enables effective bidirectional control of modality reliance across diverse benchmarks. Our findings identify an effective control mechanism to align MLLM predictions with task-specified modality priorities. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a small set of attention heads, called arbitration heads, that causally determine whether an MLLM follows visual or textual evidence under modality conflict. A training-free intervention biases these heads toward a designated trusted modality at inference time, giving bidirectional control of modality reliance.
AI.motivation: MLLMs become unreliable when their input modalities disagree, and they may favour a modality that is not the most reliable for the task. This motivates inference-time control of how the model arbitrates between modalities.
AI.method: Causal analysis identifies arbitration heads whose activity influences whether predictions follow visual or textual evidence. A lightweight, training-free intervention biases these heads toward a designated trusted modality at inference time.
AI.result: The identified heads are stable across calibration set sizes and generalise across settings, and steering them gives effective bidirectional control of modality reliance across diverse benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The arbitration heads form an effective control mechanism for aligning MLLM predictions with task-specified modality priorities.

title: World In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot Manipulation
summary: Trained action policies write manipulation skill into network weights, tying what is learned to the distribution it is learned from. In-context learning (ICL) avoids this coupling but has not matched trained policies, because a demonstration recorded in another scene carries no feedback from the world the robot currently faces. We observe that what an agent learns in context is semantic, recording task steps and object roles rather than visual appearance, so experience gathered in one world transfers to another. Based on this insight, we propose World In-Context Learning (WICL), a paradigm in which a frozen model starts from a demonstration, rehearses the task in a world such as a simulator, and writes the feedback into its context rather than its weights. We build RoboScript, a modular infrastructure that implements WICL for agentic manipulation. From a single demonstration, RoboScript learns each task through rehearsal in simulation, freezes the learned knowledge as a Task Memory, and deploys the frozen memory on new scenes with data isolation that ensures every deployment input is available on a real robot. On all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboScript reaches 83.4% mean success across clean and randomized settings with one demonstration per task and no gradient updates, exceeding the strongest trained action policy by over 20 points. The method generalizes across visual distributions, improves through reflection, scales with the foundation model, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment memory adaptation. With a world in the loop, a robot can learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights. All code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes World In-Context Learning (WICL), where a frozen model learns a task from one demonstration by rehearsing it in a world such as a simulator and storing the feedback in its context rather than its weights. The RoboScript system reaches 83.4% mean success on all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, more than 20 points above the strongest trained action policy.
AI.motivation: Trained action policies store manipulation skill in network weights, which ties them to their training distribution. In-context learning avoids this coupling but has not matched trained policies, because a demonstration recorded in another scene gives no feedback from the robot's current world.
AI.method: The authors observe that in-context learning captures semantic content (task steps and object roles) rather than visual appearance, so experience gathered in one world transfers to another. RoboScript learns each task from a single demonstration through simulated rehearsal, freezes the result as a Task Memory, and deploys it on new scenes with data isolation so that every deployment input is available on a real robot.
AI.result: Across all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, RoboScript reaches 83.4% mean success over clean and randomized settings with one demonstration per task and no gradient updates, exceeding the strongest trained action policy by over 20 points. The method generalizes across visual distributions, improves through reflection, scales with the foundation model, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment memory adaptation.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that with a world in the loop, a robot can learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights.

title: Reframe: Observation-Aligned Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Visual Reasoning
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) offer complementary routes to post-training. For visual agents, however, tool use presents two related challenges. Models may overlook useful tool-returned observations, while poorly grounded actions can limit the evidence available for subsequent distillation. We introduce Reframe, a post-training framework that treats the observation state, rather than only the output distribution, as an object of alignment. First, Ground-Drop-GRPO (GD-GRPO) trains spatial and temporal specialists with evidence-aware rewards and stochastic removal of the original visual input, encouraging them to acquire grounded evidence and use the returned observations. Second, Observation-Gated-MOPD (OG-MOPD) replaces deficient tool actions with canonical ones mid-rollout and resumes distillation from the repaired observation. The two stages complement each other, as learning to rely on tool-returned observations can help the policy benefit from observation repair. Neither stage requires a task-specific SFT cold start. Extensive experiments over 14 image and video benchmarks demonstrate that Reframe outperforms both Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD. Ablation results show that GD-GRPO increases observation dependence and tool gain compared with outcome-based GRPO.

AI.tldr: Reframe is a post-training framework for visual agents that aligns the observation state, not only the output distribution, using two stages: Ground-Drop-GRPO for grounded specialists and Observation-Gated-MOPD for mid-rollout repair of tool actions. It outperforms both Mix-RL and vanilla multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) across 14 image and video benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Visual agents that use tools may overlook useful tool-returned observations, and poorly grounded actions limit the evidence available for later distillation. Agentic RL and MOPD offer complementary post-training routes, but neither handles these two problems directly.
AI.method: Ground-Drop-GRPO (GD-GRPO) trains spatial and temporal specialists with evidence-aware rewards and stochastic removal of the original visual input, so they learn to use grounded evidence and returned observations. Observation-Gated-MOPD (OG-MOPD) replaces deficient tool actions with canonical ones mid-rollout and resumes distillation from the repaired observation. Neither stage needs a task-specific SFT cold start.
AI.result: Reframe outperforms both Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD on 14 image and video benchmarks. Ablations show that GD-GRPO increases observation dependence and tool gain compared with outcome-based GRPO.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that the two stages complement each other, because learning to rely on tool-returned observations helps the policy benefit from observation repair.

title: Engagement Estimation in Human-Robot and Human-Human Interactions across Domain, Age and Culture: MultiMediate'26 Challenge
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, ACM MultiMedia 2026 Grand Challenge Baseline Paper
summary: Understanding engagement in human interaction is essential for modelling assistive and context-aware AI systems. Previously, the MultiMediate challenge has focused on estimating momentary continuous engagement values in adult conversation across cultures, achieving high levels of generalisability across domains. However, engagement can be measured in different metrics and manifest differently between children and adults. MultiMediate'26 therefore expands the evaluated domain set to include the PInSoRo dataset of Child-Child and Child-Robot play sessions in English. These sessions were annotated categorically with task and social engagement, diversifying engagement types, age ranges and interaction types. In this paper, we describe the MultiMediate'26 challenge and its goals, introduce the NoXi, NoXi-J, MPIIGI, and PInSoRo datasets, showcase extracted multi-modal features, present our baseline model for engagement estimation across all domains, and discuss challenge submissions and approaches. In an effort to provide a transparent and welcoming challenge environment, baseline code, leaderboard, datasets, and extracted features are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the MultiMediate'26 challenge for estimating continuous engagement, extending the earlier adult-conversation benchmark to child-child and child-robot play sessions. It releases four datasets (NoXi, NoXi-J, MPIIGI, PInSoRo), extracted multi-modal features, a baseline model, a leaderboard and the challenge submissions.
AI.motivation: Earlier MultiMediate challenges covered only adult conversation across cultures. Engagement is measured with different metrics and looks different in children than in adults, so a benchmark is needed that spans more domains, age groups and interaction types.
AI.method: The challenge adds the PInSoRo dataset, which contains English child-child and child-robot play sessions annotated categorically with task and social engagement. It packages NoXi, NoXi-J, MPIIGI and PInSoRo with multi-modal features and a baseline engagement estimator that covers all domains.
AI.result: The paper reports the challenge goals, the datasets and features, the baseline, and the approaches taken by challenge submissions. Baseline code, leaderboard, datasets and features are public.
AI.conclusion: The authors position the challenge as a transparent, open benchmark for engagement estimation across domains, ages and interaction types.

title: Semantic-Enhanced Sparse Temporal Modeling for Dynamic Engagement Estimation in Multimodal Interactions
summary: Dynamic engagement estimation aims to infer participants' evolving engagement states from continuous multimodal interaction streams. Existing approaches typically combine acoustic, pose, and visual representations with temporal models to capture observable interaction patterns. However, conversational semantics are difficult to align with frame-level engagement annotations in the same manner as continuous audio-visual signals, leaving dialogue context less effectively exploited in existing temporal modeling pipelines. Moreover, engagement annotations often evolve smoothly over time, making dense frame-level modeling computationally redundant and potentially sensitive to local annotation noise. To address these issues, we propose SEST, a Semantically-Enhanced Sparse Temporal framework that models engagement-related information from both semantic and temporal perspectives. SEST leverages Multimodal Large Language Models to extract multimodal semantic embeddings, providing dialogue-aware contextual information beyond conventional frame-level features. In parallel, SEST replaces dense-to-dense temporal modeling with a sparse-to-dense pathway, where continuous frame sequences are first encoded into compact temporal dynamics to reduce redundant computation and broaden temporal coverage, then fused with semantic context and recovered to the original label resolution for dense engagement prediction. Experiments on the MEE2026 benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of SEST, which achieved first place in the challenge.

AI.tldr: SEST is a semantically enhanced sparse temporal framework for dynamic engagement estimation that combines multimodal LLM semantic embeddings with a sparse-to-dense temporal pathway. It took first place in the MEE2026 challenge.
AI.motivation: Existing engagement models combine acoustic, pose and visual features with temporal models but align dialogue semantics poorly with frame-level labels. Dense frame-level modelling is also computationally redundant and sensitive to local annotation noise, because engagement labels change smoothly over time.
AI.method: SEST uses Multimodal Large Language Models to extract multimodal semantic embeddings that carry dialogue-aware context. In parallel, it encodes continuous frame sequences into compact temporal dynamics, fuses them with the semantic context, and restores the original label resolution for dense prediction.
AI.result: Experiments on the MEE2026 benchmark show that SEST is effective and achieved first place in the challenge.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that modelling engagement semantically and sparsely in time is effective for dynamic engagement estimation, as the first-place result on MEE2026 shows.

title: Benchmarking Neural Image Compression with DCT-Based Spectral Diagnostics
comment: 17 pages, including supplementary material. Code: this https URL
summary: Neural image compression (NIC) models are commonly evaluated with scalar rate-distortion metrics, which do not show how a codec treats individual spatial frequencies. We propose a benchmark that probes codecs with the DCT basis matrix and single-frequency test images. We measure relative off-target energy (leakage), the fraction of reconstruction energy outside the probed frequency, together with target-frequency gain. Exact decompositions and bounds relate these measurements to reconstruction error. At operating points nearest 1 bpp, the BMSHJ, MBT, and Cheng2020 models leave 80-97% of their reconstructed high-band energy outside the target bin and have target-frequency gains of 0.02-0.23, whereas TCM and FTIC attain off-target energy in the classical-codec range. Both probe types identify behavior absent from scalar metrics: released Cheng2020-Anchor models produce extreme pre-clamp outputs on isolated single-frequency inputs. Finally, decoder-only fine-tuning with natural-image and leakage losses reduces basis off-target energy by 90-99.8% across all eight evaluated architectures while keeping the bitstream fixed, at a Kodak PSNR cost of 0.09-0.59 dB.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a benchmark that probes neural image compression codecs with DCT basis matrices and single-frequency test images, measuring off-target energy (leakage) and target-frequency gain. It finds that several codecs leave most of their high-band energy outside the probed frequency, and that decoder-only fine-tuning reduces this leakage substantially.
AI.motivation: Neural image compression models are usually evaluated with scalar rate-distortion metrics, which do not show how a codec handles individual spatial frequencies.
AI.method: The benchmark feeds codecs DCT basis images and single-frequency images and measures relative off-target energy (the fraction of reconstruction energy outside the probed frequency) and target-frequency gain. Exact decompositions and bounds relate these measurements to reconstruction error. Decoder-only fine-tuning then uses natural-image and leakage losses while keeping the bitstream fixed.
AI.result: At operating points near 1 bpp, BMSHJ, MBT and Cheng2020 leave 80-97% of reconstructed high-band energy outside the target bin, with target-frequency gains of 0.02-0.23, whereas TCM and FTIC reach the classical-codec range. Released Cheng2020-Anchor models give extreme pre-clamp outputs on isolated single-frequency inputs. Decoder-only fine-tuning reduces basis off-target energy by 90-99.8% across all eight architectures, at a Kodak PSNR cost of 0.09-0.59 dB.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that both probe types reveal codec behaviour that scalar metrics miss, and that leakage can be reduced substantially at a small cost in PSNR.

title: Covariate-Conditioned One-Step Diffusion for Multi-Horizon 3D Brain MRI Prediction in Aging and Neurodegeneration
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027
summary: Predicting longitudinal brain changes from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can help characterize structural progression associated with aging and neurodegeneration. However, diffusion-based forecasting typically requires iterative denoising, limiting inference efficiency. We propose a covariate-conditioned one-step diffusion framework for multi-horizon prediction of 3D gray-matter density (GMD) maps. Rather than directly generating future anatomy, the model predicts longitudinal GMD changes through residual prediction in a single denoising step. The predicted changes are added to the baseline GMD map to reconstruct future anatomy. The model is conditioned on baseline anatomy, age, diagnosis, APOE4 allele count, and continuous follow-up time. Training combines mean squared error with a Pearson correlation loss to improve the spatial agreement between predicted and observed GMD changes. A unified model supports prediction horizons from 2 to 10 years. On the held-out ADNI test set, our method achieves a $\Delta$-Pearson of 0.478, mean squared error (MSE) of $5.176 \times 10^{-3}$, and structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 0.979, with $\Delta$-Pearson reaching 0.582 at 10 years. Without retraining, external evaluation on AIBL yields a $\Delta$-Pearson of 0.450, MSE of $4.016 \times 10^{-3}$, and SSIM of 0.985. Ablation studies further demonstrate the benefits of residual prediction, covariate conditioning, and correlation-based supervision. Code: this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a covariate-conditioned one-step diffusion model that predicts 3D gray-matter density changes over 2 to 10 years from baseline brain MRI. A single denoising step produces residual changes that are added to the baseline map.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based forecasting of brain MRI usually needs iterative denoising, which limits inference efficiency for longitudinal prediction of aging and neurodegeneration.
AI.method: The model predicts residual GMD changes in one denoising step and adds them to the baseline GMD map to reconstruct future anatomy. It is conditioned on baseline anatomy, age, diagnosis, APOE4 allele count and continuous follow-up time, and is trained with mean squared error plus a Pearson correlation loss. One unified model covers horizons from 2 to 10 years.
AI.result: On the held-out ADNI test set, the method reaches a Delta-Pearson of 0.478, MSE of 5.176 x 10^-3 and SSIM of 0.979, with Delta-Pearson reaching 0.582 at 10 years. Without retraining, external evaluation on AIBL gives a Delta-Pearson of 0.450, MSE of 4.016 x 10^-3 and SSIM of 0.985. Ablations confirm the benefits of residual prediction, covariate conditioning and correlation-based supervision.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that residual one-step prediction with covariate conditioning and correlation-based supervision gives accurate multi-horizon forecasts of brain change, and that the model transfers to an external cohort without retraining.

title: UniLatent: Cross-Embodiment Transfer via Latent Observation Alignment
summary: Robot datasets are costly to collect and are usually tied to a specific embodiment, making it difficult to reuse demonstrations across robots with different geometry, appearance, and kinematics. We introduce UniLatent, a cross-embodiment transfer framework that reduces the embodiment-induced observation gap in a shared latent space. UniLatent renders paired source-target robot observations in simulation and aligns a source visual encoder to a frozen target encoder. A policy trained on encoded source demonstrations can then run directly on target observations, with no pixel-level image translation. Across three simulation tasks and two target robot arms, UniLatent reaches up to 93% zero-shot success, exceeding the strongest pixel-translation baseline by over 30 points on average. In real-world xArm-to-Franka transfer, fine-tuning with only 10 target demonstrations per task yields 27/30 successful rollouts. Code, videos and data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: UniLatent is a cross-embodiment transfer framework that aligns a source robot's visual encoder to a frozen target encoder in a shared latent space, so a policy trained on source demonstrations runs on target observations without pixel-level translation. It reaches up to 93% zero-shot success in simulation and 27/30 successful rollouts in real xArm-to-Franka transfer after fine-tuning with 10 target demonstrations per task.
AI.motivation: Robot datasets are costly to collect and tied to a specific embodiment, so demonstrations are hard to reuse across robots with different geometry, appearance and kinematics.
AI.method: UniLatent renders paired source and target robot observations in simulation and trains the source visual encoder to align with a frozen target encoder. A policy trained on encoded source demonstrations is then run directly on target observations.
AI.result: Across three simulation tasks and two target robot arms, UniLatent reaches up to 93% zero-shot success, exceeding the strongest pixel-translation baseline by over 30 points on average. In real-world xArm-to-Franka transfer, fine-tuning with only 10 target demonstrations per task gives 27/30 successful rollouts.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that aligning latent observations closes much of the embodiment gap, so demonstrations can be reused across arms with little target data.

title: Frequency-consistent synthesis and selective transfer for medical image analysis
summary: Complementary imaging is not always available, and realistic synthesis does not necessarily improve downstream analysis. Here we introduce a training framework linking medical image synthesis to task learning through adaptive frequency consistency and selective feature transfer. Image-specific frequency constraints encourage consistency of structure and detail. Features are transferred only when a teacher using synthetic images achieves a lower task-error score than the student by a task-specific margin on a labelled training sample. Evaluations across five datasets show improved translation fidelity with three adversarial and diffusion-based translators trained without paired supervision, alongside gains in brain-tumour segmentation on tumour-containing slices and lesion centre-point detection. All 105 reported paired comparisons yielded point estimates favouring the proposed methods, including 36 external translation comparisons on post?treatment MRI without retraining. These findings support synthetic modalities as task-oriented complements to acquired scans when complementary imaging is unavailable.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training framework that links medical image synthesis to downstream task learning through adaptive frequency consistency and selective feature transfer. Synthetic images are used only when they help a task, and the method improves translation fidelity and task performance across five datasets.
AI.motivation: Complementary imaging is often unavailable, and realistic synthesis does not necessarily improve downstream analysis.
AI.method: Image-specific frequency constraints encourage consistency of structure and detail. Features are transferred from a teacher trained on synthetic images to a student only when the teacher's task error is lower than the student's by a task-specific margin on a labelled training sample.
AI.result: Across five datasets, the methods improve translation fidelity for three adversarial and diffusion-based translators trained without paired supervision. They also improve brain-tumour segmentation on tumour-containing slices and lesion centre-point detection. All 105 reported paired comparisons have point estimates favouring the proposed methods, including 36 external translation comparisons on post-treatment MRI without retraining.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that synthetic modalities can serve as task-oriented complements to acquired scans when complementary imaging is unavailable.

title: Noise-Regularized Training for Learned Image Compression
comment: 22 pages, 4 figures. Accepted as a Spotlight paper at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Learned image compression (LIC) is trained almost exclusively on clean images: the only stochastic perturbation in the loop is an additive uniform proxy injected in the latent domain to keep the entropy model differentiable. Outside compression, by contrast, a long line of work---from Tikhonov regularization and contractive autoencoders through denoising score matching and modern diffusion models---has established that Gaussian noise at the input of a network with a clean target acts as a structured probe of the data manifold rather than as data augmentation. Building on this view, we introduce noise-regularized training for LIC: at every training step we add Gaussian noise to the encoder input while keeping the distortion target, the latent uniform proxy, the hyperprior, and the entropy coding pipeline unchanged. The recipe is architecture-agnostic and adds essentially no training or inference overhead. Across backbones and operating regimes it yields consistent BD-Rate gains: -2.60% on a reproduced ELIC and -0.85% / -1.05% / -2.38% on the Base/Medium/Large scales of a variable-rate DMCI codec, with DMCI-Large reaching -22.02% against VTM-22.0. A second-order expansion of the noisy RD loss accounts for these gains: because the noise enters upstream of the analysis transform, it converts the clean RD objective into a structured $O(\sigma^{2})$ regularizer comprising an information-weighted encoder-Jacobian penalty (rate side) and a Frobenius contractive penalty on the end-to-end reconstruction map (distortion side). A finite-difference Lipschitz analysis shows corresponding sensitivity reductions of ~12% for the encoder and ~8% for the end-to-end codec, while an exact-JVP test further shows preferential contraction of high-information directions. Code and trained models are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper applies noise-regularized training to learned image compression by adding Gaussian noise to the encoder input at every step. This gives consistent BD-Rate gains across backbones, including -22.02% against VTM-22.0 for DMCI-Large.
AI.motivation: Learned image compression is trained almost only on clean images, while work in other areas has shown that Gaussian noise at the input acts as a structured probe of the data manifold rather than as augmentation.
AI.method: At each training step, Gaussian noise is added to the encoder input while the distortion target, the latent uniform proxy, the hyperprior and the entropy coding pipeline stay unchanged. The recipe is architecture-agnostic and adds essentially no training or inference overhead. A second-order expansion of the noisy rate-distortion loss gives an O(sigma^2) regularizer with an information-weighted encoder-Jacobian penalty and a Frobenius contractive penalty on the reconstruction map.
AI.result: BD-Rate gains are -2.60% on a reproduced ELIC and -0.85%, -1.05% and -2.38% on the Base, Medium and Large scales of a variable-rate DMCI codec, with DMCI-Large reaching -22.02% against VTM-22.0. A finite-difference Lipschitz analysis shows sensitivity reductions of about 12% for the encoder and 8% for the end-to-end codec, and an exact-JVP test shows preferential contraction of high-information directions.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that noise at the encoder input acts as a regularizer that explains the rate-distortion gains, and that the recipe is a low-cost change applicable to many codecs.

title: Polarization Aware Deep Learning Framework for SAR Despeckling
summary: Speckle is an inherent characteristic of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery that complicates image interpretation and the extraction of reliable information. Although deep-learning-based despeckling methods have demonstrated promising performance, their applicability across different polarimetric configurations is often limited by the need for specialized architectures or separate training procedures. This paper presents a unified deep-learning framework for despeckling single-, dual-, and full-polarization SAR data using a single trained convolutional neural network. The proposed approach adopts a common nine-channel representation of the polarimetric covariance matrix and a polarization-aware masking strategy to accommodate different configurations without modifying the network architecture. Qualitative and quantitative comparison on three different scenes from different sensors demonstrate competitive performance across the considered experiments and support the feasibility of a unified, polarization-flexible approach to SAR despeckling across different polarimetric configurations.

AI.tldr: The paper presents one deep-learning network that despeckles single-, dual- and full-polarization SAR images, using a common nine-channel covariance representation and polarization-aware masking. It is competitive on three scenes from different sensors.
AI.motivation: Deep-learning despeckling methods often need specialized architectures or separate training for each polarimetric configuration, which limits their use across configurations.
AI.method: The framework represents the polarimetric covariance matrix as a common nine-channel input and applies a polarization-aware masking strategy. A single convolutional network handles all configurations without changes to its architecture.
AI.result: Qualitative and quantitative comparisons on three scenes from different sensors show competitive performance across the experiments.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that a unified, polarization-flexible despeckling approach is feasible across different polarimetric configurations.

title: Beyond Prompt Attacks: Least-Action Auditing of Concept Erasure
summary: Concept erasure, or concept unlearning, in text-to-image diffusion models is usually audited with prompt attacks. A prompt attack tests whether one conditioning string still retrieves the erased concept. It does not measure the probability that the frozen generator still assigns to that concept. We introduce least-action auditing of this residual probability, and evaluate it on Stable Diffusion concept-erasure checkpoints. The least-action barrier is the minimum control cost of driving the frozen reverse process into a detector-defined concept event. This cost equals the path-space KL divergence of conditioning the model on the event, and therefore the event's negative log-probability. The estimate $\Delta S_{\mathrm{rob}}$ uses a CLIP$\wedge$DINOv2 consensus terminal, with no retraining and no adversarial prompt. Across $18$ erased concept-mechanism pairs spanning object classes and NSFW nudity, $\Delta S_{\mathrm{rob}}$ predicts deployment leakage counted on $1{,}500$ fresh samples per model by detectors excluded from the audit (pooled Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.76$, $p{=}5{\times}10^{-4}$). Within every audited concept, the eraser with the higher barrier leaks less ($18/18$). On NSFW nudity the barrier orders the standard erasers exactly: UCE $\Delta S_{\mathrm{rob}}{=}3.9$ (leak $16.4\%$) $<$ ESD $75.5$ ($9.8\%$) $<$ RECE $224.5$ ($1.4\%$), while Safe Latent Diffusion (SLD) stays near zero and leaks $85.5\%$ under explicit prompts. The same trajectories repair deployed checkpoints. An audit-guided closed-form patch reduces UCE nudity leakage from $16.2\%$ to $0/1{,}500$ and RECE church leakage by $3.3\times$, where direction-count-matched random edits fail.

AI.tldr: The paper audits concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models by measuring the residual probability the frozen generator assigns to an erased concept, rather than using prompt attacks. The resulting least-action barrier predicts deployment leakage across 18 erased concept-mechanism pairs and orders erasers consistently.
AI.motivation: Concept erasure is usually audited with prompt attacks, which test whether one conditioning string still retrieves the concept. They do not measure the probability that the frozen generator still assigns to that concept.
AI.method: The least-action barrier is the minimum control cost of driving the frozen reverse process into a detector-defined concept event. This cost equals the path-space KL divergence of conditioning on the event, which is the event's negative log-probability. The estimate Delta S_rob uses a CLIP and DINOv2 consensus terminal, with no retraining and no adversarial prompt.
AI.result: Across 18 erased concept-mechanism pairs covering object classes and NSFW nudity, Delta S_rob predicts deployment leakage measured on 1,500 fresh samples per model by detectors excluded from the audit (pooled Spearman rho = -0.76, p = 5e-4). Within every audited concept, the eraser with the higher barrier leaks less (18/18). On NSFW nudity, UCE (barrier 3.9, leak 16.4%), ESD (75.5, 9.8%) and RECE (224.5, 1.4%) are ordered consistently, while Safe Latent Diffusion stays near zero barrier and leaks 85.5% under explicit prompts. An audit-guided closed-form patch cuts UCE nudity leakage from 16.2% to 0 of 1,500, and cuts RECE church leakage by 3.3 times, where random edits with matched direction counts fail.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that the least-action barrier is a prompt-free audit that predicts deployed leakage and can guide repairs of deployed checkpoints.

title: Dataset Collections: Challenges of Large-Scale Data Aggregation in 3D Medical Image Datasets
summary: The development of deep learning-based medical AI depends on high-quality annotated data. Yet, dataset creation remains constrained by the need for expert radiologist annotations, limiting curated datasets to relatively small cohorts. To overcome this limitation, recent efforts increasingly aggregate disparate public datasets into large-scale dataset collections. However, combining datasets at scale often obscures data provenance, introducing substantial risks of reuse propagation, unintended leakage, bias amplification and distorted data distributions. In this work, we study these problems on a massive collection of 565k 3D radiological images across 1034 public datasets and provide practical resources to address them. Firstly, we formalize dataset collections as a distinct paradigm in medical image analysis and characterize their structural challenges, including reuse propagation, duplication, and provenance fragmentation. Secondly, we perform a large-scale empirical study of duplication on this collection and demonstrate extensive exact and near-duplicate reuse across public datasets via perceptual hashing and manual tracing, identifying a lower bound of 118k duplicate pairs. We make the perceptual hashes publicly accessible for comparison through our website, providing researchers with a standardized reference for identifying potential overlaps and shared provenance. Thirdly, since hashing alone cannot detect all duplicates, we introduce MAP (Metadata for Aggregation and Provenance), a lightweight, portable metadata profile for documenting provenance, known overlaps, and deduplication decisions in dataset collections. Our contributions help dataset collections shift from coarse aggregations to reliable and provenance-aware data scaling mechanisms in medical image analysis. A web tool supporting our work is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the structural problems of aggregating public 3D medical imaging datasets, using 565k radiological images from 1034 public datasets. It finds at least 118k duplicate pairs and introduces MAP, a metadata profile for documenting provenance and deduplication decisions.
AI.motivation: Expert annotation limits curated medical datasets to small cohorts, so public datasets are increasingly combined into large collections. Combining them obscures provenance and risks reuse propagation, leakage, bias amplification and distorted distributions.
AI.method: The authors formalize dataset collections as a distinct paradigm and characterize their challenges, including reuse propagation, duplication and provenance fragmentation. They run a large-scale duplication study using perceptual hashing and manual tracing, and publish the perceptual hashes. They also introduce MAP (Metadata for Aggregation and Provenance), a lightweight portable profile, because hashing alone cannot detect all duplicates.
AI.result: The study finds extensive exact and near-duplicate reuse across public datasets, with a lower bound of 118k duplicate pairs among 565k 3D radiological images from 1034 datasets.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that dataset collections should move from coarse aggregation to provenance-aware data scaling, supported by the hashes, the MAP profile and a web tool.

title: BATCH: Behavior Alignment for Cross-Embodiment Learning from Humans
summary: Human demonstrations provide a scalable source of diverse manipulation data, but leveraging them for robot learning remains challenging due to differences in embodiment, viewpoint, action spaces, and temporal structure. We introduce BATCH, a cross-embodiment learning framework that explicitly aligns human and robot behaviors. BATCH learns self-supervised temporal representations with a cycle-consistency objective to establish cross-embodiment correspondences without manual annotation. We further introduce two complementary training objectives that leverage these correspondences within an autoregressive videoaction diffusion model: behavior-aligned co-training and human-to-robot style transfer. On real-world manipulation tasks, BATCH improves generalization to unseen task configurations compared with training on unaligned data and prior cross-embodiment baselines, with additional gains from the style-transfer objective. Our results demonstrate that explicit behavior alignment enables more effective transfer from human demonstrations to robot policies.

AI.tldr: BATCH is a cross-embodiment learning framework that aligns human and robot behaviour with self-supervised temporal representations trained by a cycle-consistency objective. It improves generalization to unseen task configurations in an autoregressive video-action diffusion model.
AI.motivation: Human demonstrations are a scalable source of manipulation data, but differences in embodiment, viewpoint, action space and temporal structure make them hard to use for robot learning.
AI.method: BATCH learns self-supervised temporal representations with a cycle-consistency objective to find cross-embodiment correspondences without manual annotation. Two objectives use these correspondences in an autoregressive video-action diffusion model: behaviour-aligned co-training and human-to-robot style transfer.
AI.result: On real-world manipulation tasks, BATCH improves generalization to unseen task configurations over training on unaligned data and over prior cross-embodiment baselines, with additional gains from the style-transfer objective.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that explicit behaviour alignment enables more effective transfer from human demonstrations to robot policies.

title: FAIR Universe Weak Lensing ML Uncertainty Challenge: Dataset and Cosmological Inference Competition
comment: 10+7 pages, 2+4 figures, 2+1 tables. Key results of the NeurIPS 2025 FAIR Universe Weak Lensing ML Challenge Phase 1. The challenge dataset is publicly available at Zenodo: this https URL. Challenge GitHub repository: this https URL
summary: Weak gravitational lensing is a powerful cosmological probe that enables direct mapping of the matter distribution and precise constraints on the fundamental parameters governing structure formation in the universe. In recent years, machine learning has shown strong potential for extracting cosmological information from weak-lensing data beyond traditional summary statistics. However, progress has been limited by the lack of standardized benchmarks that capture the complexity of the dataset, simulator imperfections, and various systematic biases encountered in realistic analyses. To address this gap, we present the FAIR Universe Weak Lensing Machine Learning Uncertainty Challenge, one of the NeurIPS 2025 competitions, as a benchmark dataset and evaluation study. Our dataset reflects realistic weak-lensing observations, incorporating multiple systematic biases, and thereby providing a controlled testbed for robust cosmological inference under uncertainties. We summarize the main methodological advances developed by the winners of our challenge, including data augmentation with conditional optimal transport, an AI-agent-driven approach for parameter inference, ensemble learning, Vision Transformer-based architectures, and physics-informed feature integration. By unifying the benchmark dataset and the winning solutions, this work provides a community resource for developing and evaluating machine learning methods for weak lensing cosmology and, more broadly, for scientific inference under systematic uncertainties.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the FAIR Universe Weak Lensing Machine Learning Uncertainty Challenge, a NeurIPS 2025 competition, as a benchmark dataset with realistic systematic biases for cosmological inference. It also summarizes the methods of the winning teams.
AI.motivation: Machine learning for extracting cosmology from weak-lensing data lacks standardized benchmarks that capture simulator imperfections and systematic biases found in realistic analyses.
AI.method: The dataset reflects realistic weak-lensing observations with multiple systematic biases. The paper summarizes the winning solutions, which use conditional optimal transport for data augmentation, an AI-agent-driven approach to parameter inference, ensemble learning, Vision Transformer architectures and physics-informed feature integration.
AI.result: The paper unifies the benchmark dataset with the winning solutions as an evaluation study. The abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The authors position the work as a community resource for developing and evaluating machine learning methods for weak-lensing cosmology and for scientific inference under systematic uncertainties.

title: OfficeTwin: Realizing 3D Reconstruction of Redundant Scenes through Partial Viewpoint Perception
summary: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction turns an uncalibrated monocular stream into a dense point cloud in a single inference pass, orders of magnitude faster than classical structure-from-motion (e.g., COLMAP), and reliable on the weakly textured, repetitive surfaces where keypoint matching fails outright. However, raw point clouds lack the object identity, physical properties, and watertight volume required for robot learning. This gap widens under robot-native capture. A camera mounted on a robot constrained to a few degrees of freedom sees each object only partially, and the repetitive, weakly textured structure of an office makes distinct workstations nearly indistinguishable, leaving redundant and partial observations that downstream reconstruction cannot resolve. Existing image-to-3D generation methods struggle with these conditions, hallucinating geometry under incomplete views and confusing repeated instances. We present OfficeTwin, a robot-native framework that converts these incomplete observations into simulation-ready digital twins. OfficeTwin first imposes metric and structural constraints, then exploits the office's structural redundancy by registering repeated cubicles into a shared canonical frame, where complementary observations recover geometry occluded in any single view without hallucination. On a real office scan, OfficeTwin recovers every cubicle as an individually watertight, metric solid, outperforming feed-forward reconstruction and generative baselines that fail to produce simulation-ready assets.

AI.tldr: OfficeTwin converts partial, redundant robot-captured views of an office into watertight, metric, simulation-ready digital twins by registering repeated cubicles into a shared canonical frame. On a real office scan it outperforms feed-forward reconstruction and generative baselines.
AI.motivation: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction gives dense point clouds quickly but without object identity, physical properties or watertight volumes needed for robot learning. Robot-mounted cameras see objects only partially, and repetitive, weakly textured office structure makes workstations nearly indistinguishable.
AI.method: OfficeTwin first imposes metric and structural constraints, then exploits the office's structural redundancy by registering repeated cubicles into a shared canonical frame. Complementary observations across cubicles recover geometry occluded in any single view, without hallucination.
AI.result: On a real office scan, OfficeTwin recovers every cubicle as an individually watertight, metric solid. Feed-forward reconstruction and generative baselines fail to produce simulation-ready assets.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that exploiting structural redundancy in robot-native capture yields simulation-ready digital twins where existing methods do not.

title: Evaluating classification and explainability in multimodal petrographic image analysis
summary: Automated thin-section classifiers increasingly combine plane-polarised and cross-polarised light (PPL and XPL), two complementary views central to petrographic identification. Classification accuracy alone does not reveal whether model errors reflect mineralogical relationships, how predictions depend on each optical view, or whether attribution maps identify regions that influence model decisions. Here, we examine these complementary aspects of the released LITHOS dual-stream vision transformer using outputs from an earlier evaluation of 105,802 expert-annotated grains across 25 categories. Classification errors frequently followed the label taxonomy: 72.6\% of misclassified plagioclase, microcline and sanidine grains were assigned the generic Feldspar label, while 87.1\% of quartz-family grains received a label within that family, compared with 66.6\% assigned their exact label. Replacing the XPL input with its per-channel spatial means produced a greater reduction in true-class probability than equivalent PPL replacement in 20 of 25 categories, but not in the three quartz categories. Five explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) attribution procedures generated visually distinct maps for identical inputs. In a superpixel-deletion analysis involving 30 grains from 29 thin sections, method-minus-random contrasts ranged from $-0.043$ to $0.057$, with all 41 simultaneous 95\% confidence intervals including zero. Together, these findings show that error structure, modality sensitivity and attribution behaviour capture distinct aspects of model performance that cannot be established from classification accuracy or visual inspection of attribution maps alone.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates the released LITHOS dual-stream vision transformer for thin-section petrography, using plane-polarised and cross-polarised light, and goes beyond accuracy to examine error structure, modality reliance and explainability maps. It shows that these aspects capture distinct facets of model behaviour that accuracy alone does not reveal.
AI.motivation: Classification accuracy does not reveal whether model errors reflect mineralogical relationships, how predictions depend on each optical view, or whether attribution maps identify regions that influence decisions.
AI.method: The authors analyse outputs from an earlier evaluation of 105,802 expert-annotated grains across 25 categories. They replace the cross-polarised input with its per-channel spatial means and compare the drop in true-class probability with the equivalent plane-polarised replacement. They also compare five explainable AI attribution methods and run a superpixel-deletion analysis on 30 grains from 29 thin sections.
AI.result: Of misclassified plagioclase, microcline and sanidine grains, 72.6% were labelled as the generic Feldspar, while 87.1% of quartz-family errors stayed within that family, compared with 66.6% assigned the exact label. Cross-polarised replacement reduced true-class probability more than plane-polarised replacement in 20 of 25 categories, but not in the three quartz categories. Method-minus-random contrasts ranged from -0.043 to 0.057, and all 41 simultaneous 95% confidence intervals included zero.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that error structure, modality sensitivity and attribution behaviour each capture distinct aspects of performance that accuracy and visual inspection of attribution maps cannot establish.

title: EmbodiedIntentBench: Benchmarking Intent-Driven Runtime Adaptation for Mobile Robotic Missions
comment: Paper is currently under review. Authors' version posted for personal use and not for redistribution
summary: Mobile robotic sensing systems must adapt to operator requirements, limited resources, changing connectivity, and observation opportunities shaped by physical motion. Evaluating runtime strategies therefore requires assessing whether their decisions fulfill mission objectives, beyond isolated perception accuracy or execution efficiency. We present EmbodiedIntentBench, a benchmark for intent-driven runtime adaptation in mobile robotic missions. It represents mission intent through structured contracts for coverage, temporal evidence, reporting, urgency, and resources, and couples simulated unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) workloads with causal, resource-accounted execution. Computation decisions affect mission time, resource use, and which observations can contribute evidence. We evaluate fixed and adaptive perception strategies in multi-phase missions and under changing urgency, connectivity, and battery conditions. In the multi-phase Depot study, a configuration with 87.5% full-bank target recall across visible target observations completes only 1 of 16 missions, whereas a lower-recall configuration completes 14. In an ablation, ignoring execution-induced observation loss increases aggregate mission success and reverses the ordering of two runtime strategies. Replays using Jetson AGX Orin CPU and GPU profiles change the relative success of local and remote strategies. In selected Jetson GPU-profile replays, intent-driven adaptation reduces modeled task energy by up to 28% with unchanged mission success. EmbodiedIntentBench provides an extensible framework for evaluating runtime decisions against mission fulfillment under physical and resource constraints.

AI.tldr: EmbodiedIntentBench is a benchmark for intent-driven runtime adaptation in mobile robotic missions, using simulated UAV workloads with resource-accounted execution. It shows that evaluating runtime strategies by mission fulfilment can change the ranking of strategies.
AI.motivation: Mobile robotic sensing must adapt to operator requirements, limited resources, changing connectivity and motion-dependent observations. Evaluating runtime decisions therefore requires measuring mission fulfilment, not only perception accuracy or execution efficiency.
AI.method: The benchmark expresses mission intent as structured contracts covering coverage, temporal evidence, reporting, urgency and resources. It couples simulated UAV workloads with causal, resource-accounted execution, so computation decisions affect mission time, resource use and which observations count as evidence. Fixed and adaptive perception strategies are tested in multi-phase missions under changing urgency, connectivity and battery conditions.
AI.result: In the multi-phase Depot study, a configuration with 87.5% full-bank target recall across visible target observations completes 1 of 16 missions, while a lower-recall configuration completes 14. An ablation shows that ignoring execution-induced observation loss raises aggregate mission success and reverses the ordering of two runtime strategies. Jetson AGX Orin CPU and GPU profile replays change the relative success of local and remote strategies. In selected Jetson GPU-profile replays, intent-driven adaptation reduces modelled task energy by up to 28% with unchanged mission success.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that EmbodiedIntentBench offers an extensible framework for judging runtime decisions by mission fulfilment under physical and resource constraints.

title: Learning a Unified Cross-Model Semantic Dictionary via Gated Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoders
comment: The 40th Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Foundation models pretrained on similar data distributions tend to learn overlapping semantic structure, but their representations are distinct due to different model architecture, pretraining objectives and protocols. This prevents unified interpretability and cross-model feature reuse. Existing approaches extract interpretable concepts from individual models and align these concepts in a shared coordinate system using cross-reconstruction objectives, but the alignment only applies to latent coordinates while the concepts themselves remain model-specific and cannot be shared or reused. This paper introduces the Gated Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoder (GB-SAE), which casts unified cross-model interpretability as a representation factorization problem and solves it by simultaneously learning a unified shared dictionary and multiple private model-specific dictionaries via a gated bottleneck sparse autoencoder framework. The shared dictionary encodes the cross-model common semantic structure in unified concepts that are reusable across all participating models (and beyond), while each private dictionary comprises residual concepts that capture model-specific biases. We evaluate GB-SAE with distinct foundation models including ViT, SigLIP, DINOv2, and ConvNeXt. GB-SAE demonstrates superior reconstruction capability, unified and faithful interpretability, strong reusability and generalization to unseen models and downstream tasks. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Gated Bottleneck Sparse Autoencoder (GB-SAE), which learns one shared dictionary of semantic concepts across foundation models together with private model-specific dictionaries. It is evaluated on ViT, SigLIP, DINOv2 and ConvNeXt.
AI.motivation: Foundation models with similar data distributions learn overlapping semantic structure, but their representations differ, which prevents unified interpretability and cross-model feature reuse. Existing alignment methods align only latent coordinates, while the concepts remain model-specific.
AI.method: GB-SAE treats unified cross-model interpretability as a representation factorization problem. It learns a shared dictionary of concepts reusable across all participating models, and a private dictionary per model that holds residual, model-specific concepts, all within a gated bottleneck sparse autoencoder framework.
AI.result: The abstract reports superior reconstruction capability, unified and faithful interpretability, strong reusability, and generalization to unseen models and downstream tasks, across ViT, SigLIP, DINOv2 and ConvNeXt. It gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that factorizing representations into shared and private dictionaries gives a unified, reusable interpretation across models.

title: Compact Quantum Channel Attention for Static ASL Recognition: A Controlled Study with Parameter-Matched Baselines
summary: Hybrid quantum-classical models often report good accuracy on image tasks, but it is rarely clear whether the quantum part is responsible. This paper proposes QCA-DenseNet, a static American Sign Language (ASL) recognition pipeline in which an eight-qubit variational circuit acts as a channel-attention gate on DenseNet121 features. The quantum channel attention (QCA) gate has 17,464 parameters, 7.51 times fewer than a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) block. The pipeline is tested on 1,815 MU HandImages images by holding out one of five signers at a time, and a frozen-backbone ablation uses small parts of the Kaggle ASL Alphabet data. On unseen signers, QCA-DenseNet reaches 94.50% mean accuracy, above SE (93.72%) and within 0.28 points of the best model. A matched classical MLP and a model without attention perform about the same, and no difference is significant. QCA gives a much smaller attention gate without a detectable loss in accuracy, but no quantum advantage.

AI.tldr: QCA-DenseNet adds an eight-qubit variational circuit as a channel-attention gate on DenseNet121 for static ASL recognition. Matched controls show that its accuracy is no better than classical attention, so the paper finds a smaller attention gate but no quantum advantage.
AI.motivation: Hybrid quantum-classical models often report good image accuracy, but it is rarely clear whether the quantum component causes the gain.
AI.method: The quantum channel attention (QCA) gate has 17,464 parameters, 7.51 times fewer than a squeeze-and-excitation (SE) block. It is evaluated on 1,815 MU HandImages with leave-one-signer-out testing across five signers. A frozen-backbone ablation uses parts of the Kaggle ASL Alphabet data. A parameter-matched classical MLP and a model without attention are included as controls.
AI.result: On unseen signers, QCA-DenseNet reaches 94.50% mean accuracy, above SE (93.72%) and within 0.28 points of the best model. The matched classical MLP and the model without attention perform about the same, and no difference is significant.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that QCA gives a much smaller attention gate without a detectable loss in accuracy, but shows no quantum advantage.

title: HSGNav: Hypothesis Scene Graphs for Multi-Scale Lifelong Navigation under Object Relocation
summary: In real homes, assistive robots must repeatedly locate targets from large furniture to tiny tabletop items, as people move objects between household surfaces. Uniformly instantiating detections at different scales as 3D objects can be brittle for small on-surface items; without explicit object-state validation, stale entries may persist after scene changes. Our key insight is to separate persistent 3D furniture entities from revisable surface-object hypotheses, retaining their visual evidence without requiring independent object geometry. We formalize this design as the Hypothesis Scene Graph (HSG), which preserves small-object evidence and supports local revision without rebuilding the stable entity topology. Building on HSG, HSGNav uses this separation for multi-scale lifelong navigation: retrieval selects entity or hypothesis evidence according to target scale, exploration acquires additional surface observations, and verification confirms target presence or invalidates contradicted hypothesis records. Because existing lifelong benchmarks such as GOAT-Bench rarely require mid-episode memory invalidation or multi-scale search, we introduce FAROS-Bench (Find And Re-find Objects across Scales) for mid-episode relocation of surface objects and multi-scale find goals. Experiments show that HSGNav performs competitively on GOAT-Bench while substantially outperforming prior methods on FAROS-Bench.

AI.tldr: HSGNav is a navigation method for assistive robots that separates persistent 3D furniture entities from revisable surface-object hypotheses in a Hypothesis Scene Graph (HSG). It performs competitively on GOAT-Bench and outperforms prior methods on the new FAROS-Bench, which tests object relocation and multi-scale search.
AI.motivation: Assistive robots must find targets from large furniture to small tabletop items as people move objects. Treating small surface objects as 3D objects can be brittle, and without object-state validation, stale entries can persist after scene changes. Existing lifelong benchmarks rarely require mid-episode memory invalidation or multi-scale search.
AI.method: The Hypothesis Scene Graph keeps furniture as persistent entities and small on-surface objects as hypotheses that keep their visual evidence without independent geometry, and supports local revision. HSGNav selects entity or hypothesis evidence by target scale, acquires extra surface observations during exploration, and verifies targets, invalidating contradicted hypothesis records. The authors introduce FAROS-Bench (Find And Re-find Objects across Scales) for mid-episode relocation and multi-scale find goals.
AI.result: HSGNav performs competitively on GOAT-Bench and substantially outperforms prior methods on FAROS-Bench. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that separating persistent entities from revisable hypotheses supports lifelong navigation under object relocation at multiple scales.

title: Seeing Isn't Enough: Unlocking Visual Reasoning by Bridging the Reasoning-Access Gap with TIGER
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) inherit strong textual reasoning capabilities from their language backbones and text pretraining, but often fail to apply the same level of competency to visual inputs. We show that this degradation cannot be attributed to only perception failures, by evaluating models on semantically-equivalent text and rendered-text image inputs: models can accurately read text in the images and recover near-text performance when provided their own transcriptions, but just cannot reason well on the images directly. We characterize this discrepancy as a modality reasoning-access gap, where models fail to route perceived visual content into existing reasoning machinery accessible with text. To bridge this, we propose TIGER (Text-to-Image Gap-targeted training for Enhanced Reasoning), which first mines synthetic modality counterfactuals where a model succeeds on a text problem but fails when provided the corresponding rendered image, and post-trains the model on the image input via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), along with SFT and DPO variants. Importantly, although trained exclusively on synthetic rendered-text images with no multimodal annotations, TIGER results in model performance improvements across diverse real-world visual benchmarks including geometric diagrams (MathVerse), multi-disciplinary sciences (EMMA, MMMU), complex charts (ChartQAPro), and embodied spatial reasoning (RoboSpatial-Home). TIGER also complements existing state-of-the-art RLVR visual reasoning methods, yielding further performance gains. Analysis involving reasoning-subspace activation and activation patching provide support indicating that TIGER helps to align visual-to-reasoning pathways toward text reasoning states. Our implementation is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper attributes weak visual reasoning in multimodal LLMs to a modality reasoning-access gap, where perceived visual content is not routed into the text reasoning machinery, and proposes TIGER, a training method on synthetic rendered-text images that improves real-world visual reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: MLLMs reason well on text but much worse on semantically equivalent images, and the authors show this is not only a perception failure since models can read the image text and recover near-text performance when given their own transcriptions.
AI.method: TIGER mines synthetic modality counterfactuals where a model succeeds on a text problem but fails on the rendered image, then post-trains on the image input with GRPO, plus SFT and DPO variants, using no multimodal annotations.
AI.result: Training only on synthetic rendered-text images improves performance on MathVerse, EMMA, MMMU, ChartQAPro and RoboSpatial-Home, and it adds further gains on top of existing state-of-the-art RLVR visual reasoning methods; activation analysis and activation patching suggest visual-to-reasoning pathways move toward text reasoning states.
AI.conclusion: The gap is a routing problem between perception and reasoning rather than only a perception deficit, and targeting it with synthetic counterfactual data offers a route to better visual reasoning without multimodal annotation.

title: EgoVeil: Personalized Privacy Reasoning for Egocentric Video
summary: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) enable AI systems to interpret egocentric video. Yet continuous visual capture raises privacy concerns because sensitive content is pervasive and varies across users and contexts. We present EgoVeil, a personalized privacy reasoning system that determines which visual content to obscure based on individual preferences while retaining context useful for downstream assistance. It converts localized visual regions into structured semantic observations and combines a privacy reasoner with an explicit user-specific memory for personalized privacy reasoning. This design supports personalization and continual adaptation as preference evidence accumulates. We evaluate on in-the-wild data from 10 smart-glasses users under a cross-user chronological protocol. EgoVeil achieves 91.93% balanced accuracy and 84.42% Mask recall, outperforming direct VLM baselines and other controlled privacy reasoning baselines. Our results show that personalized, adaptive privacy reasoning better aligns privacy preservation with individual preferences while retaining the visual context needed for effective smart-glasses assistance.

AI.tldr: EgoVeil is a personalized privacy reasoning system for egocentric video that decides which visual regions to obscure according to each user's preferences while keeping the context needed for assistance.
AI.motivation: Continuous capture by smart glasses exposes sensitive content that varies across users and contexts, and direct VLM baselines do not adapt to individual privacy preferences.
AI.method: EgoVeil converts localized visual regions into structured semantic observations and combines a privacy reasoner with an explicit user-specific memory that accumulates preference evidence over time for continual adaptation.
AI.result: On in-the-wild data from 10 smart-glasses users under a cross-user chronological protocol, EgoVeil reaches 91.93% balanced accuracy and 84.42% Mask recall, outperforming direct VLM baselines and other controlled privacy reasoning baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicit personalized memory with adaptive reasoning aligns privacy protection with individual preferences while preserving the visual context that smart-glasses assistance needs.

title: STABLE: A Continual Learning Optimizer with Adaptive Drift Control
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Continual learning suffers from catastrophic forgetting, leading to the loss of past knowledge and unstable adaptation across task streams. Existing approaches typically address this issue through replay buffers, architectural changes, or additional regularization terms. We argue that forgetting is a consequence of unstable learning dynamics, which may benefit from an optimizer-level solution. The main challenge is that learning dynamics are time-dependent, as demonstrated by empirical phenomena such as the stability gap. First, we formally prove that, for distance-based classifiers, bounded parameter drift guarantees bounded margin erosion under a local score-stability condition. Based on this insight, we propose STABLE, a primal-dual optimizer with adaptive drift control. STABLE enforces a drift budget by increasing the dual variable when the budget is violated and decreasing it otherwise. This results in high stability without penalizing plasticity. Experiments on long-horizon unimodal streams and CLIP-based multimodal streams show that vanilla PEFT baselines trained with STABLE match or outperform specialized continual learning methods. In the multimodal setting, STABLE further preserves zero-shot transfer, matching or exceeding dedicated multimodal continual learning methods.

AI.tldr: STABLE is a continual learning optimizer that enforces a drift budget through a primal-dual update, aiming to prevent catastrophic forgetting at the optimizer level without replay buffers or extra regularization terms.
AI.motivation: Existing continual learning methods rely on replay buffers, architectural changes or extra regularizers, while the authors argue forgetting stems from unstable learning dynamics that the time-dependent stability gap makes hard to control.
AI.method: The authors prove that for distance-based classifiers, bounded parameter drift guarantees bounded margin erosion under a local score-stability condition, and then propose STABLE, a primal-dual optimizer whose dual variable rises when the drift budget is violated and falls otherwise.
AI.result: On long-horizon unimodal streams and CLIP-based multimodal streams, vanilla PEFT baselines trained with STABLE match or outperform specialized continual learning methods, and in the multimodal setting STABLE preserves zero-shot transfer while matching or exceeding dedicated multimodal methods.
AI.conclusion: Controlling parameter drift at the optimizer level gives high stability without sacrificing plasticity, so simple PEFT backbones can match specialized continual learning approaches.

title: Task-Critical Part Alignment Improves Imitation of Object Interactions
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at ICAR 2025. This is the preprint version; the published version may differ slightly
summary: This paper presents enhancements to the DINOBot framework for imitation learning of object-object interactions. We introduce two key contributions aimed at improving the accuracy and efficiency of alignment in imitation-based robotic tasks. First, we integrate RANdom SAmple Consensus (RANSAC) for outlier rejection during the alignment phase, effectively mitigating the impact of noisy depth data and spurious feature matches. This improves robustness when transferring demonstrations to real-world applications. Second, we refine the semantic correspondence process by focusing on task-relevant interaction regions, ensuring that the learned representation prioritizes critical object features that influence successful manipulation. We evaluated our approach in a range of real-world manipulation tasks, including picking, insertion, shaking, and pouring, using a robotic system. The experimental results demonstrate an overall improvement of 13.8% in task success rates compared to the baseline, along with faster convergence in the alignment process. These results highlight the effectiveness of our enhancements in improving precision and efficiency for object-object interaction imitation in robotics.

AI.tldr: The paper enhances the DINOBot framework for imitation of object-object interactions by adding RANSAC outlier rejection during alignment and by focusing semantic correspondence on task-relevant interaction regions.
AI.motivation: Imitation learning of object interactions suffers from noisy depth data and spurious feature matches during alignment, and correspondence should prioritize the object features that matter for successful manipulation.
AI.method: RANSAC is integrated for outlier rejection in the alignment phase, and the semantic correspondence process is refined to concentrate on task-relevant interaction regions.
AI.result: Across real-world picking, insertion, shaking and pouring tasks, the approach improves task success by 13.8% over the baseline and converges faster in alignment.
AI.conclusion: Filtering outliers and emphasizing task-critical parts improves precision and efficiency in robotic object-object interaction imitation.

title: Constrained Look-ahead Guidance for Interference-Aware Flow Editing
summary: Diffusion and flow models enable powerful generative modeling, but controlled editing remains challenging due to the need to balance source fidelity and edit compliance along the generative trajectory. We propose a principled, inversion-free framework for flow-based image editing from a trajectory centric perspective. Rather than relying on inversion or heuristic guidance, we introduce a one-step look-ahead mechanism that evaluates the effect of candidate updates on both edit and fidelity rewards estimated via denoising, and adjusts the current update based on this evaluation. At each step, our method applies reward-driven corrections guided by the look-ahead evaluation under an explicit fidelity constraint, resulting in stable and coherent trajectory evolution. This look-ahead design mitigates gradient interference between edit and fidelity objectives by anticipating their interaction in future states, leading to improved trade-offs. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves stronger semantic edits while better preserving source content compared to existing strong baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an inversion-free flow-editing method that uses a one-step look-ahead, evaluated on edit and fidelity rewards, to correct each generative update under a fidelity constraint.
AI.motivation: Controlled editing with diffusion and flow models needs to balance source fidelity against edit compliance, but inversion and heuristic guidance are unreliable, and edit and fidelity gradients interfere with each other.
AI.method: At each step the method anticipates the effect of candidate updates on edit and fidelity rewards, estimated via denoising, using a one-step look-ahead, and applies reward-driven corrections under an explicit fidelity constraint.
AI.result: The approach yields stronger semantic edits while better preserving source content than existing strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: Anticipating how edit and fidelity objectives interact in future states yields more stable trajectories and better trade-offs for flow-based image editing.

title: Selective Cooperative Perception via Blind Spot Reasoning and Agentic Dialogue with Vision-Language Models
summary: Real-time cooperative perception (CP) in multi-agent traffic environments is highly resource-intensive, which posing scalability challenges for large-scale deployment. Efficiency can be significantly improved by selectively performing CP only in safety-critical scenarios and for key occluding objects. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are well-suited for complex reasoning in dynamic and uncertain environments, making them a promising tool for this selective CP task. This study proposes a VLM-driven agentic framework for blind spot reasoning and dialogue-based CP. A mixed-model architecture is designed that integrates conventional object detection for stable perception, vision-language reasoning for identifying impactful occlusions, and a physics-based geometric module to align reasoning with real-world visibility constraints. The framework also incorporates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting mechanism to enhance interpretability and intent-aware decision-making. We collect real-world data from connected vehicles operating in urban traffic and compare the driving-critical blind spot identification and dialogue performance of four state-of-the-art VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing. This work provides a scalable, interpretable, and bandwidth-efficient alternative to conventional CP pipelines, and offers new insights into agentic communication design for future connected traffic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a VLM-driven agentic framework that decides when cooperative perception should run by identifying driving-critical blind spots and sharing perception through dialogue, aiming to reduce bandwidth and computation.
