MAAS uses region-specific projections and learned brain tokens to condition Stable Audio through a dedicated cross-attention pathway. On a 7T fMRI dataset, we demonstrate consistent improvements over baselines, including two-stage fMRI-to-latent conditioning, across both acoustic and semantic evaluation metrics. In addition, we introduce a fidelity metric grounded in a computational model of auditory neural processing, which allows us to quantify the contribution of individual auditory cortical regions to reconstructed audio representations.

AI.tldr: MAAS conditions a pretrained audio diffusion transformer directly on ROI-wise fMRI responses, without a decoder that first predicts a stimulus representation. On a 7T fMRI dataset it outperforms baselines and quantifies each auditory cortical region's contribution to reconstructed audio.
AI.motivation: Existing brain-to-audio pipelines map neural responses to predefined stimulus representations before synthesis, and direct brain conditioning has not yet been extended to audio diffusion models.
AI.method: MAAS uses region-specific projections and learned brain tokens to condition Stable Audio through a dedicated cross-attention pathway. A fidelity metric based on a computational model of auditory neural processing measures each auditory cortical region's contribution.
AI.result: On a 7T fMRI dataset MAAS shows consistent improvements over baselines, including two-stage fMRI-to-latent conditioning, on acoustic and semantic metrics.
AI.conclusion: End-to-end conditioning of an audio diffusion transformer on fMRI is a viable route to brain-to-audio reconstruction, and the fidelity metric gives an interpretable view of cortical contributions.

title: Controlled Binary Assignment Flows
summary: This paper introduces a geometric approach to the representation and learning of time-variant parametrizations of deep assignment flows, for binary data labelings on graphs. Each edge carries an optimally controlled parameter flow in a 2-dimensional totally geodesic submanifold, based on objectives derived from a non-local linear scale space representation of the input data. The aggregation of triplets of such flows in 5-dimensional totally geodesic submanifolds is learned from data. The fusion of these flows determines the trajectory in the high-dimensional symmetric parameter space and by geometric integration the layers of binary deep assignment flows. Numerical results demonstrate the expressivity and the limitation of our highly parallel geometric local synthesis approach to high-dimensional deep assignment flow parametrizations.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a geometric framework for time-variant parametrisations of deep assignment flows that label binary data on graphs. Flow parameters are learned on totally geodesic submanifolds and integrated geometrically to form the layers of binary deep assignment flows.
AI.motivation: Deep assignment flows for binary labelings on graphs need expressive, high-dimensional parametrisations, and their learning has not been approached through a geometric representation.
AI.method: Each edge carries an optimally controlled parameter flow in a 2-dimensional totally geodesic submanifold, derived from objectives based on a non-local linear scale-space representation of the input. Triplets of such flows are aggregated in 5-dimensional totally geodesic submanifolds, with the aggregation learned from data. Geometric integration yields the layers.
AI.result: Numerical results demonstrate the expressivity of the highly parallel geometric local synthesis approach and also its limitations for high-dimensional deep assignment flow parametrisations.
AI.conclusion: The geometric approach offers an expressive and parallel way to parametrise binary deep assignment flows, though it has limits in high dimensions.

title: A four-step validation protocol for radiomic survival analysis in small cohorts: a body composition case study
summary: Gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NET) lack prognostic biomarkers, and computed tomography (CT)-based body composition radiomics at the third lumbar vertebra (L3) is a promising candidate. Small cohorts make high-dimensional radiomic models prone to overfitting and single-split evaluations variable and optimistic. This methodological study proposes a four-step validation protocol for radiomic survival analysis in small cohorts: (1) false discovery rate (FDR)-corrected feature selection, (2) a dual-path comparison of prior feature selection versus embedded regularization, (3) repeated nested cross-validation (CV) and (4) a negative control with Gaussian noise features. In 78 GEP-NET patients, 535 radiomic features from five L3 compartments were used to evaluate five survival models with Harrell's concordance index (C-index), time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and integrated Brier score (IBS). Step 1 selected at least one feature in 18% of outer folds under noise (nominal level 20%) versus 84% with radiomic features. The dual-path comparison showed no consistent difference between strategies. Repeated nested CV reduced variability across seeds (41% median reduction in C-index standard deviation), but not enough to distinguish models. The nested CV C-index exceeded chance by 0.07-0.15 with radiomic features but not clearly under noise (0.40-0.42 with prior feature selection, 0.47-0.55 with embedded regularization). Frequently selected features tentatively linked greater subcutaneous fat, skeletal muscle compactness and texture to better prognosis. These findings suggest a modest prognostic signal in L3 radiomics, with considerable uncertainty that the protocol quantifies. The protocol may transfer to other small-cohort radiomic survival studies. Code: this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a four-step validation protocol for radiomic survival analysis in small cohorts and applies it to CT body-composition radiomics at L3 in gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours. The protocol finds only a modest prognostic signal with considerable uncertainty.
AI.motivation: GEP-NET lacks prognostic biomarkers, and L3 body-composition radiomics is a promising candidate. Small cohorts make high-dimensional radiomic models prone to overfitting and single-split evaluations optimistic and variable.
AI.method: The four steps are FDR-corrected feature selection, a dual-path comparison of prior feature selection versus embedded regularisation, repeated nested cross-validation, and a negative control with Gaussian noise features. Five survival models were evaluated in 78 patients using 535 features from five L3 compartments, with Harrell's C-index, time-dependent AUC and integrated Brier score.
AI.result: Under noise, step 1 selected at least one feature in 18% of outer folds, against 84% with radiomic features (nominal level 20%). Repeated nested CV reduced C-index standard deviation across seeds by a median of 41%. The nested CV C-index exceeded chance by 0.07 to 0.15 with radiomic features, but not clearly under noise (0.40 to 0.42 with prior selection, 0.47 to 0.55 with embedded regularisation). Greater subcutaneous fat, muscle compactness and texture were tentatively linked to better prognosis.
AI.conclusion: L3 radiomics shows a modest prognostic signal, and the protocol quantifies the uncertainty around it. The protocol may transfer to other small-cohort radiomic survival studies.

title: Anchor Behavior, Not Parameters: Rehearsal-Free Continual Learning with a Single Shared Prompt
summary: Prompt-based continual learning adapts a frozen pre-trained vision transformer by tuning a small set of prompt tokens. Recently, one-prompt methods which share one single prompt across all tasks make this paradigm maximally parameter efficient. The open question is how a shared prompt can keep the knowledge of old classes while being updated for new ones. Existing methods protect old knowledge in parameter space, where they freeze task-specific prompts, expand new components, or sparsely gate which tokens receive gradients. However, this method sacrifices plasticity, yet the drift it still permits in shared tokens can corrupt the prompt's function on past classes. What must be preserved is the prompt's behavior. We propose TEA-Prompt, which couples (i) a token evaluation module that assigns each prompt token a continuous, input-conditional relevance score injected into the attention logits, softly specializing tokens across tasks without discarding any of them, and (ii) an attention-behavior anchoring loss that constrains each token's attention output around class-specific query regions using only compact Gaussian query statistics without stored old images, weighted by the token's past relevance. Anchoring the attention value allows the parameters to continue updating freely, as long as their interaction remains unchanged. TEA-Prompt achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with markedly lower forgetting on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R, and CUB-200 with only 0.38M parameters. Code is publicy available at this https URL

AI.tldr: TEA-Prompt is a rehearsal-free continual learning method that uses a single shared prompt for a frozen vision transformer and anchors the prompt's attention behaviour rather than its parameters. It reaches state-of-the-art accuracy with less forgetting on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R and CUB-200 using 0.38M parameters.
AI.motivation: Single-prompt continual learning must keep old-class knowledge while updating the shared prompt. Parameter-space protection sacrifices plasticity, and drift in shared tokens can still corrupt the prompt's function on past classes.
AI.method: A token evaluation module assigns each prompt token an input-conditional relevance score injected into the attention logits, specialising tokens across tasks without discarding any. An attention-behaviour anchoring loss keeps each token's attention output near class-specific query regions, using compact Gaussian query statistics instead of stored old images and weighted by past relevance.
AI.result: TEA-Prompt achieves state-of-the-art accuracy with markedly lower forgetting on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R and CUB-200 with only 0.38M parameters.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring attention behaviour lets parameters keep learning freely while preserving the prompt's function on previous classes, without storing old data.

title: Guiding Data Allocation for Robust Subpopulation Generalization
summary: Machine learning models often achieve high average accuracy in the training data while performing poorly on test data due to subpopulation shift. A common data-centric solution is to enforce balanced subgroup proportions, but full balance can be costly, infeasible, and not always necessary. In this work, we study whether balanced training data is the unique optimal configuration for robust subpopulation generalization. We extend a Gaussian feature-model framework to theoretically characterize the performance landscape across general training subgroup distributions. We show that multiple configurations, including substantially imbalanced ones, can perform comparably to the balanced one. We further derive gradient-based directions for adjusting subgroup proportions to improve adjusted accuracy and worst-group accuracy more efficiently. These findings suggest that strategically allocating data offers a more flexible and principled path to robust performance than simple balancing. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that balanced subgroup proportions are not the unique optimal training configuration for robust subpopulation generalisation. Within a Gaussian feature-model framework, several imbalanced configurations perform comparably to the balanced one, and gradient-based directions are derived for adjusting proportions.
AI.motivation: Models often perform well on average on training data but poorly under subpopulation shift at test time. Full balancing of subgroup proportions can be costly, infeasible and not always necessary.
AI.method: The authors extend a Gaussian feature-model framework to characterise performance across general training subgroup distributions and derive gradient-based directions for adjusting subgroup proportions to improve adjusted and worst-group accuracy.
AI.result: Multiple configurations, including substantially imbalanced ones, perform comparably to the balanced configuration. The gradient-based adjustments improve adjusted accuracy and worst-group accuracy more efficiently than simple balancing.
AI.conclusion: Strategic allocation of training data offers a more flexible and principled route to robust subpopulation performance than simple balancing.

title: MAGE: Towards Generalizable Multi-timescale EEG Representations
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) data plays an important role in understanding human brain activity, with various major applications. While current approaches, which largely build on EEG foundation models, have demonstrated strong performance across datasets and tasks, they typically rely on a fixed temporal scale. This design choice limits their ability to capture characteristics of neural dynamic behavior, often spanning across multiple timescales, which are naturally captured in EEG recordings. To address this limitation, we propose MAGE (\textbf{Multi-timescale Adaptive Generalization for EEG}), a foundation model that dynamically adapts to capture and integrate information across different timescales. Specifically, MAGE combines two key mechanisms: (i) a novel multi-timescale attention mechanism, capable of learning representations across multiple temporal scales and (ii) a trainable aggregation module, that dynamically identifies and adapts to the most informative timescale of the input signal. Experimental results across seven datasets demonstrate that MAGE consistently outperforms existing EEG foundation models while using substantially fewer parameters. Moreover, our results support the hypothesis that different downstream tasks benefit from distinct temporal scales. All source code will be released.

AI.tldr: MAGE is an EEG foundation model that learns representations across multiple temporal scales through multi-timescale attention and a trainable aggregation module that selects the most informative timescale. It outperforms existing EEG foundation models on seven datasets with substantially fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Current EEG foundation models rely on a fixed temporal scale, which limits their capacity to capture neural dynamics that span multiple timescales.
AI.method: MAGE combines a multi-timescale attention mechanism that learns representations across several temporal scales with a trainable aggregation module that dynamically identifies and adapts to the most informative timescale of each input.
AI.result: Across seven datasets MAGE consistently outperforms existing EEG foundation models while using substantially fewer parameters. Different downstream tasks benefit from distinct temporal scales.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive multi-timescale modelling is a useful inductive bias for EEG foundation models, and task-dependent timescale preferences suggest that a fixed scale is a limiting choice.

title: Causal Discovery Bench: Can LLMs Autonomously Conduct Effective Experiments?
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Code: this https URL
summary: As large language model (LLM) agents get actively adopted for autonomous research, they must not only reason over existing evidence, but also design informative experiments, allocate resources, analyze sequential observations, and decide when to stop and make conclusions. Yet these capabilities remain poorly measured. We introduce Causal-Discovery-Bench (this https URL), a verifiable sandbox with configurable structural equation models and resource constraints to evaluate sequential experimental design and causal discovery without domain-semantic cues. Across 3,802 episodes with 13 models from 5 vendors, we analyze agent behavior along 40 metrics in seven families. Agents' performance exhibits a four-level difficulty hierarchy spanning single-experiment design, sequential exploration of causal relationships, resource-aware experimentation balancing cost and statistical power, and autonomous resolution of conflicting evidence. We identify a substantial performance gap between causal inference from correctly curated evidence and navigating causal discovery through autonomous experimentation: Analyzing agents' action trajectories attributes 94.5% of their mistakes to experimental design rather than to inference, which is further consolidated with ablation studies. Relaxing resource constraints alone does not reliably resolve failures in sequential discovery. In contrast, basic statistical tools substantially improve performance across multiple model families, while advanced tools provide little additional benefit when models lack prerequisite lower-level capabilities.

AI.tldr: Causal-Discovery-Bench is a verifiable sandbox for testing whether LLM agents can design experiments, allocate resources and reach causal conclusions. Across 3,802 episodes with 13 models, agent mistakes are mostly attributed to experimental design rather than inference.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly used for autonomous research, yet their ability to design informative experiments, manage resources, analyse sequential observations and decide when to stop has been poorly measured.
AI.method: The benchmark uses configurable structural equation models with resource constraints and no domain-semantic cues. Agent behaviour is analysed along 40 metrics in seven families across 3,802 episodes with 13 models from 5 vendors, with action trajectories examined and ablation studies run.
AI.result: Performance follows a four-level difficulty hierarchy, from single-experiment design through sequential exploration and resource-aware experimentation to resolving conflicting evidence. Agents make a substantial gap between inference from curated evidence and autonomous experimentation, and 94.5% of mistakes are attributed to experimental design. Relaxing resource constraints alone does not fix sequential discovery, while basic statistical tools improve performance across model families and advanced tools help little when lower-level capabilities are missing.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous causal discovery is limited mainly by experimental design rather than inference, so agents need sound design and sequential reasoning before advanced analysis tools pay off.

title: Fresh Enough to Decide: Age of Intelligence for Cost-Aware Model Synchronization in Dynamic IoT Systems
summary: Resource-constrained IoT devices cache learned models for real-time decisions, but frequent updates incur substantial bandwidth, energy, and service overhead. Because decision-relevant model differences need not grow with elapsed time, we define Age of Intelligence (AoInt) as a model-version-relative, client-specific, and action utility distortion, and formulate synchronization as a tradeoff between stale-decision regret and refresh cost. Furthermore, we develop Kullback-Leibler-aware AoInt Synchronization (KL-AoIntSync), which accumulates output-distribution changes using client-specific unlabeled probes, whereas Parameter-aware AoInt Synchronization (Param-AoIntSync) uses a server-broadcast scalar parameter change. Then, we establish pathwise guarantees with fixed client distributions, action sets, and utilities. The numerical results show that calibrated Param-AoIntSync reduces joint synchronization cost by 6.15% relative to an Instant-Parameters policy while performing comparably to KL-AoIntSync.

AI.tldr: The paper defines Age of Intelligence (AoInt), a client-specific measure of how much stale model versions distort decisions, and uses it to schedule model synchronization for IoT devices. Calibrated Param-AoIntSync cuts joint synchronization cost by 6.15% versus an Instant-Parameters policy while performing comparably to KL-AoIntSync.
AI.motivation: IoT devices cache learned models for real-time decisions, but frequent model updates cost bandwidth, energy and service overhead. Update decisions should depend on decision-relevant model differences rather than elapsed time.
AI.method: AoInt is defined as a model-version-relative, client-specific and action-utility distortion, and synchronization is formulated as a tradeoff between stale-decision regret and refresh cost. KL-AoIntSync accumulates output-distribution changes measured on client-specific unlabeled probes, while Param-AoIntSync uses a server-broadcast scalar parameter change. Pathwise guarantees are established under fixed client distributions, action sets and utilities.
AI.result: Calibrated Param-AoIntSync reduces joint synchronization cost by 6.15% relative to an Instant-Parameters policy and performs comparably to KL-AoIntSync.
AI.conclusion: Model-synchronization timing can be driven by decision-relevant distortion, and a cheap scalar signal (parameter change) can nearly match the output-based criterion.

title: Topological Deep Learning Challenge 2026: Bridging the Gap
summary: This paper describes the 2026 edition of the Topological Deep Learning Challenge: Bridging the Gap, hosted at the second Topology, Algebra, and Geometry in Data Science (TAG-DS) Conference. Where previous editions grew the modelling and data ecosystem of Topological Deep Learning (TDL), this edition set out to place Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Topological Neural Networks (TNNs) side by side under a single evaluation pipeline. Participants implemented recent state-of-the-art architectures in TopoBench, with Track 1 covering GNNs and Track 2 covering TNNs. They evaluated these implementations on shared synthetic benchmarks generated with GraphUniverse, which independently controls homophily, average degree and degree-distribution heaviness. The challenge yielded 68 qualifying submissions from 34 teams, spanning the graph, simplicial, cellular, hypergraph and combinatorial domains. For the first time, submissions were also tracked on a public leaderboard, which we summarize and analyze here. Our analysis finds that the differences between the submitted tracks are strongly task-dependent: the mean accuracy gap is modest on community detection, while on triangle counting the Track 1 mean error is 1.85 times the Track 2 mean. Several structurally informed GNNs also outperform the Track 2 mean on triangle counting.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the 2026 Topological Deep Learning Challenge, which evaluated Graph Neural Networks (Track 1) and Topological Neural Networks (Track 2) side by side on shared synthetic benchmarks. The differences between tracks are strongly task-dependent: the Track 1 mean error on triangle counting is 1.85 times the Track 2 mean.
AI.motivation: Earlier editions built the modelling and data ecosystem of Topological Deep Learning, but GNNs and TNNs had not been compared under a single evaluation pipeline.
AI.method: Participants implemented recent state-of-the-art architectures in TopoBench, with Track 1 covering GNNs and Track 2 covering TNNs. Implementations were evaluated on synthetic benchmarks generated with GraphUniverse, which independently controls homophily, average degree and degree-distribution heaviness. Submissions were tracked on a public leaderboard for the first time.
AI.result: The challenge received 68 qualifying submissions from 34 teams across graph, simplicial, cellular, hypergraph and combinatorial domains. The mean accuracy gap between tracks is modest on community detection, while on triangle counting the Track 1 mean error is 1.85 times the Track 2 mean. Several structurally informed GNNs outperform the Track 2 mean on triangle counting.
AI.conclusion: Comparing GNNs and TNNs under one pipeline shows that the better track depends on the task, so neither family dominates across tasks.

title: All roads lead to Markov kernel networks: A representation theorem for discretization-stable learning
summary: Operator learning seeks to approximate function-to-function maps in a way that remains stable when the input discretization changes, a property sometimes called "discretization invariance". We consider a quantitative refinement of this idea, called $\textit{uniform discretization stability}$, which builds on a common representation of input functions and their discretizations as probability measures and provides a Hölder bound relating output changes to the Wasserstein distance between these measures. Our main result is a representation theorem showing all uniformly discretization stable operators can be written exactly as a $\textit{stable Markov kernel network}$---an abstract architecture that is a joint generalization of transformers, Fourier neural operators (FNO), Flowers, and other successful learned operators. Our representation theorem characterizes a design space for discretization-stable operator learning; designing new architectures becomes a question of which parts of a Markov kernel network to parameterize, and how. We further show that the read kernels of these networks can be realized as solutions of regularized variational problems, with particular choices of costs and regularizers recovering the kernels of transformers, FNO, Flowers, their hybrids, and beyond. This variational formulation provides a systematic approach to architecture design, together with sufficient conditions for uniform discretization stability.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a representation theorem stating that every uniformly discretization-stable operator can be written exactly as a stable Markov kernel network, a framework that generalizes transformers, Fourier neural operators and Flowers. The read kernels of these networks are shown to arise as solutions of regularized variational problems.
AI.motivation: Operator learning should remain stable when the input discretization changes, but there was no characterization of which operators have this property or a systematic way to design architectures that have it.
AI.method: Input functions and their discretizations are treated as probability measures, and uniform discretization stability is defined via a Holder bound relating output changes to the Wasserstein distance between these measures. The representation theorem expresses such operators as stable Markov kernel networks. Read kernels are cast as solutions of regularized variational problems, with particular costs and regularizers recovering the kernels of transformers, FNO, Flowers and their hybrids.
AI.result: All uniformly discretization-stable operators admit an exact stable Markov kernel network representation. The variational formulation recovers the read kernels of transformers, FNO, Flowers and hybrids, and yields sufficient conditions for uniform discretization stability.
AI.conclusion: Designing discretization-stable operator architectures reduces to choosing which parts of a Markov kernel network to parameterize and how, with the variational view providing a systematic design approach.

title: fNIRSAtlas: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy Classification
summary: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is a promising modality for brain-computer interfaces and cognitive state decoding, but progress in machine learning for fNIRS has been limited by small, isolated datasets and inconsistent evaluation protocols. We introduce fNIRSAtlas, the largest open benchmark for fNIRS classification to date, comprising 23 classification tasks from 19 public data collections, spanning diverse experimental paradigms, including motor execution, motor imagery, mental arithmetic, working memory, and emotion recognition. fNIRSAtlas provides a fully automated pipeline from raw data to evaluation and defines standardized benchmark tasks for both cross-subject and within-subject classification, ensuring reproducible comparison of methods. We evaluate a variety of baseline models from fNIRS and related neuroimaging and time-series machine learning literature on the benchmark. Our results demonstrate that performance varies substantially across tasks and that methods validated on limited data -- especially deep learning approaches -- often fail to generalize beyond their original evaluation. fNIRSAtlas serves as an extensible, open, and reproducible benchmark to support more robust and cumulative progress in machine learning for fNIRS data. Our code and data can be found at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces fNIRSAtlas, an open benchmark of 23 fNIRS classification tasks drawn from 19 public data collections, with an automated pipeline from raw data to evaluation. Baseline results show that performance varies substantially across tasks and that deep learning methods validated on limited data often fail to generalize.
AI.motivation: Machine learning progress for functional near-infrared spectroscopy has been limited by small, isolated datasets and inconsistent evaluation protocols.
AI.method: fNIRSAtlas spans motor execution, motor imagery, mental arithmetic, working memory and emotion recognition, and defines standardized tasks for cross-subject and within-subject classification. A fully automated pipeline runs from raw data to evaluation. A range of baseline models from fNIRS, neuroimaging and time-series literature is evaluated.
AI.result: Performance varies substantially across the 23 tasks. Methods validated on limited data, especially deep learning approaches, often fail to generalize beyond their original evaluation.
AI.conclusion: fNIRSAtlas is offered as an extensible, open and reproducible benchmark for more robust and cumulative progress in fNIRS machine learning.

title: Transferring local rib responses to new component geometries in sheet forming with a graph-based Transformer
summary: Sheet metal components often consist of a global geometry, such as the corner radii and forming depth of a corner component, and local features added to it. During forming, both affect material flow. A surrogate learning all their combinations may need large training data. However, the same local feature type is often used on many global geometries. This study therefore partly decouples local features from the global geometry. The local-feature effect is first learned on one global geometry, needing fewer simulations than learning all combinations, then transferred to other global geometries via transfer learning, which can need fewer target simulations than training from scratch. A baseline-conditioned residual surrogate, R-BiLoGo, is proposed for ribs on the side walls of hot-stamped corner components. Its inputs are the baseline response and the geometric perturbation introduced by the ribs. Its outputs are the changes in displacement and thinning from the baseline. R-BiLoGo gave lower errors than a hierarchical graph-based model and a Transolver-based model on the source geometry, and on two of three selected target geometries after transfer. Across the 22 target geometries, transfer learning with 20 target simulations gave errors similar to or lower than training from scratch with 80 target simulations for about half of the targets. With the same 80 target simulations, transfer learning reduced errors for 95% of targets. The effect of the global geometry on transfer was studied with four parameter-free geometric descriptors and controlled variations across 4 corner subclasses. The benefit of transfer decreased with increasing surface distance and high-curvature change between source and target, and for targets shallower than the source. These trends were also seen in other corner types with a different magnitude.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes R-BiLoGo, a baseline-conditioned residual surrogate that learns the effect of ribs on hot-stamped corner components and transfers this effect to new global geometries. Transfer learning with 20 target simulations matches or beats training from scratch with 80 simulations for about half of 22 targets.
AI.motivation: Surrogates for sheet forming need large training sets to cover every combination of global geometry and local features, but the same local feature type recurs across many global geometries.
AI.method: The local-feature effect is learned on one source geometry and then transferred to other geometries by transfer learning. R-BiLoGo takes as inputs the baseline response and the geometric perturbation introduced by ribs, and predicts changes in displacement and thinning from the baseline. Benefit of transfer is analysed with four parameter-free geometric descriptors and controlled variations across four corner subclasses.
AI.result: R-BiLoGo gives lower errors than a hierarchical graph-based model and a Transolver-based model on the source geometry and on two of three selected targets after transfer. Across 22 targets, 20 target simulations with transfer give errors similar to or lower than 80 simulations from scratch for about half of the targets. With 80 target simulations, transfer reduces errors for 95% of targets. Transfer benefit drops with larger surface distance, higher curvature change and shallower targets.
AI.conclusion: Learning local-feature effects once and transferring them reduces the simulation budget for new corner geometries, and transfer is most effective when source and target geometries are close.

title: Coordinated Mixed-Precision KV Cache Quantization for Efficient LLM-based Multi-agent Systems
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems solve complex tasks through collaboration, but their growing, simultaneously resident key-value (KV) caches create a memory bottleneck. Applying single-model quantization policies independently ignores differences in agents' precision needs, potentially degrading collective reasoning. We introduce Coordinated Mixed-Precision KV Cache Quantization (CoMixKV), which combines online sensitivity estimation with joint agent-layer bit-width allocation under a shared memory budget. To our knowledge, CoMixKV is the first mixed-precision KV-cache quantization framework to jointly allocate precision across simultaneously resident agent caches under such a budget. The estimator derives sensitivity from a local attention-error bound using recent queries, keys, and values, without calibration data, trial quantization, or additional model passes. A shared controller combines these scores with remaining quantizable capacity and byte-level storage costs to minimize total estimated error. Allocations are refreshed as agents start or finish and new observations become available. Selected widths apply only to newly quantized blocks; recent states retain native precision and previously quantized blocks remain unchanged. Across four benchmarks and three LLM backbones at average 2-bit, 3-bit, and 4-bit settings, CoMixKV achieves strong accuracy against the evaluated quantization baselines. At the average 3-bit setting on Gemma-4-31B-it, it achieves 68.35% average accuracy, exceeding the strongest quantized baseline by 0.59%. On Qwen3-32B, it reduces peak KV-cache memory by 32.08% and achieves a 1.38x inference speedup over FullKV.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CoMixKV, which allocates mixed KV-cache quantization bit-widths jointly across all simultaneously resident agent caches in an LLM multi-agent system under a shared memory budget. At an average 3-bit setting on Gemma-4-31B-it it reaches 68.35% average accuracy, and on Qwen3-32B it cuts peak KV-cache memory by 32.08% with a 1.38x speedup over FullKV.
AI.motivation: The growing KV caches of simultaneously resident agents create a memory bottleneck, and applying single-model quantization policies independently ignores differences in agents' precision needs.
AI.method: Sensitivity is estimated online from a local attention-error bound using recent queries, keys and values, without calibration data, trial quantization or extra model passes. A shared controller combines these scores with remaining quantizable capacity and byte-level storage costs to minimize total estimated error. Allocations are refreshed as agents start or finish. Only newly quantized blocks receive the selected widths, while recent states keep native precision.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks and three LLM backbones at average 2-bit, 3-bit and 4-bit settings, CoMixKV achieves strong accuracy against the evaluated quantization baselines. At average 3-bit on Gemma-4-31B-it it reaches 68.35% average accuracy, 0.59% above the strongest quantized baseline. On Qwen3-32B it reduces peak KV-cache memory by 32.08% and gives a 1.38x inference speedup over FullKV.
AI.conclusion: Joint precision allocation across agent caches under a shared budget is a practical way to reduce multi-agent LLM memory with limited accuracy loss.

title: TrialJev: Open-Weight Single Pass Eligibility Scoring for Patient Trial Screening
comment: 38 pages. Code: this https URL. Models: this https URL
summary: Clinical trial screening requires assessing large numbers of patient-trial pairs to prioritize candidates for detailed eligibility review, often under restrictions on sharing patient records. We introduce TrialJev, an open-weight eligibility scorer that uses LoRA-adapted Qwen models and a pointer head to score natural-language answer options in a single forward pass, without autoregressive decoding. Trained on TREC Clinical Trials 2021 and evaluated on 6,975 eligible-or-excluded pairs from 50 unseen TREC 2022 synthetic patients, TrialJev achieves 80.97% (Qwen3.5-27B) and 81.84% (Qwen3.8-27B) accuracy, compared with 79.87% and 79.93% for LLMs fine-tuned on the same data to generate verdicts. In matched batch-1 measurements, verdict generation takes 2.45-2.70 times as long as the one-pass inference of TrialJev at 9B-27B. Under a common development-fitted decision correction, the two 27B TrialJev models reach 80.99% and 81.88% accuracy, compared with 81.28% for the proprietary hosted Jev API; paired confidence intervals include zero. TrialJev runs locally on a single GPU, requiring approximately 178 ms per pair at 27B, without transmitting patient text to an external model API. An A/B-logit ablation shows that avoiding decoding, rather than the pointer head alone, accounts for the measured efficiency advantage. TrialJev is intended for first-pass prioritization of candidate trials, complementing rather than replacing explanatory models and clinical review. Evaluation is limited to synthetic patients and implementation-specific timing, and clinical use has not been validated. Adapters, pointer heads, and model cards are released on Hugging Face.

AI.tldr: The paper presents TrialJev, an open-weight LoRA-adapted Qwen eligibility scorer that answers clinical-trial eligibility questions in a single forward pass by scoring answer options with a pointer head. It matches or slightly exceeds LLMs fine-tuned to generate verdicts, and runs locally at about 178 ms per pair at 27B.
AI.motivation: Clinical trial screening requires assessing many patient-trial pairs, often under restrictions on sharing patient records, and generative verdict models are slower.
AI.method: TrialJev uses LoRA-adapted Qwen models with a pointer head that scores natural-language answer options in one forward pass, without autoregressive decoding. It is trained on TREC Clinical Trials 2021 and evaluated on 6,975 eligible-or-excluded pairs from 50 unseen TREC 2022 synthetic patients. An A/B-logit ablation separates the effect of avoiding decoding from the pointer head.
AI.result: TrialJev reaches 80.97% (Qwen3.5-27B) and 81.84% (Qwen3.8-27B) accuracy, against 79.87% and 79.93% for LLMs fine-tuned to generate verdicts. Verdict generation takes 2.45 to 2.70 times as long as TrialJev single-pass inference at 9B to 27B. With a common decision correction, the 27B TrialJev models reach 80.99% and 81.88%, against 81.28% for the proprietary hosted Jev API, with paired confidence intervals including zero.
AI.conclusion: Single-pass scoring is a practical first-pass prioritization tool that runs locally and keeps patient text off external APIs, though it is limited to synthetic patients, is not validated for clinical use, and complements rather than replaces clinical review.

title: Learning Across Heterogeneous Feature Spaces with Group Robustness
summary: In clinical applications, patients undergo different combinations of tests, and machine learning models must therefore ensure accurate predictions across heterogeneous feature spaces. Current approaches upweight the patients with the highest loss, without accounting for the limited predictive information in their features preventing their loss from going any lower. Moreover, when patients' feature spaces are fully disjoint, current methods reduce to training independent models, preventing knowledge transfer across them. We propose a framework for group robust learning across heterogeneous feature spaces, where groups are patients sharing a feature space. Since a high loss may simply reflect uninformative features, we instead optimize for worst-group excess loss, the gap between a group's loss and an estimate of its achievable optimum. To allow collaboration between groups, we use group-specific encoders mapping into a shared latent space in which learnable Gaussian anchors cluster patients by outcome. On tabular and imaging medical datasets, including fully disjoint feature settings, our framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods when groups differ in their optimal losses or cannot train a good model on their own, reducing worst-group loss by up to 79% and excess loss by up to 95% with up to 18$\times$ fewer parameters.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a group robust learning framework for heterogeneous feature spaces, where patients who share a feature set form a group. It optimizes worst-group excess loss and reduces worst-group loss by up to 79% and excess loss by up to 95% with up to 18 times fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Current group-robust methods upweight high-loss patients, but high loss may reflect uninformative features rather than model failure, and when feature spaces are fully disjoint these methods reduce to training independent models with no knowledge transfer.
AI.method: The objective is the worst-group excess loss, defined as the gap between a group's loss and an estimate of its achievable optimum. Group-specific encoders map into a shared latent space containing learnable Gaussian anchors that cluster patients by outcome, enabling collaboration across groups.
AI.result: On tabular and imaging medical datasets, including fully disjoint feature settings, the framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods when groups differ in optimal losses or cannot train a good model alone. It reduces worst-group loss by up to 79% and excess loss by up to 95% with up to 18 times fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: Robustness across heterogeneous feature spaces benefits from measuring excess rather than raw loss and from a shared latent space that transfers knowledge between groups.

title: Projected Neural Additive Models as Universal Approximators
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Neural additive models (NAMs) offer interpretability but lack expressivity due to their rigid additive structure, whereas multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) achieve universal approximation at the cost of transparency. We establish the first theoretical foundation for projected neural additive models (PNAMs), which augment NAMs with a learnable linear transformation $\boldsymbol{T}$ to capture cross-variable interactions. While standard NAMs cannot approximate even the simplest interaction term $\chi_1 \chi_2$ because their cross-derivatives are identically zero, we prove that PNAMs are universal approximators and characterize the minimum number of projections required for exact polynomial representation. Furthermore, we derive an approximation rate of $\mathcal{O}(M^{-s / (N - 1)})$ for $\mathcal{C}^s$ functions (i.e., functions with $s$ continuous derivatives), where $M$ denotes the number of projections and $N$ the input dimension; this rate is known to be optimal for ridge function approximation. To recover interpretability from the projected inputs, we introduce structured sparsity regularizers and post-hoc symbolic regression techniques that enable global input ranking, parameter pruning, and the conversion of learned bases into compact analytical expressions. Experiments on knot theory invariants, MNIST, and phase field fracture mechanics demonstrate that PNAMs match or surpass similar architectures in accuracy while discovering salient features and yielding symbolic models with orders of magnitude fewer parameters.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that projected neural additive models (PNAMs), which add a learnable linear projection to NAMs, are universal approximators and gives an approximation rate for smooth functions. It also shows that interpretability can be recovered through structured sparsity and symbolic regression.
AI.motivation: Neural additive models are interpretable but cannot capture cross-variable interactions, since their cross-derivatives are identically zero and they cannot approximate even the simple term chi_1 chi_2, while MLPs are universal but opaque.
AI.method: PNAMs augment NAMs with a learnable linear transformation T. The paper characterizes the minimum number of projections needed for exact polynomial representation and derives an approximation rate of O(M^(-s/(N-1))) for C^s functions, where M is the number of projections and N the input dimension. Structured sparsity regularizers and post-hoc symbolic regression support global input ranking, parameter pruning and conversion to analytical expressions.
AI.result: Experiments on knot theory invariants, MNIST and phase field fracture mechanics show that PNAMs match or surpass similar architectures in accuracy, while discovering salient features and yielding symbolic models with orders of magnitude fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: Projections restore the expressivity of additive models with a provable guarantee, and the projected inputs remain interpretable enough to yield compact symbolic models.

title: Fast Accurate Quantum Monte Carlo without Metropolis Adjustment
summary: In quantum systems, physical quantities of interest can be expressed as expectation values of a probability distribution, which allows their estimation by Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. This approach, an instance of Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC), plays a central role in obtaining predictions of system properties relevant to condensed matter and high energy physics. The use of Hamiltonian dynamics to design a Markov kernel, known as Hybrid or Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), is widespread in quantum applications. In this context, it is standard to use an HMC kernel that is ``adjusted'' with the Metropolis-Hastings (MH) criterion, so that estimates of expectations converge to their true value in the limit of infinite sample size. However, recent work in computational statistics suggests that an \emph{unadjusted} HMC kernel can be significantly more efficient, while safely maintaining an asymptotic bias which is small relative to the error arising from the variance of the finite sample size. We adapt this approach to the QMC setting, focusing on a challenging and high-dimensional \emph{spin-fermion} model of a quantum phase transition. We find that unadjusted methods outperform adjusted HMC in terms of effective sample size per gradient call, while retaining accurate results.

AI.tldr: The paper applies unadjusted Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, which omits the Metropolis-Hastings correction, to a spin-fermion quantum phase transition model. It finds that unadjusted methods achieve higher effective sample size per gradient call than adjusted HMC while keeping accurate results.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum Monte Carlo uses HMC with a Metropolis-Hastings correction, but recent computational statistics work suggests that unadjusted kernels can be much more efficient with only a small asymptotic bias.
AI.method: The authors adapt unadjusted HMC to the quantum Monte Carlo setting and test it on a challenging, high-dimensional spin-fermion model of a quantum phase transition.
AI.result: Unadjusted methods outperform adjusted HMC in effective sample size per gradient call while retaining accurate results.
AI.conclusion: Dropping the Metropolis-Hastings correction can be a more efficient choice for quantum Monte Carlo of high-dimensional systems.

title: BiMuon: A Geometry-Aware Stochastic Bilevel Optimization Approach
summary: Stochastic bilevel optimization provides a general framework for many machine learning applications, such as hyperparameter learning, data reweighting, language model alignment, and actor-critic reinforcement learning. However, most existing bilevel optimization methods treat matrix-valued gradients as flattened vectors and perform optimization in the resulting vectorized space, ignoring the matrix structures common in modern neural networks. Moreover, the lower-level (LL) problem curvature can induce significant spectral imbalance in the upper-level (UL) geometry. Such limitations of existing bilevel optimization methods motivate us to develop BiMuon, a geometry-aware stochastic bilevel optimization method that integrates implicit hypergradient estimation in bilevel optimization with Muon-style orthogonalized updates at the UL. To our knowledge, BiMuon is the first stochastic BLO method with Muon-style orthogonalized matrix updates and an $O(\epsilon^{-4})$ iteration-complexity guarantee, matching the best-known rates achieved by Muon-type methods based on matrix parameterizations. To improve computational and parallel efficiency for models with multiple matrix parameters, we further study BiMuon for blockwise diagonal matrix approximation and derive a relative stepsize allocation rule based on UL progress and blockwise LL sensitivity. We evaluate BiMuon on representation learning and blockwise bilevel optimization, providing empirical support for our methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes BiMuon, a stochastic bilevel optimizer that combines implicit hypergradient estimation with Muon-style orthogonalized matrix updates at the upper level. It is the first stochastic bilevel method with such updates and an O(epsilon^(-4)) iteration-complexity guarantee.
AI.motivation: Existing bilevel methods flatten matrix-valued gradients into vectors and ignore matrix structure, and lower-level curvature can cause spectral imbalance in the upper-level geometry.
AI.method: BiMuon integrates implicit hypergradient estimation with Muon-style orthogonalized updates at the upper level. For models with many matrix parameters it uses a blockwise diagonal matrix approximation and a relative stepsize allocation rule based on upper-level progress and blockwise lower-level sensitivity.
AI.result: The paper claims an O(epsilon^(-4)) iteration-complexity guarantee, matching the best-known rates of Muon-type methods based on matrix parameterizations. Empirical support is given on representation learning and blockwise bilevel optimization.
AI.conclusion: Respecting matrix structure in bilevel optimization yields a method with a rate matching Muon-type methods and empirical support on the tested tasks.

title: BO-Arena: An Evolving Benchmark for High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimisation
summary: High-dimensional Bayesian optimisation (HDBO) is an increasingly crowded field with new methods proposed at every major conference, making it ever harder to answer a deceptively simple question: "Which method is currently state-of-the-art?" In this paper, we question the efficacy of benchmarking practices in the field, and find them to be systematically ineffective: multiple published works fail to benchmark against the strongest available baselines, or even include incorrect implementations of key methods. Without a shared reference implementation, such errors are difficult to detect during peer review. We therefore introduce BO-Arena, an actively maintained and extensible package providing canonical implementations of state-of-the-art algorithms, which allows researchers to develop new methods and benchmark them rigorously. Using BO-Arena, we find that what currently drives performance in HDBO is even simpler than previously thought. We use these insights to propose a new algorithm which is competitive with the state of the art on problems with many observations, without resorting to the complex GP approximations used in recent methods. Finally, we question whether there is currently sufficient evidence that any more complex method outperforms a simple Gaussian process baseline for HDBO.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BO-Arena, an actively maintained package of canonical implementations for high-dimensional Bayesian optimisation, and uses it to show that several published comparisons used weak baselines or incorrect implementations. It finds that performance is driven by simpler factors than assumed and proposes a new algorithm competitive on problems with many observations.
AI.motivation: Many high-dimensional Bayesian optimisation papers fail to benchmark against the strongest baselines or include incorrect implementations, and without a shared reference implementation such errors are hard to catch in review.
AI.method: BO-Arena provides canonical implementations of state-of-the-art algorithms in an extensible package for rigorous benchmarking. The authors use it to analyze which components drive performance and propose a new algorithm that avoids the complex GP approximations used in recent methods.
AI.result: The proposed algorithm is competitive with the state of the art on problems with many observations. The authors find that performance is even simpler than previously thought, and question whether there is sufficient evidence that any more complex method outperforms a simple Gaussian process baseline.
AI.conclusion: Benchmarking practice in high-dimensional Bayesian optimisation needs shared reference implementations, and the evidence for complex methods over a simple GP baseline is currently weak.

title: Semiprime Factorization with Discrete Diffusion and Beam Search: Scaling Laws
summary: We demonstrate that transformer architectures trained with discrete denoising diffusion and decoded via guided test-time beam search can learn to recover the prime factors of semiprime integers directly from data. Our approach establishes a new frontier for learning-based semiprime factorization, successfully factoring 68-bit integers-a substantial advance over the prior 56-bit state of the art. While computationally less efficient than classical factoring algorithms, our model requires no domain-specific number-theoretic priors and learns purely from training examples. In practice, the diffusion model acts as a generative prior, identifying promising factor candidates where exact verification or lattice-based post-processing can complete the factorization. Furthermore, we derive empirical scaling laws relating approximation quality to training data volume, model size, and test-time computation. In contrast to language, problem size is the key driver of scaling behavior. Achieving a fixed accuracy on a held-out test set requires compute that scales exponentially with bit length. Consequently, our findings pose no threat to security, as the projected compute cost required to factorize cryptographically relevant integers remains prohibitive.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that transformers trained with discrete denoising diffusion and decoded with guided test-time beam search can learn to recover prime factors of semiprimes directly from data, factoring 68-bit integers, up from a prior 56-bit state of the art. The authors also derive empirical scaling laws in which problem size, not language-like data scale, drives the scaling.
AI.motivation: Learning-based approaches to semiprime factorization had been limited to smaller integers, and their scaling behavior was unknown.
AI.method: A transformer is trained with discrete denoising diffusion and decoded with guided test-time beam search, with the diffusion model acting as a generative prior over candidate factors. Exact verification or lattice-based post-processing completes the factorization. Empirical scaling laws relate approximation quality to training data volume, model size and test-time compute.
AI.result: The method factors 68-bit semiprimes, improving on the prior 56-bit state of the art. Reaching a fixed accuracy on a held-out set requires compute that grows exponentially with bit length.
AI.conclusion: Problem size is the key driver of scaling for this task, and the projected compute needed for cryptographically relevant integers remains prohibitive, so the results pose no threat to security.

title: DisMUSE: An Efficient Distributed Singular-Spectrum-Based Optimization Approach with Theoretical Convergence Guarantee
summary: In recent years, singular-spectrum-based optimizers have attracted increasing attention due to their ability to preserve the matrix structure of neural network gradients, thereby enabling geometry-aware optimization. However, most singular-spectrum-based (SSB) approaches remain centralized, limiting their use in distributed learning infrastructures that exploit massive parallelism. Distributed SSB optimization is still at an early stage, with open questions about convergence guarantees and communication efficiency. To fill this gap, we propose the Distributed Momentum-based Spectral Estimator (DisMUSE), an efficient distributed SSB optimization framework for both data-center and federated settings. Using Muon-style exact orthogonalized momentum as the spectral update, DisMUSE integrates a recursive variance-reduced momentum estimator and achieves an $O((KT)^{-1/3})$ convergence rate, where $K$ and $T$ denote the number of nodes and local iterations per node, respectively. This rate matches the best-known rates for variance-reduced nonconvex distributed optimization. Building on this variance-reduced framework, we study two extensions. First, our DisMUSE method with finite Newton-Schulz (NS) iterations preserves the same convergence order under a uniform normalized support-spectrum condition, up to a multiplicative factor. Second, we develop a communication-efficient variant based on low-rank (LR) momentum transmission and quantify the error it introduces to the stationarity bound, characterizing the trade-off between accuracy and communication cost.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DisMUSE, a distributed singular-spectrum-based optimizer that uses Muon-style exact orthogonalized momentum with recursive variance-reduced momentum estimation and achieves an O((KT)^(-1/3)) convergence rate. Extensions include finite Newton-Schulz iterations and low-rank momentum transmission to reduce communication.
AI.motivation: Singular-spectrum-based optimizers preserve matrix structure in neural network gradients, but most remain centralized, and distributed versions lacked convergence guarantees and communication analysis.
AI.method: DisMUSE uses Muon-style exact orthogonalized momentum as the spectral update, combined with a recursive variance-reduced momentum estimator, for both data-center and federated settings. Two extensions are studied: finite Newton-Schulz iterations under a uniform normalized support-spectrum condition, and a low-rank momentum transmission variant whose error on the stationarity bound is quantified.
AI.result: The rate O((KT)^(-1/3)), where K is the number of nodes and T the local iterations per node, matches the best-known rate for variance-reduced nonconvex distributed optimization. Finite Newton-Schulz iterations keep the same convergence order up to a multiplicative factor, and the low-rank variant exposes an accuracy-communication tradeoff.
AI.conclusion: Distributed spectral optimization can achieve variance-reduced convergence rates, with the communication-saving low-rank variant trading a quantified amount of stationarity accuracy.

title: Rethinking How to Leverage Cheap Physics for Data-Efficient Neural Operators
summary: Neural operators learn mappings from PDE inputs, such as initial conditions and coefficient fields, to the corresponding solutions. Once trained, they can rapidly predict solutions for new inputs. However, obtaining input-solution pairs for supervised training often requires expensive numerical simulations, whereas PDE inputs and governing equations provide inexpensive physical information. This raises a question: how can cheap physical information reduce the need for labeled solutions? A natural approach is to use physics to select inputs for labeling, but our acquisition experiments show no consistent advantage over random sampling. This observation motivates exploring an alternative: using cheap physics to improve neural operator initialization before supervised training. We propose Physics-Informed Initialization (PI-Init), a simple yet effective method that pretrains neural operators on unlabeled inputs using physics-informed losses and retains the learned parameters for supervised fine-tuning on the labeled dataset. A linearized analysis shows that pretraining can improve downstream prediction accuracy by reducing initialization errors that limited labeled data cannot effectively correct. Experiments across diverse PDE benchmarks and neural operator architectures demonstrate improvements in predictive accuracy, out-of-distribution generalization, and label efficiency. Representative results show error reductions of up to 62.7% at the same label budget and comparable or better accuracy with 90% fewer labels, relative to supervised-only training.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Physics-Informed Initialization (PI-Init), which pretrains neural operators on unlabeled PDE inputs with physics-informed losses before supervised fine-tuning. It reports error reductions of up to 62.7% at the same label budget and comparable or better accuracy with 90% fewer labels.
AI.motivation: Labeled input-solution pairs need expensive simulations, and using physics to select inputs for labeling showed no consistent advantage over random sampling in the authors' acquisition experiments.
AI.method: PI-Init pretrains neural operators on unlabeled inputs using physics-informed losses and keeps the learned parameters as the starting point for supervised fine-tuning on the labeled dataset. A linearized analysis explains how pretraining reduces initialization errors that limited labeled data cannot correct.
AI.result: Across diverse PDE benchmarks and neural operator architectures, PI-Init improves predictive accuracy, out-of-distribution generalization and label efficiency. Representative results show error reductions of up to 62.7% at the same label budget, and comparable or better accuracy with 90% fewer labels, relative to supervised-only training.
AI.conclusion: Cheap physics is more useful for initializing neural operators than for selecting which inputs to label.

title: RAD-TFM: Robust and Domain-Adapted Tabular Foundation Models
summary: The development of tabular foundation models (TFMs) has accelerated in recent years, outperforming traditional ML methods on many tabular benchmarks. A key finding is that TFMs can be pretrained entirely on synthetic datasets, opening opportunities to design data generators that encourage desirable model properties. Prior work has mainly focused on crafting high-quality priors over generators to improve overall pretraining performance. Our key insight is that parameterizing the generator distribution enables an adversarial, distributional robustness perspective: during training, we can adapt the generator to emphasize datasets that are particularly challenging for the model, which we formalize by introducing an optimality gap measure. Further, we develop a method to align the synthetic data generation with real-world datasets from a given domain, constraining the adversary to generate realistic data. Together, these algorithms comprise the Robust and Domain-Adapted Tabular Foundation Models (RAD-TFM) pipeline, a model-agnostic adversarial training framework. Applied to the TabPFN V2 classifier, RAD-TFM improves performance across 6 diverse tabular benchmarks, with up to a 10.8 percentage-point improvement in mean normalized AUC over the strongest baseline, using fewer than 100k additional synthetic training datasets, less than 0.1% of the original pretraining data. Applying the same pipeline to TabICL V2 also improves performance across three major benchmarks, demonstrating the generality of the framework. These results highlight a promising new direction for targeted adversarial continued training of TFMs using synthetic data alone.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RAD-TFM, a model-agnostic adversarial training pipeline for tabular foundation models that adapts the synthetic pretraining generator toward challenging datasets and constrains it to realistic, domain-aligned data. Applied to TabPFN V2 it improves mean normalized AUC by up to 10.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline on six benchmarks, using under 100k extra synthetic datasets.
AI.motivation: Tabular foundation models are pretrained on synthetic data, but prior work focused on crafting priors rather than making the generator adapt to hard cases or to a target domain.
AI.method: The generator distribution is parameterized so that adversarial, distributionally robust training can emphasize datasets that are hard for the model, measured by an introduced optimality gap. A method aligns synthetic generation with real datasets from a domain, constraining the adversary to realistic data. The pipeline is applied to TabPFN V2 and TabICL V2.
AI.result: On TabPFN V2, RAD-TFM improves performance across 6 tabular benchmarks, with up to a 10.8 percentage-point gain in mean normalized AUC over the strongest baseline, using fewer than 100k additional synthetic datasets, under 0.1% of the original pretraining data. On TabICL V2 it improves performance across three major benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Targeted adversarial continued training on synthetic data alone is a promising direction for improving tabular foundation models, and the framework generalizes across two architectures.

title: Implicit Bias in State Space Models and Linear Autoregressive Training
summary: Linear State Space Models (SSMs) and linear autoregressive sequence models reuse the same parameters across a sample-dependent number of steps. As a result, different examples impose constraints through different predictors, even though all predictors share the same weights. We study this phenomenon through a general model of multiple non-homogeneous polynomial predictors with shared parameters, in a classification setting. Under standard interpolation and directional-convergence assumptions, together with a trajectory-dependent effective-degree condition, we show that gradient descent on the exponential loss converges in direction to a KKT point of an effective-degree max-margin problem. In this problem, only examples with minimal effective degree impose hard margin constraints; examples with faster-growing margins are asymptotically inactive except for feasibility. Our result provides a first-order characterization of the implicit bias in linear SSMs and linear autoregressive models. It exposes a mechanism of length bias: a longer input sequence or additional autoregressive steps may increase the example's effective degree, and the examples with the smallest effective degree dominate the limiting classifier. Our result highlights how non-homogeneity and parameter sharing alter classical homogeneous implicit-bias results.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that gradient descent on the exponential loss for linear state space models and linear autoregressive models converges in direction to a KKT point of an effective-degree max-margin problem. Only examples with minimal effective degree constrain the limiting classifier, so longer sequences can dominate the outcome through a length bias.
AI.motivation: Linear SSMs and autoregressive models reuse shared parameters across a sample-dependent number of steps, so classical homogeneous implicit-bias results do not directly apply.
AI.method: The authors study multiple non-homogeneous polynomial predictors with shared parameters in a classification setting. Under interpolation and directional-convergence assumptions, together with a trajectory-dependent effective-degree condition, they analyze gradient descent on the exponential loss.
AI.result: Gradient descent converges in direction to a KKT point of an effective-degree max-margin problem. Only examples with minimal effective degree impose hard margin constraints, while examples with faster-growing margins are asymptotically inactive except for feasibility.
AI.conclusion: The implicit bias of linear SSMs and linear autoregressive models features a length bias in which longer inputs or more autoregressive steps can raise an example's effective degree and reduce its influence on the classifier.

title: Can Time Series Foundation Models Serve as Surrogates for Power Systems Dynamic Simulation?
comment: Accepted for publication at NeurIPS 2026 Foundation Models for Temporal Systems Workshop
summary: High-fidelity dynamic simulation is essential for scientific and engineering applications, but its computational cost limits large-scale scenario screening. We investigate the use of pretrained time-series foundation models (TSFMs) as computationally efficient surrogates to address this limitation. In-context learning and post-training strategies, including retrieval-augmented reference sample selection and physics-informed regularization, are considered in the investigation. Results are benchmarked against a traditional AI model representative of the state-of-the-art in the domain. Experiments using an open-source TSFM and data from a simulated 9-bus power system indicate promising results. Retrieval augmentation improves in-context learning performance, and fine-tuning leads to superior results compared to the traditional AI model, especially when including physics-informed regularization. The fine-tuned TSFMs achieve lower errors and improved computational costs compared to the traditional AI model, and a 563$\times$ speedup compared to the original physics-based simulation.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates pretrained time-series foundation models as surrogates for power system dynamic simulation, using in-context learning and fine-tuning with retrieval augmentation and physics-informed regularization. On a simulated 9-bus system, fine-tuned models beat a traditional AI baseline and give a 563x speedup over the physics-based simulation.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity dynamic simulation is computationally expensive, which limits large-scale scenario screening.
AI.method: The study uses an open-source time-series foundation model with in-context learning, retrieval-augmented reference sample selection and post-training with physics-informed regularization. Results are compared with a traditional AI model representative of the state of the art in the domain, using data from a simulated 9-bus power system.
AI.result: Retrieval augmentation improves in-context learning. Fine-tuning gives superior results to the traditional AI model, especially with physics-informed regularization, with lower errors and improved computational cost. The fine-tuned models achieve a 563x speedup compared with the original physics-based simulation.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuned time-series foundation models are a promising computationally efficient surrogate for power system dynamic simulation, though the evidence comes from one open-source model and one 9-bus system.

title: FedLoVA: Value-Only Aggregation for Federated LoRA Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a popular parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method for fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs), especially in federated learning, due to its strong performance and communication efficiency. In practice, LoRA is applied to the query and value projections of transformer layers without considering the distinct roles of these components. In this work, we analyze the impact of these projections in federated fine-tuning of LLMs using LoRA and observe that the value projection converges significantly faster than the query projection. Motivated by this finding, we propose FedLoVA, a federated fine-tuning framework that trains LoRA adapters on both query and value projections locally while sharing only the value projection with the server. This approach reduces communication overhead while improving convergence efficiency. Experiments on natural language understanding, multilingual sentiment analysis, and generation tasks show that FedLoVA reduces the communication cost by up to $7.8\times$ compared to existing federated LLM fine-tuning baselines while achieving comparable or better performance. The code is available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FedLoVA, a federated LoRA fine-tuning framework that trains adapters on both query and value projections locally but shares only the value projection with the server. It reduces communication cost by up to 7.8 times compared with existing federated LLM fine-tuning baselines while achieving comparable or better performance.
AI.motivation: The value projection converges significantly faster than the query projection in federated LoRA fine-tuning, yet standard LoRA treats both projections alike, adding communication overhead.
AI.method: Adapters are trained on query and value projections locally, and only the value projection is aggregated with the server. The analysis motivating this design compares convergence of the two projections.
AI.result: Experiments on natural language understanding, multilingual sentiment analysis and generation tasks show communication cost reduced by up to 7.8 times relative to existing federated LLM fine-tuning baselines, with comparable or better performance.
AI.conclusion: Sharing only the faster-converging value projection cuts federated fine-tuning communication while keeping performance, improving convergence efficiency.

title: TORNADO: Adaptive Latent Stochastic Transport for Calibrated Probabilistic PDE Forecasting
summary: Probabilistic neural surrogates for PDEs enable ensemble forecasting, but often exhibit miscalibration when used for uncertainty quantification, especially in compute-constrained, few-step inference regimes. Existing generative approaches typically rely on fixed global stochasticity, which cannot adapt predictive uncertainty to the local dynamical state. We propose TORNADO, a latent probabilistic forecasting framework that formulates next-step prediction as stochastic transport between VAE encoder posteriors. Unlike existing approaches with globally prescribed stochasticity, TORNADO learns a SDE with state-dependent diffusion, enabling the predictive uncertainty to adapt to the local latent dynamics. The model is trained using analytic conditional endpoint targets derived from a Gaussian interpolant, enabling simulation-free learning. An additional energy distance regularization term improves distributional alignment. Empirically, TORNADO improves uncertainty calibration over representative generative baselines, including stochastic interpolants, diffusion models, and flow matching, while maintaining comparable predictive accuracy. Our results show that adapting stochasticity to the latent state, rather than prescribing it globally, is an effective mechanism for improving calibration in practical neural PDE forecasting settings. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TORNADO, a latent probabilistic forecaster for PDEs that models next-step prediction as stochastic transport between VAE encoder posteriors, using an SDE with state-dependent diffusion. It improves uncertainty calibration over stochastic interpolants, diffusion models and flow matching while keeping comparable predictive accuracy.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic neural PDE surrogates are often miscalibrated in few-step inference, and existing generative methods use fixed global stochasticity that cannot adapt uncertainty to the local dynamical state.
AI.method: TORNADO learns an SDE with state-dependent diffusion over VAE latents and is trained with analytic conditional endpoint targets derived from a Gaussian interpolant, which enables simulation-free learning. An energy distance regularization term improves distributional alignment.
AI.result: TORNADO improves uncertainty calibration over representative generative baselines, including stochastic interpolants, diffusion models and flow matching, while keeping predictive accuracy comparable.
AI.conclusion: Adapting stochasticity to the latent state rather than prescribing it globally is an effective route to better calibrated probabilistic PDE forecasts.

title: Transit-Oriented Land Use Planning Using Deep Reinforcement Learning
summary: Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) is a key strategy for advancing sustainable urban development by promoting high-density, mixed-use land development within walking distance of public transit stations. However, traditional TOD planning often relies on heuristic methods, making it difficult to efficiently identify quantitatively optimized transit-oriented land use patterns. This paper presents DRL4TOD, a deep reinforcement learning framework that automatically optimizes land use types and floor area ratios (FARs) around transit stations in alignment with TOD principles. DRL4TOD incorporates a graph neural network to capture spatial interdependencies among land parcels, road networks, and metro stations, and uses a DRL-based optimization strategy to assign land-use types and FARs to selected parcels. It jointly optimizes multiple objectives, including land use density, land use diversity, and transit capacity utilization, while minimizing reconstruction costs to account for development feasibility. Applied to two real-world station areas in Shanghai, DRL4TOD consistently outperforms rule-based approaches and genetic algorithms, achieving more effective TOD outcomes with lower reconstruction costs. By adjusting objective weights, the framework enables flexible prioritization, such as placing greater emphasis on cost minimization when financial feasibility is a concern. These results demonstrate DRL4TOD's potential as a decision-support tool for generating coordinated land-use and FAR configurations under planner-specified priorities, rather than prescribing a single fixed design. For policymakers, the framework provides parcel-level, constraint-aware alternatives that make trade-offs among competing objectives explicit and support targeted decisions about development intensity and feasibility.

AI.tldr: DRL4TOD is a deep reinforcement learning framework that optimizes land-use types and floor area ratios around transit stations under Transit-Oriented Development principles, and it outperforms rule-based approaches and genetic algorithms on two Shanghai station areas.
AI.motivation: Traditional TOD planning relies on heuristic methods, which make it difficult to efficiently identify quantitatively optimized transit-oriented land-use patterns.
AI.method: A graph neural network captures spatial interdependencies among land parcels, road networks and metro stations, and a DRL-based strategy assigns land-use types and FARs to selected parcels while jointly optimizing land-use density, land-use diversity and transit capacity utilization, minimizing reconstruction costs; adjustable objective weights let planners set priorities.
