AI.result: On two real-world Shanghai station areas, DRL4TOD consistently outperforms rule-based approaches and genetic algorithms, achieving more effective TOD outcomes with lower reconstruction costs.
AI.conclusion: The framework works as a decision-support tool that generates parcel-level, constraint-aware alternatives and makes trade-offs among competing objectives explicit, rather than prescribing a single fixed design.

title: A Clinical Evaluation of Conformal Prediction for Chest Radiograph Report Generation
summary: While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have improved automated radiology report generation, they remain prone to hallucinations, necessitating clinically meaningful risk-control methods. Conformal prediction (CP) provides statistical guarantees, yet existing CP approaches rely on uncalibrated automated extractors and fail to account for the clinical relevance of errors. We introduce clinical admissibility criteria (CLARITY), a framework for evaluating radiology reports that explicitly distinguishes clinically consequential errors from minor deviations. To eliminate reliance on automatic judges, we collected radiologist annotations of MLLM-generated reports using CLARITY. By benchmarking CP strategies and automatic evaluation metrics against these expert annotations, we demonstrate that commonly used admissibility proxies systematically fail to detect clinically relevant errors. Our findings reveal that automated admissibility judgments are largely decoupled from true clinical admissibility.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CLARITY, a set of clinical admissibility criteria for chest radiograph reports, and shows that commonly used automated admissibility proxies fail to detect clinically relevant errors in MLLM-generated reports.
AI.motivation: Multimodal large language models still hallucinate in radiology report generation, and existing conformal prediction approaches rely on uncalibrated automated extractors and ignore the clinical relevance of errors.
AI.method: CLARITY explicitly distinguishes clinically consequential errors from minor deviations; radiologists annotated MLLM-generated reports with it, and conformal prediction strategies and automatic evaluation metrics were benchmarked against these expert annotations.
AI.result: Commonly used admissibility proxies systematically fail to detect clinically relevant errors, and automated admissibility judgments are largely decoupled from true clinical admissibility.
AI.conclusion: Automated admissibility judgments cannot reliably stand in for expert clinical judgment in risk control for radiology report generation.

title: Plug-and-Play Verifier for Decoupling Process Reward in Stabilizing Long-Horizon Agentic Reasoning
summary: Stabilizing long-horizon reasoning requires intelligent agents to sustain useful progress across successive reasoning steps and tool interactions. Such agents are typically trained with reinforcement learning (RL), where actor-critic RL uses a learnable critic network to estimate step advantages, while critic-free methods such as GRPO eliminate critic models and rely mostly on the group variants of sparse outcome-only rewards. Both reward types leave partially useful failed trajectories either implicit or indistinguishable from entirely unproductive ones, and as reasoning horizons grow, it becomes difficult to maintain consistent reasoning trajectories. In this work, we propose a \textit{plug-and-play verifier} framework for stabilizing long-horizon reasoning through explicit verification of intermediate reasoning artifacts. Specifically, the framework decouples process verification through a unified interface that extracts intermediate reasoning artifacts from agent running trajectories, evaluates them using domain-specific verifiers, and aggregates the verification scores as bounded process reward. Then, we combine our dense verified process rewards and the sparse outcome rewards through a two-stage post-training schedule. We showed that with plug-and-play verifiers, we further stabilize the reasoning steps as last-mile self-reflection and self-consistency. Typical evaluation on HotpotQA using Qwen3.5-4B achieves a superior accuracy (60.18\%), outperforming the standard GRPO baseline (57.73\%). Our results suggest that plug-and-play verifiers provide a modular approach to learn more stable and reliable reasoning behaviors over long horizons.

AI.tldr: A plug-and-play verifier framework extracts intermediate reasoning artifacts, scores them as bounded process rewards and combines them with sparse outcome rewards, raising Qwen3.5-4B accuracy on HotpotQA above the standard GRPO baseline.
AI.motivation: Actor-critic RL needs a learnable critic, while critic-free methods such as GRPO rely on sparse outcome-only rewards, so partially useful failed trajectories remain implicit or indistinguishable from unproductive ones, and consistency is hard to maintain as reasoning horizons grow.
AI.method: A unified interface extracts intermediate reasoning artifacts from agent trajectories, domain-specific verifiers evaluate them, and the verification scores are aggregated into bounded dense process rewards, which are combined with sparse outcome rewards through a two-stage post-training schedule.
AI.result: On HotpotQA with Qwen3.5-4B, the method reaches 60.18% accuracy versus 57.73% for the standard GRPO baseline.
AI.conclusion: Plug-and-play verifiers offer a modular approach to learning more stable and reliable long-horizon reasoning, with last-mile self-reflection and self-consistency further stabilizing reasoning steps.

title: Multi-objective drift-aware MLOps agent for model retraining
summary: Deployed ML models face non-stationary data and delayed labels, yet most retraining strategies rely on fixed schedules or brittle drift thresholds that ignore operational cost. In this setting, retraining is a sequential decision problem rather than a one-time threshold choice. We present DARE (Drift-Aware Retraining Engine), an offline, event-driven retraining framework that separates ingestion, monitoring, policy decisions, training, and logging through explicit schemas and deterministic replay. We compare DARE against practical heuristic retraining baselines, including fixed-interval, threshold-persistence, and action-rate-matched fixed scheduling policies. On Airline, the locked LinUCB policy achieves a higher mean F1 while substantially reducing intervention frequency relative to heuristic and action-rate-matched baselines. Additional runtime-calibrated evaluation shows that these gains persist when measured using the cumulative update wall-clock time. These results suggest that conservative sequential retraining policies can improve performance while reducing unnecessary operational overhead under delayed feedback.

AI.tldr: DARE is an offline, event-driven retraining framework for deployed ML models; on Airline, its locked LinUCB policy achieves higher mean F1 while substantially reducing intervention frequency compared with heuristic retraining baselines.
AI.motivation: Most retraining strategies use fixed schedules or brittle drift thresholds that ignore operational cost, although retraining under non-stationary data and delayed labels is a sequential decision problem.
AI.method: DARE separates ingestion, monitoring, policy decisions, training and logging through explicit schemas and deterministic replay, and compares a locked LinUCB policy against fixed-interval, threshold-persistence and action-rate-matched fixed scheduling baselines.
AI.result: On Airline, the locked LinUCB policy achieves a higher mean F1 and substantially reduces intervention frequency relative to heuristic and action-rate-matched baselines; runtime-calibrated evaluation shows these gains persist when measured by cumulative update wall-clock time.
AI.conclusion: Conservative sequential retraining policies can improve performance while reducing unnecessary operational overhead under delayed feedback.

title: Update Slope Is Bounded by Prior Calibration: A Structural Bound and Its Contingent Empirical Signature
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI 2026). 5 pages
summary: Evaluations of LLM forecasters increasingly measure how forecasts improve as richer evidence is supplied. We identify two confounds in this update-slope metric. First, outcome-aware evidence construction substantially inflates measured responsiveness: on the same models and questions, slopes are roughly four times larger than with resolution-blinded evidence ladders. Second, update slope is a change score with a prior-dependent structural ceiling, so raw comparisons can reflect differences in starting calibration rather than updating behavior. The ceiling defines only a feasible region; whether slope and prior calibration are empirically coupled depends on headroom utilization and varies across our Manifold, ForecastBench, and ACLED pools. Despite this variability, conditioning on prior calibration roughly triples the association between intermediate updating and final Brier score under both blinded and outcome-aware construction. Question identity also explains substantially more variance than model identity across the evaluated pools. We recommend building evidence ladders blind to outcomes, conditioning on prior calibration, and reporting headroom-normalized measures alongside raw slopes.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the update slope metric for LLM forecasters is inflated by outcome-aware evidence construction and bounded by prior calibration, and recommends blind evidence ladders with headroom-normalized measures.
AI.motivation: Evaluations of LLM forecasters measure how forecasts improve as richer evidence is supplied, but outcome-aware evidence and differences in starting calibration can distort this update-slope metric.
AI.method: The authors compare outcome-aware and resolution-blinded evidence ladders on the same models and questions, analyze update slope as a change score with a prior-dependent structural ceiling, and examine its coupling with prior calibration across the Manifold, ForecastBench and ACLED pools.
AI.result: Outcome-aware evidence construction makes slopes roughly four times larger than resolution-blinded ladders; conditioning on prior calibration roughly triples the association between intermediate updating and final Brier score under both constructions; question identity explains substantially more variance than model identity.
AI.conclusion: Evidence ladders should be built blind to outcomes and conditioned on prior calibration, with headroom-normalized measures reported alongside raw slopes.

title: Reproducible LoRA Inference Through Deterministic Split-K Reduction
summary: Reproducibility is important for LoRA-adapted language models used in repeated evaluation, auditing, and decision-making. However, Split-K kernels used to introduce parallelism in low-rank LoRA multiplications can have the unintended consequence of numerical nondeterminism when partial results are combined using floating-point atomic additions. We investigate this non-determinism in vLLM across GSM8K mathematical reasoning, MBPP code generation, and Jev-style structured toxicity decisions on Civil Comments and introduce a deterministic Triton Split-K implementation. Under identical-input replay, Atomic Split-K=8 produces different FP32 shrink outputs in 97.61% of comparisons, while our Deterministic Split-K=8 shows no observed variation. Repeated atomic inference changes generated outputs in 17.30% of GSM8K and 14.96% of MBPP comparisons, sometimes altering task correctness. Structured-decision probabilities vary in 81.47% of atomic comparisons, with decision flips. Controlled tracing demonstrates how shrink-output differences propagate into the KV cache and how accumulated cache differences can change token decisions and final answers. Our deterministic Triton Split-K=8 implementation preserves parallelism, achieving 16.8-21.1% latency-based speedup over unsplit reduction with only 1.02-2.62% additional latency relative to Atomic Split-K=8.

AI.tldr: Split-K kernels in LoRA inference introduce nondeterminism in vLLM through floating-point atomic additions; a deterministic Triton Split-K implementation removes this variation while keeping parallelism and remaining faster than unsplit reduction.
AI.motivation: Reproducibility matters for LoRA-adapted language models used in repeated evaluation, auditing and decision-making, but atomic Split-K reductions produce numerical nondeterminism.
AI.method: The authors study vLLM on GSM8K, MBPP and Jev-style structured toxicity decisions on Civil Comments, introduce a deterministic Triton Split-K implementation, and trace how shrink-output differences propagate into the KV cache.
AI.result: Under identical-input replay, atomic Split-K=8 produces different FP32 shrink outputs in 97.61% of comparisons while deterministic Split-K=8 shows no observed variation; repeated atomic inference changes generated outputs in 17.30% of GSM8K and 14.96% of MBPP comparisons; structured-decision probabilities vary in 81.47% of atomic comparisons, with decision flips; deterministic Split-K=8 gives 16.8-21.1% latency speedup over unsplit reduction at 1.02-2.62% additional latency relative to atomic Split-K=8.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic Split-K preserves reproducibility of LoRA inference while retaining the parallelism benefit, at a small latency cost over nondeterministic atomic Split-K.

title: TripletAD: Weakly Supervised Anomaly Detection in Embedding Space with Rare Anomalies and Scarce Labels
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures. Under review at TMLR
summary: Many practical anomaly detection problems come with only a handful of confirmed anomalies, and the unreviewed remainder of the data cannot be trusted to be normal. We study this setting under a curated-label protocol, in which unconfirmed anomalies are removed from training rather than relabelled as normal, and propose TripletAD, a weakly supervised detector that learns a triplet-margin embedding and calibrates a linear scoring head with two soft penalties: a partial cross-entropy on labelled anomalies and a relative-contrast hinge that separates the mean scores of anomalous and normal samples. Because every mined triplet contains a labelled anomaly, the few labels are reused across the entire training set instead of being diluted by it. On 24 ADBench datasets whose inputs are pre-trained embeddings (text, image and speech vectors), TripletAD outperforms established state-of-the-art weakly supervised detectors (DevNet, PReNet and DeepSAD) and gradient-boosted trees when anomalies are rare. At a 1% anomaly rate it has the highest mean AUCPR of six methods, 20% above DevNet; on the naturally rare Speech dataset it doubles the best baseline (0.394 vs. 0.196 AUCPR); and on MVTec-AD it is best when only a quarter or half of the anomalies are labelled. Pooled over 70 rare- or sparse-label settings, it has the best average rank (2.21 of 6) and outperforms each baseline under Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction. When anomalies are more frequent it performs on par with these methods. The method needs no per-dataset tuning and is insensitive to its loss weights and training length; on raw tabular features, gradient-boosted trees remain the stronger choice.

AI.tldr: TripletAD is a weakly supervised anomaly detector that learns a triplet-margin embedding with a calibrated linear scoring head, outperforming DevNet, PReNet, DeepSAD and gradient-boosted trees when anomalies are rare on ADBench embedding datasets.
AI.motivation: Many practical anomaly detection problems have only a handful of confirmed anomalies, and existing weakly supervised detectors dilute these scarce labels across the training set.
AI.method: Under a curated-label protocol in which unconfirmed anomalies are removed rather than relabelled as normal, every mined triplet contains a labelled anomaly, and a linear scoring head is calibrated with a partial cross-entropy on labelled anomalies and a relative-contrast hinge that separates the mean scores of anomalous and normal samples.
AI.result: On 24 ADBench datasets with pre-trained embeddings, TripletAD outperforms DevNet, PReNet, DeepSAD and gradient-boosted trees when anomalies are rare; at a 1% anomaly rate it has the highest mean AUCPR of six methods, 20% above DevNet; on Speech it doubles the best baseline (0.394 vs. 0.196 AUCPR); over 70 rare- or sparse-label settings it has the best average rank (2.21 of 6); when anomalies are more frequent it performs on par with these methods.
AI.conclusion: TripletAD needs no per-dataset tuning and is insensitive to its loss weights and training length, making it a strong choice for rare-anomaly settings, while gradient-boosted trees remain stronger on raw tabular features.

title: CHARM: Certified Homology-Aware Reverse-scale Mapping via Diffusion-Guided Quotient Towers
summary: Widely used dimensionality reduction methods prioritize neighborhood or distance 1 preservation, yet planar coordinates alone cannot certify the homological type or 2 sample-level support of higher-order structures. Obtaining this evidence directly 3 is costly because simplicial complexes grow rapidly with dimension. We propose 4 Certified Homology-Aware Reverse-scale Mapping (CHARM), which combines 5 two-dimensional coordinates with certified homology records and sample-level 6 localization. Diffusion coordinates guide cover proposals; safe contractions and a 7 Cover Quotient Tower reduce the domain of structural computation; exact algebra 8 certifies and tracks homology representatives; and reverse-scale layout places their 9 supports in shared coordinates. Safe contraction preserves the homotopy type of 10 the input flag complex. The quotient tower is multiplicatively 3-interleaved with 11 the coarse-graph hop-distance Rips filtration. Verifiable distance-distortion bounds 12 give an additive guarantee between the original Euclidean and coarse-graph Rips 13 filtrations, and composite multiplicative guarantees for the tower on positive scales. 14 Across 22 datasets and 41,637 samples under a fixed configuration, CHARM 15 ranks among the top two on all 15 sample-weighted metrics for nonsynthetic data, 16 including the smallest values on all four Euclidean persistence-diagram distances. 17 It also provides 957 traceable support records across the full benchmark. On a 18 spherical shell, one certified H2 record identifies 1,578 original samples in the 19 two-dimensional view. CHARM thus combines geometric exploration with explicit 20 evidence of homological type and location.

AI.tldr: CHARM combines two-dimensional coordinates with certified homology records and sample-level localization, so that dimensionality reduction can certify the homological type and sample support of higher-order structures across 22 datasets.
AI.motivation: Common dimensionality reduction methods preserve neighborhoods or distances, but planar coordinates alone cannot certify the homological type or sample-level support of higher-order structures, and obtaining this evidence directly is costly as simplicial complexes grow.
AI.method: Diffusion coordinates guide cover proposals; safe contractions and a Cover Quotient Tower reduce the domain of structural computation while preserving the homotopy type of the input flag complex; exact algebra certifies and tracks homology representatives; reverse-scale layout places their supports in shared coordinates; verifiable distance-distortion bounds relate the tower to the Euclidean and coarse-graph Rips filtrations.
AI.result: Across 22 datasets and 41,637 samples under a fixed configuration, CHARM ranks among the top two on all 15 sample-weighted metrics for nonsynthetic data, including the smallest values on all four Euclidean persistence-diagram distances; it provides 957 traceable support records; on a spherical shell, one certified H2 record identifies 1,578 original samples in the two-dimensional view.
AI.conclusion: CHARM combines geometric exploration with explicit evidence of the homological type and location of structures.

title: Quantitative Assessment of Crystal Structure Prediction
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets. 49 pages, 21 figures, 17 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) aims to predict a material's 3D structure from its chemical composition, with applications from energy storage to biomedical devices. Despite its importance, existing evaluation frameworks suffer from key limitations: they rely on threshold-sensitive or incomparable metrics, focus predominantly on geometric performance while overlooking physical plausibility, and fail to account for polymorphism, where a chemical composition can crystallize into multiple stable structures. In parallel, recent Symmetry-Informed CSP (SICSP) methods often report results alongside standard CSP baselines while receiving crystallographic templates at inference, which constrain the search space and make SICSP a fundamentally different task. To address these limitations, we introduce an Orientation-invariant, Polymorph-Aware, Large Benchmark (OPAL-Bench) that evaluates CSP and SICSP as separate tasks. We evaluate 7 CSP and 2 SICSP methods under OPAL-Bench across 4 datasets using threshold-free geometric and physical distance metrics. Our results show that no method dominates across all metrics, and that geometric performance is not strongly correlated with physical plausibility. We also release OPAL-CSP, an SE(3)-equivariant flow-matching baseline for the CSP track that performs competitively on geometric metrics and ranks among the best on physical ones. By unifying geometric and physical metrics under a polymorph-aware protocol, OPAL-Bench enables a more comprehensive assessment of generative quality in CSP.

AI.tldr: OPAL-Bench is an orientation-invariant, polymorph-aware benchmark that evaluates crystal structure prediction (CSP) and symmetry-informed CSP (SICSP) as separate tasks using threshold-free geometric and physical metrics, and the authors release an SE(3)-equivariant flow-matching CSP baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing CSP evaluations rely on threshold-sensitive or incomparable metrics, focus on geometry while overlooking physical plausibility, ignore polymorphism, and report SICSP methods alongside standard CSP baselines even though templates make SICSP a different task.
AI.method: The benchmark evaluates 7 CSP and 2 SICSP methods across 4 datasets using threshold-free geometric and physical distance metrics, and the authors also release OPAL-CSP, an SE(3)-equivariant flow-matching baseline for the CSP track.
AI.result: No method dominates across all metrics, and geometric performance is not strongly correlated with physical plausibility; OPAL-CSP performs competitively on geometric metrics and ranks among the best on physical ones.
AI.conclusion: Unifying geometric and physical metrics under a polymorph-aware protocol enables a more comprehensive assessment of generative quality in CSP.

title: Pruning DNA Sequence
summary: Data pruning can substantially reduce training cost by removing examples that contribute little additional learning signal, but it has not been studied for DNA language-model pretraining. We introduce Sequence Pruning (SP), a dynamic pruning framework that removes genomic sequences as they become easy for the model to predict. SP uses per-sequence pretraining accuracy computed directly from the model's forward pass, requiring no separate scoring model or additional pass over the corpus. We evaluate SP across five pretraining settings spanning two corpora, three model families, and both MLM and CLM objectives, with downstream evaluation on five genomic benchmarks. SP reduces pretraining data processing by up to 96% while largely preserving downstream performance. At moderate savings, pruning improves performance by up to 1.2 MCC points over full-data pretraining; at the highest savings, pretraining uses only 4% of the baseline GPU hours with little performance loss. SP also outperforms the dynamic pruning methods InfoBatch and BPAS across most comparisons. Beyond accuracy, our framework supports alternative criteria such as perplexity and EL2N, although accuracy yields the strongest downstream performance at matched savings. These results show that genomic pretraining does not require repeatedly processing all available sequences and that dynamic sequence-level pruning can substantially improve its data and computational efficiency. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Sequence Pruning (SP) dynamically removes genomic sequences that a DNA language model already predicts well, cutting pretraining data processing by up to 96% while largely preserving downstream performance.
AI.motivation: Data pruning can reduce training cost by removing examples that add little learning signal, but it has not been studied for DNA language-model pretraining.
AI.method: SP uses per-sequence pretraining accuracy computed directly from the model's forward pass, requiring no separate scoring model or extra corpus pass; it is evaluated across five pretraining settings spanning two corpora, three model families and both MLM and CLM objectives, and it also supports perplexity and EL2N criteria.
AI.result: Pruning reduces data processing by up to 96% while largely preserving downstream performance on five genomic benchmarks; at moderate savings it improves performance by up to 1.2 MCC points over full-data pretraining; at the highest savings, pretraining uses only 4% of baseline GPU hours with little performance loss; SP outperforms InfoBatch and BPAS across most comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Genomic pretraining does not require repeatedly processing all available sequences, and dynamic sequence-level pruning can substantially improve data and computational efficiency.

title: From Task Affinities to Optimal Allocations: Probabilistic Graphical Modelling for Supervised Finetuning
summary: Supervised fine-tuning over a large pool of heterogeneous tasks is often computationally expensive, leading practitioners to train language models on a fixed training budget of carefully chosen SFT tasks. Thus, achieving strong downstream performance hinges on selecting an effective subset of tasks, or equivalently, identifying an optimal task mixture under a fixed budget constraint. In practice, supervised finetuning mixtures are often determined using simple heuristics (e.g., uniform or size-proportional sampling) that ignore task interactions, which can hurt transfer and waste budget on redundant task sources. We introduce TASKMIXPGM, a framework for learning continuous task mixtures through energy-based modelling over SFT tasks. Each task forms a node in a Markov random field, with unary potentials capturing task utility and pairwise potentials modelling inter-task relationships via behavioral divergences between predictive distributions of single-task fine-tuned models. Optimizing this objective yields task mixtures that balance utility, coverage, and redundancy. We further show that the induced set function defined over the set of such tasks is weakly submodular under budget constraints, enabling approximation guarantees for discrete task selection. Empirically, we provide a fixed, benchmark-independent mixture that improves over heuristic mixing across multiple model families and different training budgets. TASKMIXPGM also uncovers interpretable structure in task interactions, revealing complementarities and redundancies that inform effective SFT mixtures.

AI.tldr: TASKMIXPGM learns continuous SFT task mixtures through energy-based modelling over a Markov random field of tasks, yielding a fixed, benchmark-independent mixture that improves over heuristic mixing across model families and training budgets.
AI.motivation: SFT mixtures are often set by heuristics such as uniform or size-proportional sampling that ignore task interactions, which can hurt transfer and waste budget on redundant task sources.
AI.method: Each task is a node in a Markov random field, with unary potentials for task utility and pairwise potentials for inter-task relationships measured by behavioral divergences between the predictive distributions of single-task fine-tuned models; optimizing this objective balances utility, coverage and redundancy, and the induced set function is shown to be weakly submodular under budget constraints.
AI.result: The method improves over heuristic mixing across multiple model families and different training budgets, uncovers interpretable complementarities and redundancies in task interactions, and its weak submodularity yields approximation guarantees for discrete task selection.
AI.conclusion: Modelling inter-task structure yields interpretable SFT mixtures that use the training budget more effectively than heuristic mixing.

title: Finite Time Analysis of Risk-Sensitive RL via Noisy Power Iteration
summary: Estimating the principal eigenpair of a positive operator from stochastic evaluations gives rise to a noisy form of normalized power iteration: each step applies a sampled operator estimate and then renormalizes. We establish finite-time stochastic-approximation guarantees for this procedure, working in Hilbert's projective metric, which is well-suited to the multiplicative geometry of Perron--Frobenius eigenproblems. Our main application is risk-sensitive average-cost reinforcement learning (RL) with exponential utility. In this setting the Bellman equations are multiplicative, and value functions are characterized by nonlinear eigenvalue problems rather than additive fixed points. We cast both policy evaluation and control in this framework, obtaining risk-sensitive TD- and Q-learning algorithms that learn from a single Markovian trajectory. Under explicit positivity, mixing, and linear function approximation assumptions, we prove finite-time bounds on the recovered eigenvector and eigenvalue with $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity up to problem-dependent constants. The results cover both tabular and linear function approximation regimes, and through the duality between exponential utility and KL-robust control yield finite-time guarantees for KL-robust average-cost RL as well.

AI.tldr: The paper gives finite-time stochastic-approximation guarantees for noisy normalized power iteration in Hilbert's projective metric and applies them to risk-sensitive average-cost RL with exponential utility, through TD and Q-learning algorithms that learn from a single Markovian trajectory.
AI.motivation: Risk-sensitive RL with exponential utility has multiplicative Bellman equations whose value functions are characterized by nonlinear eigenvalue problems rather than additive fixed points, and finite-time guarantees for estimating the principal eigenpair from stochastic evaluations were lacking.
AI.method: Noisy normalized power iteration applies a sampled operator estimate and then renormalizes at each step; the analysis works in Hilbert's projective metric, and policy evaluation and control are cast in this framework under explicit positivity, mixing and linear function approximation assumptions.
AI.result: Finite-time bounds are proved on the recovered eigenvector and eigenvalue with Õ(ε^-2) sample complexity up to problem-dependent constants, in both tabular and linear function approximation regimes; through the duality between exponential utility and KL-robust control, the results also yield finite-time guarantees for KL-robust average-cost RL.
AI.conclusion: The eigenproblem framework supplies finite-time guarantees for both risk-sensitive and KL-robust average-cost RL.

title: Regularization Amplifies Subliminal Learning
summary: Recent work has shown that hidden biases can be transferred through data with no apparent semantic relationship to those biases. Can regularization limit this covert influence? By constraining adaptation, regularization might be expected to suppress behavioral changes on seemingly unrelated inputs. We systematically study this hypothesis in subliminal learning, as well as in related settings of covert influence, including phantom transfer and logit-linear selection. We find the opposite: regularization amplifies the transfer of hidden biases. In particular, subliminal learning is typically absent under full fine-tuning, but low-rank adaptation or explicit penalties can induce strong transfer. Phantom transfer and logit-linear selection show similar trends. Adding more data, an implicit form of regularization, also strengthens covert influence. Together, these findings suggest that the simplicity biases induced by regularization may facilitate covert influence. We further hypothesize that the level of regularization that maximizes covert transfer depends on task complexity.

AI.tldr: Contrary to the expectation that regularization suppresses covert influence, the paper finds that regularization amplifies the transfer of hidden biases in subliminal learning and related settings.
AI.motivation: Hidden biases can transfer through data with no apparent semantic relationship to them, and regularization, by constraining adaptation, was expected to suppress such covert behavioral changes on unrelated inputs.
AI.method: The authors systematically study subliminal learning and related covert-influence settings, phantom transfer and logit-linear selection, comparing full fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation, explicit penalties and added data as forms of regularization.
AI.result: Subliminal learning is typically absent under full fine-tuning, but low-rank adaptation or explicit penalties induce strong transfer; phantom transfer and logit-linear selection show similar trends; adding more data, an implicit form of regularization, also strengthens covert influence.
AI.conclusion: The simplicity biases induced by regularization may facilitate covert influence, and the level of regularization that maximizes covert transfer is hypothesized to depend on task complexity.

title: Sharp Logarithmic-Product Bounds for List Replicability of Sign Matrices
summary: List replicability measures how many accurate hypotheses suffice to contain the output of a learning rule with arbitrarily high confidence. We prove that every nonempty class of $m$ binary concepts on $n$ domain points has list replicability at most $805\ln(2m)\ln(2n)$. This resolves the logarithmic-product conjecture of Blondal, Hatami, Hatami, Lalov, and Tretiak. Hanner matrices give lower bounds of the same order, for square matrices and for explicit families with unequal logarithmic aspect ratios. The upper bound is obtained by constructing nested acyclic sets in the faces of a cube. A critical-point estimate supplies highly connected regions, weighted cell attachments keep the sets compatible across faces, and a cubical carrier theorem converts them into accurate finite covers and learning rules. Appending one constant coordinate turns list replicability into an exact geometric quantity, the face width, and graph-orientation classes satisfy exact product formulas. In particular, there are explicit classes with list replicability $4k+1$ and equivariant index $3k$, so the additive gap between the two is unbounded. We also develop entropy-tilting and two-sided Gibbs constructions, give combinatorial upper bounds adapted to structured matrices, compute exact values on classical families, and study the index of Paley matrices.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that every nonempty class of m binary concepts on n domain points has list replicability at most 805 ln(2m) ln(2n), resolving the logarithmic-product conjecture, and Hanner matrices give lower bounds of the same order.
AI.motivation: List replicability measures how many accurate hypotheses suffice to contain a learning rule's output with arbitrarily high confidence, and the logarithmic-product conjecture of Blondal, Hatami, Hatami, Lalov and Tretiak was open.
AI.method: The upper bound comes from constructing nested acyclic sets in the faces of a cube, using a critical-point estimate for highly connected regions, weighted cell attachments that keep the sets compatible across faces, and a cubical carrier theorem that turns them into accurate finite covers and learning rules; appending one constant coordinate makes list replicability an exact face width.
AI.result: The upper bound is 805 ln(2m) ln(2n), and Hanner matrices give lower bounds of the same order; explicit classes have list replicability 4k+1 and equivariant index 3k, so the additive gap between the two is unbounded; exact values are computed on classical families.
AI.conclusion: List replicability is characterized up to constants in the logarithmic-product regime, and its additive gap to the equivariant index can be unbounded.

title: Applied bifidelity material response model construction and uncertainty quantification with a sampling hypernetwork
summary: Multifidelity modeling offers a practical route to accurate prediction and uncertainty quantification when high-fidelity data are scarce but lower-fidelity data are comparatively abundant. This work develops a bifidelity Langevin sampling hypernetwork framework that constructs probabilistic neu- ral response models by learning a posterior distribution over model parameters rather than a single deterministic fit. The method combines a flexible shared-latent data representation for low- and high-fidelity responses, enabling parameter sharing and transfer learning between the fidelities. We introduce several methodological enhancements to improve the robustness and efficiency of this ap- proach, including stability-promoting drift models, staged and conditional training strategies, adap- tive initialization of Langevin trajectories, and training procedures designed to better exploit corre- lations between fidelity levels. These additions improve convergence behavior, reduce the sampling effort required to obtain representative posterior ensembles, and provide more reliable predictive uncertainty in data-limited regimes. The resulting framework makes more effective use of available multifidelity data while preserving interpretability through the learned posterior structure, yielding improved predictive performance, better uncertainty characterization, and a more stable workflow for constructing uncertainty-aware surrogate models. The method is demonstrated on experimental, high-fidelity simulation and illustrative synthetic data.

AI.tldr: A bifidelity Langevin sampling hypernetwork learns a posterior over the parameters of neural response models from low- and high-fidelity data, improving predictive performance and uncertainty characterization when high-fidelity data are scarce.
AI.motivation: Multifidelity modelling offers a practical route to accurate prediction and uncertainty quantification when high-fidelity data are scarce, while a single deterministic fit provides limited uncertainty information for surrogate models.
AI.method: A flexible shared-latent data representation covers both fidelities to enable parameter sharing and transfer, and the framework adds stability-promoting drift models, staged and conditional training, adaptive initialization of Langevin trajectories and training procedures that exploit correlations between fidelity levels.
AI.result: The enhancements improve convergence behavior, reduce the sampling effort needed for representative posterior ensembles and give more reliable predictive uncertainty in data-limited regimes; the method is demonstrated on experimental, high-fidelity simulation and illustrative synthetic data.
AI.conclusion: The framework makes more effective use of multifidelity data while keeping interpretability through the learned posterior structure, offering a more stable workflow for uncertainty-aware surrogate models.

title: HexIt: Learning Hexahedral Block Decomposition with Expert Iteration on Combinatorial Maps
summary: Decomposing a polyhedral solid into a few well-shaped hexahedral blocks is a long-standing open problem in mesh generation. We cast it as a sequential decision problem on a 3-dimensional generalised map: an agent splits edges, faces and volumes with three insert operations until every cell is a hexahedron and the mesh passes a quality threshold, and a policy that convolves over the map's involutions chooses each insert. A successful decomposition takes over a hundred decisions, and a uniformly random policy never finds one. We clone a policy from constructed decompositions and improve it by expert iteration. On held-out chamfered solids that share no boundary topology with the cloning data, the final policy solves an expected $94.4\%$ in $20$ samples, and expert iteration raises the best-of-20 solve rate on large chamfered solids from $0.203$ to $0.355$. At matched compute, PPO, GRPO and VinePPO updates all make the cloned policy worse.

AI.tldr: HexIt casts hexahedral block decomposition of polyhedral solids as a sequential decision problem on a 3D generalised map and, using cloning and expert iteration, solves an expected 94.4% of held-out chamfered solids within 20 samples.
AI.motivation: Decomposing a polyhedral solid into a few well-shaped hexahedral blocks is a long-standing open problem in mesh generation, and a uniformly random policy never finds a successful decomposition.
AI.method: An agent applies three insert operations that split edges, faces and volumes until every cell is a hexahedron and the mesh passes a quality threshold, with a policy that convolves over the map's involutions to choose each insert; the policy is cloned from constructed decompositions and improved by expert iteration.
AI.result: On held-out chamfered solids sharing no boundary topology with the cloning data, the final policy solves an expected 94.4% in 20 samples; expert iteration raises the best-of-20 solve rate on large chamfered solids from 0.203 to 0.355; at matched compute, PPO, GRPO and VinePPO updates all make the cloned policy worse.
AI.conclusion: For this combinatorial mesh-decomposition task, expert iteration on a cloned policy outperformed the tested RL fine-tuning methods at matched compute.

title: Bayesian Low-Rank Posteriors for Scalable Membership Inference
summary: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) aim to determine whether a sample was used during the training of a target model. Strong MIAs rely on reference (or shadow) models to estimate target-conditional score distributions, but training such ensembles is computationally expensive for modern large-scale Vision--Language Models (VLMs). In this work, we propose a scalable alternative that replaces explicit reference-model training with a Bayesian approximation over low-rank adaptation parameters. Specifically, we model uncertainty only within the LoRA subspace and construct a posterior from a single training run, from which we sample a diverse set of \emph{virtual reference models}. We instantiate this approach using Stochastic Weight Averaging Gaussian (SWAG), enabling efficient approximation of target-conditional score distributions at a fraction of the cost of conventional shadow-model ensembles. We evaluate the resulting attack on three downstream-adapted VLMs across two privacy-sensitive visual question answering tasks, namely Document VQA and Medical VQA. To isolate the effect of pretraining knowledge, we additionally introduce a controlled synthetic dataset. Our approach outperforms standard reference-based attacks while requiring only a single reference-model fine-tuning run, making membership inference more practical for large VLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper replaces explicit reference-model training in membership inference with virtual reference models sampled via SWAG from a Bayesian posterior over LoRA parameters, trained in a single run, and outperforms standard reference-based attacks on vision-language models.
AI.motivation: Strong membership inference attacks rely on reference or shadow models, but training such ensembles is computationally expensive for modern large-scale vision-language models.
AI.method: Uncertainty is modelled only within the LoRA subspace, and a posterior constructed from a single training run with Stochastic Weight Averaging Gaussian (SWAG) is sampled to produce a diverse set of virtual reference models that approximate target-conditional score distributions; a controlled synthetic dataset isolates the effect of pretraining knowledge.
AI.result: The attack is evaluated on three downstream-adapted VLMs across Document VQA and Medical VQA; it outperforms standard reference-based attacks while requiring only a single reference-model fine-tuning run.
AI.conclusion: The approach makes membership inference more practical for large VLMs.

title: The Fast Tree Transform
summary: The Fast Tree Transform is a locally-aggregated transform defined for arbitrary graph geometries that generalizes both the Hadamard frequency transform and the Haar wavelet transform on the circle. The pure frequency part of the transform approximately diagonalizes the graph Laplacian; this fact makes it useful as a preconditioner in geometric optimization problems. The full transform provides an only slightly-redundant representation of signals on the graph that allows sparse representation of signals that include both edges and textures.

AI.tldr: The Fast Tree Transform is a locally aggregated transform defined on arbitrary graph geometries that generalizes both the Hadamard frequency transform and the Haar wavelet transform on the circle.
AI.motivation: A transform for signals on arbitrary graphs should generalize standard frequency and wavelet transforms, approximately diagonalize the graph Laplacian for use as a preconditioner, and represent signals that contain both edges and textures sparsely.
AI.method: The transform is locally aggregated and defined for arbitrary graph geometries; its pure frequency part approximately diagonalizes the graph Laplacian, and the full transform gives an only slightly redundant representation of graph signals.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results; it states that the frequency part approximately diagonalizes the graph Laplacian, making the transform useful as a preconditioner in geometric optimization, and that the full transform allows sparse representation of signals including both edges and textures.
AI.conclusion: The transform unifies the Hadamard and Haar ideas on general graphs and offers both a preconditioner and a sparse representation at only slight redundancy.

title: Dynamic State Estimation from Sparse PMUs via Physics-Informed Graph Neural Operators
summary: This paper proposes a physics-informed graph neural operator for power system dynamic state estimation. From a sparse, intermittent measurement window at a few generator buses, the operator estimates the rotor-angle and speed trajectories of all machines, unmeasured ones included, in one forward pass. A graph-attention encoder processes the measurements, and the swing equations are imposed as a hard constraint or as a soft one with a learned correction that absorbs model errors. It is trained on simulated measurements, without state labels. With several phasor measurement units, masked training hides one from the input but keeps it in the loss. On four transmission systems, simulations show that the operator is the most accurate estimator that neither optimizes per scenario nor uses state labels, except on the smallest system at large model errors, where tuned Kalman smoothers are better. Networks trained on simulated states are more accurate on the two smallest systems but not on the 118-bus system, where the operator is faster and more accurate than hard-constrained moving-horizon estimation. Under model errors, it matches or outperforms an optimization-based benchmark at a fraction of its cost. The results hold for a detailed machine model with exact parameters seen only through voltage phasors.

AI.tldr: A physics-informed graph neural operator estimates rotor-angle and speed trajectories of all machines in a power system from sparse, intermittent PMU measurements at a few generator buses, in one forward pass and without state labels.
AI.motivation: Dynamic state estimation must recover the trajectories of all machines, including unmeasured ones, from sparse and intermittent measurements at a few generator buses.
AI.method: A graph-attention encoder processes the measurements, and the swing equations are imposed either as a hard constraint or as a soft one with a learned correction that absorbs model errors; the operator is trained on simulated measurements without state labels, and masked training hides one PMU from the input while keeping it in the loss.
AI.result: On four transmission systems the operator is the most accurate estimator that neither optimizes per scenario nor uses state labels, except on the smallest system at large model errors, where tuned Kalman smoothers are better; on the 118-bus system it is faster and more accurate than hard-constrained moving-horizon estimation; under model errors it matches or outperforms an optimization-based benchmark at a fraction of its cost.
AI.conclusion: The operator gives accurate and fast dynamic state estimation under model errors, including for a detailed machine model with exact parameters seen only through voltage phasors.

title: CALFA-KV: Joint Calibration and Fisher-Guided Anchors for 1-Bit KV Cache Compression
summary: 1-bit key-value (KV) cache compression can combine quantizer calibration with selective high-precision storage to reduce reconstruction error. We propose Calibration and Fisher-guided Anchors for KV cache compression (CALFA-KV). Offline, we jointly fit a key center, radial normalization parameters, and K/V vector codebooks to match the frozen model's projected attention output. We also estimate channel-wise Fisher-type sensitivities from squared gradients of a reference next-token cross-entropy loss. Online, we use these sensitivities to weight the squared reconstruction errors of each KV state. Here, a KV state is one token's key-value pair within one layer and KV head. We retain the highest-scoring states at high precision under a per-layer, per-KV-head budget. Under exact restoration, we bound the excess risk of score-based anchor selection relative to the optimum at the same anchor budget, where risk is the conditional mean square of the first-order loss change. With a budget of 56 additional FP16 anchors per layer and KV head, CALFA-KV (d8b8) outperforms all evaluated nominal 1-bit baselines on the mean score across seven benchmarks for each of the three models. At the same anchor budget, CALFA-KV (d8b10) uses a nominal index rate of 1.25 bits per channel and narrows the gap to BF16 to 0.90--2.01 points on the same metric.

AI.tldr: CALFA-KV compresses KV caches to 1 bit by jointly fitting quantizer calibration and keeping Fisher-guided high-precision anchors, outperforming all evaluated nominal 1-bit baselines on seven benchmarks for each of three models.
AI.motivation: 1-bit KV cache compression can reduce reconstruction error by combining quantizer calibration with selective high-precision storage, but the choice of which states to keep at high precision needs a principled criterion.
AI.method: Offline, a key center, radial normalization parameters and K/V codebooks are jointly fitted to match the frozen model's projected attention output; channel-wise Fisher-type sensitivities from squared gradients of a reference next-token cross-entropy loss weight the squared reconstruction errors online, and the highest-scoring KV states are kept at FP16 under a per-layer, per-KV-head budget.
AI.result: With 56 additional FP16 anchors per layer and KV head, CALFA-KV (d8b8) outperforms all evaluated nominal 1-bit baselines on mean score across seven benchmarks for each of three models; CALFA-KV (d8b10), at 1.25 bits per channel, narrows the gap to BF16 to 0.90-2.01 points; the paper also bounds the excess risk of score-based anchor selection relative to the optimum under exact restoration.
AI.conclusion: Joint calibration combined with Fisher-guided anchor selection makes 1-bit KV cache compression competitive with BF16 at a small per-head anchor budget.

title: FADE: Fractional Anomalous Dynamics Extrapolation for Training-Free Diffusion Transformers Acceleration
summary: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have established themselves as the preeminent paradigm for high-fidelity generative modeling across various modalities, yet their practical deployment is hindered by the severe computational overhead of iterative sampling. While recent feature-caching methods mitigate this latency through feature reuse or forecasting based on integer-order operators, they remain limited in adapting to the non-stationary and highly curved dynamics of DiT latent trajectories. In this work, we reveal that DiT feature evolution exhibits anomalous diffusion characteristics and a certain degree of spatiotemporal heterogeneity, rendering static, integer-order forecasting operators inadequate and prone to error accumulation. To address this, we propose Fractional Anomalous Dynamics Extrapolation (FADE), a unified framework for training-free diffusion transformers acceleration. FADE models DiT feature evolution via anomalous diffusion and employs a Mittag--Leffler fractional operator to better adapt to high-curvature and non-linear latent trajectories of DiTs. Leveraging the empirical observation that these complex dynamics maintain cross-sample stability, we further construct a Look-Up Table with multiple dimensions through offline profiling. This enables negligible LUT-retrieval overhead, spatiotemporally adaptive parameter retrieval during online inference. Extensive evaluations across diverse architectures and modalities demonstrate that FADE achieves state-of-the-art acceleration, preserving exceptional generation fidelity under aggressive skip intervals with negligible latency overhead. Our project page is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: FADE accelerates training-free Diffusion Transformers by forecasting their feature trajectories with a fractional, Mittag-Leffler-based anomalous diffusion operator instead of integer-order forecasting, and uses an offline look-up table to set parameters during sampling. It reports state-of-the-art acceleration with preserved fidelity under aggressive skip intervals.
AI.motivation: Feature-caching methods for DiTs rely on integer-order forecasting operators, which are static and cannot adapt to the non-stationary, highly curved, spatiotemporally heterogeneous latent trajectories of DiTs, causing error accumulation.
AI.method: The authors observe that DiT feature evolution shows anomalous diffusion behaviour and model it with a Mittag-Leffler fractional operator. A multi-dimensional look-up table is built by offline profiling, exploiting the cross-sample stability of these dynamics, so that parameters are retrieved with negligible overhead during online inference.
AI.result: The abstract reports state-of-the-art acceleration across diverse DiT architectures and modalities, with generation fidelity preserved under aggressive skip intervals and negligible latency overhead. It gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Fractional, anomalous-diffusion-based forecasting with offline-profiled adaptive parameters is a training-free route to faster DiT sampling without quality loss.

title: Intra-Option Fitted Q-Evaluation: Evaluating Hierarchical Policies from Non-Hierarchical Data
summary: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the expected return of a target policy from previously collected data without additional environment interaction. While OPE methods for flat Markovian policies are well studied, little work has addressed evaluating hierarchical policies in which a high-level policy selects temporally extended options that generate primitive actions until a termination condition is met. The primary existing approach applies per-decision importance sampling at the option level, but requires option-annotated trajectories and exhibits variance that still grows with the horizon. For non-hierarchical policies, fitted Q-evaluation (FQE) typically achieves lower error than importance sampling by leveraging the classic Bellman equation for policy evaluation; however, a naive extension of FQE to hierarchical policies results in a biased policy value estimate. In this paper, we introduce Intra-Option Fitted Q-Evaluation (IO-FQE), which estimates a value function in the augmented state-option space; this approach enables OPE of hierarchical policies even when we lack annotations of what option was run in the data. We develop two continuous-action instantiations of IO-FQE and show on long-horizon hierarchical continuous control tasks (AntMaze navigation and OGBench Puzzle manipulation) that IO-FQE eliminates the bias incurred by a naive application of FQE to hierarchical policies and substantially lowers mean squared-error compared to option-level importance sampling.

AI.tldr: IO-FQE extends fitted Q-evaluation to hierarchical policies by estimating values in the augmented state-option space, which removes the bias of naive FQE and needs no option annotations in the logged data. It yields lower mean squared error than option-level importance sampling on long-horizon continuous-control tasks.
AI.motivation: Off-policy evaluation of hierarchical policies has mostly relied on option-level importance sampling, which needs option-annotated trajectories and has variance that grows with the horizon, while naively applying FQE to hierarchical policies gives biased value estimates.
AI.method: IO-FQE learns a value function over the augmented state-option space, so the Bellman recursion applies to hierarchical policies even when the option that generated each logged action is unknown. Two continuous-action instantiations are developed.
AI.result: On AntMaze navigation and OGBench Puzzle manipulation, IO-FQE removes the bias that naive FQE incurs on hierarchical policies and substantially lowers mean squared error relative to option-level importance sampling. The abstract gives no exact figures.
AI.conclusion: Bellman-based evaluation can be extended to hierarchical policies without option annotations, offering a lower-error alternative to importance sampling for long-horizon tasks.

title: Dual-Granularity Learning for Regression with Continuous Noisy Labels
summary: Learning with noisy labels has been extensively studied for classification, yet its regression counterpart remains relatively underexplored. Unlike classification, regression involves continuous-valued targets where label noise exhibits heterogeneous magnitudes across instances, which poses conflicting requirements on the model: correcting small-to-moderate deviations requires sensitivity to label values for instance-level refinement, whereas large deviations caused by corrupted or outlying annotations render exact label values unreliable, necessitating reduced reliance on exact labels and instead leveraging ordinal structure among samples. These requirements call for methods that capture both global structure and sample-specific deviations in a unified manner. To this end, we propose GRAIN, a dual-granularity framework for robust noisy regression. At the fine-grained level, we derive an explicit residual learning mechanism from a robust loss formulation, introducing instance-specific auxiliary variables to decouple label noise from predictive signals. At the coarse-grained level, we introduce a binning-based contrastive regularization that enforces an order-preserving feature structure aligned with label proximity, addressing noise beyond the capacity of local residual refinement. The two levels are coupled via a histogram-based bridging mechanism that enables bidirectional information flow: coarse-grained structural guidance establishes a well-ordered feature space that anchors residual learning, while fine-grained residual refinement corrects instance-level deviations that structural regularization alone cannot resolve. Experimental results show that GRAIN consistently improves robustness and generalization under diverse noise conditions.

AI.tldr: GRAIN is a dual-granularity framework for regression with noisy continuous labels that combines instance-level residual learning with a coarse-grained binning-based contrastive regularizer, coupled through a histogram-based bridge. The abstract reports consistent gains in robustness and generalization under diverse noise conditions.
AI.motivation: Label-noise methods have been studied mainly for classification, while regression noise varies in magnitude across instances. Small deviations need sensitivity to label values, whereas large, outlying deviations make exact labels unreliable and call for reliance on ordinal structure.
AI.method: At the fine level, a residual learning mechanism is derived from a robust loss, with instance-specific auxiliary variables that separate label noise from the predictive signal. At the coarse level, a binning-based contrastive regularizer enforces a feature order that follows label proximity. A histogram-based bridge passes information in both directions between the two levels.
AI.result: Experiments show that GRAIN consistently improves robustness and generalization under diverse noise conditions. The abstract names no datasets, baselines or numbers.
AI.conclusion: Combining global ordinal structure with sample-specific residual correction is a unified way to make regression robust to heterogeneous label noise.

title: Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning
summary: Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) trains agents to adapt to novel tasks from test-time experience, but requires diverse training environments and reward functions. While environments are becoming cheaper to generate, it remains difficult to anticipate every objective an agent may be asked to pursue at test time. Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) learn policies from reward-free data and support zero-shot RL (ZSRL): adaptation to new objectives at test time using a large reward-labeled dataset. Recent work has shown that BFM task inference can instead be performed online without prior task-specific data. We note that this capability positions BFMs and meta-RL as alternative approaches for online adaptation to new reward functions in a fixed environment. We then ask whether we can extend BFMs to compete with meta-RL more broadly, including in novel environments, and identify four challenges: environment identification, online data collection, test-time exploration, and learning from mixed reward supervision. We study each individually, then propose MetaBFM, a hybrid method that addresses all four. During training, it combines supervised reward-following with unsupervised learning; at test time, it can interpolate between exploration, exploitation, and ZSRL-style reward inference. We demonstrate that MetaBFM can recover the in-distribution performance of supervised meta-RL while generalizing to reward functions outside the training set. Our work suggests that BFMs and meta-RL are complementary research directions whose combined strengths allow adaptive agents to learn more diverse behaviors from a fixed set of supervised objectives.

AI.tldr: MetaBFM is a hybrid method that combines Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) with meta-RL to adapt to new reward functions, including in novel environments. It reportedly matches the in-distribution performance of supervised meta-RL while generalizing to reward functions outside the training set.
AI.motivation: Meta-RL needs diverse training environments and reward functions, while BFMs support zero-shot RL only with a large reward-labelled dataset. Extending BFMs to compete with meta-RL more broadly requires solving four challenges: environment identification, online data collection, test-time exploration, and learning from mixed reward supervision.
AI.method: The authors study each of the four challenges and then propose MetaBFM, which during training combines supervised reward-following with unsupervised learning. At test time it can interpolate between exploration, exploitation, and ZSRL-style reward inference.
AI.result: The abstract states that MetaBFM recovers the in-distribution performance of supervised meta-RL and generalizes to reward functions outside the training set. No benchmarks or numbers are given.
AI.conclusion: BFMs and meta-RL are complementary research directions, and their combined strengths let adaptive agents learn more diverse behaviours from a fixed set of supervised objectives.

title: Predictive Modelling of Solid Waste Generation through Time Series Analysis
summary: Reliable forecasting of Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) production is pivotal for sustainable urban management, as it enables efficient resource planning, optimized collection schedules, and reduced environmental impacts. Existing works on MSW forecasting have some limitations, such as unavailability of granular data from lower administrative units, small datasets, limited or sometimes no consideration of important factors that can affect MSW generation, including holidays, weekends, seasonality, changes in temperature or humidity. This work presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of four popularly used time series forecasting models, namely Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average with Exogenous Regressors (SARIMAX), Prophet, Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), using a real-world MSW dataset from Sri Lanka spanning 2012-2018. A detailed factor-wise analysis is conducted to examine waste generation behaviour considering holidays, weekday-weekend variations, seasonal patterns, temperature and humidity. The results show lower waste generation during holidays and weekends, higher generation during Summer and Winter, and comparatively lower generation during Monsoon and Post-Monsoon. Temperature and humidity do not exhibit a direct linear relationship with waste generation, although their seasonal variations are associated with the changes in waste generation across different seasons. All model performances are evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), and the coefficient of determination (R2). Among the evaluated models, LSTM and SARIMAX achieve the best overall forecasting performance.

AI.tldr: The paper compares SARIMAX, Prophet, LSTM and GRU for forecasting municipal solid waste generation using a Sri Lankan dataset from 2012 to 2018, with a factor-wise analysis of holidays, weekends, seasons, temperature and humidity. LSTM and SARIMAX give the best overall forecasts.
AI.motivation: Existing MSW forecasting studies often lack granular data from lower administrative units, use small datasets, and seldom account for holidays, weekends, seasonality, temperature and humidity.
AI.method: Four time series models are compared: SARIMAX with exogenous regressors, Prophet, LSTM and GRU. A detailed factor-wise analysis examines holidays, weekday-weekend variation, seasonal patterns, temperature and humidity. Performance is measured with MAE, MAPE, RMSE and R2.
AI.result: Waste generation is lower on holidays and weekends and higher in Summer and Winter, and lower in Monsoon and Post-Monsoon. Temperature and humidity show no direct linear relationship with generation, though their seasonal variation tracks seasonal changes. LSTM and SARIMAX achieve the best overall forecasting performance. The abstract gives no error values.
AI.conclusion: Calendar and seasonal effects drive MSW generation more than weather variables taken linearly, and LSTM and SARIMAX are the strongest forecasters for this setting.

title: Detent: Batch-Invariant LLM Serving and RL Rollouts at Near-Stock Speed
summary: Reproducible evaluation, verifiable inference and on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) need an LLM engine to give a request the same output bits whichever requests share its batch. Batch-invariant kernels exist, but engines still select each kernel and its parameters from the batch. Two kernels that compute the same sum can round it differently. The engines' deterministic modes remove the choice by keeping one conservative kernel per operator and pay for it in latency. Many fast kernels are batch-invariant by themselves, so it is enough to fix the few batch-dependent values that kernel selection reads. Detent expresses kernel selection as a program that the engine executes. It finds the fewest values in this program that must be fixed and tunes them for the workload before deployment. On multi-GPU deployments of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-30B-A3B in vLLM and SGLang, Detent is batch-invariant. Tuned per load, it serves at 1.04-1.17x the latency per output token of Stock (each engine with its standard settings), against 1.67-10.3x for the deterministic modes. In SGLang it matches the GSM8K accuracy of SGLang's deterministic mode. Detent covers multiple deployment combinations, including multiple engines, GPU generations, tensor-parallel degrees, and dense and MoE models. Seeded RL rollouts of models up to Llama-3.1-70B replay bit for bit under other batches and cache splits. A trainer on Detent's kernels and values matches every rollout logprob bit for bit at 1.03x Stock's rollout time per token. BF16 GRPO then stays stable where Stock's run collapses.

AI.tldr: Detent makes LLM serving batch-invariant, so a request gets the same output bits regardless of its batch, by fixing only the few batch-dependent values that kernel selection reads and tuning them before deployment. It runs at 1.04 to 1.17 times the latency per output token of stock engines, compared with 1.67 to 10.3 times for deterministic modes.
AI.motivation: Reproducible evaluation, verifiable inference and on-policy RL need batch-invariant outputs. Existing deterministic modes remove kernel-selection variability by using one conservative kernel per operator, which costs substantial latency.
AI.method: Many fast kernels are batch-invariant on their own, so Detent expresses kernel selection as a program executed by the engine, finds the smallest set of values that must be fixed, and tunes them for the workload before deployment.
AI.result: On multi-GPU vLLM and SGLang deployments of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, Detent is batch-invariant and runs at 1.04 to 1.17 times the stock time per output token, against 1.67 to 10.3 times for deterministic modes. In SGLang it matches the GSM8K accuracy of that engine's deterministic mode. Seeded RL rollouts replay bit for bit, and a trainer on Detent's kernels matches every rollout logprob at 1.03 times Stock's rollout time per token. BF16 GRPO stays stable where the stock run collapses.
AI.conclusion: Batch invariance does not require the slowest kernels, and fixing only the batch-dependent values that matter makes exact reproducibility practical for both serving and RL training.

title: Clinical Evidence-Guided Residual Learning for Medication Recommendation with Dynamic DDI Regularization
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Supplementary PDF and detailed result tables are included as ancillary files. Code: this https URL
summary: Medication recommendation must combine patient-specific treatment evidence with the interaction structure of a prescription. The central challenge is to determine which evidence supports each medication and how strongly to regularize interactions while preserving predictive quality. We propose EviDrug, a clinical evidence-guided residual learning framework. Its clinical-memory backbone integrates a self-trained visit-aware encoder, training-case memory and one medication-set interaction block to establish a patient-specific prescription. A gated refinement head combines the backbone states with clinical associations and history-conditioned medication identities through bounded logit corrections. Drug-drug interaction (DDI) feedback adapts regularization strength using training-query predictions. Across MIMIC-IV, NWICU and SICdb, EviDrug leads twelve published-method baselines in AP, F1 and Jaccard, improving AP by 2.26, 2.06 and 1.71 percentage points over the strongest comparator. These gains come at lower parameter and runtime costs than MetaDrug. Matched controls demonstrate DDI reductions with stable predictive quality. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: EviDrug is a residual learning framework for medication recommendation that combines patient-specific clinical evidence with a drug-drug interaction (DDI) regularizer whose strength adapts to training predictions. It leads twelve published baselines in AP, F1 and Jaccard on MIMIC-IV, NWICU and SICdb, with lower parameter and runtime costs than MetaDrug.
AI.motivation: Medication recommendation must link patient treatment evidence to each drug and regulate interactions within a prescription without degrading predictive quality.
AI.method: A clinical-memory backbone combines a self-trained visit-aware encoder, training-case memory and a medication-set interaction block. A gated refinement head adds bounded logit corrections from clinical associations and history-conditioned medication identities. DDI feedback adjusts regularization strength using training-query predictions.
AI.result: EviDrug improves AP by 2.26, 2.06 and 1.71 percentage points over the strongest comparator on MIMIC-IV, NWICU and SICdb respectively. Matched controls show DDI reductions with stable predictive quality, and the method costs less in parameters and runtime than MetaDrug.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-guided residual corrections together with adaptive DDI regularization improve medication recommendation while reducing harmful interactions, at modest computational cost.

title: CONSTRAINER: Promptable Graph-Structured Optimization via Constraint Conditioning
summary: Neural methods for graph-structured optimization have achieved strong performance within individual problem classes, but are typically trained for fixed formulations, limiting reuse across related problem variants. Recent progress in foundation models has motivated shared neural backbones trained across multiple graph-structured optimization tasks; however, existing approaches primarily share instance-level representations while treating feasibility constraints implicitly. A key source of shared structure across constrained optimization problems is the constraint set itself, which often exhibits substantial overlap across tasks. We propose CONSTRAINER, a constraint-conditioned framework for graph-structured optimization that treats constraints as structured inputs. Constraint specifications are parsed into operator graphs and encoded using a graph neural network to produce invariant constraint embeddings, which condition a shared backbone model for solution prediction. We evaluate our approach on power grid optimization and mixed-integer linear programming problems, where it shows improved solution optimality and enables efficient transfer learning and generalization compared to baseline methods.

AI.tldr: CONSTRAINER is a graph-structured optimization framework that treats constraint specifications as structured inputs, encoding them with a graph neural network and using the resulting embeddings to condition a shared solution-prediction backbone. It shows better solution optimality and transfer on power grid optimization and mixed-integer linear programming.
AI.motivation: Neural solvers for graph-structured optimization are typically trained for fixed formulations, and shared foundation-style backbones usually share instance representations while handling feasibility constraints implicitly, even though constraint sets overlap substantially across tasks.
AI.method: Constraint specifications are parsed into operator graphs and encoded with a graph neural network into invariant constraint embeddings. These embeddings condition a shared backbone that predicts solutions.
AI.result: On power grid optimization and mixed-integer linear programming, the approach improves solution optimality and enables efficient transfer learning and generalization relative to baseline methods. The abstract gives no numbers.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly conditioning on constraints makes a shared backbone reusable across related constrained optimization problem variants.

title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations
summary: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer's activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. MACaQ reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and already matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11 times less quantization time. We further apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, illustrating the generality of its layer-local design and show quantization of a 122B parameter model in 64 minutes, using only 32.5GB GPU RAM.

AI.tldr: MACaQ is a fast, layer-independent post-training quantization method for MXFP4 W4A4 that applies a per-channel scale and an online block-Hadamard transform to activations and refines weights with a Hessian-aware procedure called Flip-Refinement. It achieves lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ with much less quantization time.
AI.motivation: Weight-activation quantization often needs expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers.
AI.method: Each linear layer is handled independently. Activations receive a per-channel scale and an online block-Hadamard transform, and the inverse transforms are absorbed into the weights, which avoids cross-layer dependencies and allows streaming quantization with one layer in memory at a time. Flip-Refinement is a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent step that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values, improving on round-to-nearest.
AI.result: MACaQ adds 2.3 percent end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. It reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and matches their best Llama-3-8B perplexity in 11 times less quantization time. It also applies without modification to an image diffusion model and quantizes a 122B-parameter model in 64 minutes using 32.5 GB of GPU RAM.
AI.conclusion: Layer-local transforms and coordinate-descent refinement give a simple, general and fast quantization pipeline with small inference overhead.

title: Causal Heteroscedastic Structure Learning From Incomplete Temporal data
