summary: Discovering causal structures in multivariate time series (MTS) is critical in domains such as finance and neuroscience, yet remains challenging in practice due to three distinct obstacles. First, MTS are routinely corrupted by missing values, where naive impute-then-discover pipelines distort the underlying data distribution and yield spurious causal graphs. Second, identifying instantaneous effects is difficult even on complete data, and missingness further entangles imputation with graph recovery. Third, real-world data frequently exhibits heteroscedastic noise with variance driven by both instantaneous and lagged causes, violating the core assumptions of standard discovery methods. Existing approaches fail to address these challenges concurrently, typically presuming complete data, homoscedastic noise, or strictly time-lagged relationships. Crucially, we show through ablation studies that resolving these issues sequentially, rather than jointly, leads to a substantial degradation in performance. To overcome this, we introduce Cheesefill, an optimal transport framework for causal structure learning under missingness and heteroscedastic noise. Cheesefill parameterizes causal mechanisms using conditional normalizing flows and jointly learns a stochastic correction map that refines naive imputations into trajectories consistent with the inferred causal mechanisms. Theoretically, we prove that optimizing over stochastic correction maps is equivalent to a conditional kernel reformulation of the Kantorovich problem, from which our neural parameterization yields a tractable objective. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that Cheesefill consistently outperforms existing baselines across diverse missingness regimes.

AI.tldr: Cheesefill is an optimal-transport framework for causal structure discovery in multivariate time series that jointly handles missing values and heteroscedastic noise. It learns a stochastic correction map that refines imputations so they match the inferred causal mechanisms, and it outperforms baselines across missingness regimes.
AI.motivation: Existing causal discovery methods for multivariate time series assume complete data, homoscedastic noise, or purely lagged relations. Impute-then-discover pipelines distort the data distribution, and the authors report that handling these issues sequentially rather than jointly substantially degrades performance.
AI.method: Causal mechanisms are parameterized with conditional normalizing flows. A stochastic correction map is learned jointly with the discovery model to turn naive imputations into trajectories consistent with the inferred mechanisms. The authors prove that optimizing over stochastic correction maps is equivalent to a conditional kernel reformulation of the Kantorovich problem, which gives a tractable objective.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show that Cheesefill consistently outperforms existing baselines across diverse missingness regimes. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning imputation and causal structure under optimal transport is a more reliable route to causal discovery from incomplete, heteroscedastic time series than sequential pipelines.

title: Safe Offline Reinforcement Learning using Behavior Regularisation and Latent Feasibility Guidance
summary: Safe offline reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to learn policies that maximize return while satisfying safety constraints, using a static dataset. To characterize state-wise safety, reachability analysis identifies the feasible region, defined as the set of states from which constraints can be satisfied at every future step. Policies are commonly extracted from learned value functions with advantage-weighted regression (AWR). However, AWR relies on exponentiated weights that amplify value estimation errors, whereas behavior-regularized policy gradient methods directly utilize the action gradient of the value function and often make more effective use of learned critics. We propose Feasibility-Optimized Conditional Actor Learning (FOCAL), a method that incorporates behavior-regularized policy gradients into a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) actor. FOCAL optimizes this policy using a first-order objective partitioned by feasibility, updating the actor to increase return on transitions estimated to be feasible and to reduce constraint violations on transitions estimated to be infeasible. During inference, FOCAL dynamically adjusts the scale of the latent prior according to the estimated feasibility of the state to adjust the conservatism of action sampling. Theoretically, we show that for AWR, the policy update variance depends exponentially on the advantage error, whereas for FOCAL it scales linearly with the variance of the value estimation error. Across the DSRL benchmark, FOCAL satisfies the constraints on all evaluated tasks while achieving competitive or higher returns compared to baselines.

AI.tldr: FOCAL is a safe offline RL method that trains a CVAE actor with behaviour-regularized policy gradients, partitioning the first-order objective by estimated state feasibility. It satisfies the constraints on all evaluated DSRL tasks while achieving competitive or higher returns than baselines.
AI.motivation: Advantage-weighted regression, the usual policy extraction method, uses exponentiated weights that amplify value estimation errors, whereas behaviour-regularized policy gradients use the critic's action gradient more effectively.
AI.method: FOCAL places behaviour-regularized policy gradients on a conditional variational autoencoder actor. The first-order objective is split by feasibility, increasing return on transitions estimated to be feasible and reducing constraint violations on transitions estimated to be infeasible. At inference, the latent prior scale is adjusted by the estimated feasibility of the state to set the conservatism of action sampling. Feasibility is characterized by reachability analysis.
AI.result: Across the DSRL benchmark, FOCAL satisfies the constraints on all evaluated tasks while achieving competitive or higher returns than the baselines. The theoretical claim is that the policy update variance scales linearly with the value-estimation error variance for FOCAL, versus exponentially in the advantage error for AWR.
AI.conclusion: Replacing exponential advantage weighting with first-order, feasibility-partitioned policy gradients gives safer offline policies with better-behaved updates.

title: Spectral Bias Reduction in Local Gated ReLU Architectures
comment: 24 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Preliminary version; comments welcome
summary: Neural networks trained by gradient-based methods learn the low-frequency content of a target function faster than its high-frequency content. This spectral bias is well documented, but it is much less clear which architectural choices mitigate it and which cannot. We study the question for shallow ReLU models linear in their trainable parameters, where each mode is learned at a rate given by a Gram-matrix eigenvalue, and for a general symmetric bilinear form $a(\cdot,\cdot)$, so that least-squares regression ($a=$ the $L^2$ inner product) and variational or physics-informed losses ($a=$ the $H^1$ energy form) are two instances of one analysis. Within this framework we propose gated local ReLU dictionaries, obtained by multiplying each ReLU feature by a hat partition-of-unity weight, in the spirit of partition-of-unity finite elements and overlapping Schwarz methods. The resulting Gram matrices are block-banded for any local bilinear form, with a block-Toeplitz interior whose matrix-valued symbol governs the spectrum. The two forms then behave very differently. For $L^2$ regression, the symbol is bounded away from zero, the ratio is uniform in the number of windows, and the measured spread of frequency-dependent learning rates falls from $1.9\times10^{5}$ to $4.5$ at matched model size. For the $H^1$ stiffness matrix, the symbol vanishes at zero frequency: gating leaves the $\Theta(N^2)$ conditioning intact and inverts the frequency ordering instead of removing the bias. A preconditioner built from the same interior stencil will fix the spectral bias, showing that architecture alone is not enough. Experiments on $1$D regression and Poisson problems confirm the dichotomy, and the regression effect persists when the hidden-layer parameters are trained as well.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that gating ReLU features with overlapping hat partition-of-unity weights removes spectral bias for L2 regression but not for H1 energy problems, where gating inverts the frequency ordering instead. A preconditioner from the same interior stencil is needed to fix the H1 case.
AI.motivation: Gradient-trained networks learn low frequencies faster, but it is unclear which architectural choices mitigate this bias. Least-squares regression and variational or physics-informed losses are two instances of one bilinear-form analysis that must be compared.
AI.method: For shallow ReLU models linear in their trainable parameters, a general symmetric bilinear form is analysed. The proposed gated local ReLU dictionaries multiply each ReLU feature by a hat partition-of-unity weight, in the spirit of partition-of-unity finite elements and overlapping Schwarz methods. The resulting Gram matrices are block-banded with a block-Toeplitz interior whose matrix-valued symbol governs the spectrum.
AI.result: For L2 regression the symbol stays bounded away from zero, the conditioning ratio is uniform in the number of windows, and the spread of frequency-dependent learning rates falls from 1.9 times 10^5 to 4.5 at matched model size. For the H1 stiffness matrix the symbol vanishes at zero frequency, so the Theta(N^2) conditioning remains and the frequency ordering is inverted. Experiments on 1D regression and Poisson problems confirm the dichotomy, and the regression effect persists when hidden-layer parameters are also trained.
AI.conclusion: Architecture alone can remove spectral bias for regression, but for energy-based losses a preconditioner is also required.

title: AbductionBench: Benchmarking Abductive Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: Abductive reasoning is the inference of plausible explanations for observed evidence. Evaluating this capability requires more than a single task: a system may need to generate an explanation, discriminate among competing hypotheses, revise its hypotheses as evidence arrives, or decide what evidence to seek next. Yet these capabilities are typically evaluated through isolated benchmarks with different task formulations and scoring procedures, so claims that a model is ``good at abduction'' may reflect only a narrow aspect of this capability. We introduce AbductionBench, a unified framework whose taxonomy characterizes abductive tasks. We instantiate this framework on 27 datasets spanning ten domains and evaluate eight LLMs from four model families evaluated on single-choice selection tasks. Beyond harmonizing heterogeneous tasks, AbductionBench separates final-answer evaluation from analysis of the observable reasoning traces and interaction histories produced alongside those answers. We analyze written traces as observable model outputs rather than faithful representations of internal computation, characterizing evidence use, hypothesis comparison, uncertainty, contradiction handling, and answer commitment. Jev matches or exceeds small LLMs when selecting among explanations over compact evidence but falls substantially behind on longer cases, suggesting that candidate discrimination and extended evidence integration place different demands on a system. In interactive tasks, the proportion of actions judged relevant declines at later steps, and a relevant first question is associated with a correct final answer; in the passive task, models rarely revise their initial hypothesis as new evidence arrives. Together, these findings highlight the value of evaluating abductive reasoning through both final answers and observable evidence use, hypothesis revision, and information gathering.

AI.tldr: AbductionBench is a unified benchmark for abductive reasoning in LLMs, covering 27 datasets from ten domains with a taxonomy of abductive tasks. It separates final-answer accuracy from analysis of observable reasoning traces and interaction histories, and shows that models struggle with longer evidence and rarely revise hypotheses.
AI.motivation: Abductive reasoning is assessed through isolated benchmarks with different formulations and scoring, so claims that a model is good at abduction may reflect only a narrow aspect of the capability.
AI.method: A unified taxonomy harmonizes heterogeneous abductive tasks, instantiated on 27 datasets across ten domains. Eight LLMs from four model families are evaluated on single-choice selection tasks. Written reasoning traces are analysed as observable outputs for evidence use, hypothesis comparison, uncertainty, contradiction handling and answer commitment, not as faithful records of internal computation.
AI.result: The evaluated model matches or exceeds small LLMs when selecting among explanations over compact evidence, but falls well behind on longer cases. In interactive tasks the share of relevant actions declines at later steps, and a relevant first question is associated with a correct final answer. In the passive task, models rarely revise their initial hypothesis as new evidence arrives.
AI.conclusion: Abductive reasoning should be evaluated through both final answers and observable evidence use, hypothesis revision and information gathering, since candidate discrimination and extended evidence integration place different demands on models.

title: FedSGN: Federated Sparse Grassmann Newton Learning for IoT Anomaly Detection
summary: Anomaly detection plays a critical role in securing the Internet of things (IoT). Although existing federated principal component analysis (PCA) methods can learn the subspace of normal samples without sharing raw data, they often suffer from feature redundancy that may degrade detection performance. To address this limitation, we propose a novel and effective federated sparse Grassmann Newton (FedSGN) learning method for IoT anomaly detection. Technically, our FedSGN leverages the $\ell_{2,0}$-norm constraint on the global projection matrix to eliminate redundancy and introduces an orthogonality penalty to preserve the intrinsic structure. Moreover, we develop an augmented Lagrangian solver integrated with a semismooth Newton scheme to enable parallel client updates and Grassmann projection for robustness. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves favorable overall detection performance while reducing communication overhead. The source code is publicly available at this https URL

AI.tldr: FedSGN is a federated PCA-style method for IoT anomaly detection that learns a sparse projection of normal-sample subspaces, using an l2,0-norm constraint to remove feature redundancy. It reports favourable detection performance with lower communication overhead.
AI.motivation: Federated PCA methods can learn the normal subspace without sharing raw data, but they often suffer from feature redundancy that degrades detection.
AI.method: The global projection matrix is constrained by an l2,0-norm to eliminate redundant features and regularized by an orthogonality penalty to preserve intrinsic structure. An augmented Lagrangian solver with a semismooth Newton scheme enables parallel client updates and Grassmann projection.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show favourable overall detection performance together with reduced communication overhead. The abstract gives no datasets or numbers.
AI.conclusion: Sparse, orthogonality-constrained federated subspace learning offers a practical approach to privacy-preserving IoT anomaly detection.

title: Breaking Precision Walls in First-, Second-, and Zeroth-Order Optimizers: One Constant, Set in Advance
summary: Under power-law signal decay across directions, an optimizer can fit strong directions and miss weak ones while average loss hides it. A precision wall measures the steepest decay where the weakest direction recovers within 5% in a fixed budget. On low-rank matrix sensing and quadratics one constant sets the wall: once it dominates the denominator, Adam or grafted Shampoo is momentum descent at step $\eta/c$, setting the wall; in Shampoo, matching grafting's constant to damping restores the wall after three hypotheses failed. In zeroth-order Adam, $\varepsilon$ acts against $\varepsilon^\ast$ from a mean-square spectral model; below $\varepsilon^\ast$ error hits a noise floor. Set from true curvature or spectrum on new shapes, the rule raised the wall above the same-step default by a forecast amount: on two sensing shapes by $1.96, 1.15$ (Adam) and $1.59, 1.74$ (grafted Shampoo), and on two Hadamard-rotated quadratics by $1.12, 0.73$ (zeroth-order Adam, longer budget), rising on all seeds; fixed-step momentum at that step reaches those walls. A cosine-scheduled default (small constant giving weak modes large steps) is higher on one sensing shape, matched on new seeds of the other, and lower with the rule's constant. A default step retuned per budget catches up on rotated quadratics and population logistic regression, fails at 1 query/step on two diagonal quadratics (catching up at 16), and exceeds the rule on digits logistic regression (full-batch and minibatches, where gradient noise sets the $\eta = 0.01, 0.1$ default walls). On logistic regression the rule did not raise the first-order wall: same-step default Adam was higher (its wall on 4 new shapes at the forecast stability limit), while in zeroth order on the population loss setting $\varepsilon$ raised the wall by $0.98, 0.88$.

AI.tldr: The paper analyses a precision wall, the steepest signal decay at which an optimizer still recovers the weakest direction within 5 percent in a fixed budget, and shows that one constant set in advance determines this wall for Adam, grafted Shampoo and zeroth-order Adam. A rule that sets this constant from true curvature or spectrum raises the wall above same-step defaults on new problem shapes.
AI.motivation: Under power-law signal decay, an optimizer can fit strong directions while missing weak ones, and average loss hides this failure. Default step sizes may therefore leave weak directions unrecovered.
AI.method: On low-rank matrix sensing and quadratics, a single constant controls the wall: when it dominates the denominator, Adam or grafted Shampoo behaves as momentum descent with effective step size eta over c. In zeroth-order Adam, epsilon acts against a threshold epsilon-star derived from a mean-square spectral model. A rule chooses the constant from true curvature or spectrum on new shapes.
AI.result: The rule raises the wall over the same-step default by 1.96 and 1.15 on two sensing shapes for Adam, by 1.59 and 1.74 for grafted Shampoo, and by 1.12 and 0.73 for zeroth-order Adam on two Hadamard-rotated quadratics, consistently across seeds. A cosine-scheduled default is higher on one sensing shape, matched on another, and lower than the rule. On logistic regression the rule did not raise the first-order wall, where same-step default Adam was higher. In zeroth order on the population loss, epsilon raised the wall by 0.98 and 0.88.
AI.conclusion: A single constant chosen from curvature or spectrum can move the precision wall for several optimizers, though the benefit is not uniform across problem types.

title: Spectrogram-Based CNN Autoencoder for One-Class Anomaly Detection in Machining Vibration Signals
summary: This work presents a one-class anomaly detection framework for vibration-based condition monitoring in machining processes using a convolutional neural network autoencoder. Three-axis vibration signals acquired during industrial broaching are transformed into time--frequency spectrograms and combined into a compact three-channel representation, enabling convolutional feature learning on multivariate time-series data. The autoencoder is trained exclusively on normal process data and detects anomalous strokes based on reconstruction errors. Labeled validation data are used for threshold calibration and an independent test set is reserved for final performance evaluation. To improve sensitivity to short-lived process instabilities such as chatter, a localized residual-based metric termed Segmented Vertical Error (SVE) is introduced. Experimental results on approximately 10{,}000 broaching strokes show a clear separation between normal and anomalous process conditions under strong class imbalance. The processing pipeline is additionally evaluated on an external public turning dataset as a proof of concept, indicating preliminary applicability beyond the original broaching setup. The results suggest that spectrogram-based autoencoder models can provide a practical and scalable basis for one-class anomaly detection in industrial vibration monitoring.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a one-class anomaly detector for machining vibration signals, using a CNN autoencoder trained only on normal broaching strokes over spectrogram-based three-channel inputs. A new Segmented Vertical Error metric improves sensitivity to short-lived instabilities such as chatter.
AI.motivation: Vibration-based condition monitoring in machining needs detection of short-lived process instabilities under strong class imbalance, and a practical, scalable method is needed for industrial use.
AI.method: Three-axis vibration signals from industrial broaching are converted into time-frequency spectrograms and combined into a three-channel representation. A convolutional autoencoder trained only on normal data flags anomalous strokes by reconstruction error. Labelled validation data set the threshold, and a separate test set is used for final evaluation. A localized residual metric, Segmented Vertical Error (SVE), is introduced.
AI.result: On about 10,000 broaching strokes, normal and anomalous conditions are clearly separated despite strong class imbalance. The pipeline is also applied as a proof of concept to an external public turning dataset, with preliminary applicability reported. The abstract gives no detection metrics.
AI.conclusion: Spectrogram-based autoencoders may provide a practical and scalable basis for one-class anomaly detection in industrial vibration monitoring.

title: AERO: Adaptive Ensemble-Disagreement Routing for Oracle Feedback in Sample-Efficient Online RLHF
summary: Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has driven substantial improvements across a wide range of tasks, but the cost of acquiring preference labels remains the dominant bottleneck in the alignment pipeline. While many recent alignment methods improve sample efficiency through active exploration over candidate responses, they typically query the oracle uniformly across contexts, even for contexts where the learned reward estimates are already reliable enough to provide synthetic labels. We propose Adaptive Ensemble-disagreement Routing for Oracle feedback (AERO), a fully online RLHF algorithm built on a Dyna-style model-based RL architecture, in which an ensemble-based Epistemic Reward Model (ERM) serves both as a reward posterior for exploration and as a learned preference-feedback model for synthetic labeling. AERO uses ensemble vote entropy, a Query-by-Committee disagreement measure, combined with an adaptive thresholding mechanism to decide which contexts require oracle feedback and which can instead receive ERM-based synthetic preference labels, concentrating expensive labels where they are most informative. Empirical results across different model families and scales show that AERO achieves highly competitive alignment performance while reducing the required oracle-query budget compared to online DPO and strong active-exploration baselines.

AI.tldr: AERO is an online RLHF algorithm that routes each context to either oracle preference feedback or synthetic labels from an ensemble reward model, using ensemble vote entropy with adaptive thresholding. It reports competitive alignment with a smaller oracle-query budget than online DPO and active-exploration baselines.
AI.motivation: Preference labels are the main cost in RLHF, yet active-exploration methods usually query the oracle uniformly across contexts, even where the learned reward is already reliable.
AI.method: AERO is built on a Dyna-style model-based RL architecture. An ensemble Epistemic Reward Model serves both as a reward posterior for exploration and as a learned preference model that produces synthetic labels. Query-by-Committee disagreement, measured as ensemble vote entropy with an adaptive threshold, decides whether a context needs oracle feedback or can receive ERM-based synthetic labels.
AI.result: Across different model families and scales, AERO achieves highly competitive alignment performance while reducing the required oracle-query budget compared with online DPO and strong active-exploration baselines. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Concentrating expensive oracle labels where ensemble disagreement is high makes sample-efficient online alignment cheaper without sacrificing performance.

title: ConwayNet: Interpretability, Activation Coherence, and Noise Resilience via a Game-of-Life-Inspired Lateral Inhibition in Artificial Neural Networks
summary: Deep neural networks achieve universal function approximation by stacking interconnected nonlinearities, but as a consequence they are sensitive to noise and resist mechanistic interpretation. In contrast, the local update rules of cellular automata, such as Conway's Game of Life, give rise to not merely interpretable but programmable dynamics. We explore a bridge between these worlds: a lateral inhibition in neural networks based on continuous Game-of-Life rules that derives inhibitory and excitatory responses from the layer input and blends them into the activation map in a state-conditioned way. The mechanism is differentiable and architecture-agnostic, and its regulation is imposed rather than learned: the rule's parameters are fixed and are not optimised, while the rule's values and derivatives shape training throughout the network. Wired into fully connected, convolutional, wide-residual and graph convolutional networks, it gives rise to several properties. Activation maps become coherent across space, depth and seeds, with coarse structure persisting through depth while fine detail is renewed at every layer. The co-activation graph of the hidden units departs from an Erdős--Rényi random graph: it is laid out on the image and its giant component grows in steps, as in a spatial graph. Networks started from nearly identical initialisations, under label noise, disagree on thirty times fewer test images. Saliency maps rest on the object rather than the background, and resilience to pixel noise not seen in training is substantially improved.

AI.tldr: ConwayNet adds a fixed, non-learned lateral inhibition layer based on continuous Game-of-Life rules to standard neural networks, producing more coherent, interpretable activations and better resilience to noise. The rule is differentiable and architecture-agnostic.
AI.motivation: Deep networks are sensitive to noise and hard to interpret mechanistically, whereas cellular automata such as Conway's Game of Life give interpretable and programmable local dynamics. The paper asks whether this can be bridged into standard architectures.
AI.method: A lateral inhibition module derives inhibitory and excitatory responses from the layer input using continuous Game-of-Life rules and blends them into the activation map in a state-conditioned way. The rule parameters are fixed rather than learned, while the rule values and derivatives shape training. It is inserted into fully connected, convolutional, wide-residual and graph convolutional networks.
AI.result: Activation maps become coherent across space, depth and seeds, with coarse structure persisting through depth while fine detail is renewed at each layer. The hidden-unit co-activation graph departs from an Erdos-Renyi random graph and its giant component grows in steps, as in a spatial graph. Networks from nearly identical initializations disagree on thirty times fewer test images under label noise. Saliency maps focus on the object rather than the background, and resilience to unseen pixel noise improves substantially. The abstract gives no benchmark names.
AI.conclusion: Fixed, cellular-automaton-style lateral inhibition yields more coherent, interpretable and noise-resilient networks across several architectures.

title: Universal Approximation by Equivariant Message-Passing Graph Neural Networks with a Bilinear Readout
summary: We prove universal approximation for the bilinear-readout equivariant message-passing network (BREMP), a reference architecture for equivariant graph neural network interatomic potentials. Its layers combine equivariant convolutions with affine maps, and its readout forms invariants from products of the equivariant features. We construct a one-layer feature that determines the local environment up to permutations of atoms of the same type. The construction uses spherical harmonic filters of degree no larger than the largest number of neighbors at a common distance from the center. Iterating the construction recovers the environment reachable in as many hops as there are layers, using the same bound on filter degrees at the layer cutoff. The readout approximates every continuous invariant function of the features uniformly on compact sets. Together these give universal approximation of atomic energies at a prescribed physical range using a shorter layer cutoff. We assume that, throughout the admissible class, message passing reaches all neighbors in each physical environment within a common number of layers. Finally, DPA4, an interatomic potential architecture in production use, inherits this result by approximating the BREMP layers constructed in the proof and realizing the bilinear readout.

AI.tldr: The paper proves universal approximation for the bilinear-readout equivariant message-passing network (BREMP), showing that its layers with spherical-harmonic filters of bounded degree and a bilinear readout can approximate atomic energies over a prescribed physical range using a shorter layer cutoff. The result also covers DPA4, a production interatomic potential.
AI.motivation: Equivariant graph neural network interatomic potentials are widely used, but their expressivity as universal approximators of atomic energies had not been established for this reference architecture.
AI.method: The construction builds a one-layer feature that determines the local environment up to permutations of same-type atoms, using spherical harmonic filters of degree no larger than the largest number of neighbours at a common distance from the centre. Iterating it recovers the environment reachable in as many hops as there are layers. The readout approximates every continuous invariant function of the features uniformly on compact sets. The proof assumes that message passing reaches all neighbours within a common number of layers.
AI.result: The abstract reports the theorem and its consequences rather than experimental numbers. DPA4 inherits the result by approximating the BREMP layers constructed in the proof and realizing the bilinear readout.
AI.conclusion: Equivariant message passing with a bilinear readout is a universal approximator for atomic energies, and this guarantee carries over to a deployed potential.

title: EEGFaceSem: An EEG Benchmark with Paired Generative Latents for Semantic Visual Modeling
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations and Datasets Track. Conference page: this https URL ; Project page: this https URL
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used to measure brain activity for brain-computer interface applications for its non-invasive nature and high temporal resolution. However, progress in modeling the neural responses to visual semantics has been limited by a reliance on fixed image collections that lack the fine-grained control needed to isolate fine-grained changes in visual features and their relation to perception. In this work, we present EEGFaceSem, a large-scale dataset pairing high-quality EEG with photorealistic face images synthesized from a generative model. We provide the generative latent vector for each stimulus, enabling research into the continuous mapping between a visual latent space and neural representations. Each participant's brain responses were recorded while they attended to specific semantic features (e.g., smiling, hair color) in a rapid serial visual presentation paradigm. The dataset contains EEG signals from 30 participants, totaling 67,200 time-locked EEG recordings. We present benchmarks for single-trial semantic classification under single-subject, cross-subject, and subject-adapted settings, as well as for cross-subject voting that aggregates per-stimulus predictions across participants. We further demonstrate the dataset's unique utility with two complementary applications: deriving semantic directions in the latent space for brain-supervised image editing, and conditioning a generative model on brain-decoded labels for brain-supervised image generation. Our dataset paves the way for advancing brain-computer interfaces (BCI) for semantic-level visual saliency detection and brain-supervised generative modeling. Our dataset and code are openly released at OSF (this https URL) and at HuggingFace this https URL.

AI.tldr: EEGFaceSem is an EEG dataset of 30 participants viewing photorealistic faces synthesized from a generative model, with each stimulus's latent vector released to link neural responses to a continuous visual latent space. Benchmarks cover single-trial semantic classification and two brain-supervised image applications.
AI.motivation: EEG studies of visual semantics rely on fixed image collections, which lack the fine control needed to isolate changes in visual features and their link to perception.
AI.method: Participants attended to specific semantic features such as smiling and hair colour during a rapid serial visual presentation paradigm. Stimuli are photorealistic faces generated from a generative model, and each has its latent vector. Benchmarks cover single-subject, cross-subject and subject-adapted classification, plus cross-subject voting that aggregates per-stimulus predictions.
AI.result: The dataset contains 67,200 time-locked EEG recordings from 30 participants. Benchmarks are reported for single-trial semantic classification in the three settings and for cross-subject voting. The two applications are semantic directions in latent space for brain-supervised image editing and conditioning a generative model on brain-decoded labels for brain-supervised image generation. The abstract gives no accuracy figures.
AI.conclusion: EEGFaceSem supplies a controllable, latent-linked EEG resource for semantic visual decoding, BCI research, and brain-supervised editing and generation. The dataset and code are openly released.

title: Proximal Preference Optimization: A Unified Framework for Stable and Reward-Free Alignment
summary: We introduce a proximal preference optimization framework that unifies the implicit reward formulation of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) with the trust-region stability of Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Our framework yields two complementary algorithms. P$^2$O (Proximal Preference Optimization) introduces a clipped importance ratio directly into the DPO preference margin, producing a reward-model-free algorithm that supports safe dataset reuse, bounded policy divergence, and monotonic preference improvement guarantees. PKTO (Proximal Kahneman-Tversky Optimization) extends P$^2$O by replacing the DPO margin with KTO's prospect-theoretic utility margins, adding a self-regulating adaptive baseline that tightens the effective trust region as the policy drifts, and an asymmetric weighting that handles imbalanced or asymmetric preference datasets. We provide a unified theoretical analysis, including Kullback Leibler (KL) trust-region bounds, a policy-improvement lower bound, and convergence guarantees under multi-epoch proximal updates. Empirically, P$^2$O and PKTO match or exceed DPO and KTO in alignment quality while maintaining better stability under repeated dataset reuse across multiple LLMs on three preference benchmarks. The code base is available here.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a proximal preference optimization framework that combines DPO's implicit reward with PPO-style trust-region stability, yielding two reward-model-free algorithms, P2O and PKTO. These match or exceed DPO and KTO in alignment quality while remaining more stable under repeated dataset reuse.
AI.motivation: DPO and KTO are reward-model-free but do not carry the trust-region stability of PPO, which becomes important when preference data is reused over several update epochs.
AI.method: P2O inserts a clipped importance ratio directly into the DPO preference margin. PKTO replaces the DPO margin with KTO's prospect-theoretic utility margins and adds a self-regulating adaptive baseline that tightens the trust region as the policy drifts, plus asymmetric weighting for imbalanced or asymmetric preference datasets.
AI.result: The analysis gives KL trust-region bounds, a policy-improvement lower bound and convergence guarantees under multi-epoch proximal updates. Across multiple LLMs and three preference benchmarks, P2O and PKTO match or exceed DPO and KTO and are more stable under repeated dataset reuse.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a unified, reward-model-free route to alignment that keeps the implicit reward of DPO and KTO while gaining PPO-style stability guarantees, which supports safe dataset reuse and bounded policy divergence.

title: Zeroth-Order Riemannian Optimization on Fixed-Rank Manifolds for LLM Fine-Tuning
summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization estimates descent directions from function values alone, which removes the activation storage required by backpropagation and makes it attractive for memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). Existing low-rank ZO methods either parameterize the additive update through Euclidean factors with a non-unique representation, or restrict each finite-difference direction to be low-rank. In this work, we propose to constrain each additive update block to a fixed-rank matrix manifold while keeping the pretrained weights frozen, so the learned update remains rank-constrained throughout fine-tuning. On this geometry, we build a Riemannian ZO gradient estimator that projects a random matrix onto the tangent space, normalizes it to correct the scale mismatch induced by projection, and further propose Zeroth-order Riemannian Gradient Descent (ZO-RGD) and its smoothed variant, ZO-RGD-S. We show that the ambient finite difference matches its retracted counterpart, the normalized estimator recovers the Riemannian gradient in expectation, and ZO-RGD converges under trajectory-regularity conditions. Experiments on LLM fine-tuning tasks show that the proposed algorithms are competitive with strong forward-only baselines across model families and tasks, with gains in several settings.

AI.tldr: The paper constrains each additive LLM fine-tuning update to a fixed-rank matrix manifold and optimizes it with forward-only zeroth-order Riemannian methods, ZO-RGD and ZO-RGD-S. The methods are competitive with strong forward-only baselines across model families and tasks, with gains in several settings.
AI.motivation: Existing low-rank zeroth-order methods either use Euclidean factors with a non-unique representation or restrict each finite-difference direction to be low-rank, so the learned update does not stay rank-constrained throughout fine-tuning.
AI.method: With the pretrained weights frozen, each additive update block is kept on a fixed-rank matrix manifold. The Riemannian zeroth-order gradient estimator projects a random matrix onto the tangent space and normalizes it to correct the scale mismatch introduced by projection. The paper then proposes ZO-RGD and its smoothed variant ZO-RGD-S.
AI.result: The ambient finite difference matches its retracted counterpart, and the normalized estimator recovers the Riemannian gradient in expectation. ZO-RGD converges under trajectory-regularity conditions. On LLM fine-tuning tasks the methods are competitive with forward-only baselines, with gains in several settings.
AI.conclusion: Riemannian geometry gives memory-efficient zeroth-order fine-tuning a rank-constrained update with a principled gradient estimator and convergence analysis, while matching strong forward-only baselines.

title: Learning When to Think: Adaptive Internal Computation for Reinforcement Learning
summary: Iterative neural policies usually spend the same computation on every decision, although the benefit of additional processing varies across states. We introduce Adaptive Internal Computation (AIC), an iterative policy that learns when to stop refining its latent representation and act. In AIC, we train action selection and stopping jointly, an expected-depth penalty values computation and intermediate value predictions provide auxiliary supervision. We show that when only some states benefit from further refinement, an ideal state-dependent allocator outperforms every state-independent stopping schedule at the same expected depth. With at most eight refinement steps per decision, AIC executes 3.3 steps on average across twelve benchmark tasks and lowers per-decision latency by 31--44% relative to a fixed eight-step policy on four control and robotics tasks. Its mean reward exceeds the best fixed-depth policy on seven tasks and trails it on four. Ablating adaptive stopping and value supervision separately shows that stopping accounts for most of the reward gain on PickCube and AntMaze, where it also executes more refinement steps and that supervision accounts for most of it on RareEvent.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Adaptive Internal Computation (AIC), an iterative policy that learns when to stop refining its latent representation and act. It executes 3.3 refinement steps on average, with at most eight, and lowers per-decision latency relative to a fixed eight-step policy.
AI.motivation: Iterative neural policies spend the same computation on every decision, even though the benefit of extra processing differs across states.
AI.method: Action selection and stopping are trained jointly. An expected-depth penalty sets the computation cost, and intermediate value predictions provide auxiliary supervision. The paper also gives an ideal state-dependent allocator as a reference point against state-independent stopping schedules.
AI.result: Across twelve benchmark tasks AIC executes 3.3 steps on average, and on four control and robotics tasks it lowers per-decision latency by 31 to 44 percent relative to a fixed eight-step policy. Its mean reward exceeds the best fixed-depth policy on seven tasks and trails it on four. Ablations show that adaptive stopping drives most of the reward gain on PickCube and AntMaze, while value supervision drives most of it on RareEvent.
AI.conclusion: State-dependent computation allocation can match or beat fixed-depth policies at lower expected cost, and the benefit of adaptive stopping and of auxiliary supervision depends on the task.

title: Learning Biological Hierarchies in Single-Cell Foundation Models
summary: Cell types are organized by taxonomic relationships that define lineages in the so-called cell ontology. However, most existing foundation models typically ignore cell-type lineages encoded in this cell ontology. We introduce a biologically informed foundation model called scOntoFM, which embeds hierarchical cell ontology into representation learning. Using Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) distances from the ontology graph, our framework pairs efficient offline triplet sampling with hierarchical cell-ontology learning. This approach jointly preserves local neighborhoods and shapes the global embedding geometry to reflect the ontology structure. Across diverse cell- and gene-level benchmarks, the model consistently improves performance, with especially strong gains in zero-shot settings. Our model also balances batch integration with biological structure preservation, providing complementary perspectives to existing embedding evaluation frameworks and supporting scalable biological discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper presents scOntoFM, a single-cell foundation model that embeds the hierarchical cell ontology into representation learning. It reports consistent gains across cell- and gene-level benchmarks, especially in zero-shot settings.
AI.motivation: Most existing single-cell foundation models ignore the cell-type lineages encoded in the cell ontology.
AI.method: Lowest Common Ancestor distances computed on the ontology graph drive efficient offline triplet sampling. The hierarchical cell-ontology learning objective jointly preserves local neighborhoods and shapes the global embedding geometry to reflect ontology structure.
AI.result: The model consistently improves performance on diverse cell- and gene-level benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in zero-shot settings. It balances batch integration with biological structure preservation, complementing existing embedding evaluation frameworks.
AI.conclusion: Injecting ontological hierarchy into representation learning yields embeddings that are both biologically structured and useful for scalable biological discovery.

title: Representing Tensors as Compositions for Efficient Computation on Sparse and Structured Data
summary: We propose a new mathematical formalism in which all kinds of tensors and of operations on those tensors are represented as simple function compositions. Tensors are functions from indices to values. An element-wise operation (e.g. an activation function) is a composition with a function applied to values; re-indexing (e.g. reshape, transposition) is a composition with a function applied to indices; and a reduction is a composition with both an index function, mapping each index to several indices, and a reduction operation (e.g. product, sum, max). Combined with tensor stacking, these compositions can represent most interesting kinds of tensors (e.g. dense, jagged, all kinds of sparsity patterns, matrix factorizations), as well as lazy versions of almost every operation available in modern tensor computation frameworks, including einsums between tensors of any kind. Identities between compositions can then be used to rewrite such expressions into equivalent ones, without evaluating them. For instance, the product of two sparse matrices can be rewritten so that only products between non-zero values are computed, turning a sparse problem into a dense one. Using this algebra as the intermediate representation of a tensor computation engine would shift the focus from defining operations on tensors (e.g. einsum between sparse tensors) to defining an algebra on index functions. This should reduce the codebase complexity from $\mathcal{O}(mn^2)$, with $m$ the number of binary operations between tensors and $n$ the number of tensor types, to $\mathcal{O}(m + k^2)$, with $k$ the number of types of index functions. A draft implementation of a tensor computation framework based on this algebra is publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a formalism that represents tensors and tensor operations as function compositions over indices and values. It argues that this algebra can represent dense, jagged and sparse tensors and can rewrite sparse problems into dense ones, with a draft implementation publicly available.
AI.motivation: Tensor computation frameworks define each operation on each tensor type separately, so the codebase grows with the product of the number of binary operations and tensor types.
AI.method: Tensors are functions from indices to values. Element-wise operations compose with functions on values, re-indexing composes with functions on indices, and reductions compose with an index function and a reduction operation. Tensor stacking combines these compositions, and identities between compositions rewrite expressions without evaluating them.
AI.result: The abstract argues that the algebra represents dense, jagged, sparsity-patterned and factorized tensors, and lazy versions of most operations including einsums. As an example, the product of two sparse matrices can be rewritten so that only products of non-zero values are computed. The claimed codebase complexity drops from O(mn^2) to O(m + k^2), where m is the number of binary operations, n the number of tensor types and k the number of index-function types.
AI.conclusion: Using this algebra as the intermediate representation would move the design effort from per-type operations to an algebra on index functions, reducing complexity, though the abstract presents the complexity reduction as a projection rather than a measured result.

title: Self-contained Data Cleaning for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
summary: Training datasets for unsupervised anomaly detection are often assumed to be anomaly-free, but in practice, they frequently contain malicious or anomalous contamination. This contamination severely degrades the dependability and security of downstream detection models. While some contamination-robust methods exist, they rarely generalize across different model architectures and typically rely on a priori knowledge of the contamination ratio\textemdash information that is rarely available in real-world security operations. In this paper, we propose a novel, self-contained preprocessing framework for anomaly detection that identifies and removes training set contamination without relying on known contamination ratios. Our approach performs a dynamic analysis of the cosine similarity between each data point and its reconstruction during the early training stages of an auto-encoder, mapping points into a dynamic space where anomalous regions naturally exhibit lower density. By executing ``hard cleaning''\textemdash removing all identified anomalous candidates from the training pool\textemdash we systematically improve data quality. Because this cleaning occurs at the data level, the security and reliability improvements generalize seamlessly across various downstream anomaly detection architectures. Evaluating our framework across 8 distinct models and 10 security-relevant datasets, our approach achieves up to 100\% contamination reduction, yielding average improvements of 11.2\% in F1 score and 7.3\% in classification accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a self-contained preprocessing framework that removes contaminated training samples for unsupervised anomaly detection without knowing the contamination ratio. Across 8 models and 10 security-relevant datasets it reports up to 100 percent contamination reduction, with average gains of 11.2 percent in F1 and 7.3 percent in accuracy.
AI.motivation: Unsupervised anomaly detection assumes anomaly-free training data, but real datasets are often contaminated. Existing contamination-robust methods rarely generalize across architectures and usually need the contamination ratio, which is seldom known in security operations.
AI.method: During the early training of an auto-encoder, the method analyzes the cosine similarity between each data point and its reconstruction. This maps points into a dynamic space where anomalous regions show lower density. Hard cleaning then removes all identified anomalous candidates from the training pool.
AI.result: The approach achieves up to 100 percent contamination reduction across 8 models and 10 security-relevant datasets, with average improvements of 11.2 percent in F1 score and 7.3 percent in classification accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Cleaning at the data level makes the reliability gains transfer across different downstream anomaly detection architectures without extra knowledge of the contamination ratio.

title: Structurally Separated DAG Learning with Multi-Scale Normalized Closure
summary: Continuous DAG learning commonly enforces acyclicity through scalar functions of a weighted adjacency that aggregate evidence from weighted closed walks. We add a complementary layer: matrix-valued closure logits---explicit multi-hop structural relation scores for each ordered pair---supervised alongside data fit, sparsity, and a DAGMA-style barrier on the weighted adjacency. The distinction is not scalarization of the overall objective but how path evidence is represented and exposed before aggregation. SMNC (scale-normalized multi-scale closure) builds these scores on a structural gate by repeated squaring in log space and divides each scale by its path-length budget, counteracting product-style attenuation along long cycles; diagonal entries support node-wise cycle supervision and off-diagonals optional pairwise reachability cues. In the linear model, a bounded structure--magnitude factorization ties strong effective edges to strong gates; a nonlinear induced gate offers another construction with the same intent. For sufficiently strong cycles, normalized logits admit a length-independent lower bound; under a unique-active-cycle assumption, the hard final-scale readout yields a polynomial log-gate gradient factor rather than exponential product-style decay. On cue-free, unstandardized Gaussian linear and nonlinear ER benchmarks, these models improve over DAGMA, run with default hyperparameters at a reduced budget, on denser graphs and are close to it on sparse ones.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SMNC, a scale-normalized multi-scale closure that adds matrix-valued multi-hop structural relation scores to continuous DAG learning. On cue-free Gaussian linear and nonlinear ER benchmarks it improves over DAGMA on denser graphs and is close to it on sparse ones.
AI.motivation: Continuous DAG learning enforces acyclicity through scalar functions of the weighted adjacency, which aggregate closed-walk evidence. The abstract argues that path evidence is not exposed before aggregation, and that the product-style attenuation along long cycles weakens the signal.
AI.method: Matrix-valued closure logits, which are multi-hop structural relation scores for each ordered pair, are supervised alongside data fit, sparsity and a DAGMA-style barrier. SMNC builds them on a structural gate by repeated squaring in log space and divides each scale by its path-length budget. A bounded structure-magnitude factorization ties strong edges to strong gates in the linear model.
AI.result: For sufficiently strong cycles, the normalized logits admit a length-independent lower bound, and under a unique-active-cycle assumption the final-scale readout gives a polynomial rather than exponential log-gate gradient factor. On cue-free, unstandardized Gaussian linear and nonlinear ER benchmarks the models improve over DAGMA with default hyperparameters at a reduced budget, with larger gains on denser graphs.
AI.conclusion: Exposing multi-scale path evidence before aggregation and normalizing by path length gives a more robust acyclicity signal, particularly for dense graphs, at lower computational budget.

title: SWXAI: A Unified Multimodal Explainability Library for Space Weather Forecasting and Heliophysics
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at CIKM 2026 (Resource Track), Rome, Italy, November 7-11, 2026. Code: this https URL Docs: this https URL
summary: Space weather forecasting and heliophysics increasingly rely on machine learning models that process heterogeneous inputs such as multi-viewpoint multi-wavelength solar images and rasters, multivariate time series, spatial annotations, and tabular event-level data. However, explainability workflows remain fragmented across libraries, model interfaces, and output formats, limiting reuse and reproducibility. We present SWXAI, an open-source library that unifies explainable AI (XAI) workflows for image, time-series, and tabular data in space weather forecasting and heliophysics. SWXAI provides a common, extensible interface across commonly used vision, time-series, and tabular learning models, with validation, adaptation, and persistent explanation objects. It also includes domain-grounded examples, reproducible notebooks, tests, and documentation, enabling users to inspect outputs, swap models or explainers, and extend workflows to new heliophysics datasets. SWXAI reduces modality-specific engineering overhead and supports comparable, reusable explanations across heterogeneous scientific machine learning pipelines. A benchmark against direct backend implementations shows that SWXAI substantially reduces the code users write to produce an explanation, with no practical runtime cost.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SWXAI, an open-source library that unifies explainable AI workflows for image, time-series and tabular data in space weather forecasting and heliophysics. A benchmark shows it substantially reduces the code needed to produce an explanation with no practical runtime cost.
AI.motivation: Explainability workflows in space weather and heliophysics are fragmented across libraries, model interfaces and output formats, which limits reuse and reproducibility.
AI.method: The library provides a common, extensible interface across vision, time-series and tabular models, with validation, adaptation and persistent explanation objects. It also includes domain-grounded examples, reproducible notebooks, tests and documentation, so users can swap models or explainers and extend workflows to new datasets.
AI.result: A benchmark against direct backend implementations shows that SWXAI substantially reduces the code users write to produce an explanation, with no practical runtime cost.
AI.conclusion: A unified interface reduces modality-specific engineering overhead and makes explanations comparable and reusable across heterogeneous scientific machine learning pipelines.

title: Stochastic Port-Hamiltonian Gaussian Processes for Learning from Noisy Dynamics on Lie Groups
summary: Learning predictive models for dynamics is difficult because observations are often sparse and noisy, while the underlying dynamics evolve on nonlinear configuration manifolds and are affected by environmental dissipation and stochastic disturbances. Standard neural dynamics models can fit short-term trajectories but often violate physical structure, accumulate error over long horizons, or rely on parameterizations that introduce singularities such as gimbal lock. We introduce LieSPHGP, a stochastic Gaussian-process framework for learning rigid body dynamics with port-Hamiltonian structure and stability-aware robustness. LieSPHGP represents motion on Lie groups and Lie algebras, enabling coordinate-consistent optimization without singular parameterizations. Learned mass, potential energy, dissipation, and control components retain physical roles and a separate diffusion term represents stochastic forcing. Each component is modeled by Matérn kernel Gaussian processes which capture uncertainty induced by noisy observations. To improve physical validity, Lie group exponential map updates preserve rotational constraints, while positive-definite damping ensures nonnegative deterministic energy dissipation. The implicit-explicit integrator additionally provides unconditional stability for the frozen linear damping subsystem. The resulting model learns predictive dynamics that are robust to noise, respect rigid body geometry, and capture both intrinsic motion and environmental dissipation. Experiments on various noisy rigid body benchmarks show improved prediction accuracy, stronger long-horizon stability, and better satisfaction of manifold constraints compared with neural dynamics baselines. Code, data and interactive results are available on the project website: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LieSPHGP, a stochastic Gaussian-process framework that learns rigid body dynamics with port-Hamiltonian structure on Lie groups. It reports improved prediction accuracy, stronger long-horizon stability and better manifold-constraint satisfaction than neural dynamics baselines on noisy rigid body benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Learning dynamics from sparse, noisy observations is difficult. Standard neural dynamics models can violate physical structure, accumulate error over long horizons, or use singular parameterizations such as those with gimbal lock.
AI.method: Motion is represented on Lie groups and Lie algebras, with exponential-map updates that preserve rotational constraints. Learned mass, potential energy, dissipation and control components keep physical roles, a separate diffusion term models stochastic forcing, and each component is a Matérn-kernel Gaussian process. Positive-definite damping ensures nonnegative deterministic energy dissipation, and an implicit-explicit integrator gives unconditional stability for the frozen linear damping subsystem.
AI.result: Experiments on noisy rigid body benchmarks show improved prediction accuracy, stronger long-horizon stability and better satisfaction of manifold constraints than neural dynamics baselines.
AI.conclusion: Building Lie-group geometry and port-Hamiltonian structure into a Gaussian-process model yields dynamics predictions that are robust to noise, respect rigid body geometry and capture both intrinsic motion and dissipation.

title: Online Imitation Learning for Stabilizing Vlasov--Poisson Plasmas
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 43 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables
summary: We study the problem of controlling instability in the Vlasov--Poisson plasma systems, a fundamental challenge for nuclear fusion control. Motivated by the partial observability of plasma states in practice, we investigate imitation learning algorithms that learn from a fully-observable expert controller, but operate under macroscopic measurements. We theoretically establish a separation between online and offline imitation learning --- even a small behavior cloning error leads to error compounding that exponentially amplifies instability over time. By way of contrast, the online imitation learning loss can polynomially control the stability of rollout trajectories. We then propose a DAgger-style algorithm that learns the stabilizing controller under partial observability. Simulation results on a 1D Vlasov--Poisson system demonstrate that our algorithm can effectively stabilize plasma instabilities over longer time horizons than behavior cloning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a DAgger-style imitation learning algorithm that learns a stabilizing controller for Vlasov-Poisson plasma systems under partial observability. In a 1D simulation it stabilizes instabilities over longer horizons than behavior cloning.
AI.motivation: Plasma states are only partially observable in practice, but expert controllers are designed for full observability, and a small behavior cloning error can compound and amplify instability over time.
AI.method: The learner imitates a fully observable expert while operating on macroscopic measurements. The paper proposes a DAgger-style online imitation learning algorithm for this setting.
AI.result: The paper theoretically separates online from offline imitation learning: a small behavior cloning error leads to exponential error compounding, whereas the online imitation loss controls rollout stability polynomially. Simulations on a 1D Vlasov-Poisson system show the algorithm stabilizes plasma instabilities over longer time horizons than behavior cloning.
AI.conclusion: Online imitation learning is a more reliable route than offline behavior cloning for controlling fusion-relevant plasma instabilities under partial observability, at least in the 1D setting studied.

title: BRAT: Bounded Residual-Aligned Training for Stable Multi-Pass LLM Post-Training
summary: Reinforcement learning for large language model post-training often reuses each batch of sampled rollouts for several gradient passes to amortize the cost of generation. Under such multi-pass reuse, existing objectives fail in different ways: unclipped updates collapse as the policy drifts away from the sampling policy, adding a negative baseline avoids collapse but reinforces every sampled response, and PPO-style ratio clipping cuts off gradients abruptly. We first ask why reuse is fragile. Measuring how well an update estimated from a small rollout group aligns with the KL-regularized target on held-out rollouts of the same prompts, we find that this alignment drops by nearly an order of magnitude from in-sample to held-out rollouts across three base models, suggesting that repeated passes largely overfit the sampled group. Motivated by this finding, we propose Bounded Residual-Aligned Training (BRAT), motivated by a proximal update toward a bounded reweighting of the sampling policy. BRAT assigns each token a gradient weight that decreases linearly with its probability ratio and vanishes at a trust-region boundary, and normalizes group-centered rewards by their maximum magnitude, keeping advantages zero-mean and bounded without extra hyperparameters. With four reuse passes, BRAT avoids training collapse, limits policy drift, and achieves higher average accuracy with lower seed variance on most benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes BRAT, a bounded residual-aligned objective for reinforcement learning post-training of LLMs that reuses each rollout batch for several gradient passes. With four reuse passes it avoids training collapse, limits policy drift and achieves higher average accuracy with lower seed variance on most benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reusing sampled rollouts across several passes is fragile. Unclipped updates collapse as the policy drifts, a negative baseline reinforces every sampled response, and PPO-style clipping cuts gradients abruptly. The alignment between a group-based update and the KL-regularized target falls by nearly an order of magnitude from in-sample to held-out rollouts across three base models.
AI.method: Each token receives a gradient weight that decreases linearly with its probability ratio and vanishes at a trust-region boundary. Group-centered rewards are normalized by their maximum magnitude, which keeps advantages zero-mean and bounded without extra hyperparameters.
AI.result: With four reuse passes, BRAT avoids training collapse, limits policy drift and achieves higher average accuracy with lower seed variance on most benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Bounding per-token gradient weights by the probability ratio mitigates overfitting to the sampled group, making multi-pass reuse stable without extra hyperparameters.

title: Robust and Efficient Continual Model Merging via Global Singular Subspace Separation and Restoration
summary: Continual model merging incrementally integrates task-specific models without revisiting past models or data. However, repeated merging entangles past task components and distorts their singular geometry, making balanced task-wise allocation increasingly difficult. We propose Global Singular Subspace Separation and Restoration (GS3R), which augments the merged update with a compact restoration state. At each merge, GS3R restores the retained singular geometry, separates task-wise subspaces, and globally reallocates the available rank across tasks fairly. To reduce merging-time memory overhead, we further introduce Pre-merge Restoration and Flushing (PRF). Experiments on vision, NLP, and multimodal benchmarks show that GS3R provides a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GS3R, a continual model merging method that restores and separates singular subspaces of the merged update, reallocates rank fairly across tasks, and reduces merging-time memory via Pre-merge Restoration and Flushing. Experiments on vision, NLP and multimodal benchmarks show a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
AI.motivation: Repeated merging entangles past task components and distorts their singular geometry, which makes balanced task-wise allocation increasingly difficult when task-specific models are merged without revisiting past models or data.
AI.method: GS3R augments the merged update with a compact restoration state. At each merge it restores the retained singular geometry, separates task-wise subspaces and globally reallocates the available rank across tasks. Pre-merge Restoration and Flushing (PRF) reduces merging-time memory overhead.
AI.result: Experiments on vision, NLP and multimodal benchmarks show that GS3R provides a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Restoring singular geometry and fairly reallocating rank at each merge is a practical way to keep continual merging accurate and memory-efficient.

title: Optimal Byzantine-resilient Federated Learning with User-level Differential Privacy
summary: Real-world deployment of federated learning (FL) requires resilience against adversarial clients and data privacy. Byzantine fault captures the worst-case behavior of adversarial clients, while differential privacy (DP) provides statistical guarantees against privacy loss. In particular, user-level DP guards a client's entire contribution and provides more realistic protection against information leakage. Despite intensive efforts, the minimax-optimal convergence bound of Byzantine-resilient FL with user-level DP remains open. We establish an information-theoretic lower bound for any Byzantine-resilient empirical risk minimization problem under user-level DP and heterogeneous clients. We propose ByzULDP, a central DP algorithm featuring a two-level momentum across the client and server. Client-side momentum mitigates stochastic gradient variance during robust aggregation. Unlike the fault-free case, naively combining non-linear Byzantine-resilient aggregation with central DP noise can be insufficient to guarantee convergence to a bounded neighborhood of a stationary point. Our key contribution is a server-side momentum that leverages a property specific to user-level DP, where privacy sensitivity depends on how client updates are constructed, to empower convergence. ByzULDP achieves the order-optimal convergence bound for strongly-convex objectives, with vanishing error terms decaying at the optimal $O(1/T)$ and $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ rates for strongly-convex and non-convex objectives, respectively. We corroborate our analysis with numerical experiments on real-world datasets across diverse privacy budgets.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an information-theoretic lower bound for Byzantine-resilient empirical risk minimization under user-level differential privacy and proposes ByzULDP, which achieves the order-optimal convergence bound for strongly convex objectives. The bound is also met for non-convex objectives at the O(1/sqrt(T)) rate.
AI.motivation: The minimax-optimal convergence bound for Byzantine-resilient federated learning with user-level DP was open. Naively combining non-linear robust aggregation with central DP noise can fail to guarantee convergence to a bounded neighborhood of a stationary point.
AI.method: ByzULDP is a central DP algorithm with two-level momentum across clients and server. Client-side momentum reduces stochastic gradient variance during robust aggregation. The key contribution is a server-side momentum that exploits the property that user-level privacy sensitivity depends on how client updates are constructed.
AI.result: ByzULDP achieves the order-optimal convergence bound for strongly convex objectives, with vanishing error terms decaying at O(1/T) for strongly convex and O(1/sqrt(T)) for non-convex objectives. Numerical experiments on real-world datasets across diverse privacy budgets corroborate the analysis.
AI.conclusion: Combining a matching lower bound with a server-side momentum tailored to user-level DP closes the optimality gap for Byzantine-resilient private federated learning.

title: CoupledFlow: One-Step Neural Operators for Coupled Multi-Physics PDEs
summary: This paper introduces COUPLED FLOW, a new neural operator learning framework for multi-physics PDE systems that captures the co-evolution of multiple physical processes by modeling their cross-process interactions. Unlike existing neural operator methods that primarily target single-physics settings, COUPLED FLOW employs a novel structure-constrained flow matching algorithm to learn process- specific mean velocity fields conditioned on the full multi-physics state. This enables fast and accurate one-step prediction of coupled PDE systems that would otherwise require expensive numerical simulations. A key challenge in training COUPLED FLOW however lies in sampling structure-constrained conditional flow interpolants that capture cross-process correlations and serve as training examples for flow matching. To address this challenge, we derive a multi-physics mean-flow consistency identity that characterizes cross-process interactions and defines the structure-constrained mean-flow matching loss. To provide informative training samples for flow matching with this loss, we develop a principled method for sampling correlated conditional interpolants based on posterior multi-output Gaus- sian processes, which capture richer cross-process correlations than the commonly used endpoint-conditioned linear interpolants. We also establish a theoretical re- sult showing that the Wasserstein-2 distance between the predicted and oracle PDE solution distributions is upper-bounded in terms of the structure-constrained flow matching loss and the smoothness of the learned flow. Experiments across diverse coupled PDE benchmarks demonstrate that COUPLED FLOW consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art neural operators and generative PDE solvers.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CoupledFlow, a one-step neural operator for multi-physics PDE systems that models cross-process interactions through structure-constrained flow matching. It reports consistent gains over existing neural operators and generative PDE solvers on coupled PDE benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing neural operators mainly target single-physics settings and do not capture the co-evolution of coupled physical processes. Training is also difficult because standard endpoint-conditioned linear interpolants miss cross-process correlations.
AI.method: CoupledFlow learns process-specific mean velocity fields conditioned on the full multi-physics state, using a multi-physics mean-flow consistency identity that defines a structure-constrained mean-flow matching loss. Correlated conditional interpolants are sampled from posterior multi-output Gaussian processes to provide informative training samples.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse coupled PDE benchmarks show that CoupledFlow consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art neural operators and generative PDE solvers. The paper also bounds the Wasserstein-2 distance between predicted and oracle solution distributions in terms of the structure-constrained flow matching loss and the smoothness of the learned flow.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing cross-process structure in flow matching and sampling correlated interpolants gives fast, accurate one-step prediction for coupled PDEs that otherwise need costly simulation.

title: Interpretable Cyber-Physical Attack Detection in Smart Grids: A Leakage-Controlled Multi-Testbed Evaluation of Fusion, Robustness, and Observability Limits
summary: Cyber-physical smart-grid detectors are typically treated as black boxes and validated exclusively on clean, temporally shuffled datasets, which risk overly optimistic performance claims. This work presents a multi-testbed evaluation study built around an interpretable, time-windowed fusion Random Forest, adopting the pessimistic result whenever evaluation protocols disagree. (i) On a public paired cyber-physical dataset, shuffled cross-validation is optimistic: macro-F1 falls from 0.96 to 0.88 +/- 0.06 under rolling-origin temporal evaluation. A topology-free graph convolutional network (GCN) serving as a control confirms that this lightweight model is competitive on these splits. (ii) The adaptive and adaptive-joint feature-space attacks, which are infeasible as realistic grid manipulations, degrade macro-F1 to 0.67 and 0.34, respectively. Adversarial training and randomized smoothing partially restore performance, and a physics-constrained evolution-strategy evasion on the IEEE 14-Bus testbed shows the same vulnerability pattern. (iii) On real IEC-104 traffic, the cyber view reliably catches structural attacks (recall of 0.87 to 0.98) but largely fails on semantic value manipulation (recall of 0.11 to 0.35). An observability taxonomy on the IEEE 14-Bus system reveals that stealthy false data injection defeats all three observation views. (iv) On a full AC weighted least-squares state-estimation testbed, a forecasting-aided temporal test is evaded by slow ramps precisely where a rate-invariant physics-manifold test sustains detection at a common 5% false-alarm target. A full end-to-end evaluation on IEEE 118-Bus confirms the ordering but bounds its strength: the manifold test detects every trial down to 0.05 degree/step and 0.48 at 0.02 degree/step, against 0.14 for the temporal test. All code and benchmarks are released.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates an interpretable time-windowed fusion Random Forest for smart-grid cyber-physical attack detection across several testbeds and finds that common validation practices are optimistic. Macro-F1 falls from 0.96 to 0.88 under temporal evaluation, and the detectors are weak against semantic value manipulation and some stealthy attacks.
AI.motivation: Cyber-physical smart-grid detectors are often treated as black boxes and validated only on clean, temporally shuffled datasets, which risks overly optimistic claims.
AI.method: The study uses a time-windowed fusion Random Forest, a topology-free graph convolutional network as a control, adversarial training and randomized smoothing, physics-constrained evolution-strategy evasion on the IEEE 14-Bus testbed, an observability taxonomy, and a physics-manifold test for state estimation. It adopts the pessimistic result whenever protocols disagree.
AI.result: On a public paired dataset, macro-F1 falls from 0.96 under shuffled cross-validation to 0.88 plus or minus 0.06 under rolling-origin temporal evaluation. Adaptive feature-space attacks reduce macro-F1 to 0.67 and 0.34. On real IEC-104 traffic, recall is 0.87 to 0.98 for structural attacks and 0.11 to 0.35 for semantic value manipulation. A physics-manifold test detects slow-ramp attacks that evade a forecasting-aided temporal test, at 0.48 versus 0.14 on IEEE 118-Bus at 0.02 degree per step.
AI.conclusion: Leakage-controlled, multi-testbed evaluation reveals that reported detector performance is optimistic and that rate-invariant physics-based checks can detect attacks that temporal tests miss, though semantic manipulation and stealthy false data injection remain hard to observe.

title: An Analysis of Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation
comment: This version of the paper corrects the one that was presented at the 25th International Conference on Machine Learning. We corrected condition (7) of Theorem 1 and its proof, as well as the importance-sampling update (11).
