We also made the assumptions of Theorems 1 and 2 more precise and revised the proof of Theorem 2, adding an appendix with the auxiliary results it uses
summary: We address the problem of computing the optimal Q-function in Markov decision problems with infinite state-space. We analyze the convergence properties of several variations of Q-learning when combined with function approximation, extending the analysis of TD-learning in Tsitsiklis and Van Roy (1996) to stochastic control settings. We identify conditions under which such approximate methods converge with probability 1. We conclude with a brief discussion on the general applicability of our results and compare them with several related works.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the convergence of several Q-learning variants combined with function approximation in Markov decision problems with infinite state spaces. It identifies conditions under which these methods converge with probability 1.
AI.motivation: The optimal Q-function must be computed in infinite state spaces, where function approximation is needed, and the convergence of approximate Q-learning in stochastic control settings requires analysis.
AI.method: The analysis extends the TD-learning convergence results of Tsitsiklis and Van Roy (1996) to several variations of Q-learning with function approximation.
AI.result: The paper identifies conditions under which these approximate methods converge with probability 1, and compares its results with several related works.
AI.conclusion: The results give a convergence guarantee for approximate Q-learning in stochastic control under the stated conditions, and the abstract notes that their general applicability is briefly discussed.

title: Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning
summary: Learning accurate off-policy state-action value functions (Q-functions) from offline datasets becomes harder as the task horizon grows. One-step temporal-difference (TD) learning bootstraps after every transition, so small per-step errors accumulate along the horizon, and early states can be badly misvalued even when the TD loss is small. Multi-step TD shortens this chain by following the dataset trajectory for several steps; however, since the behavior policy is often suboptimal, every followed action adds a bias, and no fixed number of steps suits a whole trajectory. In this paper, we propose Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL), a simple method that enables accurate long-horizon value learning by automatically balancing between one-step and multi-step returns. HQL extends a target through a dataset action only when the critic values it at least as highly as the best-of-N actions sampled from the BC policy, and otherwise falls back to a one-step target. We show that this rule is a principled off-policy correction that needs no action densities, which makes HQL compatible with expressive flow and diffusion policies. Experiments show that HQL avoids the failures of both one-step and multi-step TD on a combination-lock task across horizons, and outperforms prior horizon-reduction methods on long-horizon OGBench and OCBench tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL), which balances one-step and multi-step returns for off-policy value learning from offline data. It avoids the failures of both one-step and multi-step TD on a combination-lock task and outperforms prior horizon-reduction methods on long-horizon OGBench and OCBench tasks.
AI.motivation: One-step TD errors accumulate over long horizons, while multi-step TD adds bias when the behavior policy is suboptimal, and no fixed number of steps suits a whole trajectory.
AI.method: HQL extends a target through a dataset action only when the critic values that action at least as highly as the best of N actions sampled from the BC policy, and otherwise falls back to a one-step target. The rule is a principled off-policy correction that needs no action densities, so it is compatible with flow and diffusion policies.
AI.result: On a combination-lock task across horizons, HQL avoids the failures of both one-step and multi-step TD. It outperforms prior horizon-reduction methods on long-horizon OGBench and OCBench tasks.
AI.conclusion: A simple, density-free rule that adaptively chooses between one-step and multi-step targets enables more accurate long-horizon value learning and works with expressive generative policies.

title: Hydro-Dataset: A Multi-Modal Open-Source Pipeline for Nordic Hydrological Research and Foundation Model Benchmarking
comment: Accepted for presentation at ICIP Workshop 2026 and to be published as part of the conference proceedings
summary: Despite world-class snow monitoring by the Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute (SMHI) and Finnish Meteorological Institute (FMI), no station-anchored, multi-parameter snow benchmark dataset exists for the Nordic boreal domain. We present Hydro-Dataset v1.1, a reproducible open-source pipeline that harmonizes 582 SMHI meteorological observation stations across nine hydrological winters (2015/16-2023/24) into a CF-1.9 NetCDF product with 1.8~million annotated station-days. Six derived snow parameters, such as Snow Water Equivalent (SWE), snow phenology, melt rates, degree-day melt factor, rain-on-snow flags, and freeze-thaw cycles, supply benchmark-ready labels for hydrological foundation model training. ERA5-Land cross-validation (Pearson R=0.78, bias=-262mm) confirms observation-anchored SWE provides a more reliable benchmark than reanalysis for machine learning training.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Hydro-Dataset v1.1, an open-source pipeline that harmonizes 582 SMHI meteorological stations over nine hydrological winters into a CF-1.9 NetCDF benchmark of snow parameters. It finds that observation-anchored SWE is a more reliable benchmark than ERA5-Land reanalysis.
AI.motivation: No station-anchored, multi-parameter snow benchmark dataset exists for the Nordic boreal domain, despite strong snow monitoring by SMHI and FMI.
AI.method: A reproducible open-source pipeline harmonizes observations from 582 SMHI stations across the 2015/16 to 2023/24 winters into a CF-1.9 NetCDF product with 1.8 million annotated station-days. Six derived snow parameters, including SWE, snow phenology, melt rates, degree-day melt factor, rain-on-snow flags and freeze-thaw cycles, supply benchmark labels.
AI.result: ERA5-Land cross-validation gives Pearson R of 0.78 and bias of -262 mm, which the paper uses to argue that observation-anchored SWE is a more reliable benchmark than reanalysis for machine learning training.
AI.conclusion: The dataset provides benchmark-ready labels for training and evaluating hydrological foundation models in the Nordic boreal domain, with observations preferred over reanalysis as the reference.

title: DPDP: Diffusion Policy-Steered Diffusion Planner for Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: In offline reinforcement learning, diffusion models fill two roles with complementary strengths. Typically guided by a critic, a diffusion policy is value-aware and favors high-return, behavior-supported actions, but it is short-sighted: it never lays out the states it intends to visit. A diffusion planner is far-sighted, synthesizing such a long-horizon trajectory, but it is only behavior-driven at execution, realizing each planned transition using only offline this http URL is strong exactly where the other is weak. We introduce DPDP to bring them together at the planner's execution step, where a planned transition becomes an action. Reading the planner's inverse-dynamics executor as a posterior over actions: the environment's transition likelihood relates an action to the planned next state, while the behavioral prior determines its weight under the offline data. Replacing this prior with a value-optimized diffusion policy preserves the planned transition likelihood and favors valuable actions that can serve the plan. We target the resulting clean-action distribution in two ways. A training-free sampler composes policy and inverse-dynamics scores at matched action noise levels and applies Langevin correction; this route uses a shared action noise schedule and an approximately common terminal prior. A preference objective instead amortizes the transfer into a single diffusion executor. Across D4RL, DPDP improves the planner it builds on, staying competitive with reactive diffusion policies on locomotion and leading on long-horizon navigation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DPDP, which combines a value-optimized diffusion policy with a diffusion planner in offline RL by treating the planner's inverse-dynamics executor as a posterior over actions. Across D4RL it improves the planner it builds on, staying competitive on locomotion and leading on long-horizon navigation.
AI.motivation: Diffusion policies are value-aware but short-sighted, while diffusion planners are far-sighted but behavior-driven at execution, so each is strong where the other is weak.
AI.method: At the planner's execution step, DPDP replaces the behavioral prior in the inverse-dynamics posterior with a value-optimized diffusion policy, which preserves the planned transition likelihood and favors valuable actions. Two routes realize this: a training-free sampler that composes policy and inverse-dynamics scores with Langevin correction, and a preference objective that amortizes the transfer into one diffusion executor.
AI.result: Across D4RL, DPDP improves the planner it builds on, stays competitive with reactive diffusion policies on locomotion and leads on long-horizon navigation.
AI.conclusion: Combining the far-sighted planner with a value-aware policy at the action-selection step yields a better offline RL executor, with the training-free and amortized routes offering two ways to implement it.

title: Differentiable Agent-Based Modeling for Multi-Echelon Supply Chains: Gradient-Based Optimization of Heterogeneous Policies at Scale
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 2026 Annual Modeling and Simulation Conference
summary: Global supply chains rely on the interactions of thousands of heterogeneous agents, posing significant challenges for optimization. While traditional optimization often assumes homogeneity to ensure tractability, Reinforcement Learning struggles with sample inefficiency when scaling to high-dimensional state spaces. We propose a Differentiable Agent-Based Model for multi-echelon inventory management. By implementing stochastic dynamics via differentiable tensor operations, we enable direct gradient propagation through the simulation. We validate the framework by recovering theoretical Newsvendor optima without supervision. Crucially, we demonstrate ``Mass Personalization'' by optimizing 10,000 distinct agent policies simultaneously in seconds, achieving a 53% cost reduction compared to scalar baselines. Furthermore, we utilize gradient sensitivity analysis to generate causal heatmaps, accurately recovering inherent lead-time delays from the computation graph. This approach bridges the gap between simulation and optimization, enabling the efficient training of self-correcting Digital Twins.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a differentiable agent-based model of multi-echelon inventory management that propagates gradients through the simulation. It recovers Newsvendor optima without supervision and optimizes 10,000 distinct agent policies at once, reporting a 53 percent cost reduction against scalar baselines.
AI.motivation: Global supply chains involve thousands of heterogeneous agents. Traditional optimization assumes homogeneity for tractability, and reinforcement learning is sample-inefficient in high-dimensional state spaces.
AI.method: Stochastic dynamics are implemented with differentiable tensor operations, which enables direct gradient propagation through the simulation. Gradient sensitivity analysis generates causal heatmaps from the computation graph.
AI.result: The framework recovers theoretical Newsvendor optima without supervision. It optimizes 10,000 distinct agent policies simultaneously in seconds, achieving a 53 percent cost reduction compared with scalar baselines, and the heatmaps recover inherent lead-time delays.
AI.conclusion: Differentiable simulation makes heterogeneous per-agent policy optimization tractable at scale and supports self-correcting digital twins of supply chains.

title: GradReason: LLMs as Meta-Learners that Replace Training Epochs with Training-Data-Free Weight Updates
summary: Standard training recipes make a fixed number of passes over the training data, even when an epoch mostly adds mini-batch noise. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that reads the weight and gradient history of a run can replace some of these epochs with updates that compute no gradient and read no training image. In GradReason, an LLM agent is called every ten epochs. In a restricted sandbox, it analyses recent weight snapshots, epoch-mean gradients, and validation metrics, then submits a Python program that computes new weights and a plan marking each of the next ten epochs as data or virtual. A virtual epoch is kept only if it passes a forward-only check on 5,000 held-out validation images. In 120 runs on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with three architectures, Claude Opus 5.5 used 32.8% fewer data epochs than the 80-epoch recipe at 0.31 percentage points lower test accuracy (95% CI -0.72 to +0.09; 0.94 points on ResNet-18), on the recipe's own frontier of data against accuracy. Unprompted, Opus averaged recent weight snapshots in every run. This choice produced the savings: a fixed rule with the same acceptance check but extrapolations from prior work saved 5.4% of the data epochs, and the same rule with averaging added saved 25.0%. The LLM's contribution is to find a working update within a single run; once found, a fixed rule implements it equally well. An Opus run cost 0.68 USD, but at this scale the agent's latency exceeded the GPU time it saved.

AI.tldr: GradReason replaces some training epochs with updates written by an LLM agent that computes no gradient and reads no training images, cutting data epochs by 32.8% at a 0.31 percentage point accuracy cost on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.
AI.motivation: Standard recipes make a fixed number of full passes over the data, even though later epochs mostly add mini-batch noise, and it is unknown whether an LLM reading the weight and gradient history can substitute for some of them.
AI.method: Every ten epochs an LLM agent in a restricted sandbox analyses recent weight snapshots, epoch-mean gradients and validation metrics, then submits a Python program that computes new weights and a plan marking each of the next ten epochs as data or virtual; a virtual epoch is kept only if it passes a forward-only check on 5,000 held-out validation images.
AI.result: In 120 runs on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with three architectures, Claude Opus 5.5 used 32.8% fewer data epochs than the 80-epoch recipe at 0.31 points lower test accuracy (95% CI -0.72 to +0.09; 0.94 points on ResNet-18); unprompted, Opus averaged recent weight snapshots in every run, and a fixed rule with the same check and averaging saved 25.0% of data epochs versus 5.4% for a fixed rule with extrapolation alone.
AI.conclusion: The LLM's value lies in finding a working update within a single run, after which a fixed rule implements it equally well; at this scale an Opus run cost 0.68 USD and its latency exceeded the GPU time saved.

title: PIA: Agentic Physics-Informed Runtime Anomaly Detection
summary: Runtime anomaly detectors for cyber-physical systems are either learned as black boxes from normal data, which miss stealthy manipulations that keep every signal inside its normal range, or derived by hand from physical models, which requires expert effort for every plant. We introduce physicsinformed agents (PIA), in which a large language model agent writes the detector itself as a set of physical residuals, such as pump characteristics, tank mass balances, and controller logic, and refines every candidate against normal operating data through an evaluation workbench before deployment. The result is a compact, human-readable detector that runs in milliseconds and names the component behind each alarm. On the BATADAL water distribution attack benchmark, PIA with Claude Opus 5.5 reaches an F1 of 0.878 on the test attacks against 0.504 for the strongest of six statistical and deep baselines, keeps detecting attacks concealed by replayed and offset sensor readings, and attributes every detected test attack to the attacked component. Ablations show that testing hypotheses against data is decisive: agents that write residuals from the plant description alone lose up to 0.28 F1, whereas agents that see only anonymized signals recover most of the physical structure.

AI.tldr: PIA has an LLM agent write a runtime anomaly detector for cyber-physical systems as a set of physical residuals, refined against normal operating data, and reaches an F1 of 0.878 on the BATADAL water distribution attack benchmark.
AI.motivation: Learned black-box detectors miss stealthy manipulations that keep every signal in its normal range, while hand-derived physics-based detectors require expert effort for every plant.
AI.method: A large language model agent writes the detector as physical residuals such as pump characteristics, tank mass balances and controller logic, and tests every candidate against normal operating data in an evaluation workbench before deployment, yielding a compact detector that runs in milliseconds and names the responsible component.
AI.result: With Claude Opus 5.5, PIA reaches an F1 of 0.878 on BATADAL test attacks against 0.504 for the strongest of six statistical and deep baselines, keeps detecting attacks concealed by replayed and offset sensor readings, and attributes every detected test attack to the attacked component; agents writing residuals from the plant description alone lose up to 0.28 F1.
AI.conclusion: Testing hypotheses against data is decisive, and the approach yields a human-readable, component-attributing detector without per-plant expert derivation.

title: Learning Actionable Information Landscapes for Multimodal Active Sensing in Hawkmoths
summary: Animals integrate information across sensory modalities to guide exploration, suggesting that they maintain internal estimates of where actions are expected to reduce uncertainty. However, how such action-conditioned information maps are learned from multimodal sensory experience remains unclear, as previous studies have been largely confined to unimodal sensing frameworks. We introduce a multimodal predictive-coding framework for learning uncertainty-reduction maps from visual and mechanosensory observations in hawkmoth flower interaction tasks. A variational generative model trained on simulated environments recovers modality-specific information landscapes over the action space, capturing how visual patterns, surface geometry, and mechanosensory cues shape the value of exploratory actions. These learned maps are consistent with several features of hawkmoth behavior, including nonzero tracking offsets, probing along visual patterns, and geometry-dependent exploration. Applying the model to behavioral data from flower tracking and nectary search, we find that natural trajectories tend to occupy regions of high uncertainty reduction in these learned maps. Building on these observations, we develop an uncertainty-gated lexicographic algorithm that switches between information gathering and reward exploitation based on perceptual uncertainty. In nectary search, uncertainty gating improves learning relative to exploit-only, $\epsilon$-greedy, fixed-time, and uncertainty-calibrated non-lexicographic controls, with better generalization and robustness to sensory and curvature shifts. These results link information landscapes learned through generative modeling to biological sensing and embodied exploration.

AI.tldr: The paper learns action-conditioned uncertainty-reduction maps from visual and mechanosensory observations in hawkmoth flower interaction and uses them in an uncertainty-gated algorithm that improves nectary search.
AI.motivation: Animals are thought to integrate multimodal sensory information to decide where to act, but how such action-conditioned information maps are learned from multimodal experience is unclear, since prior studies were largely unimodal.
AI.method: A multimodal predictive-coding framework trains a variational generative model on simulated environments to recover modality-specific information landscapes over the action space, and an uncertainty-gated lexicographic algorithm switches between information gathering and reward exploitation based on perceptual uncertainty.
AI.result: The learned maps match hawkmoth behaviour features such as nonzero tracking offsets, probing along visual patterns and geometry-dependent exploration, and natural trajectories lie in high uncertainty-reduction regions; in nectary search, uncertainty gating improves learning over exploit-only, epsilon-greedy, fixed-time and uncertainty-calibrated non-lexicographic controls, with better generalization and robustness to sensory and curvature shifts.
AI.conclusion: The results link information landscapes learned by generative modelling to biological sensing and embodied exploration.

title: ProtLink: Sequence and Multispecies Graph Context for Protein Interaction Prediction
comment: Submitted to AI for Scientific Research at AAAI 2027
summary: Predicting protein-protein interactions (PPIs) from sequence alone is difficult, while known interaction networks may provide informative biological context. We introduce ProtLink, a sequence-conditioned graph-learning framework that combines frozen ESM-2 representations with protein interaction topology and orthogroup-mediated connections between species. We compare sequence-only models, GraphSAGE, a homogeneous graph transformer, and a heterogeneous graph transformer (HGT) for human PPI prediction. In an initial edge-level comparison, three-layer multispecies HGT with ESM-2 650M features achieves an average precision (AP) of 0.980 under random negative sampling, compared with 0.951 for the homogeneous transformer; its AP decreases to 0.878 with two-hop-preferred negatives. In controlled three-seed experiments, three-layer full-graph HGT obtains an AP of $0.9701\pm0.0022$, exceeding an orthogroup-only model ($0.9435\pm0.0094$). The corresponding two-layer comparison shows little additional benefit from non-human PPI edges, consistent with the greater message-passing depth needed to transmit their information. For human proteins excluded from training interactions, multispecies HGT achieves $0.8335\pm0.0094$ AP versus $0.6482\pm0.0052$ for a sequence-only pair model. These results identify the value, depth dependence, and limits of evolutionary graph context while distinguishing prediction of held-out edges from generalization to held-out proteins.

AI.tldr: ProtLink combines frozen ESM-2 sequence features with protein interaction topology and orthogroup-mediated cross-species connections in a graph transformer, reaching an average precision of 0.970 for human protein-protein interaction prediction.
AI.motivation: Predicting protein-protein interactions from sequence alone is difficult, while known interaction networks and evolutionary context may supply useful biological information, whose depth dependence and limits are not well characterised.
AI.method: The authors compare sequence-only models, GraphSAGE, a homogeneous graph transformer and a heterogeneous graph transformer (HGT) built on frozen ESM-2 representations, multispecies graphs and orthogroup connections.
AI.result: Three-layer full-graph HGT obtains an AP of 0.9701 plus or minus 0.0022 over three seeds, exceeding an orthogroup-only model (0.9435 plus or minus 0.0094); with two-hop-preferred negatives AP falls to 0.878, and for human proteins excluded from training interactions multispecies HGT reaches 0.8335 plus or minus 0.0094 versus 0.6482 for a sequence-only pair model; non-human edges add little at two layers.
AI.conclusion: Evolutionary graph context is valuable but depends on message-passing depth, and the results separate prediction of held-out edges from generalization to held-out proteins.

title: Unified Factored Representations Resist Catastrophic Forgetting
summary: This paper explores an unexpected connection between the quality of a neural network's (NN's) internal representation and its vulnerability to catastrophic forgetting. The representational forgetting hypothesis is that networks with unified, factored representation (UFR) can resist catastrophic forgetting without any modification to the underlying fine-tuning algorithm or network architecture. The key insight is that catastrophic forgetting may largely result from fractured entangled representation (FER): fine-tuning on only part of the input domain results in disruptive changes for other input patterns, because of how individual features are globally entangled. In contrast, if a gradient update is compatible with how a UFR network factors its representation, such an update may result in coordinated change across the input domain, alleviating catastrophic forgetting. Experiments in two domains provide evidence for this hypothesis: (1) an illustrative 1D regression task, in which UFR networks constructed by hand are compared against networks trained from scratch with SGD, and (2) an image-regression task with NNs previously shown to exhibit UFR. In both settings, UFR networks forget substantially less than their FER counterparts when repeatedly fine-tuned on UFR-compatible variations. Further experiments show that a training loss that distills UFR representations into fresh NNs reduces forgetting; along with several additional controls, these results help isolate representation as the critical factor. Together these results suggest that representational quality is an underappreciated contributor to catastrophic forgetting, and that the encouragement and maintenance of such quality may require attending to what patterns a particular NN is ready to learn.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that networks with unified, factored representations resist catastrophic forgetting without any change to the fine-tuning algorithm or architecture, and reports supporting experiments on a 1D regression task and an image-regression task.
AI.motivation: Catastrophic forgetting may largely arise from fractured entangled representations, in which fine-tuning on part of the input domain disrupts other inputs, but the role of representation quality in forgetting has not been isolated.
AI.method: The authors hand-construct unified factored representation (UFR) networks for a 1D regression task and compare them with networks trained from scratch with SGD, use image-regression networks previously shown to exhibit UFR, and add a training loss that distils UFR representations into fresh networks along with several controls.
AI.result: In both settings UFR networks forget substantially less than fractured entangled representation (FER) counterparts when repeatedly fine-tuned on UFR-compatible variations, and the distillation loss reduces forgetting.
AI.conclusion: Representational quality is an underappreciated contributor to catastrophic forgetting, and maintaining it may require attending to which patterns a network is ready to learn.

title: Where Should Models Run? A Collaborative Inference Framework for Embodied Intelligence in 6G
summary: Embodied intelligence systems rely on fast and reliable inference to enable real-time perception, reasoning, and control. Recent advances in large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) models, including Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, have significantly enhanced the capabilities of embodied agents in complex environments. However, deploying these models remains challenging due to the limited computational resources and energy budgets of robotic platforms. A fundamental question is where inference should be executed. Collaborative inference, which partitions models across end devices, edge servers, and the cloud, has emerged as a promising solution. Yet determining the optimal partitioning point remains an open problem, as it depends on wireless network conditions, model structure, and privacy requirements. This article reviews the state of the art in collaborative inference for embodied intelligence and proposes an edge-centric framework in which the edge coordinates model partitioning and execution. Through both simulation and real-world experiments over WiFi and 5G networks, we demonstrate that the optimal partitioning strategy varies with network conditions and model structure. We further identify latency-minimizing partition points for ResNet-101, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and OpenVLA-7B in collaborative inference between NVIDIA Jetson Nano or AGX Xavier devices and an AGX Thor edge server under varying wireless conditions. Finally, we discuss the future directions for collaborative inference in 6G-empowered embodied intelligence systems.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews collaborative inference for embodied intelligence and proposes an edge-centric framework in which the edge server chooses model partition points, showing that the optimal split depends on wireless conditions and model structure.
AI.motivation: Running large LLMs and vision-language-action models on resource-limited robots is hard, and the best place to execute inference across end devices, edge servers and the cloud depends on network conditions, model structure and privacy requirements that remain an open problem.
AI.method: An edge-centric framework lets the edge coordinate model partitioning and execution, evaluated through simulation and real-world experiments over WiFi and 5G with Jetson Nano or AGX Xavier devices and an AGX Thor edge server.
AI.result: The latency-minimizing partition points vary with network conditions and model structure for ResNet-101, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and OpenVLA-7B across the tested wireless conditions.
AI.conclusion: Partition choice must adapt to network and model, and the paper outlines future directions for collaborative inference in 6G-enabled embodied intelligence.

title: Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping for Token-Efficient LLM Reasoning
summary: Extended reasoning can help language models solve complex problems, but long responses often contain both useful computations and redundant checks. Conventional length penalties encourage shorter responses without distinguishing the functions of intermediate steps. We propose Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping (PCRS), a framework that combines phase identification with training-time reward allocation. We investigate two classification routes: PCRS-H with a hidden-state classifier and PCRS-T with a frozen text classifier. Our main text classifier implementation assigns overlapping reasoning, execution, and revision labels to native chunks, then uses these labels and exact repetition to adjust existing token penalties. We compare the completed configurations on six mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks and examine four reward-weight settings with the text classifier. Compared with a baseline using token-level length penalties, the default text classifier configuration reduces mean response length by 3.13%; sampled Pass@1 is approximately 62.07% for both methods, while oracle Pass@16 rises from 86.08% to 87.67%. These results show how phase-informed penalty allocation can reduce output volume and improve multi-attempt coverage without inference-time classification.

AI.tldr: PCRS shapes token penalties according to the phase of each reasoning chunk, classified by a frozen text classifier, and reduces mean response length by 3.13% on six math and science benchmarks without changing sampled Pass@1.
AI.motivation: Length penalties shorten reasoning uniformly and do not distinguish useful computation from redundant checks, so they cannot target the parts of a response that add no value.
AI.method: Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping (PCRS) combines phase identification with training-time reward allocation, using either a hidden-state classifier (PCRS-H) or a frozen text classifier (PCRS-T) that assigns overlapping reasoning, execution and revision labels to native chunks and adjusts existing token penalties with exact repetition.
AI.result: Compared with a token-level length penalty baseline, the default text classifier configuration reduces mean response length by 3.13%, sampled Pass@1 is about 62.07% for both methods, and oracle Pass@16 rises from 86.08% to 87.67%; four reward-weight settings were examined.
AI.conclusion: Phase-informed penalty allocation can reduce output volume and improve multi-attempt coverage without inference-time classification.

title: Hybrid Product Search Without the Copy: Lexical, Semantic and Filtered Retrieval Served Directly from a Data Lake
comment: 6 pages. Submitted to ISIR-eCom 2026 (workshop at IEEE BigData 2026)
summary: E-commerce catalogs increasingly live in lakehouse tables: Apache Iceberg metadata over Parquet files in object storage. Product search, however, still runs on copies of that catalog, in a lexical engine and a vector database, each with its own ingestion pipeline, schema, staleness window and bill. We show that search applications can be hosted directly on the data lake, with the lakehouse table as the single system of record. We extend Apache Pinot, a real-time OLAP engine that already serves Iceberg tables in place, with BM25 relevance scoring over its Lucene text index, corpus-wide term statistics so that scores are comparable across files, and reciprocal rank fusion in plain SQL; a real-time table fed by a stream can sit behind the same table, merged by the broker. On the Amazon ESCI benchmark (1.2M US products, 22,458 test queries), hybrid search served from the lake matches exact retrieval (nDCG@10 .361). The lake table is queryable 149 s after its files are registered, and a lake commit is searchable in 3.8 s, close to indexing directly into a search engine. On a brand-sorted lake of 277M products (0.8 TB), one 16-vCPU node answers brand-scoped vector, BM25 and client-fused hybrid searches in 6.5-9 ms (p50), sustains 1,100 vector and 635 BM25 searches per second at under 180 ms p99, and makes a commit searchable in 4.3 s. Search adds only its indexes: no copy of the catalog, no sync pipeline and no second schema, which cuts storage, rebuild time and the operational work of keeping copies consistent.

AI.tldr: The paper serves hybrid product search directly from an Apache Iceberg lakehouse table by extending Apache Pinot with BM25, corpus-wide statistics and SQL reciprocal rank fusion, removing the need for a separate search copy of the catalog.
AI.motivation: Product search runs on copies of the catalog in a lexical engine and a vector database, each with its own ingestion pipeline, schema, staleness window and cost, although the lakehouse table could be the single system of record.
AI.method: The authors extend Apache Pinot, a real-time OLAP engine that already serves Iceberg tables in place, with BM25 scoring over its Lucene text index, corpus-wide term statistics so scores are comparable across files, and reciprocal rank fusion expressed in plain SQL, with an optional real-time stream table merged by the broker.
AI.result: On the Amazon ESCI benchmark (1.2M US products, 22,458 test queries), lake-served hybrid search matches exact retrieval (nDCG@10 0.361); a lake table is queryable 149 s after file registration and a commit is searchable in 3.8 s; on a 277M-product, 0.8 TB brand-sorted lake, one 16-vCPU node answers brand-scoped searches in 6.5 to 9 ms p50, sustains 1,100 vector and 635 BM25 searches per second under 180 ms p99, and makes a commit searchable in 4.3 s.
AI.conclusion: Search needs only its own indexes, with no catalog copy, sync pipeline or second schema, which reduces storage, rebuild time and the operational cost of keeping copies consistent.

title: Finite-Sample and Communication-Efficient Networked Information Aggregation
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Building on SODA 2026 work Kearns et al. (2026), we study learning in directed acyclic graphs in which each agent observes only a subset of the input coordinates and may use the predictions of its parents as additional features. In the finite-sample protocol, the message sent along each edge is the agent's prediction vector on a shared sample, so the communication cost is linear in the sample size $m$. In this paper we study this model under communication constraints. First, we revisit the finite-sample analysis of the full-message protocol. We identify a gap in the finite-sample proof of Kearns et al. (2026) and develop a different argument that establishes a finite-sample population-risk guarantee along paths satisfying deterministic $M$-coverage. Second, we introduce a shared-sketch protocol in which each agent sends a $k$-dimensional linear sketch of its prediction vector instead of the full $m$-dimensional message, where $k\ll m$. We analyze this protocol through a reduction to least squares on the compressed sample together with an oblivious subspace embedding argument. The resulting bound separates statistics from communication: the statistical term is still governed by the original sample size $m$, while the additional error due to compression is controlled by the sketch dimension $k$. For Gaussian sketches, we obtain an explicit high-probability population-risk bound, showing that row subsampling is not the only possible communication-statistics tradeoff for networked information aggregation.

AI.tldr: The paper studies networked information aggregation under communication constraints, giving a corrected finite-sample guarantee for full-message protocols and a shared-sketch protocol whose communication is governed by sketch dimension k rather than sample size m.
AI.motivation: Kearns et al. (2026) analysed learning in agent DAGs with finite-sample full-message exchange whose communication grows linearly with the sample size, and their finite-sample proof has a gap.
AI.method: The authors develop a different argument for the full-message protocol along paths with deterministic M-coverage, and introduce a shared-sketch protocol in which each agent sends a k-dimensional Gaussian linear sketch of its m-dimensional prediction vector, analysed by reduction to least squares on the compressed sample with an oblivious subspace embedding.
AI.result: The full-message protocol obtains a finite-sample population-risk guarantee along M-covered paths, and the sketch protocol yields an explicit high-probability population-risk bound whose statistical term depends on m and whose compression error is controlled by k.
AI.conclusion: Row subsampling is not the only communication-statistics tradeoff available for networked information aggregation.

title: Prune to Probe: Causal Decision-Stability Probes for Efficient Reasoning
summary: Reasoning models often continue generating after producing an answer, yet stopping prematurely may interrupt useful verification or revision. In this work, we investigate whether targeted interventions in a model's internal computation can provide a reliable signal for when to stop reasoning. We introduce Prune-to-Probe, an inference-time controller that uses causal activation interventions to probe the stability of a model's current answer. Specifically, we identify late-MLP coordinates that contribute to post-answer continuation while excluding those important for answer completion. Once an answer is stated, Prune-to-Probe temporarily suppresses the selected coordinates and measures the resulting stopping response relative to matched random interventions. Crucially, these interventions serve only as probes: the model either returns its existing answer or resumes generation from an untouched cache. On MATH, Prune-to-Probe reduces reasoning-token forwards by 2.60%, preserving all naturally correct trajectories while repairing six errors. On MMLU-Pro, it achieves 1.145% pooled savings with no observed harm. Further analysis shows that the intervention captures decision stability rather than correctness (AUROC 0.502). These results demonstrate the potential of causal activation probes for efficient inference-time control without permanent model modification.

AI.tldr: Prune-to-Probe uses temporary causal activation interventions on late-MLP coordinates to test whether an answer is stable, letting a reasoning model stop early and reducing reasoning-token forwards by 2.60% on MATH without harm on MMLU-Pro.
AI.motivation: Reasoning models often keep generating after stating an answer, but stopping too early may cut off useful verification or revision, so a reliable stopping signal is needed.
AI.method: The controller identifies late-MLP coordinates that drive post-answer continuation while excluding those needed for answer completion; after an answer is stated it suppresses the selected coordinates and compares the stopping response with matched random interventions, returning the existing answer or resuming from an untouched cache.
AI.result: On MATH the method reduces reasoning-token forwards by 2.60%, preserves all naturally correct trajectories and repairs six errors; on MMLU-Pro it achieves 1.145% pooled savings with no observed harm; the signal tracks decision stability rather than correctness (AUROC 0.502).
AI.conclusion: Causal activation probes can enable efficient inference-time control without permanently modifying the model.

title: Target Recoverability under Selective Labels: A Failure Mode in ECG-Based Acute Coronary Syndrome Prediction
comment: Accepted to the Proceedings of Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026
summary: Medical machine learning models often learn from diagnoses observed only in patients clinicians chose to test. The biases of such selective labels are well known, but less understood is what happens when a diagnosis includes cases the model's inputs cannot detect. Because testing decisions draw on information the model does not see, these cases can appear predictable among tested patients, producing relationships that fail, and can even reverse, among the untested. We formalize this mechanism and show in simulations that it worsens as testing becomes more selective or undetectable cases more common, while models trained only on detectable cases remain informative. We empirically study electrocardiogram (ECG)-based prediction of acute coronary syndrome (ACS), which is confirmed only by invasive testing and whose subtypes differ in how clearly they appear on the ECG. Three ECG foundation models fine-tuned on revascularization, our ACS proxy, performed well among catheterized patients (AUROC 0.740-0.770) but worse than chance for 30-day major adverse cardiovascular events among untested patients (AUROC 0.381-0.478). Models trained on ECG-visible subtypes retained discrimination (AUROC 0.680-0.709), whereas a model trained on unstable angina, which can occur without ECG changes, was inversely related to risk (AUROC 0.310). Under selective labels, effective learning therefore requires prediction targets that can be inferred from the model's inputs and evaluation in the intended deployment population, which often extends beyond the patients who were tested.

AI.tldr: Under selective labels, a diagnosis that includes cases invisible to the model can make tested-population predictions look valid while they fail or reverse in the untested population, shown for ECG-based acute coronary syndrome prediction.
AI.motivation: Clinical models are trained on diagnoses observed only in tested patients, and when some diagnosed cases cannot be detected from the model's inputs, testing decisions that draw on hidden information can distort learned relationships.
AI.method: The authors formalise this mechanism and simulate how it worsens with more selective testing or more undetectable cases, then fine-tune three ECG foundation models on revascularization as an ACS proxy and compare them with models trained on ECG-visible ACS subtypes and on unstable angina.
AI.result: Foundation models performed well among catheterized patients (AUROC 0.740 to 0.770) but worse than chance for 30-day major adverse cardiovascular events among untested patients (AUROC 0.381 to 0.478); models trained on ECG-visible subtypes kept discrimination (AUROC 0.680 to 0.709), while the unstable angina model was inversely related to risk (AUROC 0.310).
AI.conclusion: Effective learning under selective labels requires prediction targets inferable from the model's inputs and evaluation in the intended deployment population, which often extends beyond the tested patients.

title: Discrete Diffusion Playground: A 2D Benchmark for Discrete Generative Models
comment: 18 pages, 7 main figures, 2 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track)
summary: Discrete diffusion is a promising framework for categorical generative modeling, but current evaluation protocols often fail to reveal whether models have actually learned the target distribution. We introduce the Discrete Diffusion Playground, a diagnostic benchmark that converts known 2D continuous distributions into binary token sequences through an exact discretized bijection. This creates a rare setting in which models are trained on discrete sequences, but generated samples can be decoded back into 2D and compared directly against a known ground-truth distribution. The benchmark spans smooth Gaussian mixtures and tilted checkerboards with sharp boundaries, disconnected support, and coordinate-dependent structure, allowing it to expose failures that are invisible in standard proxy metrics. It supports exact grid divergences, Wasserstein distances, density visualizations, and nonparametric two-sample tests, providing both quantitative evaluation and interpretable failure diagnosis. Using this testbed, we show that masked diffusion models can learn meaningful adaptive reveal orders but remain less stable than autoregressive baselines on smooth targets and largely fail on tilted checkerboards, where autoregressive models preserve the target geometry. Control experiments with reversed and interleaved token orderings show that autoregressive performance is not explained by favorable bit order alone. The Playground provides a simple but stringent benchmark for stress-testing discrete generative models and for developing evaluation metrics that detect real distributional mismatch rather than proxy performance. Our code is available at this https URL .

AI.tldr: The Discrete Diffusion Playground converts known 2D distributions into binary token sequences so generated samples can be decoded and compared with ground truth, revealing that masked diffusion models largely fail on tilted checkerboards where autoregressive models preserve geometry.
AI.motivation: Standard proxy metrics for discrete diffusion often fail to show whether models have learned the target distribution.
AI.method: An exact discretized bijection maps smooth Gaussian mixtures and tilted checkerboards with sharp boundaries, disconnected support and coordinate-dependent structure into binary token sequences, supported by exact grid divergences, Wasserstein distances, density visualizations and nonparametric two-sample tests, with reversed and interleaved token-order controls.
AI.result: Masked diffusion models learn meaningful adaptive reveal orders but are less stable than autoregressive baselines on smooth targets and largely fail on tilted checkerboards, where autoregressive models preserve the target geometry; reversed and interleaved orderings show autoregressive performance is not explained by bit order alone.
AI.conclusion: The Playground is a stringent benchmark for stress-testing discrete generative models and for metrics that detect real distributional mismatch.

title: A Hierarchical Tokenization Framework for Voxel-Level fMRI Representation Learning
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Code available at this https URL
summary: We introduce HBAR (Hierarchical Brain Activity Representation), a hierarchical tokenization framework for learning compact, multi-scale representations of neuroimaging data. HBAR organizes voxel-level resting-state fMRI into a hierarchy spanning sub-parcel voxel groups, parcels, and large-scale functional networks, enabling up to 415x compression while preserving fine-grained spatial information beyond conventional parcellation. The framework supports fixed atlas-based, fully learned, and softly prior-guided hierarchies, allowing us to systematically study the role of structured priors in brain representation learning. On HCP-YA, at approximately 415x compression, HBAR achieves higher parcel and network correlations than rate-matched flat tokenizers, while at a lower 52x compression rate, shuffling the anatomical grouping reduces parcel correlation from 0.920 to 0.886. Demographic readouts with autoregressive training also reveal potential gains from the hierarchical structure. By combining sub-parcel inputs, compact discrete tokens, and multiscale brain structure, HBAR offers a practical framework for representation learning in high-dimensional neuroimaging data.

AI.tldr: HBAR is a hierarchical tokenizer that represents resting-state fMRI from sub-parcel voxel groups up to parcels and functional networks, achieving up to 415x compression while beating rate-matched flat tokenizers on parcel and network correlations on HCP-YA.
AI.motivation: Conventional parcellations discard fine-grained spatial information, and the role of structured anatomical priors in learning brain representations has not been studied systematically.
AI.method: HBAR organizes voxel-level resting-state fMRI into a three-level hierarchy with fixed atlas-based, fully learned and softly prior-guided variants, using sub-parcel inputs, compact discrete tokens and autoregressive training for demographic readouts.
AI.result: At about 415x compression HBAR gets higher parcel and network correlations than rate-matched flat tokenizers; at 52x, shuffling the anatomical grouping lowers parcel correlation from 0.920 to 0.886; autoregressive training also suggests gains for demographic readouts from the hierarchy.
AI.conclusion: Combining sub-parcel inputs, discrete tokens and multiscale brain structure gives a practical route to representation learning on high-dimensional neuroimaging data.

title: Uncertainty-Guided Reward Labeling for Reinforcement Learning under Limited Feedback
summary: In reinforcement learning from limited feedback (RLLF), only a small fraction of an offline dataset can be labeled with rewards, and the central question is which samples should be labeled to learn a high-performing policy from the resulting partially labeled dataset. Prior work formalized this as a reward-selection problem by focusing on the selection stage while treating downstream policy learning as a black box, in a regime where queried rewards are not retained for reward-model training. We instead study the retained-label setting, where queried rewards can be stored and used to fit a reward model before policy learning. We bound the suboptimality of the learned policy in terms of two sources of error: one arising from offline RL on a fixed, offline dataset, and the other from uncertainty in the reward model. Since reward selection cannot change the offline dataset, the limited labeling budget must be used to strategically reduce reward uncertainty. Motivated by RLLF's observation that useful rewards tend to keep the agent on high-return trajectories, we introduce Successor-Guided Uncertainty REduction (SURE), a novel method that uses successor features to select rewards that are both uncertain and associated with states from which high-valued states are reachable. We formally derive SURE from a bound-induced design objective and characterize its exact one-step marginal gain. Empirically, SURE reaches near full-feedback performance with few reward labels across a variety of domains and offline-RL backbones, yielding an effective method for feedback-efficient reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: SURE selects which samples to label under a limited reward budget by using successor features to favour rewards that are uncertain and linked to states from which high-value states are reachable, approaching full-feedback performance with few labels.
AI.motivation: Prior reward-selection work in reinforcement learning from limited feedback treats policy learning as a black box and discards queried rewards, whereas retaining them for reward-model training changes which labels are worth querying.
AI.method: The authors bound suboptimality by offline RL error on a fixed dataset plus reward-model uncertainty, argue that the labelling budget should reduce reward uncertainty, and derive SURE from this bound-induced objective, characterising its exact one-step marginal gain.
AI.result: Across a variety of domains and offline-RL backbones, SURE reaches near full-feedback performance with few reward labels.
AI.conclusion: SURE is an effective method for feedback-efficient reinforcement learning under the retained-label setting.

title: Jointly Optimizing Memory, Computing and Offloading for Energy-Efficient DNN Inference
summary: In edge intelligence systems, computation offloading and dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) are widely used to improve energy efficiency. However, as applications like deep neural network (DNN) inference evolve in complexity, their demands for memory resources have progressively increased, establishing memory as a critical bottleneck that impacts both latency and energy consumption. In this paper, we propose a joint optimization scheme integrating memory, computing and offloading for energy-efficient DNN inference. We formulate the energy minimization problem under deadline constraints as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem, where the main challenge arises from the coupling between offloading and resource optimization. To address this issue, we decompose the original problem into two subproblems under a fixed offloading policy. The local subproblem is transformed into an equivalent geometric programming (GP) problem to derive the optimal memory frequency and computing frequency, while the edge subproblem is solved via convex optimization. An efficient coordinate descent (CD) algorithm is further developed to jointly optimize all variables. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm achieves near-optimal performance with the gap from the optimal policy being at most 9.3%, and reduces the energy consumption of devices by up to 16.1% compared with benchmarks without memory frequency optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper jointly optimizes memory frequency, computing frequency and offloading for energy-efficient DNN inference on edge devices, with a coordinate descent algorithm whose gap to the optimum is at most 9.3% and which cuts device energy by up to 16.1%.
AI.motivation: Memory has become a bottleneck for DNN inference latency and energy, but prior edge offloading and DVFS work largely ignores memory frequency and its coupling with offloading decisions.
AI.method: The energy minimization under deadline constraints is a mixed-integer nonlinear program; it is decomposed under a fixed offloading policy into a local subproblem, transformed into geometric programming to choose memory and computing frequencies, and an edge subproblem solved by convex optimization, with a coordinate descent algorithm optimizing all variables jointly.
AI.result: The proposed algorithm stays within 9.3% of the optimal policy and reduces device energy by up to 16.1% compared with benchmarks that lack memory frequency optimization.
AI.conclusion: Including memory frequency in joint optimization yields substantial energy savings for edge DNN inference.

title: Compositional Conformal Risk Control for Multi-Stage LLM Cascades
summary: Multi-stage large language model (LLM) cascades balance accuracy and inference cost, but reliable deployment also requires controlling error risk and identifying its sources across stages. We propose Compositional Conformal Risk Control (CompCRC), a risk-control framework for pre-specified multi-stage LLM cascades. We decompose the risk of accepting incorrect answers into additive stage-wise contributions over the full query population, linking local risk budgets to a system-level guarantee. CompCRC constructs and freezes candidate budget allocations and acceptance thresholds, selects one candidate on independent data, and certifies its stage-wise risk contributions on separate held-out data. Under conditional exchangeability, we establish a finite-sample guarantee: the marginal expected accepted-error risk of the complete deployment procedure does not exceed the global risk budget. At the reported comparison budget of $\alpha=0.45$, all three stages of CompCRC pass their local checks on MMLU, GSM8K, and HellaSwag. Compared with Global-CRC, which passes system-level risk certification at the same budget, CompCRC reduces observed accepted-error risk by 1.33--2.00 percentage points, improves final accuracy by 0.67--2.00 percentage points, and reduces weighted inference cost by 30.37\% on HellaSwag. The selected cost-based budget allocation also improves accuracy per unit cost by 10.6\%--46.7\% over uniform allocation. Further experiments show that stage-wise statistics identify stages that fail local certification checks, providing diagnostic information alongside system-level risk control.

AI.tldr: CompCRC is a conformal risk control framework for multi-stage LLM cascades that decomposes accepted-error risk into stage-wise contributions and gives a finite-sample system-level guarantee, reducing observed risk and inference cost relative to a global baseline.
AI.motivation: Multi-stage LLM cascades trade accuracy against cost, but reliable deployment also requires controlling error risk across stages and identifying which stage causes it.
AI.method: CompCRC constructs and freezes candidate budget allocations and acceptance thresholds, selects one candidate on independent data, and certifies stage-wise risk contributions on separate held-out data, with the guarantee derived under conditional exchangeability.
AI.result: At the comparison budget alpha=0.45 all three stages pass local checks on MMLU, GSM8K and HellaSwag; compared with Global-CRC, CompCRC reduces observed accepted-error risk by 1.33 to 2.00 points and improves accuracy by 0.67 to 2.00 points, and on HellaSwag cuts weighted inference cost by 30.37%; cost-based allocation improves accuracy per unit cost by 10.6% to 46.7% over uniform allocation.
AI.conclusion: Stage-wise statistics identify stages that fail local certification, giving diagnostic information alongside system-level risk control.

title: When gene summaries reveal the answers: Gene Ontology circularity in gene embedding benchmarks
comment: 31 pages, including supplementary material. GeneProv benchmark and leaderboard: this https URL
summary: A gene summary can contain the very annotations used to evaluate an embedding of its text. The Alliance of Genome Resources converts Gene Ontology (GO) annotations into sentences, which NCBI Gene displays and GenePT includes in its input. These summaries covered 6,172 of 19,256 human protein-coding genes (32.1%), including 58% of genes with one to ten linked publications. We embedded the same corpus with and without the generated summaries and refitted a function-prediction probe on each version. Among genes with one to ten publications, removal reduced the reported per-gene area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) by 0.078 with a linear probe (95% bootstrap interval 0.072-0.084) and by 0.033 with a multilayer perceptron. These estimates use a historical GO scorer that mishandled ties. The original predictions are unavailable for rescoring. A simple TF-IDF encoder also benefited from the summaries, as did models evaluated only on experimental annotations. Replacing generated summaries with UniProt function descriptions recovered much of the lost performance despite little verbatim overlap. UniProt also curates many of the evaluation labels. In mouse and yeast, we found a similar dependence on the source of the description. We introduce GeneProv to compare encoders on matched text and to examine how representation rankings change across GO recovery, non-GO endpoints and co-essentiality.

AI.tldr: Gene summaries generated from Gene Ontology annotations leak the labels used to evaluate gene embeddings, and removing them lowers function-prediction AUROC, so GO-based benchmarks overstate text-embedding performance.
AI.motivation: The Alliance of Genome Resources turns GO annotations into sentences that NCBI Gene displays and GenePT uses as input, so the evaluation labels can appear in the embedded text itself.
AI.method: The authors embedded the same gene corpus with and without generated summaries, refitted a function-prediction probe on each version, and tested a TF-IDF encoder, experimental-only annotations and UniProt function descriptions as replacements; they also introduce GeneProv to compare encoders on matched text.
AI.result: Among genes with one to ten publications, removing summaries reduced per-gene AUROC by 0.078 with a linear probe (95% bootstrap interval 0.072 to 0.084) and by 0.033 with an MLP, though these estimates use a historical GO scorer that mishandled ties; UniProt descriptions recovered much of the lost performance, and similar source dependence appeared in mouse and yeast.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark rankings of gene embeddings are sensitive to whether the input text leaks GO annotations, and UniProt also curates many of the labels, so evaluation must control for this circularity.

title: DISCOVER: Online Variance-Guided Data Discovery for Budgeted Multimodal GRPO
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Project page: this https URL
summary: Recent advances in reinforcement learning have made verifiable rewards a central post-training paradigm for improving multimodal reasoning. However, methods such as GRPO remain data- and compute-inefficient, spending rollout and annotation budget on prompts that provide little learning signal. We propose DISCOVER, an online data-discovery framework for budgeted multimodal GRPO that enables vision-language models to dynamically identify prompts that are most useful for the current policy. DISCOVER first organizes the multimodal sample pool into semantic clusters and queries a small set of density-diverse representative samples to obtain initial reward observations. During training, it estimates the utility of unannotated samples by transferring sparse reward feedback from queried samples. Since sample utility changes as the policy evolves, DISCOVER dynamically updates these estimates with recency-weighted rollout observations. It then selects only high-utility prompts for annotation using a policy-conditioned score that accounts for reward variance and difficulty. Once the discovery budget is exhausted, DISCOVER continues with utility-based replay. Experiments on ViRL39K and VLAA-Thinking with Qwen3-VL-2B show that DISCOVER substantially improves multimodal mathematical reasoning under a strict 10% unique-sample budget, outperforming budget-matched random selection, hard-example sampling, full-pool GRPO under the same training-step budget, and online selection baselines. Ablations further validate the importance of semantic coverage, online reward transfer, and stable discovery cadence, establishing DISCOVER as a practical framework for data-efficient multimodal RL post-training.

AI.tldr: DISCOVER selects a small, high-utility subset of unlabeled multimodal prompts for reward annotation during GRPO, outperforming budget-matched baselines on mathematical reasoning with a 10% unique-sample budget for Qwen3-VL-2B.
AI.motivation: GRPO spends rollout and annotation budget on prompts that yield little learning signal, and sample utility changes as the policy evolves.
AI.method: DISCOVER clusters the multimodal pool semantically, queries density-diverse representatives for initial rewards, transfers sparse rewards to unannotated samples, updates utility estimates with recency-weighted rollouts, and selects prompts with a policy-conditioned score accounting for reward variance and difficulty, then switches to utility-based replay once the discovery budget is exhausted.
AI.result: On ViRL39K and VLAA-Thinking with Qwen3-VL-2B under a strict 10% unique-sample budget, DISCOVER substantially improves multimodal mathematical reasoning over budget-matched random selection, hard-example sampling, full-pool GRPO at the same training-step budget and online selection baselines.
AI.conclusion: Semantic coverage, online reward transfer and stable discovery cadence are each important, making DISCOVER a practical data-efficient multimodal RL post-training framework.

title: ZarrFM: A Canonical Tensor Storage Architecture for EEG Foundation-Model Pretraining
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Foundation Models for the Brain and Body
summary: Statistical models for brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) increasingly require large, heterogeneous EEG corpora, yet existing datasets vary in sampling rates, channel layouts, window lengths, and storage formats, creating substantial preprocessing and I/O overhead. We propose ZarrFM, an execution-oriented representation that complements BIDS by storing a corpus as a single Zarr v3 hierarchy with indexed metadata, canonical channel spaces, explicit masks, hash-stable subject splits, verified event tables, and block-aligned sharding. On real PhysioNet recordings and synthetic corpora, we compare ZarrFM with EDF, FIF, NPY, HDF5, and Parquet. Across 200 recordings, its two-level index reduces metadata queries from 601 requests to 14. Preserving native signal codes reduces storage from 42.4 MB/hour in EDF to 22.7 MB/hour, while block-aligned sampling reaches 3,131 windows/s, up to 11 times faster than Parquet. Reads remain bit-identical across independent Zarr implementations, and concurrent failure-injected appends recover without data loss. These results show that ZarrFM can provide a compact, interoperable, and execution-efficient storage layer for large-scale EEG pretraining.

AI.tldr: ZarrFM stores an EEG corpus as a single Zarr v3 hierarchy with indexed metadata, canonical channel spaces and block-aligned sharding, cutting metadata requests from 601 to 14 and reaching 3,131 windows per second, up to 11 times faster than Parquet.
AI.motivation: EEG corpora differ in sampling rates, channel layouts, window lengths and storage formats, creating heavy preprocessing and I/O overhead for foundation-model pretraining, and BIDS alone does not provide an execution-oriented layout.
AI.method: ZarrFM complements BIDS with a single Zarr v3 hierarchy holding indexed metadata, canonical channel spaces, explicit masks, hash-stable subject splits, verified event tables and block-aligned sharding, and is compared with EDF, FIF, NPY, HDF5 and Parquet on PhysioNet recordings and synthetic corpora.
AI.result: Across 200 recordings the two-level index reduces metadata queries from 601 to 14; preserving native signal codes lowers storage from 42.4 MB per hour in EDF to 22.7 MB per hour; block-aligned sampling reaches 3,131 windows per second; reads are bit-identical across independent Zarr implementations, and failure-injected concurrent appends recover without data loss.
AI.conclusion: ZarrFM offers a compact, interoperable and execution-efficient storage layer for large-scale EEG pretraining.

title: The Race Is Decided Early! A Kernel Law Predicts Lock-In in Majority-Vote Test-Time RL
summary: Test-time reinforcement learning with majority-vote rewards trains a language model on unlabeled questions by rewarding the samples that agree with its most frequent answer. During training, each question locks into one answer, on hard questions often a wrong one, but which answer it locks into is known only after training. In this paper, we show that this outcome is decided early, in a short race driven by sampling noise between the answers that are close at the start, and we derive the probability of each outcome. With a separate logit for each answer, the runner-up wins with a normal tail probability of the initial gap, scaled by an explicit noise constant. In a network, however, the answer logits depend on shared parameters, and through the kernel of these parameters the updates of the trailing answers also change the gap of the two leaders. This spillover shifts the boundary between the starts won by each leader, and a closed form computes the shifted probability from a kernel probe and the start logits. In LoRA experiments with three models from two families, predictions made before training with the kernel frozen at its start value forecast which answer each question locks into better than a logistic model refitted on the outcomes, although they use no fitted constants. The closed form matches these predictions on the runs in which a check before training finds that the two leaders stay above the other answers, and it explains why a law that ignores the spillover needs a strongly inflated step.

AI.tldr: In majority-vote test-time RL, each question locks into an answer early in a noise-driven race, and a kernel-based closed form predicts the locked-in answer before training by accounting for spillover through shared parameters.
AI.motivation: Test-time RL with majority-vote rewards locks each unlabeled question into one answer, often a wrong one on hard questions, but the outcome is known only after training.
AI.method: The authors model the early race between close answers, derive lock-in probabilities for independent per-answer logits, and show that with shared network parameters a kernel probe and the start logits give a closed form that includes the spillover from trailing answers' updates, evaluated in LoRA experiments on three models from two families.
AI.result: Predictions made before training with the kernel frozen at its start value forecast the locked-in answer better than a logistic model refitted on outcomes, without fitted constants; the closed form matches these predictions when the two leaders stay above the other answers, and explains why a law ignoring spillover needs a strongly inflated step.
AI.conclusion: Lock-in is decided early, and shared-parameter spillover must be included to predict it accurately.

title: ClusLoad: Cluster-Guided Model Sharing for Scalable Distribution Transformer Load Forecasting
summary: Large-scale device-level load forecasting for distribution transformers is challenged by substantial cross-device heterogeneity and the deployment burden of maintaining device-specific forecasting models. Existing approaches typically rely either on device-specific models, which are difficult to scale to large transformer populations, or on global models, which reduce deployment complexity but may overlook heterogeneous load patterns across devices. To address this trade-off, this study develops a trend-clustered forecasting framework that enables model sharing among transformers with similar temporal behaviors. Representation Learning for Time Series using Time-Embeddings (T-Rep) is employed to learn compact temporal representations of transformer load series, which are subsequently grouped using a Gaussian mixture model (GMM). Representative transformers are sampled within each cluster to train cluster-specific Patch Time Series Transformer (PatchTST) models while retaining device-level predictions. The framework is evaluated using real-world 15-min operational data from nearly one thousand distribution transformers. The proposed framework reduces mean absolute error (MAE) by approximately 20% relative to the direct PatchTST baseline, achieves a high-load warning accuracy of 95.66%, while requiring only seven cluster-specific forecasting models. These results demonstrate that behavior-based device organization provides an effective balance between forecasting accuracy, deployment scalability, and risk-oriented operational support for distribution transformer management.

AI.tldr: Proposes ClusLoad, which clusters distribution transformers by learned temporal representations and trains one PatchTST model per cluster, so about seven cluster-specific models serve nearly one thousand transformers. It reduces MAE by about 20% relative to a direct PatchTST baseline.
AI.motivation: Device-specific forecasting models are hard to scale to large transformer populations, while global models reduce deployment complexity but overlook heterogeneous load patterns across devices.
AI.method: Trend-clustered model sharing: T-Rep learns compact temporal representations of load series, a Gaussian mixture model groups them, representative transformers are sampled per cluster to train cluster-specific PatchTST models, and device-level predictions are retained.
AI.result: On 15-minute operational data from nearly 1,000 distribution transformers, MAE drops by about 20% relative to the direct PatchTST baseline, high-load warning accuracy is 95.66%, and only seven cluster-specific models are required.
AI.conclusion: Behaviour-based device organization gives a balance between forecasting accuracy, deployment scalability and risk-oriented operational support for distribution transformer management.

title: TEAM: Topology-Aware, Semantic-Sensitive, General Transformer for Multimodal-Attributed Graphs
summary: Multimodal-Attributed Graphs (MAGs) organize heterogeneous data in graphs whose nodes are characterized by modalities such as text and images rather than traditional unimodal attributes. However, many representative MAG methods organize propagation around node-level states and topology-defined neighborhoods, which can obscure fine-grained modality contributions: a bounded neighborhood may contain semantically weak evidence, while compatible context need not be confined to it. To address both limitations, we propose TEAM, a modality-centric framework that constructs and encodes graph context with node-modality tokens rather than treating each node as a single interaction unit. Concretely, TEAM unfolds the local topology into a Modality Encoding Tree and performs tree-anchored semantic evidence acquisition, organizing local structural context while expanding the accessible evidence space outside the constructed local Tree. We further introduce the Modality-Source Context Transformer (MSCT), which encodes the selected node-modality tokens and coordinates interactions among modality-source groups. By retaining textual and visual attributes as separate interaction units until readout, it supports fine-grained cross-node cross-modal exchange without first collapsing them into whole-node features. Across the evaluated baselines, TEAM attains the highest reported mean on all graph-learning metrics, all three G2Text metrics, and both G2Image metrics. On Toys, it surpasses the strongest baseline by 3.37 and 2.93 percentage points in Accuracy and Macro-F1, respectively.

AI.tldr: Proposes TEAM, a modality-centric transformer for multimodal-attributed graphs that keeps text and image attributes as separate node-modality tokens instead of collapsing each node into one feature. It reports the highest mean on all graph-learning metrics and on the G2Text and G2Image metrics among the evaluated baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing MAG methods organize propagation around node-level states and topology-defined neighborhoods, which can obscure fine-grained modality contributions, include semantically weak evidence, and exclude compatible context outside the neighborhood.
AI.method: TEAM unfolds local topology into a Modality Encoding Tree, performs tree-anchored semantic evidence acquisition that expands the accessible evidence space, and uses the Modality-Source Context Transformer (MSCT) to encode selected node-modality tokens and coordinate interactions among modality-source groups until readout.
AI.result: Across the evaluated baselines TEAM attains the highest reported mean on all graph-learning metrics, all three G2Text metrics and both G2Image metrics; on Toys it surpasses the strongest baseline by 3.37 points in Accuracy and 2.93 points in Macro-F1.
AI.conclusion: Keeping textual and visual attributes as separate interaction units until readout supports fine-grained cross-node cross-modal exchange without first collapsing them into whole-node features.

title: Not Yet in the Profile: Uncertainty-Aware Dynamic User Profiling by Learning from Future Interactions
summary: On the Web, user profiling builds compact user representations from interaction histories for efficient personalization, and dynamic user profiling updates them as users' behavior and preferences change. However, new user behavior can be ambiguous, and its interpretation differs across users. To address this, we introduce Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Profile Manager (UAPM), which separates the claims in a user profile from interpretations of new behavior that are not yet confirmed, through a Profile, a Buffer, and a Rulebook. UAPM records user-specific interpretation and update rules in the Rulebook, keeps ambiguous evidence in the Buffer outside the Profile as evidence for later decisions, and writes supported general and situational characteristics to the Profile. We train UAPM with Privileged On-Policy Distillation with Dual Specialization (POPD-DS), which learns from recorded future interactions during training without access to them at deployment. Its first stage, Dual Specialization, distills a stronger model into a current-only Student and a future-informed model that becomes the Teacher. In the second stage, privileged on-policy distillation (POPD), only the fixed Teacher receives future interactions and guides the Student's own management decisions alongside task rewards. Experiments on three Web personalization tasks show that UAPM outperforms multiple baselines under the same downstream input budget, improving on the best same-budget baseline by up to 5%.

AI.tldr: Proposes UAPM, a dynamic user profiler that separates confirmed profile claims from unconfirmed interpretations of new behaviour through a Profile, a Buffer and a Rulebook. It is trained with privileged on-policy distillation that uses future interactions only during training, and it improves on the best same-budget baseline by up to 5% on three Web personalization tasks.
AI.motivation: New user behaviour is often ambiguous and its interpretation differs across users, so updating a profile directly from it risks writing unsupported claims into the profile.
AI.method: UAPM keeps user-specific interpretation and update rules in a Rulebook, holds ambiguous evidence in a Buffer outside the Profile, and writes supported general and situational characteristics to the Profile. Training uses POPD-DS: Dual Specialization distills a stronger model into a current-only Student and a future-informed Teacher, and privileged on-policy distillation (POPD) then guides the Student with the fixed Teacher and task rewards.
AI.result: On three Web personalization tasks UAPM outperforms multiple baselines under the same downstream input budget, improving on the best same-budget baseline by up to 5%.
