AI.conclusion: Separating unconfirmed interpretations from the profile, and using future interactions only as training-time privileged information, offers a way to update dynamic profiles from ambiguous behaviour without committing unsupported claims.

title: scBIG++: Learning Across Genes and Cells to Predict Single-Cell Perturbation Responses
summary: Predicting single-cell transcriptional responses to genetic and chemical interventions supports gene-function discovery and regulatory analysis. Existing studies often focus only on highly variable genes, restricting the expression changes available for downstream analysis. Cells exposed to the same intervention can also show heterogeneous expression responses, with coordinated gene programs active to different degrees. We propose scBIG++, a full-gene perturbation prediction framework that models this heterogeneity by connecting expression-adaptive gene modules with population-conditioned generation. To preserve shared gene structure while accommodating cellular variation, Gene-Relation Clustering organizes genes into common windows, within which Dynamic SoftSub learns expression-dependent submodule memberships. This shared organization enables Set-GCAE to exchange information about corresponding gene groups across control cells, placing individual representations in their source-population context. The cell representations initialize a latent flow, while their pooled summary and the perturbation representation condition response generation. Generated states are decoded into expression profiles covering all assayed protein-coding genes retained after preprocessing, supporting comprehensive analysis of perturbation-induced expression changes. Experiments across six genetic and chemical settings spanning 6,539--19,451 genes demonstrate competitive perturbation-effect recovery and full-gene expression reconstruction under unseen targets and combinations, cross-cell-line transfer, and held-out compounds. Our implementation is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes scBIG++, a full-gene framework for predicting single-cell transcriptional responses to genetic and chemical perturbations that decodes expression profiles covering all assayed protein-coding genes rather than only highly variable genes. It reports competitive perturbation-effect recovery and full-gene reconstruction across six settings.
AI.motivation: Existing studies often restrict analysis to highly variable genes, and cells exposed to the same intervention respond heterogeneously, with coordinated gene programs active to different degrees.
AI.method: Gene-Relation Clustering groups genes into common windows, Dynamic SoftSub learns expression-dependent submodule memberships within them, and Set-GCAE shares information about corresponding gene groups across control cells. Cell representations initialize a latent flow, conditioned on their pooled summary and the perturbation representation, and the generated states are decoded into expression profiles.
AI.result: Experiments across six genetic and chemical settings spanning 6,539 to 19,451 genes show competitive perturbation-effect recovery and full-gene expression reconstruction under unseen targets and combinations, cross-cell-line transfer, and held-out compounds.
AI.conclusion: The framework supports comprehensive analysis of perturbation-induced expression changes across all retained genes, not only a highly variable subset.

title: EbbFlow: PINN-Inspired Progressive Curriculum for MeanFlow Training
summary: MeanFlow learns interval-average velocity for few-step generation, but its fixed temporal sampler mixes diagonal and interior supervision throughout training. We interpret temporal coordinates as collocation points: diagonal samples provide a stochastic boundary target, whereas finite intervals supply a differential-consistency target. The diagonal fraction controls how often the consistency component appears, while interval length enters its gradient through an explicit factor. Motivated by this distinction, EbbFlow uses Temporal Supervision Allocation (TSA) to schedule the diagonal fraction and interval geometry. It starts with diagonal supervision, then admits interior samples and expands their maximum interval; a left-anchored interval law preserves coverage across time. The per-sample loss, target, backbone, and inference procedure remain unchanged. In matched class-conditional ImageNet $256\times 256$ runs without classifier-free guidance (DiT-B/2, one training seed per method, 400k updates), EbbFlow achieves 50k-sample FID of 39.65 at one network evaluation and 36.02 at two-evaluation ODE sampling, versus 44.82 and 39.86 for MeanFlow. Gradient probes show a mid-training difference in component geometry. Ablations support allocation scheduling and left-anchored intervals, although a fixed full-horizon variant performs better at one evaluation. These results suggest that temporal sampling is a useful training control whose benefits depend on the inference protocol.

AI.tldr: Proposes EbbFlow, which schedules the temporal sampling of MeanFlow training with a PINN-inspired curriculum that starts from diagonal supervision and then admits interior intervals with an expanding maximum length. On class-conditional ImageNet 256x256 it improves FID over MeanFlow at one and at two network evaluations.
AI.motivation: MeanFlow's fixed temporal sampler mixes diagonal boundary supervision and interior differential-consistency supervision throughout training, although the two play different roles.
AI.method: EbbFlow treats temporal coordinates as collocation points and uses Temporal Supervision Allocation (TSA) to schedule the diagonal fraction and the interval geometry. Intervals expand under a left-anchored interval law that preserves coverage across time, while the per-sample loss, target, backbone and inference procedure remain unchanged.
AI.result: In matched DiT-B/2 runs without classifier-free guidance (one seed per method, 400k updates), EbbFlow reaches 50k-sample FID 39.65 at one network evaluation and 36.02 at two-evaluation ODE sampling, versus 44.82 and 39.86 for MeanFlow. Ablations support the allocation schedule and left-anchored intervals, while a fixed full-horizon variant performs better at one evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Temporal sampling is a useful training control, but its benefit depends on the inference protocol.

title: Do Feature Interactions Break Explainability? Provable Explanations for Any-Order Neural Additive Models
summary: Post-hoc explanation methods for neural networks are often heuristic and lack provable guarantees. A common alternative to such methods that was studied in recent years is to compute a cardinally-minimal subset of input features that is provably sufficient to determine the model's prediction. For general neural networks, however, finding such explanations is computationally intractable. In contrast, recent work showed that this problem becomes more tractable for a particular family of neural networks, namely neural additive models (NAMs), though standard NAMs are highly restrictive because they exclude feature interactions altogether. In this work, we study the computation of provably minimal and sufficient explanations for neural networks with restricted feature interactions, bridging the gap between fully general neural networks and purely additive models. We first prove that even with constant-order interactions, the problem is $\Sigma_2^P$-hard, implying that worst-case exponential complexity is unavoidable. We then identify two provably tractable settings: one based on sparsity in the interaction structure and another based on a stronger interaction-aware notion of sufficiency. Under either of these settings, we develop algorithms that compute provable explanations for neural networks with any-order interactions while retaining much of the computational efficiency of additive models. Empirically, we show that these explanations are significantly smaller and faster to obtain than those produced by standard algorithms, while being derived from models that achieve much higher accuracy than standard NAMs. Overall, our results help expand the class of neural networks that admit efficient provable explanations, while clarifying the fundamental role of feature interactions in shaping their complexity.

AI.tldr: Shows that computing provably minimal sufficient explanations stays Sigma_2^P-hard even with constant-order feature interactions, and identifies two tractable settings that give efficient provable explanations for neural networks with any-order interactions. The explanations are significantly smaller and faster to obtain than those from standard algorithms, and the models are much more accurate than standard NAMs.
AI.motivation: Post-hoc explanations are often heuristic, and finding minimal sufficient feature subsets is intractable for general neural networks, while standard neural additive models are restrictive because they exclude feature interactions altogether.
AI.method: The authors study provably minimal and sufficient explanations for networks with restricted feature interactions and prove hardness. They then develop algorithms for two tractable settings: one based on sparsity in the interaction structure, and one based on a stronger interaction-aware notion of sufficiency.
AI.result: Empirically, the resulting explanations are significantly smaller and faster to obtain than those produced by standard algorithms, and they are derived from models that achieve much higher accuracy than standard NAMs.
AI.conclusion: The results expand the class of neural networks that admit efficient provable explanations and clarify how feature interactions shape explanation complexity.

title: MCSA: Multi-Cutoff Spectral Aggregation in SO(3) Equivariant GNNs for Interatomic Potentials
summary: Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs) based on Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (EGNNs) have achieved remarkable progress in atomistic modeling. However, accurately representing atomic interactions across different spatial scales remains challenging. In this work, we investigate the radial spectral properties of SO(3)-equivariant message passing and establish that the cutoff radius controls the characteristic spatial-frequency scale of radial interactions. Based on this analysis, we propose Multi-Cutoff Spectral Aggregation (MCSA), a plug-and-play module that aggregates radial kernels with different cutoff radii to enrich multi-scale geometric representations. To achieve efficient implementation, we exploit the compact support of radial kernels to fuse cutoff-dependent radial weights before angular tensor-product operations, avoiding redundant angular computations while preserving rotational equivariance. Extensive experiments across representative EGNN backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in energy, force, and stress prediction, as well as enhanced accuracy in higher-order properties, including phonon dispersion and lattice thermal conductivity. Further evaluations on layered materials with distinct interaction scales demonstrate the effectiveness of physically motivated cutoff selection. Code is available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes Multi-Cutoff Spectral Aggregation (MCSA), a plug-and-play module for SO(3)-equivariant graph neural network interatomic potentials that aggregates radial kernels with different cutoff radii. It gives consistent gains in energy, force and stress prediction across EGNN backbones.
AI.motivation: Equivariant GNN potentials find it challenging to represent atomic interactions across different spatial scales, and the cutoff radius controls the characteristic spatial-frequency scale of radial interactions.
AI.method: The authors analyse the radial spectral properties of SO(3)-equivariant message passing and aggregate radial kernels with different cutoffs. For efficiency they exploit the compact support of radial kernels to fuse cutoff-dependent radial weights before angular tensor-product operations, avoiding redundant angular computation while preserving rotational equivariance.
AI.result: MCSA gives consistent improvements in energy, force and stress prediction across representative EGNN backbones and better accuracy on higher-order properties, including phonon dispersion and lattice thermal conductivity. On layered materials with distinct interaction scales, physically motivated cutoff selection is shown to be effective.
AI.conclusion: Multi-scale radial aggregation with physically motivated cutoff selection enriches geometric representations for interatomic potentials.

title: FRESCO: A Novel Consistency Control for Asynchronous Pipeline Parallel Training
summary: Asynchronous pipeline parallelism can accelerate distributed model training, but suffers from instability caused by inconsistent gradient computations. We identify a fundamental source of this inconsistency: error signals are coupled to forward-time features, not just parameter states. This means that parameters may evolve as long as they preserve forward-equivalence. Leveraging this insight, we introduce FRESCO, which frames asynchronous updates as a constrained optimization problem: it finds the minimal update modification that acts trivially on the activation subspace. We demonstrate that FRESCO consistently outperforms representative asynchronous baselines in LLM pre-training, with the gains most pronounced under deep pipelines and high inconsistency levels: at pipeline depth 32, it reaches the same loss as the strongest baseline with 43% fewer iterations and 30% less wall-clock time, while requiring 8~921$\times$ less memory overhead. Moving beyond the current limitations, FRESCO establishes a new foundation for high-utilization pipeline parallel training, providing a scalable path for large-model development on diverse, resource-constrained systems.

AI.tldr: Proposes FRESCO, a consistency control for asynchronous pipeline-parallel training that treats asynchronous updates as a constrained optimization problem. In LLM pre-training at pipeline depth 32 it reaches the strongest baseline's loss with 43% fewer iterations and 30% less wall-clock time.
AI.motivation: Asynchronous pipeline parallelism speeds up distributed training but is unstable because error signals are coupled to forward-time features, not only to parameter states, so gradients are computed inconsistently.
AI.method: FRESCO finds the minimal update modification that acts trivially on the activation subspace. Parameters may therefore evolve as long as they preserve forward equivalence.
AI.result: FRESCO consistently outperforms representative asynchronous baselines in LLM pre-training, with the largest gains under deep pipelines and high inconsistency levels. At pipeline depth 32 it reaches the strongest baseline's loss with 43% fewer iterations and 30% less wall-clock time, while requiring 8 to 921 times less memory overhead.
AI.conclusion: The authors position FRESCO as a foundation for high-utilization pipeline-parallel training that scales to large models on diverse, resource-constrained systems.

title: ALETHEIA: A Multi-Frequency Eddy Current Pulsed Thermography Dataset for Neural Operator Learning in Nondestructive Testing
summary: Learning neural solvers for spatiotemporal partial differential equations (PDEs) under real-world constraints remains a key challenge in scientific machine learning, especially for inverse tasks with sparse and noisy boundary observations. We present the Aletheia dataset, the first 3D benchmark for learning data-driven solvers in the context of nondestructive testing (NDT). The dataset simulates eddy-current-induced heating in conductive solids and models the resulting transient heat propagation governed by the heat equation. Aletheia contains over 4,700 high-resolution samples across 10 excitation frequencies (1-100,kHz), each providing volumetric heat source and temperature fields over time. It supports both forward prediction of temperature evolution and inverse reconstruction of internal heat sources or defects from surface infrared measurements. Real infrared thermography data from cracked rail specimens are included for calibration and comparison. We define four canonical tasks on both regular and irregular grids and benchmark them using various neural operators. Aletheia establishes a unified platform for evaluating neural PDE solvers under realistic NDT conditions, enabling progress in reliable, data-driven inverse modeling. The dataset and code are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Presents Aletheia, a 3D benchmark of over 4,700 eddy-current pulsed thermography samples across 10 excitation frequencies from 1 to 100 kHz, for learning neural PDE solvers in nondestructive testing. Four canonical forward and inverse tasks are defined and benchmarked with neural operators.
AI.motivation: Learning neural solvers for spatiotemporal PDEs under real-world constraints is hard, especially for inverse tasks with sparse and noisy boundary observations, and the abstract describes the work as the first 3D benchmark of this kind for NDT.
AI.method: The dataset simulates eddy-current-induced heating in conductive solids and the resulting transient heat propagation governed by the heat equation, with volumetric heat source and temperature fields over time. It supports forward prediction of temperature evolution and inverse reconstruction of internal heat sources or defects from surface infrared measurements, and includes real infrared data from cracked rail specimens for calibration and comparison.
AI.result: The four tasks are defined on both regular and irregular grids and benchmarked with various neural operators. The abstract reports no specific quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Aletheia provides a unified platform for evaluating neural PDE solvers under realistic NDT conditions and for progress in reliable, data-driven inverse modelling.

title: Primitives and Paths: Predicting What Post-Training Can Do from What the Base Model Already Has
summary: Does reinforcement learning teach language models new capabilities, or merely amplify ones acquired during pre-training? The literature offers evidence for both: pass@$k$ studies suggest RL reweights latent behaviours while some controlled composition studies demonstrate gains beyond simple amplification. We argue that this question has no answer independent of the capability state of the base model, and propose a two-dimensional state space for post-trainability. The first axis, \emph{effective full-solution support}, measures whether successful trajectories can be sampled under a feasible exploration budget. The second axis, \emph{atomic primitive coverage}, measures whether the constituent skills of a solution can be executed when the burden of composition is removed. Together, these dimensions motivate three regimes -- amplification, composition-limited, and acquisition-limited -- each predicting a distinct empirical signature and calling for a distinct intervention. We propose a prospective measurement protocol and investigate the framework using synthetic composition tasks across three small language models. We find that primitive mastery alone does not guarantee that RL can learn a composition. Checkpoints that execute every primitive reliably can fail to improve when complete solutions are never sampled during training, whereas modest composition supervision that establishes nonzero support enables substantial RL gains. The framework reframes mid-training as preparation for post-training: its role is to move models into states from which RL can operate effectively.

AI.tldr: Argues that whether RL can teach a language model new capabilities depends on the base model's capability state, and proposes a two-dimensional state space whose regions predict amplification, composition-limited or acquisition-limited regimes. In synthetic composition tasks on three small language models, primitive mastery alone does not guarantee that RL learns a composition, while modest composition supervision enables substantial RL gains.
AI.motivation: Evidence on whether RL teaches new capabilities or only amplifies pre-training behaviour is mixed, from pass@k studies to controlled composition studies, and the question is usually treated as having one answer regardless of the base model.
AI.method: The two axes are effective full-solution support, which measures whether successful trajectories can be sampled under a feasible exploration budget, and atomic primitive coverage, which measures whether a solution's constituent skills can be executed when composition is removed. A prospective measurement protocol is proposed and applied to synthetic composition tasks on three small language models.
AI.result: Checkpoints that execute every primitive reliably can fail to improve when complete solutions are never sampled during training, whereas modest composition supervision that establishes nonzero support enables substantial RL gains.
AI.conclusion: Mid-training is best seen as preparation for post-training, moving models into states from which RL can operate effectively.

title: Beyond Node Attributes: A Controlled Evaluation and Ablation of Local Interaction Statistics for Ethereum Phishing Detection
summary: Methods for detecting phishing accounts on Ethereum are usually evaluated as complete pipelines that differ in features, architecture, and training protocol, which makes the contribution of interaction information hard to isolate. This paper evaluates the Unlabeled Feature Extension (UFE), a block of 12 local interaction statistics computed from each account's incoming and outgoing call and transfer edges without reading class labels. UFE is appended to the 14 source features of HEIG-Phish and tested with six model families: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM, Graph Attention Network, GraphSAGE, and Meta-IFD. Within each pair of Baseline and Plus variants, the data partition, model configuration, random seed, decision threshold, and sampled neighborhoods are identical; only the input feature block changes. Across 20 predetermined stratified partitions of the same 2,763 labeled externally owned accounts, UFE increased test Macro-F1 by 1.0 to 9.1 percentage points across the six models. Every pair improved on all 20 partitions, all Nadeau-Bengio corrected 95% confidence intervals lie above zero, and the false-positive rate decreased for all six models. An exact-edge Random Forest ablation over 10 predetermined partitions associates most of the gain with the incoming transfer-edge sum attribute; once this feature is present, an incremental contribution of the remaining 11 UFE columns was not established. The results support reporting feature-augmented baselines alongside graph models, but they show stability under re-partitioning of one static, transductive benchmark rather than temporal or cross-dataset generalization.

AI.tldr: Evaluates the Unlabeled Feature Extension (UFE), 12 local interaction statistics per Ethereum account computed without class labels, appended to the 14 HEIG-Phish features across six model families. UFE raises test Macro-F1 by 1.0 to 9.1 points and improves every pair on all 20 partitions, but an exact-edge ablation attributes most of the gain to one attribute.
AI.motivation: Ethereum phishing detection methods are usually compared as full pipelines that differ in features, architecture and training protocol, which makes the contribution of interaction information hard to isolate.
AI.method: UFE is appended to the 14 source features and tested with Logistic Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM, Graph Attention Network, GraphSAGE and Meta-IFD. Each Baseline and Plus pair shares the data partition, configuration, seed, threshold and sampled neighbourhoods, so only the input feature block changes, across 20 stratified partitions of 2,763 labeled externally owned accounts.
AI.result: UFE increases test Macro-F1 by 1.0 to 9.1 percentage points across the six models. Every pair improves on all 20 partitions, all Nadeau-Bengio corrected 95% confidence intervals lie above zero, and the false-positive rate decreases for all six models. An exact-edge Random Forest ablation over 10 partitions associates most of the gain with the incoming transfer-edge sum attribute, and an incremental contribution of the remaining 11 UFE columns was not established.
AI.conclusion: Feature-augmented baselines should be reported alongside graph models, but the stability shown holds under re-partitioning of one static transductive benchmark, not under temporal or cross-dataset generalization.

title: How Efficient Is Your Agent? Online Predictive Bounds under Budget Constraints
summary: We evaluate AI agents in an online setting where tasks arrive sequentially and, before running each task, we construct an upper predictive bound on its \emph{time-to-success}---the number of interactions until the task is completed successfully. Under a limited budget, some runs are stopped early, so their time-to-success is unobserved (right-censored), and the correctness of the bound may be unknown. We introduce \emph{\textbf{PR}edictive Bounds for \textbf{O}nline \textbf{B}udget \textbf{E}fficiency} (\texttt{PROBE}), a method for constructing calibrated upper predictive bounds while adaptively allocating a limited budget across agent tasks to reduce the anticipated coverage deficit. Our method calibrates the bounds online using inverse-probability-weighted feedback together with a correction designed to minimize coverage deficit while remaining unbiased. We prove that \texttt{PROBE} provides a coverage guarantee for any finite time horizon while satisfying the budget constraint. Experiments on software engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and instruction following show that \texttt{PROBE} attains a coverage rate closer to the target level with tighter predictive bounds than a calibrated baseline.

AI.tldr: Proposes PROBE, which constructs calibrated online upper predictive bounds on an agent's time-to-success under a limited budget, allocates budget adaptively, and proves a coverage guarantee for any finite horizon. On software engineering, retrieval-augmented generation and instruction-following tasks it reaches coverage closer to the target with tighter bounds than a calibrated baseline.
AI.motivation: When evaluating agents online under a budget, some runs are stopped early, so their time-to-success is right-censored and the correctness of the bound may be unknown.
AI.method: Before each task an upper predictive bound on time-to-success is built and calibrated online using inverse-probability-weighted feedback, together with a correction designed to minimize the coverage deficit while remaining unbiased. Budget is allocated adaptively to reduce the anticipated coverage deficit.
AI.result: PROBE attains a coverage rate closer to the target level, with tighter predictive bounds than a calibrated baseline, on software engineering, retrieval-augmented generation and instruction-following experiments, while satisfying the budget constraint.
AI.conclusion: The method gives calibrated, budget-respecting predictive bounds for evaluating agent efficiency online, with a finite-horizon coverage guarantee.

title: Shape-Adaptive Subspace-Constrained Quadratic Matrix Factorization
summary: Quadratic manifold fitting provides a flexible framework for modeling nonlinear low-dimensional structures embedded in high-dimensional spaces. However, existing methods typically employ prescribed noise models or fixed loss functions, limiting their adaptability to varying noise characteristics. To address this limitation, we propose an alternating maximum likelihood estimation method for subspace-constrained quadratic matrix factorization, termed AMLE-SQMF, which jointly estimates the quadratic manifold and the underlying noise distribution. Specifically, we model the residuals using a generalized Gaussian distribution (GGD), whose shape parameter controls the tail behavior and determines the associated fitting loss. By exploiting the closed-form maximum likelihood estimator of the scale parameter, we eliminate the scale variable and derive a profile negative log-likelihood. Based on this formulation, we develop an alternating optimization algorithm that iteratively updates the manifold parameters and estimates the noise shape parameter. This enables adaptive loss selection within a unified likelihood-based framework, without requiring prior specification of the noise characteristics. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of AMLE-SQMF in quadratic manifold fitting and its robustness to diverse noise distributions.

AI.tldr: Proposes AMLE-SQMF, an alternating maximum likelihood method for subspace-constrained quadratic matrix factorization that jointly estimates the quadratic manifold and the noise distribution through a generalized Gaussian residual model. It removes the need to prespecify a noise model or fixed loss.
AI.motivation: Existing quadratic manifold fitting methods use prescribed noise models or fixed loss functions, which limits their adaptability to varying noise characteristics.
AI.method: Residuals are modelled with a generalized Gaussian distribution whose shape parameter controls the tail behaviour and the associated fitting loss. The closed-form maximum likelihood estimator of the scale parameter gives a profile negative log-likelihood, and an alternating optimization updates the manifold parameters and estimates the shape parameter.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate effectiveness in quadratic manifold fitting and robustness to diverse noise distributions.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive loss selection within one likelihood-based framework lets the method fit manifolds without prior specification of noise characteristics.

title: PROLA: Principal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation for Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling
summary: High-resolution weather prediction is important for resolving local atmospheric patterns missed by coarse global forecasts. Large pretrained weather backbones have improved global forecasting, but adapting them to produce future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states remains challenging and costly. We formulate this setting as Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling (PSWD), a task that jointly refines spatial and temporal resolution while predicting future high-resolution trajectories. To this end, we propose a framework that decomposes prediction into spatial and temporal stages using a shared pretrained backbone, fixed numerical scaffolds, and lightweight residual heads. For backbone adaptation, we introduce PROLA (PRincipal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation), which allocates a fixed low-rank budget between pretrained weights' principal directions and their orthogonal complement. PROLA further rescales rank-1 optimizer updates using gradient signals, improving adaptation without increasing trainable rank. Experiments in the PSWD setting show that PROLA outperforms representative low-rank adaptation baselines. Further experiments across diverse datasets and tasks support the broader applicability of PROLA, showing that its benefits extend beyond the primary weather downscaling setting.

AI.tldr: Formulates predictive spatiotemporal weather downscaling (PSWD), which jointly refines spatial and temporal resolution to predict future high-resolution trajectories, and proposes PROLA, a low-rank adaptation that splits a fixed rank budget between the principal directions of pretrained weights and their orthogonal complement. PROLA outperforms representative low-rank adaptation baselines on PSWD and shows benefits on other datasets and tasks.
AI.motivation: Coarse global forecasts miss local atmospheric patterns, and adapting large pretrained weather backbones to produce future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states is challenging and costly.
AI.method: Prediction is decomposed into spatial and temporal stages using a shared pretrained backbone, fixed numerical scaffolds and lightweight residual heads. PROLA allocates the fixed low-rank budget between principal directions and the orthogonal complement, and rescales rank-1 optimizer updates using gradient signals without increasing trainable rank.
AI.result: PROLA outperforms representative low-rank adaptation baselines in the PSWD setting, and further experiments across diverse datasets and tasks show that its benefits extend beyond weather downscaling.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest PROLA is broadly applicable as an adaptation method beyond the primary weather setting.

title: When Sensors Fail: Coverage Auditing with Incomplete Sensor Records
comment: Concise author preprint; 3 pages, 1 table; no supplementary material
summary: Sensor outages can conceal prediction-interval coverage deficits behind acceptable marginal performance, while unavailable future readings leave some issued forecasts unscorable. We present a measurement-record audit that links issue-time outage duration, original target availability, and time-uniform statistical evidence. The audit retains complete forecast keys, batches all sensors and overlapping horizons at each measurement tick, and projects simultaneous covered-count and scored-count bounds onto a cumulative conditional expected coverage ratio. This target is distinguished from empirical coverage and outage-conditional population coverage. Selected traffic and air-quality results illustrate the gap between pooled and long-outage coverage; in METR-LA, only 7.6% of issued long-gap forecasts have originally observed targets. Of 30 primary sequential outage-state audits, 26 are inconclusive and four lack scored support. This concise presentation gives the core construction and selected aggregate evidence without the full experimental supplement.

AI.tldr: Presents a measurement-record audit that gives time-uniform bounds on a cumulative conditional expected coverage ratio for prediction intervals, accounting for sensor outages and unscorable forecasts. In METR-LA only 7.6% of issued long-gap forecasts have originally observed targets, and of 30 primary sequential outage-state audits, 26 are inconclusive and four lack scored support.
AI.motivation: Sensor outages can hide prediction-interval coverage deficits behind acceptable marginal performance, and unavailable future readings leave some issued forecasts unscorable.
AI.method: The audit links issue-time outage duration, original target availability and time-uniform statistical evidence. It retains complete forecast keys, batches all sensors and overlapping horizons at each measurement tick, and projects simultaneous covered-count and scored-count bounds onto a cumulative conditional expected coverage ratio, which is distinct from empirical coverage and from outage-conditional population coverage.
AI.result: Selected traffic and air-quality results illustrate the gap between pooled and long-outage coverage. In METR-LA only 7.6% of issued long-gap forecasts have originally observed targets, and of 30 primary sequential outage-state audits, 26 are inconclusive and four lack scored support.
AI.conclusion: Pooled coverage can conceal long-outage gaps, so the outage-conditioned view matters; the paper gives the core construction and aggregate evidence only, without the full experimental supplement.

title: When Credit Turns Against Tools: Transition-Aware Credit Assignment in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains language models through multi-turn tool interactions, yet their reasoning performance and tool-calling ability can decline during training. We trace this degradation to three coupled mechanisms: (1) tool-token imbalance produces negative overall tool credit when incorrect trajectories contain more tool tokens per turn than correct ones; (2) aggregation amplification can further strengthen this negative signal as token-mean aggregation gives longer incorrect trajectories greater weight in policy updates; and (3) failure-driven retries prolong trajectories as models tend to call tools again after execution errors, extending potential negative credit to recovery attempts. To counter this suppression, we propose Transition-Aware Credit Assignment (TACA), which targets the transition from reasoning to tool use through supervision of both call initiation and generation. Specifically, TACA uses Advantage Projection to enforce a nonnegative mean advantage on tool-call tokens within each prompt group through a minimal uniform shift. Additionally, TACA guides tool-use decisions with Decision Contrast, comparing rewards for tool-assisted and direct answers to the same prompt. Through Supervised Replay, it reinforces tool-call generation using calls from previously sampled correct trajectories. Across models and tasks, TACA improves performance and sustains more reliable tool interaction during training, raising mean accuracy over MT-GRPO on six reasoning benchmarks by 4.61 percentage points for Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3.61 for Qwen2.5-3B. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Traces the degradation of tool-using reasoning in agentic RL with verifiable rewards to three coupled mechanisms, and proposes TACA, Transition-Aware Credit Assignment, which raises mean accuracy over MT-GRPO on six reasoning benchmarks by 4.61 points for Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3.61 points for Qwen2.5-3B.
AI.motivation: Reasoning performance and tool-calling ability can decline during agentic RL training with multi-turn tool interactions.
AI.method: The authors identify tool-token imbalance, which yields negative overall tool credit, aggregation amplification from token-mean aggregation that favours longer incorrect trajectories, and failure-driven retries that extend negative credit to recovery attempts. TACA uses Advantage Projection to enforce a nonnegative mean advantage on tool-call tokens per prompt group through a minimal uniform shift, Decision Contrast to compare rewards for tool-assisted and direct answers, and Supervised Replay to reinforce tool-call generation from earlier correct trajectories.
AI.result: Across models and tasks TACA improves performance and sustains more reliable tool interaction during training. Mean accuracy over MT-GRPO on six reasoning benchmarks rises by 4.61 percentage points for Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3.61 for Qwen2.5-3B.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly supervising the transition from reasoning to tool use counters the suppression of tool credit that drives the training degradation.

title: Where Should a Gate Look? Input vs. State Gating in Diagonal State Space Models
summary: Modern state-space models owe much of their computational efficiency to their linear, often diagonal, dynamics. Classical recurrent neural networks instead allow nonlinear state-to-state interactions, which can be beneficial when memory updates need to depend on the past context. In this paper, we ask whether state feedback through a simple gate regulating memory updates can enhance the expressivity of diagonal state-space models. To investigate this question, we compare gates that depend on the current input, the recurrent state, or both. We establish a strict expressivity separation: for scalar models, state gating solves induction-head tasks for arbitrary vocabulary size and sequence length, whereas input gating fails on a finite instance under standard stability assumptions on the state transition matrix. Experiments show that state gating retains its advantage on induction-head tasks in higher-dimensional models, whereas input gating performs better on selective copying tasks. Together, our results show that even a simple, diagonal form of state-feedback gating can unlock capabilities unavailable to input-controlled models, while input and state gating offer complementary strengths and achieve the strongest overall performance when combined.

AI.tldr: Compares input, state and combined gating in diagonal state-space models and shows a strict expressivity separation: for scalar models, state gating solves induction-head tasks for arbitrary vocabulary size and sequence length, while input gating fails on a finite instance. Input gating performs better on selective copying, and combining both gives the strongest overall performance.
AI.motivation: Modern state-space models gain efficiency from linear, often diagonal dynamics, whereas classical RNNs allow nonlinear state-to-state interactions; the question is whether state feedback through a simple gate can add expressivity to diagonal models.
AI.method: Gates that depend on the current input, on the recurrent state, or on both are compared. The expressivity analysis covers scalar models under standard stability assumptions on the state transition matrix, and experiments test induction-head and selective copying tasks in higher-dimensional models.
AI.result: State gating retains its advantage on induction-head tasks in higher-dimensional models, whereas input gating performs better on selective copying, and combining input and state gating achieves the strongest overall performance.
AI.conclusion: Even a simple diagonal form of state-feedback gating unlocks capabilities unavailable to input-controlled models, and input and state gating are complementary.

title: OPSRL-SSP: Optimistic Posterior Sampling for Stochastic Shortest Path with Minimax-Optimal Regret
summary: We study online reinforcement learning for the stochastic shortest path (SSP) problem with unknown transition dynamics. Although existing posterior-sampling methods perform well empirically on SSPs, their regret guarantees do not achieve the minimax-optimal order. We address this limitation by proposing OPSRL-SSP, an optimistic posterior-sampling algorithm for the SSP setting. The algorithm operates in epochs and uses a logarithmic, time-dependent schedule for the number of posterior samples. To induce optimism, we augment the transition model with a pseudo-state assigned an optimistic boundary value. We establish a high-probability regret bound of $\tilde{O}(B_\star \sqrt{SAK} + B_\star S^2 A)$, where $B_\star$ is an upper bound on the expected cost of the optimal policy, $S$ and $A$ are the numbers of states and actions, respectively, and $K$ is the number of episodes. In addition, we extend the analysis to general zero-cost SSPs using a universal cost-perturbation argument. The leading term matches the minimax lower bound $\Omega(B_\star \sqrt{SAK})$, thereby addressing the open problem raised by Jafarnia-Jahromi et al. [19] for posterior sampling in the SSP setting.

AI.tldr: Proposes OPSRL-SSP, an optimistic posterior-sampling algorithm for stochastic shortest path problems with unknown transitions, with a high-probability regret bound whose leading term matches the minimax lower bound. The analysis also extends to general zero-cost SSPs.
AI.motivation: Posterior-sampling methods perform well empirically on SSPs, but their regret guarantees are not minimax-optimal, which leaves an open problem for posterior sampling in the SSP setting.
AI.method: The algorithm runs in epochs with a logarithmic, time-dependent schedule for the number of posterior samples, and induces optimism by augmenting the transition model with a pseudo-state assigned an optimistic boundary value. The extension to general zero-cost SSPs uses a universal cost-perturbation argument.
AI.result: The regret bound is O~(B* sqrt(SAK) + B* S^2 A), where B* bounds the expected cost of the optimal policy, S and A are the numbers of states and actions, and K is the number of episodes. The leading term matches the minimax lower bound Omega(B* sqrt(SAK)).
AI.conclusion: The result addresses the open problem raised by Jafarnia-Jahromi et al. for posterior sampling in SSPs by achieving minimax-optimal leading-order regret.

title: Spatial Harness: Grounding Spatial Reasoning in Executable World States with Physics Engines
summary: Spatial reasoning requires understanding how objects and observers are arranged in a scene and how their relations change with viewpoint or movement. Vision-language models (VLMs) typically perform both steps through model-internal reasoning, forming an implicit scene interpretation from partial views and imagining the consequences of spatial transformations. A misread scene can lead to a wrong answer, while even a correct interpretation does not ensure that imagined transformations satisfy spatial constraints. We introduce Spatial Harness, which represents scenes as explicit and executable world states to ground spatial reasoning in physics-engine feedback. A Perceiver integrates scene constraints extracted from the question with specialized visual estimates to place objects and cameras in a shared coordinate frame. The resulting state is instantiated in a physics engine, where a Reasoner executes viewpoint changes and uses computed measurements and rendered views to guide reasoning. We evaluate on MindCube, SAT, MMSI-Bench, and SpatialRGPT-Bench with open- and closed-weight VLMs. On MindCube, Spatial Harness improves Qwen3.5-27B from 52.70% to 71.14%, surpassing pySpatial by 7.52 percentage points. Given identical annotated object and camera poses, it reaches 98.25% versus 71.81% for model-internal reasoning. Code is publicly available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: Proposes Spatial Harness, which represents a scene as an executable world state instantiated in a physics engine, so that VLM spatial reasoning is grounded in physics-engine feedback. On MindCube it raises Qwen3.5-27B from 52.70% to 71.14%, 7.52 points above pySpatial.
AI.motivation: VLMs reason about spatial arrangements implicitly from partial views, so a misread scene leads to a wrong answer, and even a correct interpretation does not ensure that imagined transformations satisfy spatial constraints.
AI.method: A Perceiver integrates scene constraints extracted from the question with specialized visual estimates to place objects and cameras in a shared coordinate frame. The resulting state is instantiated in a physics engine, where a Reasoner executes viewpoint changes and uses computed measurements and rendered views to guide reasoning.
AI.result: Evaluated on MindCube, SAT, MMSI-Bench and SpatialRGPT-Bench with open- and closed-weight VLMs. On MindCube, Qwen3.5-27B improves from 52.70% to 71.14%, surpassing pySpatial by 7.52 points. Given identical annotated object and camera poses, it reaches 98.25% versus 71.81% for model-internal reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Executable, physics-checked world states can ground VLM spatial reasoning, and the oracle-pose comparison shows a large gap between model-internal reasoning and reasoning over the explicit state.

title: MG-Cache: Multi-Granularity Caching for Accelerating Diffusion Transformer Inference
comment: Published in Pacific Graphics 2026 (PG'26), this https URL
summary: Diffusion Transformer (DiT) models, while having become a powerful backbone for generative synthesis, suffer from high inference cost on generating high-resolution images. Diffusion caching has emerged as a promising acceleration technique to reduce inference cost. However, existing caching strategies fail to accurately identify the varying importance of different computational modules and rarely coordinate cache reusing across the timestep and layer granularities, making it difficult to control error accumulation. To address these limitations, we propose multi-granularity caching (MG-Cache) for DiTs, a novel and fully training-free approach to exploit computational redundancy both on timesteps and Transformer layers. Our core innovation contains a two-stage caching strategy: an offline timestep profiling analysis that identifies redundant timesteps for cache reuse, followed by an adaptive layer-wise caching strategy that combines input stability with importance of each Transformer layer to selectively cache stable Attention and MLP submodules. Extensive experiments on mainstream open-source DiT models validate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving significant acceleration while maintaining high fidelity to the uncached output, with up to a 4.18x acceleration on HunyuanVideo.

AI.tldr: Proposes MG-Cache, a training-free caching method for Diffusion Transformer inference that exploits redundancy across both timesteps and Transformer layers, reaching up to 4.18x acceleration on HunyuanVideo while staying close to uncached outputs.
AI.motivation: DiT inference is costly for high-resolution generation, and existing caching strategies fail to identify the varying importance of computational modules and rarely coordinate reuse across timestep and layer granularities, which makes error accumulation hard to control.
AI.method: A two-stage strategy: an offline timestep profiling analysis identifies redundant timesteps for cache reuse, followed by an adaptive layer-wise strategy that combines input stability with each layer's importance to selectively cache stable Attention and MLP submodules.
AI.result: Experiments on mainstream open-source DiT models show significant acceleration while maintaining high fidelity to the uncached output, with up to 4.18x acceleration on HunyuanVideo.
AI.conclusion: Coordinated multi-granularity caching offers a fully training-free route to faster DiT inference with controlled fidelity loss.

title: D3Tree: Learning to Prune Block-Diffusion Draft Trees for Efficient Verification
summary: Block-diffusion drafters propose a whole block of tokens in one forward pass, and draft trees built from their position-wise marginals increase the expected accepted length of speculative decoding. Every tree node occupies a query row in target verification, so under concurrent serving low-yield branches compete with other requests for verification capacity. Existing tree methods select verified nodes by draft probability under a fixed or cost-selected per-request budget, and thus always retain a prefix of the drafter's ranking. We present D3Tree, which learns which nodes of a block-diffusion draft tree are worth verifying. A tree-size head with 2H+2 parameters predicts each candidate's conditional survival from the draft state, the candidate embedding, and its draft log-probability. Thresholding the product of these scores along parent chains yields an ancestor-closed subtree whose size adapts to each request and decoding round. The head is trained on a frozen drafter with conditional labels on the full candidate tree; an optional joint mode also steers the drafter toward the retained reference path. At serving time, D3Tree verifies whole trees under light load and, under heavy load, allocates one batch-wide node budget by predicted survival, sized to the target's matrix-multiplication tiles. Retained trees share one ancestor-masked target pass, while construction, pruning, and scheduling run on the GPU and overlap with the host. Across six vision-language verifiers and 17 text and multimodal benchmarks, D3Tree is fastest in 70 of 72 load settings, with 3.2-4.0x speedup over autoregressive decoding for one request and 1.3-1.8x at 64 concurrent requests, where fixed-budget trees fall below autoregressive speed. Under a time-varying arrival trace, it has the lowest mean end-to-end latency in every arrival phase.

AI.tldr: D3Tree learns which nodes of a block-diffusion draft tree are worth verifying, pruning each request's tree per decoding round by predicted survival, and reaches 3.2-4.0x speedup over autoregressive decoding for one request and 1.3-1.8x at 64 concurrent requests.
AI.motivation: Every draft-tree node occupies a query row in target verification, so under concurrent serving low-yield branches compete with other requests for capacity, and existing tree methods keep a prefix of the drafter's probability ranking under a fixed or cost-selected budget, which leaves fixed-budget trees below autoregressive speed at high load.
AI.method: A tree-size head with 2H+2 parameters predicts each candidate's conditional survival from the draft state, the candidate embedding and its draft log-probability; thresholding the product of these scores along parent chains gives an ancestor-closed subtree, and under heavy load one batch-wide node budget is allocated by predicted survival and sized to the target's matrix-multiplication tiles, with retained trees sharing one ancestor-masked target pass.
AI.result: Across six vision-language verifiers and 17 text and multimodal benchmarks, D3Tree is fastest in 70 of 72 load settings, with 3.2-4.0x speedup over autoregressive decoding for one request and 1.3-1.8x at 64 concurrent requests, where fixed-budget trees fall below autoregressive speed; under a time-varying arrival trace it has the lowest mean end-to-end latency in every arrival phase.
AI.conclusion: Learning which draft-tree nodes to verify, instead of keeping a fixed-budget prefix of the drafter's ranking, makes speculative decoding with block-diffusion drafters adapt to concurrent serving load.

title: Self-Supervised Collapse Prevention with Score-Based Entropy Maximization
summary: Diffusion models have demonstrated the effectiveness of score-based objectives for generative modeling, yet their potential for self-supervised representation learning remains underexplored. We introduce Entropy-Based Regularization (EBReg), a framework that uses latent score estimation to regularize the latent distribution during self-supervised training. EBReg jointly learns an encoder and a latent score model, and utilizes the learned score to provide a diversity-preserving signal that prevents representational collapse. Motivated by a mutual-information lower bound, we formulate the objective as view alignment with smoothed marginal entropy maximization and optimize the marginal entropy without explicit density evaluation. The same score model can additionally be used at test time to refine corrupted representations toward the training latent distribution. Empirically, EBReg learns competitive representations on ImageNet-1K, achieving 75.57% linear-probe accuracy with ViT-L. Across diverse architectures, score-guided test-time adaptation further improves robustness on ImageNet-C, yielding an average relative accuracy gain of approximately 5%.

AI.tldr: EBReg is a self-supervised framework that uses latent score estimation to keep the representation distribution diverse and prevent collapse, and reuses the same score model for test-time refinement of corrupted representations.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-style score-based objectives are well established for generative modeling but remain underexplored for self-supervised representation learning, where representational collapse is a central risk.
AI.method: EBReg jointly learns an encoder and a latent score model, formulates the objective as view alignment with smoothed marginal entropy maximization motivated by a mutual-information lower bound, and optimizes the marginal entropy without explicit density evaluation; the learned score is also used at test time to move corrupted representations toward the training latent distribution.
AI.result: EBReg reaches 75.57% linear-probe accuracy on ImageNet-1K with ViT-L, and score-guided test-time adaptation improves robustness on ImageNet-C across diverse architectures, with an average relative accuracy gain of approximately 5%.
AI.conclusion: A learned latent score can serve both as a diversity-preserving regularizer that prevents collapse during self-supervised training and as a test-time tool for robustness.

title: The comparison of density estimation for transfer learning in Banach, Hilbert, Euclidean spaces
summary: Domain adaptation or DA methods are indispensable when target labels or computational resources are scarce, yet the domain kernel density and subspace alignment approaches completely assume a Hilbertian geometry. They measure distributional discrepancy with symmetric L2 divergences over Euclidean feature spaces or reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS). This preprint summarizes the manuscript Non-Hilbertian Domain Adaptation. Total Variation Alignment via L1 Density Regularization on Feature Manifolds, which proposes Banach Manifold Transfer Learning or BMTL. BMTL makes two coupled design decisions. The first one is that features are embedded on a geodesic manifold rather than treated as points of a flat Euclidean space, and the second one is that the density matching regularizer is formulated in an L1 Banach norm, whose minimization is equivalent, by Scheffe's theorem, to contracting the Total Variation or TV distance between domain densities, a bounded metric that weights all regions of the sample space uniformly. The L2 formulation, by contrast, squares deviations and therefore amplifies errors in the tails, over emphasizing density outliers that do not reflect meaningful distributional shift. Experiments on MNIST-USPS, COIL20, and Office+Caltech10 show consistent gains; the L1 variant beats an otherwise identical L2 ablation on every task, for example 92.44% vs. 89.80% on USPS->MNIST and surpasses the strongest baseline DMDA by +3.68% on average over twelve Office+Caltech transfers. This document situates the contribution with an explicit comparison of Euclidean, Hilbert, and Banach geometries.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Banach Manifold Transfer Learning (BMTL), which embeds features on a geodesic manifold and matches domain densities with an L1 Banach-norm regularizer equivalent to Total Variation distance, and it compares Euclidean, Hilbert and Banach geometries for domain adaptation.
AI.motivation: Domain kernel density and subspace alignment methods assume Hilbertian geometry and measure distribution shift with symmetric L2 divergences, which square deviations and so over-weight tail outliers that do not reflect meaningful distributional shift.
AI.method: BMTL makes two coupled design choices: features are treated as points on a geodesic manifold rather than in a flat Euclidean space, and the density matching regularizer is an L1 Banach-norm term whose minimization is equivalent by Scheffe's theorem to contracting the Total Variation distance between domain densities.
AI.result: Experiments on MNIST-USPS, COIL20 and Office+Caltech10 show consistent gains, the L1 variant beats an otherwise identical L2 ablation on every task (92.44% vs. 89.80% on USPS->MNIST), and it surpasses the strongest baseline DMDA by +3.68% on average over twelve Office+Caltech transfers.
AI.conclusion: Replacing the L2 density-matching term with an L1 Banach-norm formulation on a manifold gives more robust domain adaptation than the Hilbertian baselines, and the paper frames this as a case for non-Hilbertian geometry in transfer learning.

title: Computationally Efficient Offline Policy Optimization with All-Policy Linear Realizability
summary: We study offline policy optimization in finite-horizon Markov decision processes where every deterministic Markov policy has an action-value function linear in known features, with coefficient norm at most $B$. From independent complete trajectories of one unknown Markov behavior policy, and under all-policy occupancy coverage, we give an algorithm with $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ sample dependence and computational complexity polynomial in $\log(2+B)$. The algorithm performs exactly one convex regression per layer. Its stopped-return targets are the values of a single consistent Markov witness policy. A shared reference design and bounded prediction constraints convert fast clipped-regression error into pointwise confidence for the raw linear predictions. Truncated leverage controls the performance loss without requiring empirical covariance approximation at scale $B^{-2}$. Rounding confidence radii upward preserves the exact witness and yields a polynomial-time bit implementation for rational numerical inputs. The guarantees allow any fixed initial-state distribution; realizability and coverage need only be checked for deterministic policies. We also establish a covariance-coverage variant with uniform approximate realizability and polynomial dependence on $B$. A two-action lower bound shows that the accuracy exponent $2$ is necessary.

AI.tldr: The paper gives an offline policy optimization algorithm for finite-horizon MDPs with all-policy linear realizability that runs one convex regression per layer, with O~(eps^-2) sample dependence and computation polynomial in log(2+B).
AI.motivation: Offline policy optimization guarantees usually require strong coverage or realizability assumptions and costly computation, and the paper asks whether linear action-value realizability for every deterministic Markov policy can be exploited efficiently from one unknown behavior policy's trajectories.
AI.method: The algorithm performs exactly one convex regression per layer with stopped-return targets taken from a single consistent Markov witness policy; a shared reference design with bounded prediction constraints turns clipped-regression error into pointwise confidence, truncated leverage controls performance loss without empirical covariance approximation at scale B^-2, and rounding confidence radii upward yields a polynomial-time bit implementation.
AI.result: The method achieves O~(eps^-2) sample dependence and computational complexity polynomial in log(2+B) under all-policy occupancy coverage, works for any fixed initial-state distribution, requires realizability and coverage to be checked only for deterministic policies, and a two-action lower bound shows the accuracy exponent 2 is necessary; a covariance-coverage variant with polynomial dependence on B is also established.
AI.conclusion: Under all-policy linear realizability, offline policy optimization can be done with sample-optimal-exponent accuracy and polynomial computation, and the exponent of 2 is shown to be unimprovable.

title: CHANNELS4WORLD: An Environment-Scale Dataset for Wireless Foundation Models
summary: Wireless foundation models learn reusable representations across tasks, configurations, and deployment environments. Their pretraining requires environmental breadth, yet wireless datasets often sample few sites densely. We introduce Channels4World, a scene-centered dataset of 100,000 distinct outdoor RF scenes and a procedural method for generating them. Each scene links a generated environment and RF material assignments to 32 base-station (BS) positions, 16,384 UE positions, and aligned variable-length multipath and ordered interaction records at 3.5 and 7~GHz. The corpus comprises 52.43 billion physical BS-UE pairs, 104.86 billion frequency-specific evaluations, and a 29.14-TB packaged payload. Scene identity aligns geometry, placements, channels, and interactions across frequencies, allowing environmental breadth and within-scene observation density to vary independently. The public release offers predefined subsets at multiple scales and separate access to corpus components. A deterministic 90K/10K scene-level train-test split keeps both frequencies and all scene components together. We characterize morphology, RF materials, and transceiver placement across three generation profiles. Controlled propagation and path-retention analyses show that diffraction materially affects retained-link availability and multipath structure, while the retention policy reduces storage substantially with little loss in represented aggregate power. Under matched training exposure, models trained on broader scene collections perform better on held-out scenes, although an equal-episode control shows that scene count alone cannot explain the gain. By making environmental breadth explicit and controllable, Channels4World supports the development and evaluation of wireless foundation models for generalization across deployment environments.

AI.tldr: Channels4World is a dataset of 100,000 procedurally generated outdoor RF scenes linking geometry, materials, 32 base-station positions, 16,384 UE positions and multipath channel records at 3.5 and 7 GHz, intended for pretraining wireless foundation models.
AI.motivation: Wireless foundation models need environmental breadth in pretraining, but existing wireless datasets sample few sites densely, so they cover few deployment environments.
AI.method: The authors introduce a scene-centered dataset and a procedural generator that links each generated environment and its RF material assignments to base-station and UE placements and aligned variable-length multipath and ordered interaction records, with scene identity aligning data across frequencies, a deterministic 90K/10K scene-level train-test split, and a retention policy that reduces storage.
AI.result: The corpus has 52.43 billion physical BS-UE pairs, 104.86 billion frequency-specific evaluations and a 29.14-TB packaged payload; models trained on broader scene collections perform better on held-out scenes under matched training exposure, although an equal-episode control shows scene count alone does not explain the gain, and diffraction materially affects retained-link availability and multipath structure.
AI.conclusion: By making environmental breadth explicit and controllable, the dataset supports developing and evaluating wireless foundation models for generalization across deployment environments.

title: Learning to Rank Propagators in Constraint Programming
summary: The order in which propagators are executed can substantially affect the performance of constraint programming solvers, yet propagator priorities are typically determined by fixed, manually designed heuristics. In this work, we explore learning instance-dependent propagator priorities from static problem features. We formulate the task as a learning-to-rank problem, addressing the challenge that the quality of a priority assignment can be measured through solver runtime, while the desired priorities of individual propagators are not directly observable. A self-attention-based model jointly scores the propagators present in an instance and is trained using pairwise preferences derived from solver runtimes measured under randomized propagator priority assignments, with a Plackett-Luce-based ranking objective. Predicted rankings are mapped to the discrete priority levels of the Choco solver before search begins, without modifying its propagation or search procedures. We evaluate the approach on XCSP3 instances and demonstrate that propagator ordering can have a substantial impact on solving time. On a test set of 698 instances, picked out as most difficult by problem class, the learned priorities increase the number of solved instances from 634 to 654, reduce median solver runtime by 27.93%, and reduce aggregate penalized runtime (PAR1) by 12.65% compared with Choco's default priorities. We further observe that improvements vary across problem classes and show that a simple policy selecting between learned and default priorities further increases the number of solved instances. These results demonstrate the potential of learning instance-dependent propagator priorities to improve constraint programming performance, particularly on difficult instances.

AI.tldr: The paper learns instance-dependent propagator priorities for the Choco constraint programming solver from static problem features, using a self-attention ranking model trained on Plackett-Luce pairwise preferences from solver runtimes.
AI.motivation: Propagator execution order can strongly affect constraint programming solver performance, yet priorities are fixed by manually designed heuristics, and the desired priorities cannot be observed directly, only inferred from runtimes.
AI.method: A self-attention model jointly scores the propagators in an instance and is trained with a Plackett-Luce ranking objective on pairwise preferences derived from solver runtimes under randomized priority assignments; predicted rankings are mapped to Choco's discrete priority levels before search, without changing its propagation or search procedures.
AI.result: On a test set of 698 hard XCSP3 instances, the learned priorities increase solved instances from 634 to 654, reduce median runtime by 27.93% and PAR1 by 12.65% compared with Choco's default priorities, with gains varying across problem classes, and a simple policy that selects between learned and default priorities solves further instances.
AI.conclusion: Learning instance-dependent propagator priorities is a promising way to improve constraint programming performance, particularly on difficult instances.

title: How Much Training-Inference Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate?
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses, guided by a fixed teacher. Generating these responses is expensive, so systems use quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to reduce the cost. Both, however, introduce training-inference mismatch between the rollout engine and the model being trained. Such mismatch can destabilize reinforcement learning (RL), but its effects on OPD remain unclear. This paper investigates how much mismatch OPD tolerates, where its effects arise, and how training systems can use this tolerance. Measuring all mismatch sources on one scale, we examine quantization across three student-teacher pairs, with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair. OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, revealing an empirical mismatch budget. Both the quality cost of mismatch and the mismatch introduced by quantization depend on the model, with some layers particularly sensitive to reduced precision. In controlled comparisons, OPD remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL methods. Under weight noise, mismatch also shifts the prefixes reached during generation, introducing errors that per-token corrections cannot address. To put these findings into practice, we introduce a lightweight admission check that screens rollout configurations against a calibrated budget without requiring a full training run for each candidate. Model-specific FP8 recipes preserve training quality while providing capacity for at least $1.93\times$ as many KV-cache tokens as BF16. Combining FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches the same training quality $1.62\times$ sooner than synchronous BF16 training. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper measures how much training-inference mismatch on-policy distillation (OPD) tolerates, finds a mismatch budget beyond which quality degrades, and introduces an admission check plus FP8 recipes that allow more KV-cache tokens and faster training.
AI.motivation: OPD uses quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to cut generation cost, but both introduce training-inference mismatch that destabilizes RL, and its effect on OPD was unclear.
AI.method: The authors measure all mismatch sources on one scale, examining quantization across three student-teacher pairs with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair, and they introduce a lightweight admission check that screens rollout configurations against a calibrated budget without a full training run per candidate.
AI.result: OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL, and model-specific FP8 recipes preserve quality while providing at least 1.93x as many KV-cache tokens as BF16; combining FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches the same quality 1.62x sooner than synchronous BF16 training.
AI.conclusion: OPD has an empirical mismatch budget that can be calibrated and used to choose cheaper rollout configurations, so quantization and asynchrony can be adopted without loss of training quality.

title: MOMENT-DP: Momentum Aware Evaluation of Correlated Noise for Differentially Private Training
comment: 18 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Accepted to the Privacy in the Era of Large Opaque Models (PriLOM) Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Temporally correlated noise can substantially improve the utility of differentially private optimization, yet candidate mechanisms are commonly designed or evaluated using only partial information about the optimization process, such as workload structure, learning-rate schedules, or local curvature. We study whether persistent optimizer state provides additional information that can change the relative utility of privacy-valid correlated-noise mechanisms. We introduce MOMENT-DP, an optimizer-state-aware framework that models how temporally correlated privacy noise propagates through momentum-based optimization. For locally quadratic objectives, MOMENT-DP expresses privacy-induced final loss through an optimizer transfer operator that jointly captures curvature, learning-rate scheduling, momentum, and temporal noise covariance. NoiseCurve's curvature-aware quadratic criterion is recovered exactly as the zero-momentum, constant-learning-rate special case. Changing only momentum while holding curvature, schedule, privacy calibration, and candidate mechanisms fixed induces genuine mechanism-ranking reversals. The effect persists outside exact quadratic dynamics in per-example-clipped private logistic regression, while remaining unresolved in the neural regime we study. These results establish optimizer state as an under-modeled, decision-relevant axis in evaluating temporally correlated privacy noise.

AI.tldr: MOMENT-DP is an optimizer-state-aware framework for evaluating temporally correlated privacy noise in differentially private training, showing that momentum can reverse the ranking of noise mechanisms that curvature-only criteria would give.
AI.motivation: Correlated-noise mechanisms for differentially private optimization are usually designed or evaluated with partial information such as workload structure, learning-rate schedules or local curvature, without the persistent optimizer state.
AI.method: For locally quadratic objectives, MOMENT-DP expresses the privacy-induced final loss through an optimizer transfer operator that jointly captures curvature, learning-rate schedule, momentum and temporal noise covariance; NoiseCurve's curvature-aware criterion is recovered as the zero-momentum, constant-learning-rate special case.
AI.result: Changing only momentum, with curvature, schedule, privacy calibration and candidate mechanisms held fixed, induces genuine mechanism-ranking reversals; the effect persists in per-example-clipped private logistic regression and remains unresolved in the neural regime studied.
AI.conclusion: Optimizer state is an under-modeled, decision-relevant axis for evaluating temporally correlated privacy noise, so mechanism choices should account for momentum.

title: One-Shot Hierarchical Federated Clustering for Distributed Non-IID Biomedical Data Analysis
summary: In multi-institutional biomedical data analysis, comprehensive disease profiles are often fragmented across different data silos. Furthermore, local data distributions typically exhibit varying levels of granularity or even complex nested structures. Although Hierarchical Clustering (HC) is a powerful tool for exploring such data topologies, its cumbersome recursive process incurs prohibitive computational overhead and renders it highly susceptible to privacy leakage. This paper, therefore, introduces an efficient one-shot hierarchical FC framework that performs client-end (institutions) distribution exploration and server-end distribution aggregation through one-way prototype-level communication from clients to the server. Although the designed one-shot prototype transmission guarantees minimal computational overhead and mitigates privacy risks, it inevitably incurs information loss. To counteract this, a multi-granular competitive learning mechanism is proposed on the server to fuse the clusterlets, effectively maximizing the retention and mining of global distribution topologies under limited, one-way communication constraints. It turns out that the complex cluster distributions across clients can be efficiently explored, and extensive experiments comparing state-of-the-art methods on public datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed framework in balancing robust clustering, privacy preservation, and computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a one-shot hierarchical federated clustering framework in which clients send prototypes once to a server that fuses them with multi-granular competitive learning, to cluster non-IID biomedical data across institutions.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical clustering is useful for multi-institution biomedical data with nested structure, but its recursive process has prohibitive computational cost and is susceptible to privacy leakage, while data are fragmented across silos with varying granularity.
AI.method: Clients perform local distribution exploration and send one-way prototype-level communication to the server; a multi-granular competitive learning mechanism on the server fuses the resulting clusterlets to recover global distribution topology under the one-way communication constraint.
AI.result: The abstract reports that extensive experiments on public datasets, compared with state-of-the-art methods, demonstrate superiority in balancing robust clustering, privacy preservation and computational efficiency, without giving specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: One-shot prototype communication with server-side multi-granular fusion offers a practical trade-off between clustering quality, privacy and cost for federated hierarchical clustering.

title: Regret without Optimal-Arm Feedback under Reward-Dependent Delays
comment: 45 pages, 3 figures. Code and data are included as ancillary files
summary: We study stochastic bandits with reward-dependent delays, possibly infinite, whose reports omit the originating round. For each $c\in[0,1)$, Balanced Historical Optimism (BHO) has a delay term controlled by the largest suboptimal-arm quantile at level $1-c\Delta_i$, without requiring optimal-arm reports. Lower bounds give an inverse-square slack cost in the logarithmic statistical regime and linear minimax regret at $c=1$. A family with growing $K$ forces worst-case regret $\Omega(G\log K)$ for every learner, where $G=\max_i\Delta_i h_i$ is the largest gap-weighted suboptimal cutoff. Pending-triggered balance preserves BHO's weighted-cutoff bound for $c<1$ and attains the historical-greedy exploration coefficient with deterministic rewards, a unique optimum and fixed bounded delays. Gap-weighted comparisons and experiments show when shared waiting helps and what balanced exploration costs.

AI.tldr: The paper studies stochastic bandits with reward-dependent delays whose reports omit the originating round, and proposes Balanced Historical Optimism (BHO) and a pending-triggered balance variant, with lower bounds showing linear minimax regret at c=1.
AI.motivation: Existing delayed-bandit treatments assume feedback can be attributed to its originating round, but with reward-dependent, possibly infinite delays and reports that omit the round, the optimal arm's feedback may not be observable, so a method must work without optimal-arm reports.
AI.method: BHO uses for each c in [0,1) a delay term controlled by the largest suboptimal-arm quantile at level 1-c*Delta_i, and a pending-triggered balance variant preserves its weighted-cutoff bound for c<1; the analysis uses gap-weighted comparisons.
