AI.result: Lower bounds give an inverse-square slack cost in the logarithmic regime and linear minimax regret at c=1; a family with growing K forces worst-case regret Omega(G log K) for every learner, where G is the largest gap-weighted suboptimal cutoff; with deterministic rewards, a unique optimum and fixed bounded delays, the variant attains the historical-greedy exploration coefficient.
AI.conclusion: Without optimal-arm feedback, regret under reward-dependent delays is characterized by a gap-weighted cutoff, and balanced exploration recovers strong guarantees only in the regime where c is below 1.

title: JoMoHa: Joint Model--Harness Optimization with Reinforcement Learning
summary: The performance of language agents depends jointly on model weights and the harness. Optimizing either alone can be constrained by the other component, limiting overall performance gains. Our analysis of naive alternating training reveals progressive incompatibility between the model and harness, which increasingly interferes with task execution and may also undermine model training, leading to performance degradation. To coordinate the evolution of models and harnesses, we introduce JoMoHa, to our knowledge the first framework to jointly train an executable harness generation policy and a task execution policy through reinforcement learning. JoMoHa outperforms the evaluated weight-only and harness-only baselines and achieves the highest success rates among the evaluated methods on ALFWorld, WebShop, and DBBench, averaging 70.3% and reaching 97.0% on ALFWorld. By learning both task execution and runtime improvement from its own generated trajectories, JoMoHa performs recursive self-improvement (RSI).

AI.tldr: JoMoHa jointly trains an executable harness generation policy and a task execution policy with reinforcement learning, reporting higher success rates than weight-only and harness-only baselines on ALFWorld, WebShop and DBBench.
AI.motivation: The performance of language agents depends on both model weights and the harness, but optimizing either alone is limited by the other, and naive alternating training shows progressive incompatibility between model and harness that degrades performance.
AI.method: JoMoHa is a framework that trains a harness generation policy and a task execution policy jointly through reinforcement learning, learning both task execution and runtime improvement from the agent's own generated trajectories, which the authors call recursive self-improvement (RSI).
AI.result: JoMoHa outperforms the evaluated weight-only and harness-only baselines and achieves the highest success rates among the evaluated methods on ALFWorld, WebShop and DBBench, averaging 70.3% and reaching 97.0% on ALFWorld.
AI.conclusion: Coordinating the co-evolution of model and harness through joint RL is a viable route to recursive self-improvement of language agents.

title: Data-informed Adaptation of Foundation Models for Causal Effect Estimation
summary: Due to the fundamental problem of causal inference -- the impossibility of observing counterfactual outcomes -- there is always a gap between the training goal (outcome, propensity) and the inference target (CATE, ATE). Traditional causal effect estimation revolves around setting assumptions, selecting identification strategies, and choosing causal estimators, while more recently, Causal Foundation Models (CFMs), built on Prior-Data-Fitted Networks (PFNs), ease this process by pretraining on massive synthetic prior datasets. Despite their success, such amortization makes causal inference less transparent, obscuring which assumptions the model implicitly relies on for a given dataset. The high diversity of real-world data-generating processes (DGPs) and Structural Causal Models (SCMs) makes it hard to know, a priori, which causal inference strategy is compatible with a given dataset. In this work, we focus on this compatibility between an observational dataset and method-specific assumptions, and find that geometric characteristics of data embeddings -- specifically, the variogram -- provide a useful signal of whether a given causal estimation strategy is appropriate. We develop MoE-Learner, a mixture-of-causal-experts framework that embeds a dataset under multiple assumption-specific views and uses the variogram as a counterfactual-free router to assess each expert's validity. Rather than eliminating causal assumptions, this shifts their validation from a fixed, a priori choice to a criterion that can be checked directly from data geometry. MoE-Learner achieves the best average rank on benchmark datasets (IHDP, ACIC, Lalonde). Being orthogonal to (causal) foundation models, our method builds a bridge from data characteristics to causal estimation strategy rather than proposing another CFM.

AI.tldr: MoE-Learner is a mixture-of-causal-experts framework that uses the variogram of data embeddings as a counterfactual-free router to check whether each causal estimation strategy's assumptions fit a dataset, achieving the best average rank on IHDP, ACIC and Lalonde.
AI.motivation: Causal Foundation Models amortize causal inference through pretraining on synthetic priors, which makes it opaque which assumptions a given dataset implicitly relies on, and the compatibility of a dataset with method-specific assumptions is hard to know a priori.
AI.method: The framework embeds a dataset under multiple assumption-specific views and uses the variogram, a geometric property of data embeddings, as a router to assess each expert's validity without counterfactual outcomes, so assumptions are validated from data geometry rather than fixed in advance.
AI.result: MoE-Learner achieves the best average rank on the benchmark datasets IHDP, ACIC and Lalonde.
AI.conclusion: Validating causal assumptions from data geometry offers a bridge from dataset characteristics to estimation strategy, and the method is orthogonal to causal foundation models rather than a competing one.

title: ConvLUT: Rethinking Convolutional Architectures for Ultra-Low-Latency LUT-Based Inference
summary: Lookup-table (LUT)-based neural networks (NNs) offer a compelling path to ultra-low-latency inference on FPGAs. However, existing LUT-based neural networks have largely been restricted to MLP-style topologies, leaving structured vision and audio tasks underexplored. We present ConvLUT, a family of fully unrolled LUT-mappable convolutional architectures targeting the MLPerf Tiny benchmarks. It is comprised of a standard convolutional model built around a hierarchical tree of LUTs and a depthwise separable model following the MobileNet design philosophy. These architectures are enabled by four key contributions: a unified LUT-based convolutional framework supporting standard, depthwise, and pointwise convolutions under explicit fan-in constraints; a LUT-tree that addresses the $k^2c$ receptive field dimensionality bottleneck; a channel-partitioned LUT pooling layer that replaces conventional spatial pooling; and a hardware-aware iterative pruning strategy for stable convergence at scale. Evaluated on CIFAR-10, Visual Wake Words, and Keyword Spotting, ConvLUT achieves competitive accuracy with fully unrolled inference latencies below $\sim 50$ ns. On CIFAR-10 it reaches at least a $8844\times$ latency reduction over non-logic-based prior implementations, and outperforms existing MLP-style LUT-based models on the same task by at least $20$ pp in test accuracy.

AI.tldr: ConvLUT is a family of fully unrolled, LUT-mappable convolutional architectures for FPGA inference that reaches competitive accuracy on CIFAR-10, Visual Wake Words and Keyword Spotting with unrolled latencies below about 50 ns.
AI.motivation: LUT-based neural networks for ultra-low-latency FPGA inference have been largely restricted to MLP-style topologies, leaving structured vision and audio tasks underexplored.
AI.method: ConvLUT combines a standard convolutional model built around a hierarchical LUT tree with a depthwise separable model following MobileNet design, using a unified LUT-based convolutional framework under explicit fan-in constraints, a LUT tree that addresses the k^2c receptive field bottleneck, a channel-partitioned LUT pooling layer in place of spatial pooling, and hardware-aware iterative pruning.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10 ConvLUT reaches at least an 8844x latency reduction over non-logic-based prior implementations and outperforms existing MLP-style LUT-based models on the same task by at least 20 percentage points in test accuracy, with fully unrolled inference latencies below about 50 ns across the evaluated tasks.
AI.conclusion: Convolutional LUT architectures make ultra-low-latency FPGA inference viable for structured vision and audio tasks, not only MLP-style topologies.

title: Detecting Common Golfing Faults Using AI and Video-Derived Biomechanical Features
summary: Understanding how an athlete moves can improve both technique and safety, yet outside the laboratory technique is still assessed by eye. We present a pipeline that detects named golf swing faults from ordinary video, without markers or calibration. Instead of learning end to end, it tracks body pose and the clubhead in a body-centered frame, and classifies the biomechanical quantities a coach would measure, such as the height of the clubhead above the swing plane, with shallow boosted trees. We demonstrate the approach on two common faults, coming over-the-top (OTT) and early-extension (EE). On 160 swings and 143 swings from public sources it detects OTT and EE with a cross-validated ROC-AUC of 0.975 and 0.911 respectively. Because every feature is a biomechanical quantity a coach already uses, measured at a known phase of the downswing, each decision can be traced to the signals and the moments of the swing that drove it. The signals the model relies on most are the same ones a coach checks when diagnosing these faults. The pipeline processes phone video on a consumer laptop in seconds, so it could feasibly be developed into an app for golfers of all abilities and extended to other sports in which technique is judged against a biomechanical reference.

AI.tldr: The paper detects two golf swing faults, over-the-top (OTT) and early extension (EE), from ordinary phone video by tracking body pose and the clubhead and classifying biomechanical features with shallow boosted trees.
AI.motivation: Golf technique is assessed by eye outside the laboratory, and end-to-end learned classifiers would not expose the biomechanical quantities a coach uses to judge a swing.
AI.method: The pipeline tracks body pose and the clubhead in a body-centered frame without markers or calibration, computes quantities a coach would measure, such as the height of the clubhead above the swing plane, at a known phase of the downswing, and classifies them with shallow boosted trees.
AI.result: Cross-validated ROC-AUC is 0.975 for OTT on 160 swings and 0.911 for EE on 143 swings from public sources, and the pipeline processes phone video on a consumer laptop in seconds.
AI.conclusion: Because every feature is a coach-recognized biomechanical quantity, each decision can be traced to the signals and swing moments that drove it, which suggests extension to an app and to other sports judged against a biomechanical reference.

title: Hydra: Towards Transferable Multi-Task Learning on Temporal Graphs
summary: Real-world evolving networks are naturally modeled as temporal graphs (TGs), where capturing temporal dynamics is essential for predicting future graph properties that support downstream decision-making. Existing temporal graph methods have been developed primarily for single-task prediction, and little is known about their generalization across tasks or transfer to unseen networks. This leaves the challenge of multi-task graph property prediction in TGs largely open. We address this challenge by introducing Hydra, a novel architecture that integrates local connectivity features from temporal GNNs with a spectral learning module that captures global connectivity patterns. This design enables joint learning of local and global information under a multi-task objective. In multi-task classification, Hydra achieves an 8.9% relative gain in AUC over the strongest competitor. In multi-task regression, Hydra achieves competitive results in all three tasks, while obtaining the best results in two tasks with a 8.2% relative gain in MAE compared to the strongest baseline. Moreover, Hydra delivers these gains with a 22% reduction in training time compared to temporal transfer models. These results provide the first systematic evidence that multi-task transferable learning on temporal graphs is effective. By delivering consistent top-ranked performance, Hydra highlights multi-task training on temporal graphs as a promising direction toward adaptable foundation models for temporal graphs.

AI.tldr: Hydra is a temporal graph architecture that combines temporal GNN local connectivity features with a spectral module for global patterns, trained under a multi-task objective, and reports gains over the strongest competitors on multi-task classification and regression.
AI.motivation: Temporal graph methods have been developed mainly for single-task prediction, and their generalization across tasks or transfer to unseen networks is largely unknown, so multi-task graph property prediction remains open.
AI.method: Hydra integrates local connectivity features from temporal GNNs with a spectral learning module that captures global connectivity patterns, enabling joint learning of local and global information under a multi-task objective.
AI.result: In multi-task classification Hydra achieves an 8.9% relative AUC gain over the strongest competitor; in multi-task regression it is competitive on all three tasks and best on two, with an 8.2% relative MAE gain over the strongest baseline, while cutting training time by 22% compared with temporal transfer models.
AI.conclusion: The results give first systematic evidence that multi-task transferable learning on temporal graphs is effective, pointing toward adaptable foundation models for temporal graphs.

title: Boundary Mass in Feature Space as a Label-Budget Diagnostic for Representations
summary: Low-label transfer is often decided by a practical question: after a representation looks useful, how many labels are still needed to learn the downstream boundary? Transferability and probe-quality scores characterize global alignment, likelihood, margins, and calibration. Boundary-near target mass complements these diagnostics by measuring the ambiguous regions where scarce labels are most costly. We propose effective boundary complexity, a label-budget diagnostic for frozen representations and linear probes. It measures mass in a thin strip around the learned boundary and normalizes it by class balance, so dense ambiguous regions and predicted-class imbalance are both counted. We prove that, under a smooth representation map, density change and tangential surface change cancel at first order, leaving boundary-normal stretch or compression as the governing factor. This yields a cached-feature estimator that fits a probe on one split and counts independent held-out features near its boundary. Experiments support the diagnostic at three levels. Controlled transformations match the predicted law across 74 maps with 0.38% median relative error. On real frozen features, normal-direction changes move both measured boundary mass and label demand, while tangent controls preserve the first-order coefficient. A differentiable surrogate reduces measured complexity by 16-36% at matched top-1 utility. Finally, CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet experiments support boundary mass as a second-stage diagnostic for near-tied representations. Five-way experiments show strong OvR-interface backbone-ranking agreement (Spearman 0.872), while acquisition experiments show high correlations between initial boundary mass and realized label budgets across three sampling policies (0.779-0.830). Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes effective boundary complexity, a label-budget diagnostic that measures probability mass in a thin strip around a linear probe's decision boundary in frozen representation space, normalized by class balance.
AI.motivation: Transferability and probe-quality scores capture global alignment, likelihood, margins and calibration but not the ambiguous regions where scarce labels are most costly, so the number of labels needed to learn the downstream boundary is not directly measured.
AI.method: The diagnostic counts independent held-out features in a thin strip around a probe fitted on one split, normalized by class balance, using a cached-feature estimator; the authors prove that under a smooth representation map, density change and tangential surface change cancel at first order, leaving boundary-normal stretch or compression as the governing factor.
AI.result: Controlled transformations match the predicted law across 74 maps with 0.38% median relative error; normal-direction changes move both measured boundary mass and label demand; a differentiable surrogate reduces measured complexity by 16-36% at matched top-1 utility; five-way experiments show OvR-interface backbone-ranking agreement with Spearman 0.872, and initial boundary mass correlates with realized label budgets at 0.779-0.830 across three sampling policies.
AI.conclusion: Boundary mass is a useful second-stage diagnostic for near-tied representations and a predictor of label budget, complementing global transferability scores.

title: Data Manipulation Attacks Against Machine Learning Integrated Cyber-Physical Systems
summary: There is a well-established body of work demonstrating that individual machine learning (ML) algorithms can be manipulated or deceived. However, in many real-world systems, multiple ML algorithms are composed to enable automated decision-making, particularly in Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS). Often such systems use a composition of vision, planning, and other ML models to affect their internal state and ultimate take actions in the physical world. While there is a huge literature on the (in)security of ML algorithms, it is not immediately clear how an attacker might leverage their ability to trick individual learners when attacking the composition as a whole. We develop methods for creating an attack policy (a mapping from state to attack) for a data-manipulating attacker affecting a CPS or other state-machine-based AI compositions. We describe our framework, a basic threat model and corresponding methods for computing an optimal attack policy, as well as planned extensions. The goal of this work-in-progress paper is to stimulate conversation and forge new collaborations regarding the security of compositional learning.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a framework for computing optimal data-manipulation attack policies against compositions of ML components in cyber-physical systems, presented as a work-in-progress with a basic threat model.
AI.motivation: Individual ML algorithms are known to be vulnerable to manipulation, but CPS compose vision, planning and other models to drive physical actions, and it is unclear how an attacker would exploit the composition rather than one learner.
AI.method: The authors define an attack policy as a mapping from system state to attack for a data-manipulating attacker of a CPS or other state-machine-based AI composition, describe a framework and basic threat model, and give methods for computing an optimal attack policy, with planned extensions.
AI.result: The abstract reports a framework and methods for computing optimal attack policies but gives no experimental results.
AI.conclusion: Attacks on compositions of learned components are a distinct security concern, and the work aims to stimulate discussion and collaboration on compositional learning security.

title: Probing Transformer Representations Layer by Layer, Module by Module
summary: Which representation should be probed in a transformer-based foundation model? Recent work shows that the standard practice of probing the final layer is often suboptimal, as intermediate layers can provide better features. Yet, representations are still largely studied along depth alone, treating each transformer block as an atomic unit. In this work, we analyze transformer representations layer by layer, module by module. Through more than 144,000 linear probing evaluations of vision foundation models (VFMs) and large language models (LLMs), we show that layer and module choices should be considered jointly: the best layer-module pair yields substantially larger gains over the final-layer residual stream than the best layer with the residual stream fixed. Moreover, module performance can vary substantially across layers, showing that useful representations cannot be characterized by depth alone. Building on these findings, we evaluate simple fixed probing strategies: the final-layer feedforward activation (Act@100) for vision and the second normalization layer at 60% depth (LN2@60) for language. These strategies improve over the probing baseline in a majority of evaluations and recover, on average, 42% and 86% of the gains from probing the best layer-module pair for vision and language, respectively. For VFMs, these gains increase with the transfer difficulty between pretraining and downstream data.

AI.tldr: Through more than 144,000 linear probing evaluations, the paper shows that the best layer-module pair in transformers beats the final-layer residual stream, and proposes fixed probing strategies Act@100 for vision and LN2@60 for language that recover much of that gain.
AI.motivation: Probing usually uses the final layer, and although intermediate layers can help, representations have been studied by depth alone, treating each transformer block as an atomic unit.
AI.method: The authors run layer-by-module linear probing across vision foundation models and large language models and evaluate simple fixed strategies: the final-layer feedforward activation (Act@100) for vision and the second normalization layer at 60 percent depth (LN2@60) for language.
AI.result: The best layer-module pair yields substantially larger gains over the final-layer residual stream than the best layer with the residual stream fixed; the fixed strategies beat the probing baseline in a majority of evaluations and recover on average 42% of the gains for vision and 86% for language relative to probing the best layer-module pair, with vision gains rising with transfer difficulty.
AI.conclusion: Layer and module choices should be considered jointly, and the simple fixed strategies offer a practical improvement over final-layer probing.

title: UTOPI: Efficient Egocentric Long-Video Understanding in AR via User-Guided Token Pre-Compression
summary: As long-video understanding gains increasing attention, augmented reality (AR) devices are emerging as a compelling deployment platform. However, egocentric videos exhibit significant temporal redundancy, imposing substantial memory and computational burdens on resource-constrained AR hardware. To address this challenge, we introduce UTOPI, a plug-and-play pre-compression module designed specifically for egocentric long videos on AR platforms. First, we leverage user motion signals to estimate inter-frame overlap and propose a viewpoint-shift-invariant pruning algorithm. Second, we exploit eye-tracking sensors to identify user fixations, enabling the separation of attended foreground content from background and its preferential retention via a fine-tuned neural network-based adjustment mechanism. Across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, UTOPI achieves up to 95% compression while preserving performance. Code and project page are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: UTOPI is a plug-and-play pre-compression module for egocentric long-video understanding on AR devices that uses user motion and eye-tracking signals to prune redundant frames and keep attended content, achieving up to 95% compression while preserving performance.
AI.motivation: Egocentric videos have heavy temporal redundancy, which imposes substantial memory and compute burdens on resource-constrained AR hardware.
AI.method: UTOPI estimates inter-frame overlap from user motion signals with a viewpoint-shift-invariant pruning algorithm, and uses eye-tracking to identify fixations, separating attended foreground from background and preferentially retaining the foreground via a fine-tuned neural network-based adjustment mechanism.
AI.result: Across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, UTOPI achieves up to 95% compression while preserving performance.
AI.conclusion: Sensor-guided pre-compression that uses user motion and gaze is a practical way to make long egocentric video understanding feasible on AR devices.

title: Actions Should EARN Their Credit: Test-Time Adaptation and Route Consolidation for Frozen LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents can use feedback from repeated attempts to improve their decisions without updating model parameters. However, positive action credits can continue to favor actions that repeatedly achieve the same score, even when higher scores are achievable. Under a fixed interaction budget, trying new actions in the final attempts can also lower performance. We introduce EARN, a method that uses past experience to guide further progress and retain earlier performance through conditional reuse of effective action sequences. EARN reduces action credits for reaching scores repeatedly attained in earlier episodes and assigns larger credits to action segments that reach higher scores. These credits adjust the probabilities of LLM-proposed actions. During the final episodes, EARN directly replays stored actions when the current context matches the recorded context and the actions remain available, bypassing LLM candidate generation. We evaluate performance at the end of the interaction budget using the average score over the final four episodes. Across Jericho, ScienceWorld, and Crafter, EARN achieves the best score on this metric in 31 of 33 task--budget settings among the evaluated methods, including ties. Across the evaluated Jericho budgets, replay bypasses 78.9--86.3\% of candidate-generation calls in the final four episodes, averaged across games.

AI.tldr: EARN is a test-time adaptation method for frozen LLM agents that reshapes action credits to avoid repeated scores, replays stored action sequences in final episodes, and achieves the best final-four-episode average score in 31 of 33 task-budget settings on Jericho, ScienceWorld and Crafter.
AI.motivation: Positive action credits keep favoring actions that repeatedly reach the same score even when higher scores are achievable, and under a fixed interaction budget, exploring new actions in the final attempts can lower performance.
AI.method: EARN reduces credits for scores already attained in earlier episodes and gives larger credits to action segments reaching higher scores, adjusting the probabilities of LLM-proposed actions; in the final episodes it replays stored actions when the current context matches the recorded one and the actions remain available, bypassing LLM candidate generation.
AI.result: EARN achieves the best average score over the final four episodes in 31 of 33 task-budget settings among the evaluated methods, including ties, across Jericho, ScienceWorld and Crafter, and replay bypasses 78.9-86.3% of candidate-generation calls in the final four episodes, averaged across games.
AI.conclusion: Reusing past effective action sequences through reweighted credits and conditional replay lets frozen LLM agents keep earlier performance and make further progress within a fixed budget.

title: Building heterogeneous multistep workflows in automated microscopy: reward design and knowledge transfer for autonomous structure property discovery
summary: Autonomous microscopy can turn fast acquisition into scientific progress when it decides not only where to measure, but also what information to acquire, at what scan rate, and when to recalibrate the instrument. We develop a budget constrained framework for such multistep structure-property workflows. It combines explicit scientific rewards, action costs, instrument observation models, transfer of pre experiment knowledge into the online campaign, and evaluation kept independent of the controller. The transferred knowledge includes predictor accuracy and computational cost, empirical learner maturity functions that weight model-derived rewards, and drift characteristics established before controller training. Using a real electron energy-loss spectroscopy dataset, we run two complementary campaigns. In the first, the controller chooses between imaging and spectroscopy, image size, and scan speed. In the second, the instrument drifts and the controller also decides when to recalibrate. The campaigns show that response discovery and structure-property learning favor different surrogate models and acquisition strategies. They also show that simple acquisition rules form strong, practical baselines. Independent error analysis reveals where model uncertainty is and is not a reliable learning signal. In the drift campaign, explicit registration greatly improves positional accuracy, and the framework measures what this costs in spectroscopy throughput. Together, these results provide a reproducible way to design, compare, and audit autonomous experiments, and they define what microscopes must provide for deployment: independently executable actions, characterized scan and detector responses, timestamped registration telemetry, and complete action records.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a budget-constrained framework for autonomous electron microscopy workflows that choose between imaging and spectroscopy, scan settings and recalibration, using explicit scientific rewards, action costs and transferred pre-experiment knowledge, tested on a real electron energy-loss spectroscopy dataset.
AI.motivation: Autonomous microscopy has to decide not only where to measure but also what information to acquire, at what scan rate and when to recalibrate; the abstract does not state specific shortcomings of prior methods.
AI.method: A controller is trained under a budget with explicit scientific rewards, action costs, instrument observation models and transfer of pre-experiment knowledge (predictor accuracy and cost, learner maturity functions that weight model-derived rewards, and drift characteristics), with evaluation kept independent of the controller.
AI.result: In two campaigns on a real electron energy-loss spectroscopy dataset, response discovery and structure-property learning favour different surrogate models and acquisition strategies, simple acquisition rules are strong practical baselines, and explicit registration greatly improves positional accuracy under drift at a measured cost in spectroscopy throughput; independent error analysis shows where model uncertainty is and is not a reliable learning signal.
AI.conclusion: The framework gives a reproducible way to design, compare and audit autonomous experiments and specifies what microscopes must provide for deployment: independently executable actions, characterized scan and detector responses, timestamped registration telemetry and complete action records.

title: Daily Emergency Call Volume Forecasting using Univariate and Multivariate TimeGPT
comment: Keywords: Emergency calls; Prehospital emergency services; Time-series forecasting; Foundation models; TimeGPT; Univariate forecast; Multivariate forecast
summary: This study investigates the potential of TimeGPT, a pretrained foundation model for timeseries, for forecasting daily emergency call volumes. Real-world emergency call data, comprising 2,101 daily observations, are used to evaluate both univariate and multivariate forecasting settings under one-step-ahead and seven-day multi-step-ahead scenarios. The multivariate forecasting incorporates temporal, meteorological, demographic, and socioeconomic variables. A chronological training, validation, and test split is adopted to prevent information leakage, while hyperparameters are selected using the validation set through grid search and early stopping when applicable. Forecasting performance is evaluated using multiple error metrics. Its forecasting performance is compared with several established forecasting approaches, including Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average with Exogenous Regressors (SARIMAX), Poisson regression (PR), Negative Binomial regression (NBR), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM). The results show that SARIMAX achieves the best overall performance in the univariate setting. In the multivariate setting, NBR and PR provide best performance. These findings indicate that the large-scale pretraining of TimeGPT do not necessarily translate into superior forecasting accuracy for emergency call volumes. Frugal methods trained solely on the available data remain better for this application.

AI.tldr: The study tests whether TimeGPT, a pretrained time-series foundation model, forecasts daily emergency call volumes better than established methods, and finds that frugal models trained only on the available data perform better in this application.
AI.motivation: Foundation models for time series are assumed to transfer well, but their accuracy on emergency call volume forecasting, with temporal, meteorological, demographic and socioeconomic covariates, had not been established against classical baselines.
AI.method: TimeGPT is evaluated in univariate and multivariate settings on 2,101 daily observations under one-step-ahead and seven-day multi-step-ahead scenarios, with a chronological train, validation and test split, validation-based grid search and early stopping, and compared with SARIMAX, Poisson regression, Negative Binomial regression, XGBoost, MLP and LSTM.
AI.result: SARIMAX gives the best overall performance in the univariate setting, while Negative Binomial regression and Poisson regression give the best performance in the multivariate setting, across several error metrics.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale pretraining of TimeGPT does not necessarily yield superior accuracy for emergency call volume forecasting, so frugal methods trained solely on the available data remain preferable for this application.

title: GenISys: Integrated Ship Systems Design Using Subsystem-Conditional Tabular Diffussion
summary: Ship design requires coordinating coupled subsystems to satisfy engineering constraints and balance competing performance and cost objectives. Generative artificial intelligence has supported component design, but integrated ship generation must also account for interactions among hull geometry, structure, propulsion, and operation. This paper presents GenISys, a framework for generating integrated systems, demonstrated through early-stage bulk-carrier design. Its dataset contains 217,999 proposed designs, including 16,247 that satisfy the formulated engineering constraints. The proposed simultaneous conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (SCDDPM) generates subsystems together, allowing each subsystem model to respond to changes elsewhere during generation. Experiments compare this approach with monolithic whole-ship generation and sequential subsystem generation across five independent training runs per architecture. In a study targeting lower cost per tonne of cargo transported, designs were generated for a required voyage range of 5,000 nautical miles. SCDDPM produced designs satisfying the formulated engineering constraints and meeting a common low-cost target in 55.70% of generation requests, compared with 51.10% for the monolithic model and 47.54% for the sequential model. These correspond to 9.0% and 17.2% more qualifying designs, respectively, while maintaining similar estimated transport costs. These results show how generative artificial intelligence can coordinate subsystems to generate feasible, high-performing integrated systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GenISys, a framework that generates integrated ship designs by jointly producing coupled subsystems with a simultaneous conditional denoising diffusion model, demonstrated on early-stage bulk-carrier design.
AI.motivation: Generative AI has supported component-level ship design, but integrated ship generation must also account for interactions among hull geometry, structure, propulsion and operation, which sequential or whole-ship generation may not capture.
AI.method: The SCDDPM model generates all subsystems together so that each subsystem model responds to changes elsewhere during generation, trained on a dataset of 217,999 proposed designs of which 16,247 satisfy the formulated engineering constraints, and compared with monolithic whole-ship generation and sequential subsystem generation over five training runs per architecture.
AI.result: For a required voyage range of 5,000 nautical miles and a lower cost per tonne of cargo target, SCDDPM yields qualifying designs in 55.70% of generation requests versus 51.10% for the monolithic model and 47.54% for the sequential model, corresponding to 9.0% and 17.2% more qualifying designs, with similar estimated transport costs.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI can coordinate subsystems to produce feasible, high-performing integrated ship systems, not only individual components.

title: Means vs. Foundation Models for Emergency Call Forecasting
comment: Keywords: Prehospital emergency calls; Foundation models; TimeGPT; Hölder means; Lehmer means
summary: This study investigates whether generalized means can achieve forecasting performance comparable to that of TimeGPT for daily emergency call volume prediction. Specifically, two families of generalized means, the Hölder means (HM) and the Lehmer means (LM), are evaluated against fine-tuned TimeGPT across forecasting horizons ranging from one to seven days. Forecasting performance is assessed on a real-world emergency call dataset using multiple error metrics, and Diebold-Mariano test. Experimental results show that HM and LM achieve nearly identical predictive performance across all forecasting horizons. For short-term forecasting, both generalized means outperform TimeGPT, with reductions of mean absolute error (MAE) approximately 1.24\% and 2.48\% at horizons of one and three days, respectively. Conversely, TimeGPT achieves a lower error at the seven-day horizon, with an descresing of MAE by 1.98\%. However, Diebold-Mariano tests reveal no statistically significant differences between the methods at the evaluated horizons. These findings suggest that generalized means can provide competitive forecasting performance compared with a energyvore foundation model.

AI.tldr: The study shows that generalized means, namely Hölder means and Lehmer means, forecast daily emergency call volumes about as well as fine-tuned TimeGPT, with short-horizon gains over TimeGPT that are not statistically significant.
AI.motivation: Foundation models such as TimeGPT are costly for forecasting, and the question is whether simple generalized means can match their accuracy on daily emergency call prediction.
AI.method: Hölder means and Lehmer means are evaluated against fine-tuned TimeGPT for horizons from one to seven days on a real-world emergency call dataset, using multiple error metrics and the Diebold-Mariano test.
AI.result: Hölder and Lehmer means achieve nearly identical accuracy at all horizons; both beat TimeGPT at one and three days, with MAE reductions of about 1.24% and 2.48% respectively, while TimeGPT is better at seven days by about 1.98% in MAE, and Diebold-Mariano tests find no statistically significant differences at the evaluated horizons.
AI.conclusion: Generalized means can offer competitive forecasting performance compared with a large foundation model, at much lower complexity, although the observed differences are not statistically conclusive.

title: A Theoretical Reduction From Membership Inference to Reconstruction Attacks Against Learners
summary: We study reconstruction attacks, which recover training data from a learned model. In our adversarial model, the adversary designs a hard instance, drawn from a parameterized family of data distributions, and is given the parameter used to generate it. Our main contribution is a general reduction showing that, in this model, membership inference (determining whether a given datapoint was used for training) implies reconstruction: for a training set of size $n$, a membership test with recall at least $q(n)$ and false-positive rate $O(\delta^2/n^2)$ yields a reconstruction algorithm that, with probability $1 - O(\delta)$, outputs only training points, and recovers $\Omega(n \cdot q(n))$ of them in expectation. This reduction applies to any learning algorithm. For stochastic convex optimization (SCO), we make the reduction computationally efficient over exponentially large domains via structured distributions whose support is partitioned into polynomially many categories of exponentially many elements each, so that reconstruction iterates over categories rather than the full support. Combining this with an existing membership inference result for SCO, we prove that any learning algorithm achieving low excess risk over all distributions admits a polynomial-time reconstruction attack recovering $\Omega(n)$ training points, even when the underlying distribution has exponentially large support.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a general reduction showing that membership inference implies reconstruction of training data for any learning algorithm, and makes it computationally efficient for stochastic convex optimization over exponentially large domains.
AI.motivation: Membership inference and reconstruction attacks are usually studied separately, and it is unclear whether an adversary that can only test membership can recover the training data itself, especially over large domains.
AI.method: In an adversarial model where the adversary designs a hard instance from a parameterized family of distributions and receives the generating parameter, a membership test with recall at least q(n) and false-positive rate O(delta^2/n^2) is converted into a reconstruction algorithm; for stochastic convex optimization, the support is partitioned into polynomially many categories so reconstruction iterates over categories rather than the full support.
AI.result: With probability 1 - O(delta) the algorithm outputs only training points and recovers Omega(n q(n)) of them in expectation; combined with an existing membership inference result, any learner achieving low excess risk over all distributions admits a polynomial-time attack recovering Omega(n) training points, even when the distribution has exponentially large support.
AI.conclusion: Low excess risk guarantees do not protect against reconstruction of training data, since membership inference already yields a practical reconstruction attack for SCO learners.

title: Resolvent Ellipsoid for Minty Set Inclusions
comment: The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2026
summary: We study Minty set inclusion on a compact convex set $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ with a set-valued operator $A : \mathcal{X} \rightrightarrows \mathbb{R}^d$. Under the Minty promise, the goal is to compute $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and $u \in A(x)$ such that $\sup_{y \in \mathcal{X}} \langle u, x - y \rangle \le \varepsilon$. Our approach is geometric and we work in the fixed-scale constrained-resolvent oracle model, where a query at anchor $a$ is assumed to return a resolvent point $x^+$ together with the Yosida vector $g_{\eta}(a) = (a - x^+)/\eta$. We prove that each oracle response yields a sharp dichotomy: either the returned point provides an $\varepsilon$-SVI certificate, or the Yosida vector defines a strict separating normal for the Minty set. Thus, a single black-box resolvent query supplies either a certified candidate solution or a valid geometric cut. Combining this separation principle with the ellipsoid method, we obtain RESOLVENT-ELLIPSOID, an algorithm that computes an $\varepsilon$-SVI in $\mathcal{O}\!\left(\operatorname{poly}(d, \log(1/\varepsilon))\right)$ black-box oracle calls to the fixed-scale constrained resolvent. For monotone inclusions, our algorithm gives, to our knowledge, the first $\mathcal{O}\!\left(\mathrm{poly}(d, \log(1/\varepsilon))\right)$ black-box guarantee in the fixed-scale resolvent model.

AI.tldr: The paper gives RESOLVENT-ELLIPSOID, an ellipsoid-method algorithm that computes an epsilon-SVI for Minty set inclusion using O(poly(d, log(1/epsilon))) calls to a fixed-scale constrained resolvent oracle.
AI.motivation: Minty set inclusion problems with set-valued operators need black-box methods with guarantees in the fixed-scale resolvent model, and prior guarantees of this form for monotone inclusions were not available to the authors' knowledge.
AI.method: Each resolvent query at an anchor returns a point and a Yosida vector, and the paper proves a sharp dichotomy: the point is either an epsilon-SVI certificate or the Yosida vector is a strict separating normal for the Minty set; this separation principle is combined with the ellipsoid method.
AI.result: The algorithm computes an epsilon-SVI in O(poly(d, log(1/epsilon))) black-box oracle calls, which is, to the authors' knowledge, the first such black-box guarantee for monotone inclusions in the fixed-scale resolvent model.
AI.conclusion: A single resolvent query always yields either a certified candidate solution or a valid geometric cut, so polynomial-in-dimension black-box complexity is achievable for monotone inclusions.

title: Direct GPU Energy Measurements of Batch-Level Sharing in Mixture-of-Experts and Recurrent Models
summary: Energy claims for efficient neural networks are often inferred from operation counts. We report direct GPU energy measurements on two workloads that batch very differently, recurrent policies in GPU-vectorised multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) and mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, and ask one question of both: can the rows of a batch be made to share computation, across the batch and over time, at a measured saving? On recurrent policies the answer so far is no. Shared activity patterns exist but rarely last one step, masking a frozen policy fails, and trained-in masks succeed only because a fixed mask is equivalent to a narrow GRU, at 11x the energy of a small dense policy in our implementation. Test-time steering adds nothing beyond re-picking on either workload. On MoE models the answer is yes, and granularity decides how much: on Qwen3-30B-A3B, batch-aware routing reads 25-31% fewer expert weights within KL 0.05, with benchmark changes within noise at 500 items, and uses 12-18% less energy per token on a fused forward. We also introduce persistence-aware OEA, a one-parameter rule that keeps the batch-aware cut with about 40% fewer new experts per step than native routing at batch 32-64, though its energy has not yet been measured. These are pilot measurements on one GPU type, and we state their limits.

AI.tldr: Direct GPU energy measurements show that recurrent multi-agent reinforcement learning policies gain little from batch-level sharing, while batch-aware routing in Mixture-of-Experts language models reduces expert weight reads and energy per token on Qwen3-30B-A3B.
AI.motivation: Energy claims for efficient neural networks are usually inferred from operation counts rather than measured, and it is unclear whether batch rows can share computation for measured savings in recurrent and Mixture-of-Experts workloads.
AI.method: The authors measure GPU energy on GPU-vectorised recurrent MARL policies, testing shared activity patterns, frozen and trained-in masks and test-time steering, and on Qwen3-30B-A3B, testing batch-aware routing and a new one-parameter rule called persistence-aware OEA.
AI.result: On recurrent policies, shared patterns rarely last one step, masking a frozen policy fails, and trained-in masks succeed only as a narrow GRU at 11x the energy of a small dense policy; on Qwen3-30B-A3B, batch-aware routing reads 25-31% fewer expert weights within KL 0.05 with benchmark changes within noise at 500 items and 12-18% less energy per token on a fused forward, and persistence-aware OEA keeps about 40% fewer new experts per step than native routing at batch 32-64, although its energy is not yet measured.
AI.conclusion: Batch-level sharing pays off for MoE models, with granularity deciding the size of the saving, but not for the recurrent policies studied; the results are pilot measurements on one GPU type with stated limits.

title: Scalable Counterfactual Explanations for Time Series via Policy Learning
summary: Generating counterfactual (CF) explanations for time series is challenging due to complex temporal dependencies and the computational inefficiency of traditional instance-specific optimization. We propose a policy learning framework for counterfactual explanation in time series, trained as a one-step contextual-bandit policy-learning problem. By training an actor-critic agent in the latent space of a pre-trained autoencoder, our method learns a transferable policy that captures global structural regularities. Unlike existing methods that rely on iterative optimization for each new input, the learned policy enables direct generation of valid and plausible counterfactuals through a single forward pass, avoiding per-instance optimization at inference time. Experiments on 13 UCR benchmark datasets show that our framework achieves high validity and strong plausibility across multiple anomaly detection metrics. Overall, by decoupling counterfactual generation from per-instance optimization, the proposed method provides an efficient and scalable alternative to existing approaches for time series counterfactual explanations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a policy learning framework that generates counterfactual explanations for time series in a single forward pass, by training an actor-critic agent in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder.
AI.motivation: Counterfactual explanations for time series are hard to produce because of complex temporal dependencies, and existing methods rely on costly per-instance optimization at inference time.
AI.method: Counterfactual generation is cast as a one-step contextual bandit problem, and an actor-critic agent is trained in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder so that the learned policy captures global structural regularities and can be transferred.
AI.result: On 13 UCR benchmark datasets the framework achieves high validity and strong plausibility across multiple anomaly detection metrics, while avoiding per-instance optimization at inference.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling counterfactual generation from per-instance optimization gives an efficient and scalable alternative for time series counterfactual explanations.

title: Variational Approach to Optimal IPS Estimator for Multi-logger Off-Policy Evaluation
summary: We study off-policy evaluation (OPE) in contextual bandits with data collected from multiple logging policies. Inverse propensity scoring (IPS) is a standard approach to OPE and extends naturally to the multi-logger setting. However, as highlighted by Agarwal et al. [2017], neither balanced nor weighted IPS consistently outperforms the other in this setting. We resolve this dilemma by deriving an optimal IPS estimator with sample-dependent weights that minimize variance subject to unbiasedness. Using a variational calculus approach, we obtain closed-form optimal weights, yielding an estimator that is unbiased and achieves asymptotically optimal variance within a generalized weighted-IPS estimator class. Instead of a reward model, the estimator needs only a $K\times K$ matrix and a $K$-vector of moments, where $K$ is the number of logging policies, and we quantify how much efficiency this costs relative to the semiparametric oracle. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that our estimator generally improves on existing multi-logger IPS methods. We also extend our estimator to a doubly robust form by incorporating a conditional reward estimator. We compare the resulting DR extension with the semiparametrically efficient DR estimator of Kallus et al. [2021], both theoretically and empirically. We show that the two estimators achieve the same asymptotic variance when the conditional reward estimator is consistent, while our estimator can retain semiparametric efficiency under certain forms of reward misspecification. Empirically, the proposed DR estimator often achieves lower estimation error than the existing DR baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a closed-form optimal IPS estimator for off-policy evaluation with multiple logging policies, which minimizes variance subject to unbiasedness, and extends it to a doubly robust form.
AI.motivation: With data from several logging policies, neither balanced nor weighted IPS consistently dominates the other, as noted by Agarwal et al. (2017), leaving the choice of estimator unresolved.
AI.method: Sample-dependent weights are obtained by variational calculus to minimize variance subject to unbiasedness, requiring only a K by K matrix and a K-vector of moments, where K is the number of logging policies; the doubly robust extension adds a conditional reward estimator and is compared with the semiparametrically efficient DR estimator of Kallus et al. (2021).
AI.result: The estimator generally improves on existing multi-logger IPS methods on benchmark datasets and achieves asymptotically optimal variance within a generalized weighted-IPS class; the DR extension often has lower estimation error than the existing DR baseline, and matches the asymptotic variance of the Kallus et al. estimator when the reward estimator is consistent.
AI.conclusion: The estimator retains semiparametric efficiency under certain forms of reward misspecification, where the Kallus et al. estimator does not, while the efficiency cost relative to the semiparametric oracle is quantified.

title: Autonomous Continual Learning and Knowledge Transfer via Cortex-Inspired Neural Assemblies
summary: Unlike the brain, artificial neural networks (ANNs) suffer from "catastrophic forgetting": complete overwriting of solutions when re-training on new functions ("concept shift") or on a disjoint domain of the current function ("domain shift"). ANNs require each batch of data to be roughly representative of the complete distribution, a typically expensive and impractical requirement. In this paper, we introduce Functional Task Networks (FTNs), a method of continual learning and knowledge transfer modeled after several properties of the mammalian neocortex. FTN is formulated as a distributed, stochastic mixture of experts in which a sparse, binary routing mask is computed at inference time using a small support sample of input-output pairs. Per-batch reconfiguration of the router during training, together with mask-overlap-filtered replay, shapes a basis of overlapping, partially trained subnetworks. Unrelated tasks route through mostly separate assemblies, related tasks overlap on shared components. On block-sequentially trained continual learning and knowledge transfer tasks FTN retains solutions nearly as well as disjoint-mask isolation and attains the lowest pre-update head-start loss among matched-architecture comparators. The learned mask-overlap geometry tracks the known concept-sharing structure where available. We show experimentally that under correlated concept shift, support-set mask reconfiguration is necessary even for retention. Under domain shift, the distributed bank with replay is sufficient to handle retention without the configurer. Forward transfer, or head-start, and backward transfer, are also contributed by support-set mask configuration.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Functional Task Networks, a continual learning method that routes each input through a sparse binary mask over a distributed mixture of experts, so that unrelated tasks use mostly separate subnetworks and related tasks share components.
AI.motivation: Artificial neural networks suffer catastrophic forgetting under concept shift and domain shift and need batches that are representative of the full distribution, which is an impractical requirement.
AI.method: A sparse binary routing mask is computed at inference from a small support sample of input-output pairs; per-batch router reconfiguration during training and mask-overlap-filtered replay shape a basis of overlapping, partially trained subnetworks.
AI.result: On block-sequential continual learning and knowledge transfer tasks, the method retains solutions nearly as well as disjoint-mask isolation and gets the lowest pre-update head-start loss among matched-architecture comparators; mask overlap tracks known concept-sharing structure, and support-set mask reconfiguration is necessary for retention under correlated concept shift while replay with the distributed bank suffices under domain shift.
AI.conclusion: Support-set mask configuration contributes both forward transfer (head-start) and backward transfer, so routing by support samples is a practical route to continual learning and knowledge transfer.

title: The Dark Matter of Clinical Data: An Identification Limit on Disentangling Physiology from Care Process in electronic health records
comment: 24 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Supplementary Information and code are provided as ancillary files. Interactive companion with narrated explainers: this https URL
summary: Representations learned from electronic health record (EHR) data encode patient physiology together with the clinical process that decides what is measured, when, and for whom. We formalize the data-generating process with latent physiology, ordering intent, laboratory values that exist only when measured, a learned representation, and clinical environments, and analyze two strategies for undoing this entanglement. First, no division of the information carried by laboratory "value" and "ordering" channels is identified from a single dataset: when ordering depends on the analyte, its distribution among untested patients is not recoverable, and a sentinel code for the undefined recorded value makes it carry all the entropy of the ordering indicator, fixing partial information decomposition (PID) for every redundancy measure satisfying the Williams-Beer axioms and invariant under injective re-encoding. Second, cross-site invariance of representation-conditional outcomes is a falsifiable implication of biological invariance taken jointly with exclusion and representation-sufficiency conditions, but not an identification strategy: we construct observationally equivalent models that disagree about biological invariance, whether the invariance test fails or passes. For binary physiology this happens exactly when case mix differs, the representation is lossy, and physiology affects the outcome. A worked example yields a 9.6-percentage-point cross-site gap under an unchanged biological mechanism. Tests performed for every patient remove the ordering gate, and measured tests can restore identification: biological invariance is identified when a test exactly summarizes outcome-relevant physiology, or, for binary physiology, when two tests with independent errors are available at sites with different case mix. Cross-site analyses should be reported as tests of a stated joint hypothesis.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that in EHR data, physiology and care process cannot be separated from a single dataset when ordering depends on the analyte, and shows that cross-site invariance tests are tests of a joint hypothesis rather than identification strategies.
AI.motivation: Representations learned from EHR data mix patient physiology with the clinical process that decides what is measured, when and for whom, and existing approaches do not state when this entanglement can be undone.
AI.method: The data-generating process is formalized with latent physiology, ordering intent, laboratory values that exist only when measured, a learned representation and clinical environments; the authors analyze partial information decomposition of the value and ordering channels under the Williams-Beer axioms and construct observationally equivalent models for cross-site invariance tests.
AI.result: No division of the value and ordering information is identified from a single dataset, since a sentinel code for the undefined value makes it carry all the entropy of the ordering indicator; invariance tests can fail or pass for observationally equivalent models; a worked example yields a 9.6-percentage-point cross-site gap under an unchanged biological mechanism; measured tests for every patient remove the ordering gate, and biological invariance is identified when a test exactly summarizes outcome-relevant physiology or when two tests with independent errors are available at sites with different case mix.
AI.conclusion: Cross-site analyses should be reported as tests of a stated joint hypothesis rather than as identification of biological invariance.

title: Spectral Rank and Step-Direction Dynamics in Language-Model Post-Training
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR). Details: this https URL
summary: Language-model post-training modifies weights through cumulative updates and successive displacements, yet existing studies report seemingly conflicting spectral properties: nearly full-rank updates and low stable-rank changes. We show these observations are compatible and characterize update directions during training. For singular values following $\sigma_i \propto i^{-\alpha}$ with $0 < \alpha \leq 1/2$, we prove that stable rank becomes negligible relative to fixed-energy rank as dimension increases. Full singular value decompositions of selected OLMo-2-7B updates confirm this separation: three proximal policy optimization (PPO) attention updates have stable ranks of 9.6-18.3 but require 532-1,222 singular components to capture 80% of their energy. We next compute consecutive checkpoint-displacement cosines from full-model inner products. Across nine publicly released reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) stages, all 131 adjacent pairs have negative cosines on their native checkpoint grids, including PPO and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trajectories. Supervised fine-tuning comparisons across four model families show configuration-dependent alignment, including negative late-training cosines for Mistral and FP32 Llama. Finally, a controlled OLMo-2-1B study with three paired seeds and a 2,048-token response cap compares group-relative advantages against a learned critic with generalized advantage estimation (GAE). At matched 60-rollout windows, late-training mean cosines are +0.259 and +0.012, respectively; the paired critic-minus-group difference is -0.247 (seed-level 95% interval [-0.358, -0.137]). These findings distinguish spectral concentration, energy coverage, and trajectory direction, and demonstrate that the advantage system influences directional alignment under matched training conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper reconciles conflicting spectral observations of language-model post-training updates, showing that updates can be nearly full-rank in energy coverage while having low stable rank, and that RLVR checkpoint displacements have consistently negative adjacent cosines.
AI.motivation: Existing studies report seemingly conflicting spectral properties of post-training updates, namely nearly full-rank updates and low stable-rank changes, and the directional behaviour of successive updates is not well characterized.
AI.method: For singular values decaying as i to the power minus alpha with 0 < alpha at most 1/2, the authors prove that stable rank becomes negligible relative to fixed-energy rank as dimension grows; they check full SVDs of OLMo-2-7B updates, compute consecutive checkpoint displacement cosines across nine RLVR stages and four SFT model families, and run a controlled OLMo-2-1B study with three paired seeds comparing group-relative advantages with a learned critic and generalized advantage estimation.
AI.result: Three PPO attention updates have stable ranks of 9.6 to 18.3 but need 532 to 1,222 singular components to capture 80% of their energy; all 131 adjacent checkpoint pairs across nine RLVR stages have negative cosines on their native grids; SFT cosines are configuration-dependent; at matched 60-rollout windows late-training mean cosines are +0.259 for the critic and +0.012 for group-relative advantages, a paired difference of -0.247 with seed-level 95% interval [-0.358, -0.137].
AI.conclusion: Spectral concentration, energy coverage and trajectory direction are distinct properties, and the advantage estimator measurably influences directional alignment of post-training updates under matched conditions.

title: Payoff-Aware Prediction of Population Game Dynamics
summary: Population game dynamics describe how aggregate behavior evolves in response to payoff signals. In many applications, the payoff function may change, and the goal is to predict the population trajectory induced by a new payoff design before trajectory data under that design are available. We study this problem as $\textbf{payoff-aware prediction of population game dynamics}$. Standard dynamics learning methods fit the motion observed under training payoffs, but do not separate the payoff-dependent incentive from the payoff-independent response structure needed for prediction under new payoffs. Building on the existing framework of Riemannian game dynamics, we propose PA-RmD, a payoff-aware learning method that keeps payoff information explicit and learns the payoff-independent response structure from data. Theoretically, we show that the learned model preserves fixed-payoff Nash equilibria and derive finite-time one-step prediction bounds under shared-response and payoff-coverage conditions. Empirically, we evaluate PA-RmD on synthetic zero-sum and potential games, as well as a YouTube Trending multi-country dataset, showing that our method performs well under changing payoff designs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PA-RmD, a payoff-aware learning method for predicting population game trajectories under new payoff designs, by keeping payoff information explicit and learning a payoff-independent response structure from data.
AI.motivation: Standard dynamics learning fits motion under training payoffs and does not separate payoff-dependent incentives from payoff-independent response structure, so it cannot predict trajectories under new payoffs.
AI.method: Building on Riemannian game dynamics, PA-RmD keeps payoff information explicit and learns the payoff-independent response structure from data.
AI.result: The learned model preserves fixed-payoff Nash equilibria, and finite-time one-step prediction bounds are derived under shared-response and payoff-coverage conditions; on synthetic zero-sum and potential games and a YouTube Trending multi-country dataset the method performs well under changing payoff designs.
AI.conclusion: Payoff-aware modelling enables prediction of population dynamics under payoff designs not seen in training data, provided the shared-response and payoff-coverage conditions hold.

title: APO2CS: Advantage-Aware Preference Optimization for Two-Level Constructive Search in Combinatorial Optimization
summary: Preference optimization has emerged as a promising alternative to reward-based training for neural combinatorial optimization. However, existing methods typically rely on binary pairwise labels, which discard the magnitude of solution-quality differences and provide supervision only at the complete-solution level. We propose Advantage-aware Preference Optimization for Two-level Constructive Search (APO2CS), a preference-based training objective for constructive neural solvers that integrates both macro-level and micro-level supervision. At the macro level, APO2CS enriches pairwise preferences with an advantage term derived from objective-value differences. At the micro level, it compares partial trajectories, thereby providing denser supervision throughout the sequential construction process. The resulting objective can be used either to train a policy from scratch or to fine-tune a pretrained one. Experimental results show that APO2CS improves the expressiveness and search capability of preference learning for combinatorial optimization, while demonstrating strong effectiveness and adaptability across multiple combinatorial optimization tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes APO2CS, a preference optimization objective for neural constructive combinatorial solvers that adds advantage-weighted macro-level preferences and micro-level comparisons of partial trajectories.
AI.motivation: Existing preference optimization for neural combinatorial optimization uses binary pairwise labels, which discard the magnitude of solution-quality differences and supervise only complete solutions.
AI.method: At the macro level, pairwise preferences are enriched with an advantage term derived from objective-value differences; at the micro level, partial construction trajectories are compared to give denser supervision throughout sequential construction; the objective can train a policy from scratch or fine-tune a pretrained one.
AI.result: The abstract reports that APO2CS improves the expressiveness and search capability of preference learning and shows strong effectiveness and adaptability across multiple combinatorial optimization tasks, without giving specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Combining macro and micro preference supervision with advantage information is an effective training objective for constructive neural combinatorial solvers.

title: Efficient Online Submodular Maximization with Bandit Feedback
summary: We study online monotone submodular maximization under a cardinality constraint with bandit feedback. On each round, the learner selects at most $k$ elements from a ground set of size $n$ and observes only the value of the selected set. We develop an efficient algorithm achieving $O\!\left(k\sqrt{nT\log(n/k)}\right)$ expected $(1-1/e)$-regret over $T$ rounds. To our knowledge, this is the first polynomial-time algorithm with $\sqrt{T}$ dependence on the horizon for arbitrary monotone submodular functions in the bandit setting. Our approach uses randomized sampling and a carefully constructed potential to reduce online submodular maximization to online linear optimization over the probability simplex.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a polynomial-time algorithm for online monotone submodular maximization under a cardinality constraint with bandit feedback, achieving O(k sqrt(nT log(n/k))) expected (1-1/e)-regret.
AI.motivation: Under bandit feedback, where only the value of the selected set is observed, earlier polynomial-time methods for arbitrary monotone submodular functions did not achieve square-root dependence on the horizon.
AI.method: The approach uses randomized sampling and a carefully constructed potential to reduce online submodular maximization to online linear optimization over the probability simplex.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves O(k sqrt(nT log(n/k))) expected (1-1/e)-regret over T rounds, which the authors state is the first polynomial-time algorithm with sqrt(T) dependence on the horizon for arbitrary monotone submodular functions in this bandit setting.
AI.conclusion: Reducing bandit submodular maximization to online linear optimization over the simplex yields efficient algorithms with optimal-order square-root horizon dependence.

title: KKT-Perturbation-Aware Communication for Fully Distributed Online Convex Optimization with Nonseparable Coupling
summary: Nonseparable costs and coupled constraints in distributed online convex optimization often arise when system performance and operational constraints depend on the joint configuration of all agents and cannot be decomposed into individual contributions. Such nonseparability leads to fully distributed decision-making with challenging partial local information, where each agent evaluates its local primal-dual update using estimated global information via a local belief of the joint action and the shared Lagrange multiplier to be exchanged with neighbors. While the belief consensus established by prior works ensures no-regret learning, exchanging beliefs comprising full-dimensional primal and dual states at every round imposes a communication overhead that scales with both the joint decision dimension and the network size. Existing event-triggered schemes typically activate communication according to state variation or consensus error. Under nonseparable coupling, however, errors of equal magnitude can produce markedly different perturbations after passing through the KKT operator. We therefore propose a randomized KKT-perturbation-aware communication mechanism, where the triggering of each agent's primal and dual communication channels depends on their impact on the KKT operator. The proposed mechanism transfers the adaptive-sampling principle of coordinate descent from allocating computation across decision blocks to allocating communication across information channels: channels with larger estimated perturbations receive greater priority for refresh. Under standard regularity assumptions, the resulting algorithm achieves $O({T}^{2/3})$ expected static regret and $O({T}^{2/3})$ expected cumulative constraint violation. Numerical experiments demonstrate improved learning and constraint-enforcement performance per transmitted bit over belief consensus baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a randomized KKT-perturbation-aware communication mechanism for fully distributed online convex optimization with nonseparable coupling, which refreshes primal and dual channels in proportion to their estimated effect on the KKT operator.
AI.motivation: Exchanging full-dimensional belief states every round imposes communication overhead that scales with the joint decision dimension and network size, and existing event-triggered schemes respond to state variation or consensus error, which misjudges impact under nonseparable coupling.
AI.method: Each agent's primal and dual communication channels are triggered randomly according to their estimated perturbations after the KKT operator, transferring the adaptive-sampling principle of coordinate descent from computation to communication.
AI.result: Under standard regularity assumptions the algorithm achieves O(T^(2/3)) expected static regret and O(T^(2/3)) expected cumulative constraint violation, and numerical experiments show better learning and constraint enforcement per transmitted bit than belief consensus baselines.
AI.conclusion: Prioritizing communication by KKT-perturbation impact reduces communication cost while preserving no-regret learning and constraint satisfaction in fully distributed settings.

title: MOOD: Benchmarking Post-Hoc OOD Detection for Materials Property Prediction
summary: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is essential for deploying machine learning models in high stakes scientific applications, yet methods that flag OOD inputs without retraining the model have been validated almost exclusively on image classification. We introduce MOOD (Materials Out-of-Distribution Detection), a benchmark for evaluating whether these post-hoc OOD detectors transfer to graph neural networks (GNNs) on materials property prediction. MOOD evaluates 15 post-hoc detectors and 2 supervised diagnostic probes across 4 GNN architectures, 5 MatBench tasks, and 15 physically motivated compositional and structural shifts, yielding 264 evaluation settings and over 13,000 AUROC measurements across three encoder training seeds. Our evaluation reveals three key findings. First, current post-hoc detectors perform near chance; all 15 detectors achieve an AUROC around 0.5. Second, detector failures decompose into two regimes: method bottlenecks and encoder bottlenecks. Method bottlenecks arise when supervised probes can separate in-distribution (ID) from OOD samples but unsupervised detectors fail, meaning that the embeddings contain OOD signal that current detectors do not extract. Encoder bottlenecks arise when even supervised probes fail to separate ID from OOD samples, indicating that the relevant shift is not accessible in the frozen GNN representation. Third, when OOD prediction error exceeds ID error, the AUROC of distance-based and density-based detectors correlates with the size of that gap. Collectively, these findings indicate that reliable OOD detection in scientific domains requires representation learning strategies that explicitly preserve OOD relevant signal, particularly for tasks where current GNN architectures encode no extractable signal at all.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks 15 post-hoc out-of-distribution detectors for graph neural networks on materials property prediction and finds that nearly all perform near chance, with failures traced to either the detection method or the encoder.
AI.motivation: Post-hoc OOD detectors have been validated almost only on image classification, and it is unknown whether they transfer to graph neural networks for materials property prediction, where reliable OOD flags matter for scientific use.
AI.method: MOOD evaluates 15 post-hoc detectors and 2 supervised diagnostic probes across 4 GNN architectures, 5 MatBench tasks and 15 physically motivated compositional and structural shifts, giving 264 evaluation settings and over 13,000 AUROC measurements across three encoder training seeds.
AI.result: All 15 detectors achieve AUROC around 0.5; failures split into method bottlenecks, where supervised probes separate ID from OOD but unsupervised detectors do not, and encoder bottlenecks, where even supervised probes fail; for distance-based and density-based detectors, AUROC correlates with the gap when OOD prediction error exceeds ID error.
AI.conclusion: Reliable OOD detection in scientific domains requires representation learning that explicitly preserves OOD-relevant signal, since current GNN encoders in some tasks carry no extractable signal for it.

title: DeltaForge: A Post-hoc Mixture-of-Experts VLA for Multi-Domain Autonomous Driving
summary: Fleets of driving vision-language-action (VLA) models are developed one domain at a time: each operator finetunes a shared base model on private data, producing specialized experts that are costly to consolidate into a single model. Weight merging loses accuracy as heterogeneous domains accumulate, and dense mixture-of-experts routing is prohibitively expensive to combine them. We present DeltaForge, to our knowledge the first post-hoc mixture-of-experts VLA for driving, which consolidates N independently finetuned per-domain models into a single multi-domain model from their weights and a small proxy set alone. When different operators finetune the same base model, their weight updates end up sharing a lot of structure. We exploit this by decomposing all the updates together using singular value decomposition (SVD), splitting each one into a shared part (the same across all domains) and a tiny domain-specific part. The router then only needs to work with those tiny domain-specific pieces, not the full expert weights, which is what keeps the approach efficient.
