Then two cooperating clip-level blind routers, one over the VLM reasoning experts and one over the flow-matching dynamics experts, are trained from soft labels on the proxy dataset. Across six diverse domains spanning urban, off-road, and highway driving on cars, trucks, and all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), DeltaForge approaches the accuracy of the per-domain experts and surpasses every merging, routing, centralized, and federated baseline at close to single-model parameter and compute cost. Adding a new domain requires only projecting its weight update onto the shared basis with no end-to-end retraining needed. The resulting model also generalizes to domain combinations it was never explicitly trained on.

AI.tldr: DeltaForge consolidates N independently fine-tuned per-domain driving VLA models into one mixture-of-experts model from their weights and a small proxy set, using a shared SVD basis so that routing works on small domain-specific components.
AI.motivation: Driving VLA models are fine-tuned per domain by different operators, and weight merging loses accuracy as heterogeneous domains accumulate while dense mixture-of-experts routing is prohibitively expensive.
AI.method: All per-domain weight updates are decomposed jointly by singular value decomposition into a shared part and a small domain-specific part, and two clip-level blind routers, one over VLM reasoning experts and one over flow-matching dynamics experts, are trained from soft labels on the proxy dataset.
AI.result: Across six domains spanning urban, off-road and highway driving on cars, trucks and ATVs, DeltaForge approaches the accuracy of per-domain experts and surpasses every merging, routing, centralized and federated baseline at close to single-model parameter and compute cost; adding a domain needs only projecting its update onto the shared basis, and the model generalizes to domain combinations not seen in training.
AI.conclusion: Post-hoc consolidation through a shared SVD basis is an efficient route to a single multi-domain driving VLA model without end-to-end retraining.

title: Are UFOs Real? Introducing Unified Factored Organizers
summary: Implicit in much research in deep learning is the assumption that if a network achieves low loss, then it must have learned a good representation of its training data. Recent work by Kumar et al. (2025, arXiv:2505.11581) questions this assumption, arguing that networks trained with conventional gradient descent achieve low loss despite learning fractured entangled representations (FER), leaving related concepts disconnected and unrelated concepts entangled inappropriately. Kumar et al. further show that dramatically better representations are possible: a network evolved through an open-ended, human-in-the-loop process learned unified factored representations (UFR) that capture the regularities of the domain far better than a counterpart with nearly identical outputs trained with conventional gradient descent. Inspired by UFR, this paper introduces unified factored organizers (UFOs), networks trained to model regularities in the representations of other networks. A network can then be trained both to achieve low loss on its task objective and to align its representations with the model learned by the UFO. Networks trained with UFOs are shown to learn qualitatively superior representations in an image-regression domain where representations are easily interpretable. To provide quantitative evidence for the impact of UFOs on representation learning, a transformer is trained with and without UFO regularization to grok a modular arithmetic problem set. When combined with weight decay, UFOs can reduce the number of transformer training steps needed to grok by more than 10x relative to weight decay alone. Without weight decay, UFOs can reduce the number of transformer training steps needed to grok by more than 100x relative to an unregularized baseline. If UFOs are real, they suggest a new paradigm where loss functions themselves are trained to learn an effective model of good representation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces unified factored organizers (UFOs), networks trained to model regularities in other networks' representations, and uses them as regularizers that speed up grokking of modular arithmetic by more than 10x with weight decay and more than 100x without it.
AI.motivation: Low loss does not guarantee good representations, as Kumar et al. (2025) argue that conventionally trained networks learn fractured entangled representations, and dramatically better unified factored representations need an open-ended, human-in-the-loop process.
AI.method: A UFO is trained to model regularities in the representations of other networks, and a network is trained both on its task objective and to align its representations with the model learned by the UFO; a transformer is trained with and without UFO regularization on a modular arithmetic task.
AI.result: In an image-regression domain the UFO-trained networks learn qualitatively superior representations; with weight decay, UFOs cut the training steps needed to grok by more than 10x relative to weight decay alone, and without weight decay by more than 100x relative to an unregularized baseline.
AI.conclusion: If the approach holds, loss functions could themselves be trained to encode an effective model of good representation, suggesting a new paradigm for representation learning.

title: Can Hindsight Critics Guide Delayed Actors?
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Accepted for publication at the AJCAI2026 conference. Cite as: "López, F. M., & Cruz, F. (2026). Can Hindsight Critics Guide Delayed Actors?. In Australasian Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (pp. 1-10). Cham: Springer International Publishing."
summary: Sensory delays create temporal misalignments between the state of the environment and the observations available to an agent, turning Markovian control problems into partially observable ones. In this work, we inquire whether such misalignments can be mitigated during training by using hindsight to recover aligned state-action transitions. We introduce Hindsight Critics, an asymmetric extension of the Soft Actor-Critic for reinforcement learning under partial observability. The critics are trained on hindsight-aligned transitions whereas the actor learns from the resulting privileged value estimates despite only having access to delayed observations. Comparisons against delay-aware and unaware baselines on the DelayBench suite show that Hindsight Critics can partially compensate for observation delays without requiring modifications to the agent's observations during deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Hindsight Critics, an asymmetric Soft Actor-Critic extension in which critics learn from hindsight-aligned transitions while the actor acts on delayed observations, partially compensating for sensory delays.
AI.motivation: Sensory delays misalign the environment state and the agent's observations, which turns Markovian control into partially observable control, and it is unclear whether this misalignment can be reduced during training.
AI.method: Critics are trained on hindsight-aligned state-action transitions, while the actor learns from the resulting privileged value estimates but only has access to delayed observations; no changes are made to the observations at deployment.
AI.result: Comparisons against delay-aware and delay-unaware baselines on the DelayBench suite show that Hindsight Critics partially compensate for observation delays.
AI.conclusion: Hindsight-based critic training can mitigate the effects of observation delay in reinforcement learning without modifying the deployed agent's inputs.

title: Tropical Gaussian Anticoncentration: Optimal Instance-Dependent Bounds for Online Learning in Extensive-Form Games
summary: We study the minimax regret of full-information online decision making in extensive-form games. For prediction with expert advice, the optimal regret is $\Theta(\sqrt{T\log K})$, where $K$ is the number of experts, or equivalently, the number of normal-form actions. For treeplex strategy spaces, existing efficient algorithms, including KOMWU and online mirror descent with the weight-one dilated entropy regularizer, achieve regret $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T\log|\mathcal{V}|})$, where $\mathcal{V}$ is the set of reduced normal-form strategies. We prove that this logarithmic dependence is minimax optimal in the worst-case full-information reward model. The main difficulty is that pure plans in a treeplex are not independent experts: their rewards are correlated through the recursive structure of decisions and observations. To capture this correlation, we introduce tropical Gaussian formulae, recursive Gaussian expressions built from maxima and normalized sums which preserve the variance. The index count of such a formula matches the number of reduced normal-form continuation plans in the corresponding subtree. Our main analytic result shows that every log-balanced tropical Gaussian formula with index count $N$ has Gaussian width $\Omega(\sqrt{\log N})$. While a direct approach struggles to recover this lower bound, our proof uses a spherical entropy profile to measure scale-dependent separation among the Gaussian directions, and then applies Turán's theorem and Sudakov minoration to obtain the width lower bound. Applying this result to treeplexes gives an oblivious hard distribution with valid transition outcome and Rademacher terminal rewards, establishing a regret lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{T\log|\mathcal{V}|})$. This matches known upper bounds up to universal constants and shows that the DilEnt/KOMWU dependence on the reduced normal-form complexity is unavoidable.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that the logarithmic dependence on the number of reduced normal-form strategies in existing efficient algorithms for treeplex online learning is minimax optimal, via a matching regret lower bound of Omega(sqrt(T log|V|)).
AI.motivation: Pure plans in a treeplex are correlated through the recursive decision and observation structure, so they are not independent experts and standard prediction-with-experts lower bounds do not transfer directly.
AI.method: The authors introduce tropical Gaussian formulae, recursive Gaussian expressions built from maxima and normalized sums that preserve variance, and prove a Gaussian width lower bound of Omega(sqrt(log N)) for log-balanced formulae using a spherical entropy profile, Turan's theorem and Sudakov minoration, then build an oblivious hard distribution from it.
AI.result: The lower bound Omega(sqrt(T log|V|)) matches the known upper bounds of KOMWU and online mirror descent with the weight-one dilated entropy regularizer up to universal constants.
AI.conclusion: The dependence of DilEnt and KOMWU on the reduced normal-form complexity is unavoidable in the worst-case full-information reward model, so the algorithms are instance-optimal in this logarithmic sense.

title: When Does Physics Beat Data? Data-Efficient Traffic State Estimation with Amortized PINNs
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the SSTDM workshop, IEEE ICDM 2026
summary: Traffic state estimation (TSE) reconstructs traffic density at unmonitored locations from a sparse set of sensors. Data-driven models work well when sensors are dense but degrade sharply as coverage thins. We show that imposing the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards conservation law as a physics-informed prior makes TSE more data-efficient. On four real corridors (NGSIM, I-80, PeMS04, PeMS08), physics-informed estimators generalise to held-out sensors where data-driven models, including classical and deep kriging, overfit the observed ones. On the two shock-rich corridors the effect is a clear crossover: as more sensors are held out, data-driven models collapse while the physics-informed estimator degrades gracefully, leading the no-physics network by about 26-38% at 85-90% held out and the strongest classical kriging by about 10-21% at 90%. A matched smoothness prior does not reproduce the gain, and an extended Kalman filter on the same LWR model is outperformed on the shock corridors, so the advantage comes from how the conservation law is imposed. Finally, one loss-conditional PINN removes the per-corridor loss-weight search, matching a 20-point search at about 5x lower cost.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that imposing the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards conservation law as a physics-informed prior makes traffic state estimation more data-efficient than data-driven and kriging baselines when sensors are sparse.
AI.motivation: Data-driven traffic state estimation models perform well with dense sensors but degrade sharply as sensor coverage thins, and existing approaches do not exploit the conservation law.
AI.method: The authors train physics-informed estimators that impose the LWR conservation law as a prior, compare them with classical and deep kriging and an extended Kalman filter on the same LWR model, and add a loss-conditional PINN that removes the per-corridor loss-weight search.
AI.result: On four real corridors (NGSIM, I-80, PeMS04, PeMS08), the physics-informed estimators generalise to held-out sensors where data-driven models overfit; on the two shock-rich corridors the physics-informed estimator leads the no-physics network by about 26-38 percent at 85-90 percent held out and the strongest classical kriging by about 10-21 percent at 90 percent held out, while the loss-conditional PINN matches a 20-point search at about 5x lower cost.
AI.conclusion: The advantage comes from how the conservation law is imposed rather than from a generic smoothness prior, which means physics priors can make sparse-sensor traffic estimation practical.

title: On the Global Convergence of Stochastic Adam for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: The Adam optimizer is widely used to train neural networks with highly nonlinear and nonconvex objective functions. Remarkably, Adam often drives the empirical training loss nearly to zero. This phenomenon has been partially explained by neural tangent kernel (NTK) analyses of gradient descent (GD) and stochastic gradient descent (SGD). However, analyzing Adam presents additional challenges. Its first-moment momentum couples stochastic gradients across iterations, while its adaptive second-moment preconditioner depends on the same stochastic gradient used in the update. In this paper, we establish linear convergence guarantees for Adam in training sufficiently wide two-layer neural networks with either full-batch or minibatch gradients. For full-batch Adam, we construct a Lyapunov function to control the effect of historical momentum. For minibatch Adam, our analysis builds on an exact virtual-iterate representation, a conditional analysis of the dependence between stochastic gradients and adaptive preconditioners, and uniform concentration bounds for the second-moment estimates. We prove geometric decay of the empirical loss for full-batch Adam and geometric decay in restricted expectation on a high-probability event for minibatch Adam. Beyond regression, we extend our convergence analysis to physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for solving the Poisson equation, where differential operators and separate sampling of interior and boundary points introduce additional challenges. We establish analogous global convergence guarantees for both deterministic and stochastic Adam under explicit conditions on network width and Adam's parameters, characterizing the effects of minibatch size on convergence. These results help bridge the gap between Adam's empirical success and its theoretical understanding, providing sharper convergence guarantees for PINNs than existing analyses.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes linear (geometric) convergence guarantees for Adam when training sufficiently wide two-layer neural networks with full-batch or minibatch gradients, and extends the analysis to PINNs for the Poisson equation.
AI.motivation: Adam's momentum couples stochastic gradients across iterations and its second-moment preconditioner depends on the same stochastic gradient used in the update, which existing NTK analyses of GD and SGD do not handle.
AI.method: For full-batch Adam the authors construct a Lyapunov function to control historical momentum; for minibatch Adam they use an exact virtual-iterate representation, a conditional analysis of the dependence between stochastic gradients and preconditioners, and uniform concentration bounds for second-moment estimates.
AI.result: The authors prove geometric decay of the empirical loss for full-batch Adam and geometric decay in restricted expectation on a high-probability event for minibatch Adam, with analogous guarantees for deterministic and stochastic Adam on PINNs for the Poisson equation under explicit conditions on network width and Adam's parameters.
AI.conclusion: The results give sharper convergence guarantees for PINNs than existing analyses and characterise how minibatch size affects convergence, narrowing the gap between Adam's empirical success and its theory.

title: Late but Valuable: Why Deadlines Change the Measured Value of LLM Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly plan and run experiments in automated laboratories. These experiments keep running while the model reasons and run on schedules with hard deadlines. If an LLM-generated answer arrives late, the system executes a safe fallback action instead, such as rejecting a sample. This creates a systems problem that standard serving metrics do not capture. An answer that matches the fallback adds no value, and answers that differ from the fallback may require more reasoning time. Reporting answer quality and latency separately can therefore overstate the value of reasoning. We test this on synthetic sample decisions, where the best choice is known exactly and a runtime enforces the deadline. We compare one LLM's fast mode, which answers directly, with its thinking mode, which reasons first. In a prespecified replay of 1,200 new decisions, thinking answers that missed a deadline were worth about five times as much as on-time ones. Multiplying the on-time rate by the mean answer value predicted about twice the value that thinking delivered. This prediction overstated thinking's advantage over fast mode by 0.0241 per decision, and by 0.0191 in a repeat on 300 new decisions. Both 95% confidence intervals excluded zero. In a single-GPU Qwen3-8B experiment using simultaneous request bursts, raising the number of requests from 8 to 56 reduced the share of thinking answers that met a 45 s deadline from 79.2% to 1.4%, although total output tripled. Evaluations of LLM agents for laboratories should therefore measure each answer's value and arrival time together and score the action that actually runs.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that LLM reasoning should be valued by answer quality and arrival time together, since in deadline-bound laboratory systems a late thinking answer is worth about five times more than an on-time one and reporting quality and latency separately overstates reasoning's value.
AI.motivation: Standard serving metrics do not capture that a late LLM answer triggers a safe fallback action, so reporting answer quality and latency separately can overstate the value of reasoning in automated laboratories.
AI.method: The authors test LLM fast mode versus thinking mode on synthetic sample decisions with known best answers and a runtime that enforces a deadline, using a prespecified replay of 1,200 decisions and a repeat on 300 new decisions, plus a single-GPU Qwen3-8B experiment with simultaneous request bursts.
AI.result: Thinking answers that missed a deadline were worth about five times as much as on-time ones, and multiplying the on-time rate by the mean answer value predicted about twice the value delivered; this overstated thinking's advantage over fast mode by 0.0241 per decision in the replay and by 0.0191 in the repeat, with 95 percent confidence intervals excluding zero. In the Qwen3-8B burst experiment, raising requests from 8 to 56 cut the share of thinking answers meeting a 45 s deadline from 79.2 percent to 1.4 percent, although total output tripled.
AI.conclusion: Evaluations of LLM agents for laboratories should measure each answer's value and arrival time together and score the action that actually runs.

title: CRAFT-GBM: Selecting Best Features for Gradient-Boosted Machine Learning
summary: Feature subsampling is used to accelerate gradient-boosted trees, yet standard approaches fix the feature count in advance and largely ignore the split-gain evidence accumulated during training. We introduce CRAFT-GBM (Confidence-Ranked Adaptive Feature Tracking), a native LightGBM extension that uses this evidence to adapt which---and, by default, how many---features are searched each boosting round. CRAFT-GBM transforms root-split gains into bounded observations and constructs joint time-uniform bounds valid under adaptive, non-stationary training histories. In its default endogenous mode, after initialization, CRAFT-GBM retains exactly the features that cannot yet be ruled out as best, letting the selected feature-set size $K_t$ emerge from training history rather than a pre-specified fraction. With probability at least $1-\delta$, every feature with the largest expected gain is retained jointly across all rounds after initialization. When a feature fraction $f$ is specified instead, CRAFT-GBM ranks features by their interval point estimates and provides an approximate top-$K$ guarantee for feature budget $K_f$. We implement CRAFT-GBM within LightGBM while preserving its native feature-bundling representation, and evaluate it across 14 public and synthetic dataset families and four noise-augmented settings. In the fully endogenous setting, CRAFT-GBM reduces per-fit training time by 39.74\% with 1.04\% lower test loss in the geometric mean across all 18 RQ1 experiments. Under pre-specified feature fraction $f$, Exogenous CRAFT-GBM also yields aggregate training-time reductions up to 13.52 percentage points larger than random feature subsampling, with no increase in aggregate test loss relative to full-feature LightGBM. Accumulated training evidence can thus support adaptive feature search with statistical guarantees while retaining the practical advantages of native gradient boosting.

AI.tldr: CRAFT-GBM is a native LightGBM extension that adapts which features, and by default how many, are searched each boosting round using split-gain evidence with time-uniform confidence bounds.
AI.motivation: Feature subsampling in gradient-boosted trees usually fixes the feature count in advance and ignores the split-gain evidence accumulated during training.
AI.method: The method turns root-split gains into bounded observations, builds joint time-uniform bounds valid under adaptive, non-stationary training histories, and in its endogenous mode retains exactly the features that cannot yet be ruled out as best; with a specified feature fraction it ranks features by interval point estimates for an approximate top-K guarantee.
AI.result: In the fully endogenous setting CRAFT-GBM reduces per-fit training time by 39.74 percent with 1.04 percent lower test loss in the geometric mean across 18 RQ1 experiments on 14 public and synthetic dataset families and four noise-augmented settings; under a pre-specified feature fraction the exogenous variant gives training-time reductions up to 13.52 percentage points larger than random feature subsampling with no aggregate test-loss increase relative to full-feature LightGBM.
AI.conclusion: Accumulated training evidence can support adaptive feature search with statistical guarantees while keeping the practical advantages of native gradient boosting.

title: LBSNet: Lightweight Brain State Modeling via Learnable Spectral Prototypes for EEG-Based Fatigue Detection
summary: EEG-based fatigue detection requires modeling spectral information across bands and its temporal variation. Recent methods combine multi-band modeling with adaptive temporal processing, yet how spectral structure across bands should influence the contribution of each temporal interval remains insufficiently explored. We propose LBSNet, a lightweight network that uses prototype-based brain-state modeling to link local spectral structure with temporal aggregation. LBSNet extracts compact multi-band features through band-specific temporal convolution, shared spatial projections, and cross-band recalibration. Within each window, relative spectral activity is encoded as a normalized descriptor and softly matched to learnable spectral prototypes. Prototype assignments and learned prototype importance jointly determine temporal weights for power aggregation, allowing the spectral pattern of each window to guide its contribution to the prediction. Subject-independent experiments on SEED-VIG and SADT show that LBSNet outperforms seven baselines while maintaining low computational cost. Ablation and visualization analyses support prototype-guided temporal weighting, while the learned prototypes reveal a gradual redistribution of relative cross-band spectral states with increasing fatigue. The code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: LBSNet is a lightweight EEG fatigue detection network that uses learnable spectral prototypes to weight temporal windows by their cross-band spectral pattern.
AI.motivation: Existing EEG fatigue methods that combine multi-band modeling with adaptive temporal processing do not explore how spectral structure across bands should set the contribution of each temporal interval.
AI.method: LBSNet extracts multi-band features with band-specific temporal convolution, shared spatial projections and cross-band recalibration, encodes each window's relative spectral activity as a normalized descriptor, softly matches it to learnable prototypes, and uses assignments and learned prototype importance to set temporal weights for power aggregation.
AI.result: In subject-independent experiments on SEED-VIG and SADT, LBSNet outperforms seven baselines while keeping computational cost low, and ablation and visualization analyses support prototype-guided temporal weighting.
AI.conclusion: The learned prototypes show a gradual redistribution of relative cross-band spectral states as fatigue increases, suggesting an interpretable link between spectral structure and fatigue.

title: An Evaluation of Tabular Foundation Models as Training-Free World Models
summary: World models are widely considered to be a potential key component of model-based reinforcement learning and robot planning, but typically require task-specific training on substantial interaction data. We investigate whether a pretrained tabular foundation model (TabFM) can serve as a training-free dynamics model for world modeling by framing next-state prediction as in-context regression over transition pairs, and where such a model helps and where it breaks. Across synthetic dynamical systems and robot locomotion benchmarks, TabFM is more accurate than LSTM and MLP models trained from scratch on the same limited transitions in almost all settings, and among regressors fitted to the same data it is the most accurate on locomotion, while a Gaussian process is more accurate on smooth low-dimensional systems. However, models trained on the full dataset remain substantially better on most systems. When rolled out autoregressively over multiple steps, TabFM's accuracy depends strongly on how much context it is given. With a short context, its rollouts quickly degrade to the level of a trivial baseline, whereas with a long context they improve substantially and, on one locomotion task, exceed a trained LSTM. Inference is also about three orders of magnitude slower than an LSTM. Overall, in their current state, we find that training-free priors are useful as predictors when data are scarce and enough context is available, but they are not yet a substitute for trained world models in planning.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates a pretrained tabular foundation model used in context as a training-free dynamics model and finds it is useful with scarce data and enough context but is not yet a substitute for trained world models in planning.
AI.motivation: World models for model-based RL and robot planning usually need task-specific training on substantial interaction data, and it is unclear whether a pretrained tabular foundation model can serve as a training-free alternative.
AI.method: Next-state prediction is framed as in-context regression over transition pairs, and the TabFM is compared with LSTM and MLP models trained from scratch on the same limited transitions, with regressors fitted to the same data and a Gaussian process, across synthetic dynamical systems and robot locomotion benchmarks, including multi-step autoregressive rollouts with varying context length.
AI.result: TabFM is more accurate than LSTM and MLP trained from scratch in almost all settings and is the most accurate regressor on locomotion, while a Gaussian process is more accurate on smooth low-dimensional systems; models trained on the full dataset remain substantially better on most systems. Rollout accuracy depends strongly on context length, and with long context it exceeds a trained LSTM on one locomotion task, while inference is about three orders of magnitude slower than an LSTM.
AI.conclusion: Training-free priors are useful predictors when data are scarce and enough context is available, but they are not yet a substitute for trained world models in planning.

title: Constrained Variational Policy Optimization for Hybrid Action Spaces
comment: 29 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables. This work extends constrained variational policy optimization from continuous-action spaces to hybrid discrete-continuous action spaces
summary: Constrained reinforcement learning in hybrid action spaces must coordinate discrete modes and mode-conditioned continuous controls under long-horizon cost constraints. Existing constrained hybrid-action methods typically optimize factorized policies directly in parameter space, whereas Constrained Variational Policy Optimization (CVPO) separates nonparametric improvement from parametric projection in its original continuous-action formulation. We introduce Hybrid Constrained Variational Policy Optimization (H-CVPO), extending this variational framework to hybrid action spaces. Under boundedness and strict feasibility, its constrained E-step has zero duality gap and, when the dual optimum is attained at positive temperature, yields a closed-form joint target distribution over hybrid actions through exponential reward-cost reweighting. Using the exact hybrid KL decomposition, we formulate a factorized M-step that fits both policy components to this target under separate discrete and conditional-continuous trust regions. For exact E/M updates, we prove fixed-reference surrogate improvement and conditional reward-cost bounds with a sufficient feasibility-margin condition. For approximate updates, we establish the existence of a dual minimizer under continuity on a compact domain and use residual-based admissibility to determine whether to project the target. Ablations identify cost-aware reweighting as an important contributor to constraint control. Extensive experiments in simulated hybrid-control environments show that H-CVPO achieves favorable reward-cost trade-offs compared with hybrid-action baselines.

AI.tldr: H-CVPO extends the variational constrained policy optimization framework to hybrid discrete-continuous action spaces, with a closed-form joint target from exponential reward-cost reweighting and a factorized M-step.
AI.motivation: Existing constrained hybrid-action methods optimize factorized policies directly in parameter space, whereas CVPO separates nonparametric improvement from parametric projection only for continuous actions.
AI.method: Under boundedness and strict feasibility the constrained E-step has zero duality gap and yields a closed-form joint target over hybrid actions through exponential reward-cost reweighting, and an M-step using the exact hybrid KL decomposition fits discrete and conditional-continuous policy components to this target under separate trust regions.
AI.result: For exact E and M updates the authors prove fixed-reference surrogate improvement and conditional reward-cost bounds under a feasibility-margin condition, and for approximate updates they establish existence of a dual minimizer under continuity on a compact domain; in simulated hybrid-control environments H-CVPO achieves favorable reward-cost trade-offs against hybrid-action baselines, with ablations identifying cost-aware reweighting as an important contributor to constraint control.
AI.conclusion: The variational framework transfers to hybrid action spaces with theoretical guarantees for exact updates and a residual-based admissibility rule for approximate ones.

title: Attention Is Only as Good as Its Witnesses: When Higher-Order Layers Help, and When They Do Not
comment: 25 pages, 5 figures, 7 supplementary tables. Code (Apache 2.0): this https URL ; demo and tutorial: this https URL
summary: Transformers stop learning graph search as graphs grow, and learn the card game SET only after many distinct questions, although attention can represent both. We read these failures, and the uneven record of higher-order attention, from what a layer sums over: each layer we study computes the partition function of a family of witnesses and reads it at a temperature. Two laws follow. The depth law is a known result of logic, which we state for these layers: L layers over two-step walks reach exactly 2^L - 1 steps, just as a logical statement with L nested clauses of the form "there is a vertex such that" sees exactly that far. We build a construction that reaches this far, checked in Lean, and, when vertices carry no names, no such network reaches further. The size law is the cost of reading at a temperature, which logic does not have: existence is read correctly at every size, in the worst case, if and only if inverse temperature times margin is at least the logarithm of the number of candidates. Layers built on these laws, and on two principles that we test, learn where Transformers fail. One propagator layer trained on 49-vertex graphs answers every question at every search depth on 250-vertex graphs. Given the modulus 3, exponential Newton computes the softmax of 2-simplicial attention over pairs exactly in 3^d n operations for d clocks; with six clocks it learns SET from as few deals as 2-simplicial attention and transfers from 8- to 20-card tables. On CLRS-30 without hints, a 186,000-parameter block of OR-join and power-mean channels matches (within half a point) or beats a model of at least 73 million parameters on 9 of 12 graph tasks of the official test set, and on 8 of 12 with freshly drawn test graphs. The same account explains where pair layers did not help and where parallel layers must loop.

AI.tldr: The paper explains when higher-order attention layers help by reading each layer as the partition function of a family of witnesses at a temperature, yielding a depth law tied to logic and a size law on reading existence reliably.
AI.motivation: Transformers fail to keep learning graph search as graphs grow and learn the card game SET only after many distinct questions, and the record of higher-order attention is uneven without a principled account.
AI.method: Each studied layer is viewed as computing the partition function of a witness family read at a temperature; the depth law is stated for layers over two-step walks, a construction is checked in Lean, and the size law gives the condition that inverse temperature times margin is at least the logarithm of the number of candidates; the authors build propagator, exponential Newton and OR-join and power-mean layers based on these laws and two principles they test.
AI.result: A single propagator layer trained on 49-vertex graphs answers every question at every search depth on 250-vertex graphs; with six clocks, a 2-simplicial variant learns SET from as few deals as 2-simplicial attention and transfers from 8-card to 20-card tables; on CLRS-30 without hints a 186,000-parameter block matches within half a point or beats a model of at least 73 million parameters on 9 of 12 graph tasks of the official test set, and on 8 of 12 with freshly drawn test graphs.
AI.conclusion: The same account explains where pair layers did not help and where parallel layers must loop, so the witness-based view predicts when higher-order attention is useful.

title: Decision Aware Origin-Destination Demand Estimation with Structurally Constrained Data
summary: Origin-destination (OD) demand plays an important role in transportation system design and management applications. Conventional OD estimation methods typically judge estimation quality based on how estimated demand aligns with observed traffic data and historical demand patterns. We argue that data alignment alone is insufficient; how errors in OD estimates influence downstream decision quality should also be considered. This paper develops a decision aware OD demand estimation framework that leverages structurally constrained traffic data to characterize an admissible demand region, within which we identify OD estimates that would lead to least regret in the downstream decision. Therefore, our OD estimates are both data-consistent and decision-relevant. Methodologically, we approximate the admissible demand region induced by physical network constraints through a geometric representation, which regularizes the search over feasible OD estimates. Within this regularized region, we use a convex surrogate of downstream regret to obtain a tractable decision aware optimization problem. Numerical experiments show that the proposed framework consistently reduces decision regret relative to conventional estimation benchmarks, demonstrating the value of aligning OD demand estimation with downstream decision quality.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a decision-aware origin-destination demand estimation framework that picks, within a structurally admissible demand region, the estimates that minimize a convex surrogate of downstream decision regret.
AI.motivation: Conventional OD estimation judges quality only by agreement with observed traffic data and historical demand, ignoring how estimation errors affect downstream decision quality.
AI.method: The admissible demand region induced by physical network constraints is approximated by a geometric representation that regularizes the search over feasible OD estimates, and a convex surrogate of downstream regret gives a tractable decision-aware optimization problem.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show that the framework consistently reduces decision regret relative to conventional estimation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Aligning OD demand estimation with downstream decision quality yields estimates that are both data-consistent and decision-relevant.

title: Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System for ICU Discharge Risk Assessment
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures. Code available at this https URL
summary: Unplanned 30-day intensive care unit (ICU) readmission is a critical benchmark for evaluating healthcare quality. Most predictive models assume readmission risk depends solely on a patient's individual pathophysiological state, ignoring hospital operational context and resource capacity. In practice, discharge decisions are dynamic trade-offs between patient stability and bed turnover pressures. To address this gap, we develop an Operation-aware Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for ICU discharge risk assessment. The system combines multi-agent collaborative extraction with self-evolving retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to eliminate template noise from progress notes, while constructing departmental workload indicators alongside admission flow features, continuous vital signs, and sparse medical codes (ICD/DRG). Addressing severe class imbalance (about 10.5% readmissions) and alarm fatigue, we implement data normalization, class reweighting, and decision-threshold calibration. In 20 independent runs across 20,000 ICU stays from MIMIC-III, empirical findings demonstrate that: vital signs alone have limited predictive capacity under real-world class imbalance (PR-AUC of 0.1387 +/- 0.0086); directly concatenating raw text embeddings degrades decision tree performance (XGBoost and LightGBM PR-AUC drop to 0.3893 and 0.4030); whereas an end-to-end multimodal fine-tuning architecture (Transformer E2E FineTune) utilizing layer-wise parameter freezing and differential learning rates reverses text negative transfer, achieving the highest AUROC of 0.8288 +/- 0.0110, PR-AUC of 0.4373 +/- 0.0310, and F1-Score of 0.4757 +/- 0.0196. Operational indicators supply independent risk signals, laying an engineering foundation for high-utility clinical decision support tools.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an operation-aware multimodal CDSS for 30-day ICU readmission risk that combines clinical notes, vital signs, medical codes and hospital workload features, with a fine-tuned Transformer reaching the highest reported AUROC on MIMIC-III.
AI.motivation: Most readmission models assume risk depends only on the patient's physiological state and ignore hospital operational context and bed-turnover pressure, and class imbalance of about 10.5 percent readmissions and alarm fatigue complicate prediction.
AI.method: The system uses multi-agent collaborative extraction with self-evolving RAG to remove template noise from progress notes, constructs departmental workload indicators alongside admission flow, vital signs and ICD/DRG codes, applies normalization, class reweighting and threshold calibration, and compares text-handling strategies including a Transformer with layer-wise freezing and differential learning rates.
AI.result: Across 20 independent runs on 20,000 MIMIC-III ICU stays, vital signs alone reached a PR-AUC of 0.1387 plus or minus 0.0086; directly concatenating raw text embeddings lowered XGBoost and LightGBM PR-AUC to 0.3893 and 0.4030; the end-to-end Transformer fine-tuning reached AUROC 0.8288 plus or minus 0.0110, PR-AUC 0.4373 plus or minus 0.0310 and F1 0.4757 plus or minus 0.0196.
AI.conclusion: Operational indicators supply independent risk signals and the work lays an engineering foundation for clinical decision support tools with high utility.

title: Pairwise distortion distribution for compression and quantization
summary: Choosing the latent dimension is a critical challenge in data compression, where conventional hyperparameter optimization is costly and ad hoc. Intrinsic dimension provides a good alternative, which connects information-theoretic notions such as Renyi information dimension (RID) to rate-distortion dimension and random codebook compression. In this work, we introduce the pairwise distortion distribution (PDD) and its asymptotic limit, pairwise dimension (PD), which generalize the correlation integral to general distortion measures. We show that PD bounds RID, and PDD provides a lower bound for random codebook quantization performance, which can guide a practical use for compression, quantization, and dimensionality reduction applications.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the pairwise distortion distribution and its asymptotic pairwise dimension, which generalize the correlation integral to general distortion measures and link intrinsic dimension to compression performance.
AI.motivation: Choosing the latent dimension in data compression is costly and ad hoc, and existing intrinsic dimension notions such as Renyi information dimension are not directly tied to rate-distortion for general distortion measures.
AI.method: The authors define the pairwise distortion distribution as a generalization of the correlation integral to arbitrary distortion measures and take its asymptotic limit as the pairwise dimension.
AI.result: The paper shows that pairwise dimension bounds Renyi information dimension and that the pairwise distortion distribution gives a lower bound on random codebook quantization performance.
AI.conclusion: These quantities can guide practical choices of latent dimension for compression, quantization and dimensionality reduction.

title: ShiftCache: Fast and Exact Indel Effect Prediction by Reusing Shifted Reference Encodings
summary: Sequence-to-function models such as AlphaGenome and Borzoi read up to a megabase of DNA and score a genetic variant by comparing their predictions for the reference and alternate sequences. Insertions and deletions (indels) are costly to score, because an indel usually shifts the unchanged DNA after it onto a different pooling grid, which prevents direct reuse of the reference's encoder activations. The AlphaGenome Atlas scored more than 100 million indels with three full model passes each, although the DNA after an indel matches the reference shifted by the indel's length. We present ShiftCache, an exact reuse system that encodes each shifted reference once and shares it among all variants scored in the same window with the same shift. ShiftCache copies every encoder output a variant can reuse and recomputes the rest in batched tiles. On held-out AlphaGenome windows shared by many indels, in strict fp32 on one A6000, ShiftCache is 3.5 to 6.5$\times$ faster than deduplicated dense execution and 1.6 to 2.7$\times$ faster than our adaptation of layer-by-layer reuse to indels. It is 3.5 to 4.1$\times$ faster than dense reimplementations of two published analyses with Borzoi and AlphaGenome, and 2.6$\times$ faster than dense execution with Enformer. Scoring each variant in its own centered 131 kb window makes ShiftCache only 1.36$\times$ faster than deduplicated dense execution, and highly diverse insertion lengths or many dispersed edits can make it slower than layer-by-layer reuse or dense execution. For encoders that meet our conditions, ShiftCache computes the same predictions as dense execution in exact arithmetic. On an A6000, every checked output of the default AlphaGenome and Borzoi runs matches dense execution within an absolute and relative tolerance of $10^{-5}$. With larger tile batches, with Enformer or on an H100, a small fraction of values exceeds this tolerance.

AI.tldr: ShiftCache is an exact reuse system that encodes each shifted reference window once and shares it among indels with the same shift, making indel effect scoring with sequence-to-function models faster while matching dense outputs.
AI.motivation: Scoring indels with models such as AlphaGenome and Borzoi is costly because an indel shifts downstream DNA onto a different pooling grid, which blocks direct reuse of reference encoder activations, and the AlphaGenome Atlas ran three full passes for over 100 million indels.
AI.method: ShiftCache encodes each shifted reference once, shares the encoding among all variants in the same window with the same shift, copies every reusable encoder output and recomputes the rest in batched tiles.
AI.result: On held-out AlphaGenome windows in strict fp32 on one A6000, ShiftCache is 3.5 to 6.5 times faster than deduplicated dense execution and 1.6 to 2.7 times faster than an adaptation of layer-by-layer reuse, and 2.6 times faster than dense Enformer execution; scoring each variant in its own centered 131 kb window reduces the speedup to 1.36 times, and with default AlphaGenome and Borzoi runs on an A6000 all checked outputs match dense execution within tolerance 1e-5.
AI.conclusion: For encoders that meet its conditions ShiftCache computes the same predictions as dense execution in exact arithmetic, but it can be slower for diverse insertion lengths or many dispersed edits, and larger tile batches, Enformer or an H100 can exceed the tolerance for a small fraction of values.

title: MixRoute: Rethinking Single-Distribution Training for Generalizable Neural Routing
summary: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) is a promising paradigm for solving routing problems, yet its generalization across diverse data distributions remains a critical bottleneck. Existing methods typically tackle cross-distribution generalization through complex multi-distribution training or intricate meta-learning schemes, implicitly presuming that single-distribution training yields a weak zero-shot baseline. In this paper, we demonstrate that the potential of single-distribution training has been substantially underestimated and can be unlocked by a simple architectural inductive bias: Mix Normalization. To approach this, we first construct a comprehensive benchmark spanning three representative routing problems and 179 fine-grained datasets, capturing diverse shifts in node coordinates, customer demands, capacity and time windows. Building on this benchmark, we propose MixRoute, a neural framework that adaptively combines normalization statistics at different granularities to mitigate varying distribution shifts. Trained exclusively on uniform distributions, MixRoute generalizes effectively to a wide range of unseen distributions without any distribution-specific adaptation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MixRoute consistently achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot generalization. Our work revisits normalization as a parsimonious alternative for zero-shot generalization against complex training-adaptation schemes.

AI.tldr: MixRoute shows that single-distribution training with Mix Normalization, an adaptive combination of normalization statistics at different granularities, yields state-of-the-art zero-shot generalization for neural routing solvers.
AI.motivation: Existing neural combinatorial optimization methods improve cross-distribution generalization with complex multi-distribution training or meta-learning, assuming single-distribution training gives a weak zero-shot baseline.
AI.method: The authors build a benchmark of three routing problems with 179 fine-grained datasets covering shifts in node coordinates, customer demands, capacity and time windows, and propose MixRoute, which adaptively combines normalization statistics at different granularities and is trained only on uniform distributions.
AI.result: MixRoute generalizes effectively to a wide range of unseen distributions without distribution-specific adaptation and consistently achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot generalization in extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: Normalization is a parsimonious alternative to complex training and adaptation schemes for zero-shot generalization in neural routing.

title: FireGate: Bounding Behaviour Change Before Training in Continual RL Fine-Tuning
summary: Fine-tuning a deployed language model on one task after another can change behaviour that should stay fixed, such as earlier skills, general chat or refusals. Today, such forgetting is found only after training, on the benchmarks someone chose to run. This work bounds, before training, how often its outputs change on chosen prompt distributions. FireGate places each task's update, such as a new LoRA, behind a gate, which is a classifier on the model's frozen lower layers that decides for each prompt whether the update is used. Where no gate fires, the model computes exactly what the old one computes. As a result, on any prompt distribution, every bounded behaviour score changes by at most the gates' firing rate there over a whole task stream. Calibrating each gate on unlabeled prompts of what must not change fixes that rate before training, with a PAC guarantee, whatever weights training produces. Forgetting is thus bounded by the gate's false-alarm rate, and its price is the gate's power: no update, gated or not, that changes as few protected outputs can change new-task outputs more often than the best test of that level tells new-task prompts from protected ones. On reinforcement-learning streams of up to five tasks, gated training keeps the earlier tasks and changes 3.3% of held-out chat responses, whereas ungated training changes 91.8%. Across seven models, the gain kept behind the gate follows its firing rate on new-task prompts, measured before training. The certificate covers the gated model as deployed, on the prompt distributions sampled for calibration, not against an adversary who searches for prompts that fire the gate.

AI.tldr: FireGate bounds, before training, how often a continually fine-tuned language model changes its outputs on chosen prompt distributions by gating each task update behind a calibrated classifier.
AI.motivation: Forgetting of earlier skills, general chat and refusals during sequential fine-tuning is currently found only after training and only on the benchmarks someone chose to run.
AI.method: Each task's update, such as a new LoRA, sits behind a gate that is a classifier on the frozen lower layers and decides per prompt whether the update is used; where no gate fires the model computes what the old model computes, and each gate is calibrated on unlabeled prompts that must not change to fix its firing rate before training with a PAC guarantee.
AI.result: On reinforcement-learning streams of up to five tasks, gated training keeps earlier tasks and changes 3.3 percent of held-out chat responses, whereas ungated training changes 91.8 percent; across seven models the gain kept behind the gate follows the firing rate on new-task prompts, measured before training.
AI.conclusion: Forgetting is bounded by the gate's false-alarm rate, at the cost of reduced power on new-task prompts, and the certificate holds for sampled calibration distributions but not against adversarial prompts that search for gate firings.

title: HyInv Technical Report
summary: Inverse folding designs amino-acid sequences for a given protein backbone, and screening needs many candidates that are both diverse and well folded. We present HyInv, a 1.96-million-parameter backbone-conditioned graph network with an encoder-decoder architecture, trained by Hyra 2.0, the research agent developed by our team: pretrained with random-order autoregressive sequence modeling, followed by structure-reward reinforcement learning. At inference, a grouped draft-and-rewrite sampler that uses separate draft and rewrite temperatures improves refolding TM-score at matched diversity. An optimized implementation with BF16 numerics designs 128 sequences for a 402-residue backbone in 50.6 ms on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU, about 52 times faster than the reference sampler, and an exact FP32 path that returns the reference sequences is 8.7 times faster. Across five benchmark datasets and seven dataset-predictor combinations, HyInv reaches a higher average scTM than all ten external baselines at comparable or higher sequence diversity, with large margins over ProteinMPNN and ProteinZero V2. The same default setting supports de novo backbones, pocket-constrained libraries, enzyme redesign with the catalytic site kept, and loop redesign. We have released our code and model at this https URL.

AI.tldr: HyInv is a 1.96-million-parameter backbone-conditioned graph network for inverse folding that reaches a higher average scTM than ten external baselines across five benchmark datasets and runs fast on a single GPU.
AI.motivation: Screening protein design needs many candidate sequences that are both diverse and well folded, and existing inverse-folding tools such as ProteinMPNN and ProteinZero V2 fall short on these goals.
AI.method: HyInv uses an encoder-decoder graph network pretrained with random-order autoregressive sequence modeling and then tuned with structure-reward reinforcement learning, and samples with a grouped draft-and-rewrite procedure that uses separate draft and rewrite temperatures, with an optimized BF16 implementation and an exact FP32 path.
AI.result: HyInv reaches a higher average scTM than all ten external baselines at comparable or higher sequence diversity across five benchmark datasets and seven dataset-predictor combinations, with large margins over ProteinMPNN and ProteinZero V2; it designs 128 sequences for a 402-residue backbone in 50.6 ms on one H20 GPU, about 52 times faster than the reference sampler, and the exact FP32 path is 8.7 times faster.
AI.conclusion: The same default setting supports de novo backbones, pocket-constrained libraries, enzyme redesign with the catalytic site kept and loop redesign, and the code and model are released.

title: Reward-Estimated Hypergradient for Bilevel Reinforcement Learning with Black-Box Follower
summary: Hypergradient (HG) methods for bilevel reinforcement learning (RL) typically assume a white-box follower whose reward is known. In practice, however, the leader rarely knows the follower's reward function and can only observe its trajectories. We address this black-box setting and propose Reward-Estimated Hypergradients (RE-HG), which recovers the follower's reward from these trajectories via inverse RL (IRL). Yet IRL identifies the reward only up to potential-based shaping, a transformation that leaves the follower's behavior unchanged but biases the HG. We prove that, for linear rewards, this bias cancels when IRL estimates are aggregated across sufficiently diverse dynamics, which the leader's own updates naturally supply. To handle finite samples, RE-HG truncates small eigenvalues of the aggregated feature covariance, restoring the identifiable subspace and stabilizing the estimation. Experiments show that RE-HG estimates gradients aligned with a white-box Oracle and achieves comparable performance; empirically, the truncation also suppresses HG explosions, letting RE-HG avoid local optima that trap the Oracle in sharp reward landscapes.

AI.tldr: RE-HG enables hypergradient-based bilevel RL when the follower's reward is unknown by recovering it from trajectories via inverse RL and removing the shaping bias with aggregation over diverse dynamics.
AI.motivation: Hypergradient methods for bilevel RL assume a white-box follower whose reward is known, but in practice the leader only observes follower trajectories, and inverse RL recovers rewards only up to potential-based shaping, which biases the hypergradient.
AI.method: For linear rewards the authors show the shaping bias cancels when IRL estimates are aggregated across sufficiently diverse dynamics, which the leader's own updates supply, and to handle finite samples RE-HG truncates small eigenvalues of the aggregated feature covariance to restore the identifiable subspace.
AI.result: Experiments show that RE-HG estimates gradients aligned with a white-box Oracle and achieves comparable performance, and the truncation suppresses hypergradient explosions so RE-HG avoids local optima that trap the Oracle in sharp reward landscapes.
AI.conclusion: Bilevel RL with a black-box follower can match white-box hypergradient performance once reward recovery is made identifiable through aggregation and eigenvalue truncation.

title: HyPLM Technical Report
summary: Protein language models (PLMs) are standard tools for variant-effect prediction, protein annotation and design, but the compute needed to train and serve them keeps growing. We present HyPLM-Flash, an efficient and open PLM trained by Hyra 2.0, the research agent developed by our team. HyPLM-Flash is a 650-million-parameter masked language model trained on 726 billion tokens, 0.73 times the data of ESM-2 650M and a fifth to an eighth of the data of E1-600M and ESM C 600M. It runs on an inference engine with fused kernels and INT8 matrix multiplication, embedding about 130,000 residues per second on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU, 1.9 to 2.7 times faster than other 600M-class encoders. In a matched evaluation against 28 public checkpoints on 32 tasks, HyPLM-Flash reaches a ProteinGym zero-shot Spearman correlation of 0.409, statistically tied with ESM-2 650M, ESM C 600M and E1-600M, and the highest organismal-fitness score among self-supervised single-sequence models. It gives the best long-range contact precision of all models evaluated, including ESM-2 15B and ESM C 6B, and a lower masked-residue loss than ESM-2 650M, ESM C 600M and E1-600M on held-out sequences and on recently released PDB chains. Matching state-of-the-art accuracy at a fraction of the training and inference cost, HyPLM-Flash sets a new Pareto frontier for protein language models. We have released the model weights and the inference engine at this https URL.

AI.tldr: HyPLM-Flash is an open 650-million-parameter protein language model trained on 726 billion tokens that matches leading 600M-class encoders on ProteinGym while embedding residues 1.9 to 2.7 times faster.
AI.motivation: Training and serving protein language models needs ever more compute, so the authors seek a model that matches state-of-the-art accuracy at a lower cost.
AI.method: The model is a masked language model trained on 726 billion tokens, about 0.73 times the data of ESM-2 650M, and runs on an inference engine with fused kernels and INT8 matrix multiplication; it was trained by the Hyra 2.0 research agent.
AI.result: HyPLM-Flash reaches a ProteinGym zero-shot Spearman correlation of 0.409, statistically tied with ESM-2 650M, ESM C 600M and E1-600M, embeds about 130,000 residues per second on one H20 GPU, and gives the best long-range contact precision among 28 public checkpoints evaluated on 32 tasks, including ESM-2 15B and ESM C 6B.
AI.conclusion: The model sets a new Pareto frontier for protein language models in accuracy against training and inference cost, and its weights and inference engine are released.

title: Scalable Bayesian Optimization for Efficient Exploration of Moire Patterns
summary: Large materials design spaces often contain rare high-performing configurations that are difficult to identify through trial-and-error exploration or purely representative machine-learning (ML) sampling. In this work, we present FruBO, a flexible Bayesian Optimization framework for accelerating the discovery of optimal configurations in computationally demanding materials design problems. As a case study, we investigate multilayer Moiré patterns generated by the superposition of six rotated hexagonal lattices, where the objective is to identify the rotational conformation that maximizes pore-size uniformity, quantified using the Jain fairness index. The resulting benchmark contains 600,000 unique configurations and exhibits a highly skewed objective distribution, making the global optimum difficult to locate by random sampling. We compare random exploration, Gaussian Process-based Bayesian Optimization, and Bayesian Optimization using a lightweight CatBoost surrogate with committee-based uncertainty estimation. Random sampling identifies the global optimum only after 533,012 evaluations, requiring approximately 31 hours, while Gaussian Process-based BO becomes impractical due to GPU memory exhaustion after 290 acquired samples. In contrast, FruBO with CatBoost identifies the global optimum after 1,470 acquired samples and approximately 1.15 hours. These results demonstrate that scalable surrogate models can substantially improve the feasibility and efficiency of BO in large nanomaterials design spaces.

AI.tldr: The paper applies Bayesian optimization with a CatBoost surrogate and committee-based uncertainty to find the most pore-size-uniform configuration in a 600,000-configuration Moire pattern design space, reaching the global optimum far faster than random sampling or Gaussian process BO.
AI.motivation: Rare high-performing configurations in large materials design spaces are hard to find by trial-and-error or by representative ML sampling, and Gaussian process BO becomes impractical at this scale.
AI.method: FruBO is a flexible BO framework evaluated on superposed rotated hexagonal lattices, with the Jain fairness index as the objective; it compares random exploration, Gaussian process BO and BO with a lightweight CatBoost surrogate using committee-based uncertainty estimation.
AI.result: Random sampling needs 533,012 evaluations (about 31 hours) to find the global optimum, Gaussian process BO runs out of GPU memory after 290 acquired samples, and FruBO with CatBoost finds the global optimum after 1,470 acquired samples in about 1.15 hours.
AI.conclusion: Scalable surrogate models can substantially improve the feasibility and efficiency of Bayesian optimization in large nanomaterials design spaces.

title: FocusBranch: Combinatorial Branch-and-Bound for $\ell_0$ Neural Network Robustness Verification
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 32 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables
summary: Verifying the local robustness of neural networks under $\ell_0$ perturbations is inherently combinatorial, as it must reason over all sparse subsets of $\epsilon$ perturbed pixels. This paper presents FocusBranch, a combinatorial branch-and-bound framework for $\ell_0$ robustness verification. The key insight is to make the $\ell_0$-ball decomposable and branchable using a node abstraction, which consists of a focus pixel set $\mathcal{S}$ and a level $l$, permitting at most $\epsilon-l$ pixels outside $\mathcal{S}$. This abstraction unifies two branching mechanisms: concrete nodes branch through upper shadows to fix additional perturbed locations, while super nodes branch through covering designs to cover many perturbation cases with fewer child nodes. FocusBranch proves node safety by concretizing linear relaxations over node-constrained $\ell_0$-balls and recursively branches on unknown nodes. Rather than relying on a fixed verification plan, it samples nodes across levels to estimate safe rates and costs, then selects a starting level and branching strategy predicted to minimize verification time. Experiments on fully connected and convolutional classifiers for MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 show that FocusBranch verifies $\ell_0$ robustness effectively across architectures and outperforms state-of-the-art verifiers. The code is available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: FocusBranch is a combinatorial branch-and-bound verifier for l0 robustness of neural networks that uses node abstractions over focus pixel sets and levels to branch efficiently and outperforms state-of-the-art verifiers on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10.
AI.motivation: Verifying local robustness under l0 perturbations is combinatorial because it must reason over all sparse subsets of perturbed pixels, and existing verifiers do not handle this efficiently.
AI.method: A node abstraction with a focus pixel set and a level permits at most epsilon minus level pixels outside the set; concrete nodes branch through upper shadows to fix extra perturbed locations, super nodes branch through covering designs to cover many cases with fewer children, node safety is proven by concretizing linear relaxations, and a sampling step estimates safe rates and costs to choose the starting level and strategy.
AI.result: FocusBranch verifies l0 robustness effectively across fully connected and convolutional classifiers for MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 and outperforms state-of-the-art verifiers.
AI.conclusion: Unifying the two branching mechanisms with sampling-based planning makes exact l0 robustness verification practical across architectures, and the code is publicly available.

title: MambaPD: Bidirectional Selective State Space Model for Parkinson's Disease Detection from Resting-State EEG
summary: Typical diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) occurs only after significant dopaminergic loss, while resting-state EEG abnormalities like alpha slowing and reduced coherence occur earlier. While many published EEG-based PD detectors claim accuracy greater than 95%, many use epoch-level splits which leak subject identity. I introduce MambaPD, a bidirectional selective state space model for resting-state EEG-based PD detection, blending the channel mixing, patch tokenization and bidirectional Mamba encoder. It is compared with four baselines (TCN, BiLSTM with attention, EEGNet and a patch Transformer) in two public datasets (UNM, SanDiego) using subject-independent 5-fold cross-validation (checkpoints were selected on the held-out fold, so absolute estimates are optimistic). On UNM the accuracy is between 0.67 and 0.71, and MambaPD (0.714) is not statistically distinguishable from the Transformer (0.715), and TCN (0.708), with the highest sensitivity (0.82), while the lowest specificity (0.52). For the smaller SanDiego cohort, accuracy is in the range of 0.60 to 0.70, with the highest scores (0.703) from TCN and the lowest (0.601) from EEGNet, while MambaPD scores 0.631, with the lowest specificity (0.46) among the five models. The differences among the models on UNM are minor compared to the differences among folds. I report the whole pipeline, per-fold results, and the shortcomings of the protocol.

AI.tldr: MambaPD is a bidirectional selective state space model for detecting Parkinson's disease from resting-state EEG, evaluated with subject-independent cross-validation on two public datasets. It is not clearly better than the baselines, and many published claims above 95% accuracy use epoch-level splits that leak subject identity.
AI.motivation: Early Parkinson's diagnosis is hard, and resting-state EEG abnormalities such as alpha slowing and reduced coherence appear before significant dopaminergic loss, but many published EEG-based detectors claiming over 95% accuracy use epoch-level splits that leak subject identity.
AI.method: MambaPD blends channel mixing, patch tokenization and a bidirectional Mamba encoder. It is compared with TCN, BiLSTM with attention, EEGNet and a patch Transformer under subject-independent 5-fold cross-validation on the UNM and SanDiego datasets, with checkpoints selected on the held-out fold.
AI.result: On UNM, accuracy ranges from 0.67 to 0.71; MambaPD reaches 0.714, not statistically distinguishable from the Transformer (0.715) or TCN (0.708), with the highest sensitivity (0.82) but the lowest specificity (0.52). On SanDiego, accuracy ranges from 0.60 to 0.70; MambaPD scores 0.631, below TCN (0.703), with the lowest specificity (0.46) among the five models. Differences among folds are larger than differences among models.
AI.conclusion: MambaPD's gains over the baselines are minor, and the protocol and fold-to-fold variation dominate the results; the absolute estimates are optimistic because checkpoints were selected on the held-out fold.

title: BECON: Belief-Conditioned Constrained Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning under Drifting Preferences and Budgets
summary: Constrained preference-conditioned MORL typically assumes full task observability, treating preferences and safety budgets as stationary task signals. In real-world deployment, however, these signals are often unreliable proxies: intent may drift, safety tolerances may shift with context, and exposed descriptors may be noisy, delayed, or incomplete. We therefore formulate constrained preference-conditioned MORL as a partially observed task-specification problem, where the agent must navigate a fundamental conflict between unreliable external signals and latent interaction dynamics. We propose \textbf{BECON}, a belief-conditioned framework for constrained MORL with drifting preferences and budgets, which infers latent task context from recent histories to estimate preferences and safety budgets. These estimates are fused with the exposed task signal via uncertainty-dependent gates, enabling the policy to defer to observations under high epistemic uncertainty while correcting them when history is informative. The fused context jointly conditions preference optimization and context-adaptive constraint enforcement. Experiments on diverse multi-objective control tasks demonstrate that BECON consistently improves over state-of-the-art MORL baselines, achieving stronger robustness and constraint satisfaction under task drift.

AI.tldr: BECON is a belief-conditioned framework for constrained multi-objective reinforcement learning under drifting preferences and budgets. It infers latent task context from recent histories and fuses it with the exposed task signal through uncertainty-dependent gates, and reportedly improves over MORL baselines in robustness and constraint satisfaction under drift.
AI.motivation: Constrained preference-conditioned MORL assumes full task observability with stationary preferences and safety budgets, but in deployment these signals may drift, shift with context, or be noisy, delayed or incomplete.
AI.method: The authors formulate the problem as a partially observed task-specification problem. BECON infers latent task context from recent histories to estimate preferences and safety budgets, fuses these estimates with the exposed task signal via uncertainty-dependent gates, and uses the fused context to condition both preference optimization and context-adaptive constraint enforcement.
AI.result: Experiments on diverse multi-objective control tasks show that BECON consistently improves over state-of-the-art MORL baselines, with stronger robustness and constraint satisfaction under task drift. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Treating preferences and budgets as partially observed, drifting quantities, and deferring to observations only when history is uninformative, is a practical route to safer multi-objective control under unreliable task signals.

title: Exact Natarajan Dimension of Homogeneous Multiclass Linear Predictors
summary: The Natarajan dimension is a fundamental measure of the capacity of multiclass hypothesis classes and plays an important role in analyzing their generalization ability. In this paper, by establishing lower and upper bounds, we show that the exact Natarajan dimension of homogeneous multiclass linear predictors with pairwise distinct class weights is \(n(k-1)-1\), where $n$ is the dimension of the feature space and $k$ is the number of classes, for \(n,k\ge3\), \(n,k\in\mathbb N\).

AI.tldr: The paper establishes that the exact Natarajan dimension of homogeneous multiclass linear predictors with pairwise distinct class weights is n(k-1)-1, for n and k at least 3. This fixes the capacity of this hypothesis class exactly.
AI.motivation: The Natarajan dimension is a basic capacity measure for multiclass hypothesis classes and governs their generalization ability; the paper targets its exact value for homogeneous multiclass linear predictors.
AI.method: The paper proves matching lower and upper bounds on the Natarajan dimension of homogeneous multiclass linear predictors whose class weights are pairwise distinct.
AI.result: The exact Natarajan dimension is n(k-1)-1, where n is the dimension of the feature space and k is the number of classes, for n and k at least 3.
AI.conclusion: The closed form gives an exact capacity value for this class, relevant to its generalization analysis.

title: XposedMIA: Exploiting Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) for One-Shot Membership Inference Attacks
summary: Machine learning (ML) services increasingly expose explainability outputs alongside model predictions. While such explanations are intended to improve transparency, they may also reveal information about the underlying training data. In this work, we show that the local surrogate geometry employed by Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) can be repurposed as a proxy for a sample's distance to the model's decision boundary. We extend this boundary-distance view to tabular counterfactual explanations and, for the first time, to visual counterfactual explanations for image classifiers. We present XposedMIA, a one-shot, explanation-based black-box membership inference attack (MIA) framework that converts the returned explanation into a proxy for the queried sample's distance to the model decision boundary. After a one-time calibration step on a small labeled calibration set of as few as 30 samples, our attack requires only a single query for each target sample. Unlike prior label-only attacks requiring iterative queries or shadow training, our method relies solely on the predicted label and its accompanying explanation. Our evaluation indicates that XposedMIA achieves high effectiveness, with success rates of up to 0.95 using only a single query per target, revealing that releasing explanations introduces an additional channel for membership leakage.

AI.tldr: XposedMIA is a one-shot, black-box membership inference attack that exploits the explanations returned by ML services. It uses LIME's local surrogate geometry, extended to tabular and visual counterfactual explanations, as a proxy for distance to the decision boundary, and reaches success rates of up to 0.95 with a single query per target.
AI.motivation: Explainability outputs are meant to improve transparency, but they may reveal information about the training data. Prior label-only attacks need iterative queries or shadow training.
AI.method: The local surrogate geometry of LIME is repurposed as a proxy for a sample's distance to the model's decision boundary, and this view is extended to tabular and visual counterfactual explanations. After a one-time calibration on as few as 30 labeled samples, the attack needs only the predicted label and its explanation, with a single query per target sample.
AI.result: Success rates reach up to 0.95 using one query per target, showing that releasing explanations opens an additional channel for membership leakage.
AI.conclusion: Explanations can leak membership information beyond predictions, so releasing them carries a privacy cost that should be assessed.

title: Correct First, Fast Second: What a Local 7B Code Model Can and Cannot Do for GPU Kernel Optimization
summary: We study how much the interaction strategy around a fixed, locally hosted 7B-parameter code model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct) affects its ability to replace PyTorch operators with custom CUDA kernels. On 30 KernelBench tasks (levels 1-3, first 10 each, evaluated on a V100), we compare four regimes of increasing structure: zero-shot prompting, profiling-guided prompting, iterative refinement on execution feedback, and a multi-agent loop (analysis, retrieval, generation, evaluation, feedback triage) in which the same model fills four roles around a non-LLM evaluator. Three findings stand out. (1) Correctness, not speed, is the binding constraint: even correct generated kernels average 0.97-0.99x the speed of eager PyTorch, because a 7B model cannot out-write cuBLAS/cuDNN on dense GEMM and convolution; the only real wins are fused memory-bound epilogues. (2) The best strategy depends on difficulty: profiling-guided prompting is strongest overall (43% correct, 27% faster than baseline), but the agent loop is the only method that solves any level-2 fusion problem (3/10 vs. 0/10 for all others). (3) Naive agentic scaffolding is actively harmful: our first agent scored 3% correct, below zero-shot's 30%, and the decisive repairs were matching the agent's ambition to the model's competence and spending compute on best-of-n sampling under a real execution oracle (3% to 33% correct from n=1 to n=8), not on more reasoning steps.

AI.tldr: The paper tests how a fixed, locally hosted 7B code model (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct) replaces PyTorch operators with custom CUDA kernels under four interaction strategies. Correctness, not speed, is the binding constraint, and best-of-n sampling under an execution oracle is the decisive repair.
AI.motivation: It is unclear how much the interaction strategy around a fixed 7B code model affects its ability to replace PyTorch operators with custom CUDA kernels, and whether agentic scaffolding helps.
