AI.method: On 30 KernelBench tasks (levels 1-3, first 10 each, evaluated on a V100), four regimes are compared: zero-shot prompting, profiling-guided prompting, iterative refinement on execution feedback, and a multi-agent loop in which the same model fills four roles around a non-LLM evaluator.
AI.result: Profiling-guided prompting is strongest overall, at 43% correct and 27% faster than baseline. Even correct kernels average 0.97-0.99x the speed of eager PyTorch; the agent loop is the only method that solves any level-2 fusion problem (3/10 versus 0/10). The first agent scored 3% correct, below zero-shot's 30%, and best-of-n sampling under an execution oracle raised its correctness from 3% at n=1 to 33% at n=8.
AI.conclusion: A 7B model cannot out-write cuBLAS or cuDNN on dense GEMM and convolution, so real speedups come mainly from fused memory-bound epilogues; naive agentic scaffolding can hurt, and matching the agent's ambition to the model's competence matters.

title: Zero-Search Reinforcement Learning for Slay the Spire 2 with Failure-Driven Restarts
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures. Code, released policies and an in-game mod: this https URL ; records behind every table: this https URL
summary: Slay the Spire 2 (STS2) is a deck-building roguelike in which a winning run at the highest difficulty takes several hundred decisions, and most losses happen in late boss fights that a learner seldom reaches. We train agents that choose every action with one forward pass of a 6.6M-parameter entity transformer, without lookahead. Training and evaluation run the game's own compiled assembly (v0.107.1) in a headless .NET host. The host replays a run exactly from its seed and actions, so training episodes can restart from states the learner has visited, and a failure-driven curriculum allocates these restarts in proportion to where complete runs are lost. On 12,800 held-out games at Ascension 10 (A10), the released policies win 8.05% averaged over the five characters (Ironclad 15.6%, Regent 12.5%), and AlphaSpire's released networks used without search win 0.55% on a common panel. Longer A10 training raised Ironclad from 12.4% to 15.6% and Defect from 3.0% to 8.1% on these games. At Ascension 0 the released policies win 80.2%, level with the 80.3% that the tree-search agent Spire Mentor reports, while Mentor leads by 5 to 8 points from A4 upward. Run in our host on the same 2,000 A10 games, Mentor's search wins 8.8% against 8.2% for our policies, which need 21-27 ms per decision on one CPU core. GPT-6 Astra at maximum reasoning won none of 11 A10 games through our text interface. In a controlled study of 18 training runs from six random initializations, failure-driven allocation exceeds uniform restart allocation on each of three Regent initializations, by 3.6 percentage points on average, while the Silent effect is small and changes sign. Code, trained policies, an in-game mod and the records behind every table are at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper trains a 6.6M-parameter entity transformer to play Slay the Spire 2 with one forward pass per action and no lookahead, using failure-driven restarts from exactly replayable runs. The policies win 8.05% at Ascension 10 and 80.2% at Ascension 0, close to the tree-search agent Spire Mentor at Ascension 0.
AI.motivation: Winning at the highest difficulty takes several hundred decisions, and most losses happen in late boss fights that a learner seldom reaches, so training data for those states is scarce.
AI.method: The agents choose every action with one forward pass of a 6.6M-parameter entity transformer, without lookahead. Training and evaluation run the game's own compiled assembly (v0.107.1) in a headless .NET host that replays runs exactly from seed and actions, so episodes can restart from visited states, and a failure-driven curriculum allocates restarts in proportion to where complete runs are lost.
AI.result: On 12,800 held-out games at A10, the released policies win 8.05% on average over five characters (Ironclad 15.6%, Regent 12.5%); AlphaSpire's released networks used without search win 0.55% on a common panel. At A0 the policies win 80.2%, against 80.3% for Spire Mentor, which leads by 5 to 8 points from A4 upward. On the same 2,000 A10 games, Mentor's search wins 8.8% against 8.2% for the policies, which need 21-27 ms per decision on one CPU core. GPT-6 Astra at maximum reasoning won none of 11 A10 games through the text interface. Failure-driven allocation exceeds uniform restart allocation by 3.6 percentage points on average on each of three Regent initializations.
AI.conclusion: A single-pass policy with failure-driven restarts reaches strong play at low latency but trails search at higher ascensions; the gain from failure-driven allocation is confirmed on Regent, while its effect on Silent is small and changes sign.

title: TSFFormer: A Frequency-Domain Spike Transformer for Green Human Activity Recognition
summary: Wearable Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) enable pervasive Human Activity Recognition (HAR), but traditional Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) suffer from an "arithmetic-latency deadlock" due to dense floating-point MAC operations. While Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer ultra-low power, existing ones face spatial blind spots, rigid neurons, and gradient degradation. To address these, we propose TSFFormer, a purely spiking Fourier Transformer for Green HAR. It introduces two key innovations: (1) a MultiHeadFourier attention that performs frequency-domain global mixing, reducing complexity from \(O(V^2)\) to \(O(V\log V)\), eliminating spatial blind spots, and saving \(\sim\)50% GPU memory; and (2) a dual-compartment Temporal Spiking LIF (TSLIFNode) that utilizes dynamic thresholds to adapt to non-stationary rhythms and mitigate gradient degradation. Extensive experiments on 8 public IMU benchmarks demonstrate that TSFFormer surpasses state-of-the-art SNNs and even the classic DeepConvLSTM, achieving a \(\sim\)3\(\times\) faster training speed with an energy footprint of 0.1 pJ. Ablation studies confirm the synergistic effect of our modules, providing a highly accurate, ultra-low-power event-driven paradigm for wearable sensing.

AI.tldr: TSFFormer is a purely spiking Fourier Transformer for wearable human activity recognition from inertial measurement units. It reports surpassing state-of-the-art spiking networks and the classic DeepConvLSTM on 8 public benchmarks, with an energy footprint of 0.1 pJ.
AI.motivation: Wearable IMU-based activity recognition needs low power, but conventional DNNs are costly because of dense floating-point MAC operations, and existing spiking networks have spatial blind spots, rigid neurons and gradient degradation.
AI.method: MultiHeadFourier attention performs frequency-domain global mixing, reducing complexity from O(V^2) to O(V log V), which removes spatial blind spots and saves about 50% GPU memory. A dual-compartment Temporal Spiking LIF neuron (TSLIFNode) uses dynamic thresholds to adapt to non-stationary rhythms and mitigate gradient degradation.
AI.result: Across 8 public IMU benchmarks, TSFFormer surpasses state-of-the-art SNNs and DeepConvLSTM, with about 3x faster training speed and an energy footprint of 0.1 pJ. Ablation studies confirm the synergistic effect of the modules.
AI.conclusion: The authors present TSFFormer as a highly accurate, ultra-low-power, event-driven paradigm for wearable sensing.

title: Calibrating Document-Local Boundaries for Contextual Chunk Retrieval
summary: Late Chunking encodes an entire document before pooling at chunk boundaries, preserving document context in local retrieval units. Chunk-level post-training improves context-dependent retrieval, but shared context can make semantically similar same-document negatives difficult to distinguish. We study the local decision boundary between a gold chunk and its hardest sibling. Starting from InSeNT, we analyze InSeNT's within-document gradients and show that the entropy of the conditional negative allocation decreases monotonically with the scaling factor at fixed logits. We propose a two-part framework for calibrating document-local chunk boundaries. The first component adapts the discriminative scale from within-document margins, while the second exposes chunk partitions to attention during document encoding. Experiments on ConTEB and NanoBEIR show that the resulting model improves contextual chunk retrieval across the evaluated encoder settings while retaining competitive passage-level retrieval quality; ablations further characterize the distinct roles of adaptive scaling and chunk-aware routing.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-part framework that calibrates the decision boundary between a gold chunk and its hardest same-document sibling in Late Chunking retrieval. It improves contextual chunk retrieval on ConTEB and NanoBEIR while keeping competitive passage-level retrieval quality.
AI.motivation: Late Chunking encodes a whole document before pooling at chunk boundaries, preserving context, but the shared context makes semantically similar same-document negatives hard to tell apart during chunk-level post-training.
AI.method: Starting from InSeNT, the authors analyze within-document gradients and show that the entropy of the conditional negative allocation decreases monotonically with the scaling factor at fixed logits. The framework adapts the discriminative scale from within-document margins, and exposes chunk partitions to attention during document encoding.
AI.result: Experiments on ConTEB and NanoBEIR show improved contextual chunk retrieval across the evaluated encoder settings, with competitive passage-level retrieval quality; ablations characterize the distinct roles of adaptive scaling and chunk-aware routing.
AI.conclusion: Calibrating document-local boundaries, through adaptive scaling and chunk-aware attention, improves contextual chunk retrieval without giving up passage-level retrieval quality.

title: Forecast Value Add: Reward-Based Action Selection over Probabilistic Demand Forecasts
summary: Strong machine-learning ensembles capture much of the trend, seasonality, and known events in demand, yet they can still understate peaks, miss moving events, or mistake temporary changes for shifts in demand level. We address this gap by framing forecast refinement as a reward-driven decision problem. For each forecast period, we let an agent choose among values already produced by the ensemble: its base forecast, distribution-free bounds, quantiles, and a bias-corrected estimate. We evaluate these choices against context-matched historical periods, accounting for calendar position, recurring and moving events, trend, price, and promotions. We then apply a structural seasonal guard to constrain adjustments and record the model, agent, and planner contributions to every published value. We evaluate our approach across five retail, consumer-goods, and direct-to-consumer deployments over nine months. Our refined forecasts reduce mean WMAPE by 6.3% compared with the stacked machine-learning forecast for every customer, with gains reaching 16.7%, and achieve the lowest error in 35 of 45 customer-months. Compared with statistical forecasts, our approach reduces mean error by 18.7%. These results demonstrate that context-aware, auditable action selection can add forecast value beyond a strong ensemble.

AI.tldr: The paper frames forecast refinement as a reward-driven choice among values an ensemble already produces, such as the base forecast, quantiles and a bias-corrected estimate. Across five deployments over nine months, the refined forecasts reduce mean WMAPE by 6.3% against the stacked machine-learning forecast, with gains reaching 16.7%.
AI.motivation: Strong machine-learning ensembles capture trend, seasonality and known events in demand, but they can understate peaks, miss moving events, or mistake temporary changes for shifts in demand level.
AI.method: For each forecast period an agent chooses among the ensemble's base forecast, distribution-free bounds, quantiles and a bias-corrected estimate, evaluated against context-matched historical periods that account for calendar position, recurring and moving events, trend, price and promotions. A structural seasonal guard constrains adjustments, and the model, agent and planner contributions to every published value are recorded.
AI.result: Refined forecasts reduce mean WMAPE by 6.3% compared with the stacked machine-learning forecast, for every customer, with gains reaching 16.7%, and achieve the lowest error in 35 of 45 customer-months. Compared with statistical forecasts, mean error falls by 18.7%. The evaluation covers five retail, consumer-goods and direct-to-consumer deployments over nine months.
AI.conclusion: Context-aware, auditable action selection can add forecast value beyond a strong ensemble.

title: CARE-PO: Controllable Tool-Call Efficiency for LLM Agents
summary: External tool calls are a major running cost of an LLM agent, while its training objectives align almost exclusively with task completion. In a step-level diagnosis of Qwen3.5 trajectories at two model sizes on GAIA, a long-horizon tool-use benchmark, we find that most contain removable calls, at a similar rate at both sizes. Some methods add an efficiency reward to the objective to reduce the call count, but introduce problems of their own: the anchor they price calls against is computed from the policy's own rollouts (e.g., the group's shortest correct rollout) and so moves with the policy; training can drift toward a collapsed policy that issues no tool call at all, a degeneracy seen in published reports and in our 27B baseline; and a training run delivers a single operating point, so the user cannot trade efficiency against capability. We present CARE-PO (Controllable Anchored Relative Efficiency Policy Optimization) to mitigate these problems. The efficiency reward prices calls against a reference budget anchored to the task's own difficulty and fixed before training. Injecting a successful trajectory from the training data into each online GRPO rollout group and charging for evidence a trajectory never gathers ease the drift toward a collapsed call count. Shaping the cost curve by an effort tag in the prompt yields an efficiency and a capability operating point from a single training run. On GAIA, five of the six operating points across three model sizes improve on their base model in success rate and call count at once. On four held-out multi-hop benchmarks the result is size-dependent: at 27B and 4B success rate is held or raised at a lower call count, while at 9B both operating points trade success rate for fewer calls. The call count remains well above zero throughout training at all three sizes.

AI.tldr: CARE-PO is a policy optimization method that controls tool-call efficiency for LLM agents by pricing calls against a fixed, difficulty-anchored budget. On GAIA it improves success rate and call count together at five of six operating points across three model sizes, and a single training run yields several efficiency-capability trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Tool calls are a major running cost for LLM agents, yet training objectives reward almost only task completion. Existing efficiency rewards are priced against the policy's own rollouts, so the anchor drifts, training can collapse to issuing no tool calls, and a single run yields only one operating point.
AI.method: The efficiency reward prices calls against a reference budget anchored to the task's difficulty and fixed before training. A successful training trajectory is injected into each online GRPO rollout group, and trajectories are charged for evidence they never gather. An effort tag in the prompt shapes the cost curve, giving efficiency and capability operating points from one training run.
AI.result: On GAIA, five of six operating points across three model sizes improve on the base model in success rate and call count at once. On four held-out multi-hop benchmarks the result depends on size: at 27B and 4B success is held or raised at a lower call count, while at 9B both operating points trade success rate for fewer calls. The call count remains well above zero throughout training at all three sizes.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring efficiency to a fixed difficulty budget and injecting successful trajectories counters drift toward a collapsed call count, and one run exposes a tunable efficiency-capability frontier, although the held-out gains are size-dependent.

title: One-Shot Federated Graph Learning via High-Fidelity Proxies and Transferability-Guided Collaboration
summary: One-shot Federated Graph Learning (OFGL) has emerged as a communication-efficient paradigm for federated graph learning under strict bandwidth constraints, compressing collaboration into a single transmission round. Nevertheless, this extreme setting suffers from a fundamental Single-Transmission Bottleneck, which limits both the quality and utility of exchanged knowledge. First, while existing methods attempt to distill private graphs into shareable proxies, their aggressive one-shot compression inherently triggers a fidelity crisis. This compression distorts local graph topology and semantics across clients, leading to externalized knowledge underexpression. Second, although the server aggregates these proxies to update global models, current integration schemes suffer from transferability agnosticism. The server cannot reliably identify cross-client collaboration potential, thus resulting in integrated knowledge underutilization. To tackle these dual challenges, we propose FedHFT, an effective One-Shot Personalized Federated Graph Learning (OPFGL) framework that addresses this bottleneck from two perspectives, namely High-Fidelity Knowledge Externalization and Transferability-Ware Knowledge Integration. We use Fidelity-Driven Proxy Refinement to preserve client-side knowledge fidelity, and Transferability-Steered Personalized Collaboration to enable adaptive server-side collaboration. The superiority of FedHFT is validated through extensive experiments on both homophilic and heterophilic graphs. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: FedHFT is a one-shot personalized federated graph learning framework that improves the fidelity of shared knowledge through fidelity-driven proxy refinement and selects collaborators by transferability. It is validated on both homophilic and heterophilic graphs.
AI.motivation: One-shot federated graph learning cuts communication to a single transmission, but this creates a single-transmission bottleneck: aggressive compression distorts local graph topology and semantics, and current server-side integration ignores which clients can usefully transfer knowledge to each other.
AI.method: The framework has two components. High-Fidelity Knowledge Externalization uses Fidelity-Driven Proxy Refinement to preserve client-side knowledge when private graphs are distilled into shareable proxies. Transferability-Steered Personalized Collaboration lets the server integrate proxies adaptively according to cross-client collaboration potential.
AI.result: The abstract reports extensive experiments on homophilic and heterophilic graphs that validate the method's superiority, but it gives no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: Preserving proxy fidelity and steering server-side integration by transferability addresses both parts of the single-transmission bottleneck in one-shot federated graph learning.

title: Good Views Are Not Enough: Global Counterexamples for Gaussian-Regularized JEPAs
summary: Good views do not suffice to guarantee scene invariance or uniqueness up to rotation at the global optima of Gaussian-regularized JEPAs. We give globally certified counterexamples showing that the uniqueness premise of the Gaussian extension in Good Views fails for specified soft objectives. Gaussian marginal matching can reward retaining independently resampled observation variation, and this benefit can exceed its prediction cost. In a four-state model, comparison against the entire scene-only class proves that every global minimizer splits a scene and admits an equal-value partner outside its rotation orbit. In a 512-dimensional model with a complete scene basis, a spectral gap, and exact population whitening, pooled Epps-Pulley regularization still forces every global minimizer to retain nuisance and yields positive cross-modal alignment error even after the best rotation when modality nuisances are independent. Better scene alignment can also accompany worse prediction. With matched 512-label readout budgets and 1% observation noise, whitened prediction JEPA aligns better to the scene than next-token prediction but incurs 0.2872 nats/token higher linear-readout test NLL. A Bayes-risk decomposition distinguishes information lost through the observation channel from the fitted readout's difficulty using retained information. These results connect three determinants of learned representations: what views share, what regularization favors, and what a prediction task can use.

AI.tldr: The paper gives globally certified counterexamples showing that good views do not guarantee scene invariance or uniqueness up to rotation at the global optima of Gaussian-regularized JEPAs. In the stated settings, every global minimizer retains nuisance information.
AI.motivation: The earlier Good Views analysis relies on a uniqueness premise for its Gaussian extension, and the paper shows this premise fails for specified soft objectives.
AI.method: In a four-state model, comparison against the entire scene-only class shows that every global minimizer splits a scene. In a 512-dimensional model with a complete scene basis, a spectral gap and exact population whitening, pooled Epps-Pulley regularization is analyzed, and whitened prediction JEPA is compared with next-token prediction at matched 512-label readout budgets and 1% observation noise. A Bayes-risk decomposition separates information lost through the observation channel from the readout's difficulty.
AI.result: In the four-state model every global minimizer splits a scene and has an equal-value partner outside its rotation orbit. In the 512-dimensional model every global minimizer retains nuisance and yields positive cross-modal alignment error after the best rotation when modality nuisances are independent. Whitened prediction JEPA aligns better to the scene than next-token prediction but has 0.2872 nats/token higher linear-readout test NLL.
AI.conclusion: Representation quality depends on three determinants at once: what views share, what regularization favors, and what the prediction task can use; better scene alignment can coexist with worse prediction.

title: Visible Tails: Characterizing Adaptation to Unknown Moments in Heavy-Tailed Bandits
summary: Heavy-tailed bandit learners without moment parameters face an obstruction: the rewards that carry an arm's mean can stay unseen. We address the remaining part of a COLT open problem by characterizing the optimal-arm laws that permit adaptation to unknown moments at constant-factor cost. The condition, variance-core visibility, is one-sided and translation-invariant: the mean hidden in any rare event is at most a constant multiple of the standard error of the rewards that remain. A quantile-trimmed UCB index that knows the visibility constants attains the central-moment benchmark on this class, and no single strategy adapts across all visibility levels. The same index achieves logarithmic expected regret on every instance with a visible optimal arm and finite-mean rewards. On an explicit family with no higher moment, gap $\Delta$ and constant $A$, its logarithmic coefficient and the information lower bound are of order $\Delta^{-1}e^{A/\Delta}$, exponential in the inverse gap within one visibility class.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes the optimal-arm reward laws under which heavy-tailed bandit learners can adapt to unknown moments at constant-factor cost, using a one-sided condition called variance-core visibility. A quantile-trimmed UCB index achieves logarithmic regret on every instance with a visible optimal arm and finite-mean rewards.
AI.motivation: Heavy-tailed bandit learners without moment parameters face an obstruction: the rewards that carry an arm's mean may stay unseen. The paper addresses the remaining part of a COLT open problem.
AI.method: The paper introduces variance-core visibility, a one-sided, translation-invariant condition requiring that the mean hidden in any rare event be at most a constant multiple of the standard error of the rewards that remain. It proposes a quantile-trimmed UCB index that knows the visibility constants.
AI.result: The index attains the central-moment benchmark on this class, and no single strategy adapts across all visibility levels. It achieves logarithmic expected regret on every instance with a visible optimal arm and finite-mean rewards. On an explicit family with no higher moment, the logarithmic coefficient and the information lower bound are both of order Delta^-1 e^(A/Delta), exponential in the inverse gap within one visibility class.
AI.conclusion: Adaptation to unknown moments is possible for exactly the laws that satisfy visibility at constant-factor cost, and within one visibility class the difficulty can grow exponentially as the gap shrinks.

title: Do Time-Series Foundation Models Forecast Index-Futures Returns? A Preregistered Evaluation of Models, Metrics, and Input Representations
summary: We ask whether the apparent forecasting skill of frozen time-series foundation models (TSFMs) on intraday index-futures returns is incremental skill. In a pre-registered evaluation on E-mini Nasdaq-100 (NQ) and E-mini S&P 500 (ES) futures, a common panel of five zero-shot models (Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, Moirai 2.0 and TiRex), plus separate experiments with Kronos, is compared with a no-change forecast at 5-120 minutes, using native prices, log returns, volatility-standardised returns and a volume clock as inputs. On a blind set opened once, 0 of 160 model-representation-horizon-market cells beat no-change, and a Hansen SPA test gives p = 1.000 on both markets; a later retrospective hold-out, scored as a descriptive check, gives 0 of 120. Input representations change forecast magnitude but not accuracy, and a transformation-aware ridge regression does as well. Several standard measures nevertheless suggest skill. Price-level correlation exceeds 0.9996, but no-change scores higher. Within-day RankIC across forecast origins rewards a trivial revert-to-mean rule (+0.35 at 30 minutes); we derive the expected within-day covariance under a random walk in closed form, and a sign-randomised null reproduces about 95% of the observed value. One model beats HAR for 5-minute volatility, but not the EWMA its input already contains. On strongly planted synthetic signals the models recover part of the signal at 5 minutes, and recovery deteriorates at 30 minutes. Benchmark-level success of TSFMs should therefore not be assumed to carry over to low-signal domains such as intraday returns.

AI.tldr: A preregistered evaluation finds that frozen time-series foundation models show no incremental skill on intraday E-mini Nasdaq-100 and S&P 500 futures returns: none of 160 blind-set cells beats a no-change forecast. Apparent skill in standard metrics is matched by trivial rules and null baselines.
AI.motivation: Frozen time-series foundation models appear to forecast intraday index-futures returns, and the authors ask whether this is incremental skill beyond a no-change forecast.
AI.method: A preregistered evaluation compares five zero-shot models (Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, Moirai 2.0 and TiRex), plus separate experiments with Kronos, against a no-change forecast at 5-120 minutes, using native prices, log returns, volatility-standardised returns and a volume clock as inputs. It also uses a Hansen SPA test, a transformation-aware ridge regression, a closed-form within-day covariance under a random walk, and a sign-randomised null.
AI.result: On the blind set, 0 of 160 model-representation-horizon-market cells beat no-change, with Hansen SPA p = 1.000 on both markets; a later retrospective hold-out, scored descriptively, gives 0 of 120. Price-level correlation exceeds 0.9996, but no-change scores higher. Within-day RankIC rewards a trivial revert-to-mean rule (+0.35 at 30 minutes), and a sign-randomised null reproduces about 95% of the observed value. One model beats HAR for 5-minute volatility but not the EWMA that its input already contains.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark-level success of time-series foundation models should not be assumed to carry over to low-signal domains such as intraday returns, where standard measures can be satisfied by trivial rules.

title: Beyond Flat Walks: Compositional Abstraction for Autoregressive Graph Generation
summary: Autoregressive graph generators typically linearize graphs through flat node-edge walks, which can obscure higher-order structure in large and complex graphs. We introduce a hierarchical graph abstraction and coarse-to-fine generation pipeline that separates coarsening, tokenization, and decoding. This exposes three design axes: community coarsening, hierarchical tokenization, and order randomization. Across these axes, traversal-based hierarchy consistently improves distributional and structural fidelity, while its V.U.N.\ cost depends strongly on the coarsening and randomization policy. In particular, the fidelity--V.U.N.\ trade-off observed under within-community randomization is substantially reduced when traversal order is randomized across the full hierarchy. With a fixed backbone, training protocol, and matched training time across five molecular and five non-molecular benchmarks, hierarchical serialization yields consistent distributional and structural gains on all molecular datasets, while the non-molecular results further show that these gains depend on how well the supplied hierarchy aligns with structure in the target distribution. Together, these results characterize when and how hierarchical serialization benefits autoregressive graph generation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a hierarchical graph abstraction with coarse-to-fine generation for autoregressive graph generators and characterizes when hierarchical serialization helps. Traversal-based hierarchy consistently improves fidelity on molecular graphs, while gains on non-molecular graphs depend on how well the hierarchy matches the target structure.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive graph generators linearize graphs through flat node-edge walks, which can obscure higher-order structure in large and complex graphs.
AI.method: The pipeline separates coarsening, tokenization and decoding, exposing three design axes: community coarsening, hierarchical tokenization and order randomization. The comparison uses a fixed backbone, a fixed training protocol and matched training time across five molecular and five non-molecular benchmarks.
AI.result: Hierarchical serialization gives consistent distributional and structural gains on all molecular datasets. Traversal-based hierarchy improves fidelity across the axes, while its V.U.N. cost depends on the coarsening and randomization policy; randomizing traversal order across the full hierarchy substantially reduces the fidelity-V.U.N. trade-off seen under within-community randomization. On non-molecular datasets the gains depend on how well the supplied hierarchy aligns with the target distribution's structure.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical serialization benefits autoregressive graph generation when the supplied hierarchy aligns with the structure of the target distribution, and the results characterize when and how it helps.

title: Replication of Thermal Comfort Cohort Models: No Support for Improved Thermal Preference Prediction
summary: Cohort comfort models (CCMs) aim to overcome the extensive individual data requirements of personal comfort models (PCMs) by grouping occupants based on demographic and psychometric characteristics (cold start) or similar thermal preferences (warm start). We evaluated the validity of the reported CCM performance gains through (i) a methodological assessment of the original study, (ii) a replication using one of the two original datasets (DORN: 20 participants, 6 months) under a revised experimental protocol, and (iii) a replication using an independently collected dataset (PersonAI: 72 participants, 4 weeks). Classification performance was evaluated using F1-micro, as in the original study, and F1-macro to account for class imbalance. Under F1-micro, a trivial baseline that always outputs the majority class performed on par with cohort models. Under F1-macro, all cohort models achieved lower median scores than a simple baseline that makes random predictions based on the estimated distribution of thermal preferences. In our methodological assessment we identified the following key issues: Limited data per participant and per minority class, reliance on a metric insensitive to class imbalance, missing trivial baselines, inadequate cross validation strategy, and multiple occurrences of information leakage. Our findings challenge the original study's conclusion that CCMs improve thermal preference prediction. CCMs did not outperform simple class-distribution baselines. Future studies should improve experimental designs, including controlled thermal conditions, to obtain sufficient observations across thermal preference classes.

AI.tldr: A replication of cohort thermal comfort models finds no support for their claimed improvement in thermal preference prediction. Under F1-micro a majority-class baseline matches the cohort models, and under F1-macro all cohort models score below a random baseline based on the estimated class distribution.
AI.motivation: Cohort comfort models aim to overcome the data requirements of personal comfort models by grouping occupants, but the performance gains reported by the original study needed validation.
AI.method: The evaluation has three parts: a methodological assessment of the original study, a replication on the DORN dataset (20 participants, 6 months) under a revised protocol, and a replication on the independently collected PersonAI dataset (72 participants, 4 weeks). Performance is measured with F1-micro, as in the original study, and with F1-macro to account for class imbalance.
AI.result: Under F1-micro a majority-class baseline performs on par with the cohort models. Under F1-macro all cohort models achieve lower median scores than a random baseline that uses the estimated distribution of thermal preferences. The methodological issues identified include limited data per participant and per minority class, reliance on an imbalance-insensitive metric, missing trivial baselines, an inadequate cross-validation strategy, and multiple occurrences of information leakage.
AI.conclusion: The original conclusion that cohort models improve thermal preference prediction is not supported; future studies need controlled thermal conditions and enough observations per preference class.

title: NearFormer: Linear-Size Sparse Attention via Randomized Near Neighbors
summary: Graph transformers can capture long-range interactions, but their quadratic attention cost limits their use on large graphs. We introduce \emph{NearFormer}, a graph transformer whose global attention is restricted to a randomized near-neighbor (NN) graph. NearFormer uses an efficient randomized construction to connect each node to a small number of near neighbors from a broader neighborhood defined by a label-independent feature or spectral geometry. For a fixed retained budget \(k\), the resulting attention support has linear size \(\mathcal{O}(|E|+nk)\). The NN graph is built once by within-bin search and then held fixed. We use these edges as sparse global-attention supports, with optional learned attention biases, while preserving the original graph for local message passing. Experiments on long-range graph benchmarks and synthetic structural tasks show that NearFormer provides a favorable accuracy--scalability trade-off relative to local message passing, dense and sparse attention.

AI.tldr: NearFormer is a graph transformer whose global attention is restricted to a randomized near-neighbor graph, giving linear attention size O(|E|+nk) for a fixed retained budget k. It keeps the original graph for local message passing and reports a favorable accuracy-scalability trade-off.
AI.motivation: Graph transformers capture long-range interactions, but their quadratic attention cost limits their use on large graphs.
AI.method: A randomized construction connects each node to a small number of near neighbors drawn from a broader neighborhood defined by a label-independent feature or spectral geometry. The graph is built once by within-bin search and then held fixed. These edges serve as sparse global-attention supports, with optional learned attention biases, while the original graph is kept for local message passing.
AI.result: Experiments on long-range graph benchmarks and synthetic structural tasks show a favorable accuracy-scalability trade-off relative to local message passing, dense attention and sparse attention. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Restricting global attention to a fixed randomized near-neighbor graph offers a scalable alternative to dense graph attention while preserving long-range interactions.

title: An Empirical Evaluation of Quantum Kernel Stability in Network Intrusion Detection
summary: Quantum kernel methods have been proposed for network intrusion detection, yet their performance limitations are often attributed to noise in current quantum hardware. This study evaluates that assumption through a controlled analysis of Pegasos-QSVC on the NSL-KDD and ToN-IoT datasets. We perform 56 quantum experiments using one exact noiseless statevector backend and three noise-simulated superconducting backends while keeping preprocessing, PCA features, data splits, and classical baselines identical. XGBoost achieves accuracies of 98.94% on NSL-KDD and 99.41% on ToN-IoT, compared with 91.80% and 82.98% for Pegasos-QSVC. The quantum model also exhibits substantially greater seed-dependent variability. Eight runs collapse into degenerate classifiers, including four recall-collapse cases and four trivial-positive classifiers. Notably, two failures occur on the noiseless backend, demonstrating that hardware noise is not a necessary condition for classi-fier collapse. Kernel Gram matrix analysis further reveals low effective rank and severe ill-conditioning even in the absence of noise, indicating intrinsic fragility in the learned quantum representation. These results show that average accuracy alone can conceal operationally unacceptable behavior and highlight the importance of reporting worst-case performance, seed-level variability, class-specific metrics, and explicit degeneracy tests in quantum intrusion detection studies.

AI.tldr: A controlled study of Pegasos-QSVC for network intrusion detection finds that the quantum kernel model is much less accurate than XGBoost and highly seed-sensitive, with degenerate classifiers even on a noiseless backend. Average accuracy hides these failures, so the authors call for worst-case and degeneracy reporting.
AI.motivation: Quantum kernel methods have been proposed for network intrusion detection, and their limits are often blamed on hardware noise; this study tests that assumption.
AI.method: The study runs 56 quantum experiments on NSL-KDD and ToN-IoT, using one exact noiseless statevector backend and three noise-simulated superconducting backends, with preprocessing, PCA features, data splits and classical baselines held identical.
AI.result: XGBoost reaches 98.94% on NSL-KDD and 99.41% on ToN-IoT, against 91.80% and 82.98% for Pegasos-QSVC. The quantum model shows much greater seed-dependent variability: eight runs collapse into degenerate classifiers, four with recall collapse and four trivial-positive. Two failures occur on the noiseless backend, and Gram matrices show low effective rank and severe ill-conditioning even without noise.
AI.conclusion: Hardware noise is not a necessary condition for classifier collapse, so quantum intrusion detection studies should report worst-case performance, seed-level variability, class-specific metrics and explicit degeneracy tests.

title: RAIL: Representation-Aligned Imitation Learning for Student-Compatible Teacher Policies
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) from raw sensory inputs such as images or onboard sensors can be challenging due to high-dimensional observations and sparse rewards. A common strategy is to train a teacher policy with access to privileged state information and then distill it into a student policy that acts from raw inputs alone. However, when the teacher relies on information unavailable to the student, exact imitation may be impossible, creating an irreducible imitation gap. Existing approaches typically mitigate this mismatch through careful reward shaping or additional reinforcement learning on the student policy after the teacher has been trained. Instead, we introduce Representation-Aligned Imitation Learning (RAIL), which addresses the mismatch during teacher training itself. RAIL learns a latent representation shared across teacher and student observations using contrastive learning, and trains the teacher policy directly in this space. Because the teacher policy is constrained to operate on this shared space, it learns behaviors that are reproducible from student observations. This substantially reduces the imitation gap while preserving task performance. Across multiple environments, RAIL outperforms strong baselines without reward modification or post-hoc student fine-tuning, and surpasses direct reinforcement learning from raw observations. The learned representations further enable zero-shot transfer to new tasks through teacher-only training. Project site: this https URL.

AI.tldr: RAIL trains a teacher policy in a latent space shared with the student's observations, learned by contrastive learning, which reduces the imitation gap caused by privileged teacher information without reward modification or student fine-tuning. It outperforms strong baselines and direct RL from raw observations, and enables zero-shot transfer through teacher-only training.
AI.motivation: Distilling a privileged teacher into a student that acts from raw inputs can leave an irreducible imitation gap when the teacher relies on information the student lacks; existing fixes depend on reward shaping or extra student RL after teacher training.
AI.method: Representation-Aligned Imitation Learning learns a latent representation shared across teacher and student observations with contrastive learning, and trains the teacher policy directly in that space so that its behaviors are reproducible from student observations.
AI.result: Across multiple environments RAIL outperforms strong baselines without reward modification or post-hoc student fine-tuning, and surpasses direct RL from raw observations. The learned representations enable zero-shot transfer to new tasks through teacher-only training. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Addressing the teacher-student mismatch during teacher training, rather than after it, substantially reduces the imitation gap while preserving task performance.

title: Learning Evidence-Grounded Reasoning for Context-Aware Time Series Forecasting
summary: LLM-driven time series forecasting has become increasingly promising by leveraging contextual features to generate future values directly or refine forecast priors. However, incorporating contextual features alone does not ensure that models can identify which features matter for forecasting and understand what they suggest about future dynamics. We argue that the fundamental challenge is how to extract predictive evidence from contextual features and when and how to leverage it to guide forecasting decisions. In this paper, we propose CastReasoner, an evidence-grounded reasoning model for context-aware time series forecasting. Specifically, CastReasoner uses a structured chain of thought (CoT) to extract predictive evidence from contextual features, infer the future dynamics suggested by this evidence, and assess these dynamics against the forecast prior to guide adaptive forecasting decisions. To enable this capability, we design a reasoning-centric two-stage post-training framework including supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). First, we synthesize reasoning trajectories through controllable multi-teacher guidance and select high-quality ones using a novel student-aware difficulty metric. Second, we design fine-grained multi-objective rewards to further improve reasoning and forecasting. To address heterogeneous learning needs across domains in both stages, we introduce a convergence-guided data balancing strategy. Through this two-stage training, CastReasoner improves both reasoning quality and predictive accuracy. Extensive experiments across multi-domain forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that CastReasoner achieves superior forecasting performance.

AI.tldr: CastReasoner is an evidence-grounded reasoning model for context-aware time series forecasting. It uses a structured chain of thought to extract predictive evidence from contextual features and checks that evidence against the forecast prior, and it reports superior forecasting performance on multi-domain benchmarks after SFT and RL post-training.
AI.motivation: Adding contextual features does not ensure that LLM-driven forecasters identify which features matter or what they imply for future dynamics; the challenge is extracting predictive evidence and deciding when and how to use it.
AI.method: A structured chain of thought extracts predictive evidence, infers the future dynamics it suggests, and assesses these dynamics against the forecast prior. Post-training has two stages: supervised fine-tuning on reasoning trajectories synthesized through controllable multi-teacher guidance and selected by a student-aware difficulty metric, then reinforcement learning with fine-grained multi-objective rewards, using a convergence-guided data balancing strategy across domains.
AI.result: The abstract reports superior forecasting performance across multi-domain forecasting benchmarks and improvements in both reasoning quality and predictive accuracy, but gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that explicit, evidence-grounded reasoning with two-stage post-training improves context-aware forecasting.

title: The Optimal Rate Constant of Heavy-Ball Momentum on Smooth Strongly Convex Functions
comment: 41 pages, 1 figure. Code and exact certificates: this https URL
summary: The heavy-ball method with a constant step size and a constant momentum parameter accelerates gradient descent on quadratics, but no choice of the two parameters does so on the class of smooth strongly convex functions. We determine how much faster than gradient descent it can be made on this class. Writing the best worst-case rate over all tunings as $1-c(\kappa)/\kappa$, where $\kappa$ is the condition number, we prove that $c(\kappa)$ tends to $8$ in every dimension of two or more. The lower bound on the rate holds for every tuning, because a tuning that is faster than $1-8/\kappa$ on quadratics follows a slowly decaying spiral on some function of two variables. The matching upper bound comes from an explicit tuning, with nearly the momentum of Polyak's tuning and a step size about $\sqrt{\kappa}/8$ times smaller, and from a Lyapunov function whose positivity is verified in exact arithmetic. Optimally tuned heavy-ball is therefore asymptotically four times faster than gradient descent on this class.

AI.tldr: Shows that optimally tuned heavy-ball momentum on smooth strongly convex functions has a worst-case rate of 1 - c(kappa)/kappa with c(kappa) tending to 8, making it asymptotically four times faster than gradient descent on this class.
AI.motivation: The heavy-ball method accelerates gradient descent on quadratics with a constant step size and momentum, but no fixed choice of these parameters does so on the whole class of smooth strongly convex functions, and the achievable speedup on this class was unknown.
AI.method: The lower bound comes from a spiral construction on a two-variable function showing that no tuning faster than 1 - 8/kappa on quadratics can work on the class. The matching upper bound comes from an explicit tuning with near-Polyak momentum and a step size about sqrt(kappa)/8 times smaller, certified by a Lyapunov function whose positivity is verified in exact arithmetic.
AI.result: The best worst-case rate constant c(kappa) tends to 8 in every dimension two or more, so the upper and lower bounds match asymptotically.
AI.conclusion: Optimally tuned heavy-ball is asymptotically four times faster than gradient descent on smooth strongly convex functions, which settles the achievable rate constant for this class.

title: A Modular Perspective for Modeling MARL Systems
comment: 71 pages. 18 figures. Associated repository: this https URL
summary: The growing complexity of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has fragmented the literature, obscuring underlying architectural choices behind diverse implementations. This fragmentation makes it difficult to evaluate critical modeling dimensions in isolation, identify how components affect the resulting system dynamics, and compare, reuse, or combine contributions across the literature. This paper proposes a modular perspective for modeling, analyzing, and implementing MARL systems. We decompose them into eight functional modules: agents, environments, learning, reward modeling, training and execution modes, communication, modeling of other agents, and evaluation criteria. For each module, we clarify its role and review representative approaches. We instantiate this decomposition in MARLKIT, a framework whose modules are explicit and interchangeable. MARLKIT demonstrates how the proposed perspective supports transparent experimental assumptions and the controlled variation and combination of MARL mechanisms. Experiments illustrate its ability to prototype, compare, reuse and combine modules while making differences between configurations explicit. Overall, the paper provides a structured perspective on MARL modeling and implementation, offering a common language for making modeling choices explicit, supporting clearer descriptions of MARL approaches, and supporting more controlled experimentation through the systematic isolation and combination of MARL mechanisms.

AI.tldr: Proposes a modular decomposition of multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) systems into eight functional modules and implements it in the MARLKIT framework, whose modules are explicit and interchangeable.
AI.motivation: The growing complexity and diversity of MARL implementations have fragmented the literature, obscuring architectural choices and making it hard to evaluate, compare, reuse or combine components.
AI.method: Decomposes MARL systems into agents, environments, learning, reward modeling, training and execution modes, communication, modeling of other agents, and evaluation criteria. For each module it clarifies the role and reviews representative approaches, then instantiates the decomposition as the MARLKIT framework.
AI.result: Experiments illustrate that MARLKIT can prototype, compare, reuse and combine modules while making differences between configurations explicit. The abstract reports no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: The paper gives a common structured language for MARL modeling choices and a basis for more controlled experimentation through isolating and combining mechanisms.

title: Evidence or Marginal? What Moment-Vector Propagation Computes in Polynomial Density Neurons
comment: 33 pages, 12 figures, 33 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: When a neuron's input is lost, or known through a belief $q$, what should it output? For a neuron storing a joint polynomial density $N$ with input density $D$, two formulas compete. $p_\mathrm{CD}=E_q[N]/E_q[D]$ costs one matrix-vector product; Hierarchical Correlation Reconstruction introduces it as a constant-denominator approximation to $p_\mathrm{EU}=E_q[N/D]$. For a density model both are exact answers to different questions: $p_\mathrm{CD}$ is Bayesian updating with the belief as virtual evidence; $p_\mathrm{EU}$ installs the belief as a new marginal (Jeffrey's rule). With a missing input $p_\mathrm{CD}$ returns the model's conditional; $p_\mathrm{EU}$ generally does not. This post hoc reading is proved, and illustrated outside the pair family up to $k=8$ inputs; it has no pre-registered test, only one exploratory real-data pilot. Post hoc, closed forms fall within a factor 2 of all 112 measured gaps, and negative density begins near input correlation $1/k$. In a pre-registered synthetic study (up to 32 inputs), 5 of 15 hypotheses are supported, 2 inconclusive and 8 not supported, including all three on transfer beyond equicorrelated Gaussians. Post hoc, where $p_\mathrm{EU}$ is defined, truncation usually outweighs the gap for Beta beliefs in pair neurons; triple neurons under flat and data beliefs are exceptions.

AI.tldr: Shows that the two candidate output formulas for a polynomial density neuron differ in meaning: p_CD is Bayesian updating with the belief as virtual evidence, while p_EU installs the belief as a new marginal (Jeffrey's rule).
AI.motivation: Hierarchical Correlation Reconstruction presents p_CD = E_q[N]/E_q[D] as a cheap constant-denominator approximation to p_EU = E_q[N/D], but for a density model the two answer different questions, and their behaviour under a missing input was unclear.
AI.method: Proves a post hoc reading of the two formulas as Bayesian updating versus Jeffrey's rule, and illustrates it outside the pair family up to 8 inputs. Tests hypotheses in a pre-registered synthetic study with up to 32 inputs and includes one exploratory real-data pilot.
AI.result: Post hoc, closed forms fall within a factor 2 of all 112 measured gaps, and negative density begins near input correlation 1/k. In the pre-registered study, 5 of 15 hypotheses are supported, 2 are inconclusive and 8 are not supported, including all three on transfer beyond equicorrelated Gaussians. For Beta beliefs in pair neurons, truncation usually outweighs the gap, with triple neurons under flat and data beliefs as exceptions.
AI.conclusion: With a missing input, p_CD returns the model's conditional while p_EU generally does not, so the two formulas should not be treated as interchangeable; the post hoc reading is proved, but the pre-registered evidence is mixed.

title: UCB-min: Combining Bandits Under Variance Heterogeneity (Extended Version)
comment: Extended version of short conference paper accepted at IEEE BigData 2026
summary: Multi-armed bandits are a natural framework for many real-world sequential decision problems, from recommender systems and clinical trials to educational test recommendation and online advertising. The performance of these algorithms depends on how they explore different arms, and exploration strategies range from variance-independent (e.g., UCB1) to variance-aware (e.g., UCB-V). In practice the reward variance of each arm is rarely known and varies widely across arms, and the reward support is often underspecified. In these cases no single rule is uniformly best: variance-independent methods are robust but loose when variances are small, while variance-aware methods are tight only when their variance estimates and the assumed support bound are reliable. Such heterogeneous, unknown variances arise in many settings, for instance when multiple objectives are scalarized into a single reward. We propose UCB-min, a per-arm adaptive meta-algorithm that selects, for each arm, the tighter of a variance-independent and a variance-aware exploration bonus, without prior knowledge of the variance regime and without reward normalization. We prove that, with UCB-V as variance-aware base, its regret is bounded by the sum of the two base bounds at the standard exploration constant, and by their per-arm minimum, up to a constant, for a larger one. We validate it on synthetic data, an educational tutoring task, and two group-recommendation benchmarks (MovieLens, Steam), showing that UCB-min consistently tracks the best base algorithm across diverse variance regimes and datasets.

AI.tldr: Proposes UCB-min, a per-arm meta-algorithm that selects the tighter of a variance-independent and a variance-aware exploration bonus, without prior knowledge of the variance regime or reward normalization.
AI.motivation: Variance-independent bandit methods such as UCB1 are robust but loose when arm variances are small, while variance-aware methods such as UCB-V are tight only when variance estimates and the support bound are reliable, and arm variances are usually unknown.
AI.method: For each arm, UCB-min chooses the tighter of a variance-independent bonus and a variance-aware bonus, using UCB-V as the variance-aware base. It needs no prior variance information and no reward normalization.
AI.result: With UCB-V as base, regret is bounded by the sum of the two base bounds at the standard exploration constant, and, for a larger constant, by their per-arm minimum up to a constant. On synthetic data, an educational tutoring task, and the MovieLens and Steam group-recommendation benchmarks, UCB-min consistently tracks the best base algorithm across variance regimes and datasets.
AI.conclusion: UCB-min adapts to heterogeneous, unknown reward variances and stays close to the best base algorithm across diverse settings.

title: Patching Up Circuit Learning via Parameter Sharing
summary: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) have emerged as generative models guaranteeing tractable probabilistic inference. However, tractability comes at the price of larger model sizes than in other generative models. As such, to scale PCs to high-dimensional data such as images, previous work has devised several parameter sharing techniques as well as fast evaluation protocols that consider learning PCs on independent image patches. In this work, we revisit this practice to highlight a surprising learnability issue: models that assume independence counterintuitively can yield better likelihoods than models that do not. To break this apparent bottleneck and to scale PCs further, we introduce a recursive parameter sharing construction (RePA) that fosters efficiency without assuming independence. We show empirically that RePA can greatly reduce time and memory consumption while yielding competitive likelihoods. Inspired by these results, we further generalize the approach to data modalities that do not inherently exhibit patch-structure (NoPA), such as tabular data, showing similar efficiency improvements, with marginal changes in likelihoods and sample quality on seven tabular datasets. Code available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Shows that probabilistic circuits trained on independent image patches can reach better likelihoods than non-independent models, and introduces recursive parameter sharing (RePA) and its generalization NoPA to scale circuits efficiently without assuming independence.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic circuits need large models to scale to high-dimensional data, and prior work scaled them by learning on independent image patches, which the authors find creates a learnability issue that hurts likelihoods when independence is dropped.
AI.method: Introduces RePA, a recursive parameter sharing construction that fosters efficiency without assuming independence. Generalizes the approach to data without patch structure as NoPA.
AI.result: RePA can greatly reduce time and memory consumption while yielding competitive likelihoods. On seven tabular datasets, NoPA shows similar efficiency improvements with marginal changes in likelihoods and sample quality.
AI.conclusion: Parameter sharing can make probabilistic circuits efficient at scale without the independence assumption, and the approach extends beyond image patches to tabular data.

title: Learning to Select Sparse Linear Solvers with Convolutional Neural Networks
summary: We investigate convolutional-neural-network (CNN) based automatic solver selection for sparse linear systems, a problem of practical importance where solver performance varies dramatically with matrix sparsity structure. A CNN is trained to regress log timing ratios between candidate solvers using spy plot images of matrix nonzero structure as input, achieving strong prediction accuracy on both held-out SuiteSparse matrices and real-world matrices from high-performance simulation codes.

AI.tldr: Trains a CNN on spy plot images of sparse matrix nonzero structure to predict log timing ratios between candidate solvers, enabling automatic solver selection for sparse linear systems.
AI.motivation: Solver performance for sparse linear systems varies dramatically with matrix sparsity structure, so choosing a suitable solver is a practical problem.
AI.method: A convolutional neural network takes spy plot images of matrix nonzero structure as input and is trained to regress log timing ratios between candidate solvers.
AI.result: The model achieves strong prediction accuracy on held-out SuiteSparse matrices and on real-world matrices from high-performance simulation codes. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Predicting solver choice from matrix structure images is a viable route to automatic sparse solver selection, with accuracy holding on real simulation matrices.

title: UniHam: A Large-Scale SOC-Complete Dataset and Benchmark for Hamiltonian Learning in Materials
summary: Accurate prediction of electronic Hamiltonians would enable broad property inference while avoiding the high computational cost of Density Functional Theory (DFT). However, progress toward general-purpose materials foundation models is limited by a data bottleneck: existing Hamiltonian datasets are typically small, lack structural diversity, and often omit essential relativistic physics such as spin--orbit coupling (SOC). We therefore construct UniHam, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset and benchmark suite comprising 100,000+ DFT-computed complex-valued Hermitian Hamiltonians with full SOC, covering 72 elements and a wide range of crystal geometries and symmetries (spanning diverse lattice types and space-group families). Building on UniHam, we benchmark two representative state-of-the-art models under a standardized protocol and introduce complementary evaluation metrics that jointly assess three dimensions: (i) Hamiltonian reconstruction accuracy, (ii) out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization across composition/symmetry shifts, and (iii) the ability to support downstream property prediction from the predicted Hamiltonians. Experiments on UniHam demonstrate that the proposed benchmark and metrics effectively differentiate model capabilities, revealing intrinsic SOC- and element-dependent failure modes, large variations in compositional OOD robustness, and the necessity of spectral-level evaluation to assess whether Hamiltonian predictions reliably support downstream electronic-structure properties. Overall, UniHam provides a reproducible, SOC-complete benchmark that can sharpen model comparisons and accelerate the development of next-generation foundation models for quantum materials.

AI.tldr: Introduces UniHam, a dataset of over 100,000 DFT-computed complex-valued Hermitian Hamiltonians with full spin-orbit coupling covering 72 elements, together with a benchmark and evaluation metrics for Hamiltonian learning.
AI.motivation: Predicting electronic Hamiltonians could avoid costly DFT, but progress toward materials foundation models is limited by small existing Hamiltonian datasets that lack structural diversity and often omit spin-orbit coupling.
AI.method: Constructs UniHam from DFT calculations across a wide range of crystal geometries and symmetries. Benchmarks two state-of-the-art models under a standardized protocol and introduces metrics for Hamiltonian reconstruction accuracy, out-of-distribution generalization across composition and symmetry shifts, and support for downstream property prediction.
AI.result: The benchmark and metrics differentiate model capabilities, revealing spin-orbit-coupling- and element-dependent failure modes, large variation in compositional OOD robustness, and the need for spectral-level evaluation to judge whether predicted Hamiltonians support downstream properties.
AI.conclusion: UniHam provides a reproducible, SOC-complete benchmark for sharper model comparison and for developing foundation models for quantum materials.

title: K-prop: Deep Online Learning by Backpropagating Temporal Kernels
comment: Accepted for publication in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 40 (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Self-recurrence represents an important component for temporal processing in neural networks, both artificial and biological, where it appears naturally in the form of leaky integration. However, due to the complex temporal dependencies of the gradient, an efficient and effective method of online training is still lacking. Here we propose K-prop, a novel online learning method for leaky neural networks. It dramatically reduces the computational and memory cost of real time recurrent learning (RTRL) by propagating kernel gains. K-prop also outperforms existing RTRL approximations and achieves performance comparable to backpropagation through time in sequence learning, classification, and reinforcement learning tasks. We further analyze how its sole approximation affects gradient quality and identify conditions under which K-prop remains accurate and effective.

AI.tldr: Proposes K-prop, an online learning method for leaky neural networks that propagates temporal kernel gains, cutting the cost of real-time recurrent learning while approaching backpropagation through time in performance.
AI.motivation: Self-recurrence is central to temporal processing, but online training of leaky networks lacks an efficient and effective method because the temporal dependencies of the gradient are complex.
AI.method: Propagates kernel gains instead of full sensitivities, which dramatically reduces the computational and memory cost of real-time recurrent learning (RTRL). The method has a single approximation, whose effect on gradient quality is analyzed.
AI.result: K-prop outperforms existing RTRL approximations and achieves performance comparable to backpropagation through time on sequence learning, classification, and reinforcement learning tasks. The paper identifies conditions under which it remains accurate and effective.
AI.conclusion: K-prop is a practical online alternative to backpropagation through time for leaky networks, with its accuracy governed by identifiable conditions.

title: LawKAN: Group-Law Layers for Composition -- When Imposing a Known Law Pays Off
comment: 20 pages main text (53 total), 15 figures, 6 tables in main text (31 incl. appendices). Code: this https URL
summary: Many tasks compose transformations by a known rule: chained rotations in robotics and navigation. Learned models relearn it, compounding error; classical estimators hardcode it and miss hardware deviations. We impose the known structure and learn only the remainder: an exact non-commutative group law sits in the node of a self-contained layer, its edges learn local increments, and a zero-initialized correction psi learns unknown deviations of the law. A pre-training criterion predicts exact representability. On fixed-angle SU(2) composition, a 54-parameter dense edge is the most accurate dense model, at 27x fewer parameters than the strongest fixed-matrix baseline, and lies 0.05 deg above the Bayes floor. On real robot arms, an isolated 306-parameter psi reaches 1.12-1.14 mm versus 1.29-1.33 mm for Gauss-Newton at N >= 60, and the recipe transfers across three vendors and two protocols. The recipe matches classical fits where the data obey the law and loses where the imposed law is not the task's.

AI.tldr: Proposes LawKAN, a layer that imposes an exact non-commutative group law at its node and learns only the remainder, which pays off when the imposed law is the correct structure for the task.
AI.motivation: Learned models must relearn known composition rules and compound error, while classical estimators hardcode the rule and miss hardware deviations.
AI.method: The exact group law sits in the node of a self-contained layer, edges learn local increments, and a zero-initialized correction psi learns unknown deviations from the law. A pre-training criterion predicts whether the law is exactly representable.
AI.result: On fixed-angle SU(2) composition, a 54-parameter dense edge is the most accurate dense model, using 27x fewer parameters than the strongest fixed-matrix baseline and lying 0.05 degrees above the Bayes floor. On real robot arms, an isolated 306-parameter psi reaches 1.12-1.14 mm versus 1.29-1.33 mm for Gauss-Newton at N >= 60, and the recipe transfers across three vendors and two protocols.
AI.conclusion: The recipe matches classical fits where the data obey the imposed law and loses where the imposed law is not the task's law, so the benefit depends on the law being correct.

title: From Likelihood Convergence to Parameter Convergence in POMDPs
summary: Likelihood-based methods are widely used to learn the parameters of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). While finite-sample guarantees for policy suboptimality exist for certain POMDP subclasses, analogous guarantees for parameter recovery remain less well understood. For any candidate POMDP parameter, we bound its parameter recovery error in terms of its likelihood gap to the ground truth, the structural conditioning of the observation and transition kernels, and the behavior policy used to collect data. The bound applies in both the undercomplete and overcomplete regimes, with the latter following naturally from the undercomplete analysis. Because the result applies to any sufficiently good candidate, it yields finite-sample guarantees for the maximum-likelihood estimator and any procedure producing a parameter with controlled likelihood gap. This is particularly useful for near-optimal learning in infinite-horizon POMDPs, where existing approaches largely rely on model-based planning with accurate transition and observation kernel estimates. The bound separates the contributions of the behavior policy and model, showing how data-collection choices, including action coverage, and their effects on mixing can accelerate parameter learning.

AI.tldr: Gives finite-sample bounds on parameter recovery error for POMDPs in terms of a candidate's likelihood gap, the conditioning of the observation and transition kernels, and the behavior policy used for data collection.
AI.motivation: Finite-sample guarantees for policy suboptimality exist for some POMDP subclasses, but analogous guarantees for parameter recovery are less well understood.
AI.method: For any candidate parameter, the bound relates its recovery error to its likelihood gap to the ground truth, the structural conditioning of the kernels, and the behavior policy. It covers undercomplete and overcomplete regimes, with the overcomplete case following from the undercomplete analysis.
AI.result: Because the bound applies to any sufficiently good candidate, it yields finite-sample guarantees for the maximum-likelihood estimator and for any procedure producing a parameter with controlled likelihood gap. It separates the contributions of the behavior policy and the model, showing how action coverage and mixing can accelerate parameter learning. The abstract reports no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: The analysis supports near-optimal learning in infinite-horizon POMDPs without relying solely on model-based planning, and shows how data-collection choices speed up parameter learning.

title: TRACE: Adaptive Trust-Region Bayesian Optimization for Open-Ended Molecular Design
summary: Optimizing molecules under small evaluation budgets requires deciding both where in chemical space to search and which candidate within that region to evaluate. We introduce Trust Region Adaptive Chemical Exploration (TRACE), a framework for open-ended molecular Bayesian optimization (BO), where candidates are generated on demand rather than selected from a fixed library. TRACE combines an objective-free graph-perturbation mechanism with a fixed, chemistry-aware Gaussian process (GP) surrogate using fragprints, a representation combining molecular fingerprints and fragment descriptors. Rather than learning the search geometry itself, TRACE makes the scale of chemical exploration explicit through a Tanimoto-similarity threshold controlling chemical extent and a cardinality budget controlling candidate-search breadth. A simple success/failure controller expands or contracts both quantities during optimization, while the GP and acquisition function select which admissible molecules to evaluate. Across six challenging molecular optimization benchmarks under matched 1,000-evaluation budgets, TRACE achieves the strongest overall sample efficiency as measured by the best molecule found as evaluations accumulate. Crossed ablations on two objectives further show that adaptive region control contributes beyond the proposal mechanism, while its benefit depends on the proposal distribution. We further apply TRACE to the stability of iron phthalocyanine (FePc), a non-precious molecular electrocatalyst whose degradation can involve loss of the Fe center. Using a first-principles density functional theory (DFT) workflow designed for accurate energy evaluation, TRACE increases the computed thermodynamic resistance to Fe dissolution from 0.42 to 2.59 eV over 80 designed evaluations.

AI.tldr: Introduces TRACE, an adaptive trust-region Bayesian optimization framework that generates molecular candidates on demand, and applies it to improve the computed stability of iron phthalocyanine.
AI.motivation: Optimizing molecules under small evaluation budgets requires choosing both where to search in chemical space and which candidate to evaluate, and fixed candidate libraries limit open-ended design.
AI.method: Combines an objective-free graph-perturbation proposal mechanism with a fixed, chemistry-aware Gaussian process surrogate built on fragprints, which combine molecular fingerprints and fragment descriptors. A Tanimoto-similarity threshold sets chemical extent and a cardinality budget sets candidate-search breadth, and a success/failure controller expands or contracts both during optimization.
AI.result: Across six molecular optimization benchmarks under matched 1,000-evaluation budgets, TRACE achieves the strongest overall sample efficiency. Crossed ablations show that adaptive region control contributes beyond the proposal mechanism, though its benefit depends on the proposal distribution. For iron phthalocyanine, DFT-computed thermodynamic resistance to Fe dissolution rises from 0.42 to 2.59 eV over 80 designed evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive trust-region control improves sample-efficient open-ended molecular design and can yield large computed stability gains for a non-precious electrocatalyst.

title: Simulation-aided Reinforcement Learning with Control Variates
comment: Accepted as a poster at NeurIPS 2026. 10 pages main text + appendix, 3 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms often rely on data collected from a target environment, which can be expensive and noisy. Although simulators can generate large amounts of additional data, standard simulation mixing approaches, which directly combine simulated and real experience, can degrade performance due to simulator inaccuracies, especially when they bias the solution away from the optimal policy. We propose a conservative simulation-aided learning method based on control variates, where simulated data is used solely to reduce variance in the learning process rather than directly shaping the learning target. We develop our approach for Policy-Evaluation, which is a fundamental building block of RL algorithms. Then we combine it within the actor-critic framework towards policy improvement, as well as extend it towards offline RL scenarios. Experiments on multiple MuJoCo benchmark tasks demonstrate improvements over standard simulation mixing approaches, highlighting control variates as an effective tool for simulation-aided reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: Proposes using simulated data only as control variates to reduce variance in reinforcement learning, rather than mixing it directly into the learning target, which avoids the bias from simulator inaccuracies.
AI.motivation: Standard mixing of simulated and real experience can degrade RL performance because simulator inaccuracies bias the solution away from the optimal policy.
AI.method: Develops a control-variate method for policy evaluation, a building block of RL algorithms. Combines it with an actor-critic framework for policy improvement and extends it to offline RL.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple MuJoCo benchmark tasks show improvements over standard simulation mixing approaches. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Control variates are an effective and conservative tool for simulation-aided reinforcement learning.

title: Certify, Report, or Refuse: Harm-Constrained Conformal Prediction for Clinical Actions
comment: Findings of the 6th Machine Learning for Health Symposium (ML4H 2026)
summary: Routing a melanoma case to routine follow-up is a serious action error that diagnostic coverage alone does not rule out. We present Harm-Constrained Risk-Optimal Conformal Prediction (HC-ROCP), a training-free framework that uses frozen classifier probabilities and adds a harm penalty when choosing prediction sets and actions. We test the resulting policies on disjoint calibration splits with multiplicity adjustment. HC-ROCP certifies supported claims, reports descriptive fallback policies, and refuses unsupported subgroup claims. We evaluate these outputs retrospectively on COVID-19 radiographs, ISIC 2019 dermoscopy, and EyePACS-to-APTOS retinopathy transfer. Across ten calibration seeds, HC-ROCP reduces COVID-19 severe-action errors from the exact risk-optimal baseline's 4.68\% to 0.54\%. At a 5\% budget, global claims are certified for COVID-19 and ISIC, but the rare squamous-cell-carcinoma claim is refused. At 1\%, all settings receive descriptive reports. For each budget, we also report the minimum severe-case count needed to pass the global harm gate with zero errors, providing a starting point for further data collection.

AI.tldr: Proposes HC-ROCP, a training-free conformal prediction framework that adds a harm penalty when choosing prediction sets and clinical actions, certifying supported claims, reporting fallback policies, and refusing unsupported subgroup claims.
AI.motivation: Diagnostic coverage alone does not rule out serious action errors, such as routing a melanoma case to routine follow-up.
AI.method: Uses frozen classifier probabilities and a harm penalty when choosing prediction sets and actions. Policies are tested on disjoint calibration splits with multiplicity adjustment and evaluated retrospectively on COVID-19 radiographs, ISIC 2019 dermoscopy, and EyePACS-to-APTOS retinopathy transfer.
