AI.result: Across ten calibration seeds, HC-ROCP reduces COVID-19 severe-action errors from 4.68% for the exact risk-optimal baseline to 0.54%. At a 5% budget, global claims are certified for COVID-19 and ISIC, while the rare squamous-cell carcinoma claim is refused; at 1%, all settings receive descriptive reports. The paper also reports the minimum severe-case count needed to pass the global harm gate with zero errors.
AI.conclusion: Harm-aware conformal policies can make clinical outputs explicitly certified, descriptive or refused, and the reported severe-case counts give a starting point for further data collection.

title: Trade Promotion Optimisation for Consumer Goods
summary: Trade promotions consume a large share of consumer-goods revenue, yet most planners still set discounts with a single, often unreliable, price elasticity per item. We present an end-to-end Trade Promotion Optimisation (TPO) system built as one chain: analogue SKUs, point elasticity, elasticity curve, price recommendation, promotional lift and net lift. Elasticity is measured at post-promo time from directional price-dip events against a rolling regular price, and at promo time by a causal estimator that residualises trend, seasonality and promotion, handles stock-out censoring with a Tobit likelihood and updates itself from the first clean promotion week. Items with weak evidence borrow the point elasticity and the curvature from analogue SKUs chosen by a cross-validated ridge model over category, brand, sub-category, price line and description. The optimiser separates self-price lift from substitution and post-promo dips and adjusts for inventory and trade funding. In a four-week promotion experiment on a 39-SKU consumer brand (mean elasticity -3.06), the plan lifts units by 20.6% and revenue by 6.9% at flat margin. Analogue pooling halves elasticity error relative to hierarchy averaging.

AI.tldr: Presents an end-to-end trade promotion optimisation system that estimates item-level price elasticity using analogue-SKU borrowing and a censoring-aware causal estimator, and recommends discounts that lift units and revenue at flat margin in a four-week experiment.
AI.motivation: Most planners set trade promotion discounts from a single, often unreliable, price elasticity per item.
AI.method: A chain from analogue SKUs and point elasticity through elasticity curve, price recommendation, promotional lift and net lift. Elasticity is measured post-promo from directional price-dip events and at promo time by a causal estimator that residualises trend, seasonality and promotion and uses a Tobit likelihood for stock-out censoring. Weak-evidence items borrow elasticity and curvature from analogue SKUs chosen by a cross-validated ridge model, and the optimiser separates self-price lift from substitution and post-promo dips.
AI.result: In a four-week promotion experiment on a 39-SKU consumer brand (mean elasticity -3.06), the plan lifts units by 20.6% and revenue by 6.9% at flat margin. Analogue pooling halves elasticity error relative to hierarchy averaging.
AI.conclusion: Pooling elasticity across analogue SKUs with a censoring-aware estimator yields a promotion plan that raises revenue without reducing margin in the tested brand.

title: CoilStellaration: A Dataset and Benchmark for Engineering-Aware Stellarator Coilset Generation
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Track on Evaluations and Datasets
summary: Stellarators are fusion devices that use externally generated, three-dimensional magnetic fields to confine hot plasma and offer a promising route to commercial fusion. Their electromagnetic coils pose a challenging design problem: they must reproduce the target magnetic field while satisfying engineering constraints and remaining practical and cost-effective to manufacture. Finding suitable geometries is a highly nonlinear inverse problem that generally has neither a closed-form nor a unique solution. This problem lies at the heart of stellarator design. We introduce CoilStellaration, a dataset and benchmark for learning the mapping between coil geometries from target plasma magnetic fields and engineering requirements. The dataset contains 177,000 optimized filamentary coilsets targeting plasma equilibria from ConStellaration, with sampled engineering requirements and achieved geometric and magnetic-field metrics. It spans multiple coil counts and field-period numbers, supporting studies of both specialized and shared models across configurations. The benchmark asks models to predict coils conditioned on a target equilibrium and requirements on coil-coil and coil-plasma spacing, curvature, and magnetic-field error. We show that magnetic-field accuracy remains the main challenge, with learned models rarely satisfying all requirements simultaneously. However, using learned predictions to initialize conventional coil optimization can accelerate early progress. We release baseline models and evaluation code to support reproducible research on both direct coil generation and learned optimization initializations. By lowering the barrier for machine learning and optimization researchers to engage with stellarator coil design, we aim to accelerate progress toward practical, cost-effective stellarator power plants.

AI.tldr: Introduces CoilStellaration, a dataset of 177,000 optimized filamentary stellarator coilsets and a benchmark for predicting coil geometries from target plasma equilibria and engineering requirements.
AI.motivation: Designing stellarator coils is a highly nonlinear inverse problem with neither a closed-form nor a unique solution, and machine learning and optimization researchers lack a benchmark to engage with it.
AI.method: The dataset targets ConStellaration plasma equilibria, with sampled engineering requirements and achieved geometric and magnetic-field metrics, across multiple coil counts and field-period numbers. The benchmark asks models to predict coils conditioned on a target equilibrium and on requirements for coil-coil and coil-plasma spacing, curvature and magnetic-field error.
AI.result: Magnetic-field accuracy remains the main challenge, and learned models rarely satisfy all requirements simultaneously. Using learned predictions to initialize conventional coil optimization can accelerate early progress. Baseline models and evaluation code are released.
AI.conclusion: The dataset lowers the barrier for machine learning and optimization researchers to work on stellarator coil design, and learned predictions are useful as initializations for conventional optimization.

title: Agnostic Marginal-Nonuniform Learning
summary: We study the problem of binary classification in the marginal-nonuniform learning framework in the agnostic setting. In this model, the constants in the learning rate may depend on the marginal distribution of the unlabeled data, but the guarantee must hold uniformly over all conditional distributions of the labels. We also study fine-grained rates. We consider two criteria. (1) The standard agnostic setting, where the learner competes with the best concept in the class. In this setting, an immediate consequence of standard agnostic PAC learning results gives us the optimal rate of $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ for every class $\mathcal{H}$ with finite $\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})$ and shows that arbitrarily slow rates are necessary otherwise. This also gives us the optimal fine-grained rate of $\sqrt{\tfrac{\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})}{n}}$. Therefore, the dependence on the marginal distribution does not help, which is in contrast to the realizable setting. (2) In the relaxed agnostic setting, where the learner competes with $(1+\lambda)$ times the error of the best concept for a fixed $\lambda \in (0,1]$, the picture from the realizable setting reappears. We obtain a trichotomy of the achievable optimal rates: exponential rates of the form $e^{-n}$ arise precisely when the class is finite; linear rates of the form $\tfrac{1}{n}$ arise when the class is infinite but $\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})$ is finite; and arbitrarily slow rates occur when $\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})=\infty$. We also obtain the optimal fine-grained rate of $\tfrac{\mathrm{uVCE}(\mathcal{H})}{\lambda n}$, where $\mathrm{uVCE}(\mathcal{H})$ is a recently introduced combinatorial complexity dimension called the uncentered $\mathrm{VC}$-eluder dimension.

AI.tldr: Studies agnostic binary classification in the marginal-nonuniform framework, showing that marginal dependence does not improve rates in the standard agnostic setting, while under a relaxed (1+lambda) criterion the optimal rates form a trichotomy.
AI.motivation: The marginal-nonuniform framework lets rate constants depend on the unlabeled marginal, and this contrasts with the realizable setting, where such dependence helps. The question is what happens in the agnostic setting, with its guarantee required to hold uniformly over all conditional label distributions.
AI.method: Analyzes two criteria: competing with the best concept in the class (standard agnostic), and competing with (1+lambda) times the best error for a fixed lambda in (0,1] (relaxed agnostic). Derives optimal and fine-grained rates, with the fine-grained rate for the relaxed case expressed through the uncentered VC-eluder dimension.
AI.result: In the standard agnostic setting the optimal rate is 1/sqrt(n) for every class with finite VC dimension, with fine-grained rate sqrt(VC/n), and arbitrarily slow rates are necessary otherwise. In the relaxed setting the rates form a trichotomy: exponential e^{-n} for finite classes, 1/n for infinite classes of finite VC dimension, and arbitrarily slow rates when VC is infinite, with fine-grained rate uVCE/(lambda n).
AI.conclusion: Marginal dependence does not help standard agnostic rates, whereas the relaxed criterion recovers a picture like the realizable setting, with a trichotomy of optimal rates.

title: TACTUS: A Robotic Palpation System for Spatially Heterogeneous Hardness Mapping of Woody Breast Myopathy
summary: Woody breast (WB) myopathy is a spatially heterogeneous fibro-degenerative condition of the broiler Pectoralis major muscle. Existing mechanical reference methods rely on single-point or sequential compression measurements, limiting characterization of spatial hardness variability. This study presents TACTUS (Tactile Adaptive Conformal 3D Uniform Sensing), an automated tactile array that generates thickness-normalized, three-dimensional hardness maps at 20 anatomically distributed locations within approximately 30 s. TACTUS integrates 20 independently motorized tactuators with force-sensing resistors and encoder-driven linear actuators, alongside a LiDAR depth camera for surface profiling and adaptive compression. The system was evaluated using 100 broiler breast fillets across four WB severity classes (Normal, Mild, Moderate, Severe). TACTUS identified significant force differences among severity classes (ANOVA, p < 0.001), with the strongest differentiation in the cranial region and a significant caudal effect not detected by texture-analyzer measurements. Fillet-level TACTUS force showed moderate but significant correlation with texture-analyzer measurements (Pearson r = 0.441, p < 0.001). Semivariogram, local change entropy, and heterogeneity analyses revealed increasing and anatomically structured hardness variability with WB severity. These findings demonstrate TACTUS as an automated, operator-independent platform for spatially resolved mechanical characterization and ground-truth generation to support hyperspectral and near-infrared spectroscopy-based WB classification systems.

AI.tldr: Presents TACTUS, a robotic tactile array that produces spatial 3D hardness maps of broiler breast fillets at 20 anatomical locations within about 30 seconds, to characterize woody breast myopathy.
AI.motivation: Existing mechanical reference methods use single-point or sequential compression, which limits characterization of spatial hardness variability in woody breast myopathy.
AI.method: Integrates 20 independently motorized tactuators with force-sensing resistors and encoder-driven linear actuators, plus a LiDAR depth camera for surface profiling and adaptive compression. Evaluated on 100 broiler breast fillets across four woody breast severity classes (Normal, Mild, Moderate, Severe).
AI.result: TACTUS identifies significant force differences among severity classes (ANOVA, p < 0.001), with the strongest differentiation in the cranial region and a significant caudal effect that texture-analyzer measurements do not detect. Fillet-level force correlates moderately with texture-analyzer measurements (Pearson r = 0.441, p < 0.001). Hardness variability increases with severity and is anatomically structured.
AI.conclusion: TACTUS is an automated, operator-independent platform for spatially resolved mechanical characterization and ground-truth generation to support hyperspectral and near-infrared classification of woody breast.

title: Scaling Taxonomy-Free Image Labeling with Generative AI: A Multimodal
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 4th CJ Workshop at KDD 2025 (this https URL), also related: this https URL
summary: Providing real-time multimodal insights into images is challenging because it requires low latency, high description accuracy, and scalable solutions that are both cost-effective and efficient. For example, given a new image of an outfit, we would like to generate insights that the image depicts "earth tones" and "linen pants" and allow users to explore similar ideas along these themes. Traditional strategies to generate such insights would typically involve building taxonomies producing a golden set labeled by humans, training models on these datasets, and deploying these models for online inference services. Such workflows are constrained by fixed taxonomy, high labeling cost, limited labeling coverage in sample space, and human errors and expertise gaps in labelers. In addition, these methods are expensive and cumbersome to iterate over time. Recent trends have started exploring generative AI models for online insights, but this method suffers from long latency and prohibitive costs to support a high volume of requests or large amounts of offline labeling needs. We present Generative Labeling On Clusters (GLOC) as a solution to provide highly scalable, cost-effective, low latency, and high accuracy online image insight services. GLOC leverages highly optimized image embeddings to form image clusters that are semantically close to each other for the purpose of the type of insights, and summarizes the insights at the cluster level, which effectively generalizes to members in the cluster. At Pinterest, GLOC powers image descriptors and pivot query suggestions for Hybrid Search, which is a multimodal search service enabling users to search with both an image and a text query. Our offline and online A/B tests demonstrate that GLOC significantly outperforms previous methods, delivering improvements in quality and efficiency.

AI.tldr: Presents GLOC (Generative Labeling On Clusters), which clusters image embeddings and summarizes insights per cluster with generative AI, giving scalable, low-latency image insight services; it is deployed at Pinterest for Hybrid Search.
AI.motivation: Taxonomy-based labeling is costly, fixed and limited in coverage, while per-image generative AI has long latency and prohibitive cost at high request volume or for large offline labeling.
AI.method: Forms image clusters from optimized embeddings that are semantically close for the type of insight wanted, and summarizes insights at the cluster level so they generalize to members of the cluster.
AI.result: At Pinterest, GLOC powers image descriptors and pivot query suggestions for Hybrid Search, a multimodal search service that takes both image and text queries. Offline and online A/B tests show that GLOC significantly outperforms previous methods in quality and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Cluster-level generative labeling is a scalable, cost-effective and accurate alternative to taxonomy-based or per-image generative labeling for online image insights.

title: KiteNorm: Variance Regularisation for Stable and Scalable Post-LN Transformers
summary: Post-LayerNorm Transformers have seen limited practical adoption due to enduring difficulties in scaling them to large depths. While prior research has focused on stabilising Post-LayerNorm by improving conditioning at initialisation, stability often deteriorates when models are trained with large learning rates, forcing additional compromises. In the decoder-only settings we study, existing Post-LayerNorm methods fail to outperform strong Pre-LayerNorm baselines. We propose KiteNorm, a post-norm training method designed to break this trend by constraining hidden-state variance. This approach is motivated by a bound on the LayerNorm Jacobian suggesting that variance growth contributes to gradient vanishing, alongside empirical evidence linking it to rank collapse. KiteNorm combines residual scaling and variance regularisation to maintain stability throughout training, supported by scalarised double-normalisation that provides separately learnable scales for the skip and residual branches. Across decoder-only Transformers up to 1.3B parameters, KiteNorm improves training stability and outperforms leading baselines at their optimal learning rates, with scaling laws favouring KiteNorm across depth, width, batch size, and training budget. Ablations show that each component is necessary for the full stability and performance gains.

AI.tldr: Proposes KiteNorm, a post-LayerNorm training method that constrains hidden-state variance using residual scaling and variance regularization, outperforming leading baselines on decoder-only Transformers up to 1.3B parameters.
AI.motivation: Post-LayerNorm Transformers are hard to scale to large depths and become unstable at large learning rates, and in the decoder-only settings studied, existing post-LN methods fail to outperform strong Pre-LayerNorm baselines.
AI.method: Constrains hidden-state variance, motivated by a bound on the LayerNorm Jacobian suggesting that variance growth contributes to gradient vanishing, and by empirical evidence linking variance to rank collapse. Combines residual scaling and variance regularization with scalarised double-normalisation, which gives separately learnable scales for the skip and residual branches.
AI.result: On decoder-only Transformers up to 1.3B parameters, KiteNorm improves training stability and outperforms leading baselines at their optimal learning rates, with scaling laws favouring it across depth, width, batch size and training budget. Ablations show each component is necessary for the full stability and performance gains.
AI.conclusion: Variance regularization with residual scaling keeps post-LN Transformers stable and competitive at scale, with favourable scaling behaviour.

title: $Σ$-LeWM: Learning World Models via S-Information for Robot Control
summary: World models have increasingly been applied as a model-based control method for robotics tasks such as manipulation and locomotion. While early world model architectures relied on decoders to prevent mode collapse and learn a predictable latent space, recent works on world models, such as Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture or LeWorldModel, increasingly aim to learn embeddings without a grounding decoder, utilising only a latent forward dynamics predictor and a stabilising entropy term. In this paper, we set out to demonstrate that the further introduction of two additional latent losses to LeWorldModel, a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor, enforces further structure on the latent embedding, leading to further gains in both performance and planning efficiency. These are critical properties for improving the applicability of such methods to real-time model-based control of real-world robots. We demonstrate these gains on standard world model benchmarks and two simulated robot manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: Proposes Sigma-LeWM, which adds a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor as latent losses to LeWorldModel, reporting further gains in performance and planning efficiency for robot control.
AI.motivation: Recent joint-embedding world models learn embeddings without a grounding decoder, using a latent forward dynamics predictor and a stabilising entropy term, and the authors aim to add more structure to these latent embeddings for real-time model-based control of real robots.
AI.method: Adds two latent losses to LeWorldModel: a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor, which enforce further structure on the latent embedding.
AI.result: The gains in performance and planning efficiency are demonstrated on standard world model benchmarks and on two simulated robot manipulation tasks. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Additional latent dynamics losses give a more structured embedding, which the authors argue is more applicable to real-time model-based control of real-world robots, though the evidence given is from simulation.

title: Smartphone-Enabled Depth-Aware Transillumination Imaging for Detection of Chicken Breast Fillet Myopathies in Chicken Fillets
summary: Woody Breast (WB) myopathy is a major quality defect in broiler chickens characterized by fibrosis, increased tissue hardness, and altered structural properties that affect product quality. Conventional palpation is subjective and labor-intensive, while many non-destructive methods require specialized equipment or substantial computational resources. This study developed a smartphone-based transillumination and 3D point-cloud framework for non-destructive WB severity classification. A total of 267 chicken breast fillets, including normal breast (NB, n = 87), mild WB (MWB, n = 85), and severe WB (SWB, n = 95), were evaluated using RAW transillumination images and 3D point clouds acquired with an iPhone 16 Pro. A total of 91 features, comprising 14 image-derived, 76 geometric, and one physics-informed Beer-Lambert attenuation feature, were extracted. Partial correlation controlling for thickness revealed a significant association between image characteristics and WB severity (r = 0.413, p < 0.0001), indicating optical information independent of fillet geometry. SWB tissue exhibited approximately 26% greater light attenuation per unit thickness than NB. The 2D-only models achieved approximately 82% test accuracy, while the multimodal ensemble combining Fusion-DGCNN, XGBoost, and physics-guided logistic regression (PGLR) achieved approximately 90% accuracy. These findings demonstrate the complementary value of optical, geometric, and physics-informed features and establish the feasibility of smartphone-based, non-destructive WB severity assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a smartphone-based framework that combines transillumination images and 3D point clouds from an iPhone 16 Pro to classify woody breast (WB) myopathy severity in 267 chicken fillets non-destructively. A multimodal ensemble reaches about 90% test accuracy, versus about 82% for 2D-only models.
AI.motivation: Woody breast is a major quality defect in broilers, but conventional palpation is subjective and labor-intensive, and many non-destructive methods need specialized equipment or heavy computation.
AI.method: Smartphone RAW transillumination images and 3D point clouds yield 91 features (14 image-derived, 76 geometric, and one physics-informed Beer-Lambert attenuation feature). A Fusion-DGCNN, XGBoost and physics-guided logistic regression (PGLR) ensemble combines them, with partial correlation controlling for fillet thickness.
AI.result: Image characteristics correlate with WB severity after controlling for thickness (r = 0.413, p < 0.0001). Severe WB tissue shows about 26% greater light attenuation per unit thickness than normal breast. The 2D-only models reach about 82% test accuracy and the multimodal ensemble about 90%.
AI.conclusion: Optical, geometric and physics-informed features are complementary, and the results establish the feasibility of smartphone-based non-destructive WB severity assessment.

title: Agentic-OPD: Recovering Forgotten Agent Capabilities via On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Tasks
comment: 10 pages of main text, 24 pages total including references and appendix
summary: Reinforcement learning is now the mainstream paradigm for training LLMs on agentic tasks, yet standard practice keeps only the best-validation checkpoint and discards the rest. We show that this is lossy: in GRPO training of LLM agents, the best-validation checkpoint fails on problems that earlier checkpoints from the same run had already solved, and the union of problems solved across checkpoints far exceeds any single one. The discarded checkpoints thus form a teacher pool obtained at no additional training cost, which on-policy distillation (OPD) can mine to recover the lost coverage. Mining this pool raises two challenges: i) which checkpoint to distill from, as no checkpoint dominates the others and complementarity to the student is problem-specific; ii) where to trust it, as even a well-chosen teacher is only locally superior, so indiscriminate distillation overwrites behavior the student has already mastered. We propose Agentic-OPD, which treats the best-validation checkpoint as the student and all saved checkpoints as frozen teacher candidates, using the student's evolving capability gaps to guide both teacher selection and supervision filtering: the HCN policy (Highest Coverage Next) dynamically selects teachers by weighted coverage of the student's unsolved problems, while the LAD module (Locality-Aware Distillation) confines transfer to failed student rollouts on problems where the teacher performs better. Across five agentic task domains and 24 benchmarks and task subsets, Agentic-OPD improves over its initialization checkpoint by up to 7.4 points, with a 4B student surpassing the latest frontier models GPT-5.6 and DeepSeek-V4.1 on deep search. Agentic-OPD recasts a finished RL run as a reusable pool of policies and establishes post-RL capability recovery as a stage orthogonal to improvements in the RL algorithm itself.

AI.tldr: Agentic-OPD recovers capability lost when RL training discards intermediate checkpoints by distilling from the pool of saved checkpoints into the best-validation student. It improves over its initialization by up to 7.4 points across five agentic domains and 24 benchmarks, and a 4B student surpasses GPT-5.6 and DeepSeek-V4.1 on deep search.
AI.motivation: Standard RL practice keeps only the best-validation checkpoint, but in GRPO agent training earlier checkpoints solve problems the final one fails, so the union of solved problems far exceeds any single checkpoint.
AI.method: The best-validation checkpoint is the student and all saved checkpoints are frozen teachers. The HCN (Highest Coverage Next) policy selects teachers by weighted coverage of the student's unsolved problems, and the LAD (Locality-Aware Distillation) module restricts transfer to failed student rollouts on problems where the teacher is better.
AI.result: Across five agentic task domains and 24 benchmarks and task subsets, the method improves over its initialization checkpoint by up to 7.4 points. A 4B student surpasses GPT-5.6 and DeepSeek-V4.1 on deep search.
AI.conclusion: A finished RL run becomes a reusable pool of policies, and post-RL capability recovery is established as a stage orthogonal to improvements in the RL algorithm.

title: Inversion-Free High-Dimensional Counterfactual Inference
summary: Counterfactual inference is the task of answering hypothetical "what-if" queries about a unit, given an observational dataset, modeling assumptions, and a causal graph. This enables a modeler to reason about hypothetical scenarios that cannot otherwise be answered without assumptions or a causal graph. The simpler case involves a causal graph with scalar 1-D variables that denote different attributes in the data-generation process. While the literature is clear in the 1-D case, extending this to settings with high-dimensional nodes (e.g., images) remains challenging. Conventionally, in the literature, methods recover the latent state from the factual image (inversion), generate counterfactual attributes from the graph, and render the counterfactual image from the latent state using the updated attributes. In our work, we investigate the necessity of the inversion step in computing high-dimensional counterfactuals. We first discuss moving from the scalar 1-D case to the higher-dimensional case. Secondly, we discuss the relevance of the inversion step and evaluate an inversion-free counterpart repurposed from the image-editing literature. Finally, on image datasets such as CelebA and ADNI, we benchmark our approach using two measures: namely, effectiveness and identity preservation. While effectiveness is a measure of how faithfully the counterfactual attribute is rendered, identity preservation measures whether the same unit (image) is being rendered, both of which are crucial for high-dimensional counterfactual inference. We present the tradeoffs of using inversion-based and inversion-free approaches in our work.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether the inversion step, which recovers a latent state from a factual image, is needed for high-dimensional counterfactual inference. It evaluates an inversion-free method adapted from image editing and benchmarks it on CelebA and ADNI against inversion-based approaches.
AI.motivation: Counterfactual inference is well understood for scalar 1-D variables, but extending it to high-dimensional nodes such as images is hard. Conventional pipelines depend on an inversion step whose necessity has not been examined.
AI.method: The authors move the scalar 1-D framework to higher dimensions and evaluate an inversion-free counterpart repurposed from image editing. They measure effectiveness (how faithfully the counterfactual attribute is rendered) and identity preservation (whether the same image is rendered).
AI.result: The abstract reports benchmark results on CelebA and ADNI for both measures but gives no specific numbers. It presents the tradeoffs between inversion-based and inversion-free approaches.
AI.conclusion: Inversion and inversion-free approaches trade off effectiveness against identity preservation, and the choice between them depends on that tradeoff.

title: What the Loss Curve Misses: FP4 Pretraining Slows the Acquisition of Rare Facts
summary: Low-precision pretraining is usually judged by validation loss. We ask whether matching loss also means learning rare facts as efficiently. We train transformers from scratch with emulated 4-bit matrix multiplications on synthetic biographies with controlled exposure counts, on their own and mixed into web text. NVFP4 needs 1.32$\times$ and 1.52$\times$ as many exposures as BF16 to match its recall while validation loss differs by only 0.5% and 2%, and 1.26$\times$ and 1.30$\times$ when both models are evaluated with BF16 matrix multiplications. Under our primary readout, the exposure cost is about 1.2$\times$ at matched loss. Zero-mean gradient noise reproduces the cost of quantizing only the backward pass, which barely moves the loss. In a controlled experiment at twice the NVFP4 error, noise fed only to Adam's second-moment estimate acts like a lower learning rate and its cost fades, whereas noise in the update lowers its signal-to-noise ratio and carries about two thirds of the cost through the end of training. Raising the learning rate to offset the smaller average step does not recover the cost, either for this noise or for NVFP4. Gradient statistics of BF16 checkpoints rank the costs of formats, partial quantizations and noise controls without fitting (Spearman 0.96). We suggest measuring rare-fact acquisition alongside loss when evaluating low-precision recipes.

AI.tldr: Training transformers with emulated 4-bit (NVFP4) matmuls needs more exposures to learn rare facts than BF16 training, even when validation loss is nearly matched. The paper argues that loss alone misses this cost and that rare-fact acquisition should be measured alongside it.
AI.motivation: Low-precision pretraining is judged by validation loss, but the question is whether matching loss also means learning rare facts as efficiently.
AI.method: Transformers are trained from scratch with emulated 4-bit matrix multiplications on synthetic biographies with controlled exposure counts, alone and mixed into web text. Zero-mean gradient noise is used as a controlled stand-in for quantization error, and noise is applied separately to the Adam second-moment estimate and to the update.
AI.result: NVFP4 needs 1.32x and 1.52x as many exposures as BF16 to match recall, while validation loss differs by only 0.5% and 2%. Under the primary readout the cost is about 1.2x at matched loss. Gradient statistics of BF16 checkpoints rank the costs without fitting (Spearman 0.96).
AI.conclusion: Low-precision recipes should be evaluated by rare-fact acquisition as well as loss, since the cost is not captured by loss and is not recovered by raising the learning rate.

title: Mitigating Agentic Deception via Evaluation-Side Partially Observable Games
comment: 44 pages, 10 figures. Code: this https URL Project website: this https URL
summary: As large language models become more capable agents, they can exhibit deceptive behaviors, cheating human for higher rewards while appearing helpful. We attribute this failure to evaluation-side partial observability, where models are evaluated mainly from final outcome, without checking the faithfulness of underlying reasoning, tool use, and environmental effects. Prior mitigations address this partial observability by predefined evaluator latent belief space or one-shot monitoring, which do not extend to free-form language space and vulnerable to stronger deceptions that evade simple monitoring. In this work, we formulate deception mitigation as an Evaluation-Side Partially Observable Extensive Form Game (e-PoG), a max-min framework in which an agent maximizes reward, a monitor minimizes the agent's payoff by exposing deception from the full interaction trajectory, and a fixed verifier validates the monitor's claims and converts them into penalties. We define the solution concept as a Subgame-Perfect Oversight Equilibrium (SPOE) between agent and monitor, and prove its existence in finite games. With a perfect verifier, every SPOE is faithful; with an imperfect verifier, the guarantee persists if verifier errors do not reverse the ranking of monitor actions. To achieve faithful SPOE, we derive a two-timescale policy gradient algorithm and enhance the pipeline empirically with NLI verification and deterministic checks. Experiments with Gemma3-4B-IT and Qwen3-4B/8B on Agentic Role-Playing, SearchQA, and WebShop show that e-PoG mitigates multiple emergent deception modes, outperforming the strongest baselines by 26.0% in deception mitigation and by up to 39.8% in task success. These gains persist under weak-to-strong supervision. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper frames deception mitigation in LLM agents as an evaluation-side partially observable extensive-form game (e-PoG), with a monitor exposing deception and a verifier converting claims into penalties. The method outperforms the strongest baselines by 26.0% in deception mitigation and by up to 39.8% in task success.
AI.motivation: Agents can cheat while appearing helpful because evaluation sees mainly final outcomes and not the faithfulness of reasoning, tool use and environment effects. Prior mitigations use predefined latent belief spaces or one-shot monitoring, which do not extend to free-form language and miss stronger deceptions.
AI.method: The authors model the agent and monitor as a max-min game in which the monitor exposes deception from the full trajectory and a fixed verifier validates its claims. They define a Subgame-Perfect Oversight Equilibrium (SPOE), prove its existence in finite games, and derive a two-timescale policy gradient algorithm enhanced with NLI verification and deterministic checks.
AI.result: Experiments with Gemma3-4B-IT and Qwen3-4B/8B on Agentic Role-Playing, SearchQA and WebShop show mitigation of several emergent deception modes. Gains over the strongest baselines are 26.0% in deception mitigation and up to 39.8% in task success, and they persist under weak-to-strong supervision.
AI.conclusion: With a perfect verifier every SPOE is faithful, and with an imperfect verifier the guarantee holds if verifier errors do not reverse the ranking of monitor actions.

title: Where Does Alignment Emerge and What Does It Mean? A Closer Look at the Platonic Representation Hypothesis
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Neural Network Artifacts as a New Data Modality (Spotlight)
summary: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that neural networks are converging toward similar representation spaces. As language models become more capable, their representations are aligning with those of vision models. However, recent work has questioned whether this trend continues to hold for newer language models. Moreover, it has been shown that representation similarity metrics can be confounded by model depth and width, requiring appropriate baselines for interpretation. In this work, we first investigate where alignment emerges between unimodal models across model layers and representation dimensions. Next, we find that the PRH capability-alignment trend persists for newer models as long as the captions are sufficiently clean and informative. Finally, we contextualize cross-modal alignment, introducing unimodal and multimodal baselines on various datasets. Our results show that the cross-modal representational alignment of unimodal models can surpass that of explicitly aligned vision-language models, but remains substantially behind the alignment observed for models of the same modality. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper examines where cross-modal alignment emerges between unimodal language and vision models and whether the Platonic Representation Hypothesis trend holds for newer models. It finds that unimodal models can align across modalities more than explicitly aligned vision-language models, but still remain far below same-modality alignment.
AI.motivation: Recent work questions whether the Platonic Representation Hypothesis trend of growing language-vision alignment continues for newer language models, and similarity metrics can be confounded by model depth and width.
AI.method: The authors study alignment across model layers and representation dimensions between unimodal models. They test the capability-alignment trend for newer models with clean, informative captions, and they add unimodal and multimodal baselines on several datasets to contextualize cross-modal alignment.
AI.result: The capability-alignment trend persists for newer models as long as captions are sufficiently clean and informative. Cross-modal alignment of unimodal models can surpass that of explicitly aligned vision-language models, but remains substantially behind same-modality alignment.
AI.conclusion: Cross-modal alignment is a real but limited phenomenon, and interpreting it requires appropriate unimodal and multimodal baselines.

title: Vendi Anomaly Scores for Efficient and Accurate Anomaly Detection
comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Main Track
summary: Anomaly detection (AD) is a critical for trustworthy machine learning and scientific discovery. Existing methods typically define anomalies through local density, isolation heuristics, or distance from a fitted distribution, making them sensitive to neighborhood scale, partitioning choices, or restrictive distributional assumptions. In this work, we introduce a new paradigm by formulating anomaly detection from a diversity perspective. We propose the $\textit{Vendi Anomaly Score}$ (VAS), which detects anomalies by quantifying how much a sample changes the diversity of the dataset, as measured by the Vendi score, when removed. VAS captures both local redundancy and global data structure without relying on density estimation or partitioning heuristics. Moreover, VAS requires no hyperparameter tuning, instead adapting automatically to the spectral structure of the data. VAS is non-parametric and scales linearly with dataset size. Across 148 benchmark embedding datasets derived from 10 source datasets and 4 embedding architectures, VAS achieves state-of-the-art AD performance. We further validate VAS on large-scale ImageNet experiments, where it remains robust as both contamination rate and dataset scale increase.

AI.tldr: The Vendi Anomaly Score (VAS) detects anomalies by measuring how much each sample changes dataset diversity, as quantified by the Vendi score, when it is removed. It achieves state-of-the-art anomaly detection across 148 benchmark embedding datasets and remains robust on large-scale ImageNet experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing anomaly detectors rely on local density, isolation heuristics or distance from a fitted distribution, which makes them sensitive to neighborhood scale, partitioning choices or restrictive distributional assumptions.
AI.method: Anomalies are scored by the change in the Vendi diversity measure when a sample is removed. The method is non-parametric, needs no density estimation or partitioning, requires no hyperparameter tuning, adapts to the spectral structure of the data, and scales linearly with dataset size.
AI.result: Across 148 benchmark embedding datasets derived from 10 source datasets and 4 embedding architectures, VAS achieves state-of-the-art AD performance. It stays robust as contamination rate and dataset scale grow on ImageNet experiments.
AI.conclusion: Formulating anomaly detection as a diversity problem gives a hyperparameter-free, scalable alternative that captures both local redundancy and global structure.

title: Adaptive Quantization Preserves Fast Rates for TD Learning over Rate-Limited Channels
summary: Motivated by reinforcement learning subject to communication constraints, we study a policy evaluation problem with linear function approximation over a rate-limited channel. In our setup, an agent interacting with an unknown environment (modeled as a Markov Decision Process) transmits quantized estimates of a temporal-difference (TD) learning update direction to a server over a finite-capacity channel. Our goal is to investigate to what extent one can preserve the statistical convergence rates achievable when the channel has infinite capacity. To that end, we propose a new algorithm called Batched Adaptively Quantized TD (BAQ-TD), which uses batching to reduce the variance of the transmitted information, and adaptive quantization to encode innovations. We prove a high-probability finite-time error bound for BAQ-TD, and show that, above a certain finite channel capacity, BAQ-TD preserves the convergence rate of unquantized TD up to logarithmic factors. Specifically, for a $d$-dimensional value function parameter, we establish that transmitting a total of $\mathcal{O}(d \log(T))$ bits over a horizon of length $T$ suffices to achieve the order-optimal rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/T)$, marking an exponential improvement in communication-complexity over prior work.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes BAQ-TD, a batched adaptively quantized temporal-difference algorithm for policy evaluation over a rate-limited channel. It proves that O(d log T) transmitted bits suffice to reach the order-optimal O~(1/T) rate of unquantized TD, an exponential improvement in communication complexity over prior work.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning under communication constraints must send value updates over finite-capacity channels, and it is unclear how much of the convergence rate achievable with infinite capacity can be preserved.
AI.method: An agent in an MDP with linear function approximation transmits quantized TD update directions to a server. BAQ-TD uses batching to reduce the variance of transmitted information and adaptive quantization to encode innovations.
AI.result: The authors prove a high-probability finite-time error bound. Above a certain finite channel capacity, BAQ-TD preserves the rate of unquantized TD up to logarithmic factors, with O(d log T) bits over horizon T giving O~(1/T).
AI.conclusion: Quantized TD can match the statistical rate of the unquantized algorithm with far less communication, and the communication complexity improves exponentially over prior work.

title: Kolmogorov-Chapman Maps: Trajectory-Free Learning for Simulating Molecular Dynamics
summary: Stochastic differential equations (SDEs) describe stochastic processes across a wide range of scientific domains, including physics, biology, and finance. Although individual numerical integration steps are inexpensive, observing meaningful events or transitions can require millions of sequential steps, resulting in substantial wall-clock simulation time and poor hardware utilization. Deep learning offers an alternative by amortizing many integration steps into a single neural network forward pass, potentially enabling much faster simulation. However, existing supervised approaches typically require long simulated trajectory data, which restricts their applicability. In this work, we introduce Kolmogorov-Chapman Maps (KC-Maps), a method for learning the transition kernel of an SDE that relies only on the trajectory-free marginal samples together with the known drift and diffusion coefficients. Given an initial time and state of a process, KC-Maps models its distribution integrated to any given time, corresponding to the weak solution of the SDE. To recover the correct dynamics, KC-Maps satisfies two key properties: (i) it satisfies the boundary conditions, which we incorporate directly into the neural network architecture, and (ii) it respects the Kolmogorov--Chapman equation, which provides an efficient training objective. We empirically demonstrate that KC-Maps learns to integrate the dynamics of peptide molecular systems and outperforms classical molecular dynamics in terms of GPU-hours.

AI.tldr: Kolmogorov-Chapman Maps (KC-Maps) learn the transition kernel of an SDE from trajectory-free marginal samples plus known drift and diffusion, so one forward pass approximates many integration steps. On peptide molecular systems it outperforms classical molecular dynamics in GPU-hours.
AI.motivation: Observing transitions in stochastic simulations can require millions of sequential steps, and existing supervised neural approaches need long simulated trajectory data, which limits their use.
AI.method: The model maps an initial time and state to the distribution at any later time, approximating the weak solution of the SDE. It builds the boundary conditions into the network architecture and trains with the Kolmogorov-Chapman equation as the objective.
AI.result: KC-Maps learns to integrate the dynamics of peptide molecular systems and outperforms classical molecular dynamics in terms of GPU-hours. The abstract gives no specific figures.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-free learning of SDE transition kernels is a practical route to faster molecular simulation than classical methods.

title: How to start a conversation proactively?
comment: The article is accepted in IEEE RO-MAN 2026. The dataset is available at this https URL
summary: Proactively initiating a conversation is a fundamental social competence and a critical capability for social robots. However, determining how and when to start a conversation in a given situation remains an open challenge, primarily due to the lack of a principled definition of conversational context. While recent large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive conversational fluency, they are predominantly turn-reactive and often produce generic or monotonous openers when tasked with initiating interaction, even when contextual information is available. Such limitations are particularly problematic for embodied social robots, where inappropriate or poorly timed initiations can negatively affect user engagement and rapport. In this work, we propose a schema of contextual variables that jointly characterize situations relevant for proactive conversation initiation. The schema is designed to structure perceptual, situational, and interactional cues such that they can be effectively exploited by language models. Furthermore, motivated by the absence of suitable training data, we introduce a curated dataset of contextually-aligned conversation openers (CCO) covering diverse everyday scenarios. Using this dataset, we fine-tune small language models (SLMs) to generate proactive conversation initiations. Through a comparative evaluation involving zero-shot LLMs, off-the-shelf SLMs, and our fine-tuned models, we demonstrate that explicit contextual structuring and targeted data curation substantially improve the quality and contextual appropriateness of conversation openers. Our results highlight the importance of context modeling for proactive social interaction and provide actionable building blocks for conversational robots.

AI.tldr: The paper structures the context for proactive conversation initiation in social robots and releases a curated dataset of contextually aligned conversation openers (CCO). Fine-tuned small language models trained on it produce more contextually appropriate openers than zero-shot LLMs and off-the-shelf SLMs.
AI.motivation: LLMs are turn-reactive and tend to produce generic or monotonous openers, and there is no principled definition of conversational context or suitable training data for proactive initiation by embodied social robots.
AI.method: A schema of contextual variables covers perceptual, situational and interactional cues so that language models can use them. The authors curate the CCO dataset across everyday scenarios and fine-tune small language models on it.
AI.result: A comparative evaluation of zero-shot LLMs, off-the-shelf SLMs and the fine-tuned models shows that explicit context structuring and targeted data curation substantially improve opener quality and contextual appropriateness.
AI.conclusion: Context modeling matters for proactive social interaction, and the schema and dataset are actionable building blocks for conversational robots.

title: Grounding Insight: An Artificial Affect Signal for Human-Centric Explainability of RL Agents
summary: In Human-Interactive Robot Learning (HIRL), human teachers assess learning progress by observing agent behavior. However, Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents often fail to express learning progress in human-interpretable ways, leading to suboptimal or counterproductive teaching. This work proposes "Insight": a human-interpretable affective signal grounded in the RL process. It is specifically designed to address the "Absence of learning" human teacher mental model misalignment - the misconception that a failing or exploring agent is broken, underpowered or not learning at all - by signaling an agent's "Aha!" Insight moment. The signal is derived from the absolute Temporal Difference (TD) error making it easily implementable in other RL agents. To ground this signal, five design criteria were formulated: Relevance, Interpretability, Faithfulness, Scalability, Generalizability. The structural construct validity was assessed through simulation, examining micro and macro dynamics and event-related sensitivity. Micro dynamics reveal that Insight captures meaningful learning events at the appropriate time and magnitude. Macro dynamics demonstrate that the signal follows the agent's learning phases and reflects overall progress. Event-related sensitivity shows, the signal distinguishes the saliency of environment interactions, such as positive rewards versus "trauma-like" negative events. These results demonstrate that technical RL dynamics can be effectively packaged into human-like affective substrates to close the teacher-learner loop.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "Insight", a human-interpretable affective signal derived from the absolute TD error of an RL agent, to show teachers when the agent is learning. Simulations show it tracks learning events, learning phases and the saliency of positive and negative events.
AI.motivation: In human-interactive robot learning, teachers judge progress from behavior, and RL agents often fail to show learning in interpretable ways. This leads to the "absence of learning" misconception, in which a failing or exploring agent looks broken.
AI.method: The signal is computed from the absolute TD error, so it is easy to implement in other RL agents. Five design criteria (Relevance, Interpretability, Faithfulness, Scalability, Generalizability) guide it, and its structural construct validity is assessed through simulation of micro and macro dynamics and event-related sensitivity.
AI.result: Micro dynamics show that Insight captures meaningful learning events at appropriate time and magnitude. Macro dynamics follow the agent's learning phases and overall progress. Event-related sensitivity separates positive rewards from trauma-like negative events. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Technical RL dynamics can be packaged into human-like affective signals that help close the teacher-learner loop.

title: Preference-Augmented Distributional Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Sensitive Navigation
summary: Ensuring safe and reliable navigation under diverse sources of uncertainty remains a central challenge for autonomous systems. Within distributional reinforcement learning (DistRL), Implicit Quantile Networks (IQN) have attracted interest for navigation under uncertainty because they enable risk adaptation through flexible quantile sampling. Existing approaches, however, typically use a fixed or randomly sampled Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) level during training and adjust the risk level during deployment using hand-tuned hyperparameters or external sensor signals. This scalar-CVaR formulation confines learning to a narrow family of tail-risk preferences, creating a mismatch between training-time preference exposure and deployment-time risk adjustment. We instead represent variations in risk preference as shifts in quantile-weight distributions and expose the agent to diverse preferences through preference-guided exploration. At deployment, we optimize against the worst-case preference distribution to derive a conservative policy that accounts for multiple risk profiles. This reduces hyperparameter tuning and reliance on limited sensor signals under partial observability. Experiments across simulated environments and vehicle platforms show that our method reduces collisions while improving task success.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a preference-augmented distributional RL method for navigation under uncertainty. It replaces a single CVaR level with shifts in quantile-weight distributions and optimizes against the worst-case preference distribution, which reduces collisions and improves task success in simulated and vehicle experiments.
AI.motivation: IQN-based distributional RL usually fixes or randomly samples one CVaR risk level in training and adjusts it at deployment with hand-tuned parameters or external sensor signals. This creates a mismatch between training-time preference exposure and deployment-time risk adjustment.
AI.method: Risk preferences are represented as shifts in quantile-weight distributions, and diverse preferences are exposed during training through preference-guided exploration. At deployment the policy is optimized against the worst-case preference distribution to get a conservative policy over multiple risk profiles.
AI.result: Experiments in simulated environments and on vehicle platforms show that the method reduces collisions while improving task success. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Covering a distribution of risk preferences reduces hyperparameter tuning and reliance on limited sensor signals under partial observability.

title: Efficient Learning of Differentiable MPC Policies on the GPU via Smoothed ADMM and First-Order Reinforcement Learning
summary: Differentiable model predictive control (MPC) enables structured, constraint-aware policies to be optimized end-to-end. However, learning MPC policies faces two bottlenecks: (1) nonsmooth sensitivities at active-set transitions and (2) expensive policy evaluation, since each requires an optimization solve. We first introduce SmoothedTurboMPC, a GPU-parallel differentiable MPC solver combining sequential quadratic programming (SQP) with a log-barrier-smoothed alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) inner solver. Its design enables smooth gradients, exact sensitivities at convergence, and efficient execution on GPUs. Second, to efficiently train MPC policies, we pair our solver with first-order reinforcement learning (FORL) using Short-Horizon Actor-Critic (SHAC), which reuses rollout MPC solutions instead of repeatedly re-evaluating them. Comparisons with state of the art solvers show that the approach achieves up to $4.4\times$ higher end-to-end training throughput. On a vehicle racing task, our method achieves higher returns than MPC PPO with a $46\times$ speedup, training on 3.3 million transitions in only 7 minutes. Finally, we use the framework to train a more reliable MPC racing policy via RL with domain randomization, and validate it on a full-scale race car. We integrate our advances into the open-source TurboMPC solver.

AI.tldr: SmoothedTurboMPC is a GPU-parallel differentiable MPC solver that pairs SQP with a log-barrier-smoothed ADMM inner solver, and it is trained with first-order RL (SHAC) that reuses rollout MPC solutions. It reaches up to 4.4x higher end-to-end training throughput and a 46x speedup over MPC PPO on a vehicle racing task.
AI.motivation: Learning differentiable MPC policies faces nonsmooth sensitivities at active-set transitions and expensive policy evaluation, since each evaluation requires an optimization solve.
AI.method: The solver combines sequential quadratic programming with a log-barrier-smoothed ADMM inner solver to give smooth gradients, exact sensitivities at convergence and efficient GPU execution. It is paired with first-order RL using Short-Horizon Actor-Critic (SHAC), which reuses rollout MPC solutions instead of re-solving them.
AI.result: Compared with state-of-the-art solvers, the approach achieves up to 4.4x higher end-to-end training throughput. On a vehicle racing task it earns higher returns than MPC PPO with a 46x speedup, training on 3.3 million transitions in 7 minutes. A racing policy trained with domain randomization is validated on a full-scale race car.
AI.conclusion: The advances make differentiable MPC policy training much faster and yield a more reliable racing policy, and the solver is released in the open-source TurboMPC.

title: A Systematic Comparison of In-Context Learning Strategies for Peptide Property Prediction in Low-Data Regimes
summary: Peptide sequence-property relationships are often highly non-linear, but can be learned with machine learning models and exploited for the design of new materials and bioactive compounds. Various methods based on transformer architectures have become available for molecular property predictions. These foundation models promise straightforward inference and prediction of properties of new materials through in-context learning. Benchmarks of individual model architectures exist, but a systematic comparison of various foundation models against classical baselines on similar datasets is lacking. Here, we provide a systematic evaluation of the predictive performance of various in-context learning strategies. We compare several large language models, tabular foundation models, and typed decision models against an XGBoost baseline. We evaluate predictive performance on binary and multiclass classification tasks on pH-dependent surface activ-ity, IR spectral signatures, self-assembly, and anti-cancer activities. Our results show that ICL is competitive, yet does not significantly outperform classical baselines, and performance varies between models and tasks. Our findings further suggest that language models use both in context examples and knowledge acquired during pretraining to infer properties of unseen samples. This finding indicates that pretrained models can leverage the existing literature for predictions, but may also bias their predictions towards established sequence-property relationships.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically compares in-context learning (ICL) strategies for peptide property prediction in low-data regimes, pitting LLMs, tabular foundation models and typed decision models against an XGBoost baseline. ICL is competitive but does not significantly outperform classical baselines, and performance varies across models and tasks.
AI.motivation: Foundation models promise prediction of new material properties through in-context learning, but no systematic comparison against classical baselines on similar peptide datasets existed.
AI.method: Several LLMs, tabular foundation models and typed decision models are evaluated with in-context learning against an XGBoost baseline. Binary and multiclass classification are assessed on pH-dependent surface activity, IR spectral signatures, self-assembly and anti-cancer activity.
AI.result: ICL is competitive with the XGBoost baseline but does not significantly outperform it, and results vary between models and tasks. Language models appear to use both in-context examples and pretraining knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained models can draw on the literature for predictions, but this may also bias them toward established sequence-property relationships.

title: Domain Adaptive Graph Neural Networks for Neutrino Experiments
comment: This was also accepted in the ML4PS 2026 workshop
summary: Weakly interacting particles such as neutrinos require highly efficient and precise detection methods to enable searches for new physics. Deep learning, and particularly Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), has shown promise for reconstruction tasks in liquid argon time projection chamber (LArTPC) neutrino experiments. However, differences between simulations and experimental data introduce domain shifts that can degrade model performance and potentially mimic or obscure new-physics signals. Here, we demonstrate that robust learning across datasets can still be achieved by using domain adaptation during training. We introduce, to our knowledge for the first time, domain-adaptation-enabled GNNs for robust LArTPC reconstruction tasks. We use MicroBooNE open dataset as our labeled source domain, and introduce four perturbed datasets as our unlabeled target domains-- including a fixed scale variation, moderate and severe gaussian noise, and a signal variation as a function of the position in the detector. The inclusion of adversarial-based domain adaptation during training improves performance for all four target domains, without a substantial drop in performance in the source domain. Precision in the target domain was improved up to 0.19 and recall up to 0.37, depending on the variation and the network task. These results demonstrate a potential of domain adaptation to bridge the gap between simulations and experiments, and build more trustworthy models for current and future LArTPC neutrino experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper applies adversarial domain adaptation to graph neural networks for reconstruction in LArTPC neutrino experiments, training on MicroBooNE open data as the labeled source and four perturbed datasets as unlabeled targets. It improves target-domain performance without a substantial source-domain drop, with precision up to 0.19 and recall up to 0.37 higher.
AI.motivation: Differences between simulation and experimental data create domain shifts that degrade GNN reconstruction and could mimic or obscure new-physics signals.
AI.method: Adversarial domain adaptation is used during GNN training. The four unlabeled target domains are a fixed scale variation, moderate and severe Gaussian noise, and a signal variation as a function of detector position.
AI.result: Adversarial adaptation improves performance on all four target domains without a substantial drop in source-domain performance. Target precision improves by up to 0.19 and recall by up to 0.37, depending on the variation and the network task.
AI.conclusion: Domain adaptation can bridge the gap between simulations and experiments and support more trustworthy models for LArTPC neutrino experiments.

title: Done Is Not Correct: Measuring Silent Failures and Self-Verification Calibration When LLM Agents Take CAD Actions
comment: 18 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Benchmark, harness, per-attempt records and a 3D viewer: this https URL (archived at this https URL)
summary: When a large language model (LLM) agent writes parametric CAD code from a natural-language specification, syntactic success decouples from semantic correctness. We release a benchmark and harness that measure this gap directly: 13 specification tasks whose every requirement maps to machine-checkable properties of the produced B-rep, measured by the kernel against published tolerance bands, with reference solutions and the full graded attempt corpus. The exact, self-audited oracle isolates two quantities no prior CAD benchmark reports: the silent-failure rate (a valid, renderable solid, an explicit completion claim, and at least one failed semantic check) and completion-claim calibration. Across four models from four vendors (156 attempts per architecture), single-shot agents claimed completion on 98% of attempts and were silently wrong on 14.1%; a tool-use loop that enforces measure-then-claim cut silent failures to 3.2% and raised claim precision from 64% to 96%, and a four-model ablation attributes the change to the claim contract rather than the feedback. A planner-coder-checker pipeline matched that precision at lower coverage with no success gain. Stated confidence was miscalibrated single-shot (ECE 0.32) and became informative under verification for three of four models. Hardening our own oracle flipped 18 of 519 regraded verdicts from pass to fail and none in reverse; a blind expert audit overturned 3 of the 18 silent failures outside the one ambiguously specified task; and fourfold scaling of every tolerance band leaves the contrast intact.

AI.tldr: The paper releases a benchmark of 13 CAD specification tasks and measures how often LLM agents write CAD code that is syntactically valid but semantically wrong. Single-shot agents claimed completion on 98% of attempts and were silently wrong on 14.1%, while a verify-then-claim tool loop cut silent failures to 3.2%.
AI.motivation: Syntactic success in parametric CAD code decouples from semantic correctness, and no prior CAD benchmark measures the silent-failure rate or completion-claim calibration.
AI.method: Each requirement in the 13 tasks maps to machine-checkable properties of the B-rep, measured by the kernel against published tolerance bands, with reference solutions and the full attempt corpus. The oracle is self-audited, and the silent-failure rate and claim calibration are defined from it.
AI.result: Across four models from four vendors (156 attempts per architecture), single-shot agents claimed completion on 98% of attempts and were silently wrong on 14.1%. A tool-use loop enforcing measure-then-claim cut silent failures to 3.2% and raised claim precision from 64% to 96%. A planner-coder-checker pipeline matched that precision at lower coverage with no success gain. Single-shot confidence was miscalibrated (ECE 0.32).
AI.conclusion: The gain comes from the claim contract rather than the feedback alone, and verification makes stated confidence informative for three of four models.

title: Statistical Geometry of Group Actions: Symmetry, Transport, Estimation
summary: We study variational inference in the presence of distributional symmetry, focusing on the interaction between two distinct group actions on a sample space: a symmetry action that leaves a reference distribution invariant, and a transport action that generates a parametric variational family by pushforward. By analyzing the algebraic structure of the total transformation group generated by both actions and the induced adjoint representation of the symmetry group on the transport Lie algebra, we establish that the Riemannian gradient of the Kullback--Leibler divergence at the true transport parameter is constrained to lie in the trivial representation of the symmetry group. Consequently, symmetry forces the gradient to vanish along all non-trivial representations. Combining this representation-theoretic constraint with parameter identifiability yields an orthogonal decomposition of the transport Lie algebra into three interpretable subspaces: an identifiability kernel (along which the objective is locally constant), a bias subspace (where the gradient may be nonzero due to model misspecification), and a symmetry-breaking subspace (where the gradient is forced to vanish by symmetry alone). Finally, we characterize the residual bias directions in terms of distributional mismatch between the base model and the standardized target, and derive an explicit Stein-type moment-matching condition that eliminates this bias, extending the location-scale results of (Margossian and Saul, 2025) to general Lie group transformation families.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes variational inference under distributional symmetry and decomposes the transport Lie algebra into an identifiability kernel, a bias subspace and a symmetry-breaking subspace. It shows that symmetry forces the KL gradient to vanish along non-trivial representations and derives a Stein-type moment-matching condition that removes residual bias.
AI.motivation: Variational inference with symmetric reference distributions and parametric transport families has not been analyzed through the joint algebra of symmetry and transport actions, and existing location-scale results do not cover general Lie group families.
AI.method: The authors study the total transformation group generated by a symmetry action and a transport action, and the induced adjoint representation on the transport Lie algebra. They apply representation theory to the Riemannian KL gradient and combine it with parameter identifiability.
AI.result: The Riemannian KL gradient at the true transport parameter lies in the trivial representation, so it vanishes along all non-trivial representations. This gives an orthogonal three-way decomposition, and residual bias is characterized by distributional mismatch between the base model and the standardized target.
AI.conclusion: The location-scale results of Margossian and Saul (2025) extend to general Lie group transformation families, with an explicit Stein-type moment-matching condition that eliminates the bias.

title: Agibot: An Open-Source Modular Swerve-Drive Robot Platform for Agricultural Robotics Research and Education
comment: 14 pages. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on AgriFood Electronics (TAFE)
summary: Agricultural production faces persistent labor shortages and increasing demand for automation, yet progress in agricultural robotics remains constrained by the limited availability of affordable, flexible, and accessible research platforms. This paper presents Agibot, an open-source, modular, low-cost agricultural robotics platform designed for autonomy research and experimentation, with potential applications in hands-on robotics education. The platform integrates four-wheel independent swerve drive, swappable computing, distributed embedded control, multimodal sensing, and configurable manipulation within a unified sense-plan-act-verify framework supporting perception, control, navigation, manipulation, and autonomous task verification. The platform was evaluated through representative row-crop navigation and manipulation tasks under varying lighting and soil conditions. Experiments demonstrated reliable lane following, autonomous row-to-row navigation, target identification, seed dispensing, plant manipulation, and closed-loop verification of task success. Its modular architecture supports independent testing, modification, and validation of autonomy components for rapid prototyping and experimentation. These proof-of-concept tasks, controller-tuning studies, and integrated trials demonstrate the platform's research capabilities, while its accessible and reconfigurable design supports its use for hands-on robotics education. By combining affordability, modularity, open-source accessibility, configurable manipulation, and end-to-end sense-plan-act-verify autonomy, Agibot provides a practical platform for agricultural robotics research, technology development, and workforce training.

AI.tldr: Agibot is an open-source, modular, low-cost agricultural robot platform with four-wheel independent swerve drive, swappable computing and configurable manipulation. Proof-of-concept experiments show reliable lane following, row-to-row navigation, seed dispensing, plant manipulation and closed-loop task verification.
AI.motivation: Agricultural robotics research is constrained by the lack of affordable, flexible and accessible research platforms, while labor shortages and automation demand grow.
AI.method: The platform integrates swerve drive, swappable computing, distributed embedded control and multimodal sensing within a sense-plan-act-verify framework covering perception, control, navigation, manipulation and autonomous task verification. Its modules can be tested and modified independently.
AI.result: Row-crop navigation and manipulation tasks under varying lighting and soil conditions show reliable lane following, autonomous row-to-row navigation, target identification, seed dispensing, plant manipulation and closed-loop verification of task success. The abstract gives no quantitative metrics.
AI.conclusion: The platform is a practical base for agricultural robotics research, technology development and workforce training, given its affordability, modularity and open-source design.

title: Is Recursive Self-Improvement Safe?
comment: To appear in IEEE Intelligent Systems
summary: The phrase recursive self-improvement (RSI) refers to the idea of an AI system designing and creating another, better AI system, which in turn designs and creates an even better one, and so on. While the idea has a long history, it has always been an abstract, futuristic idea -- until recently. Today's frontier AI has attained a set of abilities, including in programming, mathematics, research, tool use, and working coherently over extended periods of time, that make RSI seem plausible. AI companies are starting to pursue it, but many of the involved people are also expressing concerns, asking whether humanity should really set this in motion and under what conditions. I will discuss the situation, argue that we do not even have clear frameworks for thinking about the likely outcomes of RSI, and do a quick game-theoretic analysis of how to choose whether to initiate RSI when another party is making the same choice.

AI.tldr: This position paper argues that recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which an AI system designs a better successor, is now plausible given frontier capabilities. It contends that clear frameworks for predicting its outcomes are lacking and gives a quick game-theoretic analysis of whether to initiate RSI when another party is doing the same.
AI.motivation: Frontier AI now has abilities in programming, mathematics, research, tool use and extended coherent work that make RSI seem plausible, and AI companies are beginning to pursue it while many researchers voice concerns.
AI.method: The author discusses the situation and gives a quick game-theoretic analysis of the decision to initiate RSI when another party faces the same choice. The abstract does not describe experiments.
AI.result: The abstract reports no empirical results. Its main claim is that frameworks for thinking about likely RSI outcomes do not yet exist.
AI.conclusion: Whether to initiate RSI under competition is a strategic question that current frameworks do not adequately address, and the paper calls for clearer thinking about it.

title: Restoring General and Improving Domain-Specific Safety in Fine-Tuned LLMs Without Retraining
summary: Safety-aligned language models are known to suffer degradation in refusal behavior following domain-specific fine-tuning, even when the fine-tuning data is entirely benign. The predominant mitigation strategy, preference optimization on the fine-tuned model, is computationally expensive and requires domain-specific preference data that is often unavailable in practice. We propose SPECTRA, a training-free, weight-level method that restores refusal behavior by transferring the base model's refusal direction into the fine-tuned model's weights via an activation-aware, low-rank update, requiring no gradient-based optimization or domain-specific safety data. The low-rank design restricts the intervention to the subspace most causally active on harmful inputs, leaving benign behavior largely undisturbed by construction. Empirically, SPECTRA substantially improves refusal behavior across a comprehensive safety evaluation, while preserving general coherence, domain-specific knowledge, and producing negligible change in false refusal rates.

AI.tldr: SPECTRA restores refusal behavior in safety-aligned LLMs after benign domain-specific fine-tuning, without retraining. It transfers the base model's refusal direction into the fine-tuned weights through an activation-aware low-rank update while keeping general coherence and domain knowledge.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning degrades refusal behavior even on benign data, and the standard fix of preference optimization is expensive and needs domain-specific preference data that is often unavailable.
AI.method: The base model's refusal direction is transferred into the fine-tuned model's weights via an activation-aware, low-rank update. The low-rank design limits the change to the subspace most causally active on harmful inputs, and no gradient optimization or domain safety data is needed.
AI.result: SPECTRA substantially improves refusal behavior across a comprehensive safety evaluation, while preserving general coherence and domain-specific knowledge, with negligible change in false refusal rates.
AI.conclusion: Training-free, weight-level restoration of refusal behavior is a practical alternative to costly preference optimization after fine-tuning.

title: Continual Instruction Tuning for LLM-ased Management of Continuum Resources
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Research and Innovation in Scalable and Efficient Deep Learning (RISE-DL 2026), co-located with the 16th International Conference on the Internet of Things (IoT 2026), Newcastle upon Tyne, UK, November 2026. The Version of Record will appear in the ACM proceedings of IoT 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for resource management across the Cloud-Edge continuum. However, embedding LLMs directly inside latency-sensitive control loops places inference latency, execution jitter, and hallucination risks on the critical path.
