This study argues for a different use of LLMs: a continually instruction-tuned intent compiler that runs once per management intent or declared context change, above a fast, deterministic tactical controller that handles all low-latency runtime actions. We formulate intent compilation as a continual instruction tuning problem, because management intents arrive sequentially and accumulate while infrastructure and workload contexts drift. Unlike recent LLM-based management frameworks, our design scores the model's outputs by execution, so that catastrophic forgetting can be measured in the executed objective of the underlying controller. On a continuum simulator with a 2B backbone and parameter-efficient adapters, preliminary results show that naive sequential tuning forgets earlier intents in the executed objective, that replay of stored examples nearly prevents this forgetting, and that the tuned compact compiler performs on par with simpler translators while being more robust than a grammar parser to rephrased intents.

AI.tldr: Proposes using an LLM as a continually instruction-tuned intent compiler that runs once per management intent, above a fast deterministic controller, and measures forgetting of earlier intents by the executed objective. Preliminary simulator results show naive sequential tuning forgets, replay nearly prevents it, and the compact compiler matches simpler translators and beats a grammar parser on rephrased intents.
AI.motivation: Embedding LLMs directly in latency-sensitive control loops puts inference latency, execution jitter and hallucination risk on the critical path, and existing LLM-based management frameworks do not measure forgetting by the executed controller objective while intents accumulate and contexts drift.
AI.method: Intent compilation is formulated as continual instruction tuning of a 2B backbone with parameter-efficient adapters, with model outputs scored by execution on a continuum simulator, comparing naive sequential tuning against replay of stored examples.
AI.result: Naive sequential tuning forgets earlier intents in the executed objective, replay nearly prevents this forgetting, and the tuned compact compiler performs on par with simpler translators while being more robust than a grammar parser to rephrased intents.
AI.conclusion: The LLM is best used off the critical path to compile intents above a deterministic controller, and replay-based continual tuning is needed to keep earlier intents; the results are preliminary and come from a simulator.

title: Sparse Predict and Demote: Optimal Scheduling with Minimal Size Advice
summary: Knowledge of job sizes is crucial for optimizing the mean response time in single-server scheduling. However, predictions of job sizes are typically inexact and may be costly to obtain. Thus, a long-standing research question is: what is the minimal information about job sizes required to obtain near-optimal mean response time? We introduce a novel policy, \emph{Sparse Predict and Demote (SPD)}, and prove that it achieves order-optimal mean response time in heavy traffic while requiring only one-bit job-size predictions for a vanishing fraction of arrivals. SPD achieves heavy-traffic order-optimality even in situations when predictions are (i) inexact up to any fixed multiplicative error bound, and (ii) costly, i.e., the server is used to compute predictions and is thus unavailable to serve jobs while processing prediction queries. Finally, we use numerical experiments to illustrate that SPD maintains near-optimal performance beyond the heavy-traffic regime.

AI.tldr: Introduces Sparse Predict and Demote (SPD), a single-server scheduling policy that reaches order-optimal mean response time in heavy traffic using one-bit job-size predictions for only a vanishing fraction of arrivals. The policy stays order-optimal even when predictions carry any fixed multiplicative error and cost server time to compute.
AI.motivation: Job-size knowledge is crucial for minimizing mean response time, but predictions are typically inexact and costly, and it was an open question how little information about job sizes suffices for near-optimal mean response time.
AI.method: SPD sends one-bit predictions for a vanishing fraction of arrivals and demotes jobs accordingly, with analysis that accounts for inexact predictions under a fixed multiplicative error bound and for the server being unavailable while it computes predictions.
AI.result: The paper proves SPD achieves order-optimal mean response time in heavy traffic under both inexact and costly predictions, and numerical experiments show it keeps near-optimal performance beyond the heavy-traffic regime.
AI.conclusion: Near-optimal scheduling needs only minimal, sparse, one-bit job-size information, which lowers the cost of prediction-based scheduling.

title: The World Model Planning Accelerator (WMPA): Hardware-Algorithm Co-Design for Embedded AI in Robotics
summary: Embedded AI is moving from perception to prediction. Robots now use world models$\unicode{x2014}$learned simulators that predict the outcome of candidate actions in a compressed latent space before any is executed. Every predicted step must be computed on board within a tight power and thermal budget, yet the energy these steps fundamentally require, and how far real hardware sits from it, have not been characterized. We derive lower bounds on the arithmetic operations and the CMOS dynamic energy of a latent state transition from information theory and Boolean circuit complexity. Profiling a DreamerV3-style Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) shows that every rollout operation is memory-bandwidth bound and that a GPU consumes at least $5.9\times10^{10}$ times the CMOS energy floor. Transient 3D thermal simulations show that this inefficiency is also a thermal one, since sustained back-to-back planning heats a millimeter-scale silicon tile to 556 K even behind an ideal copper heat spreader. Guided by this chain from bound to bottleneck, we propose the World Model Planning Accelerator (WMPA), a chip architecture for embedded world model planning that combines near-memory computation, real-time entropy estimation, variable-precision rollout units, and copy-on-write latent scratchpads. With a design target of 40x lower power, the same tile stays near ambient at 306 K in simulation, pointing toward practical planning on thermally constrained robots.

AI.tldr: Derives information-theoretic and circuit-complexity lower bounds on the operations and CMOS energy of a latent world-model state transition, profiles a DreamerV3-style RSSM, and proposes the WMPA chip architecture for embedded world-model planning with a design target of 40x lower power.
AI.motivation: Robots increasingly plan with world models on board under tight power and thermal budgets, yet the energy these steps fundamentally require and how far real hardware sits from that floor had not been characterized.
AI.method: The authors derive arithmetic and CMOS dynamic energy lower bounds, profile an RSSM to find bottlenecks, run transient 3D thermal simulations, and design WMPA with near-memory computation, real-time entropy estimation, variable-precision rollout units and copy-on-write latent scratchpads.
AI.result: Every rollout operation is memory-bandwidth bound, a GPU consumes at least 5.9x10^10 times the CMOS energy floor, and sustained planning heats a millimeter-scale tile to 556 K behind an ideal copper spreader; the simulated WMPA design at 40x lower power stays near ambient at 306 K.
AI.conclusion: The gap between GPU energy and the physical floor is also a thermal problem, and the proposed architecture points toward practical world-model planning on thermally constrained robots, although the 40x power figure is a design target.

title: The Power of Two Choices in Dynamic Pricing: As Good As Full Feedback, Instance-Wise
summary: We study the dynamic pricing problem, where a firm sells a product to $T$ myopic customers and their values are independent samples from an unknown value distribution $F$. With posted prices, the firm only sees whether each customer buys, and the minimax regret is $\widetilde \Theta(T^{2/3})$ [KL03]. A menu instead offers several options, each selling the product with some probability at some expected payment. Infinitely many menu options allow the seller to fully reveal customer values, reducing the regret to $\Theta(\sqrt T)$. How many options are needed? Perhaps surprisingly, a second menu option suffices, achieving the same regret as infinite menus (up to $\log$ factors). This holds broadly: without knowing any property of $F$, our algorithm with two menu options attains $\tilde O(\sqrt T)$ regret in general, $\tilde O(T^{1/3})$ regret for monotone-hazard-rate distributions, and $\tilde O(T^{d/(d+1)})$ instance-dependent regret when $d\in(0,1)$ is a suitable notion of "dimension". All are optimal even with infinite menus. Moreover, we argue, via a novel lower-bound construction, that our algorithm is near-optimal for each problem instance. Along the way, we study the query complexity of revenue maximization, where an algorithm issues a query to each customer to learn the property of interest (either the best price or the CDF) up to some precision. We show that interval queries suffice to achieve the same query complexity as value queries (up to $\log$ factors) for both properties and across several classes of value distributions. We provide a new interval-query algorithm for each property. The best-price-estimation algorithm is the key ingredient in our main dynamic pricing algorithm, and the CDF-estimation algorithm underpins a simpler algorithm attaining $\tilde O(\sqrt T)$ regret with three menu options.

AI.tldr: Shows that a seller offering only two menu options in dynamic pricing against myopic customers with unknown value distribution attains the same regret as infinitely many menu options, up to log factors. The algorithm is also shown to be near-optimal for each problem instance.
AI.motivation: Posted prices give minimax regret of order T^{2/3}, infinite menus reduce regret to order sqrt(T) by fully revealing values, and it was unclear how many menu options are actually needed.
AI.method: The authors design a two-option menu algorithm that needs no knowledge of the value distribution, analyze it under general, monotone-hazard-rate and dimension-dependent instance conditions, and build a novel lower-bound construction; they also study query complexity of revenue maximization with interval queries.
AI.result: The two-option algorithm attains regret of order sqrt(T) up to log factors in general, T^{1/3} for monotone-hazard-rate distributions, and T^{d/(d+1)} instance-dependently for a suitable dimension d in (0,1); interval queries match value-query complexity, and a CDF-estimation variant gives sqrt(T) regret with three options.
AI.conclusion: Two menu options are enough to match the full-information regret of infinite menus, and the same rates are optimal even with infinite menus, so menu richness beyond two adds nothing in these settings.

title: LEGIT: Live Eligibility Gating over Identifier Tries for Constrained Decoding of Heterogeneous Pages
summary: A generative recommender names each candidate with a short token sequence, a Semantic ID, and recommends by generating those tokens. Some generative recommenders, including the Uber Eats search engine we are building, write a whole results page, stores with their menu items, in one decoding pass. Every Semantic ID on such a page must name a real store or item that is eligible for the search, such as a store that delivers to the user's location, and that is not already on the page. Each item must also belong to the store above it. A trie over the catalog keeps identifiers real, but eligibility and repetition change with every request and token, and the grammar-constrained decoder we tried could not enforce these changing rules exactly and quickly. We call this constraint LEGIT, for live eligibility gating over identifier tries. Numbering trie leaves depth first turns each rule into a range lookup over one store trie and one item trie, and every generated page passes an independent catalog check. On one NVIDIA B200 GPU with one or two requests per decode step, a direct implementation that walks the trie on the GPU makes each token about 5 times as slow as unconstrained decoding. Across 36 implementations, hardware counters and ablations are consistent with kernel launches and CPU-GPU waits as the source of this slowdown. Our fastest implementation walks the trie on the CPU while the GPU runs the model, needs no custom kernel, and cuts time per output token by 65.9 percent against the direct GPU implementation, to about 1.7 times the unconstrained cost. This implementation is also the fastest on a page layout that puts each item before its store.

AI.tldr: Presents LEGIT, a constrained-decoding method that enforces live eligibility and no-repeat rules on Semantic IDs when a generative recommender writes a whole results page in one decoding pass, using depth-first trie numbering so each rule becomes a range lookup. The fastest variant walks the trie on the CPU while the GPU runs the model.
AI.motivation: A generative search page must contain only real, currently eligible, non-duplicate stores and items, with each item belonging to its store, and the grammar-constrained decoder the authors tried could not enforce these changing rules exactly and quickly.
AI.method: Trie leaves are numbered depth first so eligibility and repetition checks become range lookups over one store trie and one item trie, and each page is independently checked against the catalog; 36 implementations were compared on one NVIDIA B200 with one or two requests per decode step.
AI.result: A direct GPU trie walk makes each token about 5 times slower than unconstrained decoding, and the CPU-side trie walk cuts time per output token by 65.9 percent against it, to about 1.7 times the unconstrained cost, and is also fastest on the item-before-store layout.
AI.conclusion: Hardware counters and ablations point to kernel launches and CPU-GPU waits as the cause of the slowdown, so overlapping CPU trie walks with GPU model execution is a practical way to keep exact constraints affordable.

title: A Topological Encoder Decoder Framework for Temporal Graph Learning
summary: Most temporal graph learning methods reduce future prediction to discriminative inference over past interactions, focusing on edges or node labels for a largely persistent set of nodes. This view breaks down when new nodes and edges appear, since the future graph becomes a new object with changing size, composition, and structure. We address this gap by framing temporal graph prediction as an inverse topology problem. Instead of predicting edges directly, we first predict a multiscale topological descriptor of the future graph and then reconstruct a plausible future snapshot that realizes this descriptor under inductive constraints. This approach makes global structure and node churn explicit prediction targets and produces forecasted graphs that downstream tasks can evaluate without retraining. Across 14 temporal graph datasets, we evaluate our method, TOPOGED, on node, link, and graph property prediction and compare it against state-of-the-art temporal graph models. TOPOGED significantly improves node-level forecasting accuracy over the strongest baseline, with a macro average of 0.49 versus 0.05. It also outperforms baselines in 60% of graph-structure metric evaluations and substantially increases macro-average edge prediction metrics, from near-zero to 0.12. Our results show that topology-guided graph forecasting can predict inductive future snapshots whose structure supports multiple downstream evaluations.

AI.tldr: Proposes TOPOGED, which forecasts temporal graphs by first predicting a multiscale topological descriptor of the future graph and then reconstructing an inductive future snapshot that realizes it. It is evaluated across 14 temporal graph datasets on node, link and graph property prediction.
AI.motivation: Existing temporal graph methods predict future edges or labels over a largely persistent node set, which breaks down when new nodes and edges appear and the future graph changes in size, composition and structure.
AI.method: The authors reframe temporal graph prediction as an inverse topology problem, predicting a multiscale topological descriptor and then reconstructing a plausible future snapshot under inductive constraints so downstream tasks can evaluate it without retraining.
AI.result: TOPOGED improves node-level forecasting over the strongest baseline with a macro average of 0.49 versus 0.05, outperforms baselines on 60% of graph-structure metric evaluations, and raises macro-average edge prediction from near zero to 0.12.
AI.conclusion: Topology-guided forecasting can produce inductive future snapshots whose structure supports several downstream evaluations, making global structure and node churn explicit prediction targets.

title: DiSARM: Diverse and Surprising Association Rule Mining with Large Language Models
summary: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) aims to discover informative patterns in large datasets. For transactional data, Association Rule Mining (ARM) is an established approach that facilitates EDA by efficiently generating candidate patterns. Beyond efficient mining, identifying informative rules has also been extensively studied through both objective and subjective interestingness measures. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for assessing subjective interestingness using world knowledge. Nevertheless, relying solely on LLMs raises concerns about scalability and statistical reliability. Building on prior ARM research, we propose a hybrid framework, DiSARM, that leverages the world knowledge of LLMs to assess the subjective interestingness of rules, while maintaining statistical reliability and promoting diversity among the selected rules. Across three transactional datasets, experiments demonstrate that DiSARM effectively combines statistical reliability with surprise and diversity, offering a promising approach to ADE from transactional data.

AI.tldr: Presents DiSARM, a hybrid framework that uses LLM world knowledge to score the subjective interestingness of association rules, while keeping statistical reliability and selecting a diverse set of rules. Experiments on three transactional datasets show it combines reliability with surprise and diversity.
AI.motivation: Association rule mining generates many candidate patterns, but relying solely on LLMs to judge subjective interestingness raises concerns about scalability and statistical reliability.
AI.method: The framework combines statistical rule mining with LLM-based assessment of subjective interestingness, and promotes diversity among the selected rules.
AI.result: Across three transactional datasets, DiSARM effectively combines statistical reliability with surprise and diversity in the selected rules, according to the abstract, though the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid use of LLM world knowledge with statistical mining offers a promising approach to exploratory data analysis on transactional data.

title: GEAR: A GPU-Accelerated Global Solver for Bounded Continuous Nonlinear Programs via Linear Bound Propagation
summary: We present a novel GPU-accelerated global solver for constrained nonlinear programming (NLP) inspired by the efficient linear bound propagation framework in neural network (NN) verification. Existing work on NN verification, a problem that can be cast as feasibility detection for a nonlinear objective, demonstrated orders-of-magnitude speedups with the linear bound propagation-based framework when compared to traditional solvers. Extending this paradigm to global nonlinear programming requires addressing many challenges: a global constrained NLP solver must effectively exploit all, possibly unstructured, nonlinear constraints to improve the objective, whereas NN verification typically handles simple input box constraints over a well-structured NN and does not directly optimize an objective function. We address these challenges by fully exploiting the linear bounds produced by bound propagation: these linear bounds can be viewed as relaxations of nonlinear constraints and used to provide lower bounds, check infeasibility, and guide the search for a primal solution. In addition, we propose tighter linear relaxations for bilinear, quotient, and other commonly used nonlinear functions in NLP problems, and a projected augmented Lagrangian method tightly coupled to our dual solving procedure to produce primal solutions. Our method solves 421 of 505 bounded and continuous NLP problems in the GAMS and MINLPLib benchmarks under a 180-second limit, more than each of the six global solvers we compare with, including Gurobi and BARON (commercial), and SCIP (open-source). Sixteen of these problems are certified by none of the six global solvers; all of them contain exponential, logarithmic, or trigonometric terms, which are often challenging for traditional approaches. Project webpage is at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Presents GEAR, a GPU-accelerated global solver for bounded continuous nonlinear programs that adapts linear bound propagation from neural network verification and couples it with a projected augmented Lagrangian method. It solves 421 of 505 GAMS and MINLPLib problems within 180 seconds, more than six compared global solvers.
AI.motivation: NN verification shows large speedups from linear bound propagation, but global constrained nonlinear programming must exploit general unstructured nonlinear constraints and optimize an objective, which verification does not require.
AI.method: The linear bounds are used as relaxations to derive lower bounds, check infeasibility and guide primal search, with tighter linear relaxations for bilinear, quotient and other common nonlinear functions, and a projected augmented Lagrangian method tightly coupled to dual solving.
AI.result: GEAR solves 421 of 505 bounded continuous NLP problems under a 180-second limit, more than each of six global solvers including Gurobi, BARON and SCIP; 16 of the problems are certified by none of the six solvers, and all contain exponential, logarithmic or trigonometric terms.
AI.conclusion: Linear bound propagation from NN verification can be carried over to global nonlinear programming and is competitive with leading commercial and open-source solvers, especially on transcendental problems.

title: TimeHF 2.0: Multimodal, Multivariate, and Multi-Region Collaborative Forecasting for Large-Scale Retail Supply Chains
summary: Large-scale retail supply chains need sales forecasts for specified products, future dates or planning windows, and regions under the conditions available at the forecast origin. Regional sparsity, changing environments, volatile sales, and unfamiliar business situations make these dimensions difficult to model together. We introduce TimeHF 2.0, a multimodal, multivariate, and multi-region collaborative forecasting framework that makes flexibly expressed business knowledge usable in numerical prediction. A coverage-aware directed encoder integrates regional sales and applicable covariates. A semantic alignment module transfers language-model hidden representations of natural-language plans and domain experience into target-specific forecasting context. Learning against sales observations connects these meanings to numerical evidence, allowing business users to supply experience, future plans, and changing circumstances without defining a new numerical feature for each description. Text-conditioned future queries and shared/routed experts adapt prediction to the supplied context. An ordered-distribution head allocates fine resolution to routine fluctuations and coarse resolution to extreme sales movements, while daily/window learning connects forecasts to cumulative planning quantities. Online parallel forecasting at JD yields relative accuracy improvements of 18.25% and 17.94% for national daily and planning-window sales, and 19.44% and 18.99% for DC daily and planning-window sales, over the original production deep learning baseline. Component comparisons, loss-design results, and product-type analyses examine the roles of regional information, covariates, business knowledge, context-dependent processing, and robust planning-oriented learning.

AI.tldr: Introduces TimeHF 2.0, a multimodal, multivariate, multi-region forecasting framework that lets business users express plans and experience in natural language and feeds them into numerical sales forecasts. Online deployment at JD improves relative accuracy by about 18 to 19 percent over the production deep learning baseline.
AI.motivation: Large-scale retail forecasting must handle regional sparsity, changing environments, volatile sales and unfamiliar business situations, and business knowledge is hard to use in numerical prediction without defining a new feature for each description.
AI.method: A coverage-aware directed encoder integrates regional sales and covariates, a semantic alignment module maps language-model representations of plans and domain experience into forecasting context, text-conditioned future queries and shared/routed experts adapt predictions, and an ordered-distribution head with daily and window learning targets planning quantities.
AI.result: Online parallel forecasting at JD yields relative accuracy gains of 18.25% and 17.94% for national daily and planning-window sales, and 19.44% and 18.99% for DC daily and planning-window sales, over the original production deep learning baseline.
AI.conclusion: Natural-language business knowledge can be connected to numerical sales evidence and improve large-scale retail forecasts, with component and loss-design analyses examining which parts drive the gains.

title: NeuroHorizon: Long-Horizon Forecasting of Neural Population Activity with Hierarchical Memory
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Main Track). 25 pages, including references, appendices, and the NeurIPS paper checklist
summary: Long-horizon forecasting of neural population activity tests whether a model has captured dynamics that remain predictive well beyond the observed history. Prediction quality typically declines as the horizon grows, yet neither short-horizon accuracy nor teacher-forced evaluation, which supplies the true activity preceding each predicted step, reveals how well models sustain predictions from an initial history alone. We compare direct multi-step prediction and autoregressive rollout on spiking recordings across horizons and introduce NeuroHorizon, which pairs event-based spike encoding with a causal decoder for population firing rates. Its hierarchical prediction memory keeps recent predictions at full temporal resolution and compresses earlier ones into segment summaries, giving the decoder both local detail and longer-range context. Under teacher-forced training this memory holds ground-truth activity, whereas during rollout it holds the model's own predictions. To reduce this mismatch, we train with scheduled sampling, progressively exposing the decoder to its own predictions. From 500 ms of macaque motor-cortex activity, NeuroHorizon achieves the highest forward-prediction score among the evaluated autonomous models at all four horizons from 100 to 1000 ms, and its per-bin predictions remain above a mean-firing-rate baseline across nearly the full 1 s window. Complementary experiments on macaque sensorimotor and mouse multi-region recordings show that performance generally increases with model and data size, alongside improved prediction after cross-subject pretraining and fine-tuning. Together, these results clarify how forecasting performance changes across horizons and offer an effective approach to long-horizon forecasting of neural population activity.

AI.tldr: Introduces NeuroHorizon, a long-horizon forecaster of neural population activity that pairs event-based spike encoding with a causal decoder and hierarchical prediction memory, trained with scheduled sampling. From 500 ms of macaque motor-cortex activity it gives the best autonomous forward prediction at horizons from 100 to 1000 ms.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon forecasting quality usually declines with horizon, and neither short-horizon accuracy nor teacher-forced evaluation shows how well models sustain predictions from an initial history alone.
AI.method: Direct multi-step prediction and autoregressive rollout are compared on spiking data, and NeuroHorizon keeps recent predictions at full resolution while compressing earlier ones into segment summaries, with scheduled sampling to reduce the mismatch between teacher-forced training and rollout.
AI.result: NeuroHorizon achieves the highest forward-prediction score among evaluated autonomous models at all four horizons from 100 to 1000 ms, stays above a mean-firing-rate baseline across nearly the full 1 s window, and improves with model and data size and with cross-subject pretraining on other recordings.
AI.conclusion: The results clarify how forecasting performance changes with horizon and offer an effective approach to long-horizon forecasting of neural population activity.

title: SLA-Aware Task Offloading in the IoT Edge-Cloud Continuum: Class-Weighted Deep Reinforcement Learning Against an Exact Optimum
summary: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is often used to decide where Internet of Things (IoT) tasks with different latency limits run in the edge-cloud continuum, yet some methods give every missed task the same penalty and few compare their agents with an optimal policy. This benchmark study builds four offloading systems small enough to solve exactly by dynamic programming and measures reward and learner against the optimum. A bonus for a met limit makes each miss cost its penalty plus the bonus, which shifts the class weights of published per-class rewards. A class-blind penalty stays 65% to 118% above the optimal cost even with a perfect learner, while a corrected per-class penalty comes within 0.13% of the optimum. With a per-class reward, tuned proximal policy optimization (PPO) agents come within 9% to 11% of the optimum in the smallest system, and the corrected one beats a tuned reservation rule in 9 of 10 seeds. In larger systems the agents stay 41% to 76% above the optimum, and a tuned rule beats their mean. Training ten times longer does not close this gap, and a PPO-Lagrangian agent with reachable targets does no better than the per-class reward.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks deep reinforcement learning for IoT task offloading against exact dynamic-programming optima on four small systems, and shows that a class-blind penalty leaves costs far above optimal while a corrected per-class penalty comes within 0.13% of the optimum. Tuned PPO agents remain 41% to 76% above the optimum in larger systems.
AI.motivation: Some offloading methods give every missed deadline the same penalty and few compare agents against an optimal policy, even though a bonus for a met latency limit changes the class weights of published per-class rewards.
AI.method: Four offloading systems small enough to solve exactly by dynamic programming are built, and reward and learner performance are measured against the optimum, comparing class-blind and corrected per-class penalties, tuned PPO, PPO-Lagrangian and a tuned reservation rule.
AI.result: A class-blind penalty stays 65% to 118% above the optimal cost even with a perfect learner, a corrected per-class penalty comes within 0.13% of the optimum, tuned PPO comes within 9% to 11% of the optimum in the smallest system, and in larger systems agents stay 41% to 76% above the optimum; training ten times longer does not close the gap.
AI.conclusion: The reward design matters more than training effort for these problems, and the reward shaping that matches the optimum still leaves learned agents well short of it in larger systems.

title: The Delta Gap: Cellular World Models for Perturbation Response Prediction Are Far Harder Than Global Correlation Implies
summary: Cellular world models aim to predict how cells respond to genetic perturbations, analogous to world models in reinforcement learning. Perturbation response models are evaluated almost exclusively by global Pearson correlation between predicted and observed transcriptomes. We show this metric is dominated by thousands of non-responsive genes and severely inflates apparent performance. On the Replogle K562 screen (509 unseen perturbations, 5000 genes), GEARS achieves global Pearson 0.977, but its delta Pearson is only 0.076. A trivial baseline predicting mean training delta achieves 0.267, which is 3.5x better than GEARS. Our primary contribution is methodological: we identify and quantify this delta gap as a systematic evaluation artifact, and propose delta-space evaluation as the primary benchmark. We provide two post-hoc corrections (RWR on co-expression graphs and kNN matching) and show that 2.8x of the remaining gap lies in perturbation representation geometry, not decoder capacity. We further show the gap is partially addressable end-to-end: delta-aligned training (lambda = 3.0) raises delta Pearson to 0.179 on Replogle (2.35x over GEARS) and surpasses the trivial baseline on direction accuracy (0.680 vs 0.567) and gene recovery (1.52 vs 1.19); combined with kNN it reaches 0.217. An amplitude-calibration variant (eta = 0.3) further raises gene recovery to 2.16 while reaching 0.218. Critically, these representations transfer zero-shot across cell lines: from Replogle K562 to unseen Norman A549, the delta-aligned model reaches 0.328 on 741 shared genes, 4.7x a trivial baseline and 2.1x standard GEARS. This is the first systematic quantification of the delta gap, and the first diagnostic framework localizing the residual gap to perturbation representation geometry via an oracle upper bound.

AI.tldr: Shows that global Pearson correlation greatly inflates performance of cellular perturbation response models because it is dominated by non-responsive genes, and proposes delta-space evaluation as the primary benchmark. Delta-aligned training raises delta Pearson on the Replogle K562 screen from 0.076 for GEARS to 0.179, and the representations transfer zero-shot to Norman A549.
AI.motivation: Perturbation response models are evaluated almost only by global Pearson correlation between predicted and observed transcriptomes, which the authors argue hides how poorly they predict actual perturbation effects.
AI.method: The authors quantify the delta gap, test post-hoc corrections with random walk with restart on co-expression graphs and kNN matching, train with a delta-aligned objective at lambda equal to 3.0, add an amplitude-calibration variant at eta equal to 0.3, and use an oracle upper bound to localize the residual gap.
AI.result: On Replogle K562 with 509 unseen perturbations, GEARS reaches global Pearson 0.977 but delta Pearson 0.076, a trivial mean-delta baseline reaches 0.267, delta-aligned training reaches 0.179, and combined with kNN 0.217; the delta-aligned model reaches 0.328 on 741 shared genes for unseen Norman A549.
AI.conclusion: The delta gap is a systematic evaluation artifact, and about 2.8 times the remaining gap lies in perturbation representation geometry rather than decoder capacity, so delta-space evaluation should be the standard benchmark.

title: Audit Before You Merge: Provenance, Probing, and Continual LoRA Composition
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 17 tables. ICML 2026 Workshop on Continual Adaptation at Scale (CATS). Code: this https URL
summary: Post-hoc merging of public LoRA adapters is an attractive gradient-free path to continual adaptation, but reliable measurement of catastrophic forgetting in this setting depends on infrastructure that prior work has not addressed. We treat each adapter merge as a sequential task in a continual-learning setting, with the instruction-tuned base model's capabilities as Task 0, and study forgetting on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Public adapter hubs contain modules that fail basic provenance checks: silent base-version mismatches and near-zero delta norms whose inclusion inflates measured interference by ~10pp. We propose a two-check audit (base-model match, non-trivial delta norm) and a leakage-free probing protocol as preconditions for any forgetting study in this setting. On an audited 4-adapter set, naive merging causes -10.5pp on GSM8K and -18.3pp on HumanEval, while Task Arithmetic at lambda=0.5 sits within a standard error of the unmerged baseline. A coordinate search including negative coefficients identifies the math adapter as probe-optimal at lambda=-0.5, outside the reach of positive-only mergers, suggesting forgetting has structure that negation-aware merging may exploit. The same protocol replicates on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, where 2 of 4 candidate adapters fail the audit and the audited merge reproduces the same merge-method ranking on GSM8K, supporting that our findings are not Llama-specific.

AI.tldr: Argues that public LoRA adapters must pass provenance audits before post-hoc merging can be used to study continual forgetting, proposes a two-check audit and a leakage-free probing protocol, and shows that Task Arithmetic at lambda=0.5 stays within a standard error of the unmerged baseline on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
AI.motivation: Post-hoc merging of public LoRA adapters is a gradient-free route to continual adaptation, but reliable measurement of forgetting depends on infrastructure that prior work has not addressed, and public hubs contain adapters with base-version mismatches and near-zero deltas.
AI.method: Each merge is treated as a sequential task with the instruction-tuned base model as Task 0, adapters are checked for base-model match and non-trivial delta norm, a leakage-free probing protocol is used, and a coordinate search including negative coefficients is run; the protocol is replicated on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3.
AI.result: On an audited 4-adapter set, naive merging causes -10.5pp on GSM8K and -18.3pp on HumanEval, while Task Arithmetic at lambda=0.5 sits within a standard error of the unmerged baseline, and the math adapter is probe-optimal at lambda=-0.5; on Mistral 2 of 4 candidate adapters fail the audit and the merge-method ranking on GSM8K is reproduced.
AI.conclusion: Unaudited adapters can inflate measured interference by about 10pp, so provenance checks are a precondition for forgetting studies, and negation-aware merging may exploit structure that positive-only mergers cannot reach.

title: CyberBinGym: Can AI Agents Turn Binary Patches into Real Exploits?
summary: Security fixes usually reach users as compiled updates, but deployment delays leave unpatched systems exposed. During this window, comparing patched and unpatched binaries can reveal how to exploit a vulnerability, turning a defensive update into actionable information for attackers. Existing benchmarks do not measure this capability: they expose source code, rely on human-crafted challenges, or evaluate binary comprehension without requiring exploitation. We introduce CyberBinGym, a benchmark containing 100 tasks derived from real vulnerabilities in 53 widely used projects, spanning six vulnerability families and three levels of analysis complexity. Agents receive stripped vulnerable and patched binaries without source code or vulnerability information, and must combine static and dynamic analysis to recover and exploit the vulnerability. Evaluation separately measures vulnerability recovery through differential crash testing and end-to-end exploitation through flag retrieval, with trajectory audits to reject reward hacking. The strongest evaluated agent recovers the target vulnerability in 88% of tasks and exploits it in 20%. Providing the patched binary raises its exploit rate from 10% to 25% on a matched 20-task subset; with standard binary hardening enabled, it still exploits two of its 20 previously successful tasks. These results demonstrate that current agents can turn released binary patches into working exploits in a controlled setting, although exploitation remains unreliable. These capabilities lower the barriers to targeting unpatched software and compress defenders' effective response window, increasing the urgency of timely patch deployment.

AI.tldr: Introduces CyberBinGym, a benchmark of 100 tasks from real vulnerabilities in 53 projects in which agents must recover and exploit a bug from stripped vulnerable and patched binaries. The strongest agent recovers the vulnerability in 88% of tasks and exploits it in 20%.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks expose source code, rely on human-crafted challenges, or test binary comprehension without requiring exploitation, so the capability to turn released patches into exploits was not measured.
AI.method: Agents receive stripped binaries without source or vulnerability information and must combine static and dynamic analysis, with recovery measured by differential crash testing, exploitation by flag retrieval, and trajectory audits used to reject reward hacking.
AI.result: The strongest evaluated agent recovers the target vulnerability in 88% of tasks and exploits it in 20%; providing the patched binary raises its exploit rate from 10% to 25% on a matched 20-task subset, and with standard binary hardening it still exploits two of its 20 previously successful tasks.
AI.conclusion: Current agents can turn released binary patches into working exploits in a controlled setting, although exploitation is unreliable, which shrinks defenders' response window and makes timely patch deployment more urgent.

title: Trainability-Simulability Tradeoff in Parameterized IQP-based Reinforcement Learning Policies
summary: Parameterized instantaneous quantum polynomial-time (IQP) circuits generate distributions conjectured to be hard to sample classically. As reinforcement learning (RL) policies, their $2^n$ measurement outcomes are typically mapped to a smaller action space by a classical decoder. This aggregation can mitigate initialization concentration while making the policy classically simulable. We characterize this tradeoff through the decoder's Fourier--Pauli expansion. Under independent uniform initialization, we express policy variance as an exact sum over groups of nonconstant Pauli components with identical active-generator signatures. Each group contributes its squared aggregate coefficient times $2^{-r}$, where $r$ is the binary rank of its active generators. An inverse-polynomial aggregate coefficient with logarithmic rank prevents exponential policy concentration. Sparse Pauli expansions and contiguous action bins permit efficient classical additive estimation of action probabilities. We introduce a majority decoder combining protected low-weight components with exponentially large exact Fourier support, preserving initialization nonconcentration while excluding polynomial-size enumeration of the exact expansion. Numerical experiments corroborate the variance laws. In ten-qubit CartPole experiments, majority achieves higher returns than recursive parity and the tested local readouts, while higher-weight Pauli sectors contribute an increasing relative share of gradient magnitude during training. A complementary 21-qubit block-chain policy outperforms an extensive pool of fully connected classical neural networks in episode efficiency, even though its bounded-width structure permits efficient classical simulation. These results guide decoder design for quantum and quantum-inspired RL, distinguishing policy nonconcentration, learning performance, and classical simulability.

AI.tldr: Analyzes the trade-off in IQP-circuit reinforcement learning policies between avoiding initialization concentration and keeping the policy classically simulable, and introduces a majority decoder that keeps nonconcentration while avoiding full enumeration. In ten-qubit CartPole it achieves higher returns than recursive parity and the tested local readouts.
AI.motivation: Mapping the exponentially many IQP measurement outcomes to a smaller action space can mitigate initialization concentration but may make the policy classically simulable, and the trade-off between the two had not been characterized.
AI.method: The decoder's Fourier-Pauli expansion gives an exact sum for policy variance under uniform initialization, with each group of Pauli components contributing its squared aggregate coefficient times 2^{-r} for binary rank r; a majority decoder combines protected low-weight components with exponentially large exact Fourier support.
AI.result: In ten-qubit CartPole the majority decoder achieves higher returns than recursive parity and the tested local readouts, and a 21-qubit block-chain policy outperforms a large pool of fully connected classical networks in episode efficiency despite being efficiently simulable.
AI.conclusion: Policy nonconcentration, learning performance and classical simulability are distinct properties, and the variance laws guide decoder design for quantum and quantum-inspired RL.

title: AutoC2V: Synthesis-Guided LLM Training for QoR-Optimized C++-to-Verilog Generation
summary: High-level synthesis (HLS) can translate C/C++ kernels into register-transfer level (RTL) designs, yet generating high-quality hardware still relies heavily on manual pragma tuning and repeated synthesis evaluation. We propose AutoC2V, a C++-to-Verilog generation framework driven by real synthesis feedback that enables large language models (LLMs) to directly generate RTL with improved quality of results (QoR) from synthesizable C++ kernels. We construct training data from real synthesis results, including synthesizable C++ source code, the corresponding Verilog RTL, QoR metrics, and optimization objectives. Using this dataset, we align the model toward synthesis-aware RTL generation through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To reduce the high cost of repeatedly invoking real synthesis during GRPO, we design the QoR Prediction Reward Model (QoR RM), which predicts latency and resource metrics by encoding RTL into long-context semantic representations, thereby providing low-cost and continuous QoR reward signals for policy optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that AutoC2V not only substantially improves RTL functional pass rates, but also achieves superior latency and resource optimization compared to the unfine-tuned base model, representative HLS optimization approaches (HLSPilot, LLM-DSE, and AutoDSE), and advanced general-purpose commercial models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek v4 Pro, and GLM-5.2). These results indicate that combining real synthesis data with efficient QoR reward modeling can further improve the ability of LLMs to generate high-quality RTL.

AI.tldr: Presents AutoC2V, which trains LLMs with supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on real synthesis feedback to generate Verilog RTL directly from C++ kernels, using a QoR prediction reward model in place of costly repeated synthesis. It improves RTL functional pass rates and latency and resource quality over the base model and HLS optimization baselines.
AI.motivation: High-level synthesis still relies heavily on manual pragma tuning and repeated synthesis evaluation, and calling real synthesis inside reinforcement learning is expensive.
AI.method: Training data pairs C++ kernels with Verilog, QoR metrics and objectives from real synthesis, with SFT followed by GRPO, using a QoR Prediction Reward Model that encodes RTL into long-context representations to predict latency and resource metrics as continuous rewards.
AI.result: AutoC2V substantially improves RTL functional pass rates and achieves better latency and resource optimization than the unfine-tuned base model, HLSPilot, LLM-DSE, AutoDSE, and several commercial and open models, as reported in the abstract without specific figures.
AI.conclusion: Combining real synthesis data with an efficient learned QoR reward can further improve the ability of LLMs to generate high-quality RTL.

title: Firepool: Brokering Warm GPU Capacity for Agentic and RL Workloads at LinkedIn
summary: AI agents and reinforcement-learning (RL) trainers run thousands of short, isolated GPU jobs: tool calls, verifiers, and rollouts. A job often finishes in seconds, but starting a GPU pod for it takes 20-35 s even when the container image is already on the node, and minutes when it is not. A warm pod removes the wait only if it can serve the next job, and keeping pods warm must neither waste GPUs nor leak state between callers. Firepool, the sandbox and execution broker behind agentic and RL workloads at LinkedIn, meets both requirements. It makes pods interchangeable by building them from a shared base image per hardware profile and binding each job's code, extra dependencies, and cluster topology when the job starts. It keeps them warm cheaply and safely by reusing a pod only for the caller that used it last, staging zero-VRAM standby pods in fractional GPU shares alongside active pods, and capping the GPUs that warm pools may hold via queue-driven budgets. Over a sampled peak period in production, Firepool serves 94.7% of 3,206 pod requests from warm or standby capacity. In paired benchmarks with fixed-duration jobs on production H200 nodes, agent and RL loops finish 13x and 10.8x faster than with a fresh pod per job; against a fresh reuse tag per job, warm reuse cuts p90 start latency from 59.1 s to 3.5 s. When a job cannot reuse the previous pod, standby promotion shortens the handover wait from 51 s to 0.94 s. In local and simulated runs, a keep-alive matched to the loop's pauses keeps the latency benefit while holding about half the capacity of an always-on pool.

AI.tldr: Describes Firepool, LinkedIn's sandbox and execution broker that keeps interchangeable warm GPU pods for agentic and RL jobs, cutting job-start waits while avoiding idle GPU waste and state leaks. Paired benchmarks on production H200 nodes show agent and RL loops finishing 13x and 10.8x faster than with a fresh pod per job.
AI.motivation: Short GPU jobs take 20 to 35 seconds to start a pod even with the image on the node, and minutes without it, while keeping pods warm must neither waste GPUs nor leak state between callers.
AI.method: Pods are built from a shared base image per hardware profile and bind each job's code, dependencies and topology at start, a pod is reused only for the caller that last used it, zero-VRAM standby pods share fractional GPU slices with active pods, and queue-driven budgets cap the GPUs warm pools may hold.
AI.result: Over a sampled production peak, Firepool serves 94.7% of 3,206 pod requests from warm or standby capacity; warm reuse cuts p90 start latency from 59.1 s to 3.5 s against a fresh reuse tag per job, and standby promotion shortens handover from 51 s to 0.94 s; a keep-alive matched to loop pauses holds about half the capacity of an always-on pool in simulated runs.
AI.conclusion: Warm, per-caller-safe reuse with standby promotion removes most start latency for agentic and RL workloads at a fraction of always-on capacity cost.

title: A Gamified Framework for Conflict-Driven Design: Discovering Strategies for Collaborative Resilience with Multi-Agent Learning
comment: 10 pages, 11 figures, 1 table. Author version of a paper published in the proceedings of ACADIA 2025: Computing for Resilience
summary: Conflicting stakeholder objectives make it difficult to coordinate investments in urban resilience. We model conflict-driven urban design as a non-zero-sum digital board game in which stakeholder agents allocate scarce resources and balance individual payoffs against shared urban development and resilience objectives. We use multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to train policies and examine their behavior across three settings. On a 4 x 4 board, learned policies reach about 84% of the total return found by a simulated annealing benchmark. On an 8 x 8 board with spatial and resource constraints, trained agents favor projects that improve resilience in self-play. In a 12 x 12 simulation initialized from historical maps of Tatsumi, Tokyo, trained agents achieve a mean total score of 452.1, compared with 357.3 for a random-policy baseline across 10,000 simulation runs. Gains in adaptability, sustainability, flood resistance, and greenery come with reductions in vitality and density. A human-in-the-loop interface supports replay and lets participants take over stakeholder decisions, providing a testbed for exploring these trade-offs in participatory urban planning.

AI.tldr: Models conflict-driven urban resilience design as a non-zero-sum digital board game and trains multi-agent reinforcement learning stakeholder policies that favor resilience projects in self-play. On a 12 x 12 simulation of Tatsumi, Tokyo, trained agents score a mean total of 452.1 against 357.3 for a random policy.
AI.motivation: Conflicting stakeholder objectives make it hard to coordinate investment in urban resilience, and a testbed is needed to explore the trade-offs in participatory planning.
AI.method: Stakeholder agents allocate scarce resources and balance individual payoffs against shared development and resilience objectives, MARL trains policies across 4 x 4, 8 x 8 and 12 x 12 boards with spatial and resource constraints, and a human-in-the-loop interface supports replay and takeover.
AI.result: On the 4 x 4 board learned policies reach about 84% of the total return found by simulated annealing; on the 8 x 8 board agents favor resilience projects in self-play; on the 12 x 12 Tatsumi simulation the mean total is 452.1 versus 357.3 for random over 10,000 runs, with gains in adaptability, sustainability, flood resistance and greenery but reductions in vitality and density.
AI.conclusion: The framework reveals real trade-offs between resilience gains and vitality and density, providing a testbed for participatory urban planning.

title: Sampling-based Model Predictive Control as Sequential Monte Carlo Inference
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). Code: this https URL
summary: Sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) is treated as a family of distinct algorithms: predictive sampling, MPPI, the cross-entropy method, and their biased, colored-noise, and annealed variants all sample control sequences and reweight them by cost. We show a single Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) inference algorithm implements them all, specified by three independent axes: the proposal, the update rule that reduces cost-weighted particles to a nominal plan, and the effective-sample-size threshold for resampling. We evaluate SMC-based planning on MuJoCo non-linear control, open-loop navigation through obstacle fields, 7-DoF motion planning, and non-prehensile push-T, in simulation and on a Franka FR3. Resampling combats particle degeneracy at long horizons. At a 28-knot horizon in our navigation domain it cut the collision rate by 30% over non-resampling baselines. Programmable proposals improve push-T success over perturbative baselines, improving from 1% to 100% in simulation and 10% to 90% on hardware.

AI.tldr: Shows that predictive sampling, MPPI, the cross-entropy method and their variants are all instances of one Sequential Monte Carlo inference algorithm, specified by proposal, update rule and resampling threshold. Resampling reduces collisions at long horizons, and programmable proposals raise push-T success from 1% to 100% in simulation and from 10% to 90% on hardware.
AI.motivation: Sampling-based MPC is usually treated as a family of distinct algorithms, obscuring their common structure and the design choices that separate them.
AI.method: The authors cast sampling-based MPC as SMC over control sequences with three independent axes, the proposal, the update rule that reduces weighted particles to a nominal plan, and the effective-sample-size threshold for resampling, evaluated on MuJoCo control, navigation, 7-DoF motion planning and push-T, including a Franka FR3.
AI.result: Resampling cut the collision rate by 30% over non-resampling baselines at a 28-knot horizon in navigation, and programmable proposals raised push-T success from 1% to 100% in simulation and from 10% to 90% on hardware.
AI.conclusion: A single SMC view unifies sampling-based MPC variants and clarifies which axis to change, with resampling handling particle degeneracy and proposal design improving non-prehensile manipulation.

title: Guiding future global temperature distributions with simulations and observations
summary: Assessing climate risks requires projections of daily temperature distributions, including rare and spatially widespread extremes. Climate simulations are costly and biased, while correcting them toward observations risks suppressing inter-model differences. We train a single machine-learning emulator, a conditional diffusion model, on seventeen CMIP6 models and ERA5 reanalysis to generate spatially coherent daily temperature fields conditioned on model identity, date, and CO2-equivalent concentration. At sampling time, diffusion guidance reduces model biases by steering each emulated climate-model distribution toward observations, with its strength selected through perfect-model experiments using withheld simulated futures. Observational influence decreases with projection horizon and forcing. Across seventeen synthetic targets, guidance more than halves median biases in the 1st and 99th percentiles of daily temperature, improves probabilistic scores and reliability, and reduces median annual global-mean temperature RMSE by 32-57% across three emission scenarios. In a detailed benchmark, guidance also outperforms established bias corrections on daily-field probabilistic scores. Efficient sampling generates large ensembles without further climate simulations. For example, our framework corrects CMIP6's roughly threefold historical overestimate of extreme-heat coverage, yet projects that concurrent extremes will affect nearly half of global land on a typical day in the 2080s under SSP3-7.0.

AI.tldr: Trains a conditional diffusion emulator on 17 CMIP6 models and ERA5 and uses diffusion guidance toward observations to correct model biases in daily temperature distributions. Guidance more than halves median biases in the 1st and 99th percentiles and cuts median annual global-mean RMSE by 32% to 57% across three scenarios.
AI.motivation: Assessing climate risk needs daily temperature distributions including rare extremes, but simulations are costly and biased, and correcting them toward observations can suppress inter-model differences.
AI.method: A single conditional diffusion model is conditioned on model identity, date and CO2-equivalent concentration, and at sampling time guidance steers each emulated model distribution toward observations, with strength chosen through perfect-model experiments using withheld simulated futures.
AI.result: Across 17 synthetic targets guidance more than halves median biases in the 1st and 99th percentiles of daily temperature, improves probabilistic scores and reliability, outperforms established bias corrections on daily-field scores, and corrects CMIP6's roughly threefold historical overestimate of extreme-heat coverage.
AI.conclusion: Guided emulation generates large ensembles without new simulations and projects that concurrent extremes will affect nearly half of global land on a typical day in the 2080s under SSP3-7.0, with observational influence decreasing with horizon and forcing.

title: Approximate Recall, Approximate Forecasts: Recall as a Diagnostic for LLM Forecasting Errors
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures (including appendix). Accepted as a Spotlight at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Forecasting as a New Frontier of Intelligence
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit approximate recall: they retain coarse associations about past events while losing fidelity on specific details. Past research on LLMs has quantified different models' forecasting ability in real-world events using prediction markets, but has not studied how losing said fidelity impacts their forecasting abilities. For example: while an LLM correctly recalls that the answer to: ''Did Anna Sawai win the Best Drama Actress in the 76th Emmy Awards?'' is ''Yes,'' it incorrectly states the event date as September 22 rather than September 15. In this paper, we introduce a novel metric called the Recall Fidelity Score to study how imprecision in internalized knowledge propagates to forecasting capability on future events. On resolved historical markets, we find that higher local recall fidelity around semantically similar past events predicts lower forecasting error on resolved markets, and the same signal predicts smaller distance from open markets prices.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Recall Fidelity Score, a metric for how imprecise an LLM's internalized knowledge of past events propagates into its forecasting ability. On resolved historical prediction markets, higher local recall fidelity around semantically similar past events predicts lower forecasting error and smaller distance from open market prices.
AI.motivation: LLMs retain coarse associations about past events but lose fidelity on specific details, and prior work measuring LLM forecasting on prediction markets has not studied how this loss of fidelity affects forecasting.
AI.method: The authors define a novel Recall Fidelity Score that measures local recall fidelity around semantically similar past events and relate it to forecasting error on resolved markets and to distance from open market prices.
AI.result: On resolved historical markets, higher local recall fidelity around semantically similar past events predicts lower forecasting error, and the same signal predicts smaller distance from open market prices.
AI.conclusion: Recall fidelity can serve as a diagnostic for LLM forecasting errors, showing that imprecision in internalized knowledge affects forecasting on future events.

title: Zero-Shot VLA Adaptation with Retrieved Guidance
summary: Pre-training large parametric "Vision-Language-Action" (VLA) models on large demonstration datasets has recently yielded promising results for general-purpose manipulation. However, these models still struggle under even small domain shifts relative to the training data, such as changes in camera viewpoint, background, object identity, or robot morphology. Motivated by the success of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in language models, we pursue retrieval to boost VLA performance. Specifically, we seek to leverage retrieval from domain-mismatched, "in-the-wild" demonstration datasets like DROID to guide a VLA's behavior in a new target domain. To achieve this, we introduce RAGu, which overcomes robotics-specific challenges for RAG: (1) It incorporates simple geometric calibration to transform source demonstrations into the target setup and reduce cross-domain differences. (2) It uses a coarse-to-fine retrieval strategy that selects, from a large pool of pre-warped candidates, the trajectory most compatible with the base VLA. (3) It guides the VLA's flow-matching inference procedure rather than seeking to retrain the base model or expand its limited context window. We evaluate RAGu across real-world, simulation, sim-to-real transfer, and cross-embodiment humanoid manipulation. We find it improves real-world VLA success rates from 20% to 80% and outperforms the closest-related baselines in sim. Project website: this http URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RAGu, a retrieval-augmented method that adapts a frozen vision-language-action policy to a new domain by retrieving and calibrating demonstrations from a mismatched in-the-wild dataset such as DROID. The retrieved trajectories guide the base model's flow-matching inference without retraining it.
AI.motivation: Pre-trained VLA models struggle under small domain shifts such as changes in camera viewpoint, background, object identity or robot morphology, and retraining or enlarging their limited context window is costly.
AI.method: RAGu applies simple geometric calibration to transform source demonstrations into the target setup, uses a coarse-to-fine retrieval strategy to select the trajectory most compatible with the base VLA from a pool of pre-warped candidates, and uses the retrieved trajectory to guide flow-matching inference.
AI.result: RAGu improves real-world VLA success rates from 20% to 80% and outperforms the closest related baselines in simulation; the abstract also reports evaluation on sim-to-real transfer and cross-embodiment humanoid manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval from mismatched demonstration datasets, with geometric calibration and guided inference, can boost VLA performance in a new target domain without retraining the base model.

title: Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning for an Options Market Maker: An Empirical Study with Real S&P 500 Options
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Authors listed alphabetically by last name
summary: Options market makers absorb client order flow and must hedge the resulting inventory risk under trading frictions. We study whether an option hedging reinforcement learning (RL) agent trained on historical market data outperforms three alternatives in tail-risk protection: (i) traditional delta hedging, (ii) simple hedge-ratio rules, and (iii) the same agent trained in simulated markets. Most RL hedging agents are trained in model-generated markets that do not capture the crashes and volatility regimes present in real data. We introduce an empirical replay environment using S&P 500 option data from 1996 to 2017 and compare against a matched geometric Brownian motion (GBM) environment, a stochastic-volatility (SABR) simulator, and a hybrid that values historical paths with Black-Scholes, all sharing the same portfolio mechanics, stochastic arrivals, costs, and test period. We train a distributional Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (TD3) agent and evaluate it out of sample over 2018-2023. The agent trained on empirical data reduces Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) tail loss by 3.1% compared to delta hedging and outperforms every hedge-ratio rule chosen during the training period and every alternative training environment. The reduction reaches 8.9% in volatile and falling markets, but reverses to a cost of 7-10% in rising markets. Empirical training induces a state-dependent short net delta: the policy under-hedges negative-delta books, most strongly after prices have fallen. This tilt disappears with GBM training and is weaker with SABR or hybrid training. These findings suggest that exposure to historical market dynamics can materially change a tail-risk hedging policy, although the evidence rests on a single test path and the edge is regime-conditional.

AI.tldr: The paper trains a distributional TD3 reinforcement learning hedging agent on real S&P 500 option data from 1996 to 2017 and tests it out of sample over 2018 to 2023. The agent trained on empirical data reduces CVaR tail loss by 3.1% relative to delta hedging, and the benefit is regime-conditional.
AI.motivation: Most RL hedging agents are trained in model-generated markets that do not capture the crashes and volatility regimes present in real data, so their tail-risk performance may be misleading.
AI.method: The authors build an empirical replay environment using S&P 500 option data and compare it against a matched geometric Brownian motion environment, a SABR stochastic-volatility simulator and a hybrid environment that values historical paths with Black-Scholes, all sharing the same portfolio mechanics, arrivals, costs and test period.
AI.result: The empirically trained agent reduces CVaR tail loss by 3.1% against delta hedging and outperforms every hedge-ratio rule chosen during training and every alternative training environment. The reduction reaches 8.9% in volatile and falling markets but becomes a cost of 7-10% in rising markets, and empirical training induces a state-dependent short net delta that disappears with GBM training.
AI.conclusion: Exposure to historical market dynamics can materially change a tail-risk hedging policy, but the evidence rests on a single test path and the edge is regime-conditional.

title: Improving Analytic Constants via Interpretable AI-Guided Lean Proof Refinement
summary: AI agents are increasingly capable of discovering new mathematical results, yet their reasoning and generated proofs can be difficult to understand and verify. We introduce an interpretable framework for AI-guided mathematical discovery, focused on improving quantitative bounds on analytic constants. Our key insight is that existing proofs often contain slack in intermediate lemmas, which can be tightened without reconstructing the entire argument. To exploit this structure, we represent proofs as partially-formalized Lean blueprints: human-interpretable dependency graphs of definitions, lemmas, and theorems. An AI agent then iteratively refines the Lean code while preserving the blueprint's dependency structure, allowing local improvements to automatically propagate to a verified final bound. This interpretable structure allows humans to inspect the agent's refinements and understand how local improvements propagate to the final theorem. For Grothendieck's constant ($\mathcal{K}_G$), we obtain $$ \mathcal{K}_G \leq \frac{\pi}{2\log(1+\sqrt{2})} - 10^{-17}, $$ an explicit numerical improvement over Krivine's 1977 bound. For Korenblum's constant ($\mathcal{K}_K$), we obtain $$ \mathcal{K}_K \geq 0.356565, $$ improving Wang's 2025 bound of $0.3554$. Our experiments demonstrate the potential of both partial formalization and iterative agentic refinement for interpretable mathematical discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an interpretable framework in which an AI agent iteratively refines partially formalized Lean blueprints to tighten slack in intermediate lemmas and improve bounds on analytic constants. It yields a new upper bound for Grothendieck's constant and a new lower bound for Korenblum's constant.
AI.motivation: AI agents can discover new mathematical results, but their reasoning and generated proofs are hard to understand and verify.
AI.method: Proofs are represented as partially formalized Lean blueprints, which are human-interpretable dependency graphs of definitions, lemmas and theorems. An AI agent refines the Lean code while preserving the blueprint's dependency structure so that local improvements propagate automatically to a verified final bound.
AI.result: For Grothendieck's constant the paper obtains an explicit upper bound of pi over twice log(1 + sqrt 2) minus 10^-17, improving Krivine's 1977 bound. For Korenblum's constant it obtains a lower bound of 0.356565, improving Wang's 2025 bound of 0.3554.
AI.conclusion: Partial formalization combined with iterative agentic refinement shows potential for interpretable mathematical discovery, since humans can inspect how local improvements affect the final theorem.

title: Rule-table structure of life-like cellular automata: activity, asymmetry, sensitivity, and the propagation storage factorisation
summary: What structure on the rule space of a cellular-automaton family exposes which rules can support which behaviours? For the 262,144 life-like rules -- the two-dimensional outer-totalistic family containing Conway's Game of Life -- the standard coordinate, Langton's activity parameter, is long known to be too coarse. I organise the family by three symmetry-derived rule-table coordinates: an unweighted activity, a birth-survival asymmetry (odd under the swap of birth and survival), and the Vichniac-Binder Boolean-derivative sensitivity in closed form, whose centre-bit component vanishes exactly on the centre-blind (B=S) submanifold. The cardinality coordinates lambda, delta are necessary but never sufficient to certify behaviour; the centre-bit sensitivity labels the B=S submanifold on which the paper's one exact exclusion holds. Combined with an exhaustive enumeration of every rule's compact gliders, still lifes and oscillators (three-by-three seed, period at most sixteen), they expose a hierarchical factorisation: the birth condition is a narrow gate deciding whether anything can propagate, the survival condition tunes storage, and every compact-glider-supporting rule is birth-light and survival-rich. One exclusion is exact: no B=S rule supports a compact glider at that footprint, proven by exhaustive enumeration and closing only for compact-footprint patterns -- 36 B=S rules ship at four-by-four seed and 40 at five-by-five. Two dynamical results frame the whole: glider-capable rules that random sampling never expresses show that capability is certifiable from the table while its expression is only estimable from dynamics; and every uncatalogued rule producing a richly Life-like ecology turns out to be a Conway or HighLife variant on the neighbour counts its trajectories actually visit.

AI.tldr: The paper organizes the 262,144 life-like cellular automaton rules using three symmetry-derived rule-table coordinates and shows that the birth condition gates whether anything can propagate while the survival condition tunes storage. It also proves that no B=S rule supports a compact glider at the stated footprint.
AI.motivation: Langton's activity parameter is too coarse to expose which life-like rules can support which behaviours, so a better structure on the rule space is needed.
AI.method: The author introduces an unweighted activity, a birth-survival asymmetry and the Vichniac-Binder Boolean-derivative sensitivity, combined with an exhaustive enumeration of compact gliders, still lifes and oscillators on a three-by-three seed with period at most sixteen.
AI.result: The centre-bit sensitivity labels the B=S submanifold, and every compact-glider-supporting rule is birth-light and survival-rich. The paper proves by exhaustive enumeration that no B=S rule supports a compact glider at that footprint, with 36 such rules at four-by-four seed and 40 at five-by-five.
AI.conclusion: Capability to support behaviour is certifiable from the rule table, while its actual expression is only estimable from dynamics, and the rule-table coordinates give a hierarchical factorisation of the family.

title: Network Contention State Aware Dynamic Optimizer for Accelerator Collective Communication Libraries
summary: Collective Communication Libraries (CCL) are critical for large-scale distributed AI/ML training, yet their configurations are determined by static heuristics that do not account for real-time network conditions. Our empirical study shows that these heuristics perform near-optimally in contention-free environments, but degrade substantially under background traffic. To address this, we present a cooperative multi-agent run-time optimizer for accelerator collective communication. Our approach employs a two-agent architecture: (i) detector- a Long Short Term Memory(LSTM) recurring neural network fed classifier head with a sequential probability ratio test that distinguishes sustained contention from transient spikes; and (ii) selector- a configuration selector built on a Dueling Double DQN (D3QN) with Conservative Q-Learning that adapts configuration parameters in response. We implemented this dynamic tuner over NCCL, a widely used CCL developed by NVIDIA. When evaluated on Chameleon Cloud's isolated bare-metal cluster, this dynamic tuning approach reduces AllReduce latency by 36% over NCCL and 32% over a fully converged AutoCCL. We further evaluated it across six real AI workloads spanning convolutional networks, transformers, and recommendation architectures. Our multi-agent tuner approach delivers up to 65% speedups on Delta cluster with NVIDIA A100 GPUs and Slingshot-11 fabric internode connectivity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-agent run-time tuner for NCCL collective communication that uses an LSTM-based detector to separate sustained network contention from transient spikes and a D3QN selector to adjust configuration parameters. On a bare-metal cluster it reduces AllReduce latency by 36% over NCCL and 32% over a converged AutoCCL.
AI.motivation: Collective communication library configurations rely on static heuristics that perform near-optimally without background traffic but degrade substantially under contention.
AI.method: A detector, an LSTM classifier head with a sequential probability ratio test, distinguishes sustained contention from transient spikes, and a selector built on a Dueling Double DQN with Conservative Q-Learning adapts configuration parameters in response. The tuner is implemented over NCCL.
AI.result: On Chameleon Cloud's isolated bare-metal cluster the approach reduces AllReduce latency by 36% over NCCL and 32% over a fully converged AutoCCL. Across six real AI workloads spanning convolutional networks, transformers and recommendation architectures, it delivers up to 65% speedups on the Delta cluster with NVIDIA A100 GPUs and Slingshot-11 fabric.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, contention-aware tuning of collective communication configurations can substantially improve distributed AI training performance over static heuristics.

title: RoutingTrie: Metadata Routing for Constrained Generative Retrieval
summary: Advances in large language models and semantic IDs (SIDs) have brought generative retrieval (GR) into industrial applications. These systems must return items that satisfy request metadata constraints as well as relevance requirements. A catalog trie ensures SID validity, but filtering metadata only after generation wastes computation on rejected candidates and may leave too few eligible results. We propose RoutingTrie to incorporate metadata constraints before beam selection. RoutingTrie maintains one shared SID trie and builds a compact index for each metadata field using Dense Bitset or Sparse List. We derive a storage cost formula to guide the choice between these index representations for different field distributions. During decoding, field probes determine whether requested values occur below candidate edges and produce a combined mask that guides beam selection. Experiments on ShopTrie, our configurable synthetic benchmark, demonstrate compact storage and efficient CPU and GPU probing across diverse metadata distributions. In a production replay, RoutingTrie raises Hit@100 from 67.5\% to 96.1\%, a gain of 28.6 percentage points, with only 1.1 ms latency increase. We will release the ShopTrie generator, benchmark scripts, and RoutingTrie CPU and Triton GPU implementations to support reproducibility.

AI.tldr: RoutingTrie applies request metadata constraints before beam selection in generative retrieval, using one shared semantic-ID trie with a compact per-field index. In a production replay it raises Hit@100 from 67.5% to 96.1% with only 1.1 ms added latency.
AI.motivation: Filtering metadata only after generation wastes computation on rejected candidates and may leave too few eligible results in industrial generative retrieval systems.
AI.method: RoutingTrie keeps one shared SID trie and builds for each metadata field a Dense Bitset or Sparse List index, chosen with a derived storage cost formula. During decoding, field probes determine whether requested values occur below candidate edges and produce a combined mask that guides beam selection.
