AI.result: Experiments on the authors' configurable synthetic benchmark ShopTrie show compact storage and efficient CPU and GPU probing across diverse metadata distributions. In a production replay, Hit@100 rises from 67.5% to 96.1%, a gain of 28.6 percentage points, with a 1.1 ms latency increase.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating metadata constraints into decoding improves constrained generative retrieval, and the authors plan to release the benchmark generator, scripts and CPU and Triton GPU implementations.

title: Toward universal excited-state machine-learned potentials: a local excitation Hamiltonian for size consistency and transferability
comment: 24 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables, Supplementary Information (19 pages) included. Dataset: this https URL. Code and trained models: this https URL, this https URL
summary: Universal machine-learned interatomic potentials could make excited-state simulations across chemical space routine, but excitation energies, unlike ground-state energies, are not sums of atomic contributions. The excited states of noninteracting molecules are the union of their states, which pooled multistate readouts reproduce at best for the lowest state. We introduce LEH-MACE, whose excitation energies are the eigenvalues of a local excitation Hamiltonian assembled from atom-centred blocks, so this union holds exactly. We generated TD-DFT energies and forces for about 300,000 equilibrium, thermal, and excited-state geometries of over 100,000 molecules. LEH-MACE's advantage over direct readouts grew with the distance from the training data and was largest above $S_1$, with about half their $S_2$ and $S_3$ errors for long conjugated oligomers. For molecule pairs, only LEH-MACE kept its single-molecule accuracy, while a softmin readout remained superior for $S_1$ dynamics of larger chromophores. Exact size consistency is thus one step toward such potentials.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LEH-MACE, a machine-learned potential whose excitation energies are eigenvalues of a local excitation Hamiltonian built from atom-centred blocks, so that size consistency holds exactly for noninteracting molecules. It is trained on about 300,000 TD-DFT geometries of over 100,000 molecules.
AI.motivation: Excitation energies are not sums of atomic contributions, so existing pooled multistate readouts reproduce the excited states of noninteracting molecules at best for the lowest state.
AI.method: The excitation energies are the eigenvalues of a local excitation Hamiltonian assembled from atom-centred blocks, which makes the union of molecular excited states exact. The model is trained on TD-DFT energies and forces for equilibrium, thermal and excited-state geometries.
AI.result: The advantage over direct readouts grows with distance from the training data and is largest above S1, with about half their S2 and S3 errors for long conjugated oligomers. For molecule pairs only LEH-MACE keeps single-molecule accuracy, while a softmin readout remains superior for S1 dynamics of larger chromophores.
AI.conclusion: Exact size consistency is a step toward universal excited-state machine-learned potentials, though a softmin readout still does better for some larger chromophores.

title: Symplectic Normal Coordinates Flow for Generative Modeling of Hamiltonian Systems
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 10 pages, 6 figures plus appendices. Code: this https URL
summary: In conditioned generative models of physical systems, the densities at different values of the conditioning parameters are often related through symplectic transformations. For stable linear Hamiltonian systems, there exists a symplectic transformation to "normal coordinates" such that the dynamics is reduced to rotations in each phase-space plane. This picture extends to the nonlinear case where, away from resonances, the Birkhoff normal form again consists of rotations in phase space, now with amplitude dependence. In this work, we introduce an invertible symplectic flow layer consisting of amplitude-dependent rotations in learned normal coordinates. We derive the condition under which the nonlinear rotation layer is symplectic and detail an architecture that guarantees it. Experiments are carried out on three conditional generative modeling problems: a synthetic chain of coupled nonlinear oscillators and two problems from accelerator physics. We show empirically that normalizing flows with the new layers achieve competitive or superior negative log-likelihoods compared to baseline flows, with gains that grow with the strength of the nonlinearity on the synthetic system.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an invertible symplectic flow layer made of amplitude-dependent rotations in learned normal coordinates and uses it in normalizing flows for conditional generative modeling of Hamiltonian systems. The layers achieve competitive or superior negative log-likelihoods compared with baseline flows.
AI.motivation: Densities at different values of the conditioning parameters in physical systems are related by symplectic transformations, and generative models should respect this structure, especially in nonlinear regimes where the Birkhoff normal form gives amplitude-dependent rotations.
AI.method: The authors derive the condition under which the nonlinear rotation layer is symplectic and design an architecture that guarantees it, then insert the layer into normalizing flows.
AI.result: On a synthetic chain of coupled nonlinear oscillators and two accelerator physics problems, the new flows achieve competitive or superior negative log-likelihoods relative to baselines, with gains that grow with the strength of nonlinearity on the synthetic system.
AI.conclusion: Symplectic normal-coordinate layers are a useful inductive bias for conditional generative models of Hamiltonian dynamics, with the benefit increasing as nonlinearity grows.

title: Rescene-ESM: an Earth system model built around a frozen AI weather model
comment: 47 pages, 6 figures, 11 Extended Data figures; Supplementary Information (20 figures, 9 tables) included
summary: Earth system models underpin climate projections, but their cost limits how many scenarios, ensemble members and impact pathways can be explored. Machine-learning weather models forecast as skillfully as physics-based models at a fraction of the cost, yet coupled to an ocean they have produced weak El Nino variability or have learned it from climate-model output, and none carries the climate through rivers to the people exposed to it. Here we present Rescene-ESM, an Earth system model whose coupler, YAHO, yokes a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon and energy components constrained by observations. Adding the couplings one at a time shows what each contributes: over a climatological ocean the AI atmosphere varies from year to year by a third of the observed amount over the oceans, and an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave ocean, the residual of the observed sea surface temperature (SST) equation as stochastic forcing and the land's moisture flux raise this step by step and bring El Nino and its teleconnections, leaving the mean climate almost unchanged. The full model simulates about 1,000 years per day on one graphics processing unit, holds the observed climate for a thousand years without drift, reproduces the observed 1979-2022 global warming, carries forced change with a physically based structure around the frozen network (transient climate response 1.60 K), routes runoff to 212 river gauges with a median seasonal-cycle correlation of 0.79 and, driven by emissions, separates the heatwave exposure of an SSP1 and an SSP3 world by a factor of 4.7 in 2081-2100, three-quarters of it through the warmer climate.

AI.tldr: Rescene-ESM is an Earth system model that couples a frozen 20.8-million-parameter AI weather model to physically formulated ocean, sea-ice, land, river and carbon components through the coupler YAHO. It runs about 1,000 simulated years per day on one GPU and reproduces observed warming and river gauge runoff.
AI.motivation: ML weather models are skillful but produce weak El Nino variability when coupled to an ocean, and none of them carries the climate through rivers to human exposure.
AI.method: The coupler YAHO links a frozen AI atmosphere to observation-constrained physical ocean, sea-ice, land, river, carbon and energy components, with couplings added one at a time to measure each contribution, including an interactive mixed layer, an equatorial wave ocean, stochastic SST residual forcing and land moisture flux.
AI.result: The full model holds the observed climate for a thousand years without drift, reproduces observed 1979-2022 warming with a transient climate response of 1.60 K, and routes runoff to 212 river gauges with a median seasonal-cycle correlation of 0.79. Driven by emissions, it separates heatwave exposure in SSP1 and SSP3 worlds by a factor of 4.7 in 2081-2100, three-quarters of it through the warmer climate.
AI.conclusion: Coupling a frozen AI atmosphere with physical components can yield a fast Earth system model that captures El Nino and carries climate impacts through rivers to exposure, providing a cheap tool for exploring scenarios and ensembles.

title: Evaluating generative samplers for lattice field theory by scale
summary: Generative samplers for lattice field theory are commonly evaluated by their effective sample size (ESS). We show that a small global ESS need not imply inaccurate long-distance observables: errors spread over many short-distance modes can dominate this diagnostic. We introduce a scale-resolved diagnostic based on the overlap between coarse-grained model and target distributions. At the lattice cutoff, this overlap determines the asymptotic ESS fraction; lower cutoffs isolate long-wavelength errors. In the exactly solvable free theory, two samplers with comparable ESS yield a $32\%$ bias and no bias in the susceptibility, respectively. In two-dimensional $\phi^4$ theory near criticality, trained diffusion samplers show the same separation of scales: their path-weight ESS fraction falls rapidly over the volumes studied, while low moments of the magnetization remain close to their target values. Varying the reference parameters substantially changes infrared observables, with little effect on the log-weight variance. Given the target magnetization distribution, a marginal Metropolis test maintains an acceptance rate of order one in our tests. Combined with exact local updates, it reduces the remaining mismatch, although residual bias remains at finite relaxation length. In the free field, uniformly bounded relative errors in the proposal mode variances give a volume-independent bound on the number of updates needed for a prescribed accuracy of the chain's stationary mode variances at fixed correlation length. The target marginal must be supplied or computed separately; estimating it from the samplers' own weights can inherit the poor global overlap.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scale-resolved diagnostic for generative samplers in lattice field theory based on the overlap between coarse-grained model and target distributions. It shows that a small global effective sample size can coexist with large errors in long-distance observables.
AI.motivation: Generative samplers are commonly judged by global effective sample size, but a small global ESS need not imply inaccurate long-distance observables, since errors spread over many short-distance modes can dominate the diagnostic.
AI.method: The authors introduce a scale-resolved overlap diagnostic between coarse-grained model and target distributions, study it in exactly solvable free theory and in two-dimensional phi^4 theory near criticality with trained diffusion samplers, and test a marginal Metropolis correction with exact local updates.
AI.result: In free theory two samplers with comparable ESS give a 32% bias and no bias in the susceptibility. In phi^4 theory the path-weight ESS fraction falls rapidly while low magnetization moments stay near target values. A marginal Metropolis test keeps acceptance of order one and reduces the mismatch, though residual bias remains at finite relaxation length.
AI.conclusion: Global ESS is an unreliable diagnostic for long-distance observables, scale-resolved overlap is needed, and the target marginal must be supplied or computed separately because estimating it from the samplers' own weights can inherit poor overlap.

title: Scalable Neural Safety Certification via Monotonicity
summary: Learning-based safety certification offers a promising route for verifying complex dynamical systems when explicit models are unavailable, but existing data-driven methods often scale poorly: they treat the system as a black box, rely on dense discretizations or Lipschitz bounds, and consequently suffer from sample complexity that grows exponentially with dimension. This paper shows that a common structural property of dynamical systems--monotonicity--can be used to break this curse of dimensionality. We develop a data-driven framework for robust safety verification and safe controller synthesis for unknown monotone systems using only simulator queries. Our main theoretical result proves that, for monotone systems with upper-closed unsafe sets, safety is completely characterized by the existence of monotone inductive barrier certificates. This structure reduces certificate verification over continuous state spaces to localized boundary checks over finitely many cells. To learn such certificates, we introduce Max-Monotone Networks, a monotone neural architecture with universal approximation guarantees for monotone functions. We then propose a training and refinement algorithm that, upon successful termination, returns formally valid neural barrier certificates and, under mild partition assumptions, requires only $O(n)$ simulator queries. Across high-dimensional benchmarks, including oscillator networks with up to $13{,}659$ states and traffic networks with $1{,}000$ states, our method certifies safety in regimes where prior approaches either do not converge or exceed memory limits. These results demonstrate that exploiting order structure can make neural safety certification both scalable and formally sound.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a data-driven framework for safety verification and controller synthesis of unknown monotone dynamical systems using only simulator queries, reducing certificate checking to localized boundary checks. It proposes Max-Monotone Networks as barrier certificates and certifies safety for systems with up to 13,659 oscillator states and 1,000 traffic states.
AI.motivation: Existing data-driven safety certification treats systems as black boxes and relies on dense discretizations or Lipschitz bounds, so its sample complexity grows exponentially with dimension.
AI.method: The authors prove that for monotone systems with upper-closed unsafe sets, safety is characterized by the existence of monotone inductive barrier certificates. They introduce Max-Monotone Networks, a monotone architecture with universal approximation guarantees for monotone functions, and a training and refinement algorithm.
AI.result: The method returns formally valid neural barrier certificates on high-dimensional benchmarks, including oscillator networks with up to 13,659 states and traffic networks with 1,000 states, in regimes where prior approaches do not converge or exceed memory limits. Under mild partition assumptions it needs only O(n) simulator queries.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting order structure can make neural safety certification both scalable and formally sound in high dimensions.

title: Optimal Polynomial-Query Approximation for Consistent Submodular Maximization with Short Lookahead
summary: Elements arrive one at a time, and after each arrival an algorithm holds a set of at most $k$ arrived elements. Its goal is a held set whose value under a monotone submodular function is close to the best value that $k$ arrived elements can achieve. The recourse of an update is the number of elements inserted into or removed from the held set, and we require it to be bounded independently of $k$ and of the number $n$ of arrivals. With evaluations only on sets of arrived elements and polynomially many of them, the best ratio a randomized algorithm can achieve is $2-\sqrt{2}\approx0.5858$. We show that seeing future arrivals raises the best ratio for polynomially many evaluations to $1-1/e\approx0.6321$, for deterministic and for randomized algorithms; no algorithm with polynomially many evaluations exceeds $1-1/e$, even when all elements are available at once. For every $\varepsilon>0$, a deterministic algorithm that sees the next $\lceil\varepsilon k/3\rceil$ arrivals keeps a set of value at least $1-1/e-\varepsilon$ times the optimum at every time, changes $O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ elements per arrival and makes $(n+1)^{O(\varepsilon^{-2})}$ evaluations. With the whole arrival sequence known in advance, a deterministic algorithm attains the same ratio with $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ changes per arrival. A randomized algorithm with the same short lookahead makes $O(n^2k)$ evaluations, changes $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ elements per arrival, and attains the same ratio in expectation at each fixed time. The main tool is a greedy algorithm with an explicit guarantee for each of its partial solutions combined with each initial segment of the known future arrivals. A second tool moves between two such solutions one element at a time while keeping the value high, and the deterministic algorithm times each move using upper bounds on the optimum from failed searches.

AI.tldr: The paper studies online consistent submodular maximization in which elements arrive one at a time and a set of at most k elements is maintained with bounded recourse. Seeing a short lookahead of future arrivals raises the best achievable ratio under polynomially many evaluations from 2 minus sqrt 2 to 1 minus 1/e.
AI.motivation: Without future information the best ratio a randomized algorithm can achieve with polynomially many evaluations is about 0.5858, and the question is how much knowing future arrivals helps.
AI.method: The authors prove a 1 minus 1/e upper bound on the ratio for polynomially many evaluations, even offline, and give a deterministic algorithm that sees the next ceil(eps k/3) arrivals, built from a greedy algorithm with guarantees on partial solutions combined with initial segments of the known future arrivals, plus a move procedure between two such solutions. A randomized variant is also given.
AI.result: For every eps greater than 0, the deterministic algorithm keeps a set of value at least 1 minus 1/e minus eps times the optimum at every time, with O(eps^-3) changes per arrival and (n+1)^O(eps^-2) evaluations. With the whole sequence known in advance it needs O(eps^-2) changes per arrival. The randomized version attains the same ratio in expectation at each fixed time with O(eps^-2) changes per arrival.
AI.conclusion: Short lookahead closes the gap to the optimal 1 minus 1/e ratio for polynomially many evaluations, showing that seeing future arrivals strictly raises achievable performance in consistent submodular maximization.

title: TALK: One-Shot Batch Design for Protein Variant Effect Prediction
summary: Protein variant effect prediction is central to understanding protein function and guiding protein engineering, yet experimental labels remain costly. In many protein experiments, the variants that can be assayed are dictated by protocol constraints, while the variants that need accurate prediction may lie in a different or broader region of the landscape. This assay-prediction mismatch makes candidate-local criteria such as predicted function, uncertainty, or exploration value insufficient for measurement design. Given a protocol-defined accessible space and a limited budget, we ask which variants should be assayed so that the resulting data best improves landscape prediction. We propose TALK, which estimates each candidate's contribution through posterior coupling between accessible and target variants and reduces redundant information within the batch. Across retrospective ProteinGym and FLIP protocols, TALK generally improves target-space prediction under limited measurement budgets. These results point to a practical two-stage workflow: first, spend a limited assay budget on variants selected to be informative for the target landscape and train a predictive model from the measured labels; then use this model to score and prioritize high-potential variants. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TALK is a one-shot batch design method for protein variant effect prediction that selects which variants to assay under a protocol-defined accessible space so that the measured data best improves prediction on a broader target landscape. It uses posterior coupling between accessible and target variants and reduces redundancy within the batch.
AI.motivation: Assayable variants are dictated by protocol constraints while the variants needing accurate prediction may lie elsewhere, so candidate-local criteria such as predicted function, uncertainty or exploration value are insufficient for measurement design.
AI.method: TALK estimates each candidate's contribution through posterior coupling between accessible and target variants and reduces redundant information within the batch under a limited budget.
AI.result: Across retrospective ProteinGym and FLIP protocols, TALK generally improves target-space prediction under limited measurement budgets.
AI.conclusion: A practical two-stage workflow is to spend a limited assay budget on target-informative variants, train a model on the measured labels, and then use it to prioritize high-potential variants.

title: Fast Approximate $\ell_p$ Chamfer Distance via Lopsided Embeddings and Structured JL
summary: For two $d$-dimensional point sets $A, B$ of size $n$, the Chamfer distance from $A$ to $B$ is defined as $\text{CH}(A,B)=\sum_{a \in A} \min_{b \in B} \mathsf{dist}(a, b)$, where $\mathsf{dist}$ is some underlying distance measure. We present efficient algorithms for approximating the Chamfer distance under the $\ell_p$ norm for $1 < p \le 2$. For the general case $1 < p < 2$, we utilize lopsided $\ell_p$ to $\ell_1$ embeddings with weak guarantees. We show that they are sufficient for preserving the Chamfer distance. In the high-dimensional regime, we use Fast Matrix Multiplication techniques to speed up the lopsided embeddings. These lead to $O(nd\cdot \mathrm{poly}(\log \log n, \log(1/\varepsilon))/\varepsilon^2)$ total time. For the specific Euclidean case ($p=2$), we leverage the Fast Johnson-Lindenstrauss Transform based on Toeplitz matrices and re-analyze the previous $\ell_1$-specific Chamfer algorithm in $\ell_2$. These achieve a runtime matching the recent state-of-the-art $\ell_1$ result of $O(nd(\log \log n + \log (1/\varepsilon))/\varepsilon^2)$, improving upon the previous $O(nd \log n/\varepsilon^2)$ bound for $\ell_2$. We also give additional results for the angular distance and upper and lower bounds in the streaming setting.

AI.tldr: The paper gives efficient algorithms for approximating the Chamfer distance under the l_p norm for 1 < p <= 2, using lopsided embeddings, Fast Matrix Multiplication and a Toeplitz-based fast Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform. The Euclidean case matches the best known l_1 runtime.
AI.motivation: Chamfer distance is widely used between point sets, and prior l_2 algorithms run in O(nd log n / eps^2) time, which the authors aim to improve.
AI.method: For the general case 1 < p < 2 the authors use lopsided l_p to l_1 embeddings with weak guarantees and show they preserve the Chamfer distance; in high dimensions they apply Fast Matrix Multiplication to speed up the embeddings. For p = 2 they use a Toeplitz-based Fast JL transform and re-analyze the l_1 algorithm under l_2.
AI.result: The general algorithm runs in O(nd poly(log log n, log(1/eps)) / eps^2) total time. The Euclidean algorithm matches the recent state-of-the-art l_1 runtime of O(nd (log log n + log(1/eps)) / eps^2), improving on the previous O(nd log n / eps^2) bound for l_2. The paper also gives results for angular distance and streaming upper and lower bounds.
AI.conclusion: Lopsided embeddings and structured JL transforms yield near-linear approximations of Chamfer distance across l_p norms, with the Euclidean case as fast as the l_1 case.

title: Learning calibrated probabilistic forecasts using Koopman mode decomposition and the continuous ranked probability score
comment: 31 pages plus appendices. 18 figures and 5 tables
summary: Well-calibrated forecasting for non-linear dynamical systems is essential in science and engineering applications such as fluid dynamics and weather prediction. We present a forecasting method combining probabilistic machine learning with the structured linear dynamics of Koopman mode decomposition. Within this framework, the observation, linear dynamics, and state reconstruction operators are constructed using standard machine learning architectures, producing predictive distributions via the pushforward of injected noise samples. The model is trained using a proper scoring rule, the continuous ranked probability score, to directly target calibrated, accurate forecasts. The approach is validated on two non-linear ordinary differential equation examples and two partial differential equation examples, vortex shedding and cavity flow, using both large and small, noisy datasets. Results demonstrate that known Koopman eigenfunctions and spectra can be identified and used for accurate forecasting. The model can also produce multi-modal predictive distributions, demonstrated for a trajectory initialised on the boundary between two basins of attraction. Uncertainty is captured by the sample ensemble spread, with spread--skill ratios close to one over the training horizon in several experiments, although for extended rollouts and noisy datasets, the ensemble may become under- or over-dispersed. In low-noise experiments, temporal rollout is generally accurate for at least twice the training horizon, and up to twenty times in some cases. Approximation quality is comparable to a deep ensemble approximation over the training horizon, but at a reduced computational cost and with better robustness in identifying Koopman eigenvalues.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a probabilistic forecasting method that combines Koopman mode decomposition with a continuous ranked probability score training objective to produce calibrated ensemble forecasts of nonlinear dynamical systems. Predictive distributions are generated by pushing injected noise through learned observation, linear dynamics and reconstruction operators.
AI.motivation: Calibrated forecasting of nonlinear dynamical systems matters in fields such as fluid dynamics and weather prediction, and the authors aim to combine probabilistic learning with the structured linear dynamics of Koopman theory.
AI.method: The observation, linear dynamics and state reconstruction operators are built from standard machine learning architectures, and the model is trained with the proper scoring rule CRPS to target calibrated accurate forecasts. It is validated on two ODE examples and two PDE examples, vortex shedding and cavity flow, with large and small noisy datasets.
AI.result: Known Koopman eigenfunctions and spectra can be identified and used for accurate forecasting, and the model can produce multi-modal predictive distributions. Spread-skill ratios are close to one over the training horizon in several experiments, and in low-noise cases rollouts are accurate for at least twice the training horizon and up to twenty times in some cases. Approximation quality is comparable to a deep ensemble at reduced computational cost, with better robustness in identifying Koopman eigenvalues.
AI.conclusion: The Koopman-CRPS approach gives accurate and reasonably calibrated probabilistic forecasts at lower cost than deep ensembles, though calibration can degrade over extended rollouts and with noisy data.

title: Variance-Reduced Stochastic Hessian-Driven Nesterov Acceleration with Adam-Style Preconditioning
summary: Stochastic first-order methods use sampled gradients to reduce per-iteration costs, but estimation errors can slow convergence and, in some settings, cause divergence. To improve gradient accuracy while retaining acceleration, we develop scalar and diagonal versions of VR-Adam-SHANG for smooth stochastic convex optimization. The methods combine STORM-type recursive estimation, Adam-style preconditioning, and SHANG's accelerated interpolation and correction, using at most two stochastic gradient evaluations per iteration without full-gradient refreshes. Under unbiased sampling, bounded variance, and mean-square smoothness of gradient noise, polynomial steps with prescribed initialization yield $O(1/K)$ mean-square gradient-estimation error and expected objective-gap bounds combining $O(1/K^2)$ initial-energy decay with an $O(1/\sqrt K)$ stochastic term after $K$ iterations. These guarantees require neither monotonicity of the preconditioner nor a uniform positive lower bound on its eigenvalues. The analysis also establishes polynomial-step convergence of projected nonrecursive Adam-SHANG-s, filling a gap in its original theory. Experiments compare the methods at matched sample-gradient budgets. In every tested setting, at least one of the two versions achieves the lowest mean terminal objective gap among all compared methods.

AI.tldr: The paper develops scalar and diagonal versions of VR-Adam-SHANG, which combine STORM-type variance-reduced gradient estimation, Adam-style preconditioning and accelerated interpolation for smooth stochastic convex optimization. It proves polynomial-step convergence bounds that combine an O(1/K^2) initial-energy decay with an O(1/sqrt K) stochastic term.
AI.motivation: Sampled gradients reduce per-iteration cost but estimation errors can slow convergence or cause divergence, so the authors want more accurate gradient estimates while keeping acceleration.
AI.method: The methods use at most two stochastic gradient evaluations per iteration without full-gradient refreshes, combining recursive STORM-type estimation, Adam-style preconditioning and SHANG's accelerated interpolation and correction. The analysis also covers projected nonrecursive Adam-SHANG-s.
AI.result: Under unbiased sampling, bounded variance and mean-square smoothness of gradient noise, the methods achieve O(1/K) mean-square gradient-estimation error and the stated objective-gap bounds. The guarantees need neither monotone preconditioners nor uniform positive eigenvalue bounds. In every tested setting at least one of the two versions has the lowest mean terminal objective gap among compared methods at matched sample-gradient budgets.
AI.conclusion: Variance-reduced accelerated methods with Adam-style preconditioning are theoretically sound and empirically competitive, and the analysis also fills a gap in the original Adam-SHANG-s theory.

title: An Adaptive, Context-Aware, and Stacked Attention Network-Based Recommendation System to Capture Users' Temporal Preference
comment: 12 pages. Accepted version of the article published in IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering. Code: this https URL
summary: Recommendation systems have become more important since the widespread use of the Internet. The large amount of information means that it is difficult for users to discover they really need. However, users' preferences can change over time because of the age and the impact of social networks. Recommendation systems must capture users' preferences and recommend suitable items, which is a difficult challenge. This study proposes a novel recommendation system that adapts to the changing preferences of users. By learning and adapting to users' changing preferences better recommendations are provided. This study uses context factors as additional information to model users' preferences more precisely. For the proposed recommendation system, the context is based on users' interaction items within each defined time interval. This study proposes two novel attention mechanisms for the recommendation system. The contextual item attention module captures contextual information, changing pattern in users' preference and the importance of items. The multi-head attention module extends the diversity of users' preferences and adapts to changing preferences. The recommendation performance is improved using additional item's temporal information to model the contextual item's representation. Experiments compare the proposed algorithm with several state-of-the-art recommendation methods using three real-world datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed context-aware recommendation model outperforms traditional methods and demonstrate the effectiveness with which contextual information is captured by the attention mechanism.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a recommendation system with two attention modules, a contextual item attention module and a multi-head attention module, that model users' changing temporal preferences using time-interval context. It is reported to outperform several state-of-the-art recommendation methods on three real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Users' preferences change over time because of age and social networks, and existing recommenders struggle to capture these changing preferences and recommend suitable items.
AI.method: Context is defined from a user's interaction items within each time interval, and two attention mechanisms are proposed: a contextual item attention module that captures contextual information, changing preference patterns and item importance, and a multi-head attention module that captures diverse and adaptive preferences. Item temporal information is used to model contextual item representations.
AI.result: Experiments on three real-world datasets show that the proposed context-aware model outperforms traditional methods and several state-of-the-art recommendation methods. The abstract gives no numerical metrics.
AI.conclusion: Interval-based contextual and multi-head attention can capture the effect of contextual information on temporal user preferences more effectively than prior methods.

title: NCCL-BOT: Closing the Loop on NCCL's Cost Model with Online Bandits
summary: NCCL picks an algorithm-protocol pair for every collective from an analytic cost model (AUTO) that never sees a measured latency. The model is a strong prior but a brittle final decision: priced on forced-arm runs, its choice is exact on most contexts and badly wrong in a few. We built NCCL-BOT, a tuner plugin that closes the loop: a per-context bandit, warm-started from the model, learns from measured latencies. We replay a forced-arm H100 sweep, tuned at 4-8 nodes and scored at 16-32, and price the model's choice on the same forced arms; that sweep has no stock-NCCL run. The bandit cuts the contexts where the model's choice loses more than 10% from 19 to 1 (p99 103% to 9.9%, mean 6.1% to 1.6%; p=0.047 over nine scenarios after Holm correction). The prior and continued learning both matter: cold-started bandits, and committing after one probe of each arm, lose more on the mean in every scenario. Supervised selectors fit once on the same data and tuned with the same budget match the mean, and their heavier tail is not significant (7 against 1 contexts above 10%, p=0.06); at seen scales they match or beat online selection. With hyperparameters frozen from H100, UCB1 cuts AUTO's p99 from 60% to 23% and from 56% to 15% on two GB200 fabrics, but its contexts above 10% go from 16 to 8 on one and from 10 to 13 on the other, and scenario-level tests do not separate the two. Live, on two latency-emulated node sets of one H100 system with one run per policy, the learners repair most of a gross AUTO error on one (selection loss 31% to 6-8% for deterministic Greedy and UCB1; average all-reduce bandwidth 1.18-1.24x stock) but average 0.94-0.99x stock on the other, and on both lose to stock below 1 MiB (on the first through plugin overhead); on H100 the cost model is exact there offline, so small sizes can be left to it. We do not show a net end-to-end win.

AI.tldr: NCCL-BOT is a tuner plugin that closes the loop on NCCL's analytic cost model with a per-context bandit warm-started from the model and updated from measured latencies. On forced-arm H100 replays it cuts contexts where the model loses more than 10% from 19 to 1, though the authors report no net end-to-end win.
AI.motivation: NCCL selects algorithm-protocol pairs from an analytic cost model that never sees measured latency, which is a strong prior but a brittle final decision that is badly wrong in a few contexts.
AI.method: A per-context bandit warm-started from the cost model learns from measured latencies. It is replayed on a forced-arm H100 sweep tuned at 4-8 nodes and scored at 16-32 nodes, and compared with cold-started bandits, supervised selectors, UCB1 on GB200 fabrics and live runs on latency-emulated node sets.
AI.result: The bandit reduces p99 loss from 103% to 9.9% and mean loss from 6.1% to 1.6% (p=0.047 over nine scenarios after Holm correction). Supervised selectors match the mean with a heavier tail that is not significant. Live, the learners repair most of a gross AUTO error on one node set but average 0.94-0.99x stock on the other and lose to stock below 1 MiB.
AI.conclusion: Online learning from a cost-model prior improves collective algorithm selection in offline replays, but the live gains are mixed and no net end-to-end win is shown.

title: CVaR Deep Optimal Stopping
summary: Risk-sensitive optimal stopping is useful when poor stopping outcomes carry substantial costs, as in option exercise, sequential medical treatment, and safety-critical control. A natural objective is Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) of the stopped reward. We develop a theoretical framework and algorithm for CVaR deep optimal stopping. The framework and algorithm address four difficulties in applying risk-sensitive reinforcement learning to optimal stopping: state augmentation, score-function pathology, blindness to success, and dependence on auxiliary networks. We isolate three structural properties of optimal stopping: single-point reward, action-independent dynamics, and sum-zero gradient. We exploit these properties to establish Markov optimality without state augmentation and derive a pathwise gradient estimator. Under bounded policy derivatives, the pathwise estimator has bounded second moments near deterministic policies, avoiding the divergence that can occur with score-function estimators. Building on this framework, we propose DIOS (Distribution-Informed Optimal Stopping) to address the remaining two difficulties. A per-time-step soft penalty combined with tail-level annealing mitigates blindness to success. Estimating the reward quantile directly from each batch removes the need for an auxiliary critic. For a fixed tail level, we establish a finite-time stationarity guarantee under regularity assumptions along the training iterates. Across the 24 main Bermudan max-call configurations, DIOS achieves the highest mean CVaR and the shortest recorded training time among the tested CVaR baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DIOS, a CVaR deep optimal stopping framework that uses a Markov formulation without state augmentation, a pathwise gradient estimator, a per-time-step soft penalty with tail-level annealing and a batch-estimated reward quantile in place of an auxiliary critic. Across 24 Bermudan max-call configurations it achieves the highest mean CVaR among tested baselines.
AI.motivation: Risk-sensitive optimal stopping matters when poor outcomes are costly, but applying risk-sensitive reinforcement learning to it faces state augmentation, score-function pathology, blindness to success and dependence on auxiliary networks.
AI.method: The authors exploit single-point reward, action-independent dynamics and sum-zero gradient to establish Markov optimality without state augmentation and derive a pathwise gradient estimator with bounded second moments near deterministic policies. DIOS adds a soft penalty with tail-level annealing and estimates the reward quantile directly from each batch.
AI.result: Across the 24 main Bermudan max-call configurations DIOS achieves the highest mean CVaR and the shortest recorded training time among tested CVaR baselines. For a fixed tail level the paper establishes a finite-time stationarity guarantee under regularity assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Structural properties of optimal stopping allow a pathwise, critic-free CVaR method that is stable and efficient, with a finite-time convergence guarantee for a fixed tail level.

title: OOM: Offload-Optimized Full-Parameter MoE Training via Memory-Execution Co-Design
comment: 19 pages, 9 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Offloading model state to host memory and streaming layer weights let a single multi-GPU node train large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. GPU memory then becomes a performance budget, shared by resident expert state, retained activations, and execution worksets. The best allocation depends on the expert execution path, batch size, and sequence length. We present OOM (Offload-Optimized MoE), a full-parameter MoE training system that co-designs expert execution and memory allocation. For expert-parallel execution, OOM updates resident experts on their owning GPUs and jointly plans state residency and MoE activation retention according to pipeline dependencies. For local execution, OOM bounds GPU worksets through dependency-aware partitioning; in hybrid models, it also retains attention results on the host to avoid costly recomputation and selectively regenerates layer boundaries through cheaper layers to make room. Calibrated cost models guide joint configuration within GPU and host budgets to minimize step time; OOM selects among the configured paths through short executions. On four H100s, OOM trains with 1M-token contexts, whereas FSDP2, ZeRO-Offload, and MegaTrain exhaust GPU memory at 512K. It also trains a 122B-parameter MoE model, on which all three exhaust host memory. On four 24 GB RTX 4090s, it trains 512K-token contexts and 1,024 1K-token sequences per step without gradient accumulation. Across matched-global-batch comparisons, OOM delivers 1.58x and 4.08x geometric-mean (up to 2.14x and 7.77x) throughput over CPU-offloaded FSDP2 on the two platforms while using the least host memory among the evaluated systems -- as little as 1/3.0 of FSDP2's.

AI.tldr: OOM is a full-parameter MoE training system that co-designs expert execution and memory allocation under host offloading, training 1M-token contexts and a 122B-parameter MoE on four H100s with higher throughput than CPU-offloaded FSDP2.
AI.motivation: With offloading, GPU memory becomes a budget shared by resident expert state, retained activations and execution worksets, and the best allocation depends on the expert execution path, batch size and sequence length.
AI.method: OOM updates resident experts on their owning GPUs and jointly plans state residency and MoE activation retention according to pipeline dependencies; it bounds GPU worksets through dependency-aware partitioning; in hybrid models it retains attention results on the host and regenerates layer boundaries through cheaper layers; calibrated cost models choose the configuration within GPU and host budgets, and short executions select among the configured paths.
AI.result: On four H100s OOM trains 1M-token contexts where FSDP2, ZeRO-Offload and MegaTrain exhaust GPU memory at 512K, and it trains a 122B-parameter MoE on which all three exhaust host memory. On four 24 GB RTX 4090s it trains 512K-token contexts and 1,024 1K-token sequences per step without gradient accumulation. Against CPU-offloaded FSDP2 it delivers 1.58x and 4.08x geometric-mean throughput (up to 2.14x and 7.77x) on the two platforms, using as little as 1/3.0 of FSDP2's host memory.
AI.conclusion: Treating GPU memory as a performance budget and co-designing expert execution with allocation makes full-parameter MoE training on a single multi-GPU node feasible at much longer contexts and larger models.

title: SWHForest: A Structural Curation and Search Layer for Large-Scale Code Corpora
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the MSR 2027 Data and Tool Showcase Track. Code: this https URL ; Data: this https URL
summary: Pre-training code language models relies on massive code corpora usually streamed over the internet. However, researchers rarely need a multi-terabyte archive in its entirety; instead, their workflow centers on curated subsets: selecting well-documented files, filtering out repetitive boilerplate, auditing for benchmark contamination, or retrieving specific code patterns. Yet, because modern corpora are typically published as file pointers and basic attributes rather than source text, no general structural layer exists to select which files to download: curating a subset requires downloading and parsing millions of files first just to discard most of them. We present SWHForest, an open-source framework and public dataset that provides this missing structural layer for any pointer-based corpus without redistributing source code. A single pass over the archive parses each file into an AST and immediately discards the source text, keeping only its structural summary. Queried locally or exposed by archive providers as a server-side filtering API, SWHForest selects matching files first (via SQL or index intersection) and downloads only surviving candidates. Across the ten largest languages of Stack-Edu (52.1M unique files, 341M definitions), SWHForest answers curation queries in milliseconds while cutting downloads by 46-72%, reducing live structural searches from hours of per-language streaming to seconds or minutes.

AI.tldr: SWHForest is an open-source structural layer for pointer-based code corpora that parses each file into an AST and keeps only its structural summary, so researchers can select files before downloading them.
AI.motivation: Modern code corpora are published as file pointers and basic attributes rather than source text, so curating a subset currently requires downloading and parsing millions of files just to discard most of them.
AI.method: A single pass over the archive parses each file into an AST and discards the source text; queries run locally via SQL or index intersection, or server-side through a filtering API that archive providers can expose, and only surviving candidates are downloaded.
AI.result: Over the ten largest languages of Stack-Edu (52.1M unique files, 341M definitions), SWHForest answers curation queries in milliseconds, cuts downloads by 46-72%, and reduces live structural searches from hours of per-language streaming to seconds or minutes.
AI.conclusion: A structural index over pointer-based corpora lets researchers curate large code datasets cheaply, reducing bandwidth and time without redistributing source code.

title: When Normality Shifts: Multi-Level WavLM Modeling for Open-World Audio Deepfake Detection
comment: Accpeted for the OWAD Workshop at ICDM 2026
summary: Audio deepfake detectors trained with known synthesis attacks can learn generator-specific shortcuts that fail as synthesis systems and acoustic conditions evolve. We investigate an attack-free alternative: a normality model trained exclusively on bona fide speech, which scores synthetic audio by its deviation from authentic representations. We propose MLN-WavLM, a method that applies shrinkage-Mahalanobis modeling to pooled hidden states from a frozen large-scale, pre-trained speech processing WavLM Base+ architecture. Evaluated on ASVspoof 2019 LA, our best attack-free variant achieves an 8.45\% Equal Error Rate (EER), closely tracking a fully supervised WavLM-HM-Conformer baseline (7.86%). However, when subjected to the ASVspoof 2021 DF domain shift, performance drops to 22.12% EER, exposing vulnerabilities in the bona-fide-calibrated operating point. Layer-wise analysis reveals that early WavLM representations dominate the ensemble. To test real-world viability, we simulated deployment streams using unlabeled threshold adaptation. While robust median/MAD recalibration easily handles in-domain contamination up to 10%, recalibrating under the 2021 DF domain shift triggers a total collapse of low-FPR recall. We conclude that while frozen source-domain normality can effectively rank deepfakes, it does not yield a stable open-world decision rule, and downstream threshold adaptation cannot rescue upstream ranking degradation.

AI.tldr: MLN-WavLM detects audio deepfakes without training on attacks, fitting a shrinkage-Mahalanobis normality model to pooled hidden states of a frozen WavLM Base+ trained only on bona fide speech.
AI.motivation: Detectors trained on known synthesis attacks learn generator-specific shortcuts that fail as synthesis systems and acoustic conditions evolve.
AI.method: A normality model trained exclusively on bona fide speech scores synthetic audio by its deviation from authentic representations, applying shrinkage-Mahalanobis modeling to pooled hidden states of a frozen WavLM Base+; layer-wise analysis and simulated deployment streams with unlabeled median/MAD threshold adaptation test viability.
AI.result: The best attack-free variant reaches 8.45% EER on ASVspoof 2019 LA, close to a fully supervised WavLM-HM-Conformer baseline at 7.86%, but rises to 22.12% EER under the ASVspoof 2021 DF domain shift. Early WavLM layers dominate the ensemble. Median/MAD recalibration handles in-domain contamination up to 10%, while recalibration under the 2021 DF shift collapses low-FPR recall.
AI.conclusion: Frozen source-domain normality can rank deepfakes effectively but does not yield a stable open-world decision rule, and downstream threshold adaptation cannot rescue upstream ranking degradation.

title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation
summary: Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. We present a robust, privacy-preserving Swarm Learning framework that makes verifiable data quality the condition for admission to the learning task. A validator joins only after a zero-knowledge attestation proves, without revealing any raw sample, that a reference model ran correctly on its private data. The attested outputs also yield a label-free class profile, so the network assembles a collectively IID validator pool from individually skewed validators as accurately as an oracle with the true labels (total-variation distance to uniform 0.025, against 0.021 for the oracle and 0.21 for random selection). Admitted validators score client updates and, through a Tendermint-style Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus, agree on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight for each submission, replacing dataset-size weighting with a quality-aware signal. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without an expensive end-to-end zero-knowledge proof. Across four benchmarks under non-IID partitions the framework matches FedAvg on clean data; under a gradient-scaling attack that collapses FedAvg to random chance, it retains 94% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-100 and over 99% on FashionMNIST, where FedAvg achieves only 2.1% and 11%. The result is a private, robust, and auditable foundation for decentralized learning.

AI.tldr: The framework admits validators into Swarm Learning only after a zero-knowledge proof that a reference model ran correctly on their private data, and uses BFT consensus to agree on quality-aware gradient masks and aggregation weights.
AI.motivation: Swarm Learning delegates validation of model updates to peers whose data may be biased, unrepresentative or adversarial, and existing protocols do not attest data quality, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface.
AI.method: A validator joins after a zero-knowledge attestation that proves, without revealing samples, that a reference model ran on its private data; the attested outputs give a label-free class profile for assembling a collectively IID validator pool; admitted validators score updates and agree through a Tendermint-style BFT consensus on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight; a challenge-based audit adapted from the cut-layer idea of Split Learning lets peers re-verify masks without full end-to-end zero-knowledge proofs.
AI.result: Under non-IID partitions across four benchmarks the framework matches FedAvg on clean data. Under a gradient-scaling attack that collapses FedAvg to random chance, it retains 94% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-100 and over 99% on FashionMNIST, where FedAvg reaches 2.1% and 11%. The validator pool's total-variation distance to uniform is 0.025, against 0.021 for an oracle using true labels and 0.21 for random selection.
AI.conclusion: Making verifiable data quality the condition for admission gives a private, robust and auditable foundation for decentralized learning.

title: MicroSim: Contrastive Graph Neural Networks for Binary Code Similarity Detection
summary: We present MicroSim, a system for binary code similarity detection that represents each function as a graph built from IDA Pro Hex-Rays microcode and compares such graphs with a contrastive Siamese graph neural network (GNN). We evaluate on the TREX cross-optimization benchmark, a corpus of 849,072 function-level microcode graphs spanning optimization levels -O0 through -O3, under a strict class-disjoint split in which no function key is shared between train and test. Under this protocol, MicroSim reaches 0.9972 area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) and 0.9762 Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), outperforming Gemini (0.9332 ROC-AUC), SAFE (0.9752), and jTrans (0.9740) retrained on the same split, as well as a structure-free Bag-of-Words (BoW) baseline (0.9484). We analyze the gap between pair classification and ranked retrieval in graph transformers, showing that Cross-domain Similarity Local Scaling (CSLS) under unified tie-resolved evaluation raises GraphGPS mean reciprocal rank (MRR) from 0.2542 to 0.2559 (R@1 = 0.1639, R@10 = 0.4561), strictly satisfying the theoretical MRR upper bound. Finally, over 5 seeds with equal compute, the pairwise cosine-embedding loss attains a slightly higher ROC-AUC ({\Delta} = -0.0256, 95% confidence interval [-0.3282, +0.2770]), whereas the supervised-contrastive information noise-contrastive estimation (InfoNCE) loss is significantly better on thresholded classification and ranked retrieval.

AI.tldr: MicroSim represents each binary function as a graph built from IDA Pro Hex-Rays microcode and compares graphs with a contrastive Siamese GNN, reaching 0.9972 ROC-AUC on a strict class-disjoint split of the TREX benchmark.
AI.motivation: Binary code similarity detection must generalize across optimization levels, and strong pair-classification results do not show how well graph transformers perform at ranked retrieval.
AI.method: Each function is a microcode graph compared by a contrastive Siamese graph neural network; the study applies Cross-domain Similarity Local Scaling (CSLS) under unified tie-resolved evaluation to ranked retrieval, and compares pairwise cosine-embedding and supervised-contrastive InfoNCE losses over 5 seeds with equal compute.
AI.result: On TREX (849,072 function-level microcode graphs, -O0 to -O3, class-disjoint split) MicroSim reaches 0.9972 ROC-AUC and 0.9762 MCC, above Gemini (0.9332 ROC-AUC), SAFE (0.9752), jTrans (0.9740) and a bag-of-words baseline (0.9484), all retrained on the same split. CSLS raises GraphGPS mean reciprocal rank from 0.2542 to 0.2559 (R@1 = 0.1639, R@10 = 0.4561). The cosine loss differs slightly in ROC-AUC (Delta = -0.0256, 95% CI [-0.3282, +0.2770]), while InfoNCE is significantly better on thresholded classification and ranked retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Microcode graphs with contrastive GNNs give strong binary similarity detection, and ranked retrieval needs its own evaluation and loss choice beyond pair classification.

title: CallCleaner: Lightweight Bioacoustic Denoising from an Audio Foundation Model
summary: Many studies of animal vocalizations require clean recordings, but animals are usually recorded in the field, with background noise from weather, vehicles, and other animals. Animal vocalization denoising is challenged by the scarcity of clean training data and the extreme diversity of animal vocalizations. Classical spectral gates leave residual noise, especially without voice activity detection (VAD), while detector-free neural denoisers designed for bioacoustics remove less noise. We show that a general-purpose source separation foundation model, SAM-Audio, removes more noise than either of these types of methods, when used without training and prompted with time spans from a simple animal VAD. To turn this heavy method into a practical tool, we distill it into CallCleaner, a 19M-parameter denoiser that needs no detector and runs ~90x faster than real time on a laptop CPU. We find that SI-SDR has limited utility in our setting as it penalizes regenerated output and conflates noise removal with call fidelity, a trade-off our separate metrics reveal. CallCleaner leaves 11 dB less noise around the call than Biodenoising, the leading neural bioacoustic denoiser with public weights, and among fast, CPU-capable systems it pushes the Pareto frontier of noise removal vs. call fidelity, without requiring a detector. We release code and weights for CallCleaner, which enables fast, private, local denoising of single-caller recordings without specialized hardware.

AI.tldr: CallCleaner is a 19M-parameter bioacoustic denoiser distilled from the SAM-Audio source separation foundation model, running about 90 times faster than real time on a laptop CPU without needing a voice activity detector.
AI.motivation: Field recordings of animal calls contain weather, vehicle and animal noise; classical spectral gates leave residual noise without VAD, and detector-free neural bioacoustic denoisers remove less noise.
AI.method: SAM-Audio is used without training and prompted with time spans from a simple animal VAD, and its behaviour is distilled into a small detector-free denoiser; because SI-SDR penalizes regenerated output and conflates noise removal with call fidelity, separate metrics are used alongside it.
AI.result: Prompted SAM-Audio removes more noise than either spectral gates or detector-free bioacoustic denoisers. CallCleaner leaves 11 dB less noise around the call than Biodenoising, the leading neural bioacoustic denoiser with public weights, and among fast CPU-capable systems it pushes the Pareto frontier of noise removal against call fidelity without a detector.
AI.conclusion: Code and weights are released for fast, private, local denoising of single-caller recordings without specialized hardware, and SI-SDR is shown to be a limited metric in this setting.

title: Review the Episodes, Refine the Lessons: Simple Memory Evolution for Embodied Agents
summary: Recent studies of embodied agents based on frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) develop harness engineering around the MLLM, such as harnesses with post-trained policies and recursive self-improvement loops. Yet whether these additions exceed the native capability of the MLLM remains unexplored. We introduce SimplEvo to explore how far an MLLM can improve under direct control when it retains its execution experience in self-written text memories. It requires no weight updates, post-trained policies, or privileged information. The MLLM writes a coordinate-free task memory once from a single demonstration. Under a strict train-test protocol, it then creates a bounded working memory on training episodes only and refines it after each episode with lessons on procedure, completion, and recovery. Both memories stay fixed at test time. On EBench, SimplEvo lifts the success rate (SR) of GPT-6-Astra under direct control from 46.7% to 81.7%, and tops the RoboDojo leaderboard with 69.63% SR and a score of 75.32. Compared with memories that also store past visual frames, SimplEvo reaches a similar SR with text memory alone while using fewer tokens. With its memories fixed, SimplEvo also generalizes to unseen layouts and randomized scene configurations. Moreover, the working memory transfers across models: written by GPT-6-Astra, it can be reused as is by weaker MLLMs and improve their performance without any adaptation of their own.

AI.tldr: SimplEvo lets a frontier MLLM improve embodied agents by writing and refining its own text memories from execution experience, with no weight updates, lifting GPT-6-Astra's success rate on EBench from 46.7% to 81.7%.
AI.motivation: Embodied agent studies add harness engineering around MLLMs, such as post-trained policies and recursive self-improvement loops, but whether these additions exceed the MLLM's native capability has not been explored.
AI.method: The MLLM writes a coordinate-free task memory once from a single demonstration, then builds a bounded working memory on training episodes only and refines it after each episode with lessons on procedure, completion and recovery; both memories are fixed at test time, and no weight updates, post-trained policies or privileged information are used.
AI.result: On EBench, SimplEvo lifts GPT-6-Astra's success rate under direct control from 46.7% to 81.7%, and it tops the RoboDojo leaderboard with 69.63% SR and a score of 75.32. Text memory alone reaches a success rate similar to memories that also store past visual frames while using fewer tokens. The memories generalize to unseen layouts and randomized scene configurations, and working memory written by GPT-6-Astra improves weaker MLLMs without their adaptation.
AI.conclusion: A frontier MLLM can improve substantially under direct control through self-written text memories alone, and these memories transfer across models.

title: K-PWM: Control-Oriented Structured Bilinear World Models under Partial Observation
summary: World models learn internal simulators of environment dynamics for prediction, planning, and control, yet learning them from limited, noisy, and partial observations remains challenging. While much progress has focused on pixel-based observations, many physical systems instead provide vector-valued measurements that reveal only part of the underlying state. We introduce K-PWM, a probabilistic world model for prediction and control under partial observation. K-PWM couples Koopman-bilinear latent dynamics with a nonlinear observation decoder and performs probabilistic latent-state inference through the learned model via extended Kalman filtering and smoothing, without a separately trained inference network. Its bilinear structure enables exact propagation of the maintained Gaussian belief through the latent transition and efficient rollouts for uncertainty-aware model predictive path integral (MPPI) control. For training K-PWM, we present a generalized expectation conditional maximization (GECM) procedure with closed-form updates for the generators, noise covariances, and latent prior, complemented by gradient-based decoder learning. A Koopman-consistent initialization selects the latent dimension from data and initializes the action-dependent dynamics. With limited training data, K-PWM achieves lower long-horizon prediction error than the evaluated baselines on partially observed Gymnasium MuJoCo systems, while substantially reducing training time relative to the strongest prediction baseline. On high-dimensional MuJoCo Menagerie robots, it achieves competitive tracking accuracy with low per-step computation times, demonstrating potential for real-time deployment. These results support structured probabilistic dynamics as a data- and compute-efficient approach to world modeling and control under partial observation.

AI.tldr: K-PWM is a probabilistic world model that couples Koopman-bilinear latent dynamics with a nonlinear observation decoder and infers latent states by extended Kalman filtering and smoothing, for prediction and MPPI control under partial observation.
AI.motivation: Many physical systems provide vector-valued measurements that reveal only part of the underlying state, and learning world models from limited, noisy, partial observations remains challenging.
AI.method: The bilinear structure gives exact propagation of the Gaussian belief through the latent transition and efficient uncertainty-aware MPPI rollouts; training uses a generalized expectation conditional maximization procedure with closed-form updates for the generators, noise covariances and latent prior, plus gradient-based decoder learning; a Koopman-consistent initialization selects the latent dimension from data.
AI.result: With limited training data K-PWM achieves lower long-horizon prediction error than the evaluated baselines on partially observed Gymnasium MuJoCo systems, while substantially reducing training time relative to the strongest prediction baseline. On high-dimensional MuJoCo Menagerie robots it achieves competitive tracking accuracy with low per-step computation times.
AI.conclusion: Structured probabilistic dynamics are a data- and compute-efficient approach to world modeling and control under partial observation, with potential for real-time deployment.

title: Music Inpainting With Similarity-Guided Latent Diffusion
comment: Accepted to ISMIR 2026. 8 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Code and audio examples: this https URL
summary: We propose a music inpainting technique combining similarity matching and a diffusion-based generative model to replace large segments of audio recordings with suitable alternatives. The proposed hybrid method, Similarity-Guided Diffusion Posterior Sampling (SimDPS), retrieves candidate replacement segments from the wider signal based on contextual similarity and uses them to guide the diffusion process toward coherent reconstructions. Being model-agnostic, the framework is compatible with any pre-trained diffusion model operating in either the waveform or latent domain. Objective evaluations demonstrate that SimDPS outperforms widely adopted RePaint and DPS methods across acoustic features and neural-embedding distance metrics. Subjective evaluations on multi-genre music datasets confirm that SimDPS enhances perceptual plausibility compared to previous diffusion-based methods and demonstrates robustness to poorly matched similarity candidates. These findings pave the way for improved music restoration and context-aware audio editing.

AI.tldr: SimDPS fills large audio segments by retrieving similar context from the wider signal and using it to guide a pre-trained diffusion model during posterior sampling, outperforming RePaint and DPS on objective and subjective measures.
AI.motivation: Replacing large segments of audio recordings requires alternatives that fit the surrounding music, and the paper compares against RePaint and DPS, two widely adopted diffusion-based methods.
AI.method: Similarity-Guided Diffusion Posterior Sampling retrieves candidate replacement segments from the wider signal by contextual similarity and uses them to guide the diffusion process; the framework is model-agnostic and works with any pre-trained diffusion model in the waveform or latent domain.
AI.result: Objective evaluation across acoustic features and neural-embedding distance metrics shows SimDPS outperforms RePaint and DPS. Subjective evaluation on multi-genre music datasets confirms higher perceptual plausibility than previous diffusion-based methods, and the method is robust to poorly matched similarity candidates.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid approach improves music restoration and context-aware audio editing.

title: Ostinato: Fast CPU-GPU MoE Inference for Local Agents via Resident Experts in Every Forward Pass
summary: Language-model agents increasingly run on workstations with a few consumer GPUs, where large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models keep part of their experts in host memory. With existing CPU-GPU engines, these agents get fast prefill or fast decode, not both: this http URL's expert cache skips forward passes of more than 32 tokens to keep the experts of decode cached, so an agent waits 2.1-2.8 s after each tool output, whereas its default layer placement shortens this wait but is 1.5-1.6$\times$ slower in decode. Our key insight is that a short prefill touches too many distinct experts to upload, yet sends 84% of its expert activations (routes) to a stable set of experts that fits in GPU memory. We present Ostinato, a CPU-GPU MoE inference engine that computes these experts on the GPUs in every forward pass without changing what the model computes. Short prefills split their routes, leaving fewer than one of a token's six routed experts per layer to the CPU; long prefills upload each distinct cold expert once; and each decode step runs as one fixed-shape CUDA graph per GPU. On real coding and customer-service agent sessions with DeepSeek-V4-Flash on four RTX 4090D GPUs, Ostinato is the fastest engine in both phases and finishes every session sooner than all six baselines. Against this http URL and KTransformers, it cuts the median wait after a tool output by 22-55% and finishes sessions 1.4-2.5$\times$ sooner.

AI.tldr: Ostinato is a CPU-GPU MoE inference engine that keeps a stable set of experts computed on GPUs in every forward pass, so both prefill and decode are fast for local agents on consumer GPUs.
AI.motivation: Existing engines give agents fast prefill or fast decode but not both: the baseline engine's expert cache skips offloaded forward passes over 32 tokens, so agents wait 2.1-2.8 s after each tool output, while its default layer placement shortens that wait but is 1.5-1.6x slower in decode.
AI.method: Short prefills split their routes so that fewer than one of a token's six routed experts per layer goes to the CPU; long prefills upload each distinct cold expert once; each decode step runs as one fixed-shape CUDA graph per GPU; the model's computation is unchanged.
AI.result: On real coding and customer-service agent sessions with DeepSeek-V4-Flash on four RTX 4090D GPUs, Ostinato is the fastest engine in both phases and finishes every session sooner than all six baselines. Against the cache-based baseline and KTransformers it cuts the median wait after a tool output by 22-55% and finishes sessions 1.4-2.5x sooner.
AI.conclusion: Keeping hot experts on the GPUs in every forward pass shortens the wait between agent turns and speeds whole sessions on consumer GPU workstations.

title: PRISM: Causal Counterfactual Minimization of Agent Tool Privileges via Information Bottleneck Role Induction
summary: This paper shifts the object of role engineering from human users to large language model (LLM) agents, and proposes PRISM to address the over-authorization that arises when an agent obtains full tool privileges through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). PRISM formulates whether a tool is necessary for a task as an intervenable causal proposition, and applies structured interventions in a sandbox to learn a counterfactual necessity model. It then compresses trajectories into discrete latent variables through an information bottleneck, and determines the number of roles from the knee of the rate-distortion curve. Finally, it formalizes pruning as a bilevel Stackelberg game, in which a generative flow network samples diverse near-optimal solutions. On three public benchmarks, AgentDojo, $\tau$-bench and ToolEmu, PRISM compresses the number of authorized tools per role by 78.3%, attains a task success rate of 78.2%, reaches a counterfactual necessity accuracy of 88.7%, and lowers the blast radius to 15.9%.

AI.tldr: PRISM reduces an LLM agent's MCP tool privileges by learning causally which tools each task needs, then clusters the resulting roles and prunes with a bilevel Stackelberg game sampled by a generative flow network.
AI.motivation: Agents that obtain full tool privileges through the Model Context Protocol are over-authorized, and role engineering has so far targeted human users rather than LLM agents.
AI.method: Whether a tool is necessary is treated as an intervenable causal proposition, and structured sandbox interventions train a counterfactual necessity model; trajectories are compressed into discrete latent variables by an information bottleneck, with the number of roles set at the knee of the rate-distortion curve; pruning is a bilevel Stackelberg game in which a generative flow network samples diverse near-optimal solutions.
AI.result: On AgentDojo, tau-bench and ToolEmu, PRISM compresses the authorized tools per role by 78.3%, attains a task success rate of 78.2%, reaches 88.7% counterfactual necessity accuracy, and lowers the blast radius to 15.9%.
AI.conclusion: Least-privilege role design can be applied to LLM agents by treating tool necessity causally, which limits how much damage an over-privileged agent can do.

title: Not All Branches Are Equal: Adaptive Semantic ID Construction for Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation models represent items as sequences of discrete tokens known as semantic IDs. Existing approaches derive these identifiers using residual or hierarchical vector quantization, assuming that tokens carry independent semantic meaning across quantization levels. Revisiting this assumption, we argue that semantic IDs should behave as hierarchical paths where each token's meaning is conditioned on its prefix. This highlights a mismatch between conventional fixed-codebook quantization and the hierarchical structure implicitly learned by generative recommenders. Motivated by this insight, we propose Adaptive Silhouette Tree (AST), a top-down divisive clustering method that constructs semantic IDs as paths within a tree structure. Unlike prior methods with fixed branching factors, AST dynamically determines the number of branches at each node by maximizing the silhouette coefficient, enabling finer partitions in dense regions and compact groupings in homogeneous ones. We further introduce constrained variants that enforce minimum probability mass during splitting to improve supervision for long-tail items. Extensive experiments on five Amazon Review datasets of varying sizes and domains show that AST significantly outperforms strong baselines. These results demonstrate that aligning semantic ID construction with the inherent hierarchical structure of generative recommenders leads to more effective recommendations.

AI.tldr: Adaptive Silhouette Tree builds semantic IDs as paths in a tree whose branching factor at each node is chosen by maximizing the silhouette coefficient, and significantly outperforms strong baselines on five Amazon Review datasets.
AI.motivation: Residual and hierarchical vector quantization assume each token carries independent meaning across levels, whereas the hierarchical structure implicitly learned by generative recommenders means each token's meaning depends on its prefix, a mismatch with fixed-codebook quantization.
AI.method: A top-down divisive clustering builds semantic IDs as hierarchical paths and dynamically sets the number of branches at each node by silhouette maximization, so dense regions are partitioned finely and homogeneous ones grouped compactly; constrained variants enforce a minimum probability mass during splitting to improve supervision for long-tail items.
AI.result: Experiments on five Amazon Review datasets of varying sizes and domains show that AST significantly outperforms strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: Aligning semantic ID construction with the hierarchical structure of generative recommenders leads to more effective recommendations.

title: HydroTuring: A physics probe benchmark testing mass, energy, and momentum conservation in hydrologic models
summary: Hydrologic models, including deep learning systems now deployed for operational flood forecasting, are evaluated primarily by how closely their simulated hydrographs match observed streamflow. However, high hydrograph skill does not guarantee physical consistency: in a synthetic calibration experiment, a conceptual model that loses 15% of its water input to an unreported sink still reaches a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.93, and no shared benchmark tests whether models obey fundamental conservation laws. Here we introduce HydroTuring (v0.1.0), a black-box benchmark of 37 physics probes that test mass (24 probes), energy (7) and momentum (6) conservation in hydrologic models. Each probe runs a controlled experiment on forcing generated at run time from a recorded seed and applies binary pass or fail criteria validated against 18 physically exact and 59 deliberately broken reference models. Across 32 evaluated models (3 exact references, 7 AI-based models and 22 process-based models), only the 3 exact references pass every probe among the 28 models scored on 5 or more probes. Process-based and AI-based models pass similar shares of their scored probes (76% and 74%), and a pre-trained flood-forecasting LSTM fails 6 of the 11 runoff-only probes it can be scored on. Furthermore, 49% of all 1,184 model-probe pairs remain unscored because models omit the required state or flux variables, while the scored failures occur in perturbation responses and state bounds rather than long-term water-budget closure. HydroTuring provides a reproducible smoke test for model development, peer review and operational deployment under an open community protocol.

AI.tldr: HydroTuring is a black-box benchmark of 37 physics probes testing mass, energy and momentum conservation in hydrologic models, showing that high hydrograph skill does not guarantee physical consistency.
AI.motivation: Hydrologic models are judged mainly by how closely hydrographs match observed streamflow, yet in a synthetic experiment a conceptual model losing 15% of its water to an unreported sink still reaches a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.93, and no shared benchmark tests conservation laws.
AI.method: Each probe runs a controlled experiment on forcing generated at run time from a recorded seed and applies binary pass or fail criteria validated against 18 physically exact and 59 deliberately broken reference models; the probes cover mass (24), energy (7) and momentum (6) conservation.
AI.result: Across 32 evaluated models (3 exact references, 7 AI-based, 22 process-based), only the 3 exact references pass every probe among the 28 models scored on 5 or more probes. Process-based and AI-based models pass similar shares of their scored probes (76% and 74%), and a pre-trained flood-forecasting LSTM fails 6 of the 11 runoff-only probes it can be scored on. 49% of all 1,184 model-probe pairs remain unscored because models omit required state or flux variables, and scored failures occur in perturbation responses and state bounds rather than long-term water-budget closure.
