AI.conclusion: HydroTuring provides a reproducible smoke test for model development, peer review and operational deployment under an open community protocol.

title: From Sound to Occupancy: Privacy-Aware Audio Sensing for Buildings
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Occupancy-based controls regulate lighting and HVAC according to whether a space is in use. Passive infrared (PIR) sensors, the most common choice, respond to motion and can report an occupied room as vacant when its occupants remain still. Sound offers an alternative cue, since seated occupants type, turn pages and cough, but microphones raise privacy concerns. We therefore study a two-stage design: an on-device encoder maps each second of audio to a short embedding, and a server-side temporal model turns the stream of embeddings into an occupancy state. To our knowledge, no publicly available dataset pairs office audio with occupancy labels, so we evaluate the two stages separately on public data. The encoder is trained on synthetic scenes that mix empty-room recordings, room impulse responses, office sounds and read speech, and tested on unseen rooms, recordings and speakers for whether a second contains a sound made by a person. On 11 real office recordings (DCASE 2013) it reaches an AUC of 0.87, against 0.76 for log-mel statistics. Attacks on the transmitted embeddings recover at most 1% of the spoken words, against 94% from log-mel frames, but still identify the speaker among 40 in 69 to 77% of the utterances. Noise-floor normalization with adversarial training, an 8-dimensional embedding, or sending only class probabilities lowers this to 38 to 55% without hurting detection. On HPDmobile, which pairs home occupancy labels with an amplitude envelope of the audio, a causal temporal model pretrained with a hierarchical contrastive loss matches hand-crafted features (AUC 0.75) and does better when only one labelled day per home is available. These results make the two-stage design a practical basis for privacy-aware acoustic occupancy sensing, with speaker identity as the one leak still to close.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-stage privacy-aware audio occupancy sensor, with an on-device encoder producing per-second embeddings and a server-side temporal model inferring occupancy, reaching AUC 0.87 on 11 real office recordings.
AI.motivation: PIR sensors can report an occupied room as vacant when occupants are still, while microphones raise privacy concerns, and no publicly available dataset pairs office audio with occupancy labels.
AI.method: An on-device encoder maps each second of audio to a short embedding, trained on synthetic scenes that mix empty-room recordings, room impulse responses, office sounds and read speech; a server-side temporal model turns the embedding stream into an occupancy state, and on HPDmobile it is a causal model pretrained with a hierarchical contrastive loss; the two stages are evaluated separately on public data.
AI.result: On 11 DCASE 2013 office recordings the encoder reaches AUC 0.87 against 0.76 for log-mel statistics. Attacks on transmitted embeddings recover at most 1% of spoken words, against 94% from log-mel frames, but still identify the speaker among 40 in 69-77% of utterances. Noise-floor normalization with adversarial training, an 8-dimensional embedding or sending only class probabilities lowers speaker identification to 38-55% without hurting detection. On HPDmobile the causal temporal model matches hand-crafted features (AUC 0.75) and does better when only one labelled day per home is available.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage design is a practical basis for privacy-aware acoustic occupancy sensing, with speaker identity the one leak that remains to be closed.

title: Recursive Pricing and Incumbent Subtree Column Generation for Solving Optimal Classification Trees
summary: Solving optimal classification tree (OCT) problems is computationally challenging because branching, routing, and leaf-assignment decisions must be optimized jointly. We develop an incumbent subtree column generation algorithm (ISCG-OCT) that exploits the recursive structure of classification trees. We first introduce a mixed set-packing and set-partitioning formulation (MSSF). We then construct a restricted master problem whose columns represent feasible subtree patterns. Unlike conventional dual-based column generation, our incumbent-centered pricing evaluates objective improvements relative to the current solution. We establish a recursive decomposition in which fixing a branching decision separates the remaining pricing problem into independent subtree subproblems, enabling exact dynamic programming. We also develop threshold-based variants that trade optimality guarantees for computational efficiency. Computational experiments on 27 benchmark datasets demonstrate competitive training and testing accuracy and substantial reductions in solution time on many instances. When initialized with a CART solution, ISCG-OCT can certify global optimality faster than warm-started mixed-integer programming solvers on selected instances. These results demonstrate how recursive pricing and structured subtree optimization can improve the computational efficiency of exact classification tree methods.

AI.tldr: ISCG-OCT is an exact column generation method for optimal classification trees whose incumbent-centered pricing decomposes recursively into independent subtree subproblems solved by dynamic programming.
AI.motivation: Optimal classification tree problems are computationally hard because branching, routing and leaf-assignment decisions must be optimized jointly.
AI.method: A mixed set-packing and set-partitioning formulation (MSSF) is solved through a restricted master problem whose columns are feasible subtree patterns; unlike dual-based column generation, pricing measures objective improvement relative to the current solution; fixing a branching decision separates the pricing problem into independent subtree subproblems solved by exact dynamic programming; threshold-based variants trade optimality guarantees for speed.
AI.result: On 27 benchmark datasets the method shows competitive training and testing accuracy and substantial solution-time reductions on many instances. Initialized with a CART solution, ISCG-OCT certifies global optimality faster than warm-started mixed-integer programming solvers on selected instances.
AI.conclusion: Recursive pricing and structured subtree optimization can improve the computational efficiency of exact classification tree methods.

title: Weight-Space Programming of Policies and Their Verification via Model Checking
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can write the weights of small neural networks directly, without gradient descent. This weight-space programming creates policies for sequential decision-making from a task description alone, but nothing guarantees that a written policy behaves as intended. We combine weight-space programming with probabilistic model checking. Given an environment modeled as a Markov decision process and a requirement in probabilistic computation tree logic (PCTL), an LLM writes all weights of a policy network, optionally repairs them on a dataset of optimal actions, and receives model-checking feedback until the requirement holds or a round limit is reached. The model checker Storm computes, rather than estimates from simulations, the probability that the policy satisfies the requirement, so every returned policy is verified. With two LLMs on three environments, the created policy of each of the 18 runs attains the optimal probability, before any dataset or model-checking feedback. Four of six policies programmed for two transporter jobs also complete three jobs with probability 1, so they generalize to a task that the LLM never saw. The pipeline also programs a policy that satisfies a complex safety requirement expressed with the PCTL until operator in all six runs. In one of them, dataset repair raised the accuracy to 98.4\% but broke the requirement, and one round of model-checking feedback restored it.

AI.tldr: An LLM writes all weights of a small policy network, which a probabilistic model checker (Storm) then verifies against a PCTL requirement, so every returned policy comes with a computed satisfaction probability.
AI.motivation: Weight-space programming lets LLMs create sequential decision policies from a task description without gradient descent, but nothing guarantees that a written policy behaves as intended.
AI.method: Given an MDP and a PCTL requirement, an LLM writes all policy network weights, optionally repairs them on a dataset of optimal actions, and receives model-checking feedback until the requirement holds or a round limit is reached; Storm computes the satisfaction probability rather than estimating it from simulations.
AI.result: With two LLMs on three environments, the policy created in each of the 18 runs attains the optimal probability before any dataset or model-checking feedback. Four of six policies programmed for two transporter jobs also complete three jobs with probability 1, so they generalize to a task the LLM never saw. The pipeline programs a policy satisfying a complex PCTL until requirement in all six runs. In one run dataset repair raised accuracy to 98.4% but broke the requirement, and one round of model-checking feedback restored it.
AI.conclusion: Pairing LLM-written policies with probabilistic model checking yields verified policies, and model-checking feedback can repair regressions introduced by dataset tuning.

title: Brain-Aligned Latent Actions: Imposing Premotor Cortex Geometry on a Robot's Action Vocabulary
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Robot manipulation results (CALVIN) will be added in a later version
summary: Robot policies increasingly act through a small vocabulary of discrete latent actions learned from unlabeled video, yet training leaves open which motion receives which code. We find this choice highly unstable: two independently trained runs of Moto's latent motion tokenizer assign the same robot clips to nearly unrelated codes (adjusted Rand index 0.001), and evaluating one tokenizer in bf16 instead of fp32 reassigns 74% of its tokens. We use this freedom to impose the representational geometry of macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv), recorded while a monkey drew shapes, on the tokenizer's code assignment, with a straight-through similarity loss trained alongside its reconstruction objective on robot video. In one training run per target, on five shape categories the loss never saw, the PMv-trained tokenizer reaches a representational similarity of 0.52 with PMv, against 0.20-0.26 for released and no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for the 95th percentile of random kinematic encoders. Kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer (-0.17 to -0.03). Two results limit the claim: a hand-picked kinematic descriptor, the stroke's initial direction, matches PMv better (0.65), and a label-shuffled PMv control scores 0.41. We specify the downstream manipulation test, on a CALVIN pipeline that reproduces Moto's published results, before running it.

AI.tldr: The paper imposes macaque premotor cortex (PMv) representational geometry on a robot video tokenizer's latent action codes through a straight-through similarity loss, reaching similarity 0.52 with PMv against 0.20-0.26 for released tokenizers.
AI.motivation: Latent action tokenizers trained on unlabeled video assign codes unstably: two runs of Moto's tokenizer give the same robot clips nearly unrelated codes (adjusted Rand index 0.001), and evaluating in bf16 instead of fp32 reassigns 74% of tokens.
AI.method: The tokenizer's code assignment is trained with a straight-through similarity loss alongside its reconstruction objective on robot video, with PMv recordings from a monkey drawing shapes as the target geometry; kinematic, language and random targets and a label-shuffled PMv control serve as comparisons.
AI.result: On five shape categories the loss never saw, the PMv-trained tokenizer reaches representational similarity 0.52 with PMv, against 0.20-0.26 for released and no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for the 95th percentile of random kinematic encoders. Kinematic, language and random targets do not transfer (-0.17 to -0.03). A hand-picked descriptor, the stroke's initial direction, matches PMv better (0.65), and a label-shuffled PMv control scores 0.41.
AI.conclusion: The result is a candidate brain-aligned prior for latent actions; the downstream manipulation test on a CALVIN pipeline that reproduces Moto's published results is specified but not yet run, so any manipulation benefit remains untested.

title: A Sequential Monte Carlo Method for Data Assimilation in Subsurface Flow Systems with Hierarchical Uncertainty
summary: Subsurface flow systems often involve hierarchical geological uncertainty, meaning both higher-level metaparameters and cell-by-cell properties are uncertain. This leads to challenges for data assimilation because both sets of parameters must be estimated. In this work we develop an adaptive-tempered sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) procedure for joint Bayesian estimation of these quantities. The method uses noncentered geological parameterizations, with geomodel realizations represented by metaparameters and Gaussian latent variables that are independent under the prior. Adaptive likelihood tempering, importance weighting, resampling, and blockwise Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) mutation are applied at each iteration. Flow surrogates are used for all function evaluations. The hierarchical SMC procedure is further extended to treat successive data assimilation. In this case, existing posterior particles are updated in a manner that accounts for correlations in surrogate model errors across observation batches. We consider two distinct 3D systems with hierarchical uncertainty. The first is a faulted carbon storage system containing three stacked aquifers and two extensive faults. Principal component analysis is used to represent target-aquifer heterogeneity, while geological metaparameters characterize uncertain aquifer and fault properties. The second is a channelized oil-water system containing three facies with uncertain properties. A latent diffusion model represents variability in channel geometry and facies realizations. For the four synthetic true models considered, SMC posterior metaparameter distributions and flow predictions agree closely with reference MCMC results. SMC, however, requires fewer function evaluations and provides speedups of 2.5--7.0 for single-stage data assimilation. Even greater speedups are achieved with multiple GPUs.

AI.tldr: An adaptive-tempered sequential Monte Carlo procedure jointly estimates higher-level geological metaparameters and cell-by-cell properties in subsurface flow models, matching reference MCMC results with 2.5-7.0x speedups for single-stage data assimilation.
AI.motivation: Subsurface flow systems have hierarchical geological uncertainty, in which both metaparameters and cell-by-cell properties are unknown and must be estimated together, which makes data assimilation difficult.
AI.method: Adaptive likelihood tempering, importance weighting, resampling and blockwise MCMC mutation are applied at each iteration, with noncentered geological parameterizations (metaparameters and independent Gaussian latent variables) and flow surrogates for all function evaluations; for successive data assimilation, existing particles are updated to account for correlated surrogate errors across observation batches.
AI.result: On a faulted three-aquifer carbon storage system and a channelized three-facies oil-water system, using PCA and a latent diffusion model for the heterogeneity respectively, SMC posterior metaparameter distributions and flow predictions agree closely with reference MCMC results for four synthetic true models. SMC requires fewer function evaluations and gives speedups of 2.5-7.0 for single-stage assimilation, with greater speedups on multiple GPUs.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical SMC procedure is an efficient alternative to MCMC for joint Bayesian estimation under hierarchical geological uncertainty, including sequential data assimilation.

title: Streaming Failure Forecasting: VLA Failure Monitors That Keep Learning After Deployment
comment: 25 pages, 13 figures, 9 tables. A short version was accepted at the Sim2Real2Field and EEAI workshops at CoRL 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Failure monitors for vision-language-action (VLA) policies are trained offline and then frozen. After deployment, lighting, objects and cameras drift, and the policy itself is updated or moved to new tasks. On recorded real-robot runs, after a switch of task or policy version, a frozen monitor fit on the old task ranks failures little better than chance. We present Streaming Failure Forecasting (SFF), a monitor that keeps learning from the one label every episode provides: whether it succeeded. SFF keeps the offline monitor's network fixed and refits only its last linear layer after each episode, at 2.18 ms per policy call on a Jetson CPU core. Its alarm threshold moves only after successes, which in simulation kept false alarms near target except when two drifts came at once. With every setting locked before testing, SFF ranks failures better than the same monitor kept frozen on 4 of 5 simulated test suites under unannounced drift, and above resetting on detected drift on every suite. Carried with its locked learner settings to 434 recorded runs of four VLAs on real SO-101 arms, replayed across unannounced switches of task or policy version, it ranks failures better than the frozen monitor for every VLA and, in an exploratory comparison, above a full reset at the true switch. A deployed failure monitor need not stay frozen: refitting its readout from outcomes is cheap and helps after the changes we tested.

AI.tldr: Streaming Failure Forecasting refits only the last linear layer of a VLA failure monitor after each episode, using the episode's success label, so the monitor keeps adapting after deployment and ranks failures better than a frozen monitor under drift.
AI.motivation: Failure monitors for vision-language-action policies are trained offline and then frozen, while lighting, objects, cameras and the policy itself change after deployment, and a frozen monitor fit on the old task ranks failures little better than chance after a switch.
AI.method: The offline monitor's network stays fixed while its last linear layer is refit after each episode from the success or failure outcome; the alarm threshold moves only after successes; the monitor runs at 2.18 ms per policy call on a Jetson CPU core, and all settings were locked before testing.
AI.result: In simulation SFF ranks failures better than the frozen monitor on 4 of 5 test suites under unannounced drift and beats resetting on detected drift on every suite, with false alarms kept near target except when two drifts came at once. On 434 recorded runs of four VLAs on real SO-101 arms, replayed across unannounced task or policy-version switches, it ranks failures better than the frozen monitor for every VLA and, in an exploratory comparison, above a full reset at the true switch.
AI.conclusion: Refitting a failure monitor's readout from outcomes is cheap and helps after the changes tested, so a deployed failure monitor need not stay frozen.

title: Homological Barriers to Stable Learning of First-Order Nash Equilibria
comment: The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2026
summary: We identify a homological barrier to stable learning of local Nash equilibria, also known as first-order Nash equilibria (FONE), in constrained non-concave differentiable games. We consider continuous deterministic learning dynamics that fix every FONE point and aim to attract all initial conditions to the full FONE set. We show that this convergence guarantee is impossible when the target set has nontrivial positive-degree cohomology, such as that arising from a loop, and the state space is compact and contractible. We exhibit this barrier in a simple non-concave quadratic zero-sum game on a box whose exact FONE set consists of a diagonal six-edge loop and an isolated point. Consequently, no such dynamics can make the full FONE set a stable global attractor. We further show that degree two is the minimal polynomial degree at which this barrier can arise and extend the construction to obtain nontrivial homology in arbitrarily high degrees. Finally, we establish that the barrier persists for sufficiently small approximate-FONE targets under small perturbations, yielding an open, positive-volume family of quadratic zero-sum games with the same homological barrier.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that no continuous deterministic learning dynamics can make the full set of first-order Nash equilibria a stable global attractor when that set has nontrivial positive-degree cohomology, such as a loop.
AI.motivation: The question is whether dynamics that fix every first-order Nash equilibrium (FONE) in constrained non-concave differentiable games can attract all initial conditions to the full FONE set, a topological requirement the paper examines.
AI.method: The analysis considers continuous deterministic dynamics on a compact, contractible state space and uses the homology of the target FONE set; the barrier is exhibited in a quadratic zero-sum game on a box whose exact FONE set is a diagonal six-edge loop plus an isolated point.
AI.result: Such convergence is impossible when the target set has nontrivial positive-degree cohomology. Degree two is the minimal polynomial degree at which the barrier can arise, and the construction extends to nontrivial homology in arbitrarily high degrees. The barrier persists for sufficiently small approximate-FONE targets under small perturbations, giving an open, positive-volume family of quadratic zero-sum games with the same barrier.
AI.conclusion: Stable global learning of the full FONE set is topologically obstructed in general, so no learning dynamics of this type can guarantee it.

title: Data-Driven Precision Control of Soft Helicoid Robots
comment: Submitted to npj Robotics. 44 pages, supplementary information included
summary: A purely data-driven method grounded in the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) was recently used to model and control nonlinear soft robotic simulators. Here, we extend the methodology to learn aSSM-reduced models from data collected from hardware soft robotic platforms. Specifically, we learn a five dimensional (5D) aSSM-reduced nonlinear ordinary differential equation (ODE) that accurately models the dynamics of a soft-helicoid trunk robot. We then use this ODE in a model predictive control scheme to demonstrate real-time precision control across various challenging closed-loop trajectory-tracking tasks, ranging from 2D to 3D trajectories with static and dynamic constraints. We find that our methodology enhances accuracy and precision across all control tasks compared to available data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning. While we focus here on a soft-helicoid trunk robot, our methodology relies solely on hardware data and is therefore applicable to a broader class of soft robotic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper learns a 5-dimensional adiabatic spectral submanifold (aSSM) reduced ODE directly from hardware data of a soft-helicoid trunk robot and uses it in model predictive control for precise real-time trajectory tracking.
AI.motivation: Prior data-driven aSSM methods were demonstrated only on simulators, and data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning are less accurate for controlling nonlinear soft robots.
AI.method: A purely data-driven aSSM-reduced model is learned from hardware data as a 5D nonlinear ODE and embedded in a model predictive control scheme for closed-loop 2D and 3D trajectory tracking with static and dynamic constraints.
AI.result: The aSSM-based controller improves accuracy and precision across all tested control tasks compared with data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning.
AI.conclusion: Because the method relies only on hardware data, it is claimed to apply to a broader class of soft robotic systems beyond the trunk robot studied.

title: CRUSTPairs: A Cross-Language Dataset of Paired C and Rust Solutions
summary: C-to-Rust migration is an active agenda, but no dataset pairs the two languages at the level of whole solutions to a shared problem. We present CRUSTPairs, 1857 C/Rust implementation pairs drawn from competitive programming archives, normalised, deduplicated, and stratified into difficulty tiers by zero-shot cross-language embedding similarity, with perrecord provenance and licensing. Cross-language retrieval is hard on this data, and harder than a single baseline would suggest: TF-IDF over shared identifiers reaches MRR 0.21 and so beats a pretrained code model at 0.19, which on the hardest quarter of the data scores 1.7x chance. Finetuning reaches 0.79, and lifts that hardest quarter 10x. Renaming every user identifier settles what is being learned: the finetuned models keep 96-97% of their accuracy without them, while the pretrained model keeps 66\% - less than the lexical baseline does - and on structurally divergent pairs the finetuned models are better without identifiers than with them.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CRUSTPairs, a dataset of 1857 aligned C and Rust solutions to competitive programming problems, and shows that cross-language retrieval on it is hard, with finetuned embeddings far outperforming lexical and pretrained baselines.
AI.motivation: No existing dataset pairs C and Rust at the level of whole solutions to a shared problem, which C-to-Rust migration research needs.
AI.method: The pairs are drawn from competitive programming archives, normalised, deduplicated and stratified into difficulty tiers by zero-shot cross-language embedding similarity, with per-record provenance and licensing; retrieval is evaluated with TF-IDF over shared identifiers, a pretrained code model and finetuned models, including identifier-renaming ablations.
AI.result: TF-IDF reaches MRR 0.21 versus 0.19 for the pretrained code model, and on the hardest quarter the pretrained model scores 1.7x chance; finetuning reaches MRR 0.79 and improves the hardest quarter 10x. With all user identifiers renamed, finetuned models keep 96-97% of their accuracy while the pretrained model keeps 66%.
AI.conclusion: Finetuned models learn structure rather than identifier names, and on structurally divergent pairs they perform better without identifiers, showing that cross-language retrieval is harder than a single baseline suggests.

title: Accelerated Reinforcement Learning for Soft Robotics: Hours Instead of Years
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) requires large amounts of interaction data or a reliable simulator, both hard to obtain for nonlinear soft robotic hardware. Recent work shows that a time-scale separation inherent to soft robot dynamics justifies their reduction to low-dimensional invariant manifolds, known as adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs). We demonstrate that an aSSM-reduced model, a simple polynomial ordinary differential equation learned purely from pre-collected data, can serve as an RL training environment. On a pneumatically actuated soft arm, we train a trajectory-tracking policy in 3 hours on a six-dimensional aSSM-reduced model and deploy it without fine-tuning, whereas reproducing this policy training extrapolates to 3 years of hardware interaction. Our policy tracks dynamic targets with 40% lower error than otherwise identical policies trained on a 4.8-million-parameter recurrent neural network (RNN) or a 1.7-million-parameter transformer, which take 13 and 100 hours to identify, against 5 minutes for our mathematically justified 6,924-parameter model.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a low-dimensional polynomial aSSM-reduced ODE learned purely from pre-collected data can serve as an RL training environment, training a soft-arm trajectory-tracking policy in 3 hours that transfers to hardware without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning on nonlinear soft robotic hardware needs either large amounts of interaction data or a reliable simulator, and both are hard to obtain.
AI.method: A six-dimensional aSSM-reduced polynomial ODE is learned from pre-collected data on a pneumatically actuated soft arm and used as the RL training environment, and its policy is compared with policies trained on a recurrent neural network and a transformer model.
AI.result: The policy trained on the aSSM model tracks dynamic targets with 40% lower error than identical policies trained on a 4.8-million-parameter RNN or a 1.7-million-parameter transformer, which take 13 and 100 hours to identify; the aSSM model has 6,924 parameters and takes 5 minutes to identify.
AI.conclusion: Time-scale separation in soft robot dynamics makes a compact, mathematically justified model enough to replace years of hardware interaction with hours of training.

title: Particle Filtering with Generative Trajectory Models for State Estimation and Control
summary: Generative models can support both state estimation and control in robotics. For control, a common approach is to use the model as a policy that directly samples actions conditioned on observation histories. However, models that jointly represent states, actions, and observations can also predict how the robot state and its environment evolve. We investigate whether these predictions can improve state estimation and control through a change in inference procedure, without modifying the pretrained model. To this end, we use particle filtering to maintain competing hypotheses about state histories. A single pretrained diffusion model generates these hypotheses along with their predicted observations and associated action proposals. As new measurements arrive, particles are reweighted according to how well their predicted observations match the measurements. While particle filtering conventionally uses these weights only for state estimation, we also use them to guide action selection, favoring proposals associated with hypotheses that better explain the observations. Simulation experiments in partially observed navigation and vision-based manipulation demonstrate improvements in both state estimation and task performance compared to action generation without filtering, using the same pretrained model and no additional test-time information.

AI.tldr: The paper uses particle filtering over hypotheses generated by a single pretrained diffusion model, reweighting particles by how well their predicted observations match measurements, and uses these weights to also guide action selection.
AI.motivation: Generative models that jointly represent states, actions and observations can predict environment evolution, but they are usually used only as policies that sample actions from observation histories.
AI.method: A pretrained diffusion model generates competing state-history hypotheses with predicted observations and action proposals; particles are reweighted as measurements arrive, and the weights guide action selection toward proposals that better explain the observations, without modifying the model or using extra test-time information.
AI.result: In simulated partially observed navigation and vision-based manipulation, the method improves state estimation and task performance compared with action generation without filtering, using the same pretrained model.
AI.conclusion: Changing the inference procedure alone, without retraining, lets a pretrained generative robot model benefit from its predictions for both state estimation and control.

title: Planners Exploit Deterministic Error: Dithered Low-Bit World Models
summary: Sampling-based planners such as MPPI and CEM query a learned world model thousands of times per control step, so low-bit world models are an obvious way to make model-based control cheaper on a robot. With round-to-nearest activation quantization and no calibration, we find that planning can collapse, by up to 100 points of success, while the world model's latent one-step prediction error stays no larger than that of a stochastic rounding scheme that plans well. At the same bit width, what decides the outcome is not the size of the rounding error but whether it persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates. Round-to-nearest leaves an error that persists, and an iterating planner drifts toward the candidates that this error favors; in TD-MPC2, holding the same dither fixed within a step or an episode brings the drift back. Dither shared by all candidates and redrawn at every iteration removes most of the damage at the same bit width and without training: at least half of it in all 19 affected Meta-World cells (task $\times$ bit width) of TD-MPC2 (median 95%), in 4 of 5 DINO-WM cells, and in all 8 affected tasks of a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2. Captured as CUDA graphs on an Ampere GPU, a W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model runs its planning rollouts 1.9-3.3$\times$ and the whole planning step 1.3-1.5$\times$ faster than FP32, though not faster than BF16 with pre-converted weights; shared dither adds at most 2.3% latency. In TD-MPC2, block-scaled NVFP4 removes most of the damage and MXFP4 part of it, which ties the failure to coarse grids with a shared scale. Hypotheses, thresholds and analysis code were fixed before the data that test them, and the hypotheses that failed are reported.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that round-to-nearest activation quantization can collapse planning in low-bit world models used by sampling-based planners, and that sharing a dither that is redrawn at every planner iteration removes most of this damage without training.
AI.motivation: Low-bit world models would make sampling-based planners such as MPPI and CEM cheaper, but planning collapses under naive quantization even when one-step prediction error is no larger than that of a scheme that plans well.
AI.method: The authors compare round-to-nearest quantization with stochastic rounding and a shared dither, test whether the rounding error persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates, and evaluate TD-MPC2 and DINO-WM, plus CUDA-graph integer and NVFP4 and MXFP4 variants.
AI.result: Planning drops by up to 100 success points under round-to-nearest, and shared dither recovers at least half of the damage in all 19 affected TD-MPC2 Meta-World cells (median 95%), in 4 of 5 DINO-WM cells, and in all 8 affected tasks of a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2; a W8A4 integer model runs planning rollouts 1.9-3.3x faster than FP32, with at most 2.3% extra latency from shared dither.
AI.conclusion: The failure comes from quantization error that persists and is shared across candidates, which lets an iterating planner drift toward favoured candidates; block-scaled NVFP4 removes most of the damage, which points to coarse grids with a shared scale as the cause.

title: CABrain: A Correlation-Aware Brain Foundation Model for EEG Decoding
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models have emerged as promising paradigms for decoding brain activity through large-scale self-supervised pretraining. Notably, most existing approaches employ masked patch reconstruction, in which randomly selected EEG patches are masked and recovered by the network. However, purely random masking may limit representation learning as informative patches from highly correlated channels often remain unmasked, causing the network to underutilize weakly correlated channels or serial dependencies. Furthermore, because these models are typically based on transformer architectures, their performance is influenced by the choice of positional encoding. Although positional encoding has been extensively explored in natural language processing and computer vision, few studies have adapted it to the unique characteristics of EEG signals. To address these limitations, this study introduces a conditional positional encoding method based on graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to explicitly model inter-channel correlations, along with an adaptive masking strategy that enhances representation learning by modulating the difficulty of masked patch reconstruction. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to integrate graph-based representations into conditional positional encoding and introduce adaptive masking within EEG foundation model pretraining. Experimental results on ten benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed GCN-based positional encoding and adaptive masking strategies, both individually and in combination, achieve state-of-the-art or competitive performance, highlighting their effectiveness in EEG foundation modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CABrain, an EEG foundation model that uses graph-convolution-based conditional positional encoding to model inter-channel correlations and an adaptive masking strategy during self-supervised pretraining.
AI.motivation: Random masking in masked EEG patch reconstruction leaves informative patches from highly correlated channels unmasked, and positional encodings designed for language and vision are poorly suited to EEG.
AI.method: A conditional positional encoding based on graph convolutional networks models inter-channel correlations, and an adaptive masking strategy modulates the difficulty of masked patch reconstruction during pretraining.
AI.result: On ten benchmark EEG datasets, the GCN-based positional encoding and adaptive masking, individually and combined, achieve state-of-the-art or competitive performance.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based positional encoding and adaptive masking are effective components for EEG foundation model pretraining.

title: Operator Learning of Microstructure-Dependent Internal-Variable Models for Inelastic Homogenization: Approximation and Complexity
summary: We study the learning of homogenized constitutive laws for inelastic heterogeneous materials, aiming to replace costly concurrent unit-cell simulations with surrogates that generalize across loading histories and microstructures. We focus on the recurrent neural operator framework, motivated by the explicit form of homogenized Kelvin--Voigt linear viscoelasticity. In this framework, internal variables enable a Markovian approximation of loading-history dependence, and neural operators represent the microstructure-dependent constitutive response. For periodic Kelvin--Voigt viscoelasticity, we prove a universal approximation theorem showing that the model can approximate the homogenized constitutive law to any prescribed accuracy, uniformly in time and over a wide set of admissible strain trajectories and microstructural property fields, in two and three dimensions. This comprises a significant extension of the existing, somewhat limited, one-dimensional theory that uses explicit solutions for piecewise constant materials. Instead, in two and three dimensions, we adopt a more versatile approximation based on the spectral representation of the memory kernel that arises from homogenization. This also enables us to give an explicit bound on the internal-variable dimension, sufficient for approximation, exhibiting logarithmic growth in the inverse relative stress error and in material contrast. Numerical experiments on viscoelasticity and crystal plasticity complement the theory, illustrating the roles of internal-variable dimension and sample complexity in learning homogenized responses from unit-cell data. Theoretical results are formally verified in Lean 4.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a universal approximation theorem for recurrent neural operators that learn homogenized constitutive laws for periodic Kelvin-Voigt viscoelasticity in two and three dimensions, with an explicit bound on the internal-variable dimension.
AI.motivation: Costly concurrent unit-cell simulations of inelastic heterogeneous materials should be replaced by surrogates that generalize across loading histories and microstructures, and the existing one-dimensional theory is limited to piecewise constant materials.
AI.method: Internal variables give a Markovian approximation of loading-history dependence and neural operators represent the microstructure-dependent response; the approximation uses a spectral representation of the homogenized memory kernel, and the authors give a bound on the internal-variable dimension that grows logarithmically in the inverse relative stress error and in material contrast.
AI.result: The model can approximate the homogenized constitutive law to any prescribed accuracy, uniformly in time and over admissible strain trajectories and microstructural fields in two and three dimensions; numerical experiments on viscoelasticity and crystal plasticity illustrate the roles of internal-variable dimension and sample complexity, and the theorems are formally verified in Lean 4.
AI.conclusion: The results extend the approximation theory of recurrent neural operators for homogenized inelastic response from one dimension to two and three dimensions, with explicit dimension bounds for learning from unit-cell data.

title: Scaling Adaptive Prompt Injection Attacks with Agent Swarms
summary: Prompt injections have emerged as one of the top security risks faced by AI agents today. Early work in prompt injection attacks looked at simple tool-call agents and static attack payloads, and were saturated since mid-2025. As of Fall 2026, human red-teaming may be nearing saturation, especially on the Gemini family of models. In this work, we argue that despite this apparent plateau, prompt injection attacks are still possible and continued effort into prompt injection defense is needed. We design a new synthetic evaluation dataset which uses random non-malicious actions as adversarial goals. Such dataset design helps us to evaluate prompt injection robustness as a model ability to respect instruction hierarchy, and disentangle this ability from model knowledge of security practices. We show that an agentic attacker of increased capabilities can reliably trick model to follow instructions in tool output in our evaluation, even for models previously considered robust on public prompt injection benchmarks such as GraySwan Arena. This shows that current frontier defenses may require proactive, automated red-teaming to remain resilient to increasingly capable adversaries.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that an agentic attacker with increased capabilities can reliably make frontier models follow instructions injected in tool output, using a synthetic dataset whose adversarial goals are random non-malicious actions.
AI.motivation: Prompt injection is a top security risk for AI agents, and earlier static attacks had saturated, so it is unclear whether robustness on public benchmarks reflects real instruction-hierarchy robustness.
AI.method: A synthetic evaluation dataset uses random non-malicious actions as adversarial goals, which separates instruction-hierarchy respect from knowledge of security practices, and an agentic attacker of increasing capability is used to generate injections.
AI.result: The agentic attacker reliably tricks models into following instructions in tool output, including models previously considered robust on public benchmarks such as GraySwan Arena.
AI.conclusion: Current frontier defenses may need proactive, automated red-teaming to stay resilient against increasingly capable adversaries.

title: DeFSM: Robust and Efficient Decentralization of Federated Submodular Maximization
summary: Submodular maximization seeks a small subset best representing a large dataset. In its federated setting, the server is a single point of failure and some clients may be Byzantine. Removing the server raises a trilemma of decentraliza- tion, efficiency, and security. We propose DeFSM, a Byzantine-robust and communication-efficient architecture that replaces the server with a lightweight smart contract and a pool of independent, consensus-free agents. Its aggregation rule, SafeGM, builds on two notions from combinatorial geometry: Tukey depth and safe points (the points lying in the convex hull of the good points wherever the bad points are). SafeGM makes the robust decision on 2D Gaussian random projections, which the contract can compute efficiently, and lifts it back as a convex combination of actual updates. Since lifting loses information, it uses the projected geometric median only when its depth certifies it, and otherwise a Tukey median. The share of bad updates is then bounded only by a count: how many there are, not what they contain. We prove, and confirm empirically, that this bound controls the solution quality. On CIFAR10 and PathMNIST, with up to 30% Byzantine clients and agents, DeFSM never collapses and retains on average about 91% of the quality of the ideal reference, the geometric median at a trusted central server. The geometric median decentralized in its best setting would retain about 96%, but the contract cannot compute it, and so each agent would have to download six times more data, or each client twice as much.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DeFSM, a Byzantine-robust and communication-efficient decentralized federated submodular maximization architecture that replaces the server with a smart contract and consensus-free agents, using a geometric aggregation rule called SafeGM.
AI.motivation: In federated submodular maximization the server is a single point of failure and some clients may be Byzantine, and removing the server creates a trilemma between decentralization, efficiency and security.
AI.method: SafeGM makes its robust decision on 2D Gaussian random projections that a contract can compute, using Tukey depth and safe points, and lifts the decision back to a convex combination of actual updates, using the projected geometric median when its depth certifies it and otherwise a Tukey median.
AI.result: On CIFAR10 and PathMNIST with up to 30% Byzantine clients and agents, DeFSM never collapses and keeps on average about 91% of the quality of the ideal central-server geometric median; the best decentralized geometric median would keep about 96% but cannot be computed by the contract.
AI.conclusion: The bound on solution quality depends only on the count of bad updates, which makes the design a practical robust alternative to a trusted central server.

title: Fade to... Red? Scheduling Coloured Noise Exploration Supports Efficient Robot Learning with Reduced Movement Jerk
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Accepted at the ACRA 2026 conference. Cite as: "López, F. M., and Cruz, F. (2026). Fade to... Red? Scheduling Coloured Noise Exploration Supports Efficient Robot Learning with Reduced Movement Jerk. In Proceedings of the Australasian Conference on Robotics and Automation (ACRA). Australian Robotics and Automation Association (ARAA)."
summary: Exploration in deep reinforcement learning (RL) for continuous control is commonly driven by temporally uncorrelated Gaussian (white) action noise, which leads to jerky motions with locally constrained exploration. In contrast, temporally correlated coloured noise, particularly pink noise, has been shown to support more efficient exploration in RL. Motivated by these findings, we inquire whether scheduling changes to the noise colour over the course of training can outperform white noise for continuous control robotics. We perform a systematic study of 49 linear schedules between white and red noise, together with generalised state-dependent exploration (gSDE), on four sparse-reward manipulation tasks with a Fetch arm and a Shadow Dexterous Hand. We find that the noise colour at the end of training does not affect learning efficiency or end performance, whereas fading towards red noise halves the jerk of exploration in every task. Balancing learning efficiency, end performance and smoothness, red noise emerges as the preferred strategy: it learns as efficiently as pink noise with almost 2-fold less movement jerk. We therefore recommend exploration schedulers that fade towards red noise as the default for off-policy robot learning.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that scheduling a change in action-noise colour from white toward red during RL training matches pink-noise learning efficiency while roughly halving movement jerk, and recommends fading toward red noise as the default for off-policy robot learning.
AI.motivation: White Gaussian action noise yields jerky motion and locally constrained exploration in continuous-control RL, while temporally correlated pink noise improves exploration efficiency, leaving open whether a noise-colour schedule can do better than white noise.
AI.method: The authors run a systematic study of 49 linear schedules between white and red noise, with and without generalised state-dependent exploration (gSDE), on four sparse-reward manipulation tasks using a Fetch arm and a Shadow Dexterous Hand.
AI.result: The noise colour at the end of training does not affect learning efficiency or final performance, while fading toward red noise halves the exploration jerk in every task; red noise learns as efficiently as pink noise with almost 2-fold less jerk.
AI.conclusion: Red-noise exploration schedules balance efficiency, end performance and smoothness, and are recommended as the default for off-policy robot learning.

title: Distilling Instructions into Weights: Closed-Form Edits Fix a Robot Policy's Misreading
comment: 23 pages, 7 figures. Project page with videos: this https URL ; code and benchmark: this https URL
summary: Generalist robot policies often fail at one step of a task they can otherwise perform. We ask whether such a failure can be repaired by editing the policy's weights directly, without gradients, training data, or a change to the instruction. Told to put the cube then the banana in the bowl, a zero-shot $\pi_{0.5}$ vision-language-action policy in RoboLab releases the cube before it reaches the bowl. Replaying 21 of these decisions under rewordings shows that it binds "in the bowl" to the wrong object. Closed-form instruction distillation copies the per-layer effect of an explicit rewording into the language model's MLP weights. On 128 held-out seeds, success rises from 27 to 106 episodes, with 81 fixed and 2 broken ($p=7\times10^{-22}$), while an update of the same size in random directions leaves success unchanged. The edit also lifts two other tasks without detectable harm on the remaining 13, and a variant that stores 0.16% of the parameter count keeps most of its effect. Placed in the action expert or action head instead, the same distillation helps less or not at all. Our released tool reproduced the fix end to end on new held-out seeds, from 8/64 to 36/64. Edits aimed at perception, a missing grasp, contact physics, or the gripper threshold did not help, and of seven blind Claude Opus editors, only the one given the misread instruction produced an edit that passed held-out scoring. These results suggest that weight edits work best when a known-good input already exists to distil. Because reruns with unchanged weights flip about a third of paired outcomes, evaluations should pair seeds, rerun the unedited policy, and confirm gains on held-out seeds.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that closed-form weight edits, which copy the per-layer effect of an explicit rewording into a vision-language-action policy's language-model MLP weights, can fix a misread instruction without gradients or new training data.
AI.motivation: Generalist robot policies can fail at a single step of a task they otherwise perform, and the question is whether such a failure can be repaired directly in the weights.
AI.method: Closed-form instruction distillation copies the per-layer effect of a rewording into the language model's MLP weights of a zero-shot pi0.5 policy in RoboLab, and the edit is compared with random-direction updates of the same size, with placements in the action expert or action head, and with perception, grasp, contact and gripper edits and blind Claude Opus editors.
AI.result: On 128 held-out seeds, success rises from 27 to 106 episodes, with 81 fixed and 2 broken (p=7x10^-22), while a same-size random update leaves success unchanged; a variant storing 0.16% of parameters keeps most of the effect, and the released tool raises held-out success from 8/64 to 36/64 on new seeds.
AI.conclusion: Weight edits work best when a known-good input exists to distil, and evaluations should pair seeds, rerun the unedited policy and confirm gains on held-out seeds because reruns flip about a third of paired outcomes.

title: How Far Must a Test Explore? Certifying Composable Read-Write Interfaces from Their Own Random Edits
summary: Random tests of stateful code check laws, like reading back a written value, at states that random writes reach. The laws hold at every state exactly when the code behaves like a record with hidden data, so a pass is taken as evidence. This can fail: the laws can hold at every sample while the code is far from any record. The laws are local, but behaving like a record is global. Self-testing and stability theorems bridge this gap when the query distribution is controlled by the tester or preserved by the tested maps, but here it is generated by the tested writes, which need not be invertible. We ask how far a test must explore. An interface has $m$ binary variables, each with a read and two writes; in a record, reads return their bits and writes set only their bits. Samples are the ends of geometric runs of mean $\ell$ of uniformly random writes from a start distribution; a tester adds its own write chains of depth $d$. The distance is the least, over records with hidden data, of the largest probability that a read or write differs from it at a sample. From one start state, law checks at $O(m^2\log m/\epsilon)$ samples certify, at fixed confidence, any threshold $\epsilon$ after geometric runs of every positive mean, while runs of fixed positive length can pass at distance $1/2$. For the worst start distribution, take $\epsilon=m^{-\beta}$ with fixed $0<\beta\le1$. For $d\le cm$ with fixed $c<1/2$, a polynomial budget of samples and writes exists exactly when $\ell=\Omega(m)$, where law checks suffice. With no runs, the least depth for this budget is $(1/2+o(1))m$. Counting samples alone, in the worst case at $\epsilon=1/(32m)$ and $d\le m/16$, the critical mean for a polynomial budget is $\Theta(m\log(m/d)/\log m)$, by exhaustive search. So one start state needs only law checks, and the worst case at these thresholds needs exploration linear in $m$ if writes are counted.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that random law checks can certify that stateful read-write code behaves like a record only when the random write runs are long enough, and it gives sample and write budgets for certifying this closeness.
AI.motivation: A passing random test of read-write laws does not show that the code behaves like a record with hidden data, because the laws are local while being a record is a global property and the queries are generated by the tested writes.
AI.method: The authors define distance to the nearest record over m binary variables with reads and writes, sample ends of geometric write runs of mean l, add tester write chains of depth d, and derive sample and depth bounds for thresholds epsilon, including an exhaustive search for the worst case.
AI.result: From one start state, law checks at O(m^2 log m / epsilon) samples certify any threshold after geometric runs of every positive mean, while fixed-length runs can pass at distance 1/2; for the worst start distribution, a polynomial budget exists exactly when the mean run length is Omega(m) for depth d at most cm with c below 1/2, and counting samples alone needs a critical mean of order m log(m/d) / log m.
AI.conclusion: One start state needs only law checks, but in the worst case certification requires exploration linear in m once writes are counted.

title: AI-Driven Discovery of Entanglement Witness in Spin Hamiltonians
summary: Entanglement is a crucial resource in quantum science and engineering, but detecting it in many-body states from experimentally accessible observables remains challenging. Here we introduce EntNet, an AI-driven framework to discover compact combinations of spin observables that accurately distinguish entangled from fully separable many-body mixed states in one-dimensional spin-$1/2$ chains governed by short-range Hamiltonians. We construct local-unitary-invariant representations of measurable Pauli correlators up to four-body order, sparsely select 16 candidate invariant feature channels, and learn their spatial structure using a Transformer architecture with rotary positional embeddings. Using only expectation values of these low-order observables, EntNet achieves $>98\%$ recall on certified entangled states with near-zero false-positive rates on separable states. Remarkably, it exhibits transferability across system sizes and distinct Hamiltonian families, including frustrated and disordered spin models, with minimal loss of accuracy. Beyond detection, EntNet provides physical insight into entanglement detection by revealing a selective spatial organization of pair correlations, while its finite-temperature decision boundary tracks the excitation gap of Jordan-Wigner quasiparticles. These results establish a transferable and physically interpretable framework for data-driven discovery of entanglement witnesses from local correlation functions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EntNet, a Transformer-based framework that learns compact spin-observable combinations to detect entanglement in 1D spin-1/2 chains from low-order Pauli correlators, transferring across system sizes and Hamiltonian families.
AI.motivation: Detecting entanglement in many-body mixed states from experimentally accessible observables is challenging, and a witness that is compact, interpretable and transferable would be valuable.
AI.method: Local-unitary-invariant representations of Pauli correlators up to four-body order are constructed, 16 invariant feature channels are sparsely selected, and their spatial structure is learned with a Transformer using rotary positional embeddings.
AI.result: Using only expectation values of low-order observables, EntNet reaches over 98% recall on certified entangled states with near-zero false-positive rates on separable states, and transfers across system sizes and to frustrated and disordered spin models with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.conclusion: The framework gives an interpretable, transferable route to data-driven entanglement witnesses, with a decision boundary that tracks the excitation gap of Jordan-Wigner quasiparticles at finite temperature.

title: The Relative Value of Demonstration Data: Execution Time Limits and Operator Mixtures in Behavior Cloning
summary: Robot demonstration datasets combine demonstrations from teleoperators of uneven experience, so collection teams need to know how many demonstrations from one group match those from another. We measure this with a data multiple: the ratio of the numbers of demonstrations two groups need for their policies to reach the same success rate. On robomimic's simulated Square and Can tasks, we train behavior-cloning policies on demonstrations from the two teleoperators robomimic labels Better and the two it labels Worse, varying dataset size and the share of Worse demonstrations. On Square, within robomimic's 25-second time limit, an all-Worse training set needs 1.55 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set. Most of this difference is late completion: policies trained on Worse demonstrations finish later, as the Worse teleoperators do, and with a 100-second limit the multiple falls to 1.11. On Can, most of the difference remains at 100 seconds. If each Worse demonstration were worth 1/1.55 of a Better one, as in an all-Worse set, a half-Better, half-Worse set on Square would need 1.22 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set. In fact, it needs 13% more than that, and this excess persists at every time limit from 20 to 200 seconds. The excess remains when training draws demonstrations uniformly instead of in proportion to their length. On Square, within the 25-second limit, switching to these Worse teleoperators is cheaper at equal success only if they earn less than a third of the Better teleoperators' hourly pay, because Worse demonstrations also take longer to record.

AI.tldr: The paper measures how many demonstrations from a worse teleoperator group equal those from a better group in robomimic behaviour cloning, finding a data multiple of 1.55 on Square under a 25-second limit that falls to 1.11 with a 100-second limit.
AI.motivation: Collection teams need to know how many demonstrations from one group of teleoperators match another group's, so that uneven operator quality can be priced into data collection.
AI.method: Behaviour-cloning policies are trained on simulated Square and Can demonstrations from robomimic's Better and Worse operators, varying dataset size and the share of Worse demonstrations, and the data multiple is the ratio of demonstrations needed to reach the same success rate.
AI.result: On Square within 25 seconds, an all-Worse set needs 1.55 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set, and most of the gap is late completion; a half-Better, half-Worse set needs 13% more demonstrations than the 1.22 times predicted from per-demonstration weights, and this excess holds at every time limit from 20 to 200 seconds.
AI.conclusion: Switching to the Worse operators is cheaper at equal success only if they earn less than a third of the Better operators' hourly pay, because their demonstrations also take longer to record.

title: Benchmarking language models and agents for scientific reasoning in evolving materials laboratories
summary: Large language models and the multi-agent systems built around them could accelerate materials discovery by connecting scientific knowledge with experimental decisions. Existing benchmarks establish capabilities in domain knowledge, multimodal interpretation and scientific tool use. As language models increasingly support materials research workflows, their ability to distinguish closely related material states and reason accurately with quantitative evidence remains insufficiently evaluated. These abilities are essential for comparing material responses, assessing mechanisms and maintaining reliable judgements as experimental evidence accumulates. We introduce MatScope to evaluate three connected capabilities. M1 tests unaided, condition-specific reasoning through 200 tasks spanning ten research functions, using aluminium and high-entropy alloys as representative material systems. M2 tests agent-assisted transfer of related knowledge to unresolved materials questions. MatEvoBench-20 tests initial forecasts across scientific dependency chains and revisions of still-hidden responses as observations accumulate. Across eleven model deployments, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, given-input calculations and many physical explanations are handled well. Fine-grained response estimates, comparisons between similar states and quantitatively supported choices remain substantially weaker. Related literature improves selected estimates, while condition and baseline mismatches limit transfer. Progressive observations calibrate some downstream responses and destabilize earlier accurate predictions. MatScope establishes measurable targets for developing reliable scientific reasoning in future self-evolving materials laboratories and materials-aware world models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MatScope, a benchmark of three connected tasks that tests language models and agents on condition-specific materials reasoning, literature-assisted transfer and forecasting with revision under progressive observations.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks cover domain knowledge, multimodal interpretation and tool use, but not whether models can distinguish closely related material states and reason accurately with quantitative evidence as experimental data accumulate.
AI.method: M1 uses 200 unaided tasks across ten research functions on aluminium and high-entropy alloys, M2 tests agent-assisted transfer of related knowledge to unresolved questions, and MatEvoBench-20 tests initial forecasts along scientific dependency chains and revisions of hidden responses as observations arrive, across eleven model deployments including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1.
AI.result: Given-input calculations and many physical explanations are handled well, while fine-grained response estimates, comparisons between similar states and quantitatively supported choices remain substantially weaker; related literature improves some estimates, and progressive observations calibrate some responses but destabilise earlier accurate predictions.
AI.conclusion: MatScope sets measurable targets for building reliable scientific reasoning in future self-evolving materials laboratories and materials-aware world models.

title: Low-rank Low Precision Training of Gaussian Processes
summary: Training Gaussian processes (GPs) at large scale is computationally challenging because evaluating the log-marginal likelihood and its gradients involves large, dense kernel matrices. We develop a scalable low-rank GP training approach that combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction. The resulting objective and its analytic gradients can be evaluated using low-rank factors, diagonal quantities, and small dense matrices, without forming the full kernel matrix or its derivatives. The complete training procedure is implemented in single precision and evaluated on nine large-scale regression datasets. Across these problems, the method reaches the reference predictive accuracy while substantially reducing training time, although the required approximation rank varies across datasets. We also study the numerical behavior of the full-kernel predictive solve and show that single precision can become limiting for ill-conditioned problems. Finally, we investigate further reducing selected matrix operations to fp16 or TF32. These lower-precision variants provide only modest additional speedups and can become unreliable when the reduced system is poorly conditioned.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scalable low-rank Gaussian process training method that combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a FITC correction, implemented in single precision, and reaches reference predictive accuracy with substantially less training time.
AI.motivation: Training Gaussian processes at large scale requires evaluating the log-marginal likelihood and its gradients with large dense kernel matrices, which is computationally prohibitive.
AI.method: The objective and its analytic gradients are computed from low-rank factors, diagonal quantities and small dense matrices without forming the full kernel matrix, and selected matrix operations are further reduced to fp16 or TF32 to test lower-precision speedups.
AI.result: Across nine large-scale regression datasets the method reaches the reference predictive accuracy with substantially reduced training time, though the required approximation rank varies by dataset; single precision can limit ill-conditioned problems, and fp16 or TF32 variants give only modest additional speedups that can become unreliable on poorly conditioned systems.
AI.conclusion: Low-rank GP training is practical in single precision for large regression, but reduced-precision variants should be used with care when the reduced system is poorly conditioned.

title: BARS: Beat-Adaptive Rap Synthesis via Flow Matching
comment: Published in ISMIR 2026 (Best Paper Award nominee). Demo: this https URL
summary: We present BARS (Beat-Adaptive Rap Synthesis), a non-autoregressive rapping voice generation model based on Flow Matching, conditioned on a beat track (instrumental backing), lyrics, and a short reference voice for zero-shot timbre control. Unlike prior autoregressive rap synthesis, where rap pace and output duration are strictly determined by the beat, BARS enables independent control over the rap tempo, allowing flexible-length generation without explicit duration prediction or phoneme-level alignment. We encode lyrics using a pretrained ByT5 encoder with a lightweight Transformer adapter trained jointly with the model, without relying on speech-pretrained text encoders, enabling natural handling of non-standard orthography (e.g., slang, abbreviations) and numerals common in rap lyrics. To address alignment instabilities, such as token skipping or repetition, under strong beat conditioning, we propose Asymmetric Scaled RoPE for cross-attention, which introduces a positional structure to facilitate sequential lyric-audio alignment learning. Furthermore, the model supports partial re-generation via span masking, enabling lyric-level editing while preserving the surrounding vocal style. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed model achieves high lyric fidelity, natural rap flow that is rhythmically coherent with the beat, and robust tempo control across a wide range of rapping styles and speeds.

AI.tldr: The paper presents BARS, a non-autoregressive flow-matching model that generates rap vocals conditioned on a beat, lyrics and a short reference voice, decoupling rap tempo from the beat so that output length is flexible.
AI.motivation: Prior autoregressive rap synthesis fixes rap pace and output duration to the beat, and alignment between lyrics and audio is unstable under strong beat conditioning, with token skipping and repetition.
AI.method: A pretrained ByT5 lyric encoder with a jointly trained Transformer adapter is used instead of speech-pretrained text encoders, and Asymmetric Scaled RoPE is applied in cross-attention to give positional structure for sequential lyric-audio alignment; span masking supports partial re-generation for lyric editing.
AI.result: The model achieves high lyric fidelity, natural rap flow that is rhythmically coherent with the beat, and robust tempo control across a wide range of rapping styles and speeds.
AI.conclusion: Independent control of rap tempo, together with span-masked re-generation, enables flexible-length rap synthesis and lyric-level editing while preserving the vocal style.

title: FALC: An Artifact-Centric Life Cycle Model and Research Agenda for AI Forensics
summary: AI systems increasingly appear in criminal investigations as tools, targets, and sources of evidence, yet AI forensics lacks a systematic account of the artifacts they produce: investigators often do not know which traces to look for, and for many traces they do find, no established analysis technique exists. In this paper we first developed the Forensic AI Life Cycle (FALC) that unlike other life cycle models shifts the focus onto the forensic artifacts created during the life cycle of an AI system. Through FALC we derived a reference list of artifacts that might serve an investigation. Second, we collected examples for crimes with AI involvement throughout FALC and questions likely to be asked when investigating these crimes. Third, we propose a taxonomy of forensic fields of expertise with a focus on the current possibility to analyze AI forensic artifacts using established techniques. For investigators, the model provides a systematic basis for identifying which artifacts to look for when an AI system is relevant to a case. For researchers, the classification shows where existing forensic methods already suffice and where new techniques are most urgently needed.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Forensic AI Life Cycle (FALC), an artifact-centric life cycle model that yields a reference list of forensic artifacts, examples of AI-involved crimes, and a taxonomy of forensic fields of expertise for AI forensics.
AI.motivation: AI forensics lacks a systematic account of the artifacts AI systems produce, so investigators often do not know which traces to look for, and many traces have no established analysis technique.
AI.method: FALC shifts the focus of life cycle models onto the forensic artifacts created at each stage, from which artifacts are derived; examples of crimes and investigative questions are collected across the life cycle, and forensic fields are classified by whether established techniques can analyse each artifact.
AI.result: The paper delivers a reference list of artifacts that might serve an investigation, a collection of crime examples with questions, and a taxonomy of forensic expertise fields; the abstract reports no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: The model gives investigators a basis for identifying which artifacts to seek, and shows researchers where existing methods suffice and where new techniques are most urgently needed.

title: SkillDuet: Co-Evolving Models and Skills through Response Feedback
summary: During reinforcement learning, experience can be both internalized in LLM parameters and retained externally as reusable textual skills. Parameter updates alter the model's behavior and the interaction experience from which new skills are extracted. These skills, in turn, guide the model's subsequent interactions and parameter updates. As the model's capabilities evolve, previously beneficial skills may become redundant or detrimental. We present SkillDuet, a framework that coordinates parameter updates and skill evolution through model response feedback. Skills extracted from on-policy trajectories guide parameter updates through OPD at every step. A response-based score, Strength, ranks candidate skills by the magnitude of the shift they induce in the current model's responses, and the highest-scoring skills are periodically consolidated into a persistent global skill set (Global). The updated model and Global jointly guide subsequent interactions, generating experience for further parameter and skill updates. With Qwen3-4B, SkillDuet achieves success rates of 98.57% on ALFWorld and 92.97% on WebShop, exceeding the matched SEED-API baseline by 2.86 and 5.47 percentage points, respectively. Ablations show that response-based skill selection and Global consolidation improve task performance. Further experiments show that the benefits of retained skills depend on both their content and their compatibility with the model. SkillDuet provides a concrete mechanism for model-skill co-evolution and skill-level recursive self-improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SkillDuet, a framework that co-evolves LLM parameters and a set of reusable textual skills by ranking candidate skills with a response-based score and consolidating the best into a persistent global skill set, reaching 98.57% on ALFWorld and 92.97% on WebShop with Qwen3-4B.
AI.motivation: During reinforcement learning, parameter updates and externally retained skills affect each other, and previously beneficial skills can become redundant or harmful as the model changes.
AI.method: Skills are extracted from on-policy trajectories and guide parameter updates through OPD at every step; a response-based score called Strength ranks candidate skills by the shift they induce in the model's responses, and the top skills are periodically consolidated into a persistent Global skill set.
AI.result: With Qwen3-4B, SkillDuet achieves 98.57% success on ALFWorld and 92.97% on WebShop, exceeding the matched SEED-API baseline by 2.86 and 5.47 percentage points, and ablations show that response-based selection and Global consolidation each improve performance.
AI.conclusion: The results offer a concrete mechanism for model-skill co-evolution and skill-level recursive self-improvement, with skill benefit depending on both content and compatibility with the model.

title: GPU-Accelerated Non-Interactive Encrypted Neural Network Training with Batched Diagonal Packing
comment: 12 pages. Research preprint. Code and evidence: this https URL
summary: Training a neural network under homomorphic encryption requires transposes, batch reductions, optimizer updates, and repeated refreshes in addition to forward matrix products. We combine rectangular diagonal packing, feature-major SIMD mini-batch lanes, baby-step giant-step evaluation, and compact optimizer state in an MIT-licensed Rust CKKS implementation. Its CUDA path keeps training and bootstrap ciphertext arithmetic on the GPU, while retaining host key generation and client operations. In a matched 100-update experiment on the main non-interactive MNIST model, device-resident bootstrapping reduces training time from 14,268.295 to 293.075 seconds, a $48.68\times$ ratio against our CPU implementation, with exactly equal decoded parameters and predictions. Including setup and final evaluation gives a $40.67\times$ ratio. A separate GPU run completes ten passes over 4,800 images in 2,967.095 seconds and achieves 90.35% test accuracy versus 90.41% for its plaintext twin. These are single-initialization results; exact CPU/GPU parameter agreement is verified at 100 updates, not for the full 1,000-update run. Earlier completed CPU runs support a larger-batch key-switch advantage and baseline-batch accuracy within the registered tolerance, but the baseline-batch normalized key-switch target is missed. The released ReBoot baseline does not meet the common security-estimator threshold, and its full-setting CPU time is unmeasured. We therefore distinguish measured acceleration of our implementation from conditional layout comparisons and do not claim unconditional superiority over ReBoot.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an MIT-licensed Rust CKKS implementation that trains encrypted neural networks with GPU-resident training and bootstrapping, reducing training time on the MNIST model by 48.68x against its CPU implementation with identical decoded parameters and predictions.
AI.motivation: Training under homomorphic encryption needs transposes, batch reductions, optimizer updates and repeated refreshes in addition to forward matrix products, making encrypted training expensive.
AI.method: The implementation combines rectangular diagonal packing, feature-major SIMD mini-batch lanes, baby-step giant-step evaluation and compact optimizer state, and its CUDA path keeps training and bootstrap ciphertext arithmetic on the GPU while key generation and client operations stay on the host.
AI.result: In a matched 100-update run on the main non-interactive MNIST model, device-resident bootstrapping cuts training time from 14,268.295 to 293.075 seconds (48.68x) with exactly equal decoded parameters and predictions, and a GPU run completes ten passes over 4,800 images in 2,967.095 seconds with 90.35% test accuracy against 90.41% for its plaintext twin; the released ReBoot baseline does not meet the common security-estimator threshold.
AI.conclusion: The paper claims measured acceleration of its own implementation and conditional layout comparisons, but not unconditional superiority over ReBoot.

title: FraudBench: A Legal Evaluation of AI Deception
summary: We introduce FraudBench, an evaluation of large language models' (LLMs) propensities to recommend, assist, or directly take actions that would constitute fraud under U.S. law. Our evaluation contains a novel dataset of 159 scenarios based on real-world U.S. court cases and validated by legal experts. We present each scenario to LLMs via three tasks at varying levels of autonomy: advising users, drafting messages for users to send, and acting directly on behalf of users (477 tasks total).
