Privacy constraints and instance-level reporting hinder the collection of diverse abnormal cases and frame-level labels, while repeated retraining for new centers increases computational cost. We introduce EvoDiff, a generative active learning framework that integrates diffusion modelling with information-theoretic objectives, evolutionary search, and curriculum-based sampling to select informative samples across heterogeneous US datasets. EvoDiff formulates sample selection as a generate-to-retrieve process, in which diffusion-based optimization in feature space guided by information gain produces synthetic probes, and only the real unlabeled samples retrieved by these probes are annotated and used for downstream training. Across six benchmarks covering fifteen datasets and 16,696 images, we evaluate EvoDiff on convolutional network and transformer-based foundation model. EvoDiff approaches fully supervised performance with substantially fewer labels, outperforms active learning baselines, and improves foundation model generalization under cross-domain external validation on unseen cohorts. A reader study with six radiologists indicates the potential to support clinical annotation workflows, with a model-based estimated 24% to 84% reduction in annotation workload at matched downstream performance.

AI.tldr: EvoDiff is a generative active learning framework that uses diffusion-based synthetic probes to retrieve only informative real ultrasound images for annotation, approaching fully supervised performance with fewer labels across six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Ultrasound AI is limited by data scarcity, costly expert annotation, privacy constraints and poor cross-center generalization, and retraining for each new center is expensive.
AI.method: EvoDiff integrates diffusion modelling with information-theoretic objectives, evolutionary search and curriculum-based sampling in a generate-to-retrieve process: diffusion optimization in feature space, guided by information gain, produces synthetic probes, and only the real unlabeled samples they retrieve are annotated and used for training.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks with fifteen datasets and 16,696 images, using a convolutional network and a transformer-based foundation model, EvoDiff approaches fully supervised performance with substantially fewer labels, outperforms active learning baselines and improves foundation-model generalization on unseen cohorts; a reader study with six radiologists and a model-based estimate indicate a 24% to 84% reduction in annotation workload at matched downstream performance.
AI.conclusion: The approach has potential to support clinical annotation workflows for ultrasound.

title: Ensemble Routing for Prompt-Adaptive Cost-Aware LLM Inference
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support Web-based services that must balance response quality and inference cost across heterogeneous requests. Conventional routing selects one model per prompt, while fixed ensembles cannot adapt their composition and cost to individual requests. We introduce PISA, a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router, and PISA-E, its extension to ensemble routing. At the core of both methods, PISA combines soft cluster memberships with model-specific predictors to estimate individual model capabilities. Building on these estimates, PISA-E jointly selects ensemble composition and cardinality under an explicit cost--quality preference that can be adjusted at inference time without retraining. A tractable ensemble-success surrogate and efficient candidate selection enable this extension without ensemble-specific training. Across four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, PISA achieves the highest macro-average cost--performance hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers in both settings. Meanwhile, PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches when prioritizing response quality, surpassing the strongest competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points under ID and OOD conditions, respectively. At selected lower-cost operating points, it also exceeds the strongest ensemble competitors' macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% and 25%, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of prompt-adaptive capability estimation for both single-model routing and selective ensembling.

AI.tldr: PISA is a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware LLM router and PISA-E extends it to ensemble routing, achieving the best cost-performance trade-offs among single-model routers and the highest task performance among ensemble approaches when quality is prioritized.
AI.motivation: Conventional routing picks one model per prompt, while fixed ensembles cannot adapt composition and cost to each request, and Web-based services must balance quality and cost across heterogeneous requests.
AI.method: PISA combines soft cluster memberships with model-specific predictors to estimate each model's capability for a prompt; PISA-E builds on these estimates to jointly choose ensemble composition and size under a cost-quality preference adjustable at inference time, using a tractable ensemble-success surrogate and efficient candidate selection without ensemble-specific training.
AI.result: Across four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution and out-of-distribution conditions, PISA achieves the highest macro-average cost-performance hypervolume among evaluated single-model routers; PISA-E surpasses the strongest ensemble competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points in macro-average task performance under ID and OOD conditions, and at selected lower-cost points reduces average inference cost by about 36% and 25% while still exceeding their performance.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-adaptive capability estimation is effective for both single-model routing and selective ensembling.

title: Multi-GPU MoE Inference with Adaptive Expert Offloading
summary: Modern Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference is constrained by GPU memory. This constraint is mitigated by expert offloading, which stores part of the model's weight in host memory and executes on demand. Though MoE architecture has computation sparsity, more GPUs are needed for serving increasingly larger frontier models. However, existing expert offloading systems overlook this need and fail to scale performance with additional GPUs. We present AdaOffload, a general and efficient multi-GPU hybrid expert execution framework that effectively handles heterogeneous hardware and workloads. We co-design GPU-CPU parallelism and GPU-CPU co-execution for decode and prefill with online workload observation that adapts to different hardware, workload, and batch size heterogeneity. We evaluated AdaOffload on five different platforms with varying GPU capability (L4, Pro6000, B200), number of GPUs, CPU capability, and NUMA topology on three different frontier open-weight models (284B to 753B). AdaOffload achieves $1.9\times$ to $15.5\times$ throughput speedups across different models over state-of-the-art systems.

AI.tldr: AdaOffload is a multi-GPU hybrid expert execution framework for MoE inference that co-designs GPU-CPU parallelism and co-execution, achieving 1.9x to 15.5x throughput speedups over state-of-the-art expert offloading systems.
AI.motivation: Expert offloading reduces GPU memory needs for MoE inference, but existing systems do not scale performance as more GPUs are added, even though larger frontier models need more GPUs.
AI.method: AdaOffload co-designs GPU-CPU parallelism and GPU-CPU co-execution for both decode and prefill, with online workload observation that adapts to hardware, workload and batch-size heterogeneity.
AI.result: Evaluated on five platforms with varying GPUs (L4, Pro6000, B200), GPU counts, CPUs and NUMA topologies, across three open-weight models of 284B to 753B parameters, AdaOffload achieves 1.9x to 15.5x throughput speedups over state-of-the-art systems.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive hybrid expert execution lets offloading-based MoE serving scale with additional GPUs across heterogeneous hardware.

title: ProofDiff: Auditable Argument-Level Comparison of AI-Generated Mathematical Proofs
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures. An earlier version of this work was accepted by the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Verifiable Coding. Code and artifacts are available at this https URL
summary: Mathematical understanding depends on the route from hypotheses to conclusion: how the parts of a proof function and which dependencies carry the argument forward. This structure can persist when wording or notation changes, while a small alteration to a hypothesis or inference can produce a different argument beneath similar prose. Formal verification can establish that a rewrite proves the same theorem, but not whether it follows the same mathematical route. Comparing informal proofs, especially those produced or revised by generative models, therefore requires reconstructing which claims, dependencies, and reasoning steps are preserved, reorganized, or replaced. We present ProofDiff, a system for comparing informal mathematical documents. It is designed to support human review, not to certify mathematical correctness. Given two documents, ProofDiff independently constructs a source-grounded argument map for each and proposes correspondences between the resulting maps. Each map captures the document's claims and reasoning steps and records the typed relations that connect them. An integrated human-review layer allows reviewers to revise the maps and correspondences while preserving an auditable history. Comparing the two argument maps provides a basis for inspecting whether the documents follow the same mathematical route and where their claims or dependencies differ. We demonstrate ProofDiff on four illustrative pairs of AI-generated proofs, ranging from a detailed proof and its concise revision to proofs using different mathematical strategies.

AI.tldr: ProofDiff is a system that builds source-grounded argument maps of two informal mathematical proofs and aligns them, so human reviewers can inspect whether the proofs follow the same mathematical route and where claims or dependencies differ.
AI.motivation: Formal verification can show that two rewrites prove the same theorem but not whether they follow the same argument, and comparing informal proofs, especially AI-generated ones, requires reconstructing which claims and dependencies are preserved, reorganized or replaced.
AI.method: Given two documents, ProofDiff independently constructs an argument map of claims, reasoning steps and typed relations for each, proposes correspondences between the maps, and provides a human-review layer that lets reviewers revise maps and correspondences with an auditable history.
AI.result: The authors demonstrate ProofDiff on four illustrative pairs of AI-generated proofs, including a detailed proof and its concise revision and proofs using different strategies; no quantitative evaluation is reported in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Argument-level comparison provides a basis for reviewing mathematical documents, though the system is designed to support human review rather than certify correctness.

title: ScreenProof: Where Is This Screen Wrong? Finding UI Faults Without a Reference
summary: A phone screen can be wrong in ways that need no reference: a label that runs off the screen, letters that touch, a line that breaks one character before its end, one button with sharp corners among round ones. We ask whether a model can box every such fault on a screenshot, given no target design and no reference image. Such a critic could serve as a cheap first pass over generated pages before a designer reviews them, but only if it stays silent on clean pages. ScreenProof poses this target-free critique over three families of faults: general faults, local style faults (one element breaks the style its page sets) and text layout faults (letter spacing, line height, line breaks). A data engine makes each fault in page code and records the changed element's box, and hard negatives change every sibling alike. No frontier judge is reliable: frontier models flag 18-62% of clean real screenshots and 18-82% of clean generated pages, find 47-72% of text layout faults, and rarely find a foreign icon (5-19%). Our small critic ProofJudge (Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA), trained on code-made pages with one to four faults each and keeping a finding only when it is confident, reaches F1 0.48, the highest of all judges (Gemini 4 Argon 0.37; open models at most 0.15; 0.46 even without the confidence cut), and is the only fault-finding judge within 15% false alarms on clean pages (2% real, 9% generated), the property such a first pass needs, at about a hundredth of Argon's cost. It finds the most general faults (59%) but fewer local style faults than Argon (25% against 41%) and fewer text layout faults than the API judges (43%; Gemini 4 Argon 47%). Against a named brand the task is harder still: models know a design language about as well as its public documentation states it.

AI.tldr: ScreenProof is a target-free benchmark and critic for finding UI faults in phone screenshots without a reference, where the small fine-tuned ProofJudge reaches the highest F1 of all judges with few false alarms on clean pages.
AI.motivation: Generated phone screens can contain faults such as overflowing labels, touching letters, broken lines or mismatched corners, and a first-pass critic is useful only if it finds faults without flagging clean pages, which frontier judges often fail to do.
AI.method: A data engine injects faults into page code over three families (general faults, local style faults and text layout faults) and records the changed element's box, with hard negatives that change all siblings alike; the critic ProofJudge is Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA, trained on code-made pages with one to four faults and keeping findings only when confident.
AI.result: ProofJudge reaches F1 0.48, the highest of all judges (Gemini 4 Argon 0.37; open models at most 0.15; 0.46 without the confidence cut), and is the only fault-finding judge within 15% false alarms on clean pages (2% real, 9% generated) at about a hundredth of Argon's cost; it finds 59% of general faults, 25% of local style faults versus 41% for Argon, and 43% of text layout faults versus 47% for Argon.
AI.conclusion: A small, confidence-filtered critic can serve as a cheap first pass over generated UI, though fault finding remains weaker on local style faults and against named brand design languages.

title: Adversarial Evaluation of Large Language Models for Patient-Friendly Radiology Report Summarization
comment: This work has been submitted to Radiology: Artificial Intelligence for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Purpose: To develop and validate a scalable adversarial evaluation framework for assessing the robustness of large language models (LLMs) that generate patient-friendly summaries of radiology reports. Methods: We introduced a clinically grounded adversarial framework that uses controlled term substitutions and impression removals across intensity levels. Using a radiologist-validated adversarial dictionary, we generated adversarial variants of CT and MRI reports. Six LLMs summarized original and adversarial impressions using 2 prompt styles, yielding 18,000 evaluation pairs. Robustness was evaluated with an automated LLM-as-a-judge framework scoring factual faithfulness, sensitivity to adversarial edits, certainty fidelity, and hallucination rate. Failure mode analysis quantified vulnerabilities in incorporating clinical modifiers. Agreement with two radiologists was assessed on 105 cases. Results: GPT-5-mini achieved the highest factual faithfulness and certainty fidelity under both adversarial edits. Under term substitution, hallucinations occurred in 28.1-30.1% of GPT-5-mini summaries, compared with 35.3-36.4% for Claude Sonnet 4.5 and 41.4-41.9% for MedGemma. Impression-removal edits were handled more robustly than term substitutions. Even for the highest-scoring summarizer, substitutions of anatomical terms were not reflected in 23.7% of summaries, diagnostic certainty in 22.3%, and descriptor terms (e.g., "substantial") in 21.2%. Judge-radiologist agreement (macro-F1: 0.55-0.56) was comparable to inter-radiologist agreement (0.53). Conclusions: Adversarial evaluation exposes clinically meaningful failure modes, including missed anatomical modifiers, altered diagnostic certainty, and omitted severity descriptors.

AI.tldr: An adversarial evaluation of six LLMs summarizing CT and MRI radiology impressions into patient-friendly language finds that term substitutions and removals frequently go unreflected, with GPT-5-mini the most faithful but still missing many modifiers.
AI.motivation: Patient-friendly radiology summaries must stay faithful to clinical modifiers, but LLM robustness to clinically meaningful input perturbations has not been systematically measured at scale.
AI.method: A radiologist-validated adversarial dictionary produced controlled term substitutions and impression removals across intensity levels in CT and MRI reports, yielding 18,000 evaluation pairs across six LLMs and two prompt styles, scored by an LLM-as-a-judge framework for faithfulness, sensitivity to edits, certainty fidelity and hallucination, and checked against two radiologists on 105 cases.
AI.result: GPT-5-mini had the highest factual faithfulness and certainty fidelity; under term substitution its summaries hallucinated in 28.1-30.1% of cases versus 35.3-36.4% for Claude Sonnet 4.5 and 41.4-41.9% for MedGemma; even for GPT-5-mini, anatomical substitutions were not reflected in 23.7% of summaries, diagnostic certainty in 22.3% and descriptors such as substantial in 21.2%; judge-radiologist macro-F1 of 0.55-0.56 was comparable to inter-radiologist agreement of 0.53.
AI.conclusion: Adversarial evaluation exposes clinically meaningful failure modes, including missed anatomical modifiers, altered diagnostic certainty and omitted severity descriptors, that should be checked before deploying such summaries.

title: Conformal Fair Decoding for Large Language Model Recommenders
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate personalized recommendations without task-specific training, but changing a protected attribute while holding interaction history fixed can alter the semantic content of recommended items. We study fairness control when model weights and full-vocabulary logits are unavailable. We propose Fair- Rec, an item-level decoding framework that uses an offline-calibrated semantic-disparity threshold and controls candidate selection as recommendation lists are generated. A hard variant filters candidates against the threshold; a soft variant trades off candidate likelihood and disparity while adapting a penalty using observed violations. Under an explicit uniform enforceability assumption, we establish a pathwise O(1/T) upper bound on the excess empirical violation rate of the soft decoder. Experiments on MovieLens-1M and Amazon Movies & TV using Qwen3-8B and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct show that the soft variant lowers measured counterfactual disparity relative to zero- =shot recommendation, UP5, and FACTER, while retaining competitive HR@10 and NDCG@10.

AI.tldr: FairRec is an item-level decoding framework that controls counterfactual semantic disparity in LLM recommendations without access to weights or full logits, with a soft variant that lowers measured disparity while keeping competitive HR@10 and NDCG@10.
AI.motivation: Changing a protected attribute while holding interaction history fixed can alter the semantic content of LLM-generated recommendations, and fairness control is needed when model weights and full-vocabulary logits are unavailable.
AI.method: An offline-calibrated semantic-disparity threshold controls candidate selection during list generation: a hard variant filters candidates against the threshold, and a soft variant trades off candidate likelihood against disparity while adapting a penalty to observed violations; under a uniform enforceability assumption the authors prove a pathwise O(1/T) upper bound on the soft decoder's excess empirical violation rate.
AI.result: On MovieLens-1M and Amazon Movies & TV with Qwen3-8B and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, the soft variant lowers measured counterfactual disparity relative to zero-shot recommendation, UP5 and FACTER while retaining competitive HR@10 and NDCG@10.
AI.conclusion: Decoding-time, item-level control offers a practical route to fairer LLM recommenders when model internals are inaccessible.

title: TripleGrader: A Web-Based Platform Supporting Collaborative Triple Annotation with Quality Grading and Inter-Rater Agreement Assessment
summary: Knowledge graphs need validated relational triples, and gold benchmarks of such triples are often built by several annotators. Most text annotation platforms focus on span tagging and compute agreement on categorical labels. They are not designed for ordinal quality grading of triples that have already been extracted. We present TripleGrader, an open-source web platform for grading subject-predicate-object triples on a 0 to 10 ordinal scale. In TripleGrader, each triple is scored independently, and peer scores stay hidden until the grader has rated it. Graders then discuss entries in threaded comments and propose revisions, which the session owner approves and publishes as new versions. For agreement, the platform computes quadratic-weighted Cohen's kappa for two raters and a quadratic-weighted Fleiss-type kappa for three or more. Graded sessions and the final benchmark are exported in common formats. We evaluated the platform in three ways. We ran 72 automated tests, including 18 workflow scenarios through the REST API. We also injected 10 error types to check whether prescribed corrections could be applied while preserving unaffected triples. On two small corpora with existing gold benchmarks, we then used the platform to curate the triples extracted by four large language models into each benchmark. Only 10% to 32% of the candidate triples could be kept unchanged, and 53% to 71% needed corrections, partly to match the benchmarks' naming conventions. Per model, 11 to 29 missing triples had to be added. On these corpora, the extracted triples therefore needed substantial human review. The source code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TripleGrader is an open-source web platform for collaborative 0-to-10 quality grading of knowledge-graph triples, with threaded discussion, versioned revisions and quadratic-weighted kappa agreement; applied to LLM-extracted triples, it shows that most candidates need human correction.
AI.motivation: Knowledge graph benchmarks need validated triples built by several annotators, but existing text annotation platforms focus on span tagging and categorical agreement and are not designed for ordinal quality grading of already extracted triples.
AI.method: Each triple is graded independently on a 0-10 ordinal scale with peer scores hidden until a grader has rated it; graders discuss entries in threaded comments and propose revisions that the session owner approves and publishes as new versions; agreement is computed with quadratic-weighted Cohen's kappa for two raters and a quadratic-weighted Fleiss-type kappa for three or more.
AI.result: The platform passed 72 automated tests, including 18 REST workflow scenarios, and correctly applied prescribed corrections for 10 injected error types while preserving unaffected triples; on two small corpora with gold benchmarks, only 10% to 32% of candidate triples from four LLMs could be kept unchanged, 53% to 71% needed corrections and 11 to 29 missing triples per model had to be added.
AI.conclusion: Triples extracted by LLMs needed substantial human review before they matched the benchmarks, so the platform supports the curation workflow that such benchmarks require.

title: SIRIS: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation Errors Matter in AI-Driven Systems Research
summary: LLM agents increasingly drive systems research and rely on simulators to evaluate candidate designs at scale. Simulators are imperfect by design: their modeling limitations can distort predictions yet leave the recommended design correct, or change which design should be selected. We introduce Siris to test whether LLMs can tell these cases apart, judging from their systems understanding when a limitation invalidates the simulator's recommendation. By perturbing a simulator, Siris constructs workload pairs with the same candidates, limitation, and simulator recommendation. The perturbation changes predictions on both workloads, yet a reference simulator supports the recommendation on only one. Evaluating thirteen frontier LLMs on LLM serving design problems, we find that identifying a limitation does not ensure a correct choice, and even the strongest models sometimes abandon valid recommendations. Self-correction through a review turn helps these models restore valid choices but introduces new errors in several others. These findings motivate evaluating systems understanding through design decisions under imperfect simulators.

AI.tldr: SIRIS tests whether LLMs can tell when simulator limitations actually invalidate a recommended systems design, finding that identifying a limitation does not ensure a correct choice and that self-correction helps some models while introducing new errors in others.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly rely on imperfect simulators for systems research, and a simulator limitation may either distort predictions without changing the correct design or change which design should be selected.
AI.method: SIRIS perturbs a simulator to build workload pairs with the same candidates, limitation and simulator recommendation, where the perturbation changes predictions on both workloads but a reference simulator supports the recommendation on only one; thirteen frontier LLMs are evaluated on LLM serving design problems, with and without a review turn for self-correction.
AI.result: Even the strongest models sometimes abandon valid recommendations; a review turn helps them restore valid choices but introduces new errors in several other models.
AI.conclusion: Systems understanding should be evaluated through design decisions made under imperfect simulators, not only by whether a limitation is identified.

title: IdealCache: Rethinking Cache Scheduling in Diffusion Transformers via Ideal Trajectories
comment: accepted 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Feature caching accelerates Diffusion Transformers by reusing intermediate computations across denoising timesteps, yet existing methods share a fundamental blind spot: they treat the standard reference denoising trajectory as the optimisation target, approximating its per-step states and thus inheriting its output as an implicit quality ceiling. We argue that this target is arbitrary -- what truly matters is the ideal result, not the intermediate path taken to reach it. We propose IdealCache, a training-free framework that abandons step-wise imitation of the reference trajectory. Instead, it anchors caching on a per-input ensemble of ideal trajectories constructed from candidate target results, aggregates their geometry into a single graph, and discovers optimal non-uniform schedules via a constrained shortest path on this graph. By decoupling from the reference process, IdealCache breaks the performance bottleneck of trajectory-approximation; our schedules can attain near-lossless fidelity in generation and even surpass on task-specific metrics (e.g., maintaining higher semantic consistency in image editing). Without retraining, IdealCache achieves 6.35x speedup on Qwen-Image, 5.84x on Qwen-Image-Edit, and 4.32x on HunyuanVideo, with competitive or superior quality across tasks.

AI.tldr: IdealCache is a training-free feature-caching method for Diffusion Transformers that schedules reuse along a shortest path over an ensemble of ideal trajectories rather than imitating the reference denoising path, reporting 6.35x, 5.84x and 4.32x speedups on three models.
AI.motivation: Existing feature-caching methods treat the standard reference denoising trajectory as the optimization target, inheriting its output as an implicit quality ceiling, although what matters is the ideal final result rather than the intermediate path.
AI.method: IdealCache builds a per-input ensemble of ideal trajectories from candidate target results, aggregates their geometry into one graph, and finds non-uniform caching schedules via a constrained shortest path on that graph, decoupling caching from the reference process.
AI.result: Schedules achieve near-lossless generation fidelity and sometimes surpass the reference on task-specific metrics, such as higher semantic consistency in image editing; achieved speedups are 6.35x on Qwen-Image, 5.84x on Qwen-Image-Edit and 4.32x on HunyuanVideo with competitive or superior quality.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring caching on ideal outcomes instead of trajectory imitation breaks the quality bottleneck of trajectory approximation without retraining.

title: MambaLoc: Lightweight Indoor Localization Using Cross-Modal Knowledge Distillation
summary: Accurate indoor localization on resource-constrained edge devices remains challenging due to the tension between modeling fidelity and computational efficiency. Wi-Fi Channel State Information (CSI) enables low-cost deployment using existing Wi-Fi infrastructure but is heavily distorted by multipath propagation. Transformer-based solutions mitigate these effects but their quadratic complexity limits real-time edge deployment. Ultra-Wideband (UWB) provides geometrically precise ranging yet requires dedicated infrastructure. We present MambaLoc, a cross-modal distillation framework that improves the accuracy-efficiency balance in CSI-based localization. MambaLoc uses a linear-time Selective State Space Model (Mamba) as a lightweight CSI student, guided during training by a UWB-Transformer teacher. A Feature Alignment Module bridges the representational gap between heterogeneous RF modalities, allowing the CSI model to inherit UWB-derived geometric structure without UWB hardware at inference. A probabilistic Gaussian Mixture regression head models multi-modal spatial ambiguity from multipath effects, avoiding the physically implausible averaging of deterministic regression. Evaluations on a real-world dataset show MambaLoc achieves a median localization error of 0.230 m, reducing error by 22.2% over a standalone Mamba baseline, while requiring 65.1% fewer FLOPs and 58% lower inference latency than Transformer-based approaches.

AI.tldr: MambaLoc is a cross-modal distillation framework in which a Mamba-based Wi-Fi CSI student learns from a UWB-Transformer teacher, reaching a median localization error of 0.230 m with 22.2% lower error than standalone Mamba and no UWB hardware at inference.
AI.motivation: Wi-Fi CSI localization is cheap but distorted by multipath, Transformer-based solutions are too costly for edge devices because of quadratic complexity, and UWB is precise but requires dedicated infrastructure.
AI.method: A linear-time Selective State Space Model (Mamba) serves as the lightweight CSI student, guided during training by a UWB-Transformer teacher through a Feature Alignment Module that bridges the RF modality gap, and a probabilistic Gaussian Mixture regression head models multi-modal spatial ambiguity instead of averaging deterministic predictions.
AI.result: On a real-world dataset MambaLoc achieves a median localization error of 0.230 m, a 22.2% reduction over standalone Mamba, while requiring 65.1% fewer FLOPs and 58% lower inference latency than Transformer-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: Cross-modal distillation improves the accuracy-efficiency balance of CSI-based indoor localization for resource-constrained edge devices.

title: A Computational Map of the Disaster Mental Health Research Landscape
summary: When disasters strike, they not only damage infrastructure, buildings, and the economy, but also affect the mental health of affected populations. Research on the mental health effects of disasters has expanded rapidly and has become an important, well-funded area of psychology, public health, and related social sciences. However, the overall structure of this research landscape has not been systematically characterized. Using large language models, we conducted a review of all articles related to terms 'disaster' and 'mental health' indexed in PubMed. 7,859 articles' metadata were retrieved using the NCBI API, and then Claude Sonnet was used to extract structured variables from the abstracts. The results indicated that earthquakes and epidemics were the most commonly studied disasters while many other disasters such as heat and cold waves have received less attention. PTSD, depression, and anxiety were well investigated but many other mental health issues (e.g., aggression, suicide) are relatively ignored. Despite enjoying relatively large sample sizes (median = 452, IQR = 142 - 1,568), the field rarely utilizes machine learning algorithms. Hypothesis significance testing, reviews, qualitative methods, and structural equation modeling are respectively most common methods while agent-based modeling, machine learning, casual inference, and NLP each appear in less than 1% of articles. Studies are limited to a small number of countries, particularly the United States, Japan, and China, while many disaster-prone regions remain substantially underrepresented. This LLM-assisted computational map provides a broad overview of the disaster mental health literature while highlighting important methodological gaps, with particular emphasis on the underutilization of computational methods that could help advance the field.

AI.tldr: An LLM-assisted review of 7,859 PubMed articles on disasters and mental health maps the field, finding concentration on earthquakes, epidemics, PTSD, depression and anxiety, and rare use of computational methods and of many countries and mental health outcomes.
AI.motivation: Research on disasters and mental health has expanded rapidly, but its overall structure has not been systematically characterized.
AI.method: Article metadata for records matching disaster and mental health terms in PubMed were retrieved via the NCBI API, and Claude Sonnet was used to extract structured variables from the abstracts for a computational map of the literature.
AI.result: Earthquakes and epidemics were the most studied disasters while heat and cold waves received less attention; PTSD, depression and anxiety were well investigated while aggression and suicide were relatively ignored; the field rarely uses machine learning (studies had a median sample size of 452, IQR 142-1,568), and hypothesis testing, reviews, qualitative methods and structural equation modeling were the most common methods, with agent-based modeling, machine learning, causal inference and NLP each in under 1% of articles; studies concentrate in the United States, Japan and China.
AI.conclusion: The map highlights methodological gaps and underuse of computational methods that could advance the field, and many disaster-prone regions remain underrepresented.

title: Too Big to Inspect? Ethically Auditing Large Datasets Through Small Samples
summary: Big techs and researchers increasingly claim that their training datasets are too large to inspect for bias and ethical problems. However, in the race to build ever-large models, they have relied on automated web scraping and no human curation. Datasets built this way absorb the stereotypes, exclusionary norms, and historical prejudices of their sources, and the models trained on them can reproduce and amplify those patterns. Because manually auditing billions of samples is humanly impossible, we need practical, effective methods to identify biases in these datasets. This paper studies the feasibility of ethically auditing large datasets through small samples and proposes a practical method for identifying structural biases by applying AI Ethics Tools (AIETs) to random samples. We applied Datasheets for Datasets, Data Statements, Data Nutrition Labels, and Data Cards to a 1% sample of Framed Multi30K, and Datasheets for Datasets to two 0.00006% samples of relaion2B-en-research-safe. Our results show that evaluating small samples with AIETs can reveal ethical problems, structural biases, and technical inconsistencies. Although industry practice assumes that identifying problems requires analyzing the entire dataset, we show that a random subset supports a viable qualitative analysis without overwhelming computational or human resources. Demonstrating that a dataset is biased does not require examining every instance: if a bias appears in a random sample, it is a flaw of the creation process. The AIETs' questions acted as provocateurs, evoking different perspectives and analysis methods for the same dataset, but the analysis and its results depended fundamentally on the human factor. We hope these findings contribute to urgent public discussions about ethics, transparency, accountability, and AI regulation by offering a practical pathway for responsibly auditing massive datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that large training datasets can be audited for ethical problems and structural biases by applying AI Ethics Tools to small random samples, and tests this on a 1% sample of Framed Multi30K and two tiny samples of relaion2B-en-research-safe.
AI.motivation: Big tech and researchers claim that web-scraped training datasets are too large to inspect, yet such datasets absorb stereotypes and prejudices that models can reproduce and amplify, and manually auditing billions of samples is impossible.
AI.method: The authors apply Datasheets for Datasets, Data Statements, Data Nutrition Labels and Data Cards to a 1% random sample of Framed Multi30K, and Datasheets for Datasets to two 0.00006% samples of relaion2B-en-research-safe, treating the tools' questions as provocateurs for qualitative analysis.
AI.result: Evaluating small samples with the AI Ethics Tools reveals ethical problems, structural biases and technical inconsistencies, and a random subset supports a viable qualitative analysis without large computational or human cost, though the analysis still depends on the human factor.
AI.conclusion: A bias found in a random sample indicates a flaw in the creation process, so examining every instance is unnecessary, and the approach offers a practical route to responsible auditing of massive datasets.

title: Tail-risk-aware Agent Safety: Constraining Tail Risks Across Multi-step LLM Agent Workflows
summary: LLM-based agents extend LLMs with tool calls, memory, planning, and retrieval to act in external environments, but they are vulnerable to attacks at different workflow steps. Existing defenses, including prompt engineering and post-training alignment, primarily improve LLM-only safety and often overlook risks that arise from multi-step execution. External verification adds guardrails to check each step separately, but it typically ignores how risks can propagate across steps. We argue that we should consider risk transitions across dependent steps through the agent workflow, rather than separate verification on a single step. In this paper, we propose \textbf{T}ail-risk-aware \textbf{A}gent \textbf{S}afety (TAS), a tail-risk-aware safety framework that models agent workflow safety as a sequence of dependent safety states and constrains the rare but extreme risks (i.e., tail risk) with a shared budget. TAS first models safety-state transitions sequentially along the workflow as an MDP to trace risk propagation, then measures a tail-sensitive risk to target rare but high-cost risks (i.e., tail risk), and constrains the risk with a shared budget to derive a step-wise safety strategy. By constraining tail risk rather than the overall average, TAS suppresses rare high-cost failures while preserving utility in normal cases. Experiments show that TAS achieves better performance compared with eleven baselines across three benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TAS, a tail-risk-aware safety framework that models LLM agent workflows as dependent safety states and constrains rare but extreme risks with a shared budget, reporting better performance than eleven baselines on three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing defenses such as prompt engineering, post-training alignment and per-step external verification focus on LLM-only safety or check each step separately, overlooking how risks propagate across dependent steps of multi-step agent execution.
AI.method: TAS models safety-state transitions along the agent workflow as an MDP to trace risk propagation, measures a tail-sensitive risk to target rare high-cost failures, and constrains that risk with a shared budget to derive a step-wise safety strategy.
AI.result: TAS achieves better performance than eleven baselines across three benchmarks, suppressing rare high-cost failures while preserving utility in normal cases.
AI.conclusion: Constraining tail risk rather than average risk offers a way to make multi-step LLM agents safer without sacrificing their usefulness in typical situations.

title: TurnFlow: Benchmarking User-State Reasoning in Multi-Turn LLM Agents via Scene-Guided User Simulation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed through conversational interfaces, yet strong single-turn performance does not imply reliability in multi-turn settings. Multi-turn assistance requires a model to maintain an evolving representation of user requirements and to reason over it before complying with later requests. Failures can therefore be subtle: models may fail to recognize a changed constraint or hidden conflict, or recognize it without enforcing it in the final response. Existing benchmarks primarily test fully specified prompts, long-context recall, or controlled domain environments, leaving open-domain requirement reconciliation undermeasured. We introduce TurnFlow, an interactive benchmark for evaluating whether models preserve, revise, and act on user requirements across turns. TurnFlow combines adaptive user simulation with verifiable judging, allowing conversations to unfold naturally while keeping hidden requirements and pass/fail criteria controlled. In our evaluation, nine LLMs achieve overall pass rates from 42.86% to 59.59% on 490 scenarios. Performance varies substantially across challenge types: models perform well on Stateful Multi-Constraint Following but remain considerably less reliable on Scope Creep and Goal Shift. These results reveal persistent limitations in reasoning over evolving user requirements across turns.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TurnFlow, an interactive benchmark that tests whether LLMs preserve, revise and act on user requirements across turns, using adaptive user simulation with verifiable judging on 490 scenarios.
AI.motivation: Strong single-turn performance does not imply multi-turn reliability, and existing benchmarks test fully specified prompts, long-context recall or controlled domains, leaving open-domain requirement reconciliation under-measured.
AI.method: TurnFlow combines adaptive user simulation with verifiable judging, keeping hidden requirements and pass/fail criteria controlled while conversations unfold naturally across challenge types such as Stateful Multi-Constraint Following, Scope Creep and Goal Shift.
AI.result: Nine LLMs achieve overall pass rates from 42.86% to 59.59% on 490 scenarios, performing well on Stateful Multi-Constraint Following but considerably less reliably on Scope Creep and Goal Shift.
AI.conclusion: The results reveal persistent limitations in how current LLMs reason over evolving user requirements across turns.

title: Beyond Query Similarity: Safety-Conditioned Cache Routing for LLM Response Reuse
summary: Semantic response caching reuses a cached response for a semantically similar query to improve LLM inference efficiency. However, query similarity alone can lead to unsafe reuse when safety conditions change. Existing approaches improve cache safety through stricter similarity checks, context-aware validation, or response verification, yet they may still miss safety conflicts between the cached response and the new request or introduce unnecessary verification overhead. We argue that safe and efficient semantic caching requires a reuse policy that makes the cached response's safety conditions explicit and uses them to guide the reuse decision with a balance between safety and utility. In this paper, we propose SafeCache, a safety-aware framework that separates candidate retrieval from safety approval and formulates semantic response reuse as a safety-conditioned routing problem. SafeCache matches each cached-response condition against the new request and aggregates the per-condition mismatches into an overall risk score. A separate contradiction guard prevents explicit conflicts from being diluted by strong matches. It further estimates matching uncertainty and calibrates the routing policy under a required unsafe-reuse target and a verifier-call budget to choose among direct reuse, selective verification, or regeneration. Experiments show that SafeCache achieves the better safety-utility trade-off among the evaluated baselines, enabling safer response reuse at comparable cache utility.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SafeCache, a safety-aware semantic response caching framework that treats cache reuse as a safety-conditioned routing problem and chooses among direct reuse, selective verification and regeneration.
AI.motivation: Semantic caching reuses responses for similar queries, but query similarity alone can cause unsafe reuse when safety conditions change, and existing fixes such as stricter similarity checks or response verification may miss conflicts or add verification overhead.
AI.method: SafeCache separates candidate retrieval from safety approval, matches each cached-response safety condition against the new request, aggregates mismatches into a risk score, uses a contradiction guard so explicit conflicts are not diluted, estimates matching uncertainty, and calibrates routing under an unsafe-reuse target and a verifier-call budget.
AI.result: SafeCache achieves the better safety-utility trade-off among the evaluated baselines, enabling safer response reuse at comparable cache utility.
AI.conclusion: Making the safety conditions of cached responses explicit and using them to guide reuse decisions allows semantic caching to be both safer and efficient.

title: D-REAL: Acceptance-Length Optimization with Unbiased Gradients for Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding efficiency depends on the number of consecutively accepted draft tokens, yet token-level training objectives do not directly optimize this quantity. We introduce D-REAL (Drafter Reinforcement of Expected Acceptance Length), a post-training method that directly optimizes expected acceptance length for a fixed decoding context. D-REAL weights position-wise draft-target distributional overlap by prefix survival probabilities along a draft-sampled prefix, faithfully capturing the sequential dependence of verification on earlier proposals. By accounting for the parameter dependence of the proposal distribution, we derive an unbiased gradient estimator for this single-round objective under stochastic verification. We evaluate D-REAL on DSpark and DFlash2 with Qwen3-8B as the target model across ten benchmarks. Starting from baselines whose mean acceptance length has plateaued, one epoch of D-REAL post-training consistently improves the benchmark-averaged mean acceptance length by up to 0.23 tokens across both architectures under greedy (T = 0.0) and stochastic (T = 1.0) sampling, translating into up to a 9.4% end-to-end serving throughput improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes D-REAL, a post-training method that directly optimises the expected acceptance length of speculative decoding drafters with an unbiased gradient estimator, improving acceptance length and serving throughput on Qwen3-8B.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding efficiency depends on the number of consecutively accepted draft tokens, but token-level training objectives do not directly optimise this quantity.
AI.method: D-REAL weights position-wise draft-target distributional overlap by prefix survival probabilities along a draft-sampled prefix, and accounts for the parameter dependence of the proposal distribution to derive an unbiased gradient estimator for a single-round objective under stochastic verification.
AI.result: On DSpark and DFlash2 with Qwen3-8B as the target across ten benchmarks, one epoch of post-training raises the benchmark-averaged mean acceptance length by up to 0.23 tokens under greedy and stochastic sampling, translating into up to a 9.4% end-to-end serving throughput improvement.
AI.conclusion: Directly optimising acceptance length can push drafters beyond plateaued token-level baselines, yielding practical serving speedups.

title: BunshinRL: Splitting Live Agent Workspaces for Memory-Efficient Agentic RL
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts interleave model reasoning with tool calls in persistent workspaces. Scaling these rollouts incurs substantial memory costs for concurrent environments, while slow tool calls delay entire rollout batches. We present BunshinRL, an agentic RL rollout system that exploits shared environment state and recurring tool calls through three techniques: memory sharing across environments, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution. These techniques build on BunshinFork, a novel live whole-workspace forking mechanism for containers. BunshinFork reconstructs process trees, shares memory copy-on-write, and preserves file, communication, and GUI state, enabling cached-state reuse and rollback after incorrect speculation. We implement BunshinRL and BunshinFork through Linux kernel module and CRIU modifications. BunshinRL reduces peak memory by up to 43%, total memory consumption by up to 51%, and end-to-end rollout latency by 23%.

AI.tldr: The paper presents BunshinRL, an agentic RL rollout system that shares memory, caches tool prefixes and speculatively executes tools across environments, built on BunshinFork, a live whole-workspace forking mechanism for containers.
AI.motivation: Agentic RL rollouts that interleave reasoning with tool calls in persistent workspaces incur heavy memory costs for concurrent environments, and slow tool calls delay entire rollout batches.
AI.method: BunshinRL uses memory sharing across environments, tool-prefix caching and speculative tool execution, built on BunshinFork, which reconstructs process trees, shares memory copy-on-write and preserves file, communication and GUI state, implemented through a Linux kernel module and CRIU modifications.
AI.result: BunshinRL reduces peak memory by up to 43%, total memory consumption by up to 51%, and end-to-end rollout latency by 23%.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting shared environment state and recurring tool calls makes large-scale agentic RL rollouts substantially cheaper in memory and latency, with rollback available after incorrect speculation.

title: Decentralised Drone Swarm Formation under Silent Failures with ACO Pheromone Claims and PSO Tuning
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures, 22 tables. Code, browser demo and raw results are included as ancillary files
summary: We study decentralised drone formation, without a central planner, under the conditions that make it hard: nobody knows how many drones are alive, failures are silent, radio is short-ranged and lossy, and actuation is noisy. In our controller, ant colony optimisation (ACO) allocates drones to picture positions through claims that behave as reinforced, evaporating pheromone and are gossiped between neighbours, so evaporation doubles as failure detection. A particle swarm optimisation (PSO) law flies the drones, a noise-buffered Voronoi filter keeps them apart, and PSO also tunes the controller offline. We prove that claims of destroyed drones vanish within bounded time, that conflicts between drones that exchange tables are resolved consistently, that survivors cover the picture to within a factor of two, and that drones cannot collide while their safety cells are feasible. On held-out seeds and with two tuned configurations, the controller formed the picture in 95-99% of runs in the hardest regime, restored it after a silent loss of half the swarm in 96-100% of runs at normal difficulty, transferred unchanged to eight unseen shapes and to 300 drones, and overlapped in 5 of 21,088 runs. A CBBA-style baseline that shares the evaporating claims but uses argmax without swaps was at least as reliable as ours once tuned with the same budget, and repaired faster, whereas ours generalised better to unseen shapes. The benefit thus comes from the pheromone dynamics and from tuning, not from ACO's stochastic construction or PSO's social terms. A centralised oracle is faster.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a decentralised drone formation controller in which ACO pheromone claims with evaporation serve as failure detection, and PSO flies and tunes the drones, with proofs and simulation results under silent failures.
AI.motivation: Decentralised drone formation is hard when the number of live drones is unknown, failures are silent, radio is short-ranged and lossy, and actuation is noisy, and existing allocation approaches need a formation method robust to these conditions.
AI.method: Ant colony optimisation allocates drones to picture positions through gossiped reinforced, evaporating pheromone claims, a particle swarm optimisation law flies the drones, a noise-buffered Voronoi filter keeps them apart, and PSO tunes the controller offline.
AI.result: On held-out seeds with two tuned configurations, the controller formed the picture in 95-99% of runs in the hardest regime, restored it after a silent loss of half the swarm in 96-100% of runs at normal difficulty, transferred to eight unseen shapes and 300 drones, and overlapped in 5 of 21,088 runs; a tuned CBBA-style baseline was at least as reliable and repaired faster, while the controller generalised better to unseen shapes.
AI.conclusion: The benefit comes from the pheromone dynamics and from tuning rather than from ACO's stochastic construction or PSO's social terms, and a centralised oracle is faster.

title: Represented but Not Used: Value-Policy Dissociation in LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents need to choose actions whose consequences unfold over multiple future steps, yet poor decisions do not reveal whether the model failed to represent those consequences or failed to use them. Mechanistic interpretability has studied internal representations of environment state and plans, but sequential decision making also requires evaluating how candidate actions change future outcomes. Reinforcement learning formalizes this as action value. We study this computation in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, and GPT-OSS-20B across a partially observed Grid environment and WebShop, a simulated web shopping environment. We find that the relative values of candidate actions are linearly decodable from intermediate hidden states, including at states where the policy prefers a worse action. We call this gap between value representation and policy choice value-policy dissociation. To investigate how represented value relates to action selection, we compare direct interventions along the value readout direction with Natural Value Transport (NVT), a transformation learned from hidden state changes that naturally result from differences in action value. While readout-direction interventions have limited and inconsistent effects, NVT more consistently influences action preferences, particularly at later layers. We also test a closed-loop controller that uses the value readout as a sensor and NVT as an actuator, observing improvements in task outcomes. These results suggest that LLM agents can represent useful prospective value without reliably translating it into policy choice.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that LLM agents linearly represent the relative values of candidate actions in hidden states even when they choose worse actions, a gap the authors call value-policy dissociation, and that a learned transport intervention influences action choice more consistently than direct readout-direction interventions.
AI.motivation: Poor decisions by LLM agents do not reveal whether the model failed to represent long-horizon consequences or failed to use them, and mechanistic interpretability has not studied how represented action values relate to action selection.
AI.method: The authors study Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and GPT-OSS-20B on a partially observed Grid environment and WebShop, decode action values from intermediate hidden states, and compare direct readout-direction interventions with Natural Value Transport, a transformation learned from hidden state changes that result from action value differences, including a closed-loop controller.
AI.result: Readout-direction interventions have limited and inconsistent effects, whereas NVT more consistently influences action preferences, particularly at later layers, and the closed-loop controller improves task outcomes.
AI.conclusion: LLM agents can represent useful prospective value without reliably translating it into policy choice, suggesting that the link between value representation and action selection is a distinct target for improvement.

title: PatternBloom: Empowering Agentic RAG with Externalized RL-Distilled Graph Patterns
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 46 pages. Code: this https URL
summary: Reinforcement-learning-trained agents for retrieval-augmented generation retrieve content (passages, knowledge-graph fragments, or hyperedges) and supervise training with outcome rewards on the final answer. Across these paradigms the reasoning route through retrieved content never leaves the language model's hidden state, conflating declarative knowledge with the procedural knowledge that recurs across queries of the same logical type; content-only methods consequently plateau as reasoning depth grows. We introduce PatternBloom, an agentic RAG framework that shifts the unit of retrieval from content (what to read) to logic (how to reason). A first RL stage scores the agent's constructed evidence graph by a frozen oracle's information gain through the Information-Density Reward (IDR), a size-normalized mutual-information surrogate. High-reward trajectories are distilled into a Graph Pattern Memory (GPM) of type-abstracted reasoning skeletons, and a second RL stage uses the Pattern-Augmented Reward (PAR) to couple policy to memory, turning procedural reasoning into a learnable, externalized structural prior. A 7B PatternBloom outperforms $27$ baselines by $+15.0$ Avg-OOD EM, with the gain compounding with reasoning depth precisely because procedural knowledge, once distilled, is reused rather than re-derived at every query. We release our code at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PatternBloom, an agentic RAG framework that retrieves reusable reasoning patterns distilled from high-reward trajectories into a Graph Pattern Memory, and reports a 7B model outperforming 27 baselines by +15.0 Avg-OOD EM.
AI.motivation: Existing RL-trained RAG agents keep the reasoning route inside the model's hidden state, conflating declarative knowledge with procedural knowledge that recurs across queries of the same logical type, so content-only methods plateau as reasoning depth grows.
AI.method: A first RL stage scores the constructed evidence graph with the Information-Density Reward, a size-normalised mutual-information surrogate computed by a frozen oracle; high-reward trajectories are distilled into a Graph Pattern Memory of type-abstracted reasoning skeletons, and a second RL stage uses the Pattern-Augmented Reward to couple the policy to this memory.
AI.result: A 7B PatternBloom outperforms 27 baselines by +15.0 Avg-OOD EM, with the gain growing with reasoning depth.
AI.conclusion: Distilling procedural reasoning into an externalised structural prior lets it be reused rather than re-derived for each query, which the authors argue is the source of the improvement.

title: Sampling Is Not Curiosity: Why LLM Agents Should Investigate
comment: Accepted to the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Position Paper Track
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended tasks, very common in research scenarios where they are required to explore, investigate, or act curiously. At inference time, an LLM is a fixed map from context to next-token distribution, the pretrained weights determine the function, and only its conditioning changes as context accumulates. Mechanisms like temperature, best-of-N, tree search, or RAG vary how the distribution is sampled or what it is conditioned on, but do not update the agent's model of the environment. We argue that current LLM agents do not explore curiously; they explore stochastically. From how curiosity is understood in the RL literature, it requires a predictive structure over how the environment responds to the agent's actions, which improves online from current interaction, drives action selection through its predicted improvement, and persists beyond the context window. Additionally, in its open-ended form, the agent should intrinsically originate what to investigate. Thus, we propose a framework defining curiosity in LLM agents, reserving the term for systems that satisfy it. In doing so, we identify the research directions its implementation opens up.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current LLM agents explore stochastically rather than curiously and proposes a definition of curiosity for LLM agents that requires a predictive structure improved online, action selection driven by predicted improvement, and persistence beyond the context window.
AI.motivation: Mechanisms such as temperature, best-of-N, tree search and RAG change how the output distribution is sampled or conditioned but do not update the agent's model of the environment, while open-ended research tasks require exploration and investigation.
AI.method: The authors draw on how curiosity is understood in the RL literature to define the requirements for curiosity in LLM agents, reserving the term for systems that meet them, including that the agent intrinsically originates what to investigate in open-ended settings.
AI.result: The paper contains no experiments; it identifies research directions that its proposed implementation of curiosity opens up.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM agents do not yet explore curiously, and a predictive, online-updated and persistent structure for environment response is needed to achieve it.

title: Receiver-Resolution APS-PDP Maps for Wireless Channels: Benchmarking and Coarse-to-Fine Modeling
summary: Angle Power Spectrum (APS) and Power Delay Profile (PDP) are receiver-facing spectra that govern beam selection and wideband equalization. Most ray-tracing benchmarks provide supervision as variable-size multipath component lists. This format does not match practical receivers, whose angular and delay resolutions are limited by array aperture and system bandwidth. As a result, learning targets are ambiguous and evaluations can change with reconstruction conventions. We introduce UrbanADPSMap, a benchmark that converts ray-traced supervision into fixed-grid APS and PDP targets by explicitly modeling bandwidth-limited and aperture-limited response kernels. By fixing the receiver-domain kernels, discretization, and validity mask, UrbanADPSMap removes reconstruction-induced target ambiguity and stabilizes downstream evaluation across methods. Built on this benchmark, we propose SpecFlowAR, a coarse-to-fine generator based on multi-scale autoregressive flow matching. The model first captures coarse dispersion structure and then refines beam-relevant peaks and low-power tails. The number of function evaluations controls the sampling budget, enabling latency and quality to be adjusted for dense spectrum queries. Experiments on the test set show that SpecFlowAR reduces BPL@5 to 2.03 dB under a unified NFE=80 budget, while improving beam utility and reducing errors of 3GPP dispersion statistics.

AI.tldr: The paper presents UrbanADPSMap, a benchmark that converts ray-traced multipath supervision into fixed-grid receiver-resolution APS and PDP targets, and SpecFlowAR, a coarse-to-fine multi-scale autoregressive flow matching generator evaluated on it.
AI.motivation: Ray-tracing benchmarks supply variable-size multipath component lists, which do not match practical receivers limited by array aperture and bandwidth, so learning targets are ambiguous and evaluations depend on reconstruction conventions.
AI.method: UrbanADPSMap models bandwidth-limited and aperture-limited response kernels to fix the receiver-domain kernels, discretisation and validity mask, and SpecFlowAR generates the spectra coarse-to-fine by first capturing dispersion structure and then refining beam-relevant peaks and low-power tails, with the number of function evaluations controlling the sampling budget.
AI.result: Under a unified NFE=80 budget on the test set, SpecFlowAR reduces BPL@5 to 2.03 dB, improves beam utility and reduces errors in 3GPP dispersion statistics.
AI.conclusion: Fixed receiver-domain targets remove reconstruction-induced ambiguity and allow latency and quality to be traded off through the sampling budget for dense spectrum queries.

title: InfoOrgBench: Can Agents Turn Scattered Information into Coherent Hierarchies?
summary: When agents organize records into folders, they may correctly group the excerpts of a design proposal yet place the proposal under the wrong owning group. Existing agent benchmarks do not directly measure such higher-level errors. We introduce InfoOrgBench, a benchmark of 150 tasks in which agents organize scattered records from meeting recaps, issue threads and design proposals into hierarchies. Integrity checks verify that every record is preserved, and a Structure Score measures agreement with the source hierarchy at every level, independent of folder names and order. We evaluate 45 systems that pair nine models with five agent harnesses. The best system scores 83.2 out of 100, but no system exceeds 78 on meeting recaps or issue threads. Model choice affects scores far more than harness choice: model means span about 27 points, whereas the average effect of each harness is below one point. More importantly, parent-level relations have higher error rates than leaf-level relations in all three domains. In design proposals, nearly half of the outputs analyzed by level make exactly this kind of error. These results show that evaluating information organization requires measuring higher-level relations separately from record preservation and local grouping.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces InfoOrgBench, a benchmark of 150 tasks that measures whether agents organise scattered records into correct hierarchies, using a Structure Score that checks higher-level relations separately from record preservation and local grouping.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks do not directly measure higher-level errors, such as placing a correctly grouped design proposal under the wrong owning group, in information organisation.
AI.method: The benchmark asks agents to organise records from meeting recaps, issue threads and design proposals into hierarchies, verifying with integrity checks that every record is preserved and scoring agreement with the source hierarchy at every level, independent of folder names and order, across 45 systems pairing nine models with five agent harnesses.
AI.result: The best system scores 83.2 out of 100, no system exceeds 78 on meeting recaps or issue threads, model choice spans about 27 points of mean score while each harness averages under one point, and parent-level relations show higher error rates than leaf-level relations in all three domains.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating information organisation requires measuring higher-level relations separately from record preservation and local grouping, since model choice matters far more than harness choice.

title: Agentic discrete-event simulation for manufacturing system design: an open 3D simulator, a benchmark and an industrial case
comment: 55 pages, 15 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to the Journal of Manufacturing Systems (special issue AI for Manufacturing). Software: this https URL (doi:https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23565564)
summary: The design of manufacturing systems relies on discrete-event simulation (DES) models that experts still build in tool-specific interfaces. AI agents can now write simulation code, but every model they write from scratch is new, unverified software. We present SimuLean, an open-source 3D DES simulator on the Unity engine designed to be programmed by AI agents: its modelling semantics are verified once, in the platform, and the agent builds and studies one model through domain-level commands, in the 3D scene or headless; physically simulated durations are calibrated for fast headless studies. We evaluated it on 18 manufacturing modelling tasks, from single machines to published production lines. A frontier agent built valid models in 93 of 108 attempts (86%), in about two minutes each; on the benchmark's interface version, two frontier agents built 105 of 108 models through domain commands alone, so that each comes with a record of how it was built. Every residual failure was silent - a model that builds and runs but answers wrongly - and only comparison with reference models revealed them all. In an industrial case, one agent working alone rebuilt, verified and studied a robotised welding workshop from a published study, in SimuLean and in SimPy. Comparing them with the published, expert-built model exposed an error in it; against the corrected model, the agent-built models agree within 1%. One agent can already build complete, realistic and traceable models for the design of manufacturing systems; independent reference models are what make them trustworthy.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SimuLean, an open-source 3D discrete-event simulator on Unity designed to be programmed by AI agents, and shows that agents can build valid manufacturing models through domain-level commands, with an industrial case verified against a published model.
AI.motivation: Manufacturing system design relies on discrete-event simulation models that experts build in tool-specific interfaces, and models written from scratch by AI agents are new, unverified software.
AI.method: SimuLean verifies its modelling semantics once in the platform, so the agent builds and studies models through domain-level commands in the 3D scene or headless, with physically simulated durations calibrated for fast headless studies, and the authors evaluated it on 18 manufacturing modelling tasks and a robotised welding workshop, comparing against SimPy and a published reference model.
AI.result: A frontier agent built valid models in 93 of 108 attempts (86%), two frontier agents built 105 of 108 models on the benchmark's interface version through domain commands alone, every residual failure was silent, and the agent-built models agree within 1% of a corrected reference model after comparison exposed an error in the published model.
AI.conclusion: One agent can build complete, traceable models for manufacturing system design, and independent reference models are what make them trustworthy.

title: An LLM-Orchestrated Multi-Modal Chatbot for Tomato Disease Consultant
comment: 14th International Conference on Multidisciplinary Research (ICMR 2026), ISBN: 978-974-474-120-2, Thaksin University Publisher, pp. 37-50, 2026 (Published)
summary: This paper introduces a chatbot developed to assist in diagnosing common diseases in tomato plants through natural language interaction. Users can describe symptoms in text. Then, the chatbot responds with the most likely disease, and basic treatment suggestions and related image-based reasoning. The system leverages pre-trained Mistral and Llama 3.2 large language models. The system is also built using LangChain and Streamlit to provide a lightweight and offline-friendly interface. This work targets to support tomato growers a fast and accessible tomato plant health guidance when the technical expertise is not available nearby, especially in the remote areas. The experimental results are promising and encourage further improvement of the chatbot for future real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper describes a LangChain and Streamlit chatbot that uses Mistral and Llama 3.2 LLMs to suggest likely tomato plant diseases, basic treatments and image-based reasoning from text descriptions of symptoms, designed to run offline.
AI.motivation: Tomato growers in remote areas often lack nearby technical expertise for plant health guidance, so a fast and accessible diagnostic aid is needed.
AI.method: Users describe symptoms in text, and the system, built with pre-trained Mistral and Llama 3.2 models, LangChain and Streamlit, returns the most likely disease, basic treatment suggestions and related image-based reasoning in a lightweight, offline-friendly interface.
AI.result: The abstract reports that the experimental results are promising, without giving specific figures.
AI.conclusion: The authors suggest the chatbot could support tomato growers with fast plant health guidance and merits further improvement toward real-world deployment.

title: Efficient LLM Adaptation with Forward-Only Passes
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference serving is undergoing rapid growth and large-scale deployment, motivating us to rethink how the inference process itself can be leveraged to enable efficient task-specific LLM adaptation. In this paper, we propose a forward-only approach for efficient LLM adaptation with forward-only passes in LLM inference serving. We exploit the angle concentration of activations induced by each singular value decomposition (SVD) component to measure its contribution-dispersed or concentrated-to the angle concentration of the hidden states. Based on this, our forward-only search then efficiently identifies the weight matrix with the highest dispersion that merits rank reduction. We then selectively remove the higher-order components and retain the lower-order components in SVD. Empirical results across diverse datasets demonstrate the competitive accuracy of our forward-only approach, while theoretical analysis shows lower peak memory and greater speedup than the gradient-based approach and greater speedup than the exhaustive search approach. The experiments further present the robustness and generalization of our forward-only approach to various LLMs with up to 57B parameters. The code is included in the supplementary material.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a forward-only LLM adaptation method that uses SVD angle concentration of activations during inference serving to select weight matrices and remove higher-order singular components, without gradient computation.
AI.motivation: LLM inference serving is growing rapidly, and the authors seek to exploit the inference process itself for efficient task-specific adaptation, avoiding the memory and time costs of gradient-based methods and exhaustive search.
AI.method: The approach measures each SVD component's contribution to the angle concentration of hidden states to find the weight matrix with the highest dispersion, then removes its higher-order components and retains the lower-order ones in a forward-only search.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse datasets show competitive accuracy, and the approach is robust and generalises to various LLMs of up to 57B parameters, with theoretical analysis indicating lower peak memory and greater speedup than gradient-based methods and greater speedup than exhaustive search.
AI.conclusion: Forward-only passes during serving can provide an efficient alternative to gradient-based LLM adaptation, though the abstract's claims rest on theoretical analysis for memory and speed.

title: Towards Identity-Preserving LLM Agents under Model Transition
summary: When an LLM agent's backend model is upgraded or replaced, operators typically reload the same persona, memory, and rules onto the new model and assume the agent will behave as before. We show this assumption requires empirical validation-and that whether identity is preserved depends on the specific model pairing. Across 5,760 compliance-testing runs in 12 regulated domains with three open-weight models, we find that some transitions produce significant behavioral drift while others do not, even when the agent's external state remains identical. Crucially, this drift is invisible to verbal verification: every model claims full policy compliance, yet actual decisions under pressure differ across models. The same external state can reorder which model is most compliant-a large positive effect on one substrate, negligible on the other two. Practitioners should treat model transitions as behavioral changes requiring action-level empirical testing, not as transparent infrastructure operations.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that replacing the backend model of an LLM agent, while keeping the same persona, memory and rules, can cause significant behavioural drift that verbal verification fails to reveal, based on 5,760 compliance-testing runs in 12 regulated domains.
AI.motivation: Operators usually assume an agent keeps its behaviour when the backend model is upgraded or replaced, and this assumption has not been empirically validated.
AI.method: The authors run 5,760 compliance-testing runs across 12 regulated domains with three open-weight models, comparing behaviour across model pairings while the external agent state remains identical.
AI.result: Some model transitions produce significant behavioural drift and others do not, every model claims full policy compliance, and actual decisions under pressure differ across models, with the same state reordering which model is most compliant.
AI.conclusion: Practitioners should treat model transitions as behavioural changes that require action-level empirical testing rather than as transparent infrastructure operations.

title: DFT-Agent Bench: Scaffold Effects and Execution Provenance in Autonomous DFT
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for first-principles materials simulation. We report empirical findings from DFT-Agent Bench, a benchmark of 200+ Quantum ESPRESSO tasks spanning relaxation, electronic structure, equation-of-state, and elastic-tensor pipelines over multiple material tiers. Each task carries a QE-derived ground truth with public-reference cross-checks where available, and a provenance audit checks whether the required QE execution contract was met. Under one execution harness, we compare a near-bare ReAct baseline with a bundled v5.1 scaffold on two models. The complete scaffold improves bands+DOS by +0.08/+0.11 and d-electron vc-relax by +0.17 on both models, while high-scoring relaxation and equation-of-state cells leave little room for improvement.
