AI.motivation: LLMs still produce incorrect solutions to hard math problems, and each verification direction has a gap: backward checking cannot ensure correct reasoning or completeness, while forward checking may overlook key constraints in long solution chains.
AI.method: BiVerify starts with backward verification, then runs forward verification of the reasoning, with direction switching, state resetting and re-verification governed by verification outcomes. Failed checks trigger revision of the candidate or the verification flow. Shared mathematical tools separate logical reasoning from precise computation.
AI.result: Evaluated on five challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks with DeepSeek, GPT and Gemini models, BiVerify exceeds the strongest representative public baseline in this work by 13.5 percentage points on average accuracy, with the margin reaching 31.2 points on GPT. Its overall performance exceeds either verification direction used alone.
AI.conclusion: Combining the two verification directions in a feedback loop yields gains beyond either direction alone, supporting bidirectional self-correction for mathematical reasoning.

title: RealEmbedBench: Benchmarking LLMs on Real-World Application-Layer Embedded Software Tasks
summary: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on general coding tasks, but their capabilities in application-layer embedded software development remain underexplored. Existing embedded benchmarks primarily focus on hardware-in-the-loop validation in simulated environments. We introduce RealEmbedBench, a benchmark of 5,142 samples covering three application-layer tasks: code generation and completion, state machine modeling and implementation, and cross-OS code translation. We evaluate six representative LLMs and find substantial performance differences across tasks and models. Project context, especially the local code window, significantly affects code generation and completion. Models perform reasonably well at state machine modeling but struggle to translate these models into executable code. Cross-OS translation performance varies substantially by direction. Translation from Harmony to RT-Thread is particularly challenging, with an average pass rate of 0.1667. These findings suggest that developers should consider local code context when using LLMs for code generation and completion and select models according to the translation direction. They also motivate the use of more real-world state machine implementation data in LLM training to narrow the gap between modeling and executable code.

AI.tldr: RealEmbedBench is a benchmark of 5,142 samples for application-layer embedded software, covering code generation and completion, state machine modeling and implementation, and cross-OS code translation. Six LLMs show large differences across tasks, and Harmony-to-RT-Thread translation is hardest with an average pass rate of 0.1667.
AI.motivation: LLM capability in application-layer embedded software development is underexplored, and existing embedded benchmarks focus mainly on hardware-in-the-loop validation in simulated environments.
AI.method: The benchmark spans three application-layer tasks: code generation and completion, state machine modeling and implementation, and cross-OS code translation. Six representative LLMs are evaluated on it.
AI.result: Performance differs substantially across tasks and models. The local code window significantly affects generation and completion. Models model state machines reasonably well but struggle to turn them into executable code. Translation performance varies by direction, with Harmony to RT-Thread averaging a pass rate of 0.1667.
AI.conclusion: Developers should supply local code context and choose models by translation direction, and more real-world state machine implementation data in training would narrow the gap between modeling and executable code.

title: GOPR-CAD: Graph-of-Operations Progressive Reasoning for CAD Generation
summary: Generating accurate CAD models requires substantial engineering expertise and careful control of geometry, topology, and mechanical constraints. Text-to-CAD aims to simplify this process, but current LLM-based methods often generate CAD programs directly. Language models remain unreliable when producing long code while coordinating coupled geometric, topological, and dimensional constraints. Consequently, executable programs may still produce structurally incorrect models, which execution rate and rendered appearance may fail to reveal. To address these limitations, we propose GOPR-CAD, an agentic Text-to-CAD pipeline based on Graph-of-Operations Progressive Reasoning. A language model acts as a decision agent over encapsulated CAD operations and progressively constructs an executable operation graph, which a deterministic compiler converts into the final CAD model. This separation requires no additional training and supports different language models. To evaluate structural fidelity, we construct MHCAD, a benchmark of 300 standard mechanical part requirements derived from Machinery's Handbook. Their explicit structures enable reference-free STEP/B-rep evaluation. GOPR-CAD achieves 82.7% Structural Yield on MHCAD, and 87.2% Structural Yield on an external CADPrompt subset.

AI.tldr: GOPR-CAD is an agentic Text-to-CAD pipeline in which an LLM builds an executable graph of encapsulated CAD operations and a deterministic compiler turns it into the final model. It reaches 82.7% Structural Yield on the 300-requirement MHCAD benchmark and 87.2% on an external CADPrompt subset.
AI.motivation: LLMs generating CAD programs directly are unreliable on long code with coupled geometric, topological and dimensional constraints, so programs that execute may still yield structurally incorrect models that execution rate and rendered appearance fail to reveal.
AI.method: A language model acts as a decision agent over encapsulated CAD operations and progressively constructs an executable operation graph, which a deterministic compiler converts into the final CAD model. The approach needs no additional training and works with different language models. The authors build MHCAD from Machinery's Handbook for reference-free STEP/B-rep evaluation.
AI.result: GOPR-CAD achieves 82.7% Structural Yield on MHCAD and 87.2% Structural Yield on an external CADPrompt subset.
AI.conclusion: Separating LLM decision making over operations from deterministic compilation gives structurally sound CAD models without training, and structural evaluation exposes errors that execution rate misses.

title: DriveFoundry: Co-Evolving Data and Model for Efficient Closed-Loop Iteration in Autonomous Driving
comment: 57 pages, 31 figures, Project page: this https URL
summary: A driving foundation model must learn reusable decision knowledge from rare critical events and apply it under strict runtime constraints. We introduce DriveFoundry, a closed-loop framework improving iteration efficiency under data and computation budgets by coupling structured causal data refinement with adaptive inference. The Data Engine builds traceable scene-candidate records linking scene evidence and factor-decision relations to candidate trajectories and outcome assessments. Candidate comparisons and counterfactual annotations clarify how scene factors affect behavioral feasibility and preference. Verified model failures guide VLM-assisted annotation and expert correction, refining training data and annotation systems. The model engine, Xiaomi-Drive-o1, unifies Perception, Causation, Action, World, and Value within a shared vision-language backbone to enable cross-task knowledge transfer. Block-wise latent refill passes candidate-specific evidence and predicted visual consequences between task blocks, connecting scene understanding, planning, and evaluation. A learned value-of-computation head selects tasks and allocates latent tokens based on expected benefit and cost, adapting inference to each decision. On PhysicalAI, the 9B model achieves the lowest ADE@1 across evaluated splits and horizons among tested models. In AlpaSim, it outperforms Alpamayo 1.5 across all metrics and achieves lower close-encounter and off-road rates than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, while trailing in progress and AlpaSim scores. For the 0.8B variant, joint training reduces 5 s minADE@6 by about 54% without altering the inference path or token budget. Adaptive inference matches full reasoning performance using only 28% of tokens. Real-vehicle tests confirm runtime feasibility, supporting a unified paradigm for learning from critical experience and dynamically allocating computation.

AI.tldr: DriveFoundry is a closed-loop framework for autonomous driving that couples a structured data engine with adaptive inference in a unified vision-language model, Xiaomi-Drive-o1. The 9B model achieves the lowest ADE@1 among tested models on PhysicalAI and outperforms Alpamayo 1.5 across all AlpaSim metrics, and adaptive inference matches full reasoning using only 28% of tokens.
AI.motivation: A driving foundation model must learn reusable decision knowledge from rare critical events and apply it under strict runtime constraints of data and computation budgets.
AI.method: The Data Engine builds traceable scene-candidate records linking scene evidence and factor-decision relations to candidate trajectories, with counterfactual annotations and VLM-assisted annotation guided by verified model failures. The model unifies Perception, Causation, Action, World and Value in one vision-language backbone, uses block-wise latent refill to pass evidence between task blocks, and uses a learned value-of-computation head to allocate latent tokens by expected benefit and cost.
AI.result: On PhysicalAI the 9B model achieves the lowest ADE@1 across evaluated splits and horizons among tested models. On AlpaSim it outperforms Alpamayo 1.5 on all metrics and has lower close-encounter and off-road rates than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, while trailing in progress and AlpaSim scores. For the 0.8B variant, joint training reduces 5 s minADE@6 by about 54%, and adaptive inference matches full reasoning with 28% of tokens. Real-vehicle tests confirm runtime feasibility.
AI.conclusion: Learning from critical experience and dynamically allocating computation within one shared backbone is presented as a unified paradigm that improves efficiency and driving performance under runtime constraints.

title: InfraRSI: Harnessing Recursive Self-Improvement for Training Infrastructure
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures, 8 tables. Project page and code: this https URL
summary: While Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) accelerates isolated algorithm and kernel synthesis, distributed LLM training depends on tightly coupled launch settings, operator kernels, and communication schedules, where single edits often hit out-of-memory (OOM) boundaries, compiler conflicts, measurement jitter, or silent numerical drift. We present InfraRSI, the agentic harness that turns open-ended human commands into verified training optimizations via a five-stage workflow: init locks editable scope and a fixed task contract over workload, loss, and timing invariants to prevent reward hacking, doctor profiles baseline phases and calibrates cluster noise, run co-optimizes launch knobs and code patches before re-verifying top candidates against the baseline and logging findings to a cross-hardware experience bank, and report and apply audit source paths, track failed-trial costs, and commit promoted changes. Rather than stepping greedily from a single incumbent, InfraRSI initializes from diverse experience-seeded configurations and fits global execution-time and censored peak-memory models across all trials, including OOMs. Using these models, it prices per-setting memory costs, revises miscalibrated LLM priors from live runs, and pairs memory-hungry optimizations with memory savers and verified code patches. Across four single- and multi-node dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM workloads, InfraRSI achieves a speedup of up to $2.75\times$ and lifts mean Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) from $17.4\%$ to $30.0\%$, outperforming existing tuners and coding agents while transferring experience across GPUs. As it improves training infrastructure efficiency, InfraRSI forms a two-level Recursive Self-Improvement loop---revising priors online within runs and distilling experience across clusters---to push foundation model scaling.

AI.tldr: InfraRSI is an agentic harness that applies recursive self-improvement to distributed LLM training infrastructure, turning open-ended commands into verified launch-setting and kernel optimizations. It achieves a speedup of up to 2.75x and lifts mean MFU from 17.4% to 30.0% across four dense and MoE workloads.
AI.motivation: Recursive self-improvement works for isolated algorithm and kernel synthesis, but distributed training depends on tightly coupled launch settings, operator kernels and communication schedules, where single edits often hit OOM limits, compiler conflicts, measurement jitter or silent numerical drift.
AI.method: A five-stage workflow (init, doctor, run, report and apply, and commit) locks editable scope and a fixed task contract over workload, loss and timing invariants to block reward hacking, calibrates cluster noise, and co-optimizes launch knobs and code patches from diverse experience-seeded starts. It fits global execution-time and censored peak-memory models across all trials including OOMs, revises LLM priors from live runs, and logs findings to a cross-hardware experience bank.
AI.result: Across four single- and multi-node dense and Mixture-of-Experts LLM workloads, InfraRSI achieves a speedup of up to 2.75x and raises mean Model FLOPs Utilization from 17.4% to 30.0%, outperforming existing tuners and coding agents while transferring experience across GPUs.
AI.conclusion: Two nested loops, revising priors within runs and distilling experience across clusters, are presented as a route to more efficient foundation model scaling through verified infrastructure optimization.

title: LiveAsset: Learning Intent Assets from Corrective Interactions for Agent Runtime Control
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents acting across web applications and online services often need multi-turn corrections to align their work with users' underspecified goals and preferences. In practice, users may identify problems in the current outcome without specifying the desired result, so learning user intentions requires interpreting each correction against the agent's preceding and revised outcomes. These expectations are often connected to a particular context, making it hard to know when they apply and how to ensure the agent later acts as the user expects. To this end, we propose LiveAsset, an intent harness that learns reusable intent assets from corrective interactions and uses them for runtime control of agent execution. LiveAsset jointly interprets each correction with the agent's original and revised results to infer user intent, incrementally updating the assets while preserving earlier requirements that remain applicable. The learned requirements guide agent execution from task entry and provide criteria for runtime verification, which uses the explanations to assess applicability before each reply is delivered and directs the agent to revise the result to address unmet requirements while preserving those already satisfied. Following a learning phase in which simulated users progressively reveal requirements through multi-turn corrections, we evaluate LiveAsset using same-task replay of the original requests on {\pi}-Bench, PERMA, and Vita and cross-task transfer on PAST-Bench and SkillEvolBench. Experiments show that LiveAsset better fulfills requirements learned from corrective interactions and improves performance on these benchmarks compared with memory, skill, and rule-based harness baselines. Code is available at this http URL.

AI.tldr: LiveAsset is an intent harness that learns reusable intent assets from multi-turn corrective interactions and uses them for runtime control of LLM agents, verifying each reply against learned requirements before delivery. It improves fulfillment of requirements and benchmark performance over memory, skill and rule-based harness baselines on same-task replay and cross-task transfer.
AI.motivation: Agents acting across web applications often need multi-turn corrections because users identify problems without stating the desired result, and learned expectations are tied to particular contexts, making it hard to know when they apply and how to ensure later compliance.
AI.method: LiveAsset jointly interprets each correction against the agent's original and revised outputs to infer intent, incrementally updates the assets while preserving still-applicable requirements, and uses them to guide execution from task entry. A runtime verifier checks each reply's applicability and directs revisions that address unmet requirements while keeping satisfied ones. A learning phase uses simulated users who reveal requirements progressively.
AI.result: Experiments on same-task replay of pi-Bench, PERMA and Vita, and on cross-task transfer to PAST-Bench and SkillEvolBench, show that LiveAsset better fulfills requirements learned from corrections and improves performance compared with memory, skill and rule-based harness baselines.
AI.conclusion: Learning reusable, context-scoped intent assets from corrections and enforcing them at runtime is presented as an effective way to align agents with underspecified user goals.

title: Same Error, Different Recovery: How Delivery Changes LLM Agent Behavior
summary: A tool-using language model must decide whether to retry a failed call, correct it, or stop and tell the user. The error text alone may not be enough: the same feedback can lead to different actions depending on where it appears in the conversation. We isolate this delivery problem by varying placement, guidance, retained history and turn structure. Two studies with plans fixed before data collection, across 13 open models from 3B to 70B parameters, compare the next action and subsequent task completion, with exact deterministic reruns. A new user turn that retains the failed exchange avoids the severe stopping failure observed in Llama models when that exchange is removed. It is non-inferior to history rewriting in pooled synthetic comparisons, but is not best for every model. We implement this form as an opt-in recovery layer within a deterministic inference engine and evaluate it on public benchmarks and a coding agent. On ToolMaze, it raises success on explicit errors by 14.2 points with 7-8B models and 10.5 points with 32-70B models; Loud/Quiet, 24 multi-turn tasks with visible failures and silent corruption, scored by final-state agreement, shows no measurable gain. A client given the exact fault kind performs better still. The findings support delivery as a distinct factor in recovery, not an engine-exclusive solution or a universal retry policy.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that where error feedback is placed in a conversation changes how tool-using LLMs act after a failed call, and that a new user turn retaining the failed exchange avoids the severe stopping failure seen in Llama models. An opt-in recovery layer raises success on explicit errors by 14.2 points with 7-8B models and 10.5 points with 32-70B models on ToolMaze.
AI.motivation: A tool-using model must decide whether to retry, correct the call or stop and tell the user, but the error text alone may not determine the action, since the same feedback can lead to different actions depending on where it appears in the conversation.
AI.method: Two studies with pre-registered plans vary placement, guidance, retained history and turn structure across 13 open models from 3B to 70B, comparing the next action and later task completion with deterministic reruns. The authors implement the form as an opt-in recovery layer in a deterministic inference engine and evaluate it on public benchmarks and a coding agent.
AI.result: Retaining the failed exchange in a new user turn is non-inferior to history rewriting in pooled synthetic comparisons but is not best for every model. On ToolMaze it raises success on explicit errors by 14.2 points with 7-8B models and 10.5 points with 32-70B models. On Loud/Quiet, 24 multi-turn tasks with visible failures and silent corruption, it shows no measurable gain, and a client given the exact fault kind performs better still.
AI.conclusion: Delivery is a distinct factor in recovery, so the gains come from how feedback is placed rather than from a single engine-specific fix or a universal retry policy.

title: Perturbation Profiles of Scanpath Classifiers: What Reading, Code-Comprehension and Video Decoders Are Sensitive To
summary: When a scanpath descriptor discriminates a task, it is rarely clear what the discrimination rests on. We propose a perturbation profile for trial-level descriptors. Five transformations each destroy one stated property while preserving a listed set of invariants: fixation order, duration-position coupling, the duration distribution, orientation and handedness, and fine spatial structure. The classifier is refit, and the drop in participant-held-out AUC is the pipeline's sensitivity to that property. Because refitting lets the learner use redundant information, this describes the refitted pipeline, not what a fitted classifier used. Intervals come from a participant bootstrap that refits; in simulations at the sample sizes analysed, where the target was zero they excluded zero at a pooled rate of at most 2.5%, and they covered the target in 99.6% of 2720 cases. We profiled seven descriptors on twelve binary problems from three public datasets: reading (SB-SAT, 95 participants), program comprehension (EMIP, up to 159) and video and game viewing (GazeBase, 60). Permuting fixation order raised the AUC of a descriptor built on mean saccade amplitude on three problems (by up to 0.23), because permutation turns amplitude into a measure of spatial spread. A "comprehension" contrast that pooled two programs reached AUC 0.70 with a spread-only baseline and fell to 0.47 within one program: the profile located the confound in stimulus layout. On native versus non-native readers, recurrence was sensitive to order and to jitter at the scale of text lines but not of characters, while a two-feature duration and amplitude descriptor reached the same AUC (0.65). A graph descriptor built on the code's tokens was the strongest non-baseline descriptor on the program contrast (0.78; 0.87 with boosted trees). The interpreted results held under longer runs and three seeds; under a second learner 15 of 16 kept t

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a perturbation profile for trial-level scanpath descriptors, which destroys one stated property at a time, refits the classifier and reads the drop in participant-held-out AUC as that property's sensitivity. Profiles of seven descriptors on twelve binary problems show, for example, that a comprehension contrast reaching AUC 0.70 falls to 0.47 within one program.
AI.motivation: When a scanpath descriptor discriminates a task, it is rarely clear what the discrimination rests on, and a classifier can exploit redundant information, so a sensitivity measure must describe the refitted pipeline rather than what a fitted classifier used.
AI.method: Five transformations each destroy one property while preserving listed invariants: fixation order, duration-position coupling, the duration distribution, orientation and handedness, and fine spatial structure. Classifiers are refit, and intervals come from a participant bootstrap that refits. Seven descriptors are profiled on twelve binary problems from SB-SAT (reading), EMIP (program comprehension) and GazeBase (video and game viewing).
AI.result: Permuting fixation order raised the AUC of a mean-saccade-amplitude descriptor on three problems by up to 0.23. A comprehension contrast that pooled two programs reached AUC 0.70 with a spread-only baseline and fell to 0.47 within one program. A graph descriptor on code tokens was the strongest non-baseline descriptor on the program contrast (0.78; 0.87 with boosted trees). Simulations reported coverage of the target in 99.6% of 2720 cases.
AI.conclusion: Perturbation profiles can locate confounds such as stimulus layout that a single AUC would hide, although the abstract's account of the results is partly truncated in the source.

title: An Interpretable Fuzzy Tree for Turbofan Remaining Useful Life with an Auditable Per-Component Diagnostic Layer
summary: Data-driven remaining useful life (RUL) estimators for turbofan engines are accurate but opaque, and their internal features typically encode remaining life rather than any specific component's state. This paper presents an interpretable genetic fuzzy tree that predicts RUL from cruise-condition sensor means on N-CMAPSS while exposing a per-component diagnostic layer inspectable rule by rule. The tree follows the engine hierarchy: sensors to component health, then to bounded component damage, spool damage, and RUL, so each level answers a different maintenance question. Training is staged so the prognostic objective cannot reshape the diagnostic layers: health leaves are fitted to physical targets and frozen, a deterministic fuzzy damage map with fleet-referenced thresholds is imposed on each component, and only the aggregation is optimized for RUL. It consumes 13 cruise-mean scalars per cycle rather than a trajectory, which removes any sequence model. On the native split it reaches 8.44 cycles RMSE on the multi-fault subset and 11.51 across all modes with 333 free parameters, 411 total rules, 32 to 12,000 times fewer than compiled baselines. An exhaustive sensor search bounds which components are diagnosable under the tested cruise-mean design, and the rule base is structured to admit formal verification, which this study does not discharge.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an interpretable genetic fuzzy tree that predicts turbofan remaining useful life from 13 cruise-condition sensor means and exposes a per-component diagnostic layer that can be inspected rule by rule. It reaches 8.44 cycles RMSE on the multi-fault subset and 11.51 across all modes on N-CMAPSS with 333 free parameters.
AI.motivation: Data-driven RUL estimators for turbofan engines are accurate but opaque, and their internal features usually encode remaining life rather than the state of any specific component.
AI.method: The tree follows the engine hierarchy from sensors to component health, then to bounded component damage, spool damage and RUL. Training is staged: health leaves are fitted to physical targets and frozen, a deterministic fuzzy damage map with fleet-referenced thresholds is imposed on each component, and only the aggregation is optimized for RUL. No sequence model is used.
AI.result: On the native N-CMAPSS split it reaches 8.44 cycles RMSE on the multi-fault subset and 11.51 across all modes, with 333 free parameters and 411 total rules, which is 32 to 12,000 times fewer than compiled baselines. An exhaustive sensor search bounds which components are diagnosable under the cruise-mean design.
AI.conclusion: The tree offers competitive accuracy with an auditable per-component diagnosis, and its structure is designed to admit formal verification, which the study does not carry out.

title: Optimizing Multi-Tier Intermediation in Programmatic Advertising: A DAG-Based Mechanism for Supply Path Optimization
summary: Digital programmatic advertising operates through complex, multi-hop supply chains. The opacity of these intermediary networks leads to significant efficiency losses, often referred to as the ``ad-tech tax.'' While current industry practices utilize heuristic Supply Path Optimization (SPO) to trim inefficient routes, they fail to optimize the equilibrium of the entire network. This paper extends previous work on Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) intermediation models by applying them to traceable programmatic supply chains mapped via the OpenRTB SupplyChain object. We introduce multi-attribute utility functions and Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) to account for substitutable routing (OR nodes) and percentage-based fee structures. Furthermore, we outline a computational methodology and experimental framework using public \texttt{schain} and \texttt{this http URL} data to benchmark optimal Nash social welfare against current uncoordinated market outcomes.

AI.tldr: The paper applies DAG-based intermediation models to OpenRTB SupplyChain paths and formulates supply path optimization as a MILP with multi-attribute utilities, substitutable routing and percentage fees. It outlines a method to benchmark optimal Nash social welfare against uncoordinated market outcomes but reports no numerical results in the abstract.
AI.motivation: Multi-hop programmatic supply chains cause efficiency losses, the so-called ad-tech tax, and heuristic supply path optimization trims inefficient routes without optimizing the equilibrium of the whole network.
AI.method: The work extends previous DAG intermediation models to traceable supply chains mapped via the OpenRTB SupplyChain object. It introduces multi-attribute utility functions and Mixed-Integer Linear Programming to model substitutable routing (OR nodes) and percentage-based fee structures.
AI.result: The abstract reports no empirical findings. It only states that the authors outline a computational methodology and experimental framework using public schain data to benchmark optimal Nash social welfare against uncoordinated outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The paper positions whole-network optimization of supply paths as a more principled alternative to heuristic SPO, with its empirical validation described as a framework rather than completed results.

title: Inside the Trading Loop: Markets, Models, and Moves with LLM Agents
comment: 37 pages, including appendices. Code and supporting materials available upon request
summary: We built a hybrid multi-agent trading system that combines large language model (LLM) analysts with momentum-based portfolio construction and rule-based execution. Company-news and macroeconomic agents return structured reports to a coordinator that sets stock weights and cash reserves. We evaluate the portfolio engine using its broker-recorded paper account, which operated with deterministic fallbacks, and compare LLM-enabled configurations through retrospective replays. From March 11 to August 28, 2026, the account returned 34.5%, compared with 14.4% for the S&P 500 fund SPY over the same dates. This raw return advantage came with a larger maximum drawdown. Reconstructed policies also finish above matched SPY and QQQ references when assessments are used in the same session or deferred to the next. Design comparisons examine cash authority, selective invocation, and response contracts. A constant-cash control gives a return estimate close to stance-based sizing, and shorter report contracts improve observed parsing but can change recommendations.

AI.tldr: A hybrid multi-agent trading system combines LLM news and macro analysts with momentum-based portfolio construction and rule-based execution. Its broker-recorded paper account returned 34.5% from March 11 to August 28, 2026, versus 14.4% for SPY, with a larger maximum drawdown.
AI.motivation: The abstract does not state an explicit motivation beyond evaluating LLM analysts within a trading system that sets stock weights and cash reserves.
AI.method: Company-news and macroeconomic agents return structured reports to a coordinator that sets stock weights and cash reserves, with momentum-based portfolio construction and rule-based execution. The paper account operated with deterministic fallbacks, and LLM-enabled configurations are compared through retrospective replays. Design comparisons examine cash authority, selective invocation and response contracts.
AI.result: The paper account returned 34.5% against 14.4% for the SPY fund over the same dates, with a larger maximum drawdown. Reconstructed policies finish above matched SPY and QQQ references when assessments are used in the same session or deferred. A constant-cash control gives a return estimate close to stance-based sizing, and shorter report contracts improve observed parsing but can change recommendations.
AI.conclusion: The raw return advantage comes with higher drawdown, and the LLM design choices affect outcomes, so the results are presented as observed performance over one period rather than as settled evidence.

title: Measuring Generative AI Content in Political Campaigns: Evidence of Rising Adoption and Non-Disclosure
summary: The use of generative AI in political campaigns has drawn public concern and policy attention. Public concerns range from distrust of candidates to skepticism about the authenticity and accuracy of political advertising, including AI-generated images and video. Nearly half of U.S. states have enacted laws that prohibit, or require disclosure of, "materially deceptive" AI-generated content (AIGC) in elections to guard against these concerns. This study measures how candidates and their campaigns produce and circulate AIGC during an election cycle. We develop two measures that estimate not only wether campaigns use AIGC, but how much they produce (magnitude) and in what forms (modality). We apply these measures to a novel dataset of text and images from the campaign websites, X accounts, and emails of 12,977 candidates for U.S. political office from 2023 to 2025. We report three findings. First, detectable AIGC from campaigns increased significantly across modalities over the observation window, and campaigns that use AIGC frequently do not disclose it. Second, incumbents' campaigns produced significantly less AIGC than challengers' campaigns. Third, candidates in states with AIGC disclosure or prohibition laws do not produce measurably less AIGC than candidates in other states. Our method and findings have implications for transparency and trust in elections, and on state laws that regulate AI use in campaigns. Because current state laws largely target mainly "materially deceptive" content, we identify additional policy mechanisms that could increase electoral transparency and improve trust as AIGC becomes more prevalent.

AI.tldr: The study measures generative AI content produced by 12,977 U.S. political candidates from 2023 to 2025 and finds that detectable AIGC rose across modalities, with frequent AIGC users often not disclosing it. Incumbents produce less AIGC than challengers, and candidates in states with disclosure or prohibition laws do not produce measurably less.
AI.motivation: Public concern and policy attention about generative AI in political campaigns, and state laws against materially deceptive AI content, call for evidence on how campaigns actually produce and circulate AIGC.
AI.method: The authors develop two measures that estimate whether campaigns use AIGC, how much they produce (magnitude) and in what forms (modality). They apply them to a new dataset of text and images from campaign websites, X accounts and emails.
AI.result: Detectable AIGC from campaigns increased significantly across modalities over the window, and frequent AIGC users often do not disclose it. Incumbents produced significantly less AIGC than challengers. Candidates in states with disclosure or prohibition laws do not produce measurably less AIGC than others.
AI.conclusion: Because current laws mainly target materially deceptive content, the authors argue for additional policy mechanisms to improve electoral transparency and trust as AIGC becomes more prevalent.

title: RADE: Risk-Adjusted Deployment Efficiency, A Framework for Routing, Memory, and Escalation in Safe LLM Systems
summary: A deployed language model does not merely answer questions. It spends computation, consumes time, consults evidence, exposes memory, invites or avoids human review, and sometimes makes mistakes whose consequences are radically unequal. Yet LLM systems are still commonly compared as if the relevant object were a single model and the relevant outcome were a single benchmark score. This paper argues that the unit of analysis should instead be the deployment policy: the mechanism that decides when to retrieve, when to remember, when to call a larger model, when to verify, and when not to answer at all. We introduce risk-adjusted deployment efficiency (RADE), a system-level objective that scores the utility a deployment delivers net of inference, retry, oversight, and priced expected failure cost, while treating harms that cannot be priced as hard budgets alongside constraints on latency, privacy, and resources. The framework brings selective routing, retrieval and governed memory, efficient specialization, uncertainty estimation, abstention, and human escalation into a common account. We then examine five deployment regimes in which the same nominal LLM capability leads to different rational architectures, and propose a reporting protocol based on risk-coverage behavior, end-to-end cost, update drift, memory exposure, evidence quality, and escalation load. The central claim is modest but consequential: frontier capability should be treated as a resource to allocate, not a default state to maintain. A safe and sustainable system is not the one that always uses the strongest model; it is the one that spends capability where the reduction in risk or increase in utility justifies the cost.

AI.tldr: RADE proposes risk-adjusted deployment efficiency as the objective for LLM systems, scoring utility net of inference, retry, oversight and priced expected failure cost, with unpriceable harms treated as hard budgets. It argues the deployment policy, not the single model, should be the unit of analysis and that frontier capability should be allocated rather than used by default.
AI.motivation: LLM systems are still compared as if the relevant object were a single model and the outcome a single benchmark score, ignoring computation, time, evidence use, memory exposure, human review and unequal consequences of mistakes.
AI.method: The authors introduce RADE as a system-level objective and bring selective routing, retrieval and governed memory, efficient specialization, uncertainty estimation, abstention and human escalation into one account. They examine five deployment regimes and propose a reporting protocol based on risk-coverage behavior, end-to-end cost, update drift, memory exposure, evidence quality and escalation load.
AI.result: The abstract reports no empirical results. Its claims are conceptual: the same nominal capability leads to different rational architectures across five regimes, and a reporting protocol is proposed.
AI.conclusion: A safe and sustainable system spends capability where it reduces risk or raises utility enough to justify cost, rather than always using the strongest model.

title: Self-Indexing Latent Memories for Access-Aware Continual Instruction Tuning of LLMs
summary: Continual instruction tuning often preserves old skills with task-private modules. Inference still requires selecting the right module from the prompt alone. We introduce Task-Isolated Latent Adapter Continual Training (TILA-CT), a replay-free method that makes each task module self-indexing. Each task receives a latent memory and adapter bank in a frozen LLM. During adaptation, the memory gathers causal-prefix information and injects task-conditioned context. For access, its persistent state provides the routing prototype used by a shared prompt-only router. On the 8-task CT-Pipeline stream, TILA-CT achieves 65.19 acquisition and 63.98 final macro score, with 1.38 points of average forgetting. A middle-reversed order gives 65.38 acquisition and 64.17 final macro score. Across 6 backbones, final scores remain within 1.5 points of acquisition. Ablations support memory-derived routing keys and causal gathering. Final macro routing accuracy is 93.9\%, and oracle routing recovers 1.21 final macro points. These results separate preserved task computation from learned access to it.

AI.tldr: TILA-CT is a replay-free continual instruction tuning method in which each task gets a latent memory and adapter bank in a frozen LLM, so the task module is self-indexing and a shared prompt-only router can select it. On an 8-task stream it reaches 65.19 acquisition and 63.98 final macro score with 1.38 points of average forgetting, and final routing accuracy of 93.9%.
AI.motivation: Continual instruction tuning preserves old skills with task-private modules, but inference still requires choosing the right module from the prompt alone.
AI.method: Each task receives a latent memory and adapter bank in a frozen LLM. During adaptation the memory gathers causal-prefix information and injects task-conditioned context, and its persistent state serves as the routing prototype for a shared prompt-only router. Ablations compare memory-derived routing keys and causal gathering.
AI.result: On the 8-task CT-Pipeline stream TILA-CT achieves 65.19 acquisition and 63.98 final macro score with 1.38 points of average forgetting. A middle-reversed order gives 65.38 and 64.17. Across 6 backbones, final scores stay within 1.5 points of acquisition. Final macro routing accuracy is 93.9%, and oracle routing would recover 1.21 final macro points.
AI.conclusion: The results separate preserved task computation from learned access to it, suggesting that routing rather than forgetting accounts for most of the remaining gap.

title: CASCoDe: A Closed-Loop Agentic Framework for Analog Sizing and Layout Co-Design
summary: Expert analog layouts differ from auto-generated ones in density and regularity, not only in legality: experts make a succession of discrete, hierarchical physical decisions and revisit each after extracted electrical results, while most existing automated flows act on a physical search space fixed before the controller runs. We present CASCoDe, a closed-loop LLM agent framework for analog netlist-to-layout design that formalizes those expert decisions as a hierarchical discrete action space-sizing selection, structural floorplan, local layout refinement, routing-attempt selection-on which the agent runs feedback-driven tree search from a circuit netlist to a verified GDS. The agent authors the circuit-specific floorplans and scripts, and an execution layer of interface adaptations over adapted tools make every action land at physical implementation and be judged by DRC, LVS, and extracted-RC simulation. On 20 SKY130 amplifiers spanning single-, two-, and three-stage topologies, CASCoDe is the only flow that delivers a DRC- and LVS-clean routed layout when meeting design specifications for every circuit. It reduces area by 59-85% (mean 71%) against a conventional P&R flow on identical PCells, raises mean device density from 0.39 to 0.74 against APPlace, MAGICAL, ALIGN and ICPI. A layout that beats every baseline in area and legality appears after 11 minutes of agent time on average, and ablations show that the structured action space and the feedback-guided tree search each reduce area and search cost.

AI.tldr: CASCoDe is a closed-loop LLM agent framework for analog netlist-to-layout design that searches a hierarchical discrete action space with feedback-driven tree search to a DRC-, LVS- and extracted-RC-verified GDS. On 20 SKY130 amplifiers it is the only flow delivering clean, spec-meeting layouts for every circuit and reduces area by 59-85% (mean 71%) against a conventional P&R flow.
AI.motivation: Expert analog layouts differ from automated ones in density and regularity, because experts make hierarchical physical decisions and revisit them after extracted electrical results, while most flows act on a physical search space fixed before the controller runs.
AI.method: The framework formalizes sizing selection, structural floorplan, local layout refinement and routing-attempt selection as a hierarchical discrete action space. The agent writes circuit-specific floorplans and scripts, and an execution layer adapts tools so that every action is judged by DRC, LVS and extracted-RC simulation.
AI.result: On 20 SKY130 amplifiers spanning single-, two- and three-stage topologies, CASCoDe is the only flow that delivers a DRC- and LVS-clean routed layout meeting specifications for every circuit. It reduces area by 59-85% (mean 71%) against a conventional P&R flow on identical PCells and raises mean device density from 0.39 to 0.74 against APPlace, MAGICAL, ALIGN and ICPI. A layout beating all baselines appears after 11 minutes of agent time on average.
AI.conclusion: The structured action space and feedback-guided tree search each reduce area and search cost in ablations, showing that expert-like hierarchical decisions improve automated analog layout.

title: State Media at Retrieval Time: A Large-Scale Audit of Russian State-Aligned Sources in AI Chatbot Responses
summary: The Pravda Network is a Russian state-aligned media aggregator, with over 110 websites and more than 15 million articles published since 2023. Given its prolific and repetitive output, emerging scholarship argues that the Pravda Network was built to influence AI systems. We conduct a large-scale audit of leading AI chatbots to understand: (1) the retrieval rates of Pravda Network articles, (2) the conditions of retrieval, and (3) whether chatbot responses affirm or caveat this content. We build a 10,000 prompt corpus from sampled Pravda Network headlines varied along two dimensions (headline rewording and user skepticism) and query 11 AI chatbots via the web interface (n=104,997 completed responses). Overall, we find susceptibility to Pravda Network retrieval to be infrequent---appearing in 7.3% of responses---and highly platform dependent---with three chatbots responsible for 94% of retrievals (this http URL, Claude, and Copilot). Among the frontier models, Claude is an outlier: ChatGPT, Gemini, and Meta AI retrieved no Pravda Network articles, likely indicative of a domain-level filtering policy. All 11 chatbots, however, retrieved other Russian state-aligned media to some degree (median=13.56% of responses). When Pravda Network articles are surfaced, caveat rates vary widely by platform (from 5.3% to 76.2%), with this http URL providing the fewest caveats. We also identify the tactic of headline washing: where 9.92% of sampled Pravda Network headlines attribute their reporting to other, often more credible, media outlets, while the articles themselves are republished from Russian state-aligned media. We discuss headline washing's potential to launder state media as independent reporting. With this audit, we provide a systematic analysis of AI chatbots' susceptibility to Russia's latest attempt to manipulate the information environment.

AI.tldr: An audit of 11 AI chatbots finds that Pravda Network articles appear in 7.3% of 104,997 responses, concentrated in three platforms, while all chatbots retrieve other Russian state-aligned media. The authors also identify headline washing, where 9.92% of Pravda headlines attribute reporting to other, more credible outlets.
AI.motivation: The Pravda Network, a Russian state-aligned aggregator of over 110 websites and more than 15 million articles since 2023, is argued to be built to influence AI systems, and the authors ask whether chatbots retrieve and endorse its content.
AI.method: The authors build a 10,000-prompt corpus from sampled Pravda headlines varied by headline rewording and user skepticism and query 11 chatbots through their web interfaces, obtaining 104,997 completed responses. They measure retrieval rates, retrieval conditions, and whether responses affirm or caveat the content.
AI.result: Pravda Network articles appear in 7.3% of responses, with three chatbots responsible for 94% of retrievals (including Claude and Copilot). Claude is an outlier among frontier models, as ChatGPT, Gemini and Meta AI retrieved none, which the authors suggest reflects domain-level filtering. All 11 chatbots retrieved other Russian state-aligned media, with a median of 13.56% of responses. Caveat rates range from 5.3% to 76.2% by platform.
AI.conclusion: Headline washing can launder state media as independent reporting, and the audit provides a systematic picture of chatbot susceptibility to this manipulation attempt.

title: Can the Remaining Answers Change the Prediction? Worst-Case Stability Checks for Personalized Rating Models
summary: Missing ratings can overturn a personalized model's current prediction. For completed models with additive response scores, exact worst case bounds check all missing assignments without changing the current predictor. We evaluate this audit retrospectively in two self-triage cohorts, 108 clinicians rating three simulated psychiatric interviews, and 126 counseling demonstrations annotated by ten experts. Under shared random half histories, Fisher adaptation based on observed ratings reduces log loss relative to response frequency by 0.1071 nats in the clinician audit (95% CI [0.0867,0.1261]) and 0.0223 in counseling (95% CI[0.0121,0.0321]). The counseling test excludes target experts and source videos from training. Certification covers 5.4% and 10.5% of targets; fixed width acquisition raises coverage to 13.7% and 28.6% at the same budgets. With weights and responses held fixed, the observed-rating update also has lower loss than an affine partial update while certifying exactly the same evaluated targets. The certificate establishes agreement with the completed model, not correctness or stability at intermediate updates. These rating tasks test the method; clinical usefulness remains untested.

AI.tldr: For completed personalized rating models with additive response scores, the paper gives exact worst-case bounds that check whether any assignment of missing ratings could change the current prediction. Retrospective tests on 108 clinicians and 126 counseling demonstrations show Fisher adaptation lowers log loss versus response frequency, while certification covers only 5.4% and 10.5% of targets.
AI.motivation: Missing ratings can overturn a personalized model's current prediction, so an audit is needed to check whether the remaining answers could change it.
AI.method: For completed models with additive response scores, exact worst-case bounds check all missing assignments without changing the current predictor. The audit is evaluated retrospectively in two self-triage cohorts, with shared random half histories and fixed-width acquisition as an alternative to raise coverage.
AI.result: Fisher adaptation based on observed ratings reduces log loss relative to response frequency by 0.1071 nats in the clinician audit (95% CI [0.0867, 0.1261]) and 0.0223 in counseling (95% CI [0.0121, 0.0321]). Certification covers 5.4% and 10.5% of targets, and fixed-width acquisition raises coverage to 13.7% and 28.6% at the same budgets.
AI.conclusion: The certificate establishes agreement with the completed model, not correctness or stability at intermediate updates, and the authors state that clinical usefulness remains untested.

title: A Bifurcation-Theoretic Framework for the Controllability of Emergent Intelligent Systems
summary: Real-world intelligent systems must reconcile two demands: the adaptability conferred by emergence and the steerability required for accountable deployment. We show that these demands are governed by two distinct bifurcations on the same object and that, consequently, increased capability does not imply increased controllability. Emergence is a bifurcation of the capability variable $S$, with criterion $\Gamma:=\mathcal F'(0)>1$ equivalent to the existence of a unique positive stable fixed point of a self-consistency equation, following solely from the concavity of $\mathcal F$. Controllability is a bifurcation of the permission variable $c$, whose dynamics include an erosion term and exhibit a saddle-node fold with hysteresis as the gate criterion $\rho^\ast$ crosses unity. Three quantitative results follow: the critical exponent distinguishes families rather than classifying the transition; the gating-cost bound $K(M)\propto\log(1+M)$ grows with scope, not capability; and the fold threshold is $\gamma_c\approx4\mu\kappa$. Calibrated in both directions, the criteria reproduce the two-dimensional Ising transition, admit two true-feedback order parameters, and reject nine candidate quantities, supporting the conclusion that the order parameter is geometric rather than capability-related. Since permission cannot be endogenized and no deployed system has been measured to satisfy $\Gamma>1$ and $\rho^\ast>1$ simultaneously, increased capability does not imply controllability.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that emergence and controllability are two distinct bifurcations on the same system object, so increased capability does not imply increased controllability. It gives three quantitative results and calibrates the criteria against the two-dimensional Ising transition.
AI.motivation: Deployable intelligent systems need both adaptability from emergence and steerability for accountable use, and the paper asks whether the two are linked. It treats them as separate dynamical phenomena rather than assuming capability brings control.
AI.method: Emergence is modelled as a bifurcation of the capability variable S with criterion Gamma = F'(0) > 1, while controllability is a saddle-node fold with hysteresis in the permission variable c as the gate criterion rho* crosses unity. The framework derives a gating-cost bound K(M) proportional to log(1+M) and a fold threshold gamma_c approximately 4 mu kappa.
AI.result: The criteria reproduce the two-dimensional Ising transition, admit two true-feedback order parameters, and reject nine candidate quantities. The critical exponent distinguishes families of transitions rather than classifying them, and the gating-cost bound grows with scope rather than capability.
AI.conclusion: The order parameter of controllability is geometric rather than capability-related, and since permission cannot be endogenized and no deployed system has been measured to satisfy Gamma > 1 and rho* > 1 together, increased capability does not imply controllability.

title: Reproducible quantum clustering for single-cell transcriptome atlases
comment: 28 pages; 5 figures and 1 table in the main text; 5 Extended Data figures, 5 Extended Data tables; Supplementary Information with 2 figures and 15 tables
summary: Current single-cell clustering pipelines discard most genes and can yield inconsistent clusters across random seeds. We introduce KQE-2, a training-free hybrid quantum-classical framework for reproducible whole-transcriptome clustering. KQE-2 maps cells into entanglement-free quantum states, enabling exact feature evaluation on classical hardware and direct checks on a quantum processor. Theoretically, we prove that removing entanglement is necessary and sufficient to bound single-qubit feature variance locally. Practically, while retraining scVI shifted 14% of cells and altered rare-type markers and drug targets, KQE-2 delivered identical biology across runs. On standard highly variable genes, the quantum encoding alone raised accuracy on a developing cortex from 0.61 to 0.79. KQE-2 scales to 11.4 million nuclei on one server, outperforming the compared methods on eight of ten complete atlases (and within the best method's run-to-run range on two), and leads on six even under standard downstream clustering.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces KQE-2, a training-free hybrid quantum-classical framework that encodes cells into entanglement-free quantum states for reproducible whole-transcriptome single-cell clustering. It reports identical biology across runs and scaling to 11.4 million nuclei on one server.
AI.motivation: Current single-cell clustering pipelines discard most genes and give inconsistent clusters across random seeds. The paper addresses this reproducibility problem for transcriptome atlases.
AI.method: KQE-2 maps cells into entanglement-free quantum states, which allows exact feature evaluation on classical hardware with direct checks possible on a quantum processor. The authors prove that removing entanglement is necessary and sufficient to bound single-qubit feature variance locally.
AI.result: Retraining scVI shifted 14% of cells and altered rare-type markers and drug targets, whereas KQE-2 gave identical biology across runs. On standard highly variable genes the quantum encoding alone raised accuracy on a developing cortex from 0.61 to 0.79, and KQE-2 outperformed the compared methods on eight of ten complete atlases.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers reproducible clustering that scales to 11.4 million nuclei on one server, and the authors position it as a stable alternative to seed-sensitive pipelines.

title: ARMOR: Adaptive Curriculum Meta-Learning for Noise-Robust RAG Reasoning
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in mitigating hallucinations by incorporating external knowledge. However, the retrieval process inevitably introduces noise, posing significant challenges to RAG robustness. Fundamentally, noise robustness is a composite competency encompassing noise identification, retrieval filtering, and robust reasoning. Unfortunately, existing methods often fail to capture this holistic nature, typically restricted to single-dimensional enhancements or hampered by noise-induced optimization interference. To address these limitations, we decompose RAG robustness into three sub-tasks: knowledge boundary perception, retrieval verification, and robust reasoning. Accordingly, we propose ARMOR, an Adaptive Curriculum Meta-Learning for Noise Robust RAG Reasoning. Inspired by the teaching process, ARMOR introduces an adaptive task scheduler as a teacher to curate training plans according to the absolute learning progress of RAG generators (Student). Distinct from GRPO, ARMOR utilizes inter-group advantage estimation during learning to effectively mitigate mode collapse caused by limited output spaces. Experiments on three complex reasoning datasets (2WikiMultiHopQA, MusiQue, and HotPotQA) indicate that ARMOR achieves synergistic improvements in retrieval noise robustness, significantly outperforming baselines in output quality.

AI.tldr: ARMOR is a curriculum meta-learning method that trains RAG generators to handle noisy retrieval by decomposing robustness into three sub-tasks. It reports significant gains over baselines on three multi-hop QA datasets.
AI.motivation: Retrieval introduces noise that undermines RAG robustness, and existing methods address only single dimensions of this composite competency or suffer from noise-induced optimization interference.
AI.method: The paper decomposes RAG robustness into knowledge boundary perception, retrieval verification and robust reasoning. An adaptive task scheduler acts as a teacher that curates training plans from the learning progress of the RAG generator, and it uses inter-group advantage estimation instead of GRPO to reduce mode collapse.
AI.result: Experiments on 2WikiMultiHopQA, MusiQue and HotPotQA indicate synergistic improvements in retrieval noise robustness and significantly better output quality than baselines. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Holistic, curriculum-based training that treats noise robustness as a composite competency can improve RAG under noisy retrieval.

title: Wireless AI Networks: Co-Adapting Communication Resources and Distributed Intelligence
summary: Distributed artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly relies on wireless networks, where communication and computing resources shape how AI tasks are configured and executed. However, resource availability alone does not determine how effectively these tasks can be supported, since different information selections and transmission strategies may yield different AI performance under the same resource constraints. To address this challenge, this article presents Wireless AI Networks as a unified design perspective for bidirectional adaptation between wireless communication and distributed intelligence. Specifically, an AI-executable resource budget characterizes candidate AI configurations, while task-level information value guides their selection and wireless resource allocation. Building on these principles, a wireless-AI co-adaptation framework coordinates resource abstraction, joint configuration and allocation, and execution feedback. Two complementary experiments illustrate this perspective: update selection and statistical correction improve federated learning under identical model-update payload budgets, while sensitivity-aware power allocation reduces model accuracy degradation under the same average transmit-power constraint. Together, these results highlight the importance of coordinating resource feasibility and task-level information value in distributed AI execution.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Wireless AI Networks as a design perspective in which wireless communication and distributed AI adapt to each other, with AI-executable resource budgets guiding resource allocation. Two experiments on federated learning and power allocation illustrate the idea.
AI.motivation: Resource availability alone does not determine how well distributed AI tasks are supported, because different information selections and transmission strategies yield different AI performance under the same resource constraints.
AI.method: The framework uses an AI-executable resource budget to characterize candidate AI configurations and task-level information value to guide their selection and wireless resource allocation. A co-adaptation loop coordinates resource abstraction, joint configuration and allocation, and execution feedback.
AI.result: In federated learning, update selection and statistical correction improve performance under identical model-update payload budgets. In sensitivity-aware power allocation, accuracy degradation is reduced under the same average transmit-power constraint.
AI.conclusion: Coordinating resource feasibility with task-level information value is important for distributed AI execution over wireless networks.

title: ACROSSVAM3.0: Resource-Bounded 4D Scene Construction and Adaptive Surface Association
summary: Combining video generation, dynamic reconstruction and monocular SLAM requires consistent coordinates, explicit handling of missing outputs and predictable memory use. We present AcrossVAM3.0, an offline system that converts text, images or monocular RGB video into a versioned point representation. Frozen components run sequentially on one GPU; map corrections update cameras, points and trajectories together. The coordination layer adds no neural parameters. Three fresh input-mode runs completed with a maximum sampled task-process-tree GPU footprint of 17.14 GB. In a frozen 16-scene video suite, every scene yielded a 4D reconstruction and 15 yielded a non-empty SLAM map. Strict cross-window matching reduced local surface error but lost long-range track coverage on TAP-Vid-DAVIS. We therefore developed multi-hypothesis adaptive surface chaining (MHAC), which retains several candidate matches and an explicit missing state. After selection on disjoint development data, MHAC improved Average Jaccard over a position-only baseline by 0.1394 on a frozen ten-video holdout (95% bootstrap interval [0.1074,0.1689]). Across 265 RoboTAP videos, the mean paired gain was 0.0610 ([0.0510,0.0715]), with 215 wins, one tie and 49 losses. These results support resource-bounded scene construction and an external tracking gain under the tested protocol. They do not establish metric scale, semantic identity or high-fidelity novel-view rendering.

AI.tldr: AcrossVAM3.0 is an offline, resource-bounded system that builds a versioned 4D point representation from text, images or monocular video. A new multi-hypothesis adaptive surface chaining method improves external tracking over a position-only baseline on two video benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Combining video generation, dynamic reconstruction and monocular SLAM requires consistent coordinates, explicit handling of missing outputs and predictable memory use. Strict cross-window matching reduced local surface error but lost long-range track coverage.
AI.method: Frozen components run sequentially on one GPU, and map corrections update cameras, points and trajectories together, with a coordination layer that adds no neural parameters. The proposed MHAC method keeps several candidate matches and an explicit missing state, and was selected on disjoint development data.
AI.result: The maximum sampled GPU footprint was 17.14 GB, and every scene in a 16-scene video suite yielded a 4D reconstruction. On a ten-video holdout MHAC improved Average Jaccard over a position-only baseline by 0.1394 (95% bootstrap interval [0.1074, 0.1689]), and across 265 RoboTAP videos the mean paired gain was 0.0610 with 215 wins, one tie and 49 losses.
AI.conclusion: The results support resource-bounded scene construction and an external tracking gain under the tested protocol, but the authors state they do not establish metric scale, semantic identity or high-fidelity novel-view rendering.

title: Correct Answers from Insufficient Histories: A Controlled Study of Agent Memory Evaluation
summary: An answer can match the reference for a complete agent history even when the reader's visible history does not determine it. We study this distinction using executable device logs. Our protocol separates reference agreement, certified evidence sufficiency, and context-appropriate behavior. Insufficiency requires two legal histories yielding byte-identical visible contexts but different answers; public chronology and query cutoffs certify sufficient prefixes. On 80 confirmation histories, Qwen3-32B matches 87 hidden references among 203 insufficient raw-prefix instances, with only seven appropriate abstentions. A fixed-input DeepSeek-V4-Flash replication matches 85 and abstains on 21 of the same 203 instances. Each reader makes 1,600 requests. Compact CSV's estimated appropriateness effects remain inconclusive: +3.16 percentage points, clustered 95% interval [0.00,6.57], for Qwen and +2.46, [-1.84,6.94], for DeepSeek. A separate held-out judge study achieves 99.38% correctness but retains support errors and truncations; a deterministic baseline solves all constructed cases. These results support an evaluation diagnosis across two hosted reader configurations, not gains for a general memory system or natural-language evidence assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that agent answers can match a reference even when the reader's visible history does not determine the answer, and it proposes a protocol that separates these properties. Results on device logs with two hosted readers suggest the evaluation, not the memory system, is the problem.
AI.motivation: Agent memory benchmarks can credit correct answers that are not supported by the history the reader can actually see, so reference agreement alone can be misleading.
AI.method: The protocol separates reference agreement, certified evidence sufficiency and context-appropriate behavior using executable device logs. Insufficiency is certified by two legal histories that yield byte-identical visible contexts but different answers, and public chronology and query cutoffs certify sufficient prefixes.
AI.result: On 80 confirmation histories, Qwen3-32B matched 87 hidden references among 203 insufficient raw-prefix instances, with only seven appropriate abstentions, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash matched 85 and abstained on 21 of the same instances. Estimated effects of compact CSV on appropriateness were inconclusive, with intervals of [0.00, 6.57] for Qwen and [-1.84, 6.94] for DeepSeek. A deterministic baseline solved all constructed cases.
AI.conclusion: The findings support an evaluation diagnosis across two hosted reader configurations, but they do not show gains for a general memory system or for natural-language evidence assessment.

title: MOTIF: LLM-Defined Material Taxonomies for OOD Property Prediction via Invariant Feature Selection
summary: Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization remains a central challenge in materials property prediction, where models must extrapolate to novel chemistries beyond the training distribution. While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong scientific reasoning, their direct use for quantitative prediction remains limited. To address this, we systematically evaluate multiple roles for LLM assistance, finding that only taxonomy-based grouping consistently improves OOD generalization over a strong kNN+GBT baseline. Building on this, we here propose MOTIF, a framework that leverages LLMs not as predictors, but as generators of candidate taxonomies that partition materials into chemically meaningful environments. These taxonomies are evaluated via training-only pseudo-OOD validation, and only those that improve generalization are retained. Invariant feature selection is then applied within each accepted taxonomy, followed by gated aggregation across taxonomies. We evaluate on 2D halide perovskites, where bandgap prediction must generalize across distinct organic spacer families. On this benchmark, MOTIF reduces mean OOD MAE from 0.122 to 0.111 eV. Under a frozen dev/test protocol, the deployable configuration further improves errors from 0.123 to 0.117 eV (electronic bandgap) and from 0.181 to 0.173 eV (optical bandgap). Beyond this primary task, we validate transferability across additional materials datasets, including 3D perovskite solar cell efficiencies and Matbench benchmarks with structure-based splits. Across domains, MOTIF consistently improves robustness under distribution shift, outperforming expert-defined groupings, rule-based heuristics, and clustering baselines, while remaining competitive with strong classical selection methods. These results demonstrate that LLMs are most effective not as predictors, but as tools for discovering structure in data.

AI.tldr: MOTIF uses LLMs to generate candidate material taxonomies, keeps only those that improve pseudo-OOD validation, and aggregates invariant-feature models across them for out-of-distribution property prediction. It reduces OOD errors on 2D halide perovskite bandgap prediction and transfers to other datasets.
AI.motivation: Materials property prediction must extrapolate to novel chemistries, and direct LLM prediction is limited, although the paper finds that taxonomy-based grouping is the one LLM role that consistently helps OOD generalization over a kNN+GBT baseline.
AI.method: The LLM acts as a generator of candidate taxonomies that partition materials into chemically meaningful environments. Taxonomies are scored on training-only pseudo-OOD validation, invariant feature selection is applied within each accepted taxonomy, and the resulting models are combined by gated aggregation.
AI.result: On the halide perovskite benchmark, mean OOD MAE fell from 0.122 to 0.111 eV. Under a frozen dev/test protocol the deployable configuration reduced errors from 0.123 to 0.117 eV for electronic bandgap and from 0.181 to 0.173 eV for optical bandgap, and it also helped on 3D perovskite solar cell efficiencies and Matbench structure-split tasks.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that LLMs are most effective as tools for discovering structure in data rather than as direct predictors, with robustness gains under distribution shift that remain competitive with strong classical selection methods.

title: Causal Signal Credit Assignment for Verilog Code Generation via Counterfactual Hardware Verification
summary: Large language models have improved Verilog generation, yet functional correctness remains difficult to optimize because simulation commonly provides a coarse module-level pass/fail outcome. Such feedback discards useful evidence from partially correct RTL modules and cannot determine whether a source statement is functionally responsible for an observed output behavior. We present a new method named Causal Signal Credit Assignment (CSCA), which is a counterfactual preference-optimization framework for Verilog generation. CSCA first performs continuous signal-level behavioral verification on sampled candidate modules. It then locates output-driving assignment spans and applies five interventions while holding the remaining module and testbench fixed. The resulting changes in signal-level errors are combined with behavioral agreement to form a continuous statement credit, which is mapped to response-token weights for strict weighted direct preference optimization. This enables CSCA to learn from locally supported statements without uniformly reinforcing an otherwise incorrect response. Built on Icarus Verilog and a CodeV-derived corpus, CSCA is evaluated on VerilogEval~2.0 and RTLLM~v2.0, including both code completion and specification-to-RTL tasks. With a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct backbone, CSCA leads the evaluated 7B-scale models and remains comparable to the much larger GPT-5.4-mini on the reported Verilog-generation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CSCA, a counterfactual preference-optimization method for Verilog generation that assigns credit to individual source statements using signal-level verification. With a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct backbone it leads the evaluated 7B-scale models and is comparable to GPT-5.4-mini on the reported benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Module-level pass/fail simulation feedback is coarse, discards evidence from partially correct RTL, and cannot tell whether a source statement is functionally responsible for an output behavior.
AI.method: CSCA runs continuous signal-level behavioral verification on sampled candidates, locates output-driving assignment spans, and applies five interventions while holding the rest of the module and testbench fixed. The resulting changes in signal-level errors, combined with behavioral agreement, form a continuous statement credit that is mapped to token weights for strict weighted direct preference optimization.
AI.result: The method is built on Icarus Verilog and a CodeV-derived corpus and is evaluated on VerilogEval 2.0 and RTLLM v2.0 for both code completion and specification-to-RTL tasks. The abstract gives no specific numbers beyond the stated comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Learning from locally supported statements, rather than uniformly reinforcing an incorrect response, helps a 7B model reach performance comparable to a much larger model on Verilog generation benchmarks.

title: LEGION: Benchmarking Language Agents on Sparse-Signal Investigation Under Adversarial Noise
summary: Autonomous language-model agents are increasingly deployed on discovery-driven tasks where signal is sparse and most retrieved information is irrelevant. Current benchmarks fail to evaluate this regime due to dense signals, cooperative environments, and ground truth typically being only a few tool calls away. We introduce Legion, a benchmark framework coupling a stochastic enterprise-telemetry simulator (Legion-Sim) with a tiered library of 74 expertly-crafted adversarial scenarios (Legion-Bench) and an evaluation protocol that scores investigation efficiency alongside detection accuracy. Scenarios are injected into freshly simulated companies, allowing independent control over confounder density and event volume. We test five agent architectures on two simulated companies and find that while recall is high (0.82-0.88) precision lags behind (0.61--0.72). They fail to find all of the indicators of compromise of the attack or mistake genuine indicators with attack related ones, which is critical in the context of cybersecurity investigation. Failures are consistent across reasoning tiers and persist across confounder density and event volume. We release Legion, the scenario library, performance on common agent architectures, and pipeline for reproducibility and extension.

AI.tldr: LEGION is a benchmark for language agents on sparse-signal security investigation, combining a simulated enterprise-telemetry environment with 74 adversarial scenarios. Five agent architectures reach high recall but lag in precision.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks use dense signals, cooperative environments and ground truth only a few tool calls away, so they do not test discovery-driven investigation where most retrieved information is irrelevant.
AI.method: The framework couples a stochastic enterprise-telemetry simulator (Legion-Sim) with a tiered library of 74 adversarial scenarios (Legion-Bench) and an evaluation protocol that scores investigation efficiency alongside detection accuracy. Scenarios are injected into freshly simulated companies, with independent control over confounder density and event volume.
AI.result: Five agent architectures on two simulated companies reached recall of 0.82 to 0.88 but precision of only 0.61 to 0.72. Agents missed some indicators of compromise or confused genuine indicators with attack-related benign ones, and failures persisted across reasoning tiers, confounder density and event volume.
AI.conclusion: The authors release the benchmark, scenario library, baseline performance and pipeline, and argue that the precision gap matters for cybersecurity investigation.

title: Disagreement-Aware Distribution Matching Distillation for Few-Step Diffusion Models
summary: Distribution Matching Distillation~(DMD) enables strong few-step diffusion generation by matching the student distribution to a pretrained teacher. Existing improvements to DMD often augment its supervision or modify its optimization machinery. We ask a complementary question: \emph{can DMD diagnose its own updates using signals already produced during training?} DMD inherently computes the discrepancy between a pretrained teacher and a fake model tracking the student distribution, but conventionally uses it primarily to determine the distribution matching direction. We find that the magnitude of this teacher--fake disagreement provides additional diagnostic information. Across extensive experiments, large disagreement in the high-noise regime consistently coincides with substantially higher-energy DMD updates. This reveals a dual role of disagreement: it determines not only \emph{where} the student should move, but also provides an intrinsic signal of \emph{how aggressively} the update should be applied. Based on this observation, we introduce Disagreement-Aware Distribution Matching Distillation (DA-DMD), which activates only in the high-noise regime and continuously modulates the update strength according to teacher--fake disagreement. DA-DMD reuses quantities already available during DMD training and requires no additional model, evaluator, or inference-time modification. We show that it exactly recovers vanilla DMD outside the selected region, reduces update energy only through selected samples, and exhibits redescending influence under extreme disagreement. Across multiple diffusion backbones, DA-DMD consistently improves few-step generation at the same inference cost. On SD3.5-L, DA-DMD improves HPSv2 from $28.23$ to $30.93$, while achieving a $64.4\%$ average win rate over DMD2.

AI.tldr: DA-DMD augments distribution matching distillation for few-step diffusion models by using the teacher-fake disagreement as a signal that modulates update strength. It improves few-step generation at the same inference cost across several backbones.
