AI.motivation: Existing DMD improvements augment supervision or change optimization, while the discrepancy between the teacher and the fake model is used mainly to set the matching direction. The paper asks whether this signal can also diagnose how aggressive each update should be.
AI.method: DA-DMD activates only in the high-noise regime and continuously scales the update strength by teacher-fake disagreement, reusing quantities already computed during DMD training. The authors show it recovers vanilla DMD outside the selected region, reduces update energy only on selected samples, and has a redescending influence under extreme disagreement.
AI.result: Across multiple diffusion backbones DA-DMD consistently improves few-step generation at the same inference cost. On SD3.5-L, HPSv2 rises from 28.23 to 30.93, and DA-DMD achieves a 64.4% average win rate over DMD2.
AI.conclusion: Disagreement carries intrinsic information about how strongly a distillation update should be applied, and using it requires no extra model, evaluator or inference change.

title: Layer Roles Matter: Mitigating Modality Imbalance in Multimodal Emotion Reasoning via Adaptive Layer Profiling
summary: Multimodal Emotion Reasoning (MER) requires perceiving and integrating emotion cues from multiple modalities. Recent advances increasingly leverage Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to enhance reasoning capacity. However, due to the inherent heterogeneity in conveying emotions across modalities, these models often suffer from modality imbalance and confront flawed emotion understanding. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis on MER models and uncover two key empirical insights. (i) In MER, modality imbalance manifests two distinct failure modes: unimodal over-reliance and insufficient cross-modal utilization, which call for different intervention strategies. (ii) MLLM layers exhibit implicit functional hierarchies in multimodal emotion processing, playing separable roles in stabilizing unimodal representations and integrating cross-modal information. Motivated by these observations, we propose a Layer-Aware Modality Rebalancing (LAMR) framework by explicitly aligning intervention strategies with layer roles. Specifically, we first introduce two quantized metrics for adaptive layer role profiling. In each layer, Modality Entropy (ME) measures the dispersion of modality contributions, and Cross-modal Intensity (CMI) captures the strength of cross-modal interactions. Then, we respectively enhance modality equilibrium in stabilization layers and cross-modal propagation in integration layers. Extensive experiments on two comprehensive MER benchmarks demonstrate that LAMR effectively mitigates modality imbalance and improves emotion reasoning across diverse MLLM backbones, without additional training.

AI.tldr: LAMR rebalances modalities in multimodal large language models for emotion reasoning by aligning interventions with the functional roles of layers. It improves emotion reasoning across backbones without additional training.
AI.motivation: Multimodal emotion reasoning with MLLMs suffers from modality imbalance, which appears as unimodal over-reliance and insufficient cross-modal use, and these two failure modes call for different interventions.
AI.method: The authors find that MLLM layers have separable roles, with stabilization layers that stabilize unimodal representations and integration layers that combine cross-modal information. They define Modality Entropy to measure dispersion of modality contributions and Cross-modal Intensity to measure cross-modal interaction strength, use them to profile layers, and enhance modality equilibrium in stabilization layers and cross-modal propagation in integration layers.
AI.result: Experiments on two MER benchmarks show that LAMR mitigates modality imbalance and improves emotion reasoning across diverse MLLM backbones. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Aligning intervention strategy with layer roles is an effective, training-free way to mitigate modality imbalance in MLLM-based emotion reasoning.

title: CHORD: Multi-resolution Compression for Multimodal Time Series
summary: Wearables, mobile devices, and IoT platforms generate multimodal time-series data continuously and at scale, making efficient storage and transfer a primary concern. The same recordings are reused after collection by many downstream models, often at different temporal resolutions, so a compressed representation should be small, useful across resolutions, and produced at a bit rate known in advance. Prior work meets parts of this: symbolic and error-bounded compressors reconstruct accurately but fix resolution at compression time, learned codecs target one signal domain, and discrete tokenizers reconstruct without accounting for rate. We introduce CHORD, a coarse-to-fine compressor for heterogeneous multimodal time series. A residual cascade orders each payload from broad to fine temporal scales and synthesizes corrections through learned shapelet-inspired atoms. A shared pathway supplies a reusable synthesis basis across modalities, while private pathways retain capacity for sensor-specific morphology. Finite scalar quantization fixes the bit width of every modality and scale, so payload size is known before encoding, and scale dropout trains each coarse-to-fine prefix to be a valid reconstruction operating point. Across seven wearable-sensing and forecasting benchmarks, CHORD stays within 0.62 points of uncompressed classification accuracy on average at the 8x target, the smallest gap of any compressed method, with all resolutions decoded from one payload.

AI.tldr: CHORD is a coarse-to-fine compressor for multimodal wearable time series that yields one payload from which all temporal resolutions can be decoded at a bit rate known in advance. It stays within 0.62 points of uncompressed classification accuracy on average at the 8x target.
AI.motivation: Downstream models reuse the same recordings at different temporal resolutions, and prior compressors either fix resolution at compression time, target a single signal domain, or ignore rate when reconstructing.
AI.method: A residual cascade orders each payload from broad to fine temporal scales and synthesizes corrections with learned shapelet-inspired atoms. A shared pathway provides a reusable synthesis basis across modalities while private pathways keep sensor-specific capacity, finite scalar quantization fixes the bit width for each modality and scale, and scale dropout trains each coarse-to-fine prefix to be a valid reconstruction.
AI.result: Across seven wearable-sensing and forecasting benchmarks, CHORD is within 0.62 points of uncompressed classification accuracy on average at the 8x target, the smallest gap of any compressed method evaluated, and all resolutions are decoded from one payload.
AI.conclusion: A single multi-resolution, fixed-rate payload can serve heterogeneous multimodal time series without sacrificing much downstream accuracy.

title: Can LLM Agents Organize Their Own Memory?
summary: In most LLM agents, weights are fixed after deployment, so new information must be retained in external memory. Existing approaches often rely on predefined records and fixed organizational rules, which cannot readily accommodate evolving tasks and interactions. This raises the question: can LLM agents organize their own memory using ordinary documents? We introduce self-organized memory (SoMem), a framework that stores memory in linked documents. The agent decides what to summarize, how to group related information, and when to revise existing topics, and every summary it produces stays linked to the original interactions as evidence. The runtime validates updates and automatically derives temporal, relational, and recent-memory views from the organized content. At query time, the agent chooses what to search and read, following document links and inspecting original evidence as needed. On LoCoMo, BEAM-100K, and LongMemEval-S, SoMem outperforms the strongest baseline by 2.66, 3.10, and 2.00 percentage points, respectively. The constructed memory can be reused across models, and additional reasoning effort can further improve answer quality. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of agents organizing and using their own persistent memory through ordinary documents. Code is available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: SoMem lets LLM agents store and organize their own memory as linked documents, with summaries that remain tied to the original interactions as evidence. It outperforms the strongest baseline on three long-context memory benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Since LLM weights are fixed after deployment, new information must live in external memory, but predefined records and fixed organizational rules do not adapt to evolving tasks and interactions.
AI.method: The agent decides what to summarize, how to group related information and when to revise topics, and the runtime validates updates and derives temporal, relational and recent-memory views. At query time the agent searches and reads, following document links and inspecting original evidence as needed.
AI.result: SoMem outperforms the strongest baseline by 2.66 points on LoCoMo, 3.10 points on BEAM-100K and 2.00 points on LongMemEval-S. The constructed memory can be reused across models, and additional reasoning effort can further improve answer quality.
AI.conclusion: Agents can organize and use their own persistent memory through ordinary documents, which the authors present as evidence of feasibility.

title: ChainCheck: Near-Perfect Evidence-Sufficiency Scores Can Conceal Sensitivity to Construction Artifacts -- Paired Conditional Contrasts that Expose an Evaluation Confound
summary: Evidence-sufficiency benchmarks ask whether a model can tell a complete passage set from one whose reasoning chain is broken. When broken sets are made by editing text, near-perfect sufficiency scores--and even positive crossed-control scores--need not demonstrate multi-hop reasoning. We present ChainCheck, an evaluation-validity audit that pairs validator-certified counterfactual cells with artifact-only baselines. In an exploratory crossed control on 2,214 HotpotQA pairs, a language-model scorer that never reads the chain reaches a nominal AUC of 0.997, and a one-string match reaches the maximum of the crossed chain-sensitivity statistic CS4 (0.500), while the 11 evaluated systems score from 0.308 to 0.484; the two statistics are different metrics. We therefore read positive CS4 as operational bridge-consistency sensitivity, not as semantic multi-hop reasoning. Every system is also sensitive to one extra edit, and the edits are detectable according to model-based naturalness ratings. On an independent HotpotQA set of 2,276 pairs, patterns pre-specified on MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA did not replicate: 5 of 6 trained readouts were edit-dominated, and the reference judge's selectivity interval [-0.007, +0.042] includes zero. Judge scores also depended on batch layout. The MuSiQue and 2Wiki records are public; the HotpotQA records and the fine-tuned checkpoints are not, so external reproduction is partial.

AI.tldr: ChainCheck is an evaluation-validity audit showing that near-perfect evidence-sufficiency scores on HotpotQA can be produced by artifacts rather than multi-hop reasoning. Paired conditional contrasts expose the confound, and the reported patterns do not replicate on an independent set.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks that build broken reasoning chains by editing text can yield high sufficiency scores that need not demonstrate multi-hop reasoning, so the validity of these scores is in question.
AI.method: The authors pair validator-certified counterfactual cells with artifact-only baselines. In an exploratory crossed control on 2,214 HotpotQA pairs they compare a language-model scorer that never reads the chain and a one-string match against the systems evaluated, and they read positive CS4 as operational bridge-consistency sensitivity.
AI.result: A scorer that never reads the chain reached a nominal AUC of 0.997, and a one-string match reached the maximum CS4 value of 0.500, while the 11 systems scored from 0.308 to 0.484. On an independent set of 2,276 pairs, the patterns pre-specified on MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA did not replicate, and the reference judge's selectivity interval [-0.007, +0.042] includes zero.
AI.conclusion: Positive sensitivity scores can reflect edit artifacts, judge scores depend on batch layout, and the authors call for reading such benchmark results with artifact-only controls.

title: AutoQS: Automated Quantization Strategy Design with Large Language Models
summary: Quantization reduces LLM deployment costs, but effective strategies must balance model quality and storage. LLM-driven search can automate strategy design through repeated proposal and evaluation. This process must identify useful strategies within a limited evaluation budget. The key challenge is that \textit{actual quantization is expensive, while inexpensive proxies may not reflect quantized-model performance.} To address this challenge, we present AutoQS, an \textbf{Auto}mated \textbf{Q}uantization \textbf{S}trategy Design with LLMs. AutoQS keeps weight precision fixed and searches group-size allocations across layers and operators under deployment constraints. Evaluation history guides coordinated LLM proposals, while deterministic validation ensures compatible allocations. An inexpensive quality proxy evaluates candidates, and an candidate repository retains alternative allocations to inform subsequent proposals. Periodic actual quantization complements these proxy evaluations with measured quality and checkpoint storage, providing feedback for further search within the evaluation budget. Experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show that AutoQS improves seven-task average accuracy over uniform-group GPTQ and AWQ by 0.70 and 1.12 percentage points, respectively, at four-bit weight precision.

AI.tldr: AutoQS uses LLMs to search layer- and operator-wise group-size allocations for weight quantization under a limited evaluation budget, with a cheap quality proxy and periodic actual quantization. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at four-bit weights it beats uniform-group GPTQ and AWQ.
AI.motivation: Actual quantization is expensive, while inexpensive proxies may not reflect quantized-model performance, so the search must find useful strategies within a limited evaluation budget.
AI.method: AutoQS keeps weight precision fixed and searches group-size allocations across layers and operators under deployment constraints. Evaluation history guides coordinated LLM proposals, deterministic validation ensures compatible allocations, and a candidate repository keeps alternative allocations. Periodic actual quantization gives measured quality and checkpoint storage as feedback.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at four-bit weight precision, AutoQS improves seven-task average accuracy over uniform-group GPTQ by 0.70 points and over AWQ by 1.12 points.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven search with proxy evaluations and periodic measurement can automate quantization strategy design, although the gains reported are modest and come from one model.

title: Enhancing Multi-Step Chemical Mechanism Prediction with Graph-Guided Preference Data
summary: Predicting multi-step chemical reaction mechanisms requires identifying plausible intermediates and correctly ordering the elementary reaction steps. Existing computational methods focus on single-step elementary reaction prediction, limiting their ability to generalize to unseen reaction spaces. We introduce a graph-guided framework for multi-step chemical mechanism prediction that leverages a chemical mechanism knowledge graph (ChemMechKG) to guide large language models (LLMs). To improve pathway prediction, we develop a graph-aligned reaction mechanism predictor (GRMP) that uses graph neural networks to generate synthetic candidate pathways for pathway optimization. During inference, we design a relation retrieval (RR) module to extract relevant graph evidence from the KG for pathway refinement. Experiments show that GRMP achieves the highest pathway accuracy among all compared methods on ChemMechQA and oMe-Gold, reaching 48.1% and 57.9%, respectively. On a fixed sample of 110 out-of-distribution reactions from ChemMechQA-Hard, GRMP achieves 36.4% top-1 pathway accuracy. LLM-as-Judge and human assessment further demonstrate its ability to generalize to unseen reactions.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a graph-guided framework that uses a chemical mechanism knowledge graph to help LLMs predict multi-step reaction mechanisms, with a GNN-based predictor that generates synthetic candidate pathways. It reports the highest pathway accuracy on two benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing computational methods handle single-step elementary reactions and do not generalize well to multi-step mechanisms in unseen reaction spaces, which require identifying intermediates and ordering steps correctly.
AI.method: The graph-aligned reaction mechanism predictor (GRMP) uses graph neural networks to generate synthetic candidate pathways for pathway optimization. A relation retrieval module extracts relevant graph evidence from the knowledge graph during inference to refine pathways.
AI.result: GRMP achieves the highest pathway accuracy among compared methods on ChemMechQA and oMe-Gold, at 48.1% and 57.9% respectively. On a fixed sample of 110 out-of-distribution reactions from ChemMechQA-Hard it reaches 36.4% top-1 pathway accuracy.
AI.conclusion: LLM-as-Judge and human assessment suggest the approach generalizes to unseen reactions, according to the authors.

title: Evaluating AI Agents for Industrial-Level Chip Floorplanning: A Framework and Empirical Study
summary: Floorplanning is an early step in turning a logical circuit into a physical chip: it positions large circuit modules and constrains the space available for subsequent logic placement and wiring. These decisions affect congestion and timing, but their physical consequences emerge through downstream implementation. For AI agents, the task requires translating engineering constraints into spatial decisions whose quality cannot be judged by successful tool execution alone. We present an evaluation framework that connects submitted layouts to a prescribed downstream implementation flow, checks geometric validity, measures physical quality, and reports resource use. On one industrial design whose 99 macros occupy approximately 71\% of a fixed L-shaped layout region, we compare our specialized system Nova-SI with general-purpose engineering agents and agents restricted to file access, obtaining complete physical measurements for 39 layout outputs. Under our 0--100 composite quality score, Nova-SI achieves a mean of 57.97 without online feedback from the prescribed power-grid and placement evaluation, compared with 31.17 for the strongest measured general-purpose configuration, GPT-6 Astra. The difference is supported by raw congestion and timing measurements and persists across scoring-sensitivity checks. Layout-level analysis further shows that similar global utilization can conceal substantially different local congestion. Together, the protocol and case study assess agents through the physical consequences of their delivered layouts and provide evidence about system performance on this industrial instance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an evaluation framework that scores AI agents by the physical quality of the chip floorplans they deliver, using a prescribed downstream implementation flow. On one industrial design, the specialized system Nova-SI outperforms general-purpose engineering agents on a 0 to 100 composite score.
AI.motivation: Floorplanning decisions affect congestion and timing only through downstream implementation, and for AI agents successful tool execution alone does not show that a layout is good, so a physically grounded evaluation is needed.
AI.method: The framework connects submitted layouts to a prescribed downstream implementation flow, checks geometric validity, measures physical quality and reports resource use. The authors compare Nova-SI with general-purpose engineering agents and with agents restricted to file access on one industrial design with 99 macros occupying about 71% of a fixed L-shaped region, obtaining complete measurements for 39 layout outputs.
AI.result: Nova-SI reached a mean composite score of 57.97 without online feedback from the power-grid and placement evaluation, compared with 31.17 for the strongest measured general-purpose configuration, GPT-6 Astra. The gap is supported by raw congestion and timing measurements and persists across scoring-sensitivity checks, and similar global utilization can hide different local congestion.
AI.conclusion: Assessing agents by the physical consequences of their layouts is a useful protocol, and the case study gives evidence about performance on this single industrial instance.

title: COMPASS: Composable Policy-Amortized Structured Search for LLM-Based Optimization Modeling
summary: Large language models offer a promising technique for translating natural-language optimization problems into solver code, but their reliability remains constrained by the quality of template retrieval. While recent structured methods improve over flat prompting through hierarchical taxonomy search, their traversal rules remain fixed or LLM-driven at inference time, leaving retrieval unable to improve from past successes and failures. This motivates treating template retrieval as a policy that can be learned from modeling experience, rather than as a static inference-time rule. We propose COMPASS, a policy-amortized framework for retrieving optimization templates in LLM-based solver modeling, which represents the template library as a directed acyclic graph and formulates retrieval as a sequential decision process over template nodes. A deep Q-network learns a reusable traversal policy from template-level judgments and execution feedback, reducing reliance on fixed heuristic traversal through feedback-driven graph navigation. To support extensible retrieval, COMPASS embeds problem descriptions and template nodes in a shared semantic space, allowing newly inserted templates to be scored from their text descriptions without redefining the action space. Experiments across multiple LLM backbones and optimization-modeling benchmarks demonstrate that COMPASS consistently improves over heuristic structured retrieval, with the largest gains on complex and mixed-category problems.

AI.tldr: COMPASS treats template retrieval for LLM-based optimization modeling as a learned policy over a template DAG, trained with a deep Q-network from execution feedback. It consistently improves over heuristic structured retrieval, with the largest gains on complex and mixed-category problems.
AI.motivation: Structured retrieval uses fixed or LLM-driven traversal rules at inference time, so retrieval cannot improve from past successes and failures in modeling experience.
AI.method: The template library is represented as a directed acyclic graph and retrieval is a sequential decision process over template nodes. A deep Q-network learns a reusable traversal policy from template-level judgments and execution feedback, and problem descriptions and template nodes share a semantic space so new templates can be scored from text without changing the action space.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple LLM backbones and optimization-modeling benchmarks show that COMPASS consistently improves over heuristic structured retrieval. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Learning retrieval as an amortized policy from modeling experience is a viable route to more reliable template retrieval and to extending the template library.

title: CRAFT-AI: Capability and Requirement Alignment for Flexible Manufacturing through Agentic AI
comment: Preprint intended for submission to the 37th European Safety and Reliability Conference (ESREL 2027)
summary: One of the fundamental needs for reaching resilient production infrastructure is flexible manufacturing, which requires translating changing production requirements into implementable system configurations. This paper introduces \textbf{CRAFT-AI}, an agentic AI approach combining natural language (NL) requirement interpretation, Asset Administration Shell (AAS)-based capability descriptions, and reusable engineering knowledge from existing manufacturing configurations. A tool-using AI agent matches requirements with available capabilities and reference implementations to generate manufacturing scenes and corresponding AAS instances. The approach is demonstrated using a Factory I/O prototype with twelve reference scenes and five illustrative manufacturing tasks of varying complexity, providing an initial feasibility assessment of the proposed AAS-enabled, system-level generative engineering approach. For the four valid user task descriptions, proper requirements, correct references to the relevant engineering knowledge, correct components and lastly a valid Factory I/O scene are generated. For the task with missing engineering knowledge and a wrong sensor selection, the user is informed about which requirements of the scene generation lack domain knowledge and also which sensor is not compatible with the selected raw material by the user with link to the related documentation. After fixing the task description, the correct scene is seamlessly generated. \textbf{CRAFT-AI} highlights the importance of safeguards for risk perception and communication in foundation model-driven solutions.

AI.tldr: CRAFT-AI is an agentic approach that turns natural-language manufacturing requirements into Asset Administration Shell capability descriptions and Factory I/O scenes by reusing engineering knowledge. A prototype with twelve reference scenes and five tasks gives an initial feasibility assessment.
AI.motivation: Resilient production needs flexible manufacturing, which requires translating changing requirements into implementable system configurations, and existing reference knowledge and capability descriptions are not easily reused for this.
AI.method: A tool-using AI agent matches requirements with available capabilities and reference implementations to generate manufacturing scenes and corresponding AAS instances. The approach combines natural-language requirement interpretation, AAS-based capability descriptions and reusable engineering knowledge from existing configurations.
AI.result: For the four valid task descriptions the system generated proper requirements, correct references, correct components and valid Factory I/O scenes. For the task with missing engineering knowledge and a wrong sensor selection, it reported which requirements lacked domain knowledge and which sensor was incompatible, and after the task description was fixed the correct scene was generated.
AI.conclusion: The authors highlight the need for safeguards for risk perception and communication in foundation-model-driven engineering solutions.

title: From Fluent Text to Ontology-Compatible Definitions: A Quality-Control Agentic Workflow
summary: Biomedical ontologies are structured knowledge systems that must evolve continuously to represent newly emerging knowledge, but their manual maintenance remains time-consuming and laborintensive. Textual definitions are especially costly because they must be readable to humans and compatible with controlled entities, relations, and logical constraints. Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising way to assist ontology engineering tasks, including definition generation. However, textual plausibility does not guarantee knowledge-system compatibility. A generated definition may be fluent and close to a reference definition, yet still fail to ground its implied entities or violate ontology-level constraints. Directly inserting such definitions into ontology libraries may therefore introduce entity-level hallucinations and logical inconsistencies. To address this problem, we propose two structured-knowledge incompatibility metrics, Entity Error Rate (EER) and Logical Inconsistency Rate (LIR), to quantify entity grounding and logical consistency for LLM-generated ontology definitions. We further develop an agentic quality-control (QC) workflow that treats definition generation as an iterative process rather than a direct decoding step: it generates definitions, extracts axioms, checks entity existence and logical consistency, and uses the resulting diagnostics to drive repair loops. Comprehensive experiments on Disease Ontology, Uberon Ontology, and Uberon-ConstraintStress demonstrate that EER and LIR complement conventional reference-based metrics by evaluating whether generated content can be grounded and checked inside the target ontology. The workflow effectively decreases EER while maintaining strong conventional text-generation performance. LIR further exposes sparse ontology-level logical failures that are invisible to text similarity metrics, although their repair remains limited.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes two incompatibility metrics, Entity Error Rate and Logical Inconsistency Rate, and an agentic quality-control workflow that iteratively repairs LLM-generated ontology definitions. The workflow lowers entity errors while keeping strong conventional text-generation scores.
AI.motivation: Fluent LLM-generated definitions for biomedical ontologies may ground entities that do not exist or violate ontology constraints, and inserting them directly can cause hallucinations and logical inconsistencies, which text similarity metrics do not reveal.
AI.method: The quality-control workflow treats definition generation as an iterative process: it generates a definition, extracts axioms, checks entity existence and logical consistency, and uses the diagnostics to drive repair loops. EER measures entity grounding and LIR measures logical consistency of generated definitions.
AI.result: Experiments on Disease Ontology, Uberon Ontology and Uberon-ConstraintStress show that EER and LIR complement reference-based metrics. The workflow effectively decreases EER while maintaining strong conventional text-generation performance, and LIR exposes sparse logical failures that text similarity misses, although their repair remains limited.
AI.conclusion: Checking generated definitions against the target ontology is needed for safe ontology maintenance, and logical repair remains an open limitation.

title: Joi-Bench-Task: Benchmarking Task Coordination in Full-duplex Voice Agents through Interactive Simulation
summary: Full-duplex voice agents enable natural, hands-free interaction, allowing users to refine requests, redirect ongoing work, and seek clarification while the agent is speaking. However, existing voice-agent benchmarks insufficiently isolate coordination between task execution and conversation. We introduce a benchmark that assesses this coordination by examining whether agents track what is being executed, what has been completed, what has been communicated, and what remains to be reported as the conversation evolves. We propose an interactive user simulator that introduces configurable interventions at designated timing in tool execution and spoken result delivery, supporting controllable and reproducible evaluation conditions. We evaluate five leading commercial voice agents along three dimensions: execution responsiveness, coordination under request changes, and coordination under interruptions. Agent evaluations reveal persistent coordination failures. Under request changes, the highest result completion rate is only 55%, indicating difficulty for current voice agents adapting to new requests while preserving earlier obligations. After user interruption, four of the five agents exhibit average information omission rates of at least 23%. These findings highlight task coordination as a central challenge for current voice agents in complex, evolving conversations.

AI.tldr: Joi-Bench-Task is a benchmark for task coordination in full-duplex voice agents, using an interactive user simulator that injects interruptions and request changes at controlled timings. Five commercial voice agents show persistent coordination failures, with at most 55% result completion under request changes.
AI.motivation: Existing voice-agent benchmarks insufficiently isolate how agents coordinate task execution with conversation as the conversation evolves, such as adapting to new requests and handling user interruptions.
AI.method: An interactive user simulator introduces configurable interventions at designated timings during tool execution and spoken result delivery, giving controllable and reproducible conditions. Agents are assessed on execution responsiveness, coordination under request changes, and coordination under interruptions.
AI.result: The highest result completion rate under request changes is only 55%. After user interruption, four of the five agents show average information omission rates of at least 23%.
AI.conclusion: Coordinating task execution with conversation is a central unsolved challenge for current voice agents in complex, evolving conversations.

title: SCALE: Small-Model-First Concept Abstraction with LLM-Guided Experience Internalization
summary: Autonomous agents must continually acquire reusable knowledge from experience without relying on costly large language model (LLM) reasoning for every decision. However, existing experience-based approaches often struggle to transform accumulated observations and reasoning into compact knowledge that lightweight models can independently apply. This paper proposes SCALE, a small-model-first framework that integrates selective LLM reasoning, experience-driven concept abstraction, and knowledge internalization. A lightweight model handles routine predictions, while prediction errors and accumulated cross-episode evidence selectively trigger LLM reflection. The LLM analyzes relevant historical experiences, generates positive and negative counterfactual examples, and proposes reusable concept hypotheses. Independently validated concepts are progressively incorporated into hierarchical neural representations, enabling lightweight models to exploit increasingly abstract knowledge. Meanwhile, mastered experiences are excluded from active memory while their original records remain available in a complete archive. Experiments across ten random seeds show that historical recall improves held-out accuracy from 87.11% to 98.28%, hierarchical concept knowledge increases difficult-case accuracy from 55.33% to 66.47%, and abstract archiving reduces active experience records from 6,000 to 1,528.

AI.tldr: SCALE is a small-model-first framework in which a lightweight model handles routine predictions while LLM reflection is triggered selectively, turning experience into hierarchical concept knowledge that the small model can apply. Across ten random seeds it raises held-out accuracy and reduces active experience records.
AI.motivation: Experience-based agents struggle to turn accumulated observations and reasoning into compact knowledge that lightweight models can apply independently, and relying on LLM reasoning for every decision is costly.
AI.method: Prediction errors and cross-episode evidence selectively trigger LLM reflection, which analyses historical experiences, generates positive and negative counterfactual examples, and proposes reusable concept hypotheses. Validated concepts are incorporated into hierarchical neural representations, and mastered experiences are moved out of active memory into a complete archive.
AI.result: Historical recall improves held-out accuracy from 87.11% to 98.28%. Hierarchical concept knowledge raises difficult-case accuracy from 55.33% to 66.47%. Abstract archiving reduces active experience records from 6,000 to 1,528.
AI.conclusion: Selective LLM reflection combined with concept abstraction and archiving lets lightweight models internalise reusable knowledge, reducing dependence on costly LLM reasoning for each decision.

title: System Optimizations for Cost-Efficient Agent Harnesses
summary: AI agent harnesses play the critical role of providing LLMs with an interface to a computing environment. Recent studies show that AI agents' task-execution accuracy depends mostly on the LLM used, while harness-side variances such as system prompts or tools have minimal impact. Rather, such harness-side variances show a larger impact on the cost of agent executions, achieving cost reductions up to 2.6 times on the same model and task. To further explore these harness-side cost optimization opportunities, we analyze the cost accumulation patterns across various agent traces and identify system opportunities to reduce token use and LLM calls without modifying the model or affecting task accuracy. Based on this analysis, we design Agency, a harness interposition platform that provides a unified abstraction and allows easy and portable implementation of harness-side system optimizations on existing off-the-shelf harnesses such as Claude Code or OpenAI Codex. Using Agency, we implement proof-of-concept optimization techniques based on our analysis and achieve cost reductions up to 35% across various real-world benchmarks on existing harnesses without compromising accuracy.

AI.tldr: Agency is a harness interposition platform that applies system-level optimisations to existing agent harnesses such as Claude Code or OpenAI Codex, cutting cost by up to 35% without modifying the model or affecting accuracy. The optimisations target token use and LLM calls.
AI.motivation: Harness-side variances such as system prompts and tools have little effect on agent accuracy but a large effect on execution cost, up to 2.6 times on the same model and task, and no portable way to apply such optimisations existed.
AI.method: The authors analyse cost accumulation patterns across agent traces to find opportunities to reduce token use and LLM calls. They build Agency, a platform with a unified abstraction for portable harness-side optimisation, and implement proof-of-concept techniques on it.
AI.result: Cost reductions of up to 35% across various real-world benchmarks on existing harnesses, without compromising accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Harness-level engineering is a practical lever for reducing agent cost, separate from choosing the model.

title: Toward Sustainable Agentic AI: Carbon Tradeoffs Across Iterative Self-Refinement and Tool-Augmented Coding
comment: Presented at the GREEN AI workshop @CIKM 2026
summary: Agentic language model systems can improve performance either by iterating on their own outputs or by using external tools in grounded environments. While these strategies can reduce error rates and substitute for larger models in some settings, their environmental cost remains relatively underexplored. We present two complementary empirical studies that estimate the energy and carbon footprint of agentic AI across settings of increasing complexity. Study~1 evaluates iterative verbal self-refinement: GPT-4.1-mini at $k = 1$--$5$ steps versus a GPT-4.1 single-pass baseline on two MATH benchmark splits. Study~2 evaluates tool-augmented agentic coding: GPT-4.1-mini, Claude Opus~4.6, and GPT-5.3-codex on SWE-bench Lite, where agents operate inside Docker-isolated environments with access to code execution and file editing tools. In Study~1, $k=3$ refinements close a 16-percentage-point accuracy gap to within 1~point, but nearly triple the carbon footprint relative to the cheap single-pass baseline while remaining below the GPT-4.1 single-pass baseline under the current token-based carbon scenario. In Study~2, GPT-5.3-codex achieves the highest resolution rate in this sample (81.2\%), ahead of Claude Opus~4.6 (68.9\%) and GPT-4.1-mini (25.0\%), but resolved-task-normalized efficiency remains mixed: GPT-4.1-mini is lowest on estimated carbon and cost per resolved task, while GPT-5.3-codex delivers substantially higher task success. All carbon estimates cover output-token inference only; prompt tokens, which exceed 99\% of tokens in Study~2, and tool execution are not charged, so the figures are lower bounds on the full agentic footprint.

AI.tldr: The paper measures the energy and carbon footprint of agentic AI in two studies, finding that iterative self-refinement nearly triples carbon for a few accuracy points, while stronger agentic coding models resolve more tasks with mixed efficiency per resolved task. Carbon estimates are lower bounds because they cover only output-token inference.
AI.motivation: The environmental cost of agentic strategies such as iterative self-refinement and tool-augmented coding is underexplored, although they can reduce error rates and substitute for larger models.
AI.method: Study 1 evaluates 1 to 5 verbal self-refinement steps of GPT-4.1-mini against a GPT-4.1 single-pass baseline on two MATH splits. Study 2 evaluates GPT-4.1-mini, Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.3-codex on SWE-bench Lite in Docker-isolated environments with code execution and file editing tools. Carbon is estimated from output-token inference only.
AI.result: With 3 refinement steps the accuracy gap of 16 points closes to within 1 point, but carbon nearly triples relative to the cheap single-pass baseline, remaining below the GPT-4.1 baseline under the token-based scenario. On SWE-bench Lite GPT-5.3-codex resolves 81.2%, Claude Opus 4.6 68.9% and GPT-4.1-mini 25.0%, and GPT-4.1-mini is lowest on carbon and cost per resolved task.
AI.conclusion: Efficiency is mixed: the cheapest model minimises footprint per resolved task, while stronger models deliver far higher success. Prompt tokens and tool execution are not charged, so the figures are lower bounds on the full agentic footprint.

title: Let the Fixer Decide: Training a Code Localizer from the Fixer's Likelihood
summary: Code localizers are usually trained to predict the files a reference patch edits, but the code a fixer needs to read is not the same as the code it changes. We propose Fixer-Guided Localization (FGL): the localizer proposes several localizations, a frozen fixer scores each by how likely it makes a verified patch, and the localizer is trained on these scores with weighted supervised fine-tuning, without running tests and without reinforcement learning. We build the full pipeline on Gemma 4 E4B for the Kaggle Gemma-4 Developer Agent competition, from 1,629 test-verified Kimi K3 trajectories. The FGL target helps the fixer find the bug as often as the teacher's localization while using 27.5% less code. On the development set, one EM round moves the agent in the expected direction compared with a matched control: more tasks reach a patch (53 vs. 46), fewer tasks get stuck reading files that do not exist (43 vs. 54), and more tasks are solved (8 vs. 6). Training also changes how the agent works: trained agents explore about three times more than the base model and write far fewer wrong patches, and the single agent solves up to 11 of 78 tasks, against 8 for the base model. An analysis of 13 evaluation runs identifies what limits a 4B agent under an 8-minute budget (time, repetition loops and edit quality) and gives practical lessons for training small coding agents. All data, code and adapters are publicly available.

AI.tldr: Fixer-Guided Localization trains a code localizer on the likelihood a frozen fixer assigns to a verified patch under each proposed localization, using weighted supervised fine-tuning with no test execution or reinforcement learning. The resulting 4B Gemma 4 based agent finds bugs as often as the teacher's localization while reading 27.5% less code.
AI.motivation: Code localizers are normally trained to predict the files a reference patch edits, but the code a fixer needs to read is not the same as the code it changes.
AI.method: The localizer proposes several localizations, a frozen fixer scores each by how likely it makes a verified patch, and the localizer is trained on these scores with weighted supervised fine-tuning. The pipeline is built on Gemma 4 E4B from 1,629 test-verified Kimi K3 trajectories.
AI.result: On the development set one EM round moves the agent in the expected direction against a matched control: 53 vs. 46 tasks reach a patch, 43 vs. 54 tasks get stuck reading nonexistent files, and 8 vs. 6 tasks are solved. The single agent solves up to 11 of 78 tasks, against 8 for the base model.
AI.conclusion: Fixer feedback is a useful training signal for small coding agents, which explore more and write fewer wrong patches. Time, repetition loops and edit quality limit a 4B agent under an 8-minute budget, and data, code and adapters are public.

title: Learning to Act with World Models by Valuing What Comes Next
summary: A sparse terminal reward tells an agent little about its steps. Much of the missing information is implicit in the environment's dynamics, because each state transition can change the conditions for success long before the reward arrives. A world model trained on real transitions can learn to predict what each action changes, but a predicted observation does not by itself show whether success has become more likely. With a binary terminal reward, PPO's critic makes this judgment by estimating the current policy's probability of success, but only for states the agent reaches. Our method, WM-PPO, elegantly brings the two together. For each action the policy samples, executed or not, the world model predicts the next observation and the critic values the predicted successor. In the policy channel, comparisons among these values give the policy auxiliary advantages; in the value channel, their mean gives the critic an auxiliary target. A shared gate weights both channels according to how reliably comparisons with similar margins predicted real outcomes earlier in training. The policy, critic and world model all learn from the agent's own interaction, with no teacher or privileged information, and only the policy is used at inference. With a comparable number of real environment steps, WM-PPO raises success from PPO's 63.5% to 87.5% on ALFWorld and from 39.3% to 52.9% on ScienceWorld. It matches the strongest PPO refinements we tested on ALFWorld and exceeds the best of them by 6.5 points on ScienceWorld. The trained policy more often completes prerequisite steps before placing an object or committing to an answer.

AI.tldr: WM-PPO uses a world model to predict the outcome of each sampled action, letting the PPO critic value the predicted successors as auxiliary advantages and value targets. It raises success on ALFWorld from 63.5% to 87.5% and on ScienceWorld from 39.3% to 52.9%.
AI.motivation: A sparse terminal reward gives little information about individual steps, and a predicted observation alone does not show whether success has become more likely.
AI.method: For each action the policy samples, executed or not, the world model predicts the next observation and the critic values the predicted successor. Comparisons among these values give the policy auxiliary advantages, and their mean gives the critic an auxiliary target. A shared gate weights both channels by how reliably comparisons with similar margins predicted real outcomes earlier in training.
AI.result: With a comparable number of real environment steps, success rises from PPO's 63.5% to 87.5% on ALFWorld and from 39.3% to 52.9% on ScienceWorld. WM-PPO matches the strongest PPO refinements tested on ALFWorld and beats the best of them by 6.5 points on ScienceWorld.
AI.conclusion: Predicted successors from a learned world model can give dense credit assignment for PPO agents under sparse binary rewards, and the trained policy completes prerequisite steps more often.

title: PARIS: A multi-agent LLM framework for end-to-end, PRISMA-guided systematic literature reviews with pre-synthesis corpus quality assessment
summary: Systematic literature reviews (SRs) remain slow and labor-intensive, and most automation tools address single stages of the workflow. We present PARIS (PRISMA Agentic Research Intelligence System), an open-source framework in which a conductor agent running in Claude Code orchestrates 15 specialized large language model (LLM) agents, from scoping a research question to exporting a manuscript draft. Agents are specified declaratively, coordinate exclusively through persisted artifacts that the conductor validates before every transition, and delegate retrieval, bibliometric analysis and scoring to deterministic Python utilities. Three human checkpoints gate study inclusion, corpus adequacy and the synthesis outline. We also introduce QualityScore, a pre-synthesis index that aggregates normalized network, bibliometric, semantic and process sub-scores into a 0-100 grade. Two case studies illustrate both: AI chatbots and university students' learning (388 records, 100 included) and AI-assisted SR methods (131 records, 123 included, QualityScore 69.1 recomputed with a proxy network sub-score). They show end-to-end feasibility across domains and the diagnostic use of QualityScore: in the first run, corpus improvements chosen at the corpus-adequacy checkpoint raised the score from 74.6 to 81.9 and the number of pre-2023 studies from 1 to 19. Audits of both runs exposed failure modes: incomplete retrieval, counts that drifted between agents, unrecorded or delegated checkpoint decisions and a grade that depends on how citation data are handled. PARIS fully supports 8 of the 27 PRISMA 2020 items and partially supports 11. Output quality has so far been judged only by an internal reviewer agent; independent validation against human reviews is the next step.

AI.tldr: PARIS is an open-source multi-agent framework in which a conductor agent running in Claude Code orchestrates 15 LLM agents across a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review, from question scoping to manuscript draft. It adds QualityScore, a 0 to 100 pre-synthesis corpus grade.
AI.motivation: Systematic reviews are slow and labour-intensive, and most automation tools address only single stages of the workflow.
AI.method: Agents are declared in specifications and coordinate only through persisted artifacts that the conductor validates before each transition. Retrieval, bibliometric analysis and scoring are delegated to deterministic Python utilities, with three human checkpoints for study inclusion, corpus adequacy and the synthesis outline. QualityScore aggregates normalised network, bibliometric, semantic and process sub-scores.
AI.result: Two case studies (388 records with 100 included, and 131 records with 123 included) ran end to end. In the first, corpus improvements raised QualityScore from 74.6 to 81.9 and pre-2023 studies from 1 to 19. Audits exposed incomplete retrieval, count drift between agents and unrecorded checkpoint decisions. PARIS fully supports 8 of the 27 PRISMA 2020 items and partly supports 11.
AI.conclusion: The framework shows end-to-end feasibility, and QualityScore works as a diagnostic tool. Output quality has been judged only by an internal reviewer agent, so validation against human reviews is the next step.

title: ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents
summary: On-policy self-distillation lets a language agent act as its own Teacher by conditioning on privileged context such as skills written from its own trajectories. Its guidance, however, is weighted by how much this context shifts token likelihoods rather than by whether it improves behavior, so errors in self-written skills return through later updates. We propose environment-calibrated on-policy self-distillation, which uses environmental outcomes to decide how much to trust the Teacher's current guidance and which self-written skills to reinforce. Command-level advantages, estimated by comparing commands executed at similar observations, scale each Teacher preference and reward reflections and skills whose induced preferences favor higher-advantage commands. Without skills at inference, 3B and 7B agents reach 90.5% and 93.3% macro success on seen ALFWorld tasks and 75.5% and 80.5% success on WebShop. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, they outperform GRPO under the same protocol by 11.0 and 7.6 percentage points, respectively. In an ablation study, supervising only executable commands rather than the Actor's full response raises 3B WebShop success from 52.3% to 75.0%.

AI.tldr: Environment-calibrated on-policy self-distillation weights a language agent's self-generated teacher guidance by environmental outcomes, using command-level advantages to decide which guidance and self-written skills to trust and reinforce. Without skills at inference, 3B and 7B agents reach 90.5% and 93.3% macro success on seen ALFWorld tasks.
AI.motivation: In on-policy self-distillation the teacher guidance is weighted by how much privileged context shifts token likelihoods rather than by whether it improves behaviour, so errors in self-written skills return through later updates.
AI.method: Command-level advantages, estimated by comparing commands executed at similar observations, scale each teacher preference and reward reflections and skills whose induced preferences favour higher-advantage commands. Supervision covers only executable commands rather than the full actor response.
AI.result: 3B and 7B agents reach 90.5% and 93.3% macro success on seen ALFWorld tasks and 75.5% and 80.5% on WebShop. On unseen ALFWorld tasks they outperform GRPO by 11.0 and 7.6 points. In an ablation, supervising only executable commands raises 3B WebShop success from 52.3% to 75.0%.
AI.conclusion: Environmental outcomes can calibrate self-distillation so that agents learn from their own reliable guidance rather than propagating errors from self-written skills.

title: Representational Alignment between Deep Neural Networks and Human Brain in Speech Processing under Audiovisual Noise
comment: Alignment between Deep Neural Networks and Human Brain
summary: Speech comprehension in the human brain is an incremental process that begins with acoustic processing and advances to linguistic processing. While recent studies have revealed that the hierarchy of deep neural networks (DNNs) correlates with the ascending auditory pathway, the exact nature of this DNN-brain alignment remains underexplored. In this study, we investigate how DNN representations align with the brain's acoustic-to-linguistic processing. Specifically, we employed neural encoding models to simulate neural responses to acoustic (i.e., speech and noise envelope) and linguistic features (i.e., word onset and surprisal). By applying representational similarity analysis (RSA), we quantified the similarity between these neural responses and the DNN embeddings generated by a pre-trained automatic speech recognition (ASR) model, both before and after fine-tuning on audiovisual noisy data. Our results demonstrate significant DNN-brain alignment: embeddings from shallow layers exhibit higher similarity to neural responses associated with acoustic features, while those from deeper layers align more closely with neural responses related to linguistic features. Importantly, the fine-tuning process enhances this alignment by improving noise processing in shallower layers and refining linguistic representations in deeper layers. These results suggest that fine-tuned DNN models can naturally develop human-like processing patterns in noisy environments, highlighting a functional alignment between the human brain and DNNs in speech representation.

AI.tldr: Representational similarity analysis shows that a pretrained ASR model's shallow layers align with acoustic brain responses and its deep layers with linguistic ones, and that fine-tuning on noisy audiovisual data strengthens this alignment.
AI.motivation: Speech comprehension proceeds from acoustic to linguistic processing, and although DNN hierarchies correlate with the ascending auditory pathway, the nature of the DNN-brain alignment remains underexplored.
AI.method: Neural encoding models simulate responses to acoustic features (speech and noise envelopes) and linguistic features (word onset and surprisal). Representational similarity analysis compares these simulated responses with embeddings from a pretrained ASR model, before and after fine-tuning on audiovisual noisy data.
AI.result: Shallow-layer embeddings are more similar to acoustic-feature responses, and deep-layer embeddings to linguistic-feature responses. Fine-tuning improves noise processing in shallow layers and refines linguistic representations in deep layers.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuned DNNs can develop human-like processing patterns in noisy environments, indicating a functional alignment between the human brain and DNN speech representations.

title: Depth as a Candidate Source: Portfolio Allocation for Recurrent Test-Time Scaling in Large Language Models
summary: Recurrent latent reasoning in large lanugage models (LLMs) scales test-time computation by increasing recurrent depth, naturally framing inference as a problem of deciding when to stop. We identify a previously overlooked limitation of this single-depth view through systematic preliminary analysis: deeper recurrence can lose correct solutions found at shallower depths, while depth-specific success sets remain broadly non-nested even after controlling for marginal accuracy. This suggests that depth determines not only computation cost, but also access to distinct candidate solutions. Motivated by this finding, we propose Depth Portfolio Allocation (DPA), which reformulates recurrent test-time scaling as budgeted allocation across depth-specific candidate sources. DPA supports both fixed portfolios and feedback-guided sequential allocation under a shared inference budget. Experiments on GSM8K, SVAMP, MultiArith, and MBPP show that mixed-depth portfolios expand oracle coverage under matched candidate counts and nominal costs, while feedback-guided allocation generally matches or improves uniform allocation and can reduce computation in high-budget settings. Code and data are avaible at : this https URL.

AI.tldr: Depth Portfolio Allocation treats recurrent test-time scaling in LLMs as budgeted allocation across depth-specific candidate sources, since different recurrence depths find non-nested sets of correct solutions. Mixed-depth portfolios expand oracle coverage, and feedback-guided allocation matches or beats uniform allocation.
AI.motivation: Single-depth recurrent inference treats depth only as a cost, but deeper recurrence can lose correct solutions found at shallower depths, so depth also governs access to distinct candidate solutions.
AI.method: DPA reformulates recurrent test-time scaling as budgeted allocation across depth-specific candidate sources. It supports fixed portfolios and feedback-guided sequential allocation under a shared inference budget.
AI.result: On GSM8K, SVAMP, MultiArith and MBPP, mixed-depth portfolios expand oracle coverage under matched candidate counts and nominal costs. Feedback-guided allocation generally matches or improves uniform allocation and can reduce computation in high-budget settings.
AI.conclusion: Treating depth as a source of candidate solutions, not only as a compute knob, makes portfolio-style allocation a sound framing of recurrent test-time scaling.

title: Reconfigurable Action Theories: A Formal Foundation for Dynamically Composable Agent Harnesses
summary: Action theories typically fix their vocabulary and causal laws, whereas agent harnesses can change their tools, providers, and policies during execution. We introduce Reconfigurable Action Theories (RAT), in which actions can change the action theory itself. A theory module in RAT contains a vocabulary, causal laws, and an initializer. A RAT configuration records the active modules and the world state. Module loading and unloading are represented by actions governed by ordinary causal laws. RAT retains the standard causal action semantics of its language fragment when the active module set is fixed. We give sufficient conditions for at most one next configuration, preservation of existing behavior when a module is added, and equal results when modules are loaded in either order. We establish the computational complexity of reasoning tasks in RAT and translate finite RAT systems into nonmonotonic causal theories and Answer Set Programming (ASP), preserving bounded executions. Experiments compare finite RAT models with executions of official DeepSeek Harness, Pi, and OpenHands implementations. RAT provides a formal basis for checking how component changes affect a harness's available actions, behavior, and reachable goals.

AI.tldr: Reconfigurable Action Theories (RAT) is a formal framework in which actions can load and unload theory modules, so the vocabulary and causal laws of an agent harness can change during execution. The paper gives formal properties, complexity results and a translation of finite RAT systems into ASP.
AI.motivation: Standard action theories fix their vocabulary and causal laws, whereas agent harnesses change tools, providers and policies during execution.
AI.method: A theory module contains a vocabulary, causal laws and an initializer, and a configuration records the active modules and world state. Module loading and unloading are actions governed by ordinary causal laws. Finite RAT systems are translated into nonmonotonic causal theories and Answer Set Programming, preserving bounded executions.
AI.result: The paper gives sufficient conditions for at most one next configuration, preservation of existing behaviour when a module is added, and equal results whichever order modules are loaded in. It establishes the complexity of reasoning tasks. Experiments compare finite RAT models with executions of the DeepSeek Harness, Pi and OpenHands implementations.
AI.conclusion: RAT provides a formal basis for checking how component changes affect a harness's available actions, behaviour and reachable goals.

title: PACE-ECG: Patient-Aware Contrastive ECG Pretraining; Leveraging Longitudinal Structure for Transferable Representations
summary: Foundation models for physiological signals are commonly evaluated on in-domain interpretation tasks, but their ability to transfer to longitudinal clinical prognosis across healthcare systems remains uncertain. We developed PACE-ECG, an ECG pretraining framework that combines contrastive learning across temporally neighbouring recordings from the same patient with clinically guided multitask supervision. We evaluated frozen ECG representations for post-myocardial-infarction all-cause mortality and incident heart failure prediction across MIMIC-IV and two external HEEDB cohorts, comparing the proposed representation with DeepECG-SSL, a state-of-the-art model, and two control baselines. Across both downstream tasks, the proposed model outperformed DeepECG-SSL in-domain (AUROC +1.9% for mortality and +4.0% for heart failure) and on external populations in HEEDB-Boston (+5.6% for mortality +10.3% for heart failure) and HEEDB-Atlanta (+6.9% for mortality +11.0% for heart failure) while using an encoder 41 times smaller and a fraction of the pretraining data. A matched ablation showed that patient-temporal pairing improved external mortality and heart failure AUROC over generic self-supervision by 7.0% and 9.4% on HEEDB-Boston and 8.9% and 9.3% on HEEDB-Atlanta. These findings indicate that pretraining-objective design greatly influences downstream transfer alongside model and data scale, and that in-domain performance alone is insufficient to establish the clinical generalisability of ECG foundation representations.

AI.tldr: PACE-ECG pretrains an ECG encoder with contrastive learning across temporally neighbouring recordings from the same patient, plus clinically guided multitask supervision. Its frozen representations transfer better than DeepECG-SSL to post-MI mortality and heart failure prediction in external cohorts, with an encoder 41 times smaller.
AI.motivation: Physiological foundation models are usually evaluated in-domain, and their ability to transfer to longitudinal clinical prognosis across healthcare systems is uncertain.
AI.method: Contrastive learning pairs temporally neighbouring recordings from the same patient, combined with clinically guided multitask supervision. Frozen representations are evaluated on post-MI all-cause mortality and incident heart failure prediction in MIMIC-IV and two external HEEDB cohorts, against DeepECG-SSL and two control baselines.
AI.result: The model beats DeepECG-SSL in-domain (AUROC +1.9% for mortality, +4.0% for heart failure) and externally in HEEDB-Boston (+5.6% and +10.3%) and HEEDB-Atlanta (+6.9% and +11.0%), using an encoder 41 times smaller and less pretraining data. Patient-temporal pairing improves external AUROC over generic self-supervision by 7.0% and 9.4% on HEEDB-Boston and 8.9% and 9.3% on HEEDB-Atlanta.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining objective design strongly affects downstream transfer, and in-domain performance alone is insufficient to establish the clinical generalisability of ECG foundation representations.

title: AMSchem: Automated Schematic Visualization of AMS Circuits via Verifiable Agentic Generation
summary: For decades, the netlist-to-schematic gap has remained a persistent challenge in design automation, especially for analog and mixed-signal (AMS) circuits. Netlists encode connectivity, not visual presentation, making their manual conversion into readable schematics time-consuming and dependent on expert conventions. The same gap leaves LLM-based design tools without structured visual feedback, forcing them to iterate on circuits they cannot see. We present AMSchem, a training-free, verifier-guided agentic framework that automatically generates human-readable schematics from AMS netlists. AMSchem separates circuit-aware visual planning (DrawingIntent) from executable schematic geometry (SchematicIR), and applies localized visual feedback with bounded, revalidated repair patches. Deterministic validators enforce device preservation, pin-net consistency, and geometric correctness throughout. For evaluation, we construct AMSchem-Bench comprising 64 circuits of 12 types. On the 40-circuit schematic subset, AMSchem with gpt-5.5 achieves 85.0\% validity (vs. 32.5\% direct generation). When integrated as a visual feedback module in LLM-based analog design, AMSchem resolves all 13 previously failed cases from AnalogCoder benchmark across five models, substantially improving the success rate. Our dataset and benchmark are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: AMSchem is a training-free, verifier-guided agent that turns AMS netlists into readable schematics by separating circuit-aware visual planning from executable schematic geometry, with deterministic validators. Its visual feedback also lets LLM-based analog design resolve all 13 previously failed AnalogCoder cases.
AI.motivation: Netlists encode connectivity rather than visual presentation, so converting them into readable schematics is slow and depends on expert conventions. LLM-based design tools also lack visual feedback on the circuits they generate.
AI.method: AMSchem separates circuit-aware visual planning (DrawingIntent) from executable schematic geometry (SchematicIR), and applies localised visual feedback with bounded, revalidated repair patches. Deterministic validators enforce device preservation, pin-net consistency and geometric correctness. The authors also build AMSchem-Bench with 64 circuits of 12 types.
AI.result: On a 40-circuit schematic subset, AMSchem with gpt-5.5 reaches 85.0% validity versus 32.5% for direct generation. As a visual feedback module in LLM-based analog design, it resolves all 13 previously failed AnalogCoder cases across five models.
AI.conclusion: Verifier-guided visual feedback can make schematic generation reliable and gives LLM design tools the visual feedback they otherwise lack, and the dataset and benchmark are released.

title: DForkTree: Accelerating Speculative Decoding with Fork-Aware Block Diffusion Draft Trees
comment: 20 pages, 13 figures, 13 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Speculative decoding speeds up language models by letting a lightweight drafter propose several future tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Block diffusion drafters such as DFlash draft a whole block in one forward pass, and DDTree builds a draft tree from their per-position distributions. Each of these distributions assumes that the drafter's own most likely continuation is correct. A tree, however, gains over a chain only on branches that leave this continuation, where the drafter's top-1 accuracy drops from 89% to 18% and its candidate lists miss the right token far more often. When re-run from the fork token, the same drafter is usually correct, so the errors come from the prefix that the distributions condition on rather than from what the drafter knows. We introduce DForkTree, a training-free method that re-anchors each branch on its own tokens. DForkTree adds n-gram statistics from the target model's own outputs to the drafter's scores as pointwise mutual information, weights them more after the fork, and builds the optimal tree under these scores exactly on the GPU. On Qwen3.5-4B and 9B, with all tree methods sharing one drafter, tree pipeline and verifier, DForkTree is the fastest tree method on every benchmark. It is up to 41.5% faster than DFlash and 15.1% faster than DDTree in the same setting, with average speedups of up to 4.75x over autoregressive decoding.

AI.tldr: DForkTree is a training-free speculative decoding method that re-anchors each draft branch on its own tokens by adding target-model n-gram statistics as pointwise mutual information, then builds the optimal tree exactly on the GPU. It is the fastest tree method tested on Qwen3.5-4B and 9B, up to 41.5% faster than DFlash.
AI.motivation: Block diffusion drafters condition every branch on the drafter's most likely continuation, but the drafter's top-1 accuracy drops from 89% to 18% off that continuation, and the errors come from the conditioning prefix rather than from the drafter's knowledge.
AI.method: The method adds n-gram statistics from the target model's outputs to the drafter's scores as pointwise mutual information, weights them more after the fork point, and builds the optimal tree under these scores exactly on the GPU.
AI.result: With all tree methods sharing one drafter, tree pipeline and verifier, DForkTree is the fastest tree method on every benchmark on Qwen3.5-4B and 9B. It is up to 41.5% faster than DFlash and 15.1% faster than DDTree, with average speedups up to 4.75x over autoregressive decoding.
AI.conclusion: Re-anchoring draft scores on branch-specific context improves tree-based speculative decoding without any training.

title: TANSAR: Editable and Attributable Correlation Matrix Memories under Correlated Keys, with Rule-Constrained Multi-Hop Knowledge Editing
summary: Correlation Matrix Memories (CMMs) store associations as sums of rank-one outer products, providing closed-form addressability, exact deletion, and linear attribution. While classical analyses assume random, orthogonal keys, semantic encoders produce correlated representations. We analyse CMMs under correlated keys using frame-theoretic coherence: (i) capacity bounds yielding an encoder-independent limit $n \le d(1+\varepsilon^2)$ for mean squared crosstalk $\varepsilon^2$; (ii) an exact characterisation of the collateral effect of deleting an association, guaranteeing that deletion never invalidates certified associations; and (iii) a geometric transparency bound demonstrating why attribution requires candidate sets of centred keys. On this basis, we introduce Topology-Aware Neuro-Symbolic Associative Retrieval (TANSAR). TANSAR traverses a directed acyclic association graph, prunes invalid paths via sound ground Horn constraints, and injects a representation derived strictly from the verified path into the residual stream of a frozen language model, guarded by a Clopper--Pearson selective-risk gate. Controlled experiments confirm all theoretical bounds. In multi-hop knowledge editing, Horn pruning reduces answer contradictions from 25.1% to 0.5%, whereas Hopfield retrieval incurs 24% contradictions when stale associations remain stored (and 0% if stale associations are removed). An end-to-end edit transaction requires 13.6 ms on a standard CPU and 2.37 ms on GPU. The symbolic component matches gold labels across all 600 ProofWriter theories and achieves 94.0% agreement on FOLIO, demonstrating sound and efficient multi-hop associative retrieval with exact unlearning.

AI.tldr: TANSAR is a neuro-symbolic associative retrieval method built on correlation matrix memories. It traverses a Horn-constrained association graph and injects verified facts into a frozen language model, reducing multi-hop editing contradictions from 25.1% to 0.5%, and its analysis gives capacity bounds and exact deletion guarantees under correlated keys.
AI.motivation: Classical analyses of correlation matrix memories assume random orthogonal keys, but semantic encoders produce correlated representations, and knowledge editing needs retrieval that stays editable and attributable.
AI.method: Frame-theoretic coherence analysis gives capacity bounds under correlated keys, an exact characterisation of the collateral effect of deleting an association, and a geometric transparency bound. TANSAR traverses a directed acyclic association graph, prunes invalid paths with sound ground Horn constraints, and injects a representation derived from the verified path into a frozen language model's residual stream, guarded by a Clopper-Pearson selective-risk gate.
AI.result: Horn pruning reduces multi-hop answer contradictions from 25.1% to 0.5%, whereas Hopfield retrieval has 24% contradictions when stale associations remain stored. An edit transaction takes 13.6 ms on CPU and 2.37 ms on GPU. The symbolic component matches gold labels on all 600 ProofWriter theories and reaches 94.0% agreement on FOLIO.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers sound and efficient multi-hop associative retrieval with exact unlearning, and controlled experiments confirm the theoretical bounds.

title: Detecting Shadow AI: Unsanctioned LLM Agents on Enterprise Endpoints: A Taxonomy, an Open Detector and a Controlled Evaluation
comment: 55 pages, 13 figures, 14 tables. Code, catalog and evaluation bench: this https URL
summary: Shadow IT, the use of technology that the IT organisation has not approved, is a long-standing governance problem. We argue that autonomous AI agents can make it grow much faster: agents make building tools nearly free, act with their user's privileges, and leave behind scripts, automations and MCP servers that are themselves unsanctioned. A simple compounding model shows that, under its assumptions, shadow IT grows exponentially once agentic artifacts reproduce faster than the organisation retires them; retiring them starts with detecting them. We then ask whether unsanctioned agents can be detected on Windows endpoints. We propose a taxonomy of nine classes of agents and six layers of endpoint footprint, and argue that rules based only on the structure of processes and connections cannot separate an agent from its behavioural twin, the same program talking to a non-AI service. We present Agent Detector, an open-source Windows detector that anchors behaviour to the identity of the remote service and correlates it with configuration, installation and execution history, using a catalog of 39 tools and 184 LLM endpoint entries; it informs users through a notice they must acknowledge instead of blocking. On a controlled bench of 12 synthetic agents, 3 AI components and 9 benign workloads, repeated 5 times on one workstation, two behavioural rules flagged every behavioural twin, while Agent Detector flagged none and detected every agent in the majority of runs. Its limits are temporal: a connection to a provider behind a shared content-delivery network is attributable only while the DNS cache holds the provider's name, one to five minutes, and an intermittent agent was seen by about one scan in three. A scan costs about 154 ms. The bench is too small to rank detectors; it maps what each kind of evidence can see: unsanctioned agents can be partly detected, and not by behaviour alone.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that autonomous AI agents accelerate shadow IT, proposes a nine-class agent taxonomy, and presents Agent Detector, an open-source Windows endpoint detector that identifies agents by the identity of the remote service they contact. On a controlled 12-agent bench it flagged no behavioural twins, while detecting every agent in most runs.
AI.motivation: Shadow IT is a long-standing governance problem, and agents make building tools nearly free and act with users' privileges, so unsanctioned artifacts can grow faster than organisations retire them. Process and connection structure alone cannot separate an agent from a benign program talking to a non-AI service.
AI.method: Agent Detector anchors behaviour to the identity of the remote service and correlates it with configuration, installation and execution history, using a catalogue of 39 tools and 184 LLM endpoint entries. It notifies users through an acknowledged notice rather than blocking. The bench has 12 synthetic agents, 3 AI components and 9 benign workloads, repeated five times on one workstation.
AI.result: Two behavioural rules flagged every behavioural twin, while Agent Detector flagged none and detected every agent in most runs. Its attribution holds only while the DNS cache keeps the provider name, one to five minutes, and an intermittent agent was seen in about one scan in three. A scan costs about 154 ms.
AI.conclusion: Unsanctioned agents can be partly detected, and not by behaviour alone. The bench is too small to rank detectors but maps what each kind of evidence can see.

title: Reconstructing hourly traffic on every street of a capital from a sparse counting network: a graph neural network applied to Paris
summary: Micro-scale air quality models require hourly traffic data on every road segment, whereas permanent counters cover only a small part of the network. A graph neural network (GNN) was developed to reconstruct hourly traffic flows on the 32,163 road segments of Paris intra-muros from the 1,573 segments equipped with a counter (4.9%). The model adapts the Graph Neural Network for Urban Interpolation (GNNUI) to a real, sparse counting network. Flows are decoded on the edges of the junction graph (one edge per segment, both directions summed), a traffic climatology serves as an offset in a zero-inflated negative-binomial likelihood, and training proceeds by masking counters. Eight-fold spatial cross-validation, with counters sharing a published series merged before splitting, distinguishes interpolation at a withheld counter in an instrumented district (R${}^2$ = 0.89, error of a quarter of the mean flow) from extrapolation to a district without counters (R${}^2$ = 0.74, a third of the mean flow). These scores hold on main axes where counters are located, while relative errors are about 50% on the few counted local streets. Ablations show that the climatology offset tends to help extrapolation. Road attributes, time cycles and the live state of the counting network matter most, while weather inputs have no significant effect. The masking rate is the only inherited hyperparameter with a clear effect.
