However, our preliminary analysis reveals two key challenges: (i) failures at different stages of skill evolution and downstream execution can produce indistinguishable outcomes, providing little guidance for targeted poisoned-task updates; and (ii) unsuccessful updates may undermine earlier progress, while simply discarding them may lead to repeated ineffective updates. To address these challenges, we propose BadEvolve, a failure-aware task-poisoning framework against self-evolving LLM agents. BadEvolve diagnoses attack failures across four stages, i.e., Induction, Activation, Following, and Effect, and directs updates toward the failing stage. It further employs rollback to preserve earlier progress and failure memory to avoid repeating ineffective updates. Extensive experiments across diverse self-evolution frameworks, benchmarks, and backbone LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of BadEvolve. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: BadEvolve is a task-level backdoor attack that poisons the evolution tasks of self-evolving LLM agents, so the agent implants backdoors into its own skills. It diagnoses failures across four stages and uses rollback and failure memory to optimize the poisoned tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing skill backdoor attacks assume direct manipulation of a victim's skills, which is impractical when skills are built internally by a trusted evolver. Iterative optimization of poisoned tasks faces indistinguishable failures across stages and wasted or regressing updates.
AI.method: BadEvolve diagnoses attack failures across four stages (Induction, Activation, Following and Effect), directs updates toward the failing stage, uses rollback to preserve earlier progress, and keeps failure memory to avoid repeating ineffective updates.
AI.result: The abstract reports that experiments across diverse self-evolution frameworks, benchmarks and backbone LLMs demonstrate the method's effectiveness, without giving specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Persistent skill evolution creates a new attack surface in which an attacker who controls only the evolution tasks can implant backdoors into an agent's skills.

title: Pixels over Symbols: Sensory Realism Improves Behavioral Alignment in Models of Cognition
summary: Computational models of cognition have traditionally relied on abstract symbolic inputs that approximate sensory experiences with simplified vector representations. This simplification reflects historical computational constraints and a long-held assumption that the details of sensory realism are incidental to the study of cognitive processes. Recent advances have enabled the development of sensory-realistic models capable of performing diverse cognitive tasks, yet whether sensory realism meaningfully shapes cognition has not been formally established. We address this gap through a large-scale empirical comparison of abstract and sensory-realistic neural network models trained on a battery of memory-dependent decision-making tasks. Our results show that sensory-realistic models mirror human behavioral response patterns significantly more than their abstract counterparts, though a substantial gap to human internal behavioral consistency remains even for the best tested models. By analyzing the internal dynamics of these systems, we find that the learned recurrent weights are not the main source of this divergence. In fact, frozen abstract-trained weights driven by sensory-realistic inputs recover the human consistency of sensory-realistic models. The resulting dynamics are also within the seed-to-seed variability of sensory-realistic models. Together, our findings argue that across a broad set of visual working-memory tasks, sensory realism accounts for a substantial portion of the model-human behavioral agreement, more than the choice of sequence architecture and comparable to the choice of vision encoder. These results suggest that findings obtained from abstract task models in neuroscience should be more carefully interpreted in light of their potential behavioral limitations.

AI.tldr: Sensory-realistic neural network models match human behavior on memory-dependent visual decision tasks significantly better than abstract symbolic-input models. Much of the model-human agreement comes from sensory realism itself rather than from the recurrent weights.
AI.motivation: Cognitive models have usually used abstract symbolic inputs, on the untested assumption that sensory realism is incidental to cognitive processes. Whether it shapes cognition had not been formally established.
AI.method: A large-scale comparison of abstract and sensory-realistic neural network models trained on a battery of memory-dependent decision-making tasks, with analysis of internal dynamics, including frozen abstract-trained recurrent weights driven by sensory-realistic inputs.
AI.result: Sensory-realistic models mirror human behavioral response patterns significantly more than abstract counterparts, though a substantial gap to human internal consistency remains even for the best models. Frozen abstract-trained weights with sensory-realistic inputs recover the human consistency of sensory-realistic models, and the dynamics lie within seed-to-seed variability.
AI.conclusion: Across visual working-memory tasks, sensory realism accounts for a substantial share of model-human agreement, more than the choice of sequence architecture and comparable to the choice of vision encoder, so abstract task models in neuroscience should be interpreted with their behavioral limitations in mind.

title: An Improved Algorithm for Quantified Boolean Formulas
summary: Quantified Boolean formula (QBF), the quantified version of Boolean satisfiability (SAT), is a fundamental problem in constraint solving. Due to the $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete nature of QBF, designing theoretically efficient QBF algorithms is much harder and receives less attention in academia. In this work, we present a new algorithm based on memoized search, which solves QBF with $n$ variables and $m$ clauses in $1.685^m\cdot\text{poly}(n)$ time and space. This is the first improvement over the $1.709^m\cdot\text{poly}(n)$ bound by Williams in over 20 years. Our technique is based on the minimum vertex cover of the conflict graphs, which was proposed to study the parameterized complexity of SAT. We extend this idea to QBF and further show that QBF is slicewise polynomial-time solvable using this parameter.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a memoized-search algorithm for Quantified Boolean Formulas (QBF) running in 1.685^m times poly(n) time and space for n variables and m clauses. This improves the 1.709^m bound of Williams, the first improvement in over 20 years.
AI.motivation: QBF is PSPACE-complete, which makes theoretically efficient algorithms hard to design and less studied than SAT.
AI.method: The algorithm is based on memoized search and uses the minimum vertex cover of conflict graphs, a parameter previously used to study the parameterized complexity of SAT, extended to QBF.
AI.result: The running time is 1.685^m times poly(n), improving on 1.709^m. The authors also show that QBF is slicewise polynomial-time solvable using this parameter.
AI.conclusion: The conflict-graph vertex cover parameter gives a better exponential-time bound for QBF and a slicewise polynomial-time characterization.

title: REINS: A Self-Evolving Agent Harness for Real-Time Trajectory Planning
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Main Track). 36 pages, 7 figures, 20 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Agent harnesses -- runtime scaffolds that wrap an LLM's reasoning loop with tool dispatch, verification, and persistent memory -- have become the standard substrate for deploying LLMs as autonomous agents, as demonstrated by Claude Code and Codex in software engineering. In trajectory planning, however, this paradigm has not taken hold: existing LLM-based trajectory planning methods either keep the LLM in the decision loop, exceeding the millisecond-level control budget, or offload it to offline rules or training-time supervision -- leaving the runtime planner non-evolving. Intermediate hybrids still lack the verification-and-consolidation loop that makes harnesses reliable. We ask: what runtime harness would let an LLM planner meet real-time constraints while self-evolving into a deployable one? We propose REINS, a harness built on three LLM-planner couplings: LLM outputs are (i) grounded to a learned variable-level dynamics model, (ii) verified via calibrated predicates and forward rollout, and (iii) consolidated into an indexed rule memory that serves future scenes in O(log n) without re-invoking the LLM. The harness closes a self-evolution loop: familiar scenes resolve by memory lookup; novel scenes invoke the LLM, whose verified outputs enrich the memory. Without modifying LLM weights, REINS attains 98%+ compliance, nearly 50% collision reduction, and 1.9-4.6 ms latency on simulated and real-world benchmarks at the tactical decision layer, with LLM invocation rate monotonically declining as memory matures. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: REINS is a runtime agent harness for real-time trajectory planning that keeps an LLM planner out of the millisecond control loop and lets it self-evolve through grounding, verification and a rule memory. It reaches 98%+ compliance and nearly 50% collision reduction with 1.9 to 4.6 ms latency.
AI.motivation: LLM trajectory planners either stay in the decision loop, exceeding millisecond control budgets, or are offloaded to offline rules or training-time supervision, leaving the runtime planner non-evolving. Existing hybrids lack a verification-and-consolidation loop.
AI.method: REINS couples the LLM planner in three ways: outputs are grounded to a learned variable-level dynamics model, verified via calibrated predicates and forward rollout, and consolidated into an indexed rule memory that serves future scenes in O(log n) without re-invoking the LLM. Familiar scenes are resolved by memory lookup, while novel scenes invoke the LLM, whose verified outputs enrich the memory.
AI.result: Without modifying LLM weights, REINS attains 98%+ compliance, nearly 50% collision reduction and 1.9 to 4.6 ms latency on simulated and real-world benchmarks at the tactical decision layer. The LLM invocation rate declines monotonically as memory matures.
AI.conclusion: The harness shows that an LLM planner can meet real-time constraints while self-evolving into a deployable planner, without updating LLM weights.

title: Mirage: Provable Defense Against LLM KV Cache Timing Side Channels with Topology-Aware Isolation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as shared multi-tenant services, relying on advanced optimizations like KV cache and prefix sharing to improve throughput and reduce latency. However, these optimizations introduce a critical vulnerability: attackers can exploit time-to-first-token (TTFT) variations between KV cache hits and misses to infer sensitive prompt tokens via prefix-matching side-channel attacks. Existing defenses indiscriminately restrict cross-tenant cache sharing, which incurs prohibitive performance overhead and negates the fundamental efficiency benefits of the KV cache. We propose Mirage, a topology-aware emission obfuscation framework that provably bounds timing leakage without sacrificing the performance gains of cache sharing. Instead of stalling the GPU or forcing redundant recomputations, Mirage delays token emission at the gateway so the attacker observes a natural cache miss distribution, while the GPU seamlessly continues serving other requests at full speed. Mirage uses a Privacy Odometer that persistently tracks the topological novelty of prefix fan-out expansions to distinguish aggressive probing from benign traffic. Once a prefix exceeds a safety threshold, Mirage engages a two-phase policy that uses a dynamic estimator to pad the TTFT to a calibrated cache-miss baseline. On a 500-sample public corpus across three models, Mirage suppresses the timing side-channel to near the random-guessing floor, while maintaining a significantly lower TTFT than defense baselines. We further show that Mirage withstands a strong adaptive adversary and the same principle carries over to semantic caching layers.

AI.tldr: Mirage defends LLM KV-cache sharing against timing side channels by delaying token emission at the gateway, so an attacker sees a natural cache-miss timing distribution without stalling the GPU. It suppresses the leak to near the random-guessing floor while keeping lower time-to-first-token than defense baselines.
AI.motivation: Cache hits and misses change time-to-first-token (TTFT), letting attackers infer prompt tokens via prefix-matching side channels. Existing defenses restrict cross-tenant cache sharing, which costs heavy performance and removes the benefit of the KV cache.
AI.method: Mirage is a topology-aware emission obfuscation framework. A Privacy Odometer tracks the topological novelty of prefix fan-out expansions to separate aggressive probing from benign traffic. Once a prefix exceeds a safety threshold, a two-phase policy uses a dynamic estimator to pad TTFT to a calibrated cache-miss baseline.
AI.result: On a 500-sample public corpus across three models, Mirage suppresses the timing side channel to near the random-guessing floor while keeping significantly lower TTFT than defense baselines. It withstands a strong adaptive adversary, and the principle extends to semantic caching layers.
AI.conclusion: Provable bounds on timing leakage are achievable without giving up the performance benefits of cache sharing in multi-tenant LLM serving.

title: RTLREX: LLM-Guided Framework for Exact High-Level RTL Recovery
summary: Hardware designs may be available only as gate-level netlists or input-output descriptions when the original register-transfer-level (RTL) design and documentation are not accessible. Low-level representations obscure word-level computation and its finite-width behavior. Recovering high-level RTL from such representations therefore helps engineers understand a circuit's functionality and enables RTL rewriting and resynthesis. A plausible function model is also insufficient unless the generated RTL is equivalent to the original circuit for all input combinations. In this paper, we present RTLREX, a large language model (LLM)-guided framework that coordinates domain-specific tools for function recovery, RTL generation, independent verification, and cost-guided rewriting. Independent verification establishes equivalence between the recovered RTL and the original circuit. The LLM uses tool feedback to select further analyses, revise candidate RTL, and propose syntax-cost reductions. Experiments on 30 benchmarks from Problem A of the ICCAD 2022 CAD Contest show that RTLREX recovers equivalent high-level RTL for all benchmarks, surpassing the state-of-the-art method WolFEx in recovery coverage. On benchmarks recovered by both methods, RTLREX reduces mean syntax cost by 20.5% relative to WolFEx. On complete truth-table benchmarks from the IWLS 2026 Contest, our framework reduces mean syntax cost by 95.7% relative to an LLM agent baseline on the benchmarks validated by both methods.

AI.tldr: RTLREX is an LLM-guided framework that recovers high-level RTL from gate-level netlists or input-output descriptions, with independent verification establishing equivalence to the original circuit. It recovers equivalent RTL for all 30 ICCAD 2022 benchmarks and beats WolFEx in recovery coverage.
AI.motivation: Gate-level netlists obscure word-level computation and finite-width behavior, and a plausible function model is insufficient unless the generated RTL is exactly equivalent to the original circuit for all inputs.
AI.method: An LLM coordinates domain-specific tools for function recovery, RTL generation, independent verification and cost-guided rewriting. Tool feedback guides the LLM in selecting analyses, revising candidate RTL and proposing syntax-cost reductions.
AI.result: On 30 benchmarks from Problem A of the ICCAD 2022 CAD Contest, RTLREX recovers equivalent high-level RTL for all benchmarks and surpasses WolFEx in recovery coverage. On benchmarks both methods recovered, mean syntax cost falls 20.5% relative to WolFEx. On IWLS 2026 complete truth-table benchmarks, mean syntax cost falls 95.7% relative to an LLM agent baseline on benchmarks validated by both methods.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLM guidance with independent verification and tool feedback yields exact, lower-cost high-level RTL recovery from low-level representations.

title: Trained, Frozen, or Absent: Identifying What a Quantum Layer Contributes to Cross-Sectional Equity Ranking
summary: Hybrid quantumclassical models are increasingly proposed for nancial prediction, but reported gains are rarely separated from the classical components around them. We study a hybrid quantum temporal convolutional network for daily cross-sectional ranking of 2000 Tokyo Stock Exchange equities under a protocol built to make the quantum contribution identiable: six conditions (circuit trained, frozen or absent, a parameter-matched classical surrogate, and the circuit alone, trained or frozen) through one code path; four walk-forward folds with ve seeds; bootstrap intervals, Deated Sharpe Ratios, backtest-overtting probabilities and family-wise error control; ve classical baselines including a gradient-boosted tree; and a locked holdout. On 500 out-of-sample days two one-sided tests place the trained-versus-frozen dierence inside 0.03 annualised Sharpe (p = 0.0055, minimum detectable eect 0.02): the circuit is equivalent to a frozen one, not merely indistinguishable from it. With the circuit as the head's only input the two are equivalent inside 0.25; against the network with no circuit the design resolves only 0.50. No condition is distinguishable from zero (best De-ated Sharpe Ratio 0.17). The holdout reproduces the ablation on a protable window, and 2000 US equities reproduce it where every condition loses money.

AI.tldr: A controlled protocol finds that a hybrid quantum temporal convolutional network's trained quantum circuit is statistically equivalent to a frozen one for daily cross-sectional ranking of 2000 Tokyo Stock Exchange equities. No condition is distinguishable from zero Sharpe ratio.
AI.motivation: Reported gains of hybrid quantum-classical financial models are rarely separated from the classical components around them, so the quantum contribution is hard to identify.
AI.method: Six conditions (circuit trained, frozen or absent; a parameter-matched classical surrogate; and the circuit alone, trained or frozen) run through one code path, with four walk-forward folds, five seeds, bootstrap intervals, Deflated Sharpe Ratios, backtest-overfitting probabilities, family-wise error control, five classical baselines including a gradient-boosted tree, and a locked holdout.
AI.result: On 500 out-of-sample days, two one-sided tests place the trained-versus-frozen difference within 0.03 annualized Sharpe (p = 0.0055, minimum detectable effect 0.02). With the circuit as the head's only input the two are equivalent within 0.25, and against the network with no circuit the design resolves only 0.50. The best Deflated Sharpe Ratio is 0.17, so no condition is distinguishable from zero. The holdout reproduces the ablation on a profitable window, and 2000 US equities reproduce it where every condition loses money.
AI.conclusion: The quantum layer adds no detectable contribution beyond a frozen circuit in this setting, so reported hybrid-model gains need component-level ablation before attribution.

title: A Geometry-Guided Feature-Space Framework for Interpretable Unsupervised 4D-STEM Analysis of Complex Multiphase Materials
summary: Rapid, high-fidelity analysis of four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) datasets from heterogeneous materials remains challenging because coexisting phases, orientation variants, local strain gradients, and intrinsic TEM thin-foil effects produce complex, overlapping diffraction signatures. Here, we present a machine-learning (ML) framework that combines physics-informed geometric descriptors with weighted high-dimensional embeddings to identify latent structural patterns with minimal prior knowledge. By constructing a regularized descriptor space before embedding and density-based clustering, the method improves cluster stability, suppresses noise-driven fragmentation, and reduces sensitivity to embedding hyperparameters. Spatial weighting produced the largest stability gain, increasing median cluster persistence from 0.04 to 0.55 while reducing the noise fraction from approximately 22% to 0%. Rotation weighting increased DBCV from 0.80 to 0.92, although the noise fraction rose from 0.2% to 1.0%, highlighting a trade-off between improved density separation and noise rejection. We validate the framework on two benchmark systems: Si/Si$_x$Ge$_{1-x}$ epitaxial layers with continuous lattice variation and deformation, and multiphase Ti-Nb alloys containing distinct phases and orientation variants. Comparisons with a pretrained vanilla autoencoder and model-free pattern vectorization show that the physics-informed geometric descriptor provides higher cluster fidelity, greater interpretability, and substantially lower dimensionality.

AI.tldr: A machine-learning framework for 4D-STEM analysis combines physics-informed geometric descriptors with weighted high-dimensional embeddings and density-based clustering to find phases and orientation variants without much prior knowledge. Spatial weighting raised median cluster persistence from 0.04 to 0.55 and cut the noise fraction from about 22% to 0%.
AI.motivation: Diffraction patterns from heterogeneous materials overlap because of coexisting phases, orientation variants, strain gradients and thin-foil effects, which makes unsupervised analysis of 4D-STEM data difficult.
AI.method: The framework builds a regularized, physics-informed geometric descriptor space before embedding and density-based clustering, with spatial and rotation weighting. It is validated on Si/SixGe1-x epitaxial layers and multiphase Ti-Nb alloys and compared with a pretrained vanilla autoencoder and model-free pattern vectorization.
AI.result: Spatial weighting raised median cluster persistence from 0.04 to 0.55 and reduced the noise fraction from about 22% to 0%. Rotation weighting raised DBCV from 0.80 to 0.92 but raised the noise fraction from 0.2% to 1.0%, a trade-off between density separation and noise rejection.
AI.conclusion: The physics-informed geometric descriptor gives higher cluster fidelity, greater interpretability and substantially lower dimensionality than the autoencoder and pattern-vectorization baselines.

title: Hybrid Source Code Change Impact Analysis
summary: Change impact analysis (CIA) helps developers identify code entities impacted by their initial changes. While several approaches for CIA were proposed, they still struggle with either low precision or low recall, thereby increasing manual effort for developers to verify the results. Furthermore, limitations in the used datasets and experimental setups can bias the results reported by many CIA approaches. In this paper, we first address the dataset limitations by manually labeling 1,931 changed code entities stemming from 263 commits of 22 open-source Java projects. Next, we introduce two variants of katIA, our code change impact analysis approach that combines static impact analysis with the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). The first variant uses a single prompt (katIA-SP) for refining an initial static impact set while the second variant uses three specialized agents (katIA-MA). The evaluation with our curated dataset shows that katIA-SP with Gemini 2.5 Flash achieved an F1-score of 22.4% when matching impacted entities by their fully qualified names (FQN) and 27.0% when matching them by their class and entity names (CE). The latter shows an improvement of 2.0 percentage points over the state-of-the-art. This score is further improved by katIA-MA which, using Gemini 2.5 Flash, yields an FQN-matching F1-score of 29.1% and a CE-matching F1-score of 33.3%. While these improvements come at the cost of increased median generation time from 0.570 s to 11.214 s and median token usage from 1,235 to 6,462 tokens, the improved performance justifies the additional cost. The comparison of three LLMs using katIA-SP finds that Gemini 2.5 Flash is the most consistent model. These results indicate that combining static impact analysis with LLM-based refinement, particularly with the multi-agent variant, can improve code change impact analysis.

AI.tldr: katIA combines static change impact analysis with LLMs, in a single-prompt variant and a three-agent variant, to refine impacted code entities. On a newly labeled dataset of 1,931 entities from 263 commits in 22 Java projects, the multi-agent variant reaches F1 of 29.1% (FQN matching) and 33.3% (class and entity name matching).
AI.motivation: Existing change impact analysis approaches have low precision or low recall, and limitations in datasets and setups can bias reported results.
AI.method: The authors manually label 1,931 changed code entities from 263 commits of 22 open-source Java projects to address dataset limitations. katIA-SP uses a single prompt to refine an initial static impact set, and katIA-MA uses three specialized agents. Gemini 2.5 Flash is the main model, and three LLMs are compared under katIA-SP.
AI.result: katIA-SP with Gemini 2.5 Flash reaches F1 of 22.4% (FQN) and 27.0% (CE), a 2.0 percentage point gain over the state of the art on CE. katIA-MA reaches 29.1% (FQN) and 33.3% (CE). Median generation time rises from 0.570 s to 11.214 s and median token usage from 1,235 to 6,462. Gemini 2.5 Flash is the most consistent of the three models.
AI.conclusion: Combining static impact analysis with LLM refinement, especially in the multi-agent form, improves change impact analysis, and the authors judge the added cost justified by the gains.

title: Slim Foundation Models for Latency-Critical Recommendation Serving
summary: Click-through rate (CTR) prediction is a core component of recommendation and advertising systems. Large language models (LLMs) offer rich semantic priors that improve prediction quality, particularly in cold-start and long-tail settings. Injecting a full-scale LLM into a CTR pipeline is, however, prohibitively expensive at inference time: existing LLM-enhanced CTR methods avoid this cost by caching LLM outputs offline rather than serving the LLM online. We propose a resource-efficient pipeline, SlimFM, that makes online LLM-based semantic modeling practical: (1) dependency-aware structured pruning compresses LLaMA3-8B by 44% to a 4.5B-parameter backbone; (2) LoRA-based field-aware fine-tuning trains the pruned model to produce discriminative field-level semantic embeddings from lightweight textual prompts; (3) a semantic-guided fusion module injects these embeddings into the feature interactions of a conventional CTR model. Across four datasets and six CTR backbones, SlimFM retains over 99% of uncompressed-model accuracy while reducing inference latency by up to 3.4x relative to existing LLM-enhanced baselines.

AI.tldr: SlimFM makes LLM-based semantic modeling practical for CTR prediction by pruning LLaMA3-8B by 44% to a 4.5B backbone and fine-tuning it to produce field-level embeddings online. It keeps over 99% of uncompressed accuracy and cuts inference latency by up to 3.4x relative to LLM-enhanced baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs improve CTR prediction in cold-start and long-tail settings, but serving a full-scale LLM online is prohibitively expensive, and existing methods cache LLM outputs offline instead.
AI.method: Dependency-aware structured pruning compresses LLaMA3-8B by 44%. LoRA-based field-aware fine-tuning trains the pruned model to produce discriminative field-level semantic embeddings from lightweight prompts. A semantic-guided fusion module injects these embeddings into a conventional CTR model's feature interactions.
AI.result: Across four datasets and six CTR backbones, SlimFM retains over 99% of uncompressed-model accuracy and reduces inference latency by up to 3.4x relative to existing LLM-enhanced baselines.
AI.conclusion: Online LLM semantic modeling can be made practical for latency-critical recommendation serving through compression and fine-tuning without large accuracy loss.

title: Advancements in Cloud-Native Systems: A Systematic Mapping Study of Reliability and Scalability across Cloud-Native, Edge-Native and AI-Enabled Systems
summary: Cloud-native systems now extend to the network edge and host artificial-intelligence (AI) workloads, including AI agents, but evidence on their reliability and scalability is scattered and uneven. We report a PRISMA 2020 systematic mapping study with an evidence-graded synthesis. Five logged OpenAlex searches on 11 October 2026 covered cloud-native systems, edge AI, agentic AI for operations, reliability of agentic applications and physical AI; 189 records from an earlier exploratory search were added separately. After 301 duplicate removals and an automated peer-review venue rule, 4,611 records were screened against written criteria and a five-level relevance scale. The review includes 1,794 primary studies from 2017-2026 and 95 secondary studies, with every decision released in Dataset S1. Each primary study was assigned to a 13-category taxonomy and graded as simulation, prototype or testbed, production data, production deployment, or not determinable from the abstract. Of 1,003 studies with a determinable level, 66.2% used prototypes or testbeds, 18.0% simulations and 15.8% production data or deployments. A 93-study synthesis core, appraised from indexed abstracts, shows production deployments of cascading-failure prevention, trace- and graph-based root-cause analysis and predictive autoscaling, and production-trace evaluations of cold-start mitigation. Edge reliability and physical AI rely mainly on simulations and testbeds. AI-agent reliability uses tool-grounded diagnosis, explicit safety properties, trace-driven repair and workload-aware scheduling, while empirical studies show that agent frameworks remain fragile. Conclusions are limited to the documented corpus. The principal gaps are production evidence for edge-native systems, shared resilience benchmarks and dependable agentic operations.

AI.tldr: A PRISMA 2020 systematic mapping study of 1,794 primary studies and 95 secondary studies finds that cloud-native, edge-native and AI-enabled systems rely mostly on prototypes, testbeds and simulations for reliability and scalability. Production evidence is concentrated in cascading-failure prevention, root-cause analysis and predictive autoscaling.
AI.motivation: Evidence on the reliability and scalability of cloud-native systems that extend to the edge and host AI workloads, including AI agents, is scattered and uneven.
AI.method: Five logged OpenAlex searches, plus 189 records from an earlier exploratory search, were screened against written criteria; 4,611 records were screened after 301 duplicate removals and an automated peer-review venue rule. Each primary study was assigned to a 13-category taxonomy and graded as simulation, prototype or testbed, production data, production deployment, or not determinable.
AI.result: Of 1,003 studies with a determinable level, 66.2% used prototypes or testbeds, 18.0% simulations and 15.8% production data or deployments. A 93-study synthesis core shows production deployments of cascading-failure prevention, trace- and graph-based root-cause analysis and predictive autoscaling, with production-trace evaluations of cold-start mitigation. Edge reliability and physical AI rely mainly on simulations and testbeds.
AI.conclusion: The principal gaps are production evidence for edge-native systems, shared resilience benchmarks and dependable agentic operations, with conclusions limited to the documented corpus.

title: Agents Propose, Code Verifies, Humans Decide: Verified Agentic Ingestion of Heterogeneous Scientific Tables into Relational Databases
summary: Public scientific datasets rarely arrive analysis-ready. They arrive as messy folders of wide matrices, long tables, spreadsheets, and per-cohort files whose keys and encodings differ, and every reanalysis must reconnect them first. A coding agent can automate this, but its mistakes can look plausible, and without an audit trail, a mistake that corrupts data can go uncaught. We present an AI-assisted ingestion pipeline built on one rule: LLM agents propose, deterministic code verifies, and humans decide. Narrow agents see compact, citable evidence about the files, never the data, and return typed proposals. A verifier with 39 check types tests each proposal against that evidence in two loops, one for the schema's structure and one for its meaning, and a human reviewer approves the schema and the load. Code compiles PostgreSQL DDL, reshapes the data, quarantines rows it cannot place, records provenance, and reconciles every staged row against the database. On four public biomedical datasets, one held out from development, 9 of 20 first proposals failed a check and every failure was caught: the loops repaired eight, and a one-line reviewer edit fixed the ninth. All 45.1 million values loaded with zero reconciliation gap. Discovering a dataset's structure took 4-7 LLM calls and preparing its data at most one more, costing under $0.50 per dataset. In a separate test, each of nine planted data errors was quarantined with a reason or recorded in an audit log.

AI.tldr: A verified agentic pipeline ingests messy scientific tables into PostgreSQL under the rule that LLM agents propose, deterministic code verifies and humans decide. On four public biomedical datasets, all 45.1 million values loaded with zero reconciliation gap, at under $0.50 per dataset.
AI.motivation: Public scientific datasets arrive as heterogeneous folders of matrices, long tables, spreadsheets and per-cohort files with differing keys and encodings, and a coding agent's plausible-looking mistakes can corrupt data without an audit trail.
AI.method: Narrow agents see compact, citable evidence about files, not the data, and return typed proposals. A verifier with 39 check types tests each proposal in two loops, one for schema structure and one for meaning. A human reviewer approves the schema and the load, and code compiles PostgreSQL DDL, reshapes data, quarantines unplaceable rows, records provenance and reconciles every staged row.
AI.result: Of 20 first proposals, 9 failed a check and all failures were caught: the loops repaired eight, and a one-line reviewer edit fixed the ninth. All 45.1 million values loaded with zero reconciliation gap. Structure discovery took 4 to 7 LLM calls, and data preparation at most one more, costing under $0.50 per dataset. In a separate test, all nine planted data errors were quarantined with a reason or recorded in an audit log.
AI.conclusion: Separating LLM proposal from deterministic verification and human approval gives an auditable and reliable route to analysis-ready scientific databases.

title: Neural Activity Synchronization-Based Fast Local Learnable Spiking Neural Network Architecture
summary: Implementing intelligent learning systems on low- power edge devices is challenging due to the high compu- tational complexity, training latency, and energy demands of traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), biologically plausible and spike-driven, come as an alternative. However, SNN training commonly relies on backpropagation through time (BPTT), which is computationally expensive, inherently global, and unsuitable for battery-driven devices. This work proposes a novel local learning framework for multi-layered SNNs inspired by Neural Activity Synchronization (NAS). Each layer updates its own weights using locally com- puted gradients. No gradient backpropagation is needed. This significantly reduces computational complexity, training latency, and energy consumption. The proposed SNN model is trained and evaluated on the MNIST dataset, achieving a classification accuracy of 97.78%. The model is also analyzed with Gaussian and salt-and-pepper noise, demonstrating robust performance across different noise levels.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a local learning framework for multi-layer spiking neural networks inspired by Neural Activity Synchronization, in which each layer updates its weights from locally computed gradients without backpropagation through time. It reaches 97.78% accuracy on MNIST with robustness to Gaussian and salt-and-pepper noise.
AI.motivation: Training SNNs with backpropagation through time is computationally expensive, global and unsuitable for battery-powered edge devices.
AI.method: Each layer of a multi-layer SNN updates its own weights using locally computed gradients, so no gradient backpropagation is needed.
AI.result: The model reaches 97.78% classification accuracy on MNIST and performs robustly under Gaussian and salt-and-pepper noise at different levels.
AI.conclusion: Local learning can reduce computational complexity, training latency and energy consumption for spiking networks on low-power edge devices, though the abstract evaluates only MNIST.

title: Statopia: A Prover--Library Ecosystem for Automated Formalization and Proof Discovery in Statistics
summary: Theoretical results in statistics and machine learning rest on long, technically delicate proofs, and fluent arguments generated by large language models are not necessarily correct. Automated formalization makes such arguments mechanically checkable, and automated proving goes further by discovering machine-checked proofs for statements whose proofs are incomplete or missing altogether. Both require reconstructing assumptions from source materials, accessing specialized mathematical infrastructure and managing long proof developments. We present Statopia, an ecosystem that jointly develops Statopia Prover, an independent agent specialized for formalizing and proving results in statistics and machine learning, and Statlib, a Lean~4 library built with the prover and organized for automated use. The prover controls its own execution without relying on external coding agents. It is built for formal proof discovery and checking existing proofs. A natural-language proof, when available, guides its search but is not required: from a statement alone, the prover develops the argument itself and constructs a Lean proof. Its workflow integrates source preparation, statement review, library supported planning and proof construction. Dynamic proof dependency graphs and task groups support parallel, resumable proof development. Statlib's shared definitions and theorem interfaces are organized for retrieval and composition by agents, and its coverage of statistics keeps expanding. Verified results and usage feedback from the prover inform reviewed library updates, so that proof development drives this expansion. A cross-platform application provides an interactive workspace for uploading source files and running tasks locally or in the cloud.

AI.tldr: Statopia is an ecosystem of a specialized prover agent, Statopia Prover, and Statlib, a Lean 4 library, for automated formalization and proof discovery in statistics and machine learning. The prover can build a Lean proof from a statement alone, without a natural-language proof.
AI.motivation: Long proofs in statistics and ML are technically delicate, LLM-generated arguments may be incorrect, and automated formalization and proving require reconstructing assumptions, accessing specialized infrastructure and managing long proof developments.
AI.method: The prover controls its own execution without external coding agents and integrates source preparation, statement review, library-supported planning and proof construction. Dynamic proof dependency graphs and task groups support parallel, resumable development. Statlib's shared definitions and theorem interfaces are organized for retrieval and composition by agents, and verified results and usage feedback drive reviewed library updates. A cross-platform application provides a workspace for local or cloud runs.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The ecosystem aims to make statistical theory mechanically checkable and to let proof development drive the expansion of the library, with coverage described as expanding.

title: Guidance at Pure Noise Erodes Speaker Similarity in Few-Step Token-Conditioned Flow-Matching TTS
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech and Language Processing. Code: this https URL
summary: Text-to-speech systems built from a language model and a flow-matching mel decoder now run the decoder with two to four Euler steps instead of the official ten or more. At two steps the word error rate (WER) is unchanged, but speaker similarity (SIM) drops by one to six points. This paper shows that most of this loss comes from classifier-free guidance on the first step. At pure noise the network can only return the conditional mean, so guidance shifts every trajectory by nearly the same vector. Later steps do not remove this shift, and its size grows with the length of the first step, so it is negligible with ten or more steps and accounts for most of the loss with two. Two training-free samplers are derived from this analysis. First-step unguided sampling (FSU) leaves the first step unguided and recovers $84$--$91\%$ of the two-step SIM loss on CosyVoice~2/3 with no significant WER increase. FSU-Mid replaces the two Euler steps by one midpoint step with an unguided first evaluation, recovers $77$--$85\%$ on IndexTTS-2 and matches the ten-step teacher on CosyVoice~2 and GLM-TTS. Both use three network function evaluations, one fewer than the official two-step sampler, and FSU-Mid gives the highest mean recovery among eight published guidance rules re-run at two steps on four decoders.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that most of the speaker-similarity loss in few-step flow-matching TTS decoders comes from classifier-free guidance applied at the first, pure-noise Euler step, and proposes two training-free samplers (FSU and FSU-Mid) that recover most of that loss with three network evaluations.
AI.motivation: Running the mel decoder of LM-based TTS with two to four Euler steps cuts cost, but at two steps speaker similarity drops by one to six points while WER is unchanged, and the cause was not isolated.
AI.method: At pure noise the network can only return the conditional mean, so classifier-free guidance shifts every trajectory by nearly the same vector, and the shift scales with the first step length. First-step unguided sampling (FSU) leaves the first step unguided; FSU-Mid replaces the two Euler steps with one midpoint step whose first evaluation is unguided.
AI.result: FSU recovers 84-91% of the two-step SIM loss on CosyVoice 2/3 with no significant WER increase. FSU-Mid recovers 77-85% on IndexTTS-2 and matches the ten-step teacher on CosyVoice 2 and GLM-TTS, and gives the highest mean recovery among eight published guidance rules re-run at two steps on four decoders. Both use three network function evaluations, one fewer than the official two-step sampler.
AI.conclusion: Guidance at pure noise is the main source of speaker-similarity degradation in few-step token-conditioned flow-matching TTS, and removing it from the first step gives a cheap training-free fix.

title: Replay Fidelity in LLM Agent Evaluation: Randomness, Hidden State, and Test Oracles in AppWorld
comment: Empirical study; 11 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables; historical AppWorld census with a bounded BFCL consistency check
summary: Reproducibility in large language model (LLM) agent evaluation depends on replay fidelity: which parts of an execution trace are reconstructed, controlled, and compared. This matters for agent debugging, failure analysis, and counterfactual evaluation of stateful tool use. We audit all 71 unsuccessful executions in a fixed historical AppWorld corpus using 284 isolated fixed-code replay attempts. Reconstructed declared settings admit 42 cases under printed-output, pre-oracle database-delta, and native-verdict/test-count checks; resetting the random-number generator before each interaction admits 68. The 26-case gap contracts to four under database/oracle checks, with one endpoint unknown. Mechanism studies identify four materialized-state discrepancies despite matching outputs and verdicts. In one admitted endpoint pair, an identical API call yields matching responses but different row effects; common future Python RNG removes that deterministic difference in two paired repetitions. A separate JWT credential-equality program and alignment controls expose authentication/write differences, with missing repetitions retained. For all 10 affected post-oracle export cases, native export from retained output trackers restores the reference comparison without changing original cached contents. A purposeful 12-case BFCL pilot shows no discrepancy under its tested public-state, return, and verdict checks. We preserve resource censoring and infrastructure deviations. The contribution is a bounded empirical characterization of replay eligibility, hidden state, and test-oracle integration, without estimating debugger accuracy, repair gains, or method-ranking distortion.

AI.tldr: The paper audits replay fidelity for the 71 unsuccessful executions in a historical AppWorld corpus and characterises which traces can be faithfully replayed, where hidden state and test-oracle integration cause discrepancies.
AI.motivation: Reproducibility of LLM agent evaluation depends on how much of an execution trace can be reconstructed, controlled and compared, which matters for debugging, failure analysis and counterfactual evaluation of stateful tool use.
AI.method: The authors run 284 isolated fixed-code replay attempts over the 71 unsuccessful AppWorld executions, check replays with printed-output, pre-oracle database-delta and native verdict/test-count checks, study materialised-state discrepancies, add a JWT credential-equality program and alignment controls, and run a 12-case BFCL pilot.
AI.result: Reconstructed declared settings admit 42 cases, and resetting the random-number generator before each interaction admits 68, leaving a 26-case gap that narrows to four under database and oracle checks, with one endpoint unknown. Four materialised-state discrepancies appear despite matching outputs and verdicts, and one endpoint pair yields different row effects from an identical API call; common future Python RNG removes that difference in two paired repetitions. The BFCL pilot shows no discrepancy under its tested checks. For all 10 affected post-oracle export cases, native export from retained trackers restores the reference comparison.
AI.conclusion: Replay eligibility, hidden state and oracle integration are real limits on reproducing agent traces; the paper is a bounded empirical characterisation and does not estimate debugger accuracy, repair gains or method-ranking distortion.

title: ErosionBench: Probing Alignment Decay in Enterprise Multi-Agent Systems
summary: As enterprises delegate consequential work to multi-agent LLM systems, benign-looking requests can escalate into unsafe actions as they propagate across sessions through poisoned shared state, long-context documents, and trusted peer messages: no single message is malicious, yet the assembled tool action is. Prior benchmarks isolate a single agent under prompt injection or score multi-agent attacks by their final output, leaving cross-session erosion of shared state out of scope. We introduce ErosionBench, an environment-grounded benchmark that executes such attacks and verifies alignment decay at the process level, scoring the realized tool call against authorized intent and provenance with deterministic contracts, not output text. Each scenario is authored as a deterministic state graph before any prose is rendered, so every state change traces to a known cause. It spans four enterprise domains and four decay mechanisms across 1,728 scenarios with matched benign controls, labeled against the OWASP Top-10 for LLM Applications, plus 198 image-based attacks, each paired with a text equivalent, so a defense must survive the same attack in either channel. Perimeter defenses suppress attacks only by over-refusing 54-92% of legitimate work, so a low attack-success rate can conceal severe over-refusal. As a reference defense, we propose a calibrated Meta-Auditor pairing synchronous state checks with asynchronous trajectory monitoring; on a family-disjoint 906-scenario held-out split it reaches 98.5% recall at a 2.9% false-positive rate. Since it monitors trajectory, not surface content, its detection is channel-invariant: the strongest auditor flags image-delivered attacks about as reliably as their text equivalents (recall gap $\leq$2 points per model). Across GPT, Gemini, and Claude auditors, calibration keeps false positives low while recall tracks model capability, strongest for Claude.

AI.tldr: ErosionBench is a process-level benchmark of cross-session alignment decay in enterprise multi-agent LLM systems, scored by the realised tool call, and it proposes a calibrated Meta-Auditor as a reference defence.
AI.motivation: Benign-looking requests can escalate into unsafe actions as they propagate through poisoned shared state, long documents and peer messages, but prior benchmarks isolate single agents or score multi-agent attacks only by final output.
AI.method: Scenarios are authored as deterministic state graphs and rendered to prose, verified against authorised intent and provenance with deterministic contracts. The benchmark spans four enterprise domains and four decay mechanisms with 1,728 scenarios, matched benign controls, OWASP Top-10 labels, and 198 image-based attacks paired with text equivalents. The reference defence, Meta-Auditor, pairs synchronous state checks with asynchronous trajectory monitoring.
AI.result: Perimeter defences suppress attacks only by over-refusing 54-92% of legitimate work. On a family-disjoint 906-scenario held-out split, Meta-Auditor reaches 98.5% recall at a 2.9% false-positive rate. Its recall gap between image and text attacks is at most 2 points per model, and recall tracks model capability across GPT, Gemini and Claude auditors, strongest for Claude.
AI.conclusion: A low attack-success rate can hide severe over-refusal, so defences must be judged on both attacks and legitimate work, and trajectory-level monitoring offers channel-invariant detection.

title: Least-Privilege Auditing of Agent Tool Calls with Intent Graphs and Reasoning-Guided Escalation
summary: LLM agents that call tools are exposed to indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden in tool outputs can steer an agent into calls the user never asked for. We present a runtime audit that derives an executable intent graph from the user's objective and the deployment's tool catalog with one LLM call per task, and checks every tool call against it with a deterministic loop that makes no LLM call (median 5.7 microseconds per call). Two further mechanisms recover utility. Lookups of the user's own state bypass the audit, because the harm of an attack lies in its write or outward step. The calls that remain flagged are escalated to a reasoning guardian, in the spirit of tool-integrated reasoning models such as START: a reasoning model that sees only the objective, the plan, the call history without tool outputs, and the flagged call, and can verify facts with a restricted Python-expression tool. A current agent showed no baseline attack success, so end-to-end validation remains open.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a runtime least-privilege audit for LLM tool calls that checks each call against an intent graph derived from the user objective, and escalates flagged calls to a reasoning guardian, to defend against indirect prompt injection.
AI.motivation: Indirect prompt injection can steer tool-using agents into calls the user never requested, and existing defences need a way to block these without losing too much utility.
AI.method: One LLM call per task derives an executable intent graph from the objective and tool catalogue, and a deterministic loop checks every tool call against it without any LLM call. Lookups of the user's own state bypass the audit, and flagged calls go to a reasoning guardian that sees only the objective, plan, call history without tool outputs, and the flagged call, with a restricted Python-expression tool for verification.
AI.result: The deterministic check takes a median of 5.7 microseconds per call. A current agent showed no baseline attack success, so end-to-end validation of the defence is still open.
AI.conclusion: The design is cheap at runtime, but its protective value has not yet been demonstrated end to end because the baseline agent was not successfully attacked.

title: Agentic Attribution of Cloud Resource Ownership
summary: Security tools raise findings across cloud environments, and AI agents now investigate and prioritize them. A finding is still resolved by people: it has to reach the people responsible for fixing it and accountable for the resource it concerns. Ownership is the organizational context that decides who that is. Where recorded, it is declared by hand in configuration management databases or owner tags and goes stale unless kept current; accounts are shared, and automation creates much of the infrastructure. The knowledge sits in work records, code history, audit logs and identity directories, encoded in each organization's own conventions. Recovering it poses four challenges: the signal is scattered across sources, none of them authoritative; the conventions that carry it differ between organizations; reaching an owner takes multi-hop links; and those related to a resource differ in the strength of their relation. We define ownership as a set of entities, people or teams, each related to the resource by one of five patterns ordered by strength. We present a reference architecture for agentic ownership attribution that derives ownership from these records instead of declaring it: it profiles an organization offline into tested signal procedures and an ownership playbook, then attributes each resource with a coordinator agent and parallel investigators, with confidence computed by rules. On 100 resources of 50 Amazon Web Services (AWS) resource types in one organization, we pool the architecture's candidates with those of an unprimed general-purpose agent and verify every evidence piece against the records. The architecture reaches 92.1% weighted recall and 86.6% weighted precision, against 54.8% and 77.4%, at 0.55 times the agent's cost per unit of coverage. The difference lies in people who build and change resources without an explicit owner, found through work records and code history.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an agentic reference architecture that attributes owners to cloud resources by deriving ownership from work records, code history, audit logs and identity directories rather than from manually declared tags.
AI.motivation: Security findings must reach the people responsible for a resource, but ownership is declared by hand in CMDBs or tags, goes stale, and is hard to recover because the signal is scattered and encoded in each organisation's own conventions.
AI.method: Ownership is defined as a set of people or teams linked to a resource by one of five patterns ordered by strength. The architecture profiles an organisation offline into tested signal procedures and an ownership playbook, then uses a coordinator agent with parallel investigators per resource, and computes confidence by rules.
AI.result: On 100 resources of 50 AWS resource types in one organisation, the architecture reaches 92.1% weighted recall and 86.6% weighted precision, against 54.8% and 77.4% for an unprimed general-purpose agent, at 0.55 times that agent's cost per unit of coverage. The gain comes from people who build and change resources without an explicit owner.
AI.conclusion: Ownership can be attributed from evidence in existing records with higher recall and precision than a general agent, and the largest gains come from implicit owners found through work records and code history.

title: On the Relative Security of Prompt Injection: Mechanised Definitions, Defences and Verdicts for LLM Agents
summary: An LLM agent that reads untrusted content, such as an email or a web page, may follow instructions hidden in it. Noninterference is too strong for such agents, since a useful agent lets untrusted content influence what it does and may disclose the user's data by design, and declassification needs a release policy written for each task. We instead state security relative to a reference agent, which runs the same plan under the same runtime monitor with a model that never obeys untrusted content. An agent is relatively secure if every leak it has is a leak the reference already has. Our framework, PlanTERS, instantiates relative security, a notion from speculative execution, with a small agent language in which the attacker chooses how the model follows instructions, a composition with runtime monitors, and attacker models that differ in what they observe. A fence theorem shows that revoking injectable tools at the first untrusted read, and never granting them back, makes every plan relatively secure at the event level on finite runs, for every model behaviour in which each injection is a single call and the model obeys on a schedule fixed in advance; with a fairness condition, this extends to possibly infinite runs. We prove or refute relative security for agents with fences, budgets, approvals, loops and dual LLMs, in Isabelle/HOL.

AI.tldr: The paper defines relative security for LLM agents, where an agent is secure if every leak it has is also a leak of a reference agent, and implements the framework as PlanTERS with Isabelle/HOL proofs of fence and other results.
AI.motivation: Noninterference is too strong for agents that read untrusted content, because a useful agent must let that content influence its actions and may disclose user data by design, and declassification needs a release policy for each task.
AI.method: Security is stated relative to a reference agent that runs the same plan under the same runtime monitor with a model that never obeys untrusted content, using a notion borrowed from speculative execution. PlanTERS combines a small agent language, a composition with runtime monitors, and attacker models that differ in what they observe.
AI.result: A fence theorem shows that revoking injectable tools at the first untrusted read, and never granting them back, makes every plan relatively secure at the event level on finite runs, for models where each injection is a single call and the model obeys on a schedule fixed in advance. With a fairness condition this extends to possibly infinite runs. Relative security is proved or refuted for agents with fences, budgets, approvals, loops and dual LLMs, in Isabelle/HOL.
AI.conclusion: Relative security gives a usable notion of prompt-injection security for agents that must use untrusted content, and fences give a provable baseline under the stated model assumptions.

title: Weight-Space Programming of Variational Quantum Circuits: Large Language Models Write Quantum Circuit Parameters Without an Optimizer
summary: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) optimize circuit angles through repeated quantum-device evaluations, often facing vanishing gradients and high optimization costs. We ask whether a large language model (LLM) can write these angles directly. Extending *weight-space programming* from classical networks to quantum circuits, we provide a frontier LLM (\gpt) with the problem, circuit, and gate conventions. Its angles are executed exactly as written, without returning losses, gradients, or accuracy feedback. Across 139 requests, we test handwritten-digit classification, VQE ground-state estimation for spin chains and H$_2$, and MaxCut QAOA, comparing against random weights, classical optimization, and optimization initialized with LLM weights on the same circuit. When parameters have interpretable structure, the LLM matches or approaches the optimizer: it achieves 95--100\% of the energy spectrum on every VQE problem, derives the exact H$_2$ ground state in closed form, finds optimal depth-one QAOA angles for every graph, and reaches 93--96\% accuracy on digits 3 versus 8 with 12--18 hand-written weights, outperforming an optimizer trained on the same ten examples. Its weights are also strong warm starts: optimization reaches its best value after a median of one evaluation rather than hundreds. Allowed to design circuits, the LLM chooses data-dependent rotation chains encoding pixel importance in all 30 cases (one qubit for binary tasks, one chain per qubit for ten classes), reaching 65\% accuracy across ten digits. Yet the approach fails in opaque weight spaces: accuracy drops to chance when fixed circuits exceed 30 weights, while optimization improves. It is also sensitive to gate conventions: 6 of 42 QAOA replies reverse mixing-angle signs and fail. We release all prompts, replies, and scores.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a frontier LLM can write variational quantum circuit angles directly, without an optimiser or loss feedback, matching or approaching optimised results when the parameters have interpretable structure and failing in opaque weight spaces.
AI.motivation: Variational quantum algorithms need many quantum-device evaluations and often suffer from vanishing gradients and high optimisation cost, so the question is whether an LLM can write the circuit parameters directly.
AI.method: The authors extend weight-space programming from classical networks to quantum circuits by giving a frontier LLM (GPT) the problem, circuit and gate conventions, executing its angles exactly as written, and returning no losses, gradients or accuracy. They test 139 requests on handwritten-digit classification, VQE for spin chains and H2, and MaxCut QAOA, against random weights, classical optimisation and optimisation warm-started from LLM weights.
AI.result: The LLM reaches 95-100% of the energy spectrum on every VQE problem, derives the exact H2 ground state in closed form, finds optimal depth-one QAOA angles for every graph, and reaches 93-96% accuracy on digits 3 versus 8 with 12-18 weights. Its weights are strong warm starts, reaching the best value after a median of one evaluation. When allowed to design circuits it reaches 65% accuracy across ten digits. Accuracy drops to chance when fixed circuits exceed 30 weights, and 6 of 42 QAOA replies reverse mixing-angle signs and fail.
AI.conclusion: LLM-written parameters are competitive when they have interpretable structure, but the approach is fragile in opaque weight spaces and sensitive to gate conventions; all prompts, replies and scores are released.

title: Treating the Model as an Untrusted Component: Deterministic Policy Enforcement, Human Approval and Taint Tracking Against Prompt Injection in Tool-Using Agents, with Validation on Open-Weights Models
comment: 23 pages, 8 figures, 18 tables. Original research contribution. Code, data and the two-rater oracle audit: this https URL
summary: Tool-using LLM agents act on instructions embedded in the data they read, so prompt injection is a structural rather than a prompt-wording problem. We compare in-prompt defences (hardened prompts, spotlighting, LLM detectors) with deterministic enforcement outside the model (four reference monitors of increasing strength), human approval and taint tracking, judged by one effect-based oracle independent of every defence in an executable environment of 13 tasks and 12 tools, with argument-fuzzing attackers and severity-weighted harm. In an evaluation with real open-weights models (Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B; 156 attack episodes per defence and model), the models proposed the attacker's call in 64% and 84% of attack episodes behind the task-bound monitor, which admitted 1.3% and 7.7%; guardrail effects depended on the model (a prompt guardrail moved obedience from 67% to 65% and from 86% to 55%, spotlighting plus a detector to 12% and 0%) against static attacks. Simulation with an assumed model covers what no real run did: under the assumed erosion law a persistent adaptive attacker or a compromised model drives every guardrail stack to 100.0% attack success, whereas the task-bound monitor holds severe actions at 0.0%; its residual (harm 0.69/10) falls by 62% under taint-triggered human review, and a human layer without a deterministic monitor fails against approval spamming unless each episode has a deterministic approval budget. Implementation quality matters: a naive monitor admits 18 of 33 effective attack variants, a hardened one 6 and a capability-bound one 1. The real-model evidence is limited to two open-weights models and static attacks, the human-approval and taint results are simulation-only, and the larger model's detector stack contradicts the assumed erosion law. Code, data, a two-rater oracle audit and a notebook for repeating the real-model evaluation are provided.

AI.tldr: The paper compares in-prompt defences with deterministic policy enforcement, human approval and taint tracking against prompt injection in tool-using agents, and finds that a task-bound deterministic monitor holds severe actions near zero attack success on open-weights models.
AI.motivation: Prompt injection is a structural problem for tool-using agents that act on instructions embedded in data, so defences that depend on prompt wording are unlikely to be reliable.
AI.method: Four reference monitors of increasing strength, human approval and taint tracking are compared with hardened prompts, spotlighting and LLM detectors in an executable environment of 13 tasks and 12 tools, judged by one effect-based oracle with argument-fuzzing attackers and severity-weighted harm. Real evaluations use Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B with 156 attack episodes per defence and model, and simulations use an assumed model of erosion.
AI.result: Behind the task-bound monitor, the models proposed the attacker's call in 64% and 84% of attack episodes, and the monitor admitted 1.3% and 7.7%. Prompt guardrails had model-dependent effects. Under the assumed erosion law, guardrail stacks reach 100.0% attack success, while the task-bound monitor holds severe actions at 0.0% with residual harm 0.69/10, reduced by 62% under taint-triggered human review. A naive monitor admits 18 of 33 effective attack variants, a hardened one 6 and a capability-bound one 1.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic enforcement outside the model is far more reliable than in-prompt defences, but the real-model evidence is limited to two open-weights models and static attacks, and the human-approval and taint results are simulation-only.

title: Qubit-to-Motion: Traceable Action Provenance in Hybrid QRL for Robotic Bin-Packing Sequencing
summary: Hybrid quantum reinforcement learning has been explored for robotic decision-making, but evaluations often emphasize task success, return, or convergence, leaving unresolved whether quantum circuit outputs influence constrained actions and remain traceable through robot execution. We present \texttt{Qubit-to-Motion}, an evidence-centered framework for support-constrained sequencing and simulated robotic placement. Four Pauli-$Z$ readouts provide the sole learned input to the actor and critic, while a support mask enforces admissible object selection. Each decision is recorded and linked via step indices and SHA-256 fingerprints to a sealed route, deterministic Cartesian and inverse-kinematics waypoints, prescribed joint motion, and MuJoCo contact replay. A frozen checkpoint is evaluated across five deterministic 30-object scene variants. All 150 placements satisfy support, containment, and settling criteria. A fixed-state zero-readout intervention changes $90.0\pm0.0\%$ of decisions, demonstrating dependence on the joint circuit representation. Mean macro travel is $34.537\pm0.206$~m, inference requires $8.60\pm1.27$~ms per route, and replay achieves $8.764\pm0.220~\mu$m mean final position error with 0.356~mm maximum interpenetration. These results establish reproducible decision-to-contact traceability. The implementation is available at \href{this https URL}{\textcolor{linkpink}{the anonymous repository}}.

AI.tldr: Qubit-to-Motion is a traceable hybrid quantum reinforcement learning framework for robotic bin-packing sequencing, in which four Pauli-Z readouts drive a support-masked policy and each decision is linked to the simulated robot's contact replay.
AI.motivation: Hybrid quantum RL evaluations for robotics report task success or return, but do not show whether quantum circuit outputs actually influence constrained actions or remain traceable through robot execution.
AI.method: Four Pauli-Z readouts are the sole learned input to the actor and critic, and a support mask enforces admissible object selection. Each decision is recorded and linked by step indices and SHA-256 fingerprints to a sealed route, Cartesian and inverse-kinematics waypoints, joint motion and MuJoCo contact replay. A frozen checkpoint is evaluated on five deterministic 30-object scene variants.
AI.result: All 150 placements satisfy support, containment and settling criteria. A fixed-state zero-readout intervention changes 90.0 plus or minus 0.0% of decisions. Mean macro travel is 34.537 plus or minus 0.206 m, inference takes 8.60 plus or minus 1.27 ms per route, and replay gives 8.764 plus or minus 0.220 micrometre mean final position error with 0.356 mm maximum interpenetration.
AI.conclusion: The framework establishes reproducible traceability from quantum-circuit decision to physical contact in simulation, showing dependence on the joint circuit representation.

title: A Physical Testbed for Self-Driving Laboratories: Comparing Bayesian and Agentic Optimization in a Minimal Closed-Loop Color Formulation Task
summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) integrate laboratory robotics and automation with AI-driven decision-making to close the design-build-test-learn (DBTL) cycle. However, physical testbeds that combine off-the-shelf hardware and AI into a functioning closed-loop workflow remain in early stages of development, and their integration with commercial laboratory automation is comparatively less developed. In this work, we develop a physical testbed that assembles and integrates commercially available laboratory automation instruments and demonstrate continuous, closed-loop, autonomous operation over 24 cumulative hours of unattended experimentation. We validate this platform on a minimal closed-loop discovery task in which the system autonomously formulates aqueous dye mixtures to match a target absorbance spectrum. The system completed six independent campaigns, each consisting of 48 closed-loop iterations over approximately four hours. In every campaign, the system autonomously selected, dispensed, and measured each mixture, with an AI-driven decision-making algorithm determining subsequent formulations without human intervention. Using this testbed, we compared the performance of two AI-driven decision-making algorithms, traditional Bayesian optimization (BO) and an agentic approach, in selecting mixtures under a fixed total-volume constraint. The agentic optimizer matched target absorbance spectra using fewer iterations than BO, with reductions up to 52%, and converged on a solution for one target that BO failed to match within 48 iterations. These results demonstrate a reference physical platform for SDLs that can evaluate both established and emerging AI strategies, including large language model (LLM)-directed optimization, before their deployment in real-world applications where experiments may be costly and time-consuming to prepare.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a low-cost physical self-driving laboratory testbed that ran 24 cumulative hours of unattended closed-loop colour formulation, and uses it to compare Bayesian optimisation with an agentic LLM-directed optimiser.
AI.motivation: Physical testbeds that integrate off-the-shelf hardware and AI into a working closed loop are at an early stage, and their integration with commercial laboratory automation is less developed.
AI.method: The authors assemble commercially available laboratory automation instruments into a testbed and run six independent campaigns of 48 closed-loop iterations each, about four hours per campaign, in which the system selects, dispenses and measures aqueous dye mixtures to match a target absorbance spectrum under a fixed total-volume constraint. Bayesian optimisation (BO) and an agentic optimiser are compared on this task.
AI.result: In every campaign the system ran without human intervention. The agentic optimiser matched target spectra with fewer iterations than BO, with reductions of up to 52%, and converged on one target that BO did not match within 48 iterations.
AI.conclusion: The testbed is offered as a reference platform for evaluating established and emerging SDL decision strategies, including LLM-directed optimisation, before deployment where experiments are costly.

title: Steering Emergent Behavior in Multi-Agent LLM Systems via Information Networks
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables; supplementary information included as an appendix
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in groups, each pursuing an individual objective while jointly determining system performance. If an operator controls which agent observes which other agent, but not their payoffs or messages, how should observations be structured to raise collective welfare? We make the information network (who observes whom) a design object, decoupled from the fixed interaction network over which agents act. Ten identical LLM agents play repeated group-decision games; by default each observes only an anonymous summary of the group's previous-round outcome, and a manager with a fixed budget adds directed observation links that reveal peers' past actions. Across 1,080 episodes and six games spanning coordination, anti-coordination, social dilemmas, and discovery, we ask how much information to share and, at a fixed budget, who should observe whom. Disclosure creates behavioral coupling: observation acts as a contagion channel whose welfare effect depends on the alignment between individually attractive behavior and the collective objective. First, the value of information is alignment-contingent: more peer information tends to help or be neutral when individual behavior is aligned with the collective goal, but under free-riding or congestion externalities it amplifies collectively harmful behavior; in a public-goods game the group does best with no information at all. We read this sign separation as a cross-game regularity within one controlled LLM population, not a model-invariant law. Second, at a fixed budget, who observes whom matters primarily when coupling is harmful: a modular "barbell" that lets sub-populations entrench harmful behavior is reliably the worst wiring, reversing the network-reciprocity intuition from human evolutionary game theory. These results argue against a default of full transparency for agent collectives.

AI.tldr: The paper treats the information network, meaning who observes whom among LLM agents, as a design object, and finds that more peer information helps only when individual and collective goals are aligned, while harmful wiring such as a modular barbell is worst.
AI.motivation: When an operator controls observation links between LLM agents but not their payoffs or messages, it is unclear how to structure observations to raise collective welfare.
AI.method: Ten identical LLM agents play repeated group-decision games. By default each sees only an anonymous summary of the group's previous outcome, and a manager with a fixed budget adds directed links that reveal peers' past actions. Across 1,080 episodes and six games covering coordination, anti-coordination, social dilemmas and discovery, the authors vary disclosure and the wiring at a fixed budget.
AI.result: The value of information depends on alignment: more peer information tends to help or be neutral when individual and collective goals align, but under free-riding or congestion amplifies harmful behaviour, and in a public-goods game the group does best with no information. At a fixed budget, wiring matters mainly when coupling is harmful, and a modular barbell that lets sub-populations entrench harmful behaviour is reliably the worst.
AI.conclusion: Full transparency should not be a default for agent collectives, and the sign of the welfare effect of disclosure is a cross-game regularity within one controlled LLM population rather than a model-invariant law.

title: ShadowBench-MCP: Measuring Shadow Invocations in MCP-Style Tool Routing
comment: Presented at the 35th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 2026)
summary: LLM agents increasingly act as routers for tools, APIs, and software-supply-chain workflows, making an execution path - rather than generated text alone - a security-relevant model output. We study shadow invocation: a task-preserving request variant that causes an LLM router to select a riskier execution path, potentially skipping validation, provenance, staging, redaction, or audit controls even though the request does not ask for a malicious action. We introduce ShadowBench-MCP, a benchmark and metric suite that separates task preservation (TPSS), operational pressure (OPSS), and route-geometric drift (RGAS), and combines them in the pre-execution SODS score. In a focused policy-ablation study using a Groq-hosted qwen/qwen3-32b router, 120 routing decisions yield 96 original-versus-variant comparisons across six security-sensitive workflows. Efficiency-first routing produces a 29.2% shadow-invocation rate and 26.7% safety-tool skip rate. Policy-aware routing reduces these to 4.2% and 1.7%, respectively, corresponding to an 85.7% relative reduction in shadow invocations. Pre-execution signals distinguish shadow routes with ROC AUC up to 0.94. These results are early, single-router evidence of a policy-dependent routing-layer security effect, not a claim of universal vulnerability.

AI.tldr: ShadowBench-MCP is a benchmark and metric suite for shadow invocations, where a task-preserving request variant causes an LLM tool router to pick a riskier execution path that skips safety controls, and policy-aware routing sharply reduces it.
AI.motivation: For LLM agents that route tools and workflows, the execution path is itself a security-relevant output, yet routers may choose riskier paths even when the request asks for nothing malicious.
AI.method: The authors define task preservation (TPSS), operational pressure (OPSS) and route-geometric drift (RGAS), combine them into a pre-execution SODS score, and run a policy-ablation study with a Groq-hosted qwen/qwen3-32b router. It produces 120 routing decisions and 96 original-versus-variant comparisons across six security-sensitive workflows.
