AI.result: Efficiency-first routing yields a 29.2% shadow-invocation rate and 26.7% safety-tool skip rate. Policy-aware routing reduces these to 4.2% and 1.7%, an 85.7% relative reduction in shadow invocations. Pre-execution signals distinguish shadow routes with ROC AUC up to 0.94.
AI.conclusion: The results are early, single-router evidence that the routing-layer security effect depends on policy, not a claim of universal vulnerability.

title: Silinx: An Open, Browser-Based HDL Design Platform for Teaching Digital Systems on FPGA Boards
summary: Many digital systems courses teach on FPGA boards whose vendor tool is no longer maintained: the Digilent Basys2 and Nexys2 (Xilinx Spartan-3E) and Nexys3 and Atlys (Spartan-6) need Xilinx ISE 14.7, discontinued since 2013 and hard to install on the computers and tablets students use today. The author presents Silinx, a free (AGPL-3.0) HDL design platform for teaching that keeps ISE's Project Navigator workflow but runs in a web browser with nothing to install. A module can be written in VHDL or Verilog, in C or C++ through Silinx HLS, which is compatible with AMD's Vitis HLS and passes all 73 of its introductory examples, or drawn as a schematic, an ASM chart, a state diagram, a Boolean function with its Karnaugh map, or a Petri net, from which its HDL is generated. Designs are checked with explanations written for beginners, simulated, run on an emulated board, built, and programmed onto a real board over WebUSB. The implementation flow is open and runs in the browser: Yosys and nextpnr compiled to WebAssembly, with Silinx's own device data, timing model and bitstream writer for the Spartan-3E and Spartan-6, built by black-box observation of ISE's documented tools; Lattice iCE40 boards use the existing open iCE40 tools, and further families are planned. ISE is the oracle: Silinx's bitstreams are byte-identical to those ISE writes for the same placed and routed design, and pass ISE's design rule check. Against ISE at the same optimization goal, the open flow uses 15% fewer slices with 14% shorter critical paths when optimizing for area, and 21% fewer slices with 8% shorter critical paths when optimizing for speed (geometric means over 45 open-source designs built by both flows). The author also describes how the platform was developed with AI coding agents under test-first project rules.

AI.tldr: Silinx is a free, browser-based HDL design platform for teaching digital systems on legacy Xilinx-based FPGA boards, with an open implementation flow that is compared against ISE and claims byte-identical bitstreams for the Spartan-3E and Spartan-6 families.
AI.motivation: Digital systems courses that use Basys2, Nexys2, Nexys3 and Atlys boards need Xilinx ISE 14.7, which has been discontinued since 2013 and is hard to install on current student devices.
AI.method: Silinx keeps the ISE Project Navigator workflow in a browser and accepts VHDL, Verilog, C or C++ through Silinx HLS, which passes all 73 of Vitis HLS's introductory examples, or graphical entry such as schematics, ASM charts, state diagrams, Karnaugh-mapped Boolean functions and Petri nets. The open flow uses Yosys and nextpnr compiled to WebAssembly, with device data and a bitstream writer built by black-box observation of ISE's documented tools, and programming over WebUSB.
AI.result: Silinx's bitstreams are byte-identical to ISE's for the same placed and routed design and pass ISE's design rule check. Against ISE at the same optimisation goal, the open flow uses 15% fewer slices with 14% shorter critical paths when optimising for area, and 21% fewer slices with 8% shorter critical paths when optimising for speed, as geometric means over 45 open-source designs.
AI.conclusion: The platform offers a maintained, zero-install route for teaching on legacy boards, and the author also describes building it with AI coding agents under test-first project rules.

title: Towards Trustworthy Mobile Speech Interaction: Ensuring Voice Authenticity and Transmission Integrity
comment: Submitted to Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies (IMWUT)
summary: The rapid progress of generative speech models has made high-fidelity voice cloning and editing cheap, fast, and widely accessible, weakening the security of voiceprint-based authentication in mobile speech interactions. Existing speech watermarking techniques focus on offline protection or watermarking synthetic speech, and thus cannot verify whether a live utterance originates from the genuine speaker at capture time. We present \textit{MoBiMark}, a real-time \textbf{mo}bile \textbf{bi}ologic speech water\textbf{mark}ing system that binds ultrasonic articulatory signatures to speech content and embeds a dynamic watermark during capture. MoBiMark emits a multi-frequency ultrasonic probe on commodity smartphones, extracts echo features from the vocal tract, and fuses them with a content-dependent speech embedding to produce a dual-layer dynamic watermark combining a persistent user identifier (UID) and a per-utterance speech identifier (SID), enabling both source authentication and propagation-time tamper detection. A jointly trained embedder and detector injects the watermark while preserving perceptual quality, and system-level optimization with INT8 quantization enables lightweight on-device deployment. Evaluated on 50 users across four smartphone models, MoBiMark achieves an average 99.79% accuracy in source and propagation attacks, with negligible impact on speech quality and intelligibility.

AI.tldr: MoBiMark is a real-time mobile speech watermarking system that binds ultrasonic articulatory signatures from the vocal tract to speech content at capture time, so that live utterances can be authenticated and tampering detected.
AI.motivation: Voice cloning has weakened voiceprint authentication, and existing speech watermarking works offline or only marks synthetic speech, so it cannot verify that a live utterance came from the genuine speaker at capture.
AI.method: The system emits a multi-frequency ultrasonic probe on commodity smartphones, extracts vocal-tract echo features, and fuses them with a content-dependent speech embedding. It produces a dual-layer dynamic watermark with a persistent user identifier (UID) and a per-utterance speech identifier (SID). A jointly trained embedder and detector inject it, and INT8 quantisation supports on-device deployment.
AI.result: Evaluated on 50 users across four smartphone models, MoBiMark achieves an average accuracy of 99.79% in source and propagation attacks, with negligible impact on speech quality and intelligibility.
AI.conclusion: Ultrasonic biologic watermarking at capture time offers source authentication and propagation-time tamper detection for mobile speech interaction.

title: HolidayFactory 1.0: Simulating, Generating, and Evaluating Industrial Robot Tasks
summary: Robots are typically evaluated in episodes that begin from a reset, while industrial work consists of repeated jobs whose outcomes affect subsequent operations. Evaluating such work at scale requires simulation of task-critical physical interactions, construction of industrial environments, and measurements of performance as scene state persists. We present HOLIDAYFACTORY 1.0, a framework for simulating, generating, and evaluating industrial robot work. Given a human-specified workplace and task, the framework defines a world pairing a scenario of scene variants and process logic with an evaluation defining a job, metrics, and a rubric. HOLIDAYFACTORY 1.0 comprises three components. HOLIDAY-SIM extends Newton's SDF-based hydroelastic contact with additional constitutive laws and a semi-implicit primal-dual solver, couples stateful actuator dynamics to articulated motion, and derives tactile and joint observations from simulated states. Agentic world construction generates simulation-ready assets and scene variants using geometric and interaction checks, and proposes task-conditioned evaluations for human confirmation and executable checks. 24/7-BENCH introduces seven industrial tasks in which jobs are evaluated without resetting the scene, measuring completed, failed, and unfinished jobs, throughput, latency, and motor energy. Controlled studies characterize the proposed contact, actuator, and tactile models and examine the effectiveness of verification-guided world construction. Experiments on scene and evaluation generation further reveal the limitations of model critics and the difficulty of ensuring that generated evaluations faithfully capture task requirements. We examine job-level evaluations with scripted trajectories (e.g., code-as-policy) but have not yet compared policies over persistent runs.

AI.tldr: HolidayFactory 1.0 is a framework for simulating, generating and evaluating industrial robot work, in which jobs are evaluated over persistent scene state without resets, using a new contact and actuator simulator and an agentic world-construction pipeline.
AI.motivation: Robots are usually evaluated in reset-started episodes, but industrial work is a sequence of jobs whose outcomes affect later operations, so evaluation at scale must preserve scene state and simulate task-critical contact.
AI.method: HOLIDAY-SIM extends Newton's SDF-based hydroelastic contact with more constitutive laws and a semi-implicit primal-dual solver, couples stateful actuator dynamics to articulated motion, and derives tactile and joint observations. Agentic world construction generates assets and scene variants with geometric and interaction checks and proposes task-conditioned evaluations for human confirmation. 24/7-BENCH defines seven industrial tasks scored by completed, failed and unfinished jobs, throughput, latency and motor energy.
AI.result: Controlled studies characterise the contact, actuator and tactile models and test verification-guided world construction. Experiments reveal the limits of model critics and the difficulty of ensuring that generated evaluations faithfully capture task requirements. Job-level evaluation is shown only with scripted trajectories, and policies have not yet been compared over persistent runs.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a basis for job-level industrial evaluation of robots, but generated evaluations still need human confirmation and comparisons of learned policies over persistent runs remain future work.

title: Publications as benchmarks: auditing AI agents on spatial transcriptomics alignment
summary: AI agents are increasingly automating data analysis, but responsible adoption requires reliable performance evaluation, which is costly in specialized scientific domains. We introduce a framework that translates scientific publications into auditable benchmarks for AI agents and demonstrate its use on spatial transcriptomics alignment tasks. Across 121 tasks, 16 baseline methods, and six AI agents, the best agents (GPT-6-Astra and Gemini-4-Argon) matched or outperformed all baselines on 80% of tasks, often using surprisingly simple heuristics. Agent performance was robust to prompting and access to pre-installed packages. Benchmark construction also uncovered errors in prior work and shortcuts in current evaluation metrics. Finally, we show that agent-generated solutions can be distilled into a reusable program that ranks in the top 10% of baseline methods on unseen data. Our framework offers a scalable way to evaluate AI agents in specialized scientific domains by leveraging and stress-testing existing papers and metrics.

AI.tldr: The paper turns scientific publications into auditable benchmarks for AI agents and applies this to spatial transcriptomics alignment, finding that the best agents match or beat all 16 baselines on 80% of 121 tasks.
AI.motivation: Responsible use of AI agents in data analysis requires reliable performance evaluation, which is costly in specialised scientific domains.
AI.method: The framework converts published papers into benchmark tasks, here 121 spatial transcriptomics alignment tasks with 16 baseline methods and six AI agents. The authors test robustness to prompting and to access to pre-installed packages, and distil agent-generated solutions into a reusable program.
AI.result: The best agents, GPT-6-Astra and Gemini-4-Argon, match or outperform all baselines on 80% of tasks, often with simple heuristics, and performance is robust to prompting and package access. Construction uncovered errors in prior work and shortcuts in current metrics. A distilled program ranks in the top 10% of baselines on unseen data.
AI.conclusion: Publications can serve as scalable, stress-tested benchmarks for evaluating AI agents in specialised scientific domains, and the process also exposes flaws in existing papers and metrics.

title: Ultrasound-Assisted Biometric Watermarking Against Face Video Deepfakes
comment: Submitted to Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies (IMWUT)
summary: Currently, artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) poses a severe threat to facial video deepfakes, and many AIGC companies employ video watermarking to mitigate unauthorized fake video usage, but its effectiveness is limited due to watermark tampering and private-model forgery. Additionally, some schemes actively add watermarks to user videos. However, current approaches focus primarily on the quality of watermark embedding in offline scenarios, and no existing work offers a solution for protecting human facial videos in real-time online applications. To fill this gap, we propose, to the best of our knowledge, a novel biometric video watermarking method, UltraGuard, for the first time. It uses the smartphone's built-in speaker and microphone to emit ultrasonic signals and capture biometric features, which are then fused with spatio-temporal dynamic features derived from the video content. The fused features are encoded as watermarks and embedded into videos in real time, enabling dynamic, content-aware watermarking throughout transmission and propagation. Extensive experimental validation demonstrates that UltraGuard can effectively defend against malicious attacks such as forgery and editing, both at the source and during propagation, proving the system's efficacy. In the future, it can be deployed on users' mobile devices to provide real-time protection for users' facial videos, thereby preventing security and privacy breaches caused by various malicious attacks.

AI.tldr: UltraGuard is a real-time biometric video watermarking method that uses a smartphone's speaker and microphone to emit ultrasound, captures biometric features, and fuses them with video dynamics to watermark facial videos during capture against deepfakes.
AI.motivation: Existing video watermarks can be tampered with or forged by private models and are mostly applied offline, so no prior work protects facial videos in real-time online use.
AI.method: The smartphone emits ultrasonic signals and captures biometric features, which are fused with spatio-temporal dynamic features derived from the video content. The fused features are encoded as watermarks and embedded into the video in real time, giving content-aware watermarking through transmission and propagation.
AI.result: The abstract reports extensive experiments showing that UltraGuard defends against forgery and editing attacks both at the source and during propagation. No quantitative results are stated in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that the method could be deployed on mobile devices to protect users' facial videos in real time against forgery and privacy breaches.

title: VeilTune: Secure Fine-Tuning of Private LoRA Adapters on Public Pretrained Language Models
summary: Fine-tuning public pretrained language models with lightweight adapters such as LoRA has become the mainstream way to adapt them to downstream tasks. A service provider often trains its adapter on a data owner's samples, so two assets need protection: the data owner's samples and the provider's adapter. Existing secure fine-tuning protocols protect the samples but reveal to the data owner intermediate results of every training step, such as the hidden representations or logits of its inputs. We show that a single step suffices to copy the adapter: from the hidden representations of one mini-batch of 32 samples, the data owner fits an adapter that agrees with the provider's on 99.2% of test inputs, and logits alone yield about 94%. Protecting both assets therefore requires that no value that depends on the adapter be revealed throughout training. We present VeilTune, to the best of our knowledge the first protocol that fine-tunes a pretrained language model with backpropagation entirely in secure multi-party computation (MPC). VeilTune computes only what the loss depends on, replaces generic MPC operators with training-aware nonlinear operators that stay accurate on the values that training produces, and obliviously skips the steps corrupted by truncation failures. On four few-shot tasks with RoBERTa-large, VeilTune nearly matches plaintext training and is 5.3 points more accurate on average than SecP-Tuning, the state-of-the-art secure fine-tuning protocol. On SST-2, it achieves a 3.5x end-to-end speedup and a 3.6x reduction in communication over SecP-Tuning, and 26x and 17x over full fine-tuning in MPC.

AI.tldr: VeilTune is a secure multi-party computation protocol that fine-tunes a pretrained language model with backpropagation entirely in MPC, so neither the data owner nor the provider learns adapter-dependent values during LoRA training.
AI.motivation: Existing secure fine-tuning protocols protect the samples but reveal intermediate values such as hidden representations or logits, and one step's hidden representations of 32 samples let the data owner copy the adapter with 99.2% agreement on test inputs.
AI.method: VeilTune computes only what the loss depends on, replaces generic MPC operators with training-aware nonlinear operators accurate on training-time values, and obliviously skips steps corrupted by truncation failures.
AI.result: On four few-shot tasks with RoBERTa-large, VeilTune nearly matches plaintext training and is 5.3 points more accurate on average than SecP-Tuning. On SST-2 it gives a 3.5x end-to-end speedup and 3.6x less communication than SecP-Tuning, and 26x and 17x over full fine-tuning in MPC.
AI.conclusion: Fully MPC-based backpropagation is practical for LoRA fine-tuning of pretrained language models and closes the leakage of adapter information that partial secure protocols leave open.

title: Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids (DASH): Latency-Agnostic Scaling of Vision-Language-Action Models for Humanoid Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a vision-language backbone with an action head, but in closed-loop control the backbone sits on the control-critical path: while it computes, the robot keeps moving, so each executed action is conditioned on an increasingly stale observation. A larger backbone therefore directly blocks reactivity, especially in humanoid dexterous manipulation. We present DASH, a Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids that removes this coupling. DASH splits the policy into a slow vision-language model (System 2) and a fast flow-matching action head (System 1) that run as concurrent processes over the LCM communication protocol, so the control rate is set by the action head alone, independent of backbone size. The action head fuses stale semantics from a frozen backbone with fresh vision from its own ResNet encoder, desynchronized training exposes it to the staleness it meets at deployment, and an adaptive temporal aggregator aligns overlapping action chunks under variable inference latency. On an asynchronous RoboTwin benchmark that charges inference latency in simulated time, DASH holds 20 Hz control rate from 0.8B to 8B backbones while the synchronous rate falls from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz, with higher success at every size. On a real humanoid with dexterous hands, DASH achieves clearly higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline.

AI.tldr: DASH decouples a slow vision-language model (System 2) from a fast flow-matching action head (System 1) that run as concurrent processes, so the robot's control rate depends only on the action head and not on backbone size.
AI.motivation: In closed-loop VLA control the backbone sits on the control-critical path, so larger backbones make each executed action condition on stale observations and reduce reactivity, which matters most for humanoid dexterous manipulation.
AI.method: The two systems run concurrently over the LCM protocol. The action head fuses stale semantics from a frozen backbone with fresh vision from its own ResNet encoder, is trained with desynchronised exposure to the staleness it meets at deployment, and uses an adaptive temporal aggregator to align overlapping action chunks under variable inference latency.
AI.result: On an asynchronous RoboTwin benchmark that charges inference latency in simulated time, DASH holds a 20 Hz control rate from 0.8B to 8B backbones, while the synchronous rate falls from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz, with higher success at every size. On a real dexterous humanoid, DASH achieves clearly higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling the backbone from the control loop removes the latency penalty of scaling VLA backbones for humanoid manipulation.

title: Harness Matters: Measuring and Dissecting Security Resilience in Web Agents
summary: Web agents extend LLMs from text generation to real-world web interaction by relying on execution harnesses that interpret user goals, perceive webpages, plan actions, and ground model decisions into browser operations. While prior work has recognized that agent security depends on more than the backend model alone, how harness design quantitatively shapes web-agent security remains insufficiently measured. To systematically study web-agent harness security, we first characterize web-agent harnesses as a four-stage execution workflow covering goal interpretation, webpage perception, reasoning and planning, and action execution. Based on this abstraction, we build WebTrap Farm, a systematic and extensible evaluation framework covering three representative attack categories: malicious user prompts, malicious prompt injection, and deceptive web design. To avoid conflating security with task capability, we use paired usability calibration tasks to separate genuine defensive behavior from capability limitations. Our evaluation shows that existing web-agent harnesses remain vulnerable to typical attacks, with some unsafe behaviors occurring even without explicit attack content, revealing harness-intrinsic security failures (RQ1). Statistical analysis further shows that both harness and backend model significantly affect security outcomes, indicating that deployed-agent security is jointly shaped by the harness and backend model (RQ2). Finally, we localize where defensive behavior emerges across workflow stages and identify more secure design mechanisms, providing actionable guidance for building more robust web agents (RQ3). These findings highlight the web-agent harness as an important security boundary and motivate moving beyond model-centric defenses toward harness-level security design.

AI.tldr: WebTrap Farm is an evaluation framework that measures how the execution harness of a web agent, as well as its backend model, shapes security against malicious prompts, prompt injection and deceptive web design.
AI.motivation: Prior work recognised that agent security depends on more than the backend model, but how harness design quantitatively affects web-agent security was not measured.
AI.method: The authors characterise web-agent harnesses as a four-stage workflow of goal interpretation, webpage perception, reasoning and planning, and action execution. They build WebTrap Farm covering three attack categories and use paired usability calibration tasks to separate genuine defensive behaviour from capability limits, then run statistical analysis over harnesses and backend models.
AI.result: Existing harnesses remain vulnerable to typical attacks, and some unsafe behaviours occur even without explicit attack content. Both harness and backend model significantly affect security outcomes. The authors also localise where defensive behaviour emerges across workflow stages and identify more secure design mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: The web-agent harness is an important security boundary, and the authors argue for moving beyond model-centric defences toward harness-level security design.

title: Thermo-VLA: A Thermal-Aware Vision-Language-Action Model with Gated Residual Modulation for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have begun incorporating thermal sensing, but existing approaches typically treat thermal images as ordinary visual inputs, providing limited support for temperature-aware relational reasoning in manipulation. To address this limitation, we propose Thermo-VLA with a ThermoRes Encoder, which decomposes thermal images into cold and hot attribute representations and injects them into the RGB token through language-conditioned residual modulation, enabling temperature-driven target selection and continuous manipulation. We further construct six real-world robotic tasks on a dual-arm Unitree G1 platform, spanning basic grounding to relational reasoning. Experiments show that Thermo-VLA achieves an average success rate of 0.86 across four thermal-dependent tasks, outperforming a pi_0.5 baseline that directly incorporates RGB-thermal observations by 18 percentage points. Under unseen-object and scene variations, Thermo-VLA maintains an average success rate of 0.78, achieving the best generalisation performance among the compared methods. Beyond thermal sensing, we transfer the same residual modulation mechanism to colour attributes and observe consistent improvements in both simulation and real-robot experiments, indicating its potential to generalise beyond thermal attributes. Project website: this https URL

AI.tldr: Thermo-VLA is a vision-language-action model that encodes thermal images into cold and hot attribute representations and injects them into RGB tokens via language-conditioned residual modulation, enabling temperature-driven target selection and manipulation. It reaches an average success rate of 0.86 on four thermal-dependent tasks, 18 percentage points above a pi_0.5 baseline using RGB-thermal input.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models that use thermal sensing treat thermal images as ordinary visual inputs, which gives limited support for temperature-aware relational reasoning in manipulation.
AI.method: A ThermoRes Encoder decomposes thermal images into cold and hot attribute representations and injects them into the RGB token stream through language-conditioned residual modulation. Six real-world tasks on a dual-arm Unitree G1 range from basic grounding to relational reasoning.
AI.result: Average success is 0.86 across four thermal-dependent tasks, versus a pi_0.5 baseline that directly takes RGB-thermal observations, which is 18 percentage points lower. Under unseen-object and scene variations the average success is 0.78, the best generalisation among compared methods. The same residual modulation applied to colour attributes gives consistent gains in simulation and on a real robot.
AI.conclusion: Residual modulation of attribute representations is a mechanism that may generalise beyond thermal attributes, not only to thermal sensing.

title: Grasp-Taxonomy Conditioning as a Mode Switch for Dexterous Grasping of Climbing Holds
summary: Dexterous grasping in robotics relies on distinct hand configurations depending on object geometry. We introduce BetaGrasp, a 3D diffusion policy that conditions a DP3-style point-cloud policy on a four-class grasp label (crimp, sloper, pinch, and jug), running on a Franka arm with a 16-DoF LEAP hand. We also introduce a climbing-hold benchmark: a spring testbed whose ratchet gives a slip-force reading in newtons. In our analysis the policy's point-cloud encoder did not separate the four holds, so the scan alone gave it little to choose a grasp from. Without the label (a DP3-style baseline), simulated rollouts from the robot's reset pose all end in a jug grasp, whatever the hold (25% correct grasp type, versus 94% for BetaGrasp). The label works as a switch for which grasp the policy performs. On 80 paired hardware trials, BetaGrasp raises average slip force from 9.6 N to 14.3 N, and grasps slipping fully off the hold drop from 44% of trials to 10%.

AI.tldr: BetaGrasp is a 3D diffusion policy that conditions a DP3-style point-cloud policy on a four-class grasp label (crimp, sloper, pinch, jug) for dexterous grasping of climbing holds on a Franka arm with a LEAP hand. The label acts as a switch that selects the grasp type and raises average slip force from 9.6 N to 14.3 N in hardware trials.
AI.motivation: Dexterous grasping depends on hand configurations that vary with object geometry, but the point-cloud encoder of the policy did not separate the four climbing holds, so the scan alone gave little basis for choosing a grasp.
AI.method: The policy conditions a DP3-style point-cloud diffusion policy on a four-class grasp-type label. A climbing-hold benchmark uses a spring testbed whose ratchet gives a slip-force reading in newtons.
AI.result: In simulation, a DP3-style baseline without the label always produced a jug grasp from the reset pose (25% correct grasp type), versus 94% for BetaGrasp. On 80 paired hardware trials, average slip force rose from 9.6 N to 14.3 N, and grasps that slipped fully off the hold fell from 44% to 10% of trials.
AI.conclusion: The grasp-type label controls which grasp the policy performs, so explicit grasp-type conditioning can supply the mode choice that the point-cloud encoder did not learn from the scan.

title: Feeling Easier, Working Harder: Cognitive Load in AI-Assisted Code Comprehension
summary: Software developers spend significant time reading and understanding code, increasingly supplemented by generative AI. While these tools aim to reduce the difficulty of reading code, interacting with them introduces a dual-task environment that may impose extraneous cognitive load that is challenging to capture. This study investigates how access to generative AI affects developers' real-time cognitive workload, code comprehension performance, and self-perceived code comprehension strategies. We conducted a 3x2 within-subjects study with 20 novice CS students reviewing Java code snippets of varying lengths with or without AI assistance, followed by an AI-unassisted comprehension quiz. Cognitive workload was continuously captured using a Detection-Response Task (tDRT) during both reading and quiz phases, and compared to post-quiz NASA-TLX and SEQ scores. AI assistance significantly increased objective cognitive workload, raising tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, yet participants' perceived workload remained unchanged. Code comprehension scores were high under both conditions, with no evidence that AI assistance improved comprehension at the difficulty levels evaluated; a ceiling effect limited power to detect benefits on harder tasks. Qualitatively, participants reported trusting the AI conditionally -verifying its output against their own reading for more complex snippets, but directly trusting it for simpler code- and, while many felt their reading process was unchanged, a notable subset shifted toward skimming or reading the AI's explanations in place of the code itself. These findings reveal that developers do not accurately perceive the cognitive resources they expend when managing AI tools. This study provides evidence of added cognitive effort associated with using generative AI, pointing towards a need to account for this dual-task penalty in software engineering tools and education.

AI.tldr: A within-subjects study with 20 novice CS students finds that generative AI assistance raises objective cognitive workload during Java code comprehension, with reaction times up 11.2%, while perceived workload stays unchanged and comprehension does not improve. Developers therefore do not accurately perceive the cognitive resources they spend on AI tools.
AI.motivation: Generative AI is meant to reduce the difficulty of reading code, but using it creates a dual-task environment that may add extraneous cognitive load that is hard to capture.
AI.method: A 3x2 within-subjects design had 20 novice students review Java snippets of varying lengths with or without AI assistance, followed by an AI-unassisted comprehension quiz. Workload was measured continuously with a Detection-Response Task (tDRT), and compared with post-quiz NASA-TLX and SEQ scores.
AI.result: AI assistance significantly raised tDRT reaction times by 11.2%, while NASA-TLX perceived workload was unchanged. Comprehension scores were high in both conditions, with no evidence that AI improved comprehension, and a ceiling effect limited power on harder tasks. Participants trusted AI conditionally, verifying it on complex snippets, and a notable subset shifted toward skimming or reading the AI explanation instead of the code.
AI.conclusion: Using generative AI carries an added cognitive cost that users do not perceive, so software engineering tools and education should account for this dual-task penalty.

title: Perils and opportunities of AI for public climate services
summary: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative and machine-learning systems, in climate services development and provision is transforming how climate information is produced, accessed, and interpreted. AI-enabled climate services offer significant opportunities for process automation, optimisation, tailoring, and the translation of complex climate data into actionable knowledge for diverse users. However, the growing reliance on privately controlled algorithms, data infrastructures, and computing facilities raises critical concerns related to governance, transparency, equity and economic sustainability, among others. While the technical architecture of climate services increasingly relies on advanced machine learning and large-scale climate models, their legitimacy as public services may be weakened in the absence of arrangements that prioritise public value and long-lasting societal benefit over profit maximisation. The tension between the public mandate of climate services and the private nature of AI infrastructure challenges traditional notions of openness. Using a consensus-based elicitation method coupled with the PESTLE framework, we analyse the political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental risks and opportunities shaping the co-production value chain of AI-enabled climate services. We draw policy-relevant conclusions for data, model and infrastructure supporting the next generation of upstream and downstream climate services as critical applications for society. Our work presents potential and plausible challenges and benefits for a pan-European, decentralised public climate service built on sovereign AI infrastructure and open governance principles.

AI.tldr: The paper analyses the political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental risks and opportunities of AI-enabled climate services using a consensus-based elicitation method with the PESTLE framework. It concludes that a pan-European, decentralised public climate service built on sovereign AI infrastructure and open governance could address these concerns.
AI.motivation: AI is changing how climate services are produced and delivered, but reliance on privately controlled algorithms, data infrastructure and computing raises governance, transparency, equity and sustainability concerns that conflict with the public mandate of climate services.
AI.method: A consensus-based elicitation method combined with the PESTLE framework is used to analyse risks and opportunities across the co-production value chain of AI-enabled climate services.
AI.result: The abstract reports potential and plausible challenges and benefits for a pan-European, decentralised public climate service built on sovereign AI infrastructure. It does not report quantitative findings.
AI.conclusion: Policy-relevant conclusions are drawn for the data, model and infrastructure that will support upstream and downstream climate services, with public value and open governance prioritised over profit.

title: Transactional Data Change for Real-Time Analytics in Lakehouses
comment: Accepted by VLDB 2026 and to be published on PVLDB Vol.19 No.13, 14 pages, 16 figures
summary: Real-time data analytics has become a key demand for lakehouses. It requires propagating data changes from the data source to the lakehouse in real time, while ensuring ACID guarantees and minimizing resource consumption and impact on analytical query performance. This is highly challenging for a data system according to the RUM conjecture, especially given the read-optimized immutable file storage layer in lakehouses. Existing lakehouses offer only git-style catalog version control on a single table, and they trade data freshness, query performance, and/or resource efficiency to achieve a barely acceptable data-change throughput. In this paper, we propose a novel data synchronization framework, Retina, that enables real-time, cost-efficient, query-performant, and fully transactional data changes in lakehouses. We implement and open-source Retina. Evaluations show that Retina delivers 10-millisecond-level data freshness and over 3.2 million row/s linear-scalable data-change throughput with low resource consumption and query-performance overhead, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art lakehouse systems and lake-compatible HTAP databases.

AI.tldr: Retina is a data synchronisation framework for lakehouses that propagates data changes in real time with full ACID transactions. It achieves 10-millisecond-level data freshness and over 3.2 million rows per second of linearly scalable change throughput, outperforming state-of-the-art lakehouse systems and lake-compatible HTAP databases.
AI.motivation: Real-time analytics needs data changes propagated into lakehouses under ACID guarantees, but read-optimised immutable file storage makes this hard. Existing lakehouses offer only git-style version control on a single table and trade off freshness, query performance or resource efficiency for barely acceptable change throughput.
AI.method: Retina is a new synchronisation framework designed to deliver real-time, cost-efficient, query-performant and fully transactional data changes in lakehouses. The authors implement it and open-source it.
AI.result: Evaluations show 10-millisecond-level data freshness and over 3.2 million row/s linearly scalable data-change throughput, with low resource consumption and query-performance overhead. It significantly outperforms state-of-the-art lakehouse systems and lake-compatible HTAP databases.
AI.conclusion: Fully transactional real-time change propagation into lakehouses can be achieved without the usual trade-offs among freshness, query performance and efficiency.

title: GeoMind: A Benchmark for Spatial Understanding in Robotic Manipulation
summary: Robotic manipulation has advanced rapidly in mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions. However, reliable manipulation in open-world environments requires robust spatial understanding: the ability to identify targets in complex layouts (spatial reasoning) and adapt to scenes that continuously evolve through interaction (spatial memory). Yet existing embodied benchmarks fall short in evaluating spatial understanding: they often introduce strong visual cues that bypass spatial reasoning, and focus on static scenes that offer little insight into an agent's capacity for spatial memory. To address this gap, we introduce GeoMind, a systematic benchmark for structured spatial understanding through tabletop manipulation. GeoMind comprises 54 evaluated task variants organized around spatial reasoning and spatial memory. It also incorporates a scalable pipeline that automates the generation and annotation of task instances with verified targets and executable interactions. Extensive evaluations across diverse embodied agents reveal their consistent weaknesses in spatial understanding. Our findings highlight that these agents struggle to track identities after spatial changes and convert relational or geometric constraints into executable actions. We release the GeoMind benchmark at this https URL.

AI.tldr: GeoMind is a benchmark of 54 tabletop manipulation task variants for evaluating spatial understanding, covering spatial reasoning and spatial memory, with an automated pipeline that generates and annotates verified task instances. Evaluations show that diverse embodied agents consistently struggle to track identities after spatial changes and to turn relational or geometric constraints into executable actions.
AI.motivation: Existing embodied benchmarks often include strong visual cues that bypass spatial reasoning and focus on static scenes, so they give little insight into spatial memory.
AI.method: The authors build GeoMind around spatial reasoning and spatial memory in tabletop manipulation, with 54 evaluated task variants. A scalable pipeline automates the generation and annotation of task instances with verified targets and executable interactions.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations across diverse embodied agents reveal consistent weaknesses in spatial understanding. Agents struggle to track identities after spatial changes and to convert relational or geometric constraints into executable actions.
AI.conclusion: Current embodied agents lack reliable structured spatial understanding, and GeoMind is released as a benchmark to measure it.

title: Embodied First Exam
summary: Early successes on agentic robotics point to a potential paradigm shift toward using coding agents to control robots. Existing robotics benchmarks are built around visuomotor policy learning, leaving it open whether coding agents can reliably control diverse robots under physical-world constraints. We therefore introduce the Embodied First Exam, a unified, comprehensive, and agent-native evaluation framework where coding agents can choose their own control approach: direct control, code to control, or train a policy to control. We hope it serves as a first exam for coding agents before they enter the physical world, with 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 robots, including 9 new suites that go beyond pick-and-place to spatial puzzles, dexterous manipulation, multi-robot interaction, dynamic whole-body control, and sim-to-sim engineering. Each task can be run in up to three evaluation settings. The Standard Setting mimics the real world: the agent receives only sensor observations and, by default, cannot reset the environment. Its Realtime variant keeps the environment running while the agent reasons. The Privileged Setting gives the agent access to the full simulator state and unlimited resets, allowing it to search for an oracle solution for training purposes. Success rates in this setting serve as an approximate upper bound. On the 456 core tasks, the strongest of eight agents, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, achieves a success rate of 34% in the Standard Setting, leaving much room for improvement. To see where agents fail, we label the stage at which failed attempts go wrong and compare failures across agents, settings, and stage categories.

AI.tldr: The Embodied First Exam is an agent-native benchmark of 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 robots, where coding agents may choose direct control, code-to-control or policy training. The strongest of eight agents, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, reaches a 34% success rate on the 456 core tasks in the Standard Setting.
AI.motivation: Robotics benchmarks are built around visuomotor policy learning, so it is unclear whether coding agents can reliably control diverse robots under physical-world constraints.
AI.method: The framework lets agents pick their own control approach (direct control, code to control, or train a policy). Nine new suites cover spatial puzzles, dexterous manipulation, multi-robot interaction, dynamic whole-body control and sim-to-sim engineering. Each task can run in up to three settings: a Standard Setting with sensor observations only and no default resets, a Realtime variant where the environment keeps running, and a Privileged Setting with full simulator state and unlimited resets.
AI.result: On the 456 core tasks the strongest of eight agents, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, achieves 34% success in the Standard Setting. The Privileged Setting success rates are reported as an approximate upper bound. Failed attempts are labelled by the stage where they go wrong and compared across agents, settings and stage categories.
AI.conclusion: Coding agents are not yet reliable for controlling robots in the physical world, with much room for improvement, and the benchmark is meant as a first exam before they enter the physical world.

title: Graph-Based RL for Sequential Rendezvous Planning with Multiple Patrolling USVs
summary: In patrol missions involving multiple unmanned surface vehicles (USVs), a designated command USV can support fleet management by sequentially rendezvousing with each patrolling USV. These operations require motion-feasible route planning and priority-aware rendezvous sequencing, with the objective of minimizing mission completion time and total tardiness relative to priority-dependent due dates. We propose a framework combining grid-based path planning, surrogate travel-time prediction, and graph-based reinforcement learning. The path planner accounts for ocean currents and approximates turn-rate constraints through multi-stage maneuvers, with path feasibility empirically validated through trajectory-tracking simulations. For rendezvous sequencing, a Feasible Transition Graph (FTG) represents candidate rendezvous events and temporally feasible transitions, enabling a graph neural network to exploit spatiotemporal rendezvous relationships for policy learning. A surrogate predicts travel times from compact current and motion features to avoid repeated path searches during FTG construction and policy training. Evaluation using grid-based path planning shows statistically significant average objective reductions of 10.5%, 3.5%, and 1.5% compared with greedy, MLP-RL, and 2-step lookahead greedy, respectively. The policy achieves these improvements while requiring approximately 1/35 of the latter's computation time. It maintains its advantage over MLP-RL under unseen priority-tier settings, with larger gains as fleet size increases.

AI.tldr: A framework combines grid-based path planning, a surrogate travel-time predictor and graph-based reinforcement learning to sequence rendezvous between a command USV and multiple patrolling USVs. It reduces the average objective by 10.5%, 3.5% and 1.5% relative to greedy, MLP-RL and 2-step lookahead greedy, at about 1/35 of the computation time of the last of these.
AI.motivation: A command USV must rendezvous sequentially with patrolling USVs under motion feasibility and priority-dependent due dates, minimising completion time and total tardiness, which requires route planning and sequencing that also respect ocean currents and turn-rate limits.
AI.method: A grid-based path planner accounts for ocean currents and approximates turn-rate constraints with multi-stage manoeuvres. A Feasible Transition Graph represents candidate rendezvous events and temporally feasible transitions, and a graph neural network learns the policy over it. A surrogate predicts travel times from compact current and motion features to avoid repeated path searches.
AI.result: The policy reduces the objective by 10.5%, 3.5% and 1.5% against greedy, MLP-RL and 2-step lookahead greedy respectively, with statistical significance reported. It needs about 1/35 of the 2-step lookahead computation time, keeps its advantage over MLP-RL under unseen priority tiers, and gains more as fleet size grows.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based reinforcement learning over feasible rendezvous transitions is an effective and efficient approach to sequencing rendezvous in multi-USV patrol missions.

title: Be My Eye: Learning to See Beyond a Robot's Own Perspective
summary: Robots operating in the real world are inherently subject to partial observability, particularly in multi-robot collaboration, where individual observations may be insufficient for effective task execution. A key challenge is leveraging complementary observations from partner robots to support collaborative decision-making. We argue that information sharing should go beyond passively transmitting raw observations or generic visual features. Instead, robots should selectively encode task-relevant information according to task objectives and execution progress. To this end, we propose a task-oriented active context sharing framework that transforms robot observations into compact representations, preserving critical information under constrained communication budgets. The framework adopts a two-stage training paradigm. In the first stage, onboard observations and task instructions are jointly encoded into compact context representations. Task-oriented future prediction and soft task-progress correspondence learning guide this collaboration-agnostic compression, preserving information about task objectives and execution progress. In the second stage, the learned representations are integrated into a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy, enabling bidirectional context exchange. Each robot combines complementary partner information with local observations to guide action generation. Action supervision jointly refines the context representations and policy, aligning information sharing with collaborative decision-making. Controlled experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains under constrained communication budgets, while three real-world experiments validate the framework in complex dual-robot tasks. These results highlight a shift from passive visual transmission toward active, task-oriented context sharing that directly supports collaborative decision-making.

AI.tldr: Be My Eye is a task-oriented active context sharing framework in which robots compress their observations into compact, task-relevant representations for partner robots under constrained communication budgets. The representations are integrated into a pretrained Vision-Language-Action policy, which yields substantial gains in controlled experiments and in three real-world dual-robot tasks.
AI.motivation: Partially observable multi-robot collaboration needs complementary observations from partners, but passively sending raw observations or generic visual features is inefficient, and robots should instead encode information according to task objectives and execution progress.
AI.method: Stage one jointly encodes onboard observations and task instructions into compact context representations, guided by task-oriented future prediction and soft task-progress correspondence learning. Stage two integrates these representations into a pretrained VLA policy for bidirectional context exchange, with action supervision refining both the context and the policy.
AI.result: Controlled experiments show substantial performance gains under constrained communication budgets, and three real-world dual-robot experiments validate the framework on complex tasks. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Information sharing moves from passive visual transmission to active, task-oriented context sharing that directly supports collaborative decision-making.

title: RecoGEM: A Serving System for Production-Scale Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation (GR) is moving industrial recommender systems (RecSys) from scoring candidate items to autoregressively generating item identifiers. This shift promises higher recommendation quality, but makes serving substantially harder: each request executes a short sequence of dependent decoding steps that explore a large item space and select promising candidates on the latency-critical path. GR not only creates structural mismatches with conventional RecSys pipelines, but also challenges the architectural and optimization assumptions of LLM serving stacks, making direct adoption of existing systems difficult. We present RecoGEM, our production GR serving system. RecoGEM uses a runtime--engine decoupling architecture to move GR-specific serving responsibilities, such as candidate-state transitions and live artifact updates, to a dedicated runtime. Its execution engine exploits GR's short token sequences, large candidate populations, and predictable step shapes to optimize self-attention, candidate selection, and execution planning. RecoGEM has been deployed for over nine months across our production lines, serving applications with hundreds of millions of users and supporting more than ten GR model families. On our OneModel production workloads, RecoGEM reaches over 1,000 QPS per serving instance with P99 latency below 35 ms and a 2.88$\times$ throughput improvement over representative baselines.

AI.tldr: RecoGEM is a production serving system for generative recommendation that decouples the runtime from the execution engine and optimises self-attention, candidate selection and execution planning for short, dependent decoding steps. On OneModel workloads it exceeds 1,000 QPS per instance with P99 latency below 35 ms and 2.88x throughput over representative baselines.
AI.motivation: Generative recommendation generates item identifiers autoregressively, which makes serving much harder than scoring candidates. It breaks the assumptions of conventional recommender pipelines and of LLM serving stacks, so existing systems are hard to adopt directly.
AI.method: RecoGEM uses a runtime-engine decoupling architecture that moves GR-specific responsibilities such as candidate-state transitions and live artifact updates to a dedicated runtime. Its execution engine exploits short token sequences, large candidate populations and predictable step shapes.
AI.result: On OneModel production workloads RecoGEM reaches over 1,000 QPS per serving instance with P99 latency below 35 ms and a 2.88x throughput improvement over representative baselines. It has been deployed for over nine months across production lines, serving applications with hundreds of millions of users and more than ten GR model families.
AI.conclusion: A GR-specific serving architecture is practical at production scale, and the paper frames runtime-engine decoupling as the key design choice.

title: Do Machine Learning Models Predict?
summary: Machine learning (ML) models are said to predict. Philosophers draw a line between accommodation and prediction, depending on whether or not the evidence a theory succeeds on was used in constructing it. Does this distinction survive when a theory is replaced by an ML model? We argue so, yet the dividing line becomes fuzzy. Whether an output of an ML model counts as an accommodation or as a prediction hinges upon the relationship between the patterns the input instantiate and those on which the model was selected through its training. Once this relation is taken into account, most successful outputs of ML models, we suggest, bear a strong accommodation character. We further trace the consequences of our account for confirmation, novelty, and scientific realism.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the philosophical distinction between accommodation and prediction survives when theories are replaced by ML models, but the dividing line becomes fuzzy. Most successful ML outputs therefore bear a strong accommodation character, which has consequences for confirmation, novelty and scientific realism.
AI.motivation: Philosophers separate accommodation (evidence used in building a theory) from prediction (evidence not used). It is unclear whether this distinction still applies when an ML model replaces the theory.
AI.method: The argument proceeds conceptually. Whether an ML output counts as accommodation or prediction depends on the relation between the patterns the input instantiates and those on which the model was selected during training.
AI.result: Once that relation is considered, most successful outputs of ML models bear a strong accommodation character. The paper also traces implications for confirmation, novelty and scientific realism.
AI.conclusion: Successful ML models should often be understood as accommodating rather than predicting, which bears on how their successes confirm theories and support realism.

title: UniOMA: Unified Optimal-Transport Multi-Modal Structural Alignment for Robot Perception
summary: Achieving generalizable and well-aligned multimodal representations remains a core challenge in robot learning. While recent approaches have attempted to align modalities by modeling conditional or higher-order statistical dependencies, they do not explicitly consider the structural coherence across modalities. In this work, we propose a novel multimodal alignment method that augments existing contrastive losses with a geometry-aware Gromov--Wasserstein (GW) distance-based regularization. To this end, we encode intra-modal geometry for each modality and reduce cross-modal structural discrepancies through a dynamically learned GW barycenter, thereby encouraging structural consistency in addition to instance-level contrastive alignment. We apply this optimal-transport-based alignment strategy to robot perception tasks involving underexplored modalities such as force and tactile signals, where modality data often exhibit varying sample densities. Extensive experiments on five robotic benchmarks show that our method improves structural alignment and downstream performance over state-of-the-art multimodal contrastive baselines across a wide range of downstream tasks, including robot and environment state prediction. Moreover, our GW-based regularization can be seamlessly integrated into most InfoNCE-like objectives.

AI.tldr: UniOMA adds a geometry-aware Gromov-Wasserstein distance regulariser to contrastive multimodal alignment, using a dynamically learned GW barycenter to keep structure consistent across modalities. It improves structural alignment and downstream performance on five robotic benchmarks, especially for force and tactile signals, and can be added to most InfoNCE-like objectives.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal alignment methods model conditional or higher-order dependencies but do not explicitly enforce structural coherence across modalities, which matters for underexplored modalities such as force and tactile signals with uneven sample densities.
AI.method: Intra-modal geometry is encoded for each modality, and cross-modal structural discrepancies are reduced through a dynamically learned Gromov-Wasserstein barycenter. This GW regularisation is added to instance-level contrastive alignment.
AI.result: Experiments on five robotic benchmarks show improved structural alignment and downstream performance over state-of-the-art multimodal contrastive baselines across tasks including robot and environment state prediction. The regularisation integrates into most InfoNCE-like objectives. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Optimal-transport-based structural regularisation is a general and seamless addition to contrastive multimodal learning for robot perception.

title: Clinical predictions using artificial intelligence in neurosurgery and its subspecialties: a systematic review and meta-analysis
summary: Artificial intelligence models for clinical prediction are proliferating across neurosurgery, but their aggregate discriminative performance, distribution along the care pathway and methodological quality are unclear. We systematically reviewed and meta-analysed these studies in neurosurgery and its subspecialities along with their risk of bias appraisal. We performed a PRISMA search for peer-reviewed original studies using AI to predict a clinical outcome in neurosurgical populations. Metrics were pooled using random effects modelling. Each study was classified as diagnostic, prognostic or forecasting and was assigned an evidence level. Clinical prediction task sub-stratification analysis was performed. Risk-of-bias was assessed using PROBAST. 1063 studies were included. Across 451 studies reporting AUC, pooled discrimination was 0.86, ranging from 0.84 (spine) to 0.87 (neuro-oncology), with extreme heterogeneity. Performance varied by clinical pathway stage, highest for diagnosis, grading and molecular tasks and lowest for post-operative tasks. Only 51 studies were using prospective data with external validation, whereas 619 rested on internal validation alone or no validation. 89 percent studies were at high risk-of-bias, driven by the analysis domain. AI models report high performance across all the neurosurgical subspecialities, concordant across AUC, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity and robust to risk-of-bias stratification. Performance is highest for imaging-anchored diagnostic tasks and lowest at decision-facing post-operative stage. However, the literature is dominated by optimism-prone, internally-validated and poorly calibrated models with extreme heterogeneity. External validation, calibration analysis and reporting guidelines adherence remain prerequisites for clinical adoption.

AI.tldr: A systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of 1063 studies finds that AI clinical prediction models in neurosurgery pool to an AUC of 0.86, with extreme heterogeneity, and that most studies are at high risk of bias and rest on internal validation alone. Performance is highest for imaging-anchored diagnostic tasks and lowest for post-operative tasks.
AI.motivation: The aggregate discriminative performance, care-pathway distribution and methodological quality of AI clinical prediction studies across neurosurgery and its subspecialties were unclear.
AI.method: A PRISMA search identified peer-reviewed original studies that use AI to predict clinical outcomes in neurosurgical populations. Metrics were pooled with random-effects modelling, each study was classified as diagnostic, prognostic or forecasting and assigned an evidence level, and risk of bias was appraised with PROBAST.
AI.result: Across 451 studies reporting AUC, pooled discrimination was 0.86, ranging from 0.84 (spine) to 0.87 (neuro-oncology), with extreme heterogeneity. Performance was highest for diagnosis, grading and molecular tasks and lowest for post-operative tasks. Only 51 studies used prospective data with external validation, while 619 relied on internal validation alone or none. 89% of studies were at high risk of bias, driven by the analysis domain.
AI.conclusion: Reported performance is high but dominated by optimism-prone, internally validated and poorly calibrated models, so external validation, calibration analysis and reporting-guideline adherence are prerequisites for clinical adoption.

title: Say Shibboleth: Fingerprinting the LLMs and Harnesses Behind Agentic Attacks
summary: We study the fingerprinting of agentic cyberattacks. Our objective is to reliably infer information about the attacker's configuration, such as LLM version and harness, from telemetry. To achieve this, we introduce a technique we call shibboleth traps: modular honeypot services designed to elicit discriminative behaviors from agentic attackers. The traps make informative interactions a condition for obtaining resources the agent seeks, eliciting model declarations and characteristic writing without requiring a successful prompt injection. To achieve harness fingerprinting, we introduce general mechanisms to indirectly probe peculiar execution behaviors of harnesses. These probes reveal how a harness masks secrets in tool output, enforces command time limits, and schedules tool calls, using only the effects visible in subsequent requests. We show that combined declarative and behavioral inference distinguishes among 15 candidate models with an average 90% top-1 accuracy, with behavioral classifiers evaluated on held-out harnesses or task families. In a separate experiment across four harnesses, fixed probe rules identify the correct harness with 92% accuracy. When instructed to conceal their identity, agents still leave useful behavioral evidence even as their declarations become uninformative.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces shibboleth traps, modular honeypot services that make informative interactions the condition for obtaining resources, and harness probes that expose execution behaviours. Combining declarative and behavioural evidence identifies among 15 candidate models with about 90% top-1 accuracy, and fixed probe rules identify the harness with 92% accuracy across four harnesses.
AI.motivation: Telemetry from agentic cyberattacks can reveal the attacker's configuration, such as LLM version and harness, which would help attribution and defence, but this needs reliable fingerprinting.
AI.method: Shibboleth traps are honeypot services designed to elicit model declarations and characteristic writing from agentic attackers without requiring a successful prompt injection. Harness fingerprinting probes how a harness masks secrets in tool output, enforces command time limits and schedules tool calls, using only effects visible in subsequent requests.
AI.result: Combined declarative and behavioural inference distinguishes 15 candidate models with an average 90% top-1 accuracy, with behavioural classifiers evaluated on held-out harnesses or task families. In a separate experiment across four harnesses, fixed probe rules identify the correct harness with 92% accuracy. When agents are told to conceal their identity, their declarations become uninformative but behavioural evidence remains.
AI.conclusion: Behavioural evidence is hard for attackers to hide, so telemetry can support fingerprinting of agentic attackers even when they conceal their declared identity.

title: Bridging Task Planning and Execution for Language-Conditioned Bimanual Manipulation
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE-RAS International Conference on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids 2026). Equal contribution by the first two authors
summary: Robots are increasingly expected to execute natural-language manipulation tasks in real-world environments. This is particularly relevant in household assistance and logistics, where clutter requires reasoning about both task objectives and execution feasibility. This challenge becomes even more pronounced for bimanual humanoid platforms, where coordinating two manipulators introduces additional interaction and kinematic constraints. We present a zero-shot vision-language framework for execution-aware bimanual manipulation that jointly reasons about task objectives and physical feasibility. Planning is grounded in a structured scene representation that combines semantic object relations with execution constraints, enabling the selection of obstacle relocations and execution choices while preserving task semantics. Compatible actions are organised into parallel bimanual stages with explicit pre- and post-conditions. A hierarchical validator evaluates these conditions under perceptual uncertainty and uses stage-level execution history to support local recovery or targeted replanning. Experiments on the CENTAURO hybrid wheeled-legged humanoid robot across nine language-conditioned manipulation scenarios show higher task success than a non-execution-aware baseline. In dedicated failure scenarios, hierarchical validation recovers from execution failures with fewer model queries than always replanning. These results demonstrate the benefits of combining execution reasoning directly into task planning. Videos and additional material are available on the Project Webpage: this https URL.

AI.tldr: A zero-shot vision-language framework for bimanual manipulation on the CENTAURO humanoid plans with a structured scene representation, organises actions into parallel bimanual stages with pre- and post-conditions, and uses a hierarchical validator for execution-aware recovery. It achieves higher task success than a non-execution-aware baseline across nine language-conditioned scenarios and recovers from failures with fewer model queries than always replanning.
AI.motivation: Language-conditioned manipulation in clutter requires reasoning about both task objectives and physical feasibility, which is harder for bimanual humanoids because two manipulators add interaction and kinematic constraints.
AI.method: Planning is grounded in a scene representation combining semantic object relations with execution constraints, which selects obstacle relocations and execution choices. Compatible actions are grouped into parallel bimanual stages with explicit pre- and post-conditions. A hierarchical validator checks these conditions under perceptual uncertainty and uses stage-level execution history for local recovery or targeted replanning.
AI.result: Experiments on the CENTAURO hybrid wheeled-legged humanoid across nine language-conditioned scenarios show higher task success than a non-execution-aware baseline. In dedicated failure scenarios, hierarchical validation recovers with fewer model queries than always replanning. The abstract gives no numerical success rates.
AI.conclusion: Combining execution reasoning directly into task planning benefits bimanual manipulation.

title: Physics-informed neural networks in the small-data regime: A controlled comparison with classical PDE surrogates
summary: Neural surrogates for engineering models are often trained on large collections of simulated solutions. We investigate whether physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can achieve accurate predictions from scarce labelled observations by incorporating governing equations and prescribed initial and boundary conditions. We introduce hierarchical loss weighting (H-PINN) and its gradient-direction-aware extension (HO-PINN), which adjust the emphasis on physical constraints according to higher-priority losses. Hierarchical PINNs are compared with Vanilla PINN, tuned gradient boosting, support-vector regression, and Gaussian-process regression on a heat equation and three heterogeneous two-phase-flow benchmarks. Experiments use 20--1000 labelled states and ten paired seeds. Each label is one coordinate--state observation, not a complete simulation. At least one PINN variant achieves the highest mean primary-target \(R^2\) in each interpolation and equation-assisted forecasting comparison at 20 and 50 labels. The advantage for water saturation persists across all tested budgets. Hierarchical weighting reduces variability across runs in selected settings. These results demonstrate that known physics can support accurate neural surrogate predictions from very few solution observations, at substantially higher fitting cost than the tested classical regressors.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical PINNs (H-PINN and its gradient-direction-aware extension HO-PINN) weight physical losses by priority and are compared with a vanilla PINN, gradient boosting, SVR and Gaussian-process regression on a heat equation and three two-phase-flow benchmarks with 20 to 1000 labels. At least one PINN variant achieves the highest mean primary-target R^2 in each interpolation and equation-assisted forecasting comparison at 20 and 50 labels.
AI.motivation: Neural surrogates for engineering models usually need large simulation datasets, and it is unclear whether physics-informed networks can predict accurately from scarce labelled observations.
AI.method: The authors introduce hierarchical loss weighting (H-PINN) and its gradient-direction-aware extension (HO-PINN), which adjust the emphasis on physical constraints according to higher-priority losses. Each label is a single coordinate-state observation rather than a full simulation, and results use ten paired seeds.
AI.result: At least one PINN variant has the highest mean primary-target R^2 in each interpolation and equation-assisted forecasting comparison at 20 and 50 labels. The water-saturation advantage persists across all tested budgets, and hierarchical weighting reduces run-to-run variability in selected settings. The PINNs cost substantially more to fit than the classical regressors.
AI.conclusion: Known physics can support accurate neural surrogate predictions from very few solution observations, at a higher fitting cost than classical regressors.

title: To SIMD or Not to SIMD: Comparing RVV vs. CGRA SoCs for Non-Linear Functions in AI
comment: Published in the H2RC workshop at the International Conference on High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis 2026
summary: Non-linear functions are an important class of operations in modern large language models. However, chip vendors building for AI have so far relied on traditional vector or scalar processing units for non-linear functions. The performance of these units has not kept pace with matrix multiplication units (MMUs), which can be found in both high-performance and edge-computing devices from almost every vendor. Reconfigurable units such as FPGAs and CGRAs have been proposed in the literature, but have not been systematically compared with traditional units backed by MMUs. In this paper, we build two SoCs: one using an RVV vector processor and the other using a latency-insensitive (\emph{elastic}) CGRA, both coupled with an MMU and driven by a single-core CPU. We then propose mappings for common feed-forward networks on our SoCs and find that the CGRA reaches a maximum speedup in clock cycles of 7.12x over RVV on the activation stage of simple point-wise non-linear functions like SiLU, whereas the RVV reaches a maximum speedup of \textbf{9.8x} over the CGRA on complex non-linear functions such as $\mathrm{softmax}$. Over the enclosing feed-forward block the corresponding maxima are 3.16x and 4.24x.

AI.tldr: The paper builds two SoCs, one with an RVV vector processor and one with an elastic CGRA, both coupled with an MMU, and compares them on non-linear functions in feed-forward networks. The CGRA reaches up to 7.12x speedup over RVV on point-wise functions such as SiLU, while RVV reaches up to 9.8x over the CGRA on softmax.
AI.motivation: Non-linear functions in LLMs are usually run on vector or scalar units that have not kept pace with matrix multiplication units, and reconfigurable units such as CGRAs have not been systematically compared with traditional units backed by MMUs.
AI.method: Two SoCs are built, one with an RVV vector processor and one with a latency-insensitive (elastic) CGRA, both coupled with an MMU and driven by a single-core CPU. Mappings for common feed-forward networks are proposed for both.
AI.result: In clock cycles, the CGRA reaches a maximum speedup of 7.12x over RVV on the activation stage of point-wise functions such as SiLU, while RVV reaches up to 9.8x over the CGRA on complex functions such as softmax. Over the enclosing feed-forward block the maxima are 3.16x for the CGRA and 4.24x for RVV.
AI.conclusion: The better unit depends on the function: the CGRA suits simple point-wise non-linearities and RVV suits complex ones such as softmax.

title: WaveGen: Truly End-to-End Waveform Generation via Internal Spectral Trajectory Learning
summary: This work proposes WaveGen, a fully end-to-end diffusion-based text-to-waveform framework based on Spectral Forcing, which jointly learns an internal spectral trajectory and the target waveform trajectory within a single model, enabling direct end-to-end text-to-waveform generation. Unlike recent TTS pipelines, WaveGen does not rely on separately trained or externally decoded intermediate representations, such as neural audio codecs, Mel-spectrogram vocoders, or VAE-based latent models. In addition, WaveGen performs internal text-speech alignment within a single model, eliminating the need for external alignment modules such as duration predictors. To preserve a truly end-to-end formulation, our framework further avoids dependence on self-supervised representations, such as BERT-based text embeddings and Wav2Vec 2.0-based semantic representations, as well as semantic distillation methods for training optimization. To achieve this, we carefully design Spectral Forcing, a model architecture with disentangled diffusion heads, and a training objective based on a multi-scale spectral $v$-loss. We further validate the scalability of end-to-end TTS models by scaling the model size from 0.1B to 0.6B parameters. Using a single architecture, open-source data, and one-stage training, without external modules such as duration predictor or REPA, WaveGen demonstrates fully end-to-end waveform generation achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Emilia training dataset. In particular, WaveGen achieves a WER of 1.47 and a SIM of 0.75 on the Seed-en benchmark. Source code and checkpoints are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: WaveGen is a fully end-to-end diffusion text-to-waveform model based on Spectral Forcing, which learns an internal spectral trajectory jointly with the waveform trajectory and needs no codecs, vocoders, duration predictors or self-supervised representations. It achieves a WER of 1.47 and SIM of 0.75 on the Seed-en benchmark after training on Emilia, with models scaled from 0.1B to 0.6B parameters.
AI.motivation: Recent TTS pipelines rely on separately trained or externally decoded intermediate representations, external alignment modules and self-supervised or distilled features, which stop them being truly end-to-end.
AI.method: Spectral Forcing uses a model architecture with disentangled diffusion heads, and the training objective is a multi-scale spectral v-loss. Text-speech alignment is learned internally in one model, with one architecture, open-source data and one-stage training.
AI.result: WaveGen achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Emilia training dataset, with a WER of 1.47 and SIM of 0.75 on the Seed-en benchmark. Scaling from 0.1B to 0.6B parameters is reported to validate the scalability of end-to-end TTS.
AI.conclusion: Fully end-to-end waveform generation from text is feasible with a single model and no external modules, and it scales with model size.

title: Perceived Agency During Agent-Avatar Control Transitions in Virtual Reality
summary: Prior beliefs about whether a virtual human (VH) is controlled by a human or a computer can shape how users interpret and respond to its behaviour. As emerging hybrid VH systems allow control to transfer between human operators and computer programs during an ongoing interaction, it remains unclear whether perceived agency updates with the actual controller or continues to reflect users' prior beliefs and first impressions. We investigated this question in a within-subject VR study with 24 participants across four conditions: always computer-controlled, computer-to-human, human-to-computer, and always human-controlled. We designed an interaction task in which participants acted as interviewers, asking the VHs a fixed set of questions. Before each interaction, participants were informed whether the VH was human- or computer-controlled, matching the actual controller at the beginning, but were unaware of possible control transitions.
