We found that perceived agency was strongly influenced by the controller presented at the beginning of the interaction, with no evidence of updating following the control transitions. Social evaluations including likeability and co-presence were generally higher in conditions where human control occurred later and covered a greater proportion of the interaction. The results suggest that prior beliefs and first impressions continued to shape perceived agency, whereas social evaluations were more sensitive to the VH's actual behaviour over the interaction.

AI.tldr: In a within-subject VR study with 24 participants, perceived agency of virtual humans tracked the controller shown at the start of an interaction and did not update after control transitions between human and computer. Social evaluations such as likeability and co-presence were more sensitive to the actual behaviour, being higher when human control came later and covered more of the interaction.
AI.motivation: Hybrid virtual humans can transfer control between human operators and programs mid-interaction, and it is unclear whether perceived agency updates with the actual controller or keeps reflecting prior beliefs.
AI.method: Participants acted as interviewers asking virtual humans a fixed set of questions across four conditions: always computer-controlled, computer-to-human, human-to-computer and always human-controlled. Participants were told the initial controller, which matched the actual one, but were unaware of later transitions.
AI.result: Perceived agency was strongly influenced by the controller presented at the start, with no evidence of updating after transitions. Likeability and co-presence were generally higher when human control occurred later and covered a greater proportion of the interaction.
AI.conclusion: Prior beliefs and first impressions continue to shape perceived agency, while social evaluations respond more to the virtual human's actual behaviour over the interaction.

title: reComposer: Editable Planning for Controllable Image Generation
summary: Prompt-based image generation makes it easy to produce visual assets, but offers little support for engaging with the creative process. Prompting collapses interdependent creative decisions into a monolithic instruction and returns a finished image, leaving control limited to revising the prompt or correcting the model's output. We present reComposer, a process-oriented image-generation interface built around editable planning, which decomposes users' evolving intent into meaningful creative decisions - such as subject, composition, or palette - and collaborates with users to explore underspecified goals and alternatives. reComposer supports conversational and direct manipulation of the plan, moving between concept-level intent and visual-level control. We evaluated reComposer with 8 design and non-design professionals. Compared to prompting, participants felt greater control and ownership while developing visual assets, exploring alternatives, and iterating on details. Our findings suggest how shifting generative AI interaction from specifying outputs to shaping process can support creative thinking alongside asset production.

AI.tldr: reComposer is a process-oriented image-generation interface that decomposes user intent into an editable plan of creative decisions, such as subject, composition or palette, which users can manipulate conversationally or directly. In a study with 8 design and non-design professionals, it gave participants greater control and ownership than prompting.
AI.motivation: Prompt-based image generation collapses interdependent creative decisions into a single instruction and returns a finished image, which limits engagement with the creative process to revising prompts or correcting outputs.
AI.method: The system builds an editable planning layer that supports conversational and direct manipulation of the plan, moving between concept-level intent and visual-level control. It also helps users explore underspecified goals and alternatives.
AI.result: Compared with prompting, participants with 8 professionals felt greater control and ownership while developing visual assets, exploring alternatives and iterating on details. The abstract reports no quantitative measures.
AI.conclusion: Shifting generative AI interaction from specifying outputs to shaping the process can support creative thinking alongside asset production.

title: Multi-Agent Screening: What Agreement and Acceptance Cannot Tell You
summary: When AI agents screen items for a costly human assessor, as in agentic search, e-discovery and AI reviewing of papers, only what they pass gets judged. We show what each kind of evidence can establish about their errors, even with unlimited data. Agreement shows that agents concur, not that they are right, however many there are. Acceptance by the assessor gives precision but only a lower bound on recall. Knowing which agents found which relevant items gives an upper bound on recall if agents' finds are not negatively correlated, and caps what one more agent can add if agents are interchangeable. Without assumptions about the agents, recall can be pinned down only by judging items they did not pass: a random sample of these estimates how many relevant items were missed, to any chosen accuracy, and the sample needed does not grow with the number of agents.

AI.tldr: The paper shows what different kinds of evidence can and cannot establish about the errors of AI agents that screen items for a costly human assessor, even with unlimited data. Agreement and assessor acceptance give limited guarantees, while recall can be pinned down only by judging items the agents did not pass.
AI.motivation: When AI agents screen items before a costly human assessor judges them, only the passed items are ever judged, so the errors among rejected items are unobserved. Existing evidence such as agent agreement and assessor acceptance is assumed to speak to correctness and recall, which it does not establish on its own.
AI.method: The authors give a formal analysis of three kinds of evidence: agreement among agents, acceptance by the assessor, and which agents found which relevant items. They derive what each one bounds, and show that a random sample of the items the agents did not pass estimates the number of missed relevant items to any chosen accuracy, with a sample size that does not grow with the number of agents.
AI.result: Agreement shows only that agents concur, not that they are right. Assessor acceptance gives precision and a lower bound on recall. Overlap of finds gives an upper bound on recall if agents' finds are not negatively correlated, and caps the added value of one more agent if agents are interchangeable. Without assumptions about the agents, recall is identified only by judging rejected items, and that sample size is independent of the number of agents.
AI.conclusion: Assessing recall in agent-based screening, as in agentic search, e-discovery and AI reviewing of papers, requires sampling the items the agents rejected, since the other kinds of evidence cannot establish recall without strong assumptions about the agents.

title: DeepChronos: Temporal Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning for Multi-Step Attack Detection
summary: Modern cyber threats commonly unfold as multi-step attacks comprising temporally and causally related phases. Current defenses commonly follow a detect first and correlate later paradigm. Intrusion detection systems classify events independently, while downstream systems reconstruct attack progression from the resulting alerts or audit records. In this context, learning-based detectors learn attack-step dependencies implicitly as statistical regularities in the data and cannot guarantee that their predictions follow the real attack progression. Conversely, correlation systems represent attack relationships explicitly, but apply this knowledge only after the underlying attack observations have been detected. We present DEEPCHRONOS, a neuro-symbolic network intrusion detection system that shifts the paradigm from detect first and correlate later to detection through logical progression. DEEPCHRONOS combines learned flow-level evidence with explicit attack-phase rules, temporal prerequisites, and previously inferred phases, allowing the evolving attack history to inform and constrain each detection decision. Evaluations on DARPA 2000 and AIT-LDS V2 show that DEEPCHRONOS improves macro F1 over purely neural baselines by up to 11.3%, eliminates causal violations under strict temporal constraints, and maintains millisecond-scale inference latency. These results demonstrate that integrating explicit attack progression knowledge into detection produces more accurate and temporally coherent multi-step attack predictions.

AI.tldr: DeepChronos is a neuro-symbolic network intrusion detection system that combines learned flow-level evidence with explicit attack-phase rules and temporal prerequisites, so detection follows the progression of multi-step attacks. On DARPA 2000 and AIT-LDS V2 it improves macro F1 over purely neural baselines by up to 11.3% and eliminates causal violations under strict temporal constraints.
AI.motivation: Current defenses detect attack events first and correlate them later. Learning-based detectors capture attack-step dependencies only implicitly and cannot guarantee that predictions follow real attack progression, while correlation systems use explicit attack knowledge only after the underlying observations are detected.
AI.method: The system combines learned flow-level evidence with explicit attack-phase rules, temporal prerequisites, and previously inferred phases, so the evolving attack history informs and constrains each detection decision. This shifts detection from detect-first-correlate-later to detection through logical progression.
AI.result: DeepChronos improves macro F1 over purely neural baselines by up to 11.3% on DARPA 2000 and AIT-LDS V2, eliminates causal violations under strict temporal constraints, and keeps millisecond-scale inference latency.
AI.conclusion: Integrating explicit attack progression knowledge into detection yields more accurate and temporally coherent multi-step attack predictions.

title: LUCQUE: A lung cancer screening dataset from Québec for reliable AI evaluation
summary: BACKGROUND: AI-based tools are expected to play a key role in lung cancer screening (LCS). The evaluation of these tools often relied on private datasets or fragmented public datasets with inconsistent availability of clinical data and expert nodule annotations. This has hindered reproducibility, comparability, and independent assessment of AI tools. To address these gaps, we present LUCQUE, a novel, large, comprehensively annotated dataset derived from LDCT lung cancer screening in Québec, which is accessible for reliable AI evaluation. METHODS: LUCQUE was curated and is hosted on PARADIM, a digital infrastructure supporting DICOM data de-identification, annotation, long-term storage and analysis. LDCT scans and clinical information were combined to a curated collection and complemented by voxel-level, expert-derived pulmonary nodule and cyst segmentations, and Lung-RADS-based lesion characteristics. Key dataset characteristics and statistics were reported, including participant demographics, imaging parameters, radiological findings, and segmented lesion characteristics. Dataset analyses were conducted according to PARADIM's model-to-data approach, in which user code is executed on the platform such that data remains on premise. RESULTS: LUCQUE currently comprises 1,678 LDCT baseline studies from 1,678 participants. Most studies were classified as Lung-RADS 2. A total of 1,776 pulmonary nodules and 60 cysts were annotated, with a median (interquartile range) volume of $89\,(56,\,159)\,\mathrm{mm}^3$ and $1,384\,(589,\,3793)\,\mathrm{mm}^3$ respectively. CONCLUSIONS: Compared to publicly available LCS datasets, LUCQUE currently represents the largest accessible annotated real-world LCS dataset. Access to LUCQUE is provided via a model-to-data approach, enabling privacy-preserving, reproducible, and independent real-world evaluation of AI tools in LCS.

AI.tldr: LUCQUE is a large, comprehensively annotated lung cancer screening dataset from LDCT scans in Quebec, hosted on the PARADIM platform and accessed through a model-to-data approach. It contains 1,678 baseline studies with 1,776 annotated pulmonary nodules and 60 cysts, and is presented as the largest accessible annotated real-world LCS dataset.
AI.motivation: AI tools for lung cancer screening have often been evaluated on private datasets or on fragmented public datasets with inconsistent clinical data and expert nodule annotations, which hinders reproducibility, comparability and independent assessment.
AI.method: LDCT scans and clinical information were combined into a curated collection on the PARADIM infrastructure, which supports DICOM de-identification, annotation, long-term storage and analysis. It was complemented with voxel-level expert segmentations of pulmonary nodules and cysts and with Lung-RADS-based lesion characteristics. Analyses run under PARADIM's model-to-data approach, in which user code executes on the platform so the data stays on premise.
AI.result: The dataset currently comprises 1,678 LDCT baseline studies from 1,678 participants, mostly classified as Lung-RADS 2. It includes 1,776 pulmonary nodules and 60 cysts, with median (interquartile range) volumes of 89 (56, 159) mm^3 for nodules and 1,384 (589, 3793) mm^3 for cysts.
AI.conclusion: Compared with publicly available lung cancer screening datasets, LUCQUE is currently the largest accessible annotated real-world one, and the model-to-data access enables privacy-preserving, reproducible and independent evaluation of AI tools.

title: Programming Prescience: Issues in Human Construction of Forecasting Bots
summary: AI models' growing capacity for complex reasoning has made them attractive tools for forecasting, or the systematic prediction of the future based on past and present data. However, should AI forecasting systems be adopted, human builders will shoulder the work of building and evaluating them. In this paper, we explore what this work looks like with a qualitative interview study with 15 builders of forecasting bots, sampled from among successful participants in a recent AI forecasting competition. Our analysis surfaces the challenges around (1) tuning a bot to acquire factual research, (2) implementing coherent reasoning, and (3) understanding how well one's bot actually does. During their work, builders frequently introduced complexity that did not pay off, and tested in ways that were opportunistic and piecemeal. Our detailed account of their challenges helps clarify what problems should be targeted in upcoming innovations in process, tools, and human-AI teaming for forecasting.

AI.tldr: The paper reports a qualitative interview study of 15 builders of AI forecasting bots, sampled from successful participants in a recent AI forecasting competition, examining the human work of building and evaluating them. It identifies challenges in tuning bots to acquire factual research, implementing coherent reasoning, and understanding bot performance.
AI.motivation: If AI forecasting systems are adopted, humans will do the work of building and evaluating them, but little was known about what that work involves.
AI.method: A qualitative interview study with 15 builders of forecasting bots, sampled from successful participants in a recent AI forecasting competition.
AI.result: The analysis surfaces challenges in (1) tuning a bot to acquire factual research, (2) implementing coherent reasoning, and (3) understanding how well one's bot actually performs. Builders often added complexity that did not pay off, and tested their bots in opportunistic and piecemeal ways.
AI.conclusion: The account clarifies which problems upcoming innovations in process, tools and human-AI teaming for forecasting should target.
